Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Re: Docket USBC-2026-0628
Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions

I am writing as a resident of Morganfield, a small community in rural western Kentucky, to oppose the proposed residence criteria and restrictions on demographic questions.

I am disabled, receive Social Security Disability Insurance and Medicare, and live on a limited fixed income. I depend on public institutions making decisions using complete, accurate information about the people and communities they serve. Census policy may sound abstract, but representation, public planning, civil-rights enforcement, and the distribution of public resources have real consequences for people like me.

I oppose excluding undocumented residents and most temporary lawful residents from the population used for congressional apportionment. The Constitution’s Fourteenth Amendment requires representatives to be apportioned according to the “whole number of persons in each State,” not only citizens or lawful permanent residents. Every person living in a community affects its schools, hospitals, emergency services, roads, housing needs, and economy. Their presence creates real responsibilities for state and local governments regardless of immigration status.

Excluding residents from the apportionment population would make some communities politically smaller on paper than they are in reality. That could reduce their representation even though public agencies must still serve the people who were excluded. It could also discourage participation in the census among mixed-status families and others who fear how government information may be used, making an accurate count more difficult.

I also oppose the proposed prohibition on questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation on questionnaires used for the decennial enumeration.

I understand that the proposed rule would still permit the Census Bureau to collect demographic information through the American Community Survey, administrative records, and other sources. That limitation should be stated accurately. It does not, however, eliminate my concern.

Race and ethnicity data help the public, researchers, courts, and government agencies identify unequal treatment and disparities involving voting, housing, healthcare, education, employment, environmental hazards, and access to public services. Sexual-orientation data can likewise help document whether LGBTQ Americans are being served fairly or experiencing disparities that would otherwise remain hidden.

Removing demographic questions from the decennial enumeration risks making the nation’s most comprehensive population record less useful for understanding who lives here and whether different communities are being treated equally. Other surveys may not provide the same coverage, geographic detail, or public confidence as information collected through the census itself.

A government cannot effectively protect people it chooses not to measure. Less demographic evidence can mean less accountability, because discrimination and unequal outcomes become harder to demonstrate when the underlying data are incomplete.

The Census Bureau describes demographic characteristics such as race as immaterial to the constitutional purpose of apportionment. But the census has responsibilities and consequences beyond calculating a single national population total. Congress requires census information for redistricting, and census data support decisions throughout federal, state, and local government. Accuracy should mean accurately understanding the population—not merely producing a number stripped of information needed to evaluate fairness.

I respectfully request that the Census Bureau withdraw the proposed restrictions on who is included in the apportionment population and withdraw the proposed prohibition on race, ethnicity, and sexual-orientation questions. At minimum, the Bureau should conduct and publish a thorough analysis of how these changes could affect census participation, data quality, redistricting, civil-rights enforcement, rural and underserved communities, and the government’s ability to identify disparities.

The census should count the people who live in this country and preserve the information necessary to ensure that all of them can be seen, represented, and protected.

Bruce Coffman
Morganfield, Kentucky

Attacks on the quality of these products, as described above, would lead to severe reductions in quality and therefore the size of the market itself. And economics impacts are minor compared to the irreparable harm of reducing public knowledge of Americans. The Census is an august institution which has spread open data and open understanding of what America is. Willfully blinding ourselves to communities of America is a short-sighted and destructive impulse. This rule should not take effect.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am a citizen of the United States of America and I am commenting as an individual. I am addressing proposed 15 CFR § 60.4 and proposed 15 CFR § 70.2. I support both sections as published.
Section 60.4:  Foreign citizens
I support counting for apportionment only U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents as of Census Day, and not counting other foreign citizens.
The constitutional purpose of the decennial census is to apportion House seats among the States according to the number of persons who belong to those States as inhabitants. “Usual residence” has never meant mere physical presence. From the First Census Act forward it has included an element of settled connection and allegiance. A person whose legal right to remain is temporary, conditional, or nonexistent does not have that connection in the same way a citizen or green-card holder does.
Apportionment is not a social-services headcount. It decides who holds political power for a decade. Including people who cannot vote, who may be required to leave, and who have no durable stake in the laws of the United States shifts seats and Electoral College votes toward jurisdictions that happen to contain large temporary or illegal populations. That is a political outcome, not a neutral count. Other federal surveys and administrative records can still measure how many people are physically present for planning and funding formulas that Congress writes separately. The apportionment base should not be one of those formulas.
Legal permanent residents have been granted an open-ended right to live here and a path that can lead to citizenship. That is a bright, administrable line. Temporary visa holders, students, and persons here illegally are not in the same category. Treating them as interchangeable with citizens for representation rewards illegal presence and temporary presence with permanent political weight. Incentives work in both directions. If presence alone confers representation, the incentive to control the border and to distinguish citizens from non-citizens weakens.
Section 70.2: Restrictions on certain demographic questions
I support the rule that no question about race, ethnicity, or sexual orientation shall appear on the short-form decennial questionnaire or any questionnaire used for the enumeration of the population.
The job of the enumeration is to count persons once, in the right place, for apportionment. Race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation are not required for that job. They have been collected for other purposes on other instruments, including the American Community Survey. Those instruments can continue. Putting identity categories on the form that produces the official national count invites the census to become a tool for sorting Americans into official groups rather than a count of equal persons.
Granular identity data has costs as well as uses. It trains institutions and citizens to treat ancestry and orientation as the primary facts about a person. It also creates a standing demand that every future policy be scored by those categories. That is a choice about political culture, not a requirement of Article I or the Fourteenth Amendment. A color-blind enumeration does not erase history or prevent later analysis. It simply refuses to make group classification part of the constitutional headcount.
Advances in record linkage and commercial data already allow detailed demographic profiles without putting those questions on the short form. The Bureau itself notes that. The short form should stay short and limited to what the Constitution requires.
Conclusion
I urge the Department of Commerce and the Census Bureau to adopt § 60.4 and § 70.2 as proposed. The 2030 Census should count citizens and lawful permanent residents for apportionment, and it should not use the enumeration questionnaire to classify the population by race, ethnicity, or sexual orientation.
Respectfully submitted.

I would like to address the constitutional context of this proposal. The 14th Amendment, written in 1868, states that "Representatives shall be apportioned among the several states according to their respective numbers, counting the whole number of persons in each state, excluding Indians not taxed." However, when the 14th Amendment was drafted, the framers could not have anticipated two critical aspects of our modern world:

The unprecedented ease with which people can now travel from anywhere in the world to enter the United States, a reality made possible by advances in transportation and technology.
The massive influx of illegal immigrants across our largely unguarded borders, as has occurred from 2021 to 2025, resulting in millions of individuals residing in the country without legal status.

Given these realities, I believe it is reasonable and necessary to reconsider how we define "the whole number of persons" for the purposes of congressional apportionment. The proposed rule, which would count only citizens and lawful permanent residents, better reflects the intent of ensuring that political representation and federal resources are allocated to those who are legally part of our national community. This change would help align the census with the interests and obligations of American citizens and legal residents, and address challenges that the framers of the 14th Amendment could not have foreseen.

Thank you for considering my comment

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing, as a public health scientist, as a mother of three children who are both white and Asian, and as a citizen of this country, to strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Decennial Census outlined in 2026-18481 (91 FR 57524). Specifically, I write to oppose the removal of race categories from the census. Removing this information will be detrimental across many areas. As a public health scientist, I will focus on concerns from that viewpoint. 

Even though Race has no inherent biological meaning, the categorization system is deeply embedded in our culture and society. As a result, these categories impact health outcomes. We must continue to collect race data in order to conduct public health research, evaluate public health programs, and track substantial and as yet persistent health disparities. 

The framework for the race categories we use today was invented by Carl Linnaeus in 1735, just as the trans-Atlantic slave trade was escalating toward its peak. The Linnaean race categories were hierarchical, dividing humanity based on skin color and geography, and ranking the groups. Linnaeus place Homo Europaeus albescens (translating to white European man) at the top, followed by Homo Americanus rubescens (translating to “red American man,” referring to people indigenous to the Americas), then Homo Asiaticus fuscus (translating to “brown Asian” man), and finally, at the bottom of the hierarchy, Homo Africanus niger (or Black African man). This purported biological hierarchy was used to justify and excuse the increasingly profitable exploitation and brutal treatment of African people through the trans-Atlantic slave trade and American chattel slavery. The same racial classification system has endured over centuries, with only minor changes to the names and the addition of a. Few categories. The mapping of the human genome provided undeniable evidence that race categories are not biologically meaningful. Humans genes, regardless of race, are 99% the same. In fact, greater genetic heterogeneity exists among people descended from different parts of Africa (all racialized in the US as Black) than between certain African and European populations. If humans were grouped into categories based on genetic similarity, the resulting groups would look nothing like our current racial classification system.

Yet, the hierarchical nature of race groups has remained deeply embedded in American culture. As recently as 1954, schools were legally segregated by race until Brown v Board of Education determined separate was not equal. Alachua County, where I attended college, did not desegregate its schools until 1970, 16 years after Brown v Board of Education. The last segregated school in the US did not desegregate until 2017. 2017! That is the year my 9 year old son was born.

Race matters because we made it matter, through policies that provide different access to opportunity based on the color of one’s skin. These discriminatory policies have yet to be fully eradicated. Those that have been corrected in recent decades still have impacts on those who experienced the discriminatory policies. These policies have contributed to substantial racial disparities in health outcomes. Black Americans are 4 times more likely to progress to kidney failure, 60% more likely to develop diabetes, and twice as likely to develop Alzheimer's Disease. 

Removing race categories from the Census will leave us blind to these disparities. But being  unable to measure a problem does not make the problem disappear.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am a mechanical engineer and a community organizer who wants the best for our country and our people. I care about a fair and accurate census because I recognize how this plays into fair democratic representation and allocation of government resources for everything from health care to disaster response. As an engineer I know first hand that bad data leads to bad decisions, and this proposed rule is a path to bad data that may lead to, for example, health and human services resources being shut down where they are needed most.

First ask: further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is good, but regulatory actions as significant as this deserve a full 90 days for the public to digest and comment.

Second, I oppose both Parts 60 and 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, to include the following:

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people. Neglecting these groups will only weaken the whole.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.

As written, the proposed rule excludes residents, results in an inaccurate count, and prohibits collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. The rule must be revised.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am from Austin, Tx where I work in the insurance industry, pay my taxes and have had enough of the scamming from this administration. I care about a fair and accurate census because it matters, accuracy and real data is not only helpful but imperative in determining so many important factors. Skewing the data makes the whole thing pointless. This is worked just fine for the past 200+ years if it ain’t broke, don’t fix it. 

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond. 

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions. 

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.


I urge you to reconsider, pretending as if some people don’t exists doesn’t actually make them not exist.

Comment: U.S. Census Bureau,I am writing to oppose the Census Bureau's proposal to remove race and ethnicity questions from the 2030 Census (Docket No. USBC-2026-0628).For decades, federal standards counted Middle Eastern and North African (MENA) Americans as White. Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I oppose the proposed restriction on asking about sexual orientation on the decennial Census questionnaire and other questionnaires used to count the population. I also urge the Census Bureau to consider how its decisions about demographic questions affect the visibility of transgender and nonbinary people.
Communities need trustworthy, privacy-protected information to understand who lives here and whether services reach them. Sexual orientation and gender identity data can help community groups, educators, researchers, and public agencies identify gaps in outreach and services, make informed decisions, and assess whether LGBTQ+ people are being overlooked. Without reliable data, it is harder to document needs or measure progress.
I understand that these questions require careful attention to privacy, wording, and public trust. Those concerns deserve serious research and community input—not a blanket rule that prevents the Bureau from asking a sexual orientation question on an enumeration questionnaire, even if a well-tested, voluntary approach could be developed. Continuing to collect information through the American Community Survey is important, but it should not be used as a reason to rule out appropriate questions on the decennial Census in advance.
Please do not finalize this restriction. Instead, consult LGBTQ+ communities, including transgender and nonbinary people; test questions for accuracy and accessibility; explain how responses would be protected; and preserve the flexibility to collect demographic information that communities need. Being counted should also mean having a fair chance to be understood.

* Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands

* Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds

 The proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census because a fair and accurate census is critical to ensuring every community is counted, fairly represented, and able to get the resources people need to live healthy lives — including sexual and reproductive healthcare. An inaccurate or incomplete census can deepen existing inequities, particularly for communities that already face disenfranchisement and barriers to healthcare. 

A fair and accurate census is essential to our health and rights. 

Census data help determine access to programs patients and their families rely on, including important programs like Medicaid, SNAP, WIC, and TANF. Accurate census data also shape political representation by determining how seats in the U.S. House of Representatives are apportioned among states and providing data used for redistricting. When communities are undercounted or excluded, they risk losing both resources and political representation. 

The Census Bureau and Department of Commerce must:

1. Count all people residing in the United States in the 2030 Census, without regard to immigration status. Excluding noncitizens from census apportionment data violates the Constitution and established legal precedent. It would suppress the count of many communities, effectively erasing them from critical datasets and depriving them of resources and congressional representation –— including resources and political representation that support access to healthcare.

2. Continue collecting race and ethnicity data and implement the 2024 OMB SPD 15 standards. Census race and ethnicity data are essential for important research across many sectors, for upholding civil rights, and for growing the economy. Extensive Census Bureau research and engagement with expert stakeholders shows that implementing the modernized 2024 OMB SPD 15 standards for race and ethnicity data collection will yield data that more accurately represent the nation’s increasingly diverse population.

4. Withdraw other proposed changes to residence criteria, including tying place of residence to tax records and "lawful residence," and the adoption of a three month enumeration period. The Census Bureau must extensively research and consult with stakeholders about the potential effects of such changes before proposing their implementation in a decennial census.

5. Halt the practice of prison gerrymandering by counting incarcerated individuals in their home communities. This will yield more accurate census data and ensure that communities receive the congressional representation to which they are entitled.

Sincerely,
Patricia Horejsi
AZ 86004

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census. These changes will not only weaken the accuracy and integrity of our nation's most important population count, but they will also harm our communities, and I strongly urge the Bureau to reject them. 

First, removing questions of race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation erases the full scope of my identity when I participate in the Census survey. These data points are not optional. They are the tools we use to enforce civil rights laws, monitor discrimination, and measure the disparities that still affect millions of people. Excluding them from the count does not make them disappear from our society, but it does make our government less equipped to handle big issues when they arise. 

The Constitution is clear: the census must count ALL persons living in the United States, regardless of their immigration or citizenship status. The proposal to exclude non-citizens, including those residents with some type of lawful status, violates more than two centuries of legal precedent. Every person counted in this country contributes to our communities, and every person deserves to be fully seen. 

The consequences of these changes will negatively impact our daily lives. The census affects everything. It determines political representation and the drawing of voting districts. It guides how billions of dollars in federal funding are used to close persistent disparities in schools, hospitals, and other government programs that are designed to improve our lives.  

The census is the foundation of our democracy. It must reflect the complete yet nuanced reality of who we are as a nation. And it must reflect the lives of our friends and neighbors who may not look, think, or speak like we do. I ask the Bureau to withdraw these proposed changes and to preserve a count that includes everyone and represents everyone. 

Thank you for considering my comment.

Sincerely,

Regina Powell

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: US Census Bureau,I urge the Census Bureau and Department of Commerce to withdraw the proposed rule changing residence criteria for the decennial Census and restricting demographic questions.The proposal would exclude foreign citizens from the population used for congressional apportionment unless they are also U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents. The Census proposes to only include people if their address is confirmed by tax records -- which could mean millions, particularly low-income families, could be missed in the decennial Census. Overall, this would leave out people who actually live in our community, including many people who are lawfully present in the United States.For all past Census counts, including the 2020 Census, foreign citizens living in the United States were generally counted where they lived and slept most of the time. That approach recognizes the basic purpose of a Census: accurately counting the people who live in our communities. The 14th Amendment requires congressional representation to be apportioned according to the “whole number of persons in each State.”I am also deeply concerned by the proposal to prohibit race and ethnicity questions, along with sexual orientation, on the decennial Census enumeration questionnaire. The Census Bureau itself recognizes the importance of race data for civil rights protections, legislative redistricting, equal employment opportunities, and identifying disparities.The 2030 Census will determine congressional, state, and local representation for the decade that follows. It must be complete, accurate, and protected from political manipulation.Please withdraw this proposed rule and preserve a Census that fairly and accurately counts our community.Peggy  [X] Plattsburgh , New York 12901

Comment:
My name is [Your Name] and I am your constituent from [City/Zip Code]. As Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander (AANHPI) Heritage Month comes to a close, I write to urge you to support AANHPI students by cosponsoring the All Students Count Act.

To the U.S. Census Bureau: 

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule titled “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005). Eliminating the collection of race and ethnic data, prohibiting the collection of sexual orientation, and leaving non-citizens out of the apportionment would significantly harm the Southeast Asian American (SEAA) and broader Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander (AANHPI) communities. I respectfully request that the Census Bureau withdraw the proposed rule and extend the comment period to December 10, 2026. 

This proposed rule would significantly harm the SEAA and AANHPI communities. The AANHPI community is not a homogenous population; it encompasses over 50 different ethnic groups and 100 languages and dialects. There are vast socioeconomic disparities within the AANHPI population, often related to their migratory and historical experience. SEAAs, such as the Cambodian, Hmong, Laotian, and Mien populations, often have higher rates of poverty and lower educational attainment rates than both the broader AANHPI and American populations. 

For SEAAs, this disparity is generally tied to their experiences escaping their countries of origin and resettlement in the United States after the Vietnam War, Secret War in Laos, and Khmer Rouge genocide in Cambodia. For example, because of the 2020 Census, we now know that the Mien population has lower educational attainment rates compared to the general American and AANHPI populations. Additionally, the data also show that Mien men have a lower educational attainment rate compared to women. Such information could only be obtained because of the census, which is the primary source for data collection and reporting of small ethnic groups. These data cannot be replicated by other surveys, including the American Community Survey. 

Accurate data, reflective of race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation, help our elected officials properly identify and address the unique needs and challenges of our communities. Prohibiting the collection of this demographic data would prevent our government officials from passing informed public policy; hamper the ability of community-based organizations to demonstrate data narratives for fundraising purposes; and inhibit the ability of students and academics studying our communities from accessing the most robust source of information on SEAAs and the broader AANHPI community. 

Thank you for taking my comment into consideration. I reiterate my request that the US Census Bureau withdraws the proposed rule; preserves the collection of race and ethnic data; and keeps its commitment to count everyone once, only once, and in the right place.

I also ask the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. Changes of this scope deserve more time for the public to review and respond.

Sincerely,
Candice Adam-Medefind

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I support residence-based census counting that includes every person living in the United States, regardless of citizenship or immigration status.

The Constitution directs that the population be enumerated. Counting all residents is essential to producing an accurate picture of the people who live in communities and rely on public infrastructure, schools, hospitals, emergency services, transportation systems, and other public resources. Citizenship status should not determine whether a person is included in the population count.

Excluding noncitizens, or attempting to remove them from the population used for apportionment and demographic purposes, would make the census less accurate. It could undercount communities with large immigrant populations, including U.S. citizens and lawful residents who live in the same households and neighborhoods. An inaccurate count could also distort congressional apportionment, redistricting, federal funding formulas, and the allocation of public resources. All people in a given area use its public resources, so undercounting will hurt Americans in states and areas with more immigrants.

A citizenship-based exclusion could discourage participation and make it more difficult to obtain accurate responses from households that include noncitizens. Census accuracy depends on public trust and on people’s willingness to provide complete information. The Bureau should avoid policies that could cause residents to fear that census participation will expose them or their family members to immigration-related consequences.

The census should continue to use usual residence as the central counting principle: each person should be counted at the place where they ordinarily live and sleep. This approach is administratively workable, consistent with the purpose of a population census, and more likely to produce reliable data than attempting to determine citizenship or immigration status for every resident.

I urge the Census Bureau to:

Count every person residing in the United States and its territories within the applicable census universe, regardless of citizenship or immigration status.
Avoid using citizenship status as a basis for excluding residents from population totals used for apportionment, redistricting, or other official demographic purposes.
Preserve clear confidentiality protections and communicate that census responses should not be used for immigration enforcement.
Conduct thorough testing and publish evidence on how any proposed citizenship-related question or residence rule would affect response rates, data quality, costs, and the accuracy of population counts.
Explain how the proposal would prevent undercounting communities that contain mixed-status households or large immigrant populations.
An accurate census must count the people who live in the country, not only the people who hold a particular legal status. I respectfully ask the Bureau to retain a residence-based approach that includes everyone.

Thank you for reviewing and considering this comment and for allowing the public to provide essential input.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Census Bureau's proposed rule to strengthen the US Census is critical to fair representation and the future of America.  

The U.S. Census should not include distorted data in its count of Americans.  By including overly generalized ethnic demographic categories, we obscure the true goal of the census and hinder its constitutionally mandated purpose: an accurate count of Americans.  

Additionally, illegal aliens and other non-legal permanent residents should not be included for apportionment. Census data is used for the apportionment of congressional seats. Non-citizens cannot legally vote and should not be used to decrease the voting power of Americans. I support the Census Bureau in advancing the correct understanding of usual residence to recognize an element of allegiance that is antithetical to the inclusion of those not legally present in our country.  

This Census Bureau should also consider adding a citizenship question to the Census survey. The Supreme Court has already held that the Constitution lawfully permits the Census Bureau to at least inquire about citizenship on the census questionnaire. "The census should absolutely include questions related to citizenship and legal presence. 

These changes would strengthen the census in its core purpose of attaining an accurate count of Americans and have my full support. 

Thank you,  

Dana Davis

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

My name is Melissa, and I’m from MI. I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). I have participated in the census my whole life. First sitting with my parents as a child and then throughout my adult life. An accurate census is important to me because it is one of the building blocks of our democracy. We need a fair accounting of all people living in the US to make accurate districting, economic and infrastructure plans.

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including:

• Count all people as the Census is designed to do. Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. They are here legally and need to be counted.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Dear Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions,

Subject: Re: Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions (Docket No. 260903-0005; RIN 0607-AA75) 

I strongly oppose the proposed rules for the census and changes to its residence rule. All persons in the United States have a right to be counted, as the 14th Amendment of the Constitution plainly establishes. This proposed rule will weaken our democracy, our systems of representation, and the doctrine of “one person, one vote.” Without an accurate count, people will not be fairly represented in Congress or state legislatures.

Comment:

* Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

* Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

* Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

* Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

* Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

* Determining state higher education funding formulas 

* Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

* Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

* Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

First, to ensure a fair and accurate census,  the Census Bureau should  extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. • Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (including children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Public Comment: Proposed Changes to the 2030 Decennial Census
Submitted by: Rev. Kim Lagree
Docket No.: USBC-2026-0628

I oppose the proposed restrictions on census residence eligibility and demographic data collection because they risk undermining constitutional representation, civil rights enforcement, public health planning, and equitable resource allocation.

With more than 25 years of experience in public health, health equity, trauma-informed systems change, and community-based initiatives, I understand that effective governance depends on accurate population data and the ability to identify and measure disparities.

Constitutional representation: The Fourteenth Amendment requires an enumeration of the whole number of persons in each state for apportionment. Excluding undocumented immigrants and certain other noncitizens would depart from longstanding census practice and risk distorting population-based representation. Citizenship and tax filing status are not equivalent to residence.

Civil rights and health equity: Race and ethnicity data are essential for identifying disparities, evaluating discrimination, assessing public programs, and directing resources. Census data provide geographic detail that other surveys and administrative records cannot automatically replace. Restricting these data would weaken the ability to measure inequities and evaluate policy outcomes.

Public health and resource allocation: Census-derived data inform health care, behavioral health, housing, education, emergency preparedness, and federal funding. Systematic undercounts can distort planning and resource distribution, particularly in underserved communities.

Methodological integrity: Tax and immigration records are not comprehensive population enumeration systems. Incomplete or outdated records may disproportionately affect mobile households, children and dependents, low-income populations, and people experiencing housing instability. The Census Bureau should independently validate administrative records and publish analyses of accuracy, differential error, and undercount risks before adopting these changes.

I urge the Census Bureau to reject exclusions that compromise inclusive enumeration, preserve race and ethnicity questions, reconsider restrictions on sexual orientation data, and publish a comprehensive assessment of the proposed changes’ legal, demographic, fiscal, and public health consequences. Meaningful consultation with civil rights organizations, public health experts, researchers, and affected communities is also essential.

An accurate census is foundational democratic and public health infrastructure. Decisions affecting representation, public investment, and civil rights must be grounded in reliable evidence and a complete accounting of the population.

Respectfully submitted,
Rev. Kim Lagree
Public Health and Systems Strategist | Trauma and Resilience Expert

Sincerely,
Kim Lagree

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am a retired preschool teacher from the state of Illinois, and I care about a fair and accurate census because I am also a former census taker for the U.S. government and understand how important and proper, accurate census is.

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including:

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census because a fair and accurate census is critical to ensuring every community is counted, fairly represented, and able to get the resources people need to live healthy lives — including sexual and reproductive healthcare. An inaccurate or incomplete census can deepen existing inequities, particularly for communities that already face disenfranchisement and barriers to healthcare. 

A fair and accurate census is essential to our health and rights. 

Census data help determine access to programs patients and their families rely on, including important programs like Medicaid, SNAP, WIC, and TANF. Accurate census data also shape political representation by determining how seats in the U.S. House of Representatives are apportioned among states and providing data used for redistricting. When communities are undercounted or excluded, they risk losing both resources and political representation. 

The Census Bureau and Department of Commerce must:

1. Count all people residing in the United States in the 2030 Census, without regard to immigration status. Excluding noncitizens from census apportionment data violates the Constitution and established legal precedent. It would suppress the count of many communities, effectively erasing them from critical datasets and depriving them of resources and congressional representation –— including resources and political representation that support access to healthcare.

2. Continue collecting race and ethnicity data and implement the 2024 OMB SPD 15 standards. Census race and ethnicity data are essential for important research across many sectors, for upholding civil rights, and for growing the economy. Extensive Census Bureau research and engagement with expert stakeholders shows that implementing the modernized 2024 OMB SPD 15 standards for race and ethnicity data collection will yield data that more accurately represent the nation’s increasingly diverse population.

3. Remove the clause banning the addition of future questions on sexual orientation. Proposed changes to demographic items should be based on research and guided by a deliberative and transparent process, including extensive stakeholder consultation.

4. Withdraw other proposed changes to residence criteria, including tying place of residence to tax records and "lawful residence," and the adoption of a three month enumeration period. The Census Bureau must extensively research and consult with stakeholders about the potential effects of such changes before proposing their implementation in a decennial census.

5. Halt the practice of prison gerrymandering by counting incarcerated individuals in their home communities. This will yield more accurate census data and ensure that communities receive the congressional representation to which they are entitled.

Sincerely,

MA 01720

Comment: The changes proposed to the 2030 census are problematic for several reasons. My largest concern is with the proposal to discontinue data collection about race and ethnicity. From infant deaths, to educational opportunities, to differential premature mortality, race impacts peoples' lives literally from the cradle to the grave. Not collecting data on race and ethnicity will not magically make these very real problems disappear. In fact, it will create a significant hindrance to addressing these issues so that all Americans, regardless of racial background, have equal opportunities to experience life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness, as our founders intended. I find it childish and repellant that the government would so explicitly play politics with a tool that is immensely useful for those of us on the ground during the real work of helping our fellow Americans achieve and improve their lives.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
My name is [Your Name] and I am your constituent from [City/Zip Code]. As Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander (AANHPI) Heritage Month comes to a close, I write to urge you to support AANHPI students by cosponsoring the All Students Count Act.

To the U.S. Census Bureau: 

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule titled “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005). Eliminating the collection of race and ethnic data, prohibiting the collection of sexual orientation, and leaving non-citizens out of the apportionment would significantly harm the Southeast Asian American (SEAA) and broader Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander (AANHPI) communities. I respectfully request that the Census Bureau withdraw the proposed rule and extend the comment period to December 10, 2026. 

This proposed rule would significantly harm the SEAA and AANHPI communities. The AANHPI community is not a homogenous population; it encompasses over 50 different ethnic groups and 100 languages and dialects. There are vast socioeconomic disparities within the AANHPI population, often related to their migratory and historical experience. SEAAs, such as the Cambodian, Hmong, Laotian, and Mien populations, often have higher rates of poverty and lower educational attainment rates than both the broader AANHPI and American populations. 

For SEAAs, this disparity is generally tied to their experiences escaping their countries of origin and resettlement in the United States after the Vietnam War, Secret War in Laos, and Khmer Rouge genocide in Cambodia. For example, because of the 2020 Census, we now know that the Mien population has lower educational attainment rates compared to the general American and AANHPI populations. Additionally, the data also show that Mien men have a lower educational attainment rate compared to women. Such information could only be obtained because of the census, which is the primary source for data collection and reporting of small ethnic groups. These data cannot be replicated by other surveys, including the American Community Survey. 

Accurate data, reflective of race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation, help our elected officials properly identify and address the unique needs and challenges of our communities. Prohibiting the collection of this demographic data would prevent our government officials from passing informed public policy; hamper the ability of community-based organizations to demonstrate data narratives for fundraising purposes; and inhibit the ability of students and academics studying our communities from accessing the most robust source of information on SEAAs and the broader AANHPI community. 

Thank you for taking my comment into consideration. I reiterate my request that the US Census Bureau withdraws the proposed rule; preserves the collection of race and ethnic data; and keeps its commitment to count everyone once, only once, and in the right place.

I also ask the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. Changes of this scope deserve more time for the public to review and respond.

Sincerely,
Chi Huynh
Honolulu, HI 96822

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census because a fair and accurate census is critical to ensuring every community is counted, fairly represented, and able to get the resources people need to live healthy lives — including sexual and reproductive healthcare. An inaccurate or incomplete census can deepen existing inequities, particularly for communities that already face disenfranchisement and barriers to healthcare. 

A fair and accurate census is essential to our health and rights. 

Census data help determine access to programs patients and their families rely on, including important programs like Medicaid, SNAP, WIC, and TANF. Accurate census data also shape political representation by determining how seats in the U.S. House of Representatives are apportioned among states and providing data used for redistricting. When communities are undercounted or excluded, they risk losing both resources and political representation.

1. Count all people residing in the United States in the 2030 Census, without regard to immigration status. Excluding noncitizens from census apportionment data violates the Constitution and established legal precedent. 2. Continue collecting race and ethnicity data and implement the 2024 OMB SPD 15 standards. Census race and ethnicity data are essential for important research across many sectors, for upholding civil rights, and for growing the economy. Extensive Census Bureau research and engagement with expert stakeholders shows that implementing the modernized 2024 OMB SPD 15 standards for race and ethnicity data collection will yield data that more accurately represent the nation’s increasingly diverse population.

3. Remove the clause banning the addition of future questions on sexual orientation. Proposed changes to demographic items should be based on research and guided by a deliberative and transparent process, including extensive stakeholder consultation.

The Census Bureau must extensively research and consult with stakeholders about the potential effects of such changes before proposing their implementation in a decennial census.

5. Halt the practice of prison gerrymandering by counting incarcerated individuals in their home communities. This will yield more accurate census data and ensure that communities receive the congressional representation to which they are entitled.

Sincerely,
Nancy Kiec
IL 60634

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). 

As an educator, I care about a fair and accurate census because census data and other federal datasets based on the census are used to make key decisions that affect our nation’s students, educators, and schools.  

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Examples of these uses include: . 

* Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. 

* Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

* Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

* Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

* Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

* Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

* Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

* Determining state higher education funding formulas 

* Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

* Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

* Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

First, to ensure a fair and accurate census,  the Census Bureau should  extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. Second, I oppose both the proposed changes to the residence criteria and the proposed regulations regarding demographic questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. The Census Bureau should  withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The Constitution requires  counting all people living in the United States. 

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (including children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count. 

Revise the tax records language so that those whose mailing address differs from their residential address (servicemembers, those with a post office box) are not excluded.  

• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for civil rights enforcement, among other uses, and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The prohibition, as written, may also restrict the collection or publication of census data on same-sex couples that was asked in 2020. 

 The proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Sincerely,
Mr. Vincent Nicoletti
Littleton, CO

Comment:

Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.  

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Sincerely,

Frank Pratt

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). 

As an educator, I care about a fair and accurate census because census data and other federal datasets based on the census are used to make key decisions that affect our nation’s students, educators, and schools.  

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Examples of these uses include: . 

* Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. 

* Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

* Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

* Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

* Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

* Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

* Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

* Determining state higher education funding formulas 

* Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

* Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

* Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

First, to ensure a fair and accurate census,  the Census Bureau should  extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. Second, I oppose both the proposed changes to the residence criteria and the proposed regulations regarding demographic questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. The Census Bureau should  withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The Constitution requires  counting all people living in the United States. 

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (including children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count. 

Revise the tax records language so that those whose mailing address differs from their residential address (servicemembers, those with a post office box) are not excluded.  

• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for civil rights enforcement, among other uses, and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The prohibition, as written, may also restrict the collection or publication of census data on same-sex couples that was asked in 2020. 

 The proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Sincerely,
Mrs Shannon Feldewerth
Arnold, MO

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am a women who lives in a small townwhere the community is aging. Not everyone works or has current tax records. We are farmers and self sufficient people but in the case of a natural disaster or major emergency we need to make sure our population is recorded accuratly. I care about a fair and accurate census because it effects parents, young people and ours seniors healthcare and security.

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Comment: 91 FR 57524  Public Comment,I am submitting this comment in opposition to the Census Bureau's proposed rule on residence criteria and demographic questions for the decennial census, 91 FR 57524 (Sept. 10, 2026). Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The United States Census was designed to obtain statistics to help a vast array of public and private entities to make rational and constructive decisions that contribute to the well-functioning of the country and its people. Once again, not asking these questions benefits no-one and just promotes a willful blindness.   
Not understanding the full population of this country and its needs is like building an airport without fully researching the long term weather, including the expected and the unexpected.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am a payroll administrator from a legal staffing firm in Denver, CO, and I care about a fair and accurate census because it will impact everyone. People and the communities they live in will be harmed, not helped, with the inaccurate numbers that will come with these changes. 

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including:

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.
As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

I have comments on three aspects of this proposed rule.

The first one is about asking about someone's citizenship during the census. I support asking about everyone's citizenship status, this is absolutely essential. Finally, I support the apportionment of districts among the states based on citizenship. Anything else is a violation of the 14th Amendment. An accurate count of U.S. citizens is essential.
