Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). 

As an educator, I care about a fair and accurate census because census data and other federal datasets based on the census are used to make key decisions that affect our nation’s students, educators, and schools.  

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Examples of these uses include: . 

* Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. 

* Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

* Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

* Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

* Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

* Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

* Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

* Determining state higher education funding formulas 

* Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

* Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

* Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

First, to ensure a fair and accurate census,  the Census Bureau should  extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. Second, I oppose both the proposed changes to the residence criteria and the proposed regulations regarding demographic questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. The Census Bureau should  withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The Constitution requires  counting all people living in the United States. 

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (including children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count. 

Revise the tax records language so that those whose mailing address differs from their residential address (servicemembers, those with a post office box) are not excluded.  

• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for civil rights enforcement, among other uses, and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The prohibition, as written, may also restrict the collection or publication of census data on same-sex couples that was asked in 2020. 

 The proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Sincerely,
Ms Barbara Benzwi
Oakland, CA

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census because a fair and accurate census is critical to ensuring every community is counted, fairly represented, and able to get the resources people need to live healthy lives — including sexual and reproductive healthcare. An inaccurate or incomplete census can deepen existing inequities, particularly for communities that already face disenfranchisement and barriers to healthcare. 

A fair and accurate census is essential to our health and rights. 

Census data help determine access to programs patients and their families rely on, including important programs like Medicaid, SNAP, WIC, and TANF. Accurate census data also shape political representation by determining how seats in the U.S. House of Representatives are apportioned among states and providing data used for redistricting. When communities are undercounted or excluded, they risk losing both resources and political representation. 

The Census Bureau and Department of Commerce must:

1. Count all people residing in the United States in the 2030 Census, without regard to immigration status. Excluding noncitizens from census apportionment data violates the Constitution and established legal precedent. It would suppress the count of many communities, effectively erasing them from critical datasets and depriving them of resources and congressional representation –— including resources and political representation that support access to healthcare.

2. Continue collecting race and ethnicity data and implement the 2024 OMB SPD 15 standards. Census race and ethnicity data are essential for important research across many sectors, for upholding civil rights, and for growing the economy. Extensive Census Bureau research and engagement with expert stakeholders shows that implementing the modernized 2024 OMB SPD 15 standards for race and ethnicity data collection will yield data that more accurately represent the nation’s increasingly diverse population.

3. Remove the clause banning the addition of future questions on sexual orientation. Proposed changes to demographic items should be based on research and guided by a deliberative and transparent process, including extensive stakeholder consultation.

4. Withdraw other proposed changes to residence criteria, including tying place of residence to tax records and "lawful residence," and the adoption of a three month enumeration period. The Census Bureau must extensively research and consult with stakeholders about the potential effects of such changes before proposing their implementation in a decennial census.

5. Halt the practice of prison gerrymandering by counting incarcerated individuals in their home communities. This will yield more accurate census data and ensure that communities receive the congressional representation to which they are entitled.

Sincerely,

AR 72713

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: [keep any/all points you would like to include in your comment]

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).
I am a retired teacher and an artist, and I care about a fair and accurate census because it is the foundation of so much of our public policy that guides how we care for our communities.
First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.
Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including:
• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.
As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I strongly oppose erasing demographic data, targeting noncitizens, and shortening the enumeration window. 

Erasing demographic data & targeting noncitizens:
Non-citizens have always been counted in the census. The 14th Amendment explicitly commands an enumeration of the “whole number of persons in each State.” It does not say “voters” or “citizens”; it says persons. When America has excluded/discounted people in the census, it was to uphold white supremacy. For example 1) in 1790, enslaved Black Americans were reduced to three-fifths of a human being for apportionment benefiting Southern states. 2)The systematic exclusion of Native Americans went on for over a century (and the government is still undercounting them today).
The proposed change would update residential requirements to exclude non-citizens from the total population count (even legal permanent residents, student/work visa holders, refugees, and DACA recipients). It also proposes adding a mandatory citizenship question was already blocked by the Supreme Court in 2019 (Department of Commerce v. New York). The Supreme Court ruling should stand. 
Additionally, undercounting the population severely weakens both public health and emergency disaster responses. During severe weather, emergency management agencies rely on population figures to determine how many shelters to open and how many medical teams to deploy. Without knowing how many people actually live in a community, effective disaster preparation is impossible. We have seen an uptick in both public health issues and disasters in recent years so this could be devastating.


Shortening enumeration window: 
Winter months present severe obstacles for rural residents, unhoused populations, and communities impacted by extreme weather. I live in TN and in January we had winter storm Fern. If a census had occurred during a severe freeze like Winter Storm Fern, thousands of displaced residents would be left uncounted just because they were temporarily displaced.

The U.S. Census Bureau's proposed rule to strengthen the US Census is critical to fair representation and the future of America.  

The U.S. Census should not include distorted data in its count of Americans.  By including overly generalized ethnic demographic categories, we obscure the true goal of the census and hinder its constitutionally mandated purpose: an accurate count of Americans.  

Additionally, illegal aliens and other non-legal permanent residents should not be included for apportionment. Census data is used for the apportionment of congressional seats. Non-citizens cannot legally vote and should not be used to decrease the voting power of Americans. I support the Census Bureau in advancing the correct understanding of usual residence to recognize an element of allegiance that is antithetical to the inclusion of those not legally present in our country.  

This Census Bureau should also consider adding a citizenship question to the Census survey. The Supreme Court has already held that the Constitution lawfully permits the Census Bureau to at least inquire about citizenship on the census questionnaire. "The census should absolutely include questions related to citizenship and legal presence. 

These changes would strengthen the census in its core purpose of attaining an accurate count of Americans and have my full support. 

Thank you,  

Lisa M Garland

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: US Census Bureau,I urge the Census Bureau and Department of Commerce to withdraw the proposed rule changing residence criteria for the decennial Census and restricting demographic questions.The proposal would exclude foreign citizens from the population used for congressional apportionment unless they are also U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents. Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census because a fair and accurate census is critical to ensuring every community is counted, fairly represented, and able to get the resources people need to live healthy lives — including sexual and reproductive healthcare. An inaccurate or incomplete census can deepen existing inequities, particularly for communities that already face disenfranchisement and barriers to healthcare. 

A fair and accurate census is essential to our health and rights. 

Census data help determine access to programs patients and their families rely on, including important programs like Medicaid, SNAP, WIC, and TANF. Accurate census data also shape political representation by determining how seats in the U.S. House of Representatives are apportioned among states and providing data used for redistricting. When communities are undercounted or excluded, they risk losing both resources and political representation. 

The Census Bureau and Department of Commerce must:

1. Count all people residing in the United States in the 2030 Census, without regard to immigration status. Excluding noncitizens from census apportionment data violates the Constitution and established legal precedent. It would suppress the count of many communities, effectively erasing them from critical datasets and depriving them of resources and congressional representation –— including resources and political representation that support access to healthcare.

2. Continue collecting race and ethnicity data and implement the 2024 OMB SPD 15 standards. Census race and ethnicity data are essential for important research across many sectors, for upholding civil rights, and for growing the economy. Extensive Census Bureau research and engagement with expert stakeholders shows that implementing the modernized 2024 OMB SPD 15 standards for race and ethnicity data collection will yield data that more accurately represent the nation’s increasingly diverse population.

3. Remove the clause banning the addition of future questions on sexual orientation. Proposed changes to demographic items should be based on research and guided by a deliberative and transparent process, including extensive stakeholder consultation.

4. Withdraw other proposed changes to residence criteria, including tying place of residence to tax records and "lawful residence," and the adoption of a three month enumeration period. The Census Bureau must extensively research and consult with stakeholders about the potential effects of such changes before proposing their implementation in a decennial census.

5. Halt the practice of prison gerrymandering by counting incarcerated individuals in their home communities. This will yield more accurate census data and ensure that communities receive the congressional representation to which they are entitled.

Sincerely,
Eileen O'Connor
FL 34243

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census because a fair and accurate census is critical to ensuring every community is counted, fairly represented, and able to get the resources people need to live healthy lives — including sexual and reproductive healthcare. An inaccurate or incomplete census can deepen existing inequities, particularly for communities that already face disenfranchisement and barriers to healthcare. 

A fair and accurate census is essential to our health and rights. 

Census data help determine access to programs patients and their families rely on, including important programs like Medicaid, SNAP, WIC, and TANF. Accurate census data also shape political representation by determining how seats in the U.S. House of Representatives are apportioned among states and providing data used for redistricting. When communities are undercounted or excluded, they risk losing both resources and political representation. 

The Census Bureau and Department of Commerce must:

1. Count all people residing in the United States in the 2030 Census, without regard to immigration status. Excluding noncitizens from census apportionment data violates the Constitution and established legal precedent. It would suppress the count of many communities, effectively erasing them from critical datasets and depriving them of resources and congressional representation –— including resources and political representation that support access to healthcare.

2. Continue collecting race and ethnicity data and implement the 2024 OMB SPD 15 standards. Census race and ethnicity data are essential for important research across many sectors, for upholding civil rights, and for growing the economy. Extensive Census Bureau research and engagement with expert stakeholders shows that implementing the modernized 2024 OMB SPD 15 standards for race and ethnicity data collection will yield data that more accurately represent the nation’s increasingly diverse population.

3. Remove the clause banning the addition of future questions on sexual orientation. Proposed changes to demographic items should be based on research and guided by a deliberative and transparent process, including extensive stakeholder consultation.

4. Withdraw other proposed changes to residence criteria, including tying place of residence to tax records and "lawful residence," and the adoption of a three month enumeration period. The Census Bureau must extensively research and consult with stakeholders about the potential effects of such changes before proposing their implementation in a decennial census.

5. Halt the practice of prison gerrymandering by counting incarcerated individuals in their home communities. This will yield more accurate census data and ensure that communities receive the congressional representation to which they are entitled.

Sincerely,
Amanda Justice
CA 91335

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

Are you serious? The demographic information has been on the Census since 1790 and you want to cut it? WHY? That's more than 200 years of data you are messing with, and how ridiculous are you to do this? Our nonsense government is already risking data integrity by scaring undocumented people with ICE, which harms EVERYONE - including documented people and citizens.

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I work in pipeline Engineering in Omaha, Nebraska, and I care about a fair and accurate census because DATA MATTERS and is a MATTER OF LIFE OR DEATH FOR PEOPLE IN MY COMMUNITY.

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people. DATA MATTERS. 
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
A la Oficina del Censo de los Estados Unidos:

Re: Docket No. 260903-0005, RIN 0607-AA75, USBC-2026-0628. “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions”

Soy residente de Puerto Rico. Someto este comentario para expresar mi oposición a las Partes 60 y 70 propuestas del Título 15 del Código de Regulaciones Federales, por el daño que causarían a un conteo completo y correcto de Puerto Rico y de los puertorriqueños.

Resido en San Juan . Residencia permanente

La propuesta no menciona a Puerto Rico ni una sola vez, aunque el Censo decenal cuenta a más de 3.2 millones de ciudadanos estadounidenses en la Isla y produce los datos con que se redibujan nuestros distritos legislativos. Las secciones 60.5 y 70.3 hablan del “stateside census” y del nivel “nacional o estatal” sin definir “Estados Unidos”. Solicito que la Oficina del Censo explique por escrito cómo aplicarían las Partes 60 y 70 en Puerto Rico y que no adopte una regla final sin hacerlo.

La sección 60.2(a) dice que la residencia habitual “debe ser consistente con” los récords contributivos, pero no dice cuáles. La mayoría de los residentes de Puerto Rico rinde planilla ante el Departamento de Hacienda, nuestra autoridad contributiva local, y no ante el IRS; los patronos emiten el Formulario 499R-2/W-2PR. Solicito que la Oficina del Censo aclare por escrito si aceptaría las planillas de Hacienda y el Formulario 499R-2/W-2PR como récords contributivos en Puerto Rico, y cómo los obtendría y parearía.

Se estima que entre el 40% y el 60% de las estructuras en Puerto Rico no tienen una dirección física de calle y número (city-style), el estándar que usan los sistemas federales, así que no se pueden validar, parear ni ubicar en un mapa. Muchas familias reciben su correspondencia en apartados postales o rutas rurales, no donde viven, y nuestras direcciones usan el campo “Urbanización” y acentos que los sistemas nacionales no parean bien. Un récord con dirección postal no prueba dónde vive una persona. Solicito que la Oficina publique las tasas de pareo de direcciones en Puerto Rico de cada fuente administrativa y que mantenga la enumeración en persona donde las direcciones no se puedan parear.

La Encuesta sobre la Comunidad de Puerto Rico y casi todas las encuestas se ajustan a estimados de población basados en el Censo decenal. La sección 70.4 dice que la ACS aún podría preguntar sobre raza y origen, pero sin esos datos en el Censo no habría punto de referencia confiable. Municipios, agencias, hospitales, universidades, organizaciones sin fines de lucro y negocios dependen de estos datos, igual que la distribución de fondos federales para salud, alimentos, educación, vivienda y recuperación de desastres. Solicito que no se adopte la Parte 70.

La Constitución de Puerto Rico exige revisar los 40 distritos representativos y los 8 senatoriales después de cada censo, a partir de datos por bloque y barrio. El mismo conteo es la base de fondos federales para salud, nutrición, educación, vivienda y recuperación de desastres en los 78 municipios. Si la regla deja fuera hogares o los ubica en su dirección postal, los mapas y los fondos de la próxima década se distorsionan. Solicito que la Oficina publique un análisis del efecto de la regla en la base poblacional de Puerto Rico antes de adoptarla.

Estos cambios son los más profundos que se han propuesto al Censo en generaciones. El periodo de comentarios, aun extendido al 2 de noviembre de 2026, no basta para que las comunidades de Puerto Rico los evalúen. Solicito una extensión adicional, audiencias públicas en español en Puerto Rico y consulta formal con el gobierno de Puerto Rico y sus municipios.

Por estas razones, solicito que la Oficina del Censo retire la regla propuesta y garantice que todas las personas en Puerto Rico y en la diáspora sean contadas, una vez y en el lugar correcto.

Gracias por considerar este comentario.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I vehemently oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census. These changes will weaken the accuracy and integrity of our nation's most important population count and harm our communities. I strongly urge the Bureau to reject them. 

First, eliminating questions of race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation erases the full scope of my identity when I participate in the Census survey. These data points are not optional. They are the tools we use to enforce civil rights laws, monitor discrimination, and measure the disparities that still affect millions of people. Excluding them from the count does not make them disappear from our society, but it does make our government less equipped to handle big issues when they arise. To characterize this proposed change as an “addition” for the purpose of “establishing standards” is disingenuous.

The United States Constitution is clear: the census must count ALL persons living in the United States, regardless of their immigration or citizenship status. The proposal to exclude non-citizens, including those residents with some type of lawful status, violates more than two centuries of legal precedent. It also purports to fix the imaginary problem of residents being counted “more than once” in order to erase non-citizens from the count. Collecting accurate data about all who reside in the U.S. does not accidentally confer citizenship, but failing to count everyone renders the Census a weak tool. 

The consequences of these changes will have a negative impact on our daily lives. The census affects everything. It determines political representation and how voting districts are drawn. It guides how billions of dollars in federal funding are used to close persistent disparities in schools, hospitals, and other government programs that are designed to improve our lives.  

The census is the foundation of our democracy. It must reflect the complete, nuanced reality of who we are as a nation. It must also reflect the lives of our friends and neighbors who may not look, think, or speak like we do. I respectfully ask the Bureau to withdraw these proposed changes and to preserve a count that includes everyone and represents everyone. 

Thank you for considering my comment.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census.

A fair and accurate census is critical to ensuring every community is counted, fairly represented, and able to get the resources people need to live healthy lives. An inaccurate or incomplete census can deepen existing inequities, particularly for communities that already face disenfranchisement and barriers to healthcare.

Protecting the most vulnerable amongst us ensures that all of us are protected. Without representation for all, it's only a matter of time before someone you know can't receive the healthcare they need and deserve.

A fair and accurate census is essential to our health and rights. 

Census data help determine access to programs patients and their families rely on. When communities are undercounted or excluded, they risk losing both resources and political representation. After rights and services are denied to one segment of our country, it is easier for those rights and services to be denied for more people -- especially children.

The Census Bureau and Department of Commerce must:

1. Count all people residing in the United States in the 2030 Census, without regard to immigration status. This is necessary if you value our Constitution and value the lives of children.

2. Continue collecting race and ethnicity data and implement the 2024 OMB SPD 15 standards. Census race and ethnicity data are essential for important research across many sectors, for upholding civil rights, and for growing the economy. Extensive Census Bureau research and engagement with expert stakeholders shows that implementing the modernized 2024 OMB SPD 15 standards for race and ethnicity data collection will yield data that more accurately represent the nation’s increasingly diverse population. Diversity is a strength of our country, which has historically enabled us to have allies throughout the world. This is one of the best ways to prevent a future war on American soil.

3. Remove the clause banning the addition of future questions on sexual orientation (or on gender identity). Proposed changes to demographic items should be based on research and guided by a deliberative and transparent process, including extensive stakeholder consultation.

4. Withdraw other proposed changes to residence criteria, including tying place of residence to tax records and "lawful residence," and the adoption of a three month enumeration period. The Census Bureau must extensively research and consult with stakeholders about the potential effects of such changes before proposing their implementation in a decennial census.

5. Halt the practice of prison gerrymandering by counting incarcerated individuals in their home communities. This will yield more accurate census data and ensure that communities receive the congressional representation to which they are entitled.

Fair and accurate data about all Americans ultimately benefits all Americans.

Sincerely,
Jennifer Brewster
NJ 07450

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

Re: Docket No. 260903-0005, RIN 0607-AA75, USBC-2026-0628. “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions”

I am Puerto Rican and live in the United States (District of Columbia). I submit this comment to oppose proposed 15 CFR Parts 60 and 70 because of the harm they would cause to a complete and accurate count of Puerto Rico and of Puerto Ricans.

The proposed rule does not mention Puerto Rico a single time, even though the decennial census counts more than 3.2 million U.S. citizens on the island and produces the data used to redraw our legislative districts. Sections 60.5 and 70.3 refer to the “stateside census” and to the “national or state level” without defining “United States.” I ask the Census Bureau to explain in writing how Parts 60 and 70 would apply in Puerto Rico, and not to finalize any rule without doing so.

Section 70.2(a) would prohibit the Hispanic-origin question, which includes the “Puerto Rican” checkbox. More people of Puerto Rican origin now live in the states than on the island, and that question is the only way the decennial census counts them. Without it, our communities in New York, Florida, Pennsylvania, Massachusetts, Connecticut, and elsewhere would disappear from the data used to enforce civil and voting rights and to plan services. I ask that Section 70.2(a) be withdrawn.

Section 60.2(a) says usual residence “should be consistent with, and evidenced by” tax records, but does not say which ones. Most Puerto Rico residents file with the Puerto Rico Department of the Treasury (Hacienda), our local tax authority, not with the IRS; employers issue Form 499R-2/W-2PR. I ask the Census Bureau to state in writing whether it would accept Hacienda returns and Form 499R-2/W-2PR as tax records in Puerto Rico, and how it would obtain and match them.

Even if the Bureau used Hacienda returns, a residence test based on tax records would leave many people in Puerto Rico out. An estimated one-third of the population doesn’t file and works in the informal economy (Caraballo-Cueto), and retirees and low-income households often file no return at all. Moreover, there is concern that a substantial share of the returns that are filed list a P.O. box or rural route as the address, which does not identify the home where the person lives. I ask that tax records not be made the proof of residence in Puerto Rico, and that self-response and field verification be accepted.

An estimated 40% to 60% of structures in Puerto Rico have no physical street-and-number (city-style) address, the standard federal systems use, so they cannot be validated, matched, or placed on a map. Many families receive mail at P.O. boxes or rural routes rather than where they live, and our addresses use an “Urbanización” line and accents that national systems don’t match well. A record with a mailing address does not prove where a person lives. I ask the Bureau to publish Puerto Rico address-match rates for every administrative source and to keep in-person enumeration wherever addresses cannot be matched.

The Bureau invites comments on adding a legal-status question to the questionnaire. I oppose it. Puerto Rico has long-established immigrant communities and many mixed-status households that include U.S. citizens. The fear such a question creates would suppress response from entire households and worsen undercounts in the barrios and municipios where they live.

The Puerto Rico Community Survey and nearly all surveys are weighted to population estimates based on the decennial census. Section 70.4 says the ACS could still ask about race and origin, but without those data in the census there would be no reliable benchmark. Municipios, agencies, hospitals, universities, nonprofits, and businesses depend on these data, as does the distribution of federal funds for health, nutrition, education, housing, and disaster recovery. I ask that Part 70 not be adopted.

These are the most sweeping changes proposed to the census in generations. Even extended to November 2, 2026, the comment period is not enough time for Puerto Rico’s communities to evaluate them. I ask for a further extension, public hearings in Spanish in Puerto Rico, and formal consultation with the Government of Puerto Rico and its municipios.

For these reasons, I ask the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that everyone in Puerto Rico and in the diaspora is counted, once, and in the right place.

Thank you for considering this comment.

Comment:
October 24, 2026
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

There is no logical reason for diminishing the accuracy of an important and historical data source like the US Census. Approving this rule will harm all Americans.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). 

As an educator, I care about a fair and accurate census because census data and other federal datasets based on the census are used to make key decisions that affect our nation’s students, educators, and schools.  

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Examples of these uses include: . 

* Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. 

* Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

* Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

* Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

* Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

* Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

* Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

* Determining state higher education funding formulas 

* Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

* Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

* Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

First, to ensure a fair and accurate census,  the Census Bureau should  extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. Second, I oppose both the proposed changes to the residence criteria and the proposed regulations regarding demographic questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. The Census Bureau should  withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The Constitution requires  counting all people living in the United States. 

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (including children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count. 

Revise the tax records language so that those whose mailing address differs from their residential address (servicemembers, those with a post office box) are not excluded.  

• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for civil rights enforcement, among other uses, and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The prohibition, as written, may also restrict the collection or publication of census data on same-sex couples that was asked in 2020. 

 The proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Sincerely,
Ms. Mary Bost
Hempstead, NY

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule: Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions.

The census has counted all residents for apportionment regardless of legal status for 230 years. 

The country has always counted native-born U.S. citizens, naturalized U.S. citizens, non-citizen U.S. nationals, lawful permanent residents and temporary migrants, such as foreign students, refugees, asylum seekers and undocumented immigrants. The census has never left out residents because of their immigration status.  This is for good reason: these are individuals who are part of our communities.  They need food and healthcare, education and the use of roads.  

The census determines the funding and representation of our communities. By not counting all people, communities will not get the resources they need for schools, hospitals, roads, firefighters and other critical services. This proposal would mean there would no longer be a complete and accurate count of our population. I strongly oppose this rule and encourage the census bureau not to enact it.  Any failure to accurately count residents makes clear a goal of seeing some lives as worth more than others. 

Article I, Section 2, Clause 3 of the U.S. Constitution mandates that an "actual Enumeration" of the population be conducted within three years of the first Congress meeting and every subsequent term of ten years. The 14th Amendment further clarifies that representatives are apportioned by counting the "whole number of persons" in each state.  This is the law, and that law should hold for every president, not just those who make a conscious choice to do what is ethically and legally right.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census because a fair and accurate census is critical to ensuring every community is counted, fairly represented, and able to get the resources people need to live healthy lives — including sexual and reproductive healthcare. An inaccurate or incomplete census can deepen existing inequities, particularly for communities that already face disenfranchisement and barriers to healthcare. 

A fair and accurate census is essential to our health and rights. 

Census data help determine access to programs patients and their families rely on, including important programs like Medicaid, SNAP, WIC, and TANF. Accurate census data also shape political representation by determining how seats in the U.S. House of Representatives are apportioned among states and providing data used for redistricting. When communities are undercounted or excluded, they risk losing both resources and political representation. 

The Census Bureau and Department of Commerce must:

1. Count all people residing in the United States in the 2030 Census, without regard to immigration status. Excluding noncitizens from census apportionment data violates the Constitution and established legal precedent. It would suppress the count of many communities, effectively erasing them from critical datasets and depriving them of resources and congressional representation –— including resources and political representation that support access to healthcare.

2. Continue collecting race and ethnicity data and implement the 2024 OMB SPD 15 standards. Census race and ethnicity data are essential for important research across many sectors, for upholding civil rights, and for growing the economy. Extensive Census Bureau research and engagement with expert stakeholders shows that implementing the modernized 2024 OMB SPD 15 standards for race and ethnicity data collection will yield data that more accurately represent the nation’s increasingly diverse population.

3. Remove the clause banning the addition of future questions on sexual orientation. Proposed changes to demographic items should be based on research and guided by a deliberative and transparent process, including extensive stakeholder consultation.

4. Withdraw other proposed changes to residence criteria, including tying place of residence to tax records and "lawful residence," and the adoption of a three month enumeration period. The Census Bureau must extensively research and consult with stakeholders about the potential effects of such changes before proposing their implementation in a decennial census.

5. Halt the practice of prison gerrymandering by counting incarcerated individuals in their home communities. This will yield more accurate census data and ensure that communities receive the congressional representation to which they are entitled.

Sincerely,
Jessie Casteel
TX 77035

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
docket id USBC-2026-0628
I am a US citizen. I was born here, my parents were born here, and my father’s parents were born here.
I disagree strenuously with the proposed exclusion of “illegal aliens (among others)” from apportionment. As you know, Amendment XIV section 2 of the Constitution requires the count to include ALL PERSONS. That must include ANY PERSON, regardless of immigration status, who has established a residence here and an intent to remain here indefinitely. Excluding persons meeting these criteria risks litigation, and I am tired of my tax money being wasted on defending the indefensible in court.
It’s ludicrous that you cite as support for this position three bills that are unlikely to become law and two more that died in a previous Congress.
I’m incensed that you are actually bragging about your illegal use of our data, for example from the Social Security Administration and the IRS, for purposes to which we did not consent. The integration you are so proud of is something that the old rules were explicitly designed to prevent. This abuse of our data is another likely target for further litigation and waste of tax dollars.
I oppose including a citizenship/legal status question on the decennial census questionnaire. We’ve had this discussion already. SCOTUS ruled against it in 2019, and cherry-picking a sentence from that ruling doesn’t alter that fact. A citizenship question would reduce the accuracy of the count of all persons. I realize that for some in this administration, that’s a feature, not a bug. Nevertheless, it’s a bug. Besides, you have been bragging about all the data you have amassed that can provide citizenship information, almost certainly more accurately and timely than the decennial census, and without the (to me) undesired side effect of degrading the accuracy of the census for apportionment purposes.
I oppose the proposed elimination of demographic questions relating to race and ethnicity or sexual orientation. One of the more un-American things this administration has done is its demonization of diversity, equity, and inclusion, which in my opinion are core American values. The data collected from the answers to these questions is necessary for “tak(ing) Care that the Laws be faithfully executed” and guaranteeing equal protection of the laws. The argument advanced by the agency that asking these questions threatens individual privacy rights is rich, coming from this administration. And I know I repeat myself, but Executive Orders are not laws. Finally, the argument that reducing the number of questions could improve the response rate, while not without merit, is cancelled out by the proposed inclusion of a question about not just citizenship, but legal status. Unlike citizenship and legal status, it is much less clear to me how comparable demographic data can be gleaned from other Agencies or even the American Community Survey. The Census is a census. A survey is a sample from a population, not a census.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: I strongly oppose eliminating race and ethnicity from the 2030 Census because these classifications are essential for accurately measuring the American population, identifying disparities, and ensuring government accountability. Rather than eliminating these categories, the federal government should improve them by establishing a distinct ancestry classification for multigenerational Black Americans descended from people enslaved in the United States and the historic American Freedmen population, while preserving the ability of individuals to identify as Black or African American. A separate classification would allow the government to distinguish this historically rooted population from more recent African and Caribbean immigrant populations for statistical research, without denying anyone their existing racial or ethnic identity. Eliminating race and ethnicity without a transparent plan for preserving detailed ancestry data could make it more difficult to measure historical inequalities, evaluate civil rights protections, and develop evidence-based policies. I urge OMB to retain race and ethnicity data collection, maintain the underlying ancestry and coding systems, and work with affected communities to develop a clear, accurate, and historically meaningful classification for American Freedmen descendants before implementing any changes to the 2030 Census. Strongly believe the census should keep population origin subgroups for data purposes.

The U.S. Census Bureau's proposed rule to strengthen the US Census is critical to fair representation and the future of America.

The census is the foundation of our democracy. It must reflect the complete yet nuanced reality of who we are as a nation. And it must reflect the lives of our friends and neighbors who may not look, think, or speak like we do. I ask the Bureau to withdraw these proposed changes and to preserve a count that includes everyone and represents everyone. 

Thank you for considering my comment.

Sincerely,
Kiera Recker

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am a mother, a healthcare worker and a citizen of Arizona and I care about a fair and accurate census because I love and care about my community.

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.
As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
A la Oficina del Censo de los Estados Unidos:

Re: Docket No. 260903-0005, RIN 0607-AA75, USBC-2026-0628. “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions”

Soy residente de Puerto Rico (Bayamón). Someto este comentario para expresar mi oposición a las Partes 60 y 70 propuestas del Título 15 del Código de Regulaciones Federales, por el daño que causarían a un conteo completo y correcto de Puerto Rico y de los puertorriqueños.

La propuesta no menciona a Puerto Rico ni una sola vez, aunque el Censo decenal cuenta a más de 3.2 millones de ciudadanos estadounidenses en la Isla y produce los datos con que se redibujan nuestros distritos legislativos. Las secciones 60.5 y 70.3 hablan del “stateside census” y del nivel “nacional o estatal” sin definir “Estados Unidos”. Solicito que la Oficina del Censo explique por escrito cómo aplicarían las Partes 60 y 70 en Puerto Rico y que no adopte una regla final sin hacerlo.

La sección 70.2(a) prohibiría la pregunta de origen hispano, que incluye el encasillado “puertorriqueño”. Hoy viven más personas de origen puertorriqueño en los estados que en Puerto Rico, y esa pregunta es la única forma en que el Censo decenal las cuenta. Sin ella, nuestras comunidades en Nueva York, Florida, Pensilvania, Massachusetts, Connecticut y otros estados desaparecerían de los datos que se usan para hacer cumplir los derechos civiles y electorales y para planificar servicios. Solicito que se elimine la sección 70.2(a).

La sección 60.2(a) dice que la residencia habitual “debe ser consistente con” los récords contributivos, pero no dice cuáles. La mayoría de los residentes de Puerto Rico rinde planilla ante el Departamento de Hacienda, nuestra autoridad contributiva local, y no ante el IRS; los patronos emiten el Formulario 499R-2/W-2PR. Solicito que la Oficina del Censo aclare por escrito si aceptaría las planillas de Hacienda y el Formulario 499R-2/W-2PR como récords contributivos en Puerto Rico, y cómo los obtendría y parearía.

Aun si la Oficina usara las planillas de Hacienda, una prueba de residencia basada en récords contributivos dejaría fuera a muchas personas en Puerto Rico. Se estima que cerca de un tercio de la población no rinde planilla y está en la economía informal (Caraballo-Cueto), y jubilados y hogares de bajos ingresos con frecuencia no rinden ninguna. Además, preocupa que una porción sustancial de las planillas que sí se rinden use un apartado postal o una ruta rural como dirección, que no identifica la vivienda donde vive la persona. Solicito que no se haga de los récords contributivos la prueba de residencia en Puerto Rico y que se acepten la autorespuesta y la verificación en el campo.

Por estas razones, solicito que la Oficina del Censo retire la regla propuesta y garantice que todas las personas en Puerto Rico y en la diáspora sean contadas, una vez y en el lugar correcto.

Gracias por considerar este comentario.

Jose Joaquin Mulinelli-Rodriguez

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census because a fair and accurate census is critical to ensuring every community is counted, fairly represented, and able to get the resources people need to live healthy lives — including sexual and reproductive healthcare. An inaccurate or incomplete census can deepen existing inequities, particularly for communities that already face disenfranchisement and barriers to healthcare. 

A fair and accurate census is essential to our health and rights. 

Census data help determine access to programs patients and their families rely on, including important programs like Medicaid, SNAP, WIC, and TANF. Accurate census data also shape political representation by determining how seats in the U.S. House of Representatives are apportioned among states and providing data used for redistricting. When communities are undercounted or excluded, they risk losing both resources and political representation. 

The Census Bureau and Department of Commerce must:

1. Count all people residing in the United States in the 2030 Census, without regard to immigration status. Excluding noncitizens from census apportionment data violates the Constitution and established legal precedent. It would suppress the count of many communities, effectively erasing them from critical datasets and depriving them of resources and congressional representation –— including resources and political representation that support access to healthcare.

2. Continue collecting race and ethnicity data and implement the 2024 OMB SPD 15 standards. Census race and ethnicity data are essential for important research across many sectors, for upholding civil rights, and for growing the economy. Extensive Census Bureau research and engagement with expert stakeholders shows that implementing the modernized 2024 OMB SPD 15 standards for race and ethnicity data collection will yield data that more accurately represent the nation’s increasingly diverse population.

3. Remove the clause banning the addition of future questions on sexual orientation. Proposed changes to demographic items should be based on research and guided by a deliberative and transparent process, including extensive stakeholder consultation.

4. Withdraw other proposed changes to residence criteria, including tying place of residence to tax records and "lawful residence," and the adoption of a three month enumeration period. The Census Bureau must extensively research and consult with stakeholders about the potential effects of such changes before proposing their implementation in a decennial census.

5. Halt the practice of prison gerrymandering by counting incarcerated individuals in their home communities. This will yield more accurate census data and ensure that communities receive the congressional representation to which they are entitled.

Sincerely,
Judith Weis
NY 10023

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census. These changes will not only weaken the accuracy and integrity of our nation's most important population count, but they will also harm our communities, and I strongly urge the Bureau to reject them. 

First, removing questions of race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation erases the full scope of my identity when I participate in the Census survey. These data points are not optional. They are the tools we use to enforce civil rights laws, monitor discrimination, and measure the disparities that still affect millions of people. Excluding them from the count does not make them disappear from our society, but it does make our government less equipped to handle big issues when they arise. 

The Constitution is clear: the census must count ALL persons living in the United States, regardless of their immigration or citizenship status. The proposal to exclude non-citizens, including those residents with some type of lawful status, violates more than two centuries of legal precedent. Every person counted in this country contributes to our communities, and every person deserves to be fully seen. 

The consequences of these changes will negatively impact our daily lives. The census affects everything. It determines political representation and the drawing of voting districts. It guides how billions of dollars in federal funding are used to close persistent disparities in schools, hospitals, and other government programs that are designed to improve our lives.  

The census is the foundation of our democracy. It must reflect the complete yet nuanced reality of who we are as a nation. And it must reflect the lives of our friends and neighbors who may not look, think, or speak like we do. I ask the Bureau to withdraw these proposed changes and to preserve a count that includes everyone and represents everyone. 

Thank you for considering my comment.

Sincerely,
Virginia Clark

I am a healthcare worker and EMT-B in suburban Chicago, Illinois, and I care about a fair and accurate census because of its implications in US and state House representative allocations, statistical analysis, constitutional requirements, and local and national demographic trends.

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including:

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities in which people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Eliminate the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Sincerely, a Chicago-area frontline emergency response and healthcare worker.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
RE: Docket USBC-2026-0628 — Proposed Census Regulations
Dear Secretary Lutnick:

As a grant professional, I rely on Census Bureau and American Community Survey (ACS) data to identify community needs, support funding applications, and demonstrate the impact of federal investments. I am concerned that the proposed changes to Census residence criteria and demographic data collection could affect the accuracy, availability, and comparability of information essential to federal grantmaking.

Changes to these data could affect funding eligibility, competitive applications, and the distribution of federal resources. Small and rural communities could be particularly affected if reliable, geographically detailed data become less available.

Before finalizing either proposal, I urge the Census Bureau to work with OMB and federal grantmaking agencies to assess the potential impacts on grant eligibility, funding allocations, community needs assessments, and program evaluation. Any alternative data sources should remain publicly accessible, timely, geographically detailed, and comparable over time.

I also encourage the Bureau to consult grant professionals and other data users to better understand these practical implications.

Thank you for considering my comments.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed changes to the 2030 Census, particularly those that could compromise the accuracy and completeness of our population data.

The fundamental purpose of the Census should be to accurately count the people living in our communities. State and local governments are responsible for serving their residents, regardless of citizenship or immigration status. Excluding certain populations or introducing barriers to participation risks producing incomplete data that undermines effective planning, resource allocation, and fair representation.

I am especially concerned about the additional burdens these changes could place on states and municipalities. Communities rely on accurate Census data to make decisions about infrastructure, schools, healthcare, emergency services, and public funding. What purpose does a Census serve if the resulting data fails to reflect the population our communities actually serve?

Equally troubling is the proposal to eliminate race and ethnicity questions. Our nation's diversity is a reality worth acknowledging, not obscuring. Removing this information risks erasing important distinctions within our population and limiting our ability to identify disparities, protect civil rights, and ensure that resources reach those who need them.

I recognize the importance of efficiency, privacy, and responsible government spending. However, these objectives should not come at the expense of accurate, inclusive, and meaningful data.

A Census should reflect America as it is, not present a diminished or incomplete picture of who we are.

I respectfully urge the Census Bureau to reconsider these proposals and prioritize the integrity, accuracy, and inclusiveness of this essential national undertaking.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
We represent a nonprofit organization serving over 60,000 individuals per year. We submit this comment in opposition to the proposed changes to the 2030 Census and urge the U.S. Department of Commerce and the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposal. In our view, it would produce an incomplete picture of our communities, weaken the information used to plan essential services, and put fair representation and public resources at risk. 
Our organization works with those seeking stable housing and greater financial security. Accurate population and demographic information help us understand local needs and plan our work. In preparing our needs assessment, we use Census Bureau data alongside local information to examine poverty, employment, health, and education. The quality of that information matters to the decisions we make and the residents we serve. 
The proposal would exclude foreign citizens who are neither U.S. citizens nor lawful permanent residents from the count used to allocate seats in the U.S. House of Representatives. That would exclude people who live and work in our communities, including international students and people with temporary work visas, as well as undocumented residents. We oppose this change. The Fourteenth Amendment calls for representation based on the “whole number of persons in each State.” We urge the Bureau to retain a count of all residents regardless of immigration status. 
Excluding residents from the count would not eliminate the needs of the communities where they live. Their children would still attend school, their households would still need housing, and local systems would still serve them. Census data help guide the distribution of federal resources. An incomplete population count could leave communities with resources that do not reflect the number of people who depend on their schools, housing, and other services. Nonprofits would face the same needs with less reliable information and potentially greater pressure to fill gaps. 
The proposed rules also raise concerns for the people we serve. The proposal would determine usual residents based on where someone spent the greatest number of days between January 3 and April 1, with tax records used as evidence of residence. A family moving from a shelter into an apartment during that period could have several addresses. A resident staying temporarily with relatives may have no tax document showing where they actually live. These situations should not result in residents being missed or counted in the wrong community. 
Tax records can help supplement a count, but they should not become a barrier to being counted accurately. An address on a tax return result may reflect an earlier home or a reliable place to receive mail. People with low incomes may also have limited or inconsistent tax returns. We ask the Bureau to preserve practical ways to count people experiencing homelessness, renters who move frequently, and families staying temporarily with others, including residents whose circumstances are not captured accurately in administrative records. 
We also oppose removing race and ethnicity questions from the decennial census. Population total alone cannot show whether different communities face unequal access to housing, education, or economic opportunities. Reliable demographic data help organizations identify disparities, assess whether services are reaching residents, and support fair housing and other civil rights work. Removing these questions would make it harder to recognize needs that can be hidden within a community-wide average. 
The proposal would leave demographic questions on the American Community Survey, but that survey serves a different purpose from the decennial count. Retaining one source does not remove the need for reliable demographic information from the census itself. We ask the Bureau to preserve race and ethnicity data collection and to address privacy and participation through sound protections, clear communication, and accessible outreach. 
Public confidence is also essential to a complete count. Residents need to understand that the census includes their community and that responding is worthwhile. Excluding groups of residents or introducing confusing residence rules could discourage participation beyond those directly affected. For organizations working with families facing housing instability or uncertainty about immigration policy, that loss of trust could make an already difficult outreach effort harder. 
For these reasons, we urge the Department of Commerce and the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposal. The Bureau should count all residents regardless of immigration status, retain residence rules that account for unstable and changing housing situations, and preserve race and ethnicity questions. We also request a fuller assessment of how changes would impact local population counts, community resources, and the information nonprofits and public agencies use to serve residents.

Comment:
I’m retired from the military, and I represent Idaho House District 25 in Twin Falls County.

As a military retiree, I appreciate that the census doesn’t just count whoever is standing in a state on Census Day. Federal personnel stationed overseas are counted back in their home states when House seats are divided, and the Supreme Court has upheld that. Foreign tourists who happen to be here on Census Day aren’t counted at all. What matters is a person’s lasting connection to this country.

I support the Bureau’s proposal to stop counting illegal aliens and people on temporary visas when it divides House seats. It’s the same idea, and it should apply to green-card holders too. New citizens take an oath giving up allegiance to any foreign country, and green-card holders haven’t taken that oath yet. A lot of them serve honorably in our military, and federal law gives them a faster path to citizenship. Once they’re citizens, they should count. Until then, they should be counted in the census but not in the numbers used to divide seats.

I also support the proposed limits on demographic questions, which take race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation off the census form. Those questions have nothing to do with a person’s ties to this country.

I’m asking the Bureau to adopt the rule and divide House seats based on U.S. citizens only, not green-card holders or any other noncitizens. I’m also asking it to give states block-level data with a clear explanation of how it was produced, in time to meet the legal deadline for redistricting. And if the population used for House seats differs from the one in the redistricting data, the Bureau should say so plainly.

Respectfully,
Rep. David Leavitt, Idaho House of Representatives, District 25
