Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

Re: Docket No. 260903-0005, RIN 0607-AA75, USBC-2026-0628. “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions”

I am a resident of Puerto Rico. I submit this comment to oppose proposed 15 CFR Parts 60 and 70 because of the harm they would cause to a complete and accurate count of Puerto Rico and of Puerto Ricans.

The decision to change the questions on the 2030 Census form significantly harms Puerto Ricans, especially those of us living on the island. First, the proposal does not mention Puerto Rico, nor does it allow us to identify as Puerto Rican. Furthermore, there is an attempt to use the residential address on file with the IRS; however, those of us living on the island file our income tax returns with the Department of the Treasury (*Departamento de Hacienda*), not the IRS. Moreover, the vast majority of us use a P.O. Box as our address when filing these returns. Another issue regarding residential addresses is that 60% of the island's inhabitants live in rural areas, where addresses are defined by a highway number, a kilometer marker, and a *barrio* (neighborhood) or sector. In light of all the points mentioned above, please take my concerns into consideration.

The proposed rule does not mention Puerto Rico a single time, even though the decennial census counts more than 3.2 million U.S. citizens on the island and produces the data used to redraw our legislative districts. Sections 60.5 and 70.3 refer to the “stateside census” and to the “national or state level” without defining “United States.” I ask the Census Bureau to explain in writing how Parts 60 and 70 would apply in Puerto Rico, and not to finalize any rule without doing so.

Section 70.2(a) would prohibit the Hispanic-origin question, which includes the “Puerto Rican” checkbox. More people of Puerto Rican origin now live in the states than on the island, and that question is the only way the decennial census counts them. Without it, our communities in New York, Florida, Pennsylvania, Massachusetts, Connecticut, and elsewhere would disappear from the data used to enforce civil and voting rights and to plan services. I ask that Section 70.2(a) be withdrawn.

Section 60.2(a) says usual residence “should be consistent with, and evidenced by” tax records, but does not say which ones. Most Puerto Rico residents file with the Puerto Rico Department of the Treasury (Hacienda), our local tax authority, not with the IRS; employers issue Form 499R-2/W-2PR. I ask the Census Bureau to state in writing whether it would accept Hacienda returns and Form 499R-2/W-2PR as tax records in Puerto Rico, and how it would obtain and match them.

Even if the Bureau used Hacienda returns, a residence test based on tax records would leave many people in Puerto Rico out. An estimated one-third of the population doesn’t file and works in the informal economy (Caraballo-Cueto), and retirees and low-income households often file no return at all. Moreover, there is concern that a substantial share of the returns that are filed list a P.O. box or rural route as the address, which does not identify the home where the person lives. I ask that tax records not be made the proof of residence in Puerto Rico, and that self-response and field verification be accepted.

An estimated 40% to 60% of structures in Puerto Rico have no physical street-and-number (city-style) address, the standard federal systems use, so they cannot be validated, matched, or placed on a map. Many families receive mail at P.O. boxes or rural routes rather than where they live, and our addresses use an “Urbanización” line and accents that national systems don’t match well. A record with a mailing address does not prove where a person lives. I ask the Bureau to publish Puerto Rico address-match rates for every administrative source and to keep in-person enumeration wherever addresses cannot be matched.

For these reasons, I ask the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that everyone in Puerto Rico and in the diaspora is counted, once, and in the right place.

Thank you for considering this comment.

Juan Santiago Torres

As a student, the data that the census provides to research and to policies that directly impact my education and my future is incredibly important. Even though the justification for these changes is that the constitutional purpose of the census is to solely inform apportionment, it is still a fact that the Census helps policymakers determine the distribution of more than $2.8 trillion a year across roughly 350 federal programs. It also informs how states distribute resources. Unless the 2030 decennial census ceases to function as a vital tool for distributing resources to underserved communities, it is heinous and ridiculous to remove essential demographic information through excluding participants based on legal status, as well as erase racial and ethnicity questions. It is wildly unconstitutional and invasive to use federal and third party resources to systematically exclude individuals with uncertain legal status from the census. It is also an egregious waste of federal resources that could be used to improve the census, not gut it. The proposed changes to the census targets critical information about race and immigration that is absolutely necessary in making our democracy representative. The changes proposed are unnecessary and actively harmful to the well-being of our nation.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am a disaster researcher living in California, and I care about a fair and accurate census because it is a tool for researchers to study the impacts of disasters on all Americans and propose policy solutions that alleviate suffering.

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census. These changes will not only weaken the accuracy and integrity of our nation's most important population count, but they will also harm our communities, and I strongly urge the Bureau to reject them. 

First, removing questions of race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation erases the full scope of my identity when I participate in the Census survey. These data points are not optional. They are the tools we use to enforce civil rights laws, monitor discrimination, and measure the disparities that still affect millions of people. Excluding them from the count does not make them disappear from our society, but it does make our government less equipped to handle big issues when they arise. 

The Constitution is clear: the census must count ALL persons living in the United States, regardless of their immigration or citizenship status. The proposal to exclude non-citizens, including those residents with some type of lawful status, violates more than two centuries of legal precedent. Every person counted in this country contributes to our communities, and every person deserves to be fully seen. 

The consequences of these changes will negatively impact our daily lives. The census affects everything. It determines political representation and the drawing of voting districts. It guides how billions of dollars in federal funding are used to close persistent disparities in schools, hospitals, and other government programs that are designed to improve our lives.  

The census is the foundation of our democracy. It must reflect the complete yet nuanced reality of who we are as a nation. And it must reflect the lives of our friends and neighbors who may not look, think, or speak like we do. I ask the Bureau to withdraw these proposed changes and to preserve a count that includes everyone and represents everyone. 

Thank you for considering my comment.

Sincerely,
Moira McKinnon

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Census Bureau's proposed rule to strengthen the US Census is critical to fair representation and the future of America.

"The census should absolutely include questions related to citizenship and legal presence.

Thank you,  

John Buzzell

I oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census because a fair and accurate census is critical to ensuring every community is counted, fairly represented, and able to get the resources people need to live healthy lives — including sexual and reproductive healthcare. An inaccurate or incomplete census can deepen existing inequities, particularly for communities that already face disenfranchisement and barriers to healthcare. 

A fair and accurate census is essential to our health and rights. 

Census data help determine access to programs patients and their families rely on, including important programs like Medicaid, SNAP, WIC, and TANF. Accurate census data also shape political representation by determining how seats in the U.S. House of Representatives are apportioned among states and providing data used for redistricting. 1. Count all people residing in the United States in the 2030 Census, without regard to immigration status. Census race and ethnicity data are essential for important research across many sectors, for upholding civil rights, and for growing the economy. 4. Withdraw other proposed changes to residence criteria, including tying place of residence to tax records and "lawful residence," and the adoption of a three month enumeration period. The Census Bureau must extensively research and consult with stakeholders about the potential effects of such changes before proposing their implementation in a decennial census.

5. Halt the practice of prison gerrymandering by counting incarcerated individuals in their home communities. This will yield more accurate census data and ensure that communities receive the congressional representation to which they are entitled.

PA 16510

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To whom it may concern at the US Census Bureau,
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).
My name is Iman Emdad, I am a resident of the state of Georgia working at a voting rights non-profit. I care about an accurate and democratic census because my work towards fair representation will be null and void if the Census Bureau implements these proposed rules. 
First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. While I appreciate the extension to November 2nd, significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond. That includes my colleagues, working in politics and advocacy. Many people working in my field cannot respond in their full capacity, individual or organizational, until after the midterm elections. I myself found that my commenting capacity was reduced due to the additional workload burden surrounding protecting free and democratic elections.
Secondly, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule changes. I oppose the rule changes for a variety of reasons, but mostly because the proposed changes risk exacerbating historical disparities between Black and white people. While I acknowledge that the full breadth of human ethnicity cannot be reduced into the number of categories on the Census alone, abandoning the numbers that we do have seems haphazardly executed at best, and devastatingly censorial at worst. Scrapping racial data in this manner would be akin to throwing “the baby, the tub, and the entire bathroom” [sic] out with the bathwater should it come to pass.
After reading through the proposed rule changes, it is evident that the current administration, whose politics have been quietly steeping but recently enumerated, has a vested interest in erasing minority political power, but specifically Black political power. Deciding against hundreds of years of data collection that enables the analysis and understanding of racial denominators in favor of an amalgamated count interrupts historical and academic data collection that allows us to acknowledge that different groups of people are different. While opportunity itself can and should be colorblind, accessible to people across races and resource backgrounds, choosing to ignore or erase our differences in the hope that they will magically disappear on their own is ludicrous.
Furthermore, another reason I oppose this rule change is because counting incarcerated people where they are incarcerated versus the communities in which they reside is also a subterfuge to dilute Black voting power. Mass incarceration is a historical development that follows Reconstruction and the end of slavery. A vast body of sociological and economic research shows that show Black people are disproportionately incarcerated; while only making about 13% of the population, they make up 37% of all incarcerated people. About 1in 5 Black men born in 2001 is projected to be incarcerated at some point in their lifetime, and studies show that 1 in 2 Black women are affected by a family member being incarcerated, and that they bear higher financial burdens as a result. Research also supports the idea that Black people tend to be incarcerated for longer than their white counterparts who commit the same crimes. The Census Bureau choosing to count incarcerated people where they are jailed rather than their home address will significantly divert federal, state, and local resources from the communities that they hope to return to. Because most states revoke the right of incarcerated felons to vote in elections, being counted in the Census is one of the remaining few ways that incarcerated people can access institutional allocation and power. Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
This comment addresses the accuracy of Social Security Administration citizenship data, which any administrative-records approach to immigration status would likely depend on.
I write about the limits of using administrative records to determine immigration status in the 2030 Census. Any such effort would likely lean on the citizenship records the Social Security Administration (SSA) keeps, and those records have accuracy problems of their own.
SSA does not automatically update a person's citizenship when they naturalize. Its policy says people need not report a change in immigration status unless they receive Social Security benefits, and the only way to fix outdated information is an in-person visit to an SSA field office. SSA itself warns that although its citizenship information is accurate for its own program purposes, "if used later for other purposes, it may not be current," because "SSA is not the custodian of U.S. citizenship records."[1]
A 2006 audit by SSA's Office of Inspector General quantified one version of the problem. Of the records SSA classified as belonging to non-citizens, 7.0 percent of those reviewed belonged to people who had since become U.S. citizens without telling SSA. The OIG projected that about 3.3 million SSA records carried these outdated citizenship codes.[2]
I urge Commerce not to rely on SSA citizenship data to determine immigration status for apportionment.
Sources:
[1] Fair Elections Center, Issue Brief: Examining Changes to USCIS's SAVE System (Feb. 2026), https://fairelectionscenter.org/uscis-save-system-report/; see also Fair Elections Center, Comment to U.S. Department of Homeland Security re: SAVE System of Records Notice (Dec. 1, 2025), https://fairelectionscenter.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/2025-12-01-Fair-Elections-re-DHS-SAVE-SORN.pdf.
[2] U.S. Social Security Administration, Office of the Inspector General, Congressional Response Report: Accuracy of the Social Security Administration's Numident File, No. A-08-06-26100 (Dec. 18, 2006), https://oig-files.ssa.gov/audits/full/A-08-06-26100.pdf.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am a data specialist and a resident of a rural community in western NY state, and I care about a fair and accurate census because it should accurately determine the distribution of necessary funds to all communities, especially rural counties with lower overall populations and a higher senior demographic.

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including:

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census because a fair and accurate census is critical to ensuring every community is counted, fairly represented, and able to get the resources people need to live healthy lives — including sexual and reproductive healthcare. An inaccurate or incomplete census can deepen existing inequities, particularly for communities that already face disenfranchisement and barriers to healthcare. 

A fair and accurate census is essential to our health and rights. 

Census data help determine access to programs patients and their families rely on, including important programs like Medicaid, SNAP, WIC, and TANF. Accurate census data also shape political representation by determining how seats in the U.S. House of Representatives are apportioned among states and providing data used for redistricting. When communities are undercounted or excluded, they risk losing both resources and political representation. 

The Census Bureau and Department of Commerce must:

1. Count all people residing in the United States in the 2030 Census, without regard to immigration status. Excluding noncitizens from census apportionment data violates the Constitution and established legal precedent. It would suppress the count of many communities, effectively erasing them from critical datasets and depriving them of resources and congressional representation –— including resources and political representation that support access to healthcare.

2. Continue collecting race and ethnicity data and implement the 2024 OMB SPD 15 standards. Census race and ethnicity data are essential for important research across many sectors, for upholding civil rights, and for growing the economy. Extensive Census Bureau research and engagement with expert stakeholders shows that implementing the modernized 2024 OMB SPD 15 standards for race and ethnicity data collection will yield data that more accurately represent the nation’s increasingly diverse population.

3. Remove the clause banning the addition of future questions on sexual orientation. Proposed changes to demographic items should be based on research and guided by a deliberative and transparent process, including extensive stakeholder consultation.

4. Withdraw other proposed changes to residence criteria, including tying place of residence to tax records and "lawful residence," and the adoption of a three month enumeration period. The Census Bureau must extensively research and consult with stakeholders about the potential effects of such changes before proposing their implementation in a decennial census.

5. Halt the practice of prison gerrymandering by counting incarcerated individuals in their home communities. This will yield more accurate census data and ensure that communities receive the congressional representation to which they are entitled.

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Examples of these uses include: . 

* Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs.

* Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

* Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

* Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

* Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

* Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

* Determining state higher education funding formulas 

* Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

* Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

* Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

First, to ensure a fair and accurate census,  the Census Bureau should  extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. Revise the tax records language so that those whose mailing address differs from their residential address (servicemembers, those with a post office box) are not excluded.

Information on race and ethnicity is critical for civil rights enforcement, among other uses, and should not be banned. Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
SUPPLEMENTAL PUBLIC COMMENT — Docket No. USBC-2026-0628 | RIN 0607-AA75 | 91 FR 57524

To the U.S. Census Bureau:

This supplemental comment addresses four requests: resolving conflicting records, preventing duplicate or omitted counts, evaluating demographic-data limitations, and identifying authority or procedures needed. I distinguish what the APA requires from what I request as sound rulemaking. Filing does not guarantee adoption; the Bureau must consider significant comments and provide a reasoned explanation. 5 U.S.C. § 553(c); Motor Vehicle Mfrs. v. State Farm, 463 U.S. 29, 43 (1983).

I. RESOLVING CONFLICTING RECORDS

Under Franklin v. Massachusetts, 505 U.S. 788, 804 (1992), usual residence may involve ties beyond physical presence. The preamble should explain: (a) what standards govern the weight given to conflicting, outdated, or incomplete records; (b) how recency, address signals, and residence rules are applied; and (c) how conflicts are resolved through hierarchical rules or verification. I also request, as sound rulemaking, a verification standard for high-risk cases—without a rigid two-source rule for every person.

II. PREVENTING DUPLICATE OR OMITTED COUNTS

The Bureau has acknowledged persistent census errors: "Persons who should have been counted are not counted at all or are counted at the wrong location . . . [and] persons who should have been counted only once are counted twice." Nat'l Ass'n v. Bureau of the Census, 382 F. Supp. 3d 349, 354 (D. Md. 2019). The proposed rule states that administrative records "can serve as reliable evidence for certain purposes," 91 FR 57524, but does not address preventing duplicates or omissions. I request that the Bureau explain: (a) its deduplication and person-linkage standards; (b) how it will remediate undercoverage of children under five; and (c) what corroboration is required for high-risk cases. These may be addressed through guidance or the preamble.

III. EVALUATING DEMOGRAPHIC-DATA LIMITATIONS

The proposed rule restricts certain demographic questions on enumeration questionnaires but does not restrict obtaining demographic data from administrative records or other surveys. 91 FR 57524. Administrative records can contain missing, outdated, or incorrectly assigned demographic information. Historical records used designations such as "free persons of color" and "mulatto" inconsistently, and these terms were "in at least some instances incorrectly used." State ex rel. Schlumbrecht v. La. St. Bd. of H., 231 So. 2d 730, 735 (La. Ct. App. 1970). I present this as a reason to evaluate the risk of misclassification—not as proof that the proposed rule has caused a specific misclassification. I request that the Bureau explain how it will: (a) evaluate the accuracy and limitations of demographic information from non-questionnaire sources; (b) distinguish racial self-identification from ancestry, tribal enrollment, and federal recognition, per Morton v. Mancari, 417 U.S. 535, 551–55 (1974), 25 U.S.C. § 5301(b), (d), and 25 C.F.R. Part 83; and (c) disclose limitations when replacement data are used.

IV. IDENTIFYING AUTHORITY OR PROCEDURES

Where safeguards cannot be established through the final rule, I request that the Bureau identify the implementation process or additional legal authority required—whether separate rulemaking, guidance, or legislative clarification for multi-source linkage and state data-sharing.

V. PRIVACY AND DATA PROTECTION

The Bureau should explain how 13 U.S.C. §§ 8–9 and other applicable confidentiality requirements will govern administrative records used for census purposes, including linked records and resulting frames. The Bureau should identify restrictions on nonstatistical use, individual-level disclosure, and access by other agencies, along with statutory exceptions. 13 U.S.C. § 9(a) (restricting use to "statistical purposes" subject to specified exceptions); 13 U.S.C. § 8(c) (prohibiting use "to the detriment of any respondent" except in Title 13 prosecutions). I further request that the Bureau explain what safeguards will prevent census-derived information from being used for individual-level law-enforcement, immigration, or voter-registration actions, and identify any limits on its authority to establish those safeguards. I note that 52 U.S.C. § 20507 governs state voter-registration list maintenance and does not impose a Census Bureau data firewall; the separation I request is a policy safeguard, not a statutory mandate.

VI. CONCLUSION

I urge the Bureau to: (1) resolve conflicting records; (2) prevent duplicate or omitted counts; (3) evaluate demographic-data limitations, including risks of misclassification; and (4) identify authority or procedures for safeguards it cannot establish through this rule. These give the Bureau three ways to respond: explain its approach, modify the rule, or identify a separate process. Filing does not guarantee adoption.

Sincerely,
Ms. Jane Wiley

Comment:

The census is the foundation of our democracy. It must reflect the complete yet nuanced reality of who we are as a nation. And it must reflect the lives of our friends and neighbors who may not look, think, or speak like we do. I ask the Bureau to withdraw these proposed changes and to preserve a count that includes everyone and represents everyone. 

Thank you for considering my comment.

Sincerely,

Damian Kuehn

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am a resident of California, and I care about a fair and accurate census because it determines who is represented in our democracy. All of us need to be counted. 

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions.

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans. I am fed up with the corrupt and power grabbing shenanigans of this administration!

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: 91 FR 57524  Public Comment,Re: Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions (Docket No. USBC-2026-0628).I am writing to oppose the Census Bureau's proposed rule, "Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions," Docket No. USBC-2026-0628, because it would produce an inaccurate count of the people living in this country.Every ten years, the census gives the country one reliable picture of who lives here. Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).  As a physician and health researcher, the Census plays a critical role in understanding the health and social needs of the community.

In particular I am writing to oppose part 60 and part 70. Implementation of these rules would exclude information on many individuals in violation of the enumeration clause of the US Constitution, Article 1, Section 2, Clause 3.  The constitution gives the Census Bureau no authority whatsoever to exclude visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
Other proposed changes significantly reduce the value of the Census. The census should continue the activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.    Incarcerated people should be counted in their home communities, not where they are imprisoned.  Most important, the proposed ban on demographic questions  does substantive harm to the health of the public, as well as civil rights enforcement; these should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.
The Census Bureau is proposing major changes and there are many who will want to comment. A full 90 days for the public to review and respond is a reasonable minimum standard. The public comment period should be extended until December 10, 2026. 
In summary:  The proposed rule as written would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).
As an Economic Development practitioner, it’s critical that the census be done in a fair, accurate and complete manner, since that data is critical to both the business community to understand the true number of people in an area for customer and potential employment reasons, and to the local governments that are providing services and want to ensure they are allocated appropriately.
As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable.
I oppose both part 60 and part 70 and urge the Bureau to revise the regulations in the following manner:
• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.
Finally, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period to a full 90 days for the public to review and respond to this critical issue.
As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census. These changes will not only weaken the accuracy and integrity of our nation's most important population count, but they will also harm our communities, and I strongly urge the Bureau to reject them.

The proposal to exclude non-citizens, including those residents with some type of lawful status, violates more than two centuries of legal precedent. Every person counted in this country contributes to our communities, and every person deserves to be fully seen. 

The consequences of these changes will negatively impact our daily lives. The census affects everything. It determines political representation and the drawing of voting districts. It guides how billions of dollars in federal funding are used to close persistent disparities in schools, hospitals, and other government programs that are designed to improve our lives.  

The census is the foundation of our democracy. It must reflect the complete yet nuanced reality of who we are as a nation. And it must reflect the lives of our friends and neighbors who may not look, think, or speak like we do. I ask the Bureau to withdraw these proposed changes and to preserve a count that includes everyone and represents everyone. 

Thank you for considering my comment.

Sincerely,
Angela Fitzpatrick

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Argument in Support of the Proposed Residence Criteria and Restrictions on Demographic Questions for the 2030 Census
The Census Bureau’s proposed rule more faithfully implements the Constitution’s command to apportion representatives according to the “whole number of persons in each State.” It refines the long-standing concept of “usual residence” to require durable legal and political ties, and confines the short-form questionnaire to information necessary for that enumeration. The proposal is consistent with the constitutional text, founding-era practice, and Supreme Court recognition that usual residence involves more than mere physical presence.

Constitutional Text and Structure
Article I, Section 2, as amended by the Fourteenth Amendment, Section 2, requires that Representatives “shall be apportioned among the several States according to their respective numbers, counting the whole number of persons in each State, excluding Indians not taxed.” The phrase “persons in each State” has never meant every individual physically present on Census Day.

The explicit exclusion of “Indians not taxed” shows that physical presence alone has never been sufficient. Temporary visitors and foreign diplomats have also historically been omitted. The proposed rule continues this approach by including U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents—those with formal, enduring permission to remain—while excluding those present unlawfully or under temporary status. This applies the existing “usual residence” standard rather than creating a new exclusion.

Founding-Era Understanding and Practice
The First Census Act of 1790 was titled “An Act providing for the enumeration of the Inhabitants of the United States.” Section 5 directed that every person whose “usual place of abode” was in a family on Census Day be returned as of that family, and that every person occasionally absent be counted “as belonging to that place in which he usually resides in the United States.” The statute focused on inhabitants and usual residence, not mere physical presence.
James Madison, in Federalist No. 54, described the apportionment rule as founded on “the aggregate number of inhabitants.” He recognized that the census would include non-voters yet framed the base as the settled population of the States. The first census was narrowly focused on a headcount for representation and taxation.

The Supreme Court has acknowledged this understanding. In Franklin v. Massachusetts, 505 U.S. 788 (1992), the Court stated that “usual residence” was the gloss given the constitutional phrase “in each State” by the first enumeration Act. The Court observed that the term “can mean more than mere physical presence, and has been used broadly enough to include some element of allegiance or enduring tie to a place.” The proposed rule applies that principle by linking inclusion to durable legal status and allegiance.

Supreme Court Precedent Trump v. New York, 592 U.S. (2020), vacated injunctions against excluding illegal aliens from the apportionment base on standing and ripeness grounds and declined to address the merits, leaving the approach open.

Evenwel v. Abbott, 578 U.S. 54 (2016), held that States may use total population, including non-citizens, for state legislative districts. That holding concerns state discretion in districting; it does not require that the federal apportionment base include persons present unlawfully.
Broader case law has long recognized that physical presence does not automatically confer full membership in the political community.

Structural and Practical Considerations
Including large numbers of persons present unlawfully or on temporary visas shifts House seats and Electoral College votes toward States that attract or tolerate high levels of illegal immigration, diluting the representational weight of citizens and lawful permanent residents elsewhere. The proposed rule reduces that distortion while still counting the permanent, lawfully settled population.

Restricting questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation on the short-form questionnaire further serves the census’s primary purpose. The Framers’ enumeration was limited in scope. Expansions into contested identity categories have raised concerns about response rates and privacy. Those topics remain available through the American Community Survey and other instruments.

Conclusion
The proposed residence criteria rest on a sound reading of the constitutional text, founding-era statutes and debates, the long-standing concept of usual residence recognized by the Supreme Court, and the need to preserve the integrity of representation. The limits on demographic questions reinforce that focus. While the issue remains contested, the proposal is consistent with the Constitution’s original design and with the discretion long exercised by Congress and the executive in administering the census.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Docket USBC-2026-0628; RIN 0607-AA75 (91 FR 57524)

I am a private citizen of California. Who we are—and who we acknowledge as a fellow citizen and a fellow human—is fundamental to this country. It is who we are at our core. Representation, the safety net, and public trust all start there. This once-a-decade comment period is where the Census Bureau should reconsider that founding question of who belongs—not as a slogan, but as an operational rule for the 2030 count. In 1900, with about 76 million people, the census asked 28 questions, including citizenship and naturalization. We can ask again on a modern, records-backed form.

It is time for us to affirmatively count. This is not the passive process a sleepy, growing country could once allow. We run the most advanced welfare system in human history, designed for better or worse for a high-trust society. A high-trust system cannot be steered with a soft or evasive headcount. Being born is a public act, just like dying. There should be no games in between. When government needs the information to count us, it gets the information. That is the least we can give—and giving clean answers is cheaper than paying taxes for waste built on a wrong count.

I support the proposed rule with these numbered asks:

1. Apportionment base. Finalize proposed §60.4: for apportionment, count U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents (green-card holders) only. Temporary visas and unauthorized presence should not draw House seats. America First means the map of power follows the people who permanently belong here under our laws. The Fourteenth Amendment apportions by "the whole number of persons in each State"; persons in a State should mean people who lawfully reside there, not anyone physically present on Census Day.

2. How to determine status. Use all of the above: match administrative records and put a citizenship question on the enumeration form. The reason is plain and stated openly: an accurate count of who lawfully belongs, so representation is right. Make records-based verification and a clear digital response path the default, with human follow-up where files conflict. Government already holds birth, death, tax, and immigration records; use them, ask the person too, and publish enough methodology for the public to hold the Bureau accountable for how status was resolved.

3. Prisoners. Keep counting people in federal, state, and local correctional facilities at the facility, as proposed. When they are released, they are released into that community. Count them where they actually are on Census Day.

4. Residence window and special situations. Keep the simple January 3–April 1 usual-residence rule in proposed §60.2. But write the clear 2020-style situation rules for college students, people with seasonal or second homes (snowbirds), and people experiencing homelessness—shelters, unsheltered locations, and domestic-violence shelters—back into the final regulation, so no one is missed or counted twice. A short general rule without those operational lines will create avoidable holes and double-counts. Spell out how the Jan–Apr day count and tax-record evidence apply to dorms and winter homes so families are not left guessing.

5. Demographics on the short form. Support proposed Part 70: drop race, ethnicity, and sexual-orientation questions from the 2030 enumeration questionnaire. Ask citizenship instead. Proposed §70.4 already leaves the American Community Survey and administrative records free to collect race and ethnicity where those separate programs need them. Your own analysis notes the ACS may not give accurate estimates for small populations, such as some tribes; fund the American Community Survey to stand on its own. I would rather have an accurate count without race than all the sampling, guessing, and gap-filling. Sampling for the apportionment population is already barred by the Census Act, as the Supreme Court held in Department of Commerce v. United States House of Representatives (1999). Count imputation for missing households was later upheld as distinct from sampling in Utah v. Evans (2002). Even so, I ask the Bureau to minimize imputation and other modeled or estimated fills, and to verify people through records. Every estimate is a guess. Measuring race for inclusion has too often only helped us see exclusion. Dr. King dreamed of a nation where his children "will not be judged by the color of their skin but by the content of their character." Move toward that vision, where we see souls, American souls, people. Organized comments will urge you to keep race on the short form; this comment period is exactly when you should reconsider and choose the citizenship question instead.

Please adopt the residence and demographic framework as proposed, with the clarifications above. Count us as Americans first.

Respectfully,
Alec Snelling
California

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.

Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Sincerely,
Resident of Sacramento County, California

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am opposed to changes to the enumeration of "the actual number of free persons" based on short-term political opinions. I would vote in favor of a Constitutional amendment to base apportionment on the number of lawfully registered voters, ignoring not only illegal aliens but prisoners, minors, parole felons, persons of unsound mind, and others not part of our democratic decision making process. However, the proposed rule does not (and cannot) redefine the basis of apportionment in this way, and singles out the peculiar category of "usual residents who are not lawful inhabitants" for special discrimination; I do not approve. Your analysis maybe right that various Founders had later thoughts about implicit notions they did not capture in the actual words of the Enumeration Clause, but these later private communications are not the words that were ratified. Enumerate everyone at their usual place of residence, or seek an amendment to honestly redefine apportionment on a modern basis eschewing any 18th century notions of the propertied paterfamilias as the cardinal political voice of a larger community for whom he casts his votes.

As a genealogist, I am keenly aware of the value to history of the demographic information collected by the census. Historical records are already full of creative nonresponses to these questions, like the nonsensical "American ethnicity" so common in old responses. If you worry that making demographic questions mandatory decreases response rates--which you assert but do not quantify--simply provide a "prefer not to respond" option.

It would be ridiculous to include a mandatory question about legal status without also providing a legal barrier between the Census Bureau data and immigration enforcement. However, such use-of-data commitments have been routinely ignored by the present administration, making future commitments of this type implausible on their face, and creating enormous non-compliance pressure of a mind you claim to be sensitive to.

Despite a certain amount of sympathy for your proposals, and with due recognition of the legal and historical evidence you have marshaled, I respectfully encourage that the present proposals be dropped in their entirety.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; ProposedResidence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). 

As an educator, I care about a fair and accurate census because census data and other federal datasets based on the census are used to make key decisions that affect our nation’s students, educators, and schools.  

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Examples of these uses include: . 

* Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. 

* Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

* Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

* Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

* Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

* Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

* Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

* Determining state higher education funding formulas 

* Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

* Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

* Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

First, to ensure a fair and accurate census,  the Census Bureau should  extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. Second, I oppose both the proposed changes to the residence criteria and the proposed regulations regarding demographic questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. The Census Bureau should  withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The Constitution requires  counting all people living in the United States. 

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (including children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count. 

Revise the tax records language so that those whose mailing address differs from their residential address (servicemembers, those with a post office box) are not excluded.  

• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for civil rights enforcement, among other uses, and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The prohibition, as written, may also restrict the collection or publication of census data on same-sex couples that was asked in 2020. 

 The proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Sincerely,
Rev. Sharon Duffy
Champaign, IL

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Re: Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions (Docket No. 260903-0005; RIN 0607-AA75) 

I am contacting you on behalf of a group of friends, family members and co-workers who are very concerned about this issue.

We strongly oppose the proposed rules for the census and changes to its residence rule. All persons in the United States have a right to be counted, as the 14th Amendment of the Constitution plainly establishes. This proposed rule will weaken our democracy, our systems of representation, and the doctrine of “one person, one vote.” Without an accurate count, people will not be fairly represented in Congress or state legislatures. 

For New Jersey, this proposal would jeopardize our representation and the resources our communities depend on. We are the nation’s most densely populated state, and one in four New Jerseyans was born outside the United States. Immigrant residents live in all 21 counties. They work in our hospitals, warehouses, farms, and small businesses, pay taxes, and send their children to public schools. Excluding or undercounting these residents would erase them from the data that shapes political power and public investment. Their communities’ needs would remain, while funding for the schools, clinics, roads, and transit systems we all share would be put at risk for the next decade. The proposal would also threaten our voice in Congress and undermine the data our Apportionment Commission and Congressional Redistricting Commission rely on to draw fair districts. 

The exclusion of questions about race and ethnicity will exacerbate the degradation of data quality, and it will lead to undercounts of Black and brown communities that are already undercounted in past censuses. If we don’t know who is living in our communities, we cannot prepare for the challenges we may face, and we will not receive adequate funds from federal programs. 

A permanent ban on sexual orientation questions is baseless and bypasses the Bureau's own process. The decennial census does not currently ask about sexual orientation. This rule would nonetheless bar the Bureau from ever adding such a question, regardless of future research or data needs. When the government prevents itself from measuring a population, it loses the ability to identify disparities, target enforcement, and evaluate whether legal protections are working. 

We strongly urge you to reject this proposed rule.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). 

I live in Mayfield Hts., Ohio, where many immigrants also live, and I care about a fair and accurate census because census data and other federal datasets based on the census are used to make key decisions that affect our nation’s students, educators, and schools.  

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Examples of these uses include:  

Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. 

Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners 

Determining the need for resources for students living in poverty 

Determining the need for resources for students with disabilities 

Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

Determining state higher education funding formulas 

Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

To ensure a fair and accurate census, I first ask the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. Significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve more time for the public to review and respond. 

Second, I oppose both the proposed changes to the residence criteria and the proposed regulations regarding demographic questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: [keep any/all points you would like to include in your comment] 

• Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people living in the United States. 

• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care. 

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count. 


As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Sincerely,
[Your information here]

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
RE: Docket USBC-2026-0628 — Proposed Census Regulations
Dear Secretary Lutnick:

As a grant professional, I rely on Census Bureau and American Community Survey (ACS) data to identify community needs, support funding applications, and demonstrate the impact of federal investments. I am concerned that the proposed changes to Census residence criteria and demographic data collection could affect the accuracy, availability, and comparability of information essential to federal grantmaking.

Census data help grant applicants demonstrate need, identify underserved populations, and establish benchmarks for program evaluation. Changes to these data could affect funding eligibility, competitive applications, and the distribution of federal resources. Small and rural communities could be particularly affected if reliable, geographically detailed data become less available.

Before finalizing either proposal, I urge the Census Bureau to work with OMB and federal grantmaking agencies to assess the potential impacts on grant eligibility, funding allocations, community needs assessments, and program evaluation. Any alternative data sources should remain publicly accessible, timely, geographically detailed, and comparable over time.

I also encourage the Bureau to consult grant professionals and other data users to better understand these practical implications.

Thank you for considering my comments.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the Department of Commerce: 

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). 

I am [add a description of who you are, such as your profession and/or state where you live], and I care about a fair and accurate census because census data and other federal datasets based on the census are used to make key decisions that affect our nation’s students, educators, and schools.  

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Examples of these uses include:  [keep any/all points you would like to include in your comment – see this site if you would like to add state-specific statistics about funding impacts:]. 

Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. 

Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

Determining state higher education funding formulas 

Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

First, to ensure a fair and accurate census,  the Census Bureau should  extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. Second, I oppose both the proposed changes to the residence criteria and the proposed regulations regarding demographic questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. The Census Bureau should  withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: [keep any/all points you would like to include in your comment] 

• Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The Constitution requires  counting all people living in the United States. 

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (including children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count. 

Revise the tax records language so that those whose mailing address differs from their residential address (servicemembers, those with a post office box) are not excluded.  

• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for civil rights enforcement, among other uses, and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The prohibition, as written, may also restrict the collection or publication of census data on same-sex couples that was asked in 2020. 

 The proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans. 

Sincerely,
Dennis R. Wylie

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I write in support of the Census Bureau's proposed rule, "Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions" (Docket No. USBC-2026-0628; RIN 0607-AA75).

The Constitution calls for an "actual Enumeration" every ten years so that representation can be fairly apportioned among the states. The decennial census is meant to be a count, not a survey or a statistical estimate. Americans' voice in Congress depends on that count being right.

In 2020, the Bureau intentionally introduced statistical noise into the population data used to draw congressional and legislative districts. Data that determine political representation should never be deliberately altered. I support proposed  70.3, which directs the Bureau to prioritize the accuracy of the population count and prohibits publishing demographic data when doing so would introduce uncertainty into national or state population counts.

I also support the proposed residence criteria. Being counted at one's "usual residence" has never meant mere physical presence on Census Day. It reflects a lasting connection to a place, which is why service members stationed abroad are still counted in their home states. Counting citizens and lawful permanent residents, and excluding foreign nationals who are here unlawfully or temporarily, follows that principle.

I support keeping the enumeration questionnaire focused on the count itself. The Bureau can continue to produce demographic and statistical information through the American Community Survey and other tools, but those products should remain separate from the constitutional headcount.

To make these reforms durable, I urge the Bureau to state clearly in the final rule that the constitutional enumeration, and the counts used for apportionment and redistricting, are fundamentally distinct from routine federal statistical products and may not be adjusted to serve other statistical purposes.

Please finalize this rule so that the 2030 Census delivers an accurate count and restores Americans' trust in how they are represented.

Respectfully,
Chris Schleif

Hortonville, WI

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am a Professor of Sociology in New Jersey, and I care about a fair and accurate census because it materially impacts my immediate community and state. New Jersey is one of the most diverse states in the country and failing to capture the demographic richness does a disservice to residents. Not counting immigrants and others would harm this state as it would significantly underestimate those in need of services from school and library access to healthcare.

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: [keep any/all points you would like to include in your comment]

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

In short, I am concerned that these changes will undercount the actual number of people who live in my region.
