This means our tax dollars will have to support the full number of people who actually live here, even if the census numbers claim differently. These proposed changes are going to cost our community more. We are struggling to pay already for the services our kids need in school, and undercounting our children, our immigrant neighbors, and our snowbird neighbors will only exacerbate this challenge. This will only make this challenge worse.

Additionally, excluding noncitizens without lawful permanent residence from census apportionment data is unconstitutional and would deprive our communities of their fair share of resources and representation.The Constitution, statutes, and settled law clearly provide that all persons residing in the United States must be counted for the apportionment of Congressional seats. Research has also shown that adding a question on citizenship to the decennial census form would have a chilling effect on census participation. If the census does not count all residents, our communities will lose resources to support their schools, hospitals, transportation infrastructure, emergency services, and more. This would harm our community because many residents rely on services such as Medicaid, Medicare Part B, SNAP, highway/transportation funds, Title I/educational services, school lunch, and Headstart/child care programs.

Eliminating census race and ethnicity data collection is unprecedented, violates statutes, and severely undermines the utility of census data for a range of critical purposes. Since the first census in 1790, every single decennial census has collected race and ethnicity data in some form. Census race and ethnicity data underpin many other critical federal datasets and serve as an irreplaceable benchmark for nearly every population-based survey and study in the U.S., ensuring that our research is reliable and leads to better outcomes for all of us. Race and ethnicity data are vital to protecting public health and safety because they allow health officials to identify and address differences in health risk factors. They are necessary to enforce civil rights laws and ensure equal opportunity for all Americans, helping to ensure fairness and strengthen the U.S. economy. Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am a 27 year old, multiracial Black American living in Rochester, NY. I am currently a project manager at a local nonprofit and I deeply care about a fair and accurate census. During my time working on health disparities among underrepresented populations such as Indigenous Americans and Black Americans, the importance of national data such as the census is pivotal to creating needs assessments to ask for funding to create programs, initiatives, and changes to our systems to reduce the gaps of disparities these groups face. I have lived and experienced the common pain points many marginalized people in the U.S. face and I am grateful to have been given the opportunity at education and in social circles where the prevailing culture exposes me to public input opportunities like this - opportunities to express the little political voice that our predecessors fought so hard for that we still get swindled out of. Knowing that key demographic metrics are being erased from the 2030 Census spells out an impending decade of under-documented suffering for those who will not be represented in those counts, thereby which evidence of disparity cannot be collected to substantiate the need for increased investments to those of us who need it the most.

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: [keep any/all points you would like to include in your comment]

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Thank you for your time in considering my input and I will hope for the best.

A concerned citizen.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: Counting everyone in the census is necessary for restoring trust in our democratic institutions. The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. I oppose this proposed rule because it departs from that constitutional mandate, risking severe harm to my community. Excluding noncitizens from the population count used for congressional apportionment and federal funding, while adding a citizenship question designed to deter participation, will suppress response rates across immigrant communities and mixed-status families who fear being targeted. An undercount here would directly strip my community of appropriate congressional representation and our fair share of federal funding for essential safety-net programs like SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, CHIP, and Title I education grants. As someone who cares about fairness and the rule of law, I urge the Bureau to withdraw this proposal and count every person living in our communities, as the Constitution requires. I am also concerned that the proposed rule erases vital Census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Decades of demographic data serve as the baseline that public and private institutions rely on to identify inequalities and direct resources where they are needed most. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities. Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. I oppose this proposed rule because it departs from that constitutional mandate, risking severe harm to my community and the entire country. Excluding noncitizens from the population count used for congressional apportionment and federal funding while adding a citizenship question designed to deter participation, will suppress response rates across immigrant communities and mixed-status families who fear being targeted. An undercount here would directly strip my community of appropriate congressional representation and our fair share of federal funding for essential safety-net programs like SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, CHIP, and Title I education grants. As someone who cares about fairness and the rule of law, I urge the Bureau to withdraw this proposal and count every person living in our communities, as the Constitution requires. 

I am also concerned that the proposed rule erases vital Census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Decades of demographic data serve as the baseline that public and private institutions rely on to identify inequalities and direct resources where they are needed most. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities.  

Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.  

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Sincerely,
Laurel Hirt
Minneapolis, MN

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am Californian resident, and I care about a fair and accurate census because data is a powerful tool to protect human rights and marginalized groups.

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including:

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Hello,

I am writing to strongly oppose the government's proposed rule (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026) that would drastically change who is counted by the U.S. Decennial Census, where they are counted, and what questions are included in the questionnaire.

I am a professor of psychology at New York University and a developmental psychologist whose research examines how stereotypes, social beliefs, and inequalities shape children's development and opportunities. I am deeply concerned about the consequences of this proposal, both for the integrity of scientific research and for the well-being of children and families across the country.

A fair and accurate census is critical to our democracy, and it should not be politicized. The Fourteenth Amendment requires congressional representation to be apportioned according to the "whole number of persons in each State," not just citizens or permanent residents. All people means all people: We should be counting citizens and non-citizens alike, regardless of immigration status.

The proposed exclusion of noncitizens who are not permanent residents is particularly troubling. This would include international students and researchers on temporary visas, many of whom live, work, pay taxes, and contribute to their communities for years. As a university professor, I see firsthand how integral these individuals are to our institutions and communities. They are residents of the United States and should be counted as such.

**As a developmental psychologist, I am especially concerned about the implications for children.** Young children are already among the most frequently undercounted groups in the census. The Census Bureau estimated that 5.4% of children under five were missed in 2020, with even larger undercounts among Black and Hispanic young children. The proposed changes risk exacerbating these disparities while simultaneously eliminating the race and ethnicity data needed to identify and address them. Inaccurate counts also have consequences for the allocation of resources to schools, health care, child care, and other services on which children and families depend.

**The proposed restrictions on demographic questions would also seriously undermine our ability to understand and address social inequality.** My research examines, among other things, how children develop beliefs about social groups and how these beliefs contribute to unequal opportunities and outcomes. Reliable, geographically detailed data on race and ethnicity are indispensable for identifying disparities, understanding their causes, and evaluating efforts to reduce them. Removing these questions from the decennial census would deprive researchers, policymakers, and communities of a uniquely comprehensive source of information.

More broadly, as a scientist, I find it deeply troubling that decisions with such far-reaching implications for data quality appear to be driven by political considerations rather than sound scientific and statistical evidence. The design of the census should be guided by rigorous research on measurement, representativeness, accuracy, and respondent privacy. The Census Bureau should be strengthening the scientific foundations of its work, not introducing restrictions that compromise the usefulness of its data.

I also strongly oppose the proposal to prohibit questions about sexual orientation from appearing on the decennial census, even though such questions have never been included. There is no scientific justification for categorically foreclosing the possibility of collecting this information in the future. Decisions about what demographic information to collect should be based on evidence of its scientific and public value, alongside careful consideration of privacy and data quality.

Finally, data from the census should continue to be made publicly available whenever possible, with appropriate safeguards for confidentiality. This includes information that allows researchers to identify same-sex couples and understand the diversity of family structures in the United States. Every family deserves to be represented in the data on which important public decisions depend.

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw this proposal and instead pursue policies that preserve the accuracy, completeness, scientific integrity, and public value of the U.S. Decennial Census.

Thank you for considering my comments.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: US Census Bureau,I urge you to withdraw the proposed 2030 Census rule, including the requirement that a person’s usual residence be consistent with and evidenced by their tax records.This requirement could leave tens of millions of people out of the Census. Many people with low incomes are not required to file tax returns, and some do not have tax records that can be used to confirm their address. Children and other household members may also be missing from available tax records.Census Bureau researchers found that 11.5 percent of people in the 2020 Census had no record in the IRS data they examined. That represents more than 38 million people who may not have the tax records needed to verify their address in the 2030 Census under this proposal.Tax records also do not always reflect where people actually live. Someone may have moved since filing a return or may use a post office box, a business address, or an accountant’s address. A tax return may omit relatives and others who share a household.These problems could cause people to be missed or counted in the wrong place, with especially harmful consequences for low-income communities. An inaccurate count would distort representation in Congress and state and local governments and affect the allocation of funding for essential programs and services.The Constitution requires congressional representation to be based on the whole number of persons in each state. Everyone deserves to be counted, regardless of whether their address can be confirmed through a tax record.Please withdraw the entire proposed rule and protect a complete, accurate, and inclusive 2030 Census.Rajni Oberoi   [X]  Glendale, California 91205

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). 

As an educator, I care about a fair and accurate census because census data and other federal datasets based on the census are used to make key decisions that affect our nation’s students, educators, and schools.  

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Examples of these uses include: . 

* Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. 

* Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

* Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

* Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

* Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

* Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

* Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

* Determining state higher education funding formulas 

* Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

* Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

* Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

First, to ensure a fair and accurate census,  the Census Bureau should  extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. Second, I oppose both the proposed changes to the residence criteria and the proposed regulations regarding demographic questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. The Census Bureau should  withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The Constitution requires  counting all people living in the United States. 

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (including children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count. 

Revise the tax records language so that those whose mailing address differs from their residential address (servicemembers, those with a post office box) are not excluded.  

• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for civil rights enforcement, among other uses, and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The prohibition, as written, may also restrict the collection or publication of census data on same-sex couples that was asked in 2020. 

 The proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Sincerely,
Mr. Matt Vawter
Vernon, IN

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am a resident of Minnesota and a retired Refugee Health Nurse and I care about a fair and accurate census because it is the vehicle by which much public health and civil rights enforcement is guided. Additionally, this country has a commitment and obligation to count ALL INDIVIDUALS. 

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).
I have a Masters in Public Policy, and I care about a fair and accurate census because it is very important in my policy research, and critical to ensuring that Congressional districts accurately reflect the population.  Census data on race and ethnicity is essential to public policy research because it allows for statistical analysis of questions about relationships between race and ethnicity and demographics such as housing, education, longevity, and more.  Generally, good public policy is based on access to more data, not less.  Banning the collection of data about sexual orientation reduces the opportunity to understand societal trends.  When collected with consent, government data sets are incredibly valuable to society and should be expanded, not restricted.

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: [keep any/all points you would like to include in your comment]
• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.
As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). 

As an educator, I care about a fair and accurate census because census data and other federal datasets based on the census are used to make key decisions that affect our nation’s students, educators, and schools.  

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Examples of these uses include: . 

* Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. 

* Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

* Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

* Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

* Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

* Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

* Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

* Determining state higher education funding formulas 

* Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

* Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

* Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

First, to ensure a fair and accurate census,  the Census Bureau should  extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. Second, I oppose both the proposed changes to the residence criteria and the proposed regulations regarding demographic questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. The Census Bureau should  withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The Constitution requires  counting all people living in the United States. 

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (including children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count. 

Revise the tax records language so that those whose mailing address differs from their residential address (servicemembers, those with a post office box) are not excluded.  

• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for civil rights enforcement, among other uses, and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The prohibition, as written, may also restrict the collection or publication of census data on same-sex couples that was asked in 2020. 

 The proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Sincerely,
Ms. Lorraine Hemans
Trenton, NJ

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: US Census Bureau,I urge you to withdraw the proposed 2030 Census rule, including the requirement that a person’s usual residence be consistent with and evidenced by their tax records.This requirement could leave tens of millions of people out of the Census. Many people with low incomes are not required to file tax returns, and some do not have tax records that can be used to confirm their address. Children and other household members may also be missing from available tax records.Census Bureau researchers found that 11.5 percent of people in the 2020 Census had no record in the IRS data they examined. That represents more than 38 million people who may not have the tax records needed to verify their address in the 2030 Census under this proposal.Tax records also do not always reflect where people actually live. Someone may have moved since filing a return or may use a post office box, a business address, or an accountant’s address. A tax return may omit relatives and others who share a household.These problems could cause people to be missed or counted in the wrong place, with especially harmful consequences for low-income communities. An inaccurate count would distort representation in Congress and state and local governments and affect the allocation of funding for essential programs and services.The Constitution requires congressional representation to be based on the whole number of persons in each state. Everyone deserves to be counted, regardless of whether their address can be confirmed through a tax record.Please withdraw the entire proposed rule and protect a complete, accurate, and inclusive 2030 Census.Deborah Crawford-Poyner   [X]  Issaquah , Washington 98029-5048

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). 

Having accurate census data is an essential first step to being an effective government that serves the people. We need to be able to properly allocate funding, accurately forecast changes in population sizes and demographics, and determine when resources are necessary to enforce and implement programming and interventions. We can’t make good decisions when we don’t have accurate data.

I believe the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. 

I am asking that the following points be seriously considered:

1.) To ensure a fair and accurate census, the Census Bureau should extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. 

2.) I oppose both the proposed changes to the residence criteria and the proposed regulations regarding demographic questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. The Census Bureau should withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

— Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The Constitution REQUIRES counting ALL people living in the United

— Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day, and so that people (including children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count. 

— Revise the tax records language so that those whose mailing address differs from their residential address (service members, those with a post office box) are not

— Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for civil rights enforcement, among other uses, and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The prohibition, as written, may also restrict the collection or publication of census data on same-sex couples that was asked in 2020. 

Thank you for your time and consideration.

Sincerely,
A concerned citizen

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Census Bureau's proposed rule to strengthen the US Census is critical to fair representation and the future of America.  

The U.S. Census should not include distorted data in its count of Americans.  By including overly generalized ethnic demographic categories, we obscure the true goal of the census and hinder its constitutionally mandated purpose: an accurate count of Americans.  

Additionally, illegal aliens and other non-legal permanent residents should not be included for apportionment. Census data is used for the apportionment of congressional seats. Non-citizens cannot legally vote and should not be used to decrease the voting power of Americans. I support the Census Bureau in advancing the correct understanding of usual residence to recognize an element of allegiance that is antithetical to the inclusion of those not legally present in our country.  

This Census Bureau should also consider adding a citizenship question to the Census survey. The Supreme Court has already held that the Constitution lawfully permits the Census Bureau to at least inquire about citizenship on the census questionnaire. "The census should absolutely include questions related to citizenship and legal presence. 

These changes would strengthen the census in its core purpose of attaining an accurate count of Americans and have my full support. 

Thank you,  

James Huggins

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am a registered nurse in Virginia, and I care about a fair and accurate census because it affects the lives of all people residing in the United States.

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed regulations governing residence criteria and demographic questions for the decennial census (15 CFR Parts 60 and 70). I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw both proposals because of their potential  to undermine accurate population counts, diminish political representation, weaken civil rights protections, and compromise the equitable distribution of public resources.

The decennial census is not merely an administrative exercise. It  is a foundational instrument of American democracy, essential to ensuring that people and communities are accurately represented and that public institutions have reliable information to meet their needs. 

First, the proposed residence criteria threaten the constitutional principle of representation based on the whole population. Section 2 of the 14th amendment requires congressional apportionment based on the "whole number of persons in each State," not merely citizens or lawful permanent residents.

Proposed statute 60.4 would exclude entire categories of people who live, work, attend school, pay taxes, and contribute to their communities. These include people with temporary lawful immigration status as well as undocumented residents. Their presence creates real demand for schools, infrastructure, transportation, emergency services, and public health systems, regardless of immigration classification.

Excluding these individuals from apportionment would diminish the representation of the communities and states where they reside. It could also compound the political marginalization of communities of color and mixed-status families, including US citizens whose communities would be represented by artificially reduced population figures.

Second, eliminating race and ethnicity questions from the decennial census would jeopardize the date necessary to identify and address discrimination. Proposed statute 70.2 would prohibit these questions on census enumeration questionnaires, despite their longstanding importance to civil rights enforcement, voting rights protections, and public policy. 

Race and ethnicity data are essential to evaluating potential racial discrimination in voting districts, educational opportunities, housing, employment, and access to public services. Without reliable, geographically detailed demographic information, governments, researchers, and civil rights organizations would face additional obstacles in identifying disparities and evaluating compliance with laws such as the Voting Rights Act and Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. 

The Census Bureau itself has acknowledged that accurate racial and ethnic population data are critical to redistricting and Voting Rights Act analysis. Removing these questions would weaken an established source of information at precisely the level of geographic detail needed to evaluate community representation.

Third, relying on administrative records instead of direct demographic self-identification introduces serious questions about data quality and equity. The Government Accountability Office's November 2024 report, 2020 Census: Coverage Errors and Challenges Inform 2030 Plans (GAO-25-107160), documented that 18% of enumerations based on administrative records lacked race information, compared with fewer than 3% of direct self-responses.

This substantial difference raises concerns about whether alternative data sources can adequately replace direct demographic questions. Administrative records may also fail to capture people with unstable housing, inconsistent documentation, or limited contact with government institutions.

The proposed requirement that usual residence be established through lawful physical presence and supported by tax records creates additional risks for vulnerable populations, including children, people experiencing homelessness, and individuals whose living arrangements do not correspond neatly to administrative documentation.

Fourth, the potential consequences for public funding and essential services demand rigorous examination. Census data inform decisions affecting public education, health care, housing assistance, transportation, and other essential services. According   to the Census Bureau, 353 federal assistance programs used Decennial Census Programs data, in whole or in part, to distribute more than $2.8 trillion in fiscal year 2021.

Changes that diminish the accuracy or completeness of census data could divert resources from communities that need them most and obscure discrimination. Race and ethnicity data are essential to ensuring civil rights. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw both proposals and preserve a full population count and direct demographic questions.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am a community college instructor in WA state, and I care about a fair and accurate census because this data is needed to support the rights of al US residents.

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: [keep any/all points you would like to include in your comment]

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.
As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Greetings,

I am writing to oppose the Census Bureau's proposal to change how Census data are collected.

Accurate, detailed data helps the government spend public dollars wisely. When agencies know who lives where and what they need, they can direct funding and services to the places they will do the most good. Removing these questions would make public spending less efficient, not more.

1. Only counting citizens is an absolute disservice to all people who live in the US, contribute to it through taxes and receive public services such as using roads or public schools.

2. Collecting data only during the winter will not provide accurate or complete information because many in Northern states travel to southern states to get away from the cold. It will also make it hard to do outreach and encourage participation in Census while dealing with weather related obstacles.

3. Collecting race and ethnicity information is very important as the data is linked to over 200 studies, the decision to remove race and ethnicity questions from the 2030 Census (Docket No. USBC-2026-0628) is absolutely counterproductive.

For decades, federal standards counted Middle Eastern and North African (MENA) Americans as White. The Bureau has decided not to use the updated standards in the 2027 American Community Survey. As a result, no federal survey would count MENA. Without accurate counts, we cannot document the health, education, and economic gaps we face, or the discrimination our communities report.

I urge the Census Bureau to:

1. Keep race and ethnicity questions on the 2030 Census, including the MENA category required by the 2024 standards.
2. Re-commit to full implementation of the 2024 revision to Statistical Policy Directive No. 15 (SPD 15), including on the American Community Survey.
3. Re-engage with community organizations, researchers, and state and local governments in a collaborative process to use more detailed data for the public good, including to direct resources more efficiently to the communities that need them most.

The Bureau says these changes will get more people to respond and protect privacy. However, I believe telling people that some of them don't count is more likely to scare people away from the census and deepen privacy fears, the very problems the Bureau says it wants to solve.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am a commercial property manager in San Diego California , and I care about a fair and accurate census because people deserve to receive recognition and services from the government for the taxes they pay..

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: [keep any/all points you would like to include in your comment]

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.
As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: US Census Bureau,I urge you to withdraw the proposed 2030 Census rule, including the requirement that a person’s usual residence be consistent with and evidenced by their tax records.This requirement could leave tens of millions of people out of the Census. Someone may have moved since filing a return or may use a post office box, a business address, or an accountant’s address. A tax return may omit relatives and others who share a household.These problems could cause people to be missed or counted in the wrong place, with especially harmful consequences for low-income communities. Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am a resident of NJ, and I believe the census should do everything in its power to accurately account for all persons living in my community.

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people!

• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.

• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.

• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.

• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.

• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population and communities. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

-A concerned NJ resident

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am a first-generation daughter of Filipino descent, a mother of two, and a proud Michigander, and I care about a fair and accurate census because fair and accurate representation is important for all citizens who comprise and contribute to our country.

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the U.S. Census Bureau’s proposed changes for the 2030 Census. The decennial census is a constitutional pillar designed to accurately enumerate the entire population of the United States. The proposed rule compromises scientific integrity, damages data accuracy, and violates the explicit intent of the census.

1. Exclusion of Non-Citizens from Apportionment
The proposal to count only U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents for congressional apportionment directly contradicts the Fourteenth Amendment, which mandates counting the "whole number of persons in each State." Excluding undocumented immigrants, students, and visa holders will result in severe, artificial undercounts. This shift politically disenfranchises states with large immigrant populations and structurally distorts federal funding for critical public infrastructure, healthcare, and education.

2. Removal of Race and Ethnicity Questions
Eliminating race and ethnicity data for the first time since 1790 is a catastrophic regression. These data metrics are legally essential for enforcing civil rights protections, specifically the Voting Rights Act. Civil rights monitoring, compliance tracking, and academic research on systemic inequalities will be completely blinded without this standardized dataset. Removing these questions does not eliminate disparities; it merely renders them impossible to track and remedy.

3. Prohibiting Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity Questions
Barring the collection of sexual orientation data continues the systematic erasure of LGBTQ+ Americans from official demographic records. Accurately counting this historically marginalized community is a prerequisite for understanding their unique economic, social, and healthcare needs. Prohibiting these questions prevents federal and local agencies from effectively directing resources to support vulnerable LGBTQ+ sub-populations.

4. Voluntary Demographics and Reliance on Administrative Data
Making standard demographic questions voluntary will sharply lower response rates and undermine data reliability. Furthermore, substituting direct enumeration with proxy administrative records (like tax files) will introduce profound biases, as low-income individuals, housing-unstable populations, and marginalized communities are routinely underrepresented in institutional data systems.

The Census Bureau must prioritize scientific accuracy and inclusivity. I urge the Bureau to withdraw the proposed changes, preserve the integrity of the decennial count, and maintain comprehensive, mandatory demographic questions for all residents.

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am Andrea, a registered nurse in Texas, and I care about a fair and accurate census because it affects the availability of community resources such as schools, libraries, and hospitals. 

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.

Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.
As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am Daniel Robbins from Sacramento,  Ca Retired, and I care about a fair and accurate census because [add a brief description of why you care].

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: [keep any/all points you would like to include in your comment]

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.
