Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). 

As an educator, I care about a fair and accurate census because census data and other federal datasets based on the census are used to make key decisions that affect our nation’s students, educators, and schools.  

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Examples of these uses include: . 

* Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. 

* Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

* Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

* Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

* Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

* Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

* Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

* Determining state higher education funding formulas 

* Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

* Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

* Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

First, to ensure a fair and accurate census,  the Census Bureau should  extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. Second, I oppose both the proposed changes to the residence criteria and the proposed regulations regarding demographic questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. The Census Bureau should  withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The Constitution requires  counting all people living in the United States. 

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (including children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count. 

Revise the tax records language so that those whose mailing address differs from their residential address (servicemembers, those with a post office box) are not excluded.  

• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for civil rights enforcement, among other uses, and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The prohibition, as written, may also restrict the collection or publication of census data on same-sex couples that was asked in 2020. 

 The proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Sincerely,
A Teacher

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am a public health survey researcher from California, and I care about a fair and accurate census because it impacts everyone from all walks of life, in all fields of profession, and in ways that range from human rights, access to healthcare, community services, proper governance, children's well-being and security, and the overall public good. While my professional work specifically would be directly impacted by an inaccurate census as we rely on accurate population figures for our survey processes and representative research, the crux of the matter does not even rest on any given individual's or organization's need to use census data for their work. The accuracy of the census is essential to communities and the people within those communities. They are the ones who will be harmed by the trickle down from administrations and organizations using less robust information, imprecise measurement, and flawed evidence in the implementation of policies, programs, and research findings. The accuracy of the census is therefore about what is fair and what is just to maintaining civil rights for all people and ensuring that everyone who lives in our country is treated fairly and with respect and dignity.

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including:

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples. As a survey researcher, I cannot stress enough how important accurate demographic census data are for the work done by millions and millions of Americans, and how widespread the negative impact would be of these bans in ways that are hard to even quantify. Whole industries could be upended by these changes -- that is how vital and far-reaching these data are.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of critical data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
A la Oficina del Censo de los Estados Unidos:

Re: Docket No. 260903-0005, RIN 0607-AA75, USBC-2026-0628. “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions”

Soy residente de Puerto Rico. Someto este comentario para expresar mi oposición a las Partes 60 y 70 propuestas del Título 15 del Código de Regulaciones Federales, por el daño que causarían a un conteo completo y correcto de Puerto Rico y de los puertorriqueños.

La propuesta no menciona a Puerto Rico ni una sola vez, aunque el Censo decenal cuenta a más de 3.2 millones de ciudadanos estadounidenses en la Isla y produce los datos con que se redibujan nuestros distritos legislativos. Las secciones 60.5 y 70.3 hablan del “stateside census” y del nivel “nacional o estatal” sin definir “Estados Unidos”. Solicito que la Oficina del Censo explique por escrito cómo aplicarían las Partes 60 y 70 en Puerto Rico y que no adopte una regla final sin hacerlo.

La sección 70.2(a) prohibiría la pregunta de origen hispano, que incluye el encasillado “puertorriqueño”. Hoy viven más personas de origen puertorriqueño en los estados que en Puerto Rico, y esa pregunta es la única forma en que el Censo decenal las cuenta. Sin ella, nuestras comunidades en Nueva York, Florida, Pensilvania, Massachusetts, Connecticut y otros estados desaparecerían de los datos que se usan para hacer cumplir los derechos civiles y electorales y para planificar servicios. Solicito que se elimine la sección 70.2(a).

La sección 60.2(a) dice que la residencia habitual “debe ser consistente con” los récords contributivos, pero no dice cuáles. La mayoría de los residentes de Puerto Rico rinde planilla ante el Departamento de Hacienda, nuestra autoridad contributiva local, y no ante el IRS; los patronos emiten el Formulario 499R-2/W-2PR. Solicito que la Oficina del Censo aclare por escrito si aceptaría las planillas de Hacienda y el Formulario 499R-2/W-2PR como récords contributivos en Puerto Rico, y cómo los obtendría y parearía.

Aun si la Oficina usara las planillas de Hacienda, una prueba de residencia basada en récords contributivos dejaría fuera a muchas personas en Puerto Rico. Se estima que cerca de un tercio de la población no rinde planilla y está en la economía informal (Caraballo-Cueto), y jubilados y hogares de bajos ingresos con frecuencia no rinden ninguna. Además, preocupa que una porción sustancial de las planillas que sí se rinden use un apartado postal o una ruta rural como dirección, que no identifica la vivienda donde vive la persona. Solicito que no se haga de los récords contributivos la prueba de residencia en Puerto Rico y que se acepten la autorespuesta y la verificación en el campo.

Por estas razones, solicito que la Oficina del Censo retire la regla propuesta y garantice que todas las personas en Puerto Rico y en la diáspora sean contadas, una vez y en el lugar correcto.

Gracias por considerar este comentario.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: US Census Bureau,I urge you to withdraw the proposed 2030 Census rule, including the requirement that a person’s usual residence be consistent with and evidenced by their tax records.This requirement could leave tens of millions of people out of the Census. Comment: 91 FR 57524  Public Comment,Re: Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions (Docket No. USBC-2026-0628).I am writing to oppose the Census Bureau's proposed rule, "Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions," Docket No. USBC-2026-0628, because it would produce an inaccurate count of the people living in this country.Every ten years, the census gives the country one reliable picture of who lives here. Congress, states, cities, and businesses use it to divide representation, distribute federal funds, and plan for the next decade. This rule would distort that picture. Lower response rates also mean more costly follow-up work, paid for by taxpayers.A bad count in 2030 cannot be corrected until at least 2040. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw this rule.Judith Hazelton   [X]  Bennington, Vermont 05201

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I write in support of the Census Bureau's proposed rule, "Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions" (Docket No. USBC-2026-0628; RIN 0607-AA75).

The Constitution calls for an "actual Enumeration" every ten years so that representation can be fairly apportioned among the states. The decennial census is meant to be a count, not a survey or a statistical estimate. Americans' voice in Congress depends on that count being right.

In 2020, the Bureau intentionally introduced statistical noise into the population data used to draw congressional and legislative districts. Data that determine political representation should never be deliberately altered. I support proposed  70.3, which directs the Bureau to prioritize the accuracy of the population count and prohibits publishing demographic data when doing so would introduce uncertainty into national or state population counts.

I also support the proposed residence criteria. Being counted at one's "usual residence" has never meant mere physical presence on Census Day. It reflects a lasting connection to a place, which is why service members stationed abroad are still counted in their home states. Counting citizens and lawful permanent residents, and excluding foreign nationals who are here unlawfully or temporarily, follows that principle.

I support keeping the enumeration questionnaire focused on the count itself. The Bureau can continue to produce demographic and statistical information through the American Community Survey and other tools, but those products should remain separate from the constitutional headcount.

To make these reforms durable, I urge the Bureau to state clearly in the final rule that the constitutional enumeration, and the counts used for apportionment and redistricting, are fundamentally distinct from routine federal statistical products and may not be adjusted to serve other statistical purposes.

Please finalize this rule so that the 2030 Census delivers an accurate count and restores Americans' trust in how they are represented.

Respectfully,
Toby Burke
Kenai, AK

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

Re: Docket No. 260903-0005, RIN 0607-AA75, USBC-2026-0628. “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions”

I am a resident of Puerto Rico (Toa Alta). I submit this comment to oppose proposed 15 CFR Parts 60 and 70 because of the harm they would cause to a complete and accurate count of Puerto Rico and of Puerto Ricans.

I am Puerto Rican and a United States citizen. A large part of my family is in the U.S., but I choose to remain in Puerto Rico. I want us to be counted accurately in the Census. I was never given the choice to become a U.S. citizen; I have no other option, as Puerto Rico is a colony of the United States rather than a free and sovereign country. I cannot vote for the President who makes decisions that affect us; I have no representation in Congress with a voice and a vote; and now, they seek to erase us from the map by failing to count us correctly. This is your responsibility. We demand transparency and an accurate count of the 3.2 million United States citizens residing in Puerto Rico.

The proposed rule does not mention Puerto Rico a single time, even though the decennial census counts more than 3.2 million U.S. citizens on the island and produces the data used to redraw our legislative districts. Sections 60.5 and 70.3 refer to the “stateside census” and to the “national or state level” without defining “United States.” I ask the Census Bureau to explain in writing how Parts 60 and 70 would apply in Puerto Rico, and not to finalize any rule without doing so.

Section 70.2(a) would prohibit the Hispanic-origin question, which includes the “Puerto Rican” checkbox. More people of Puerto Rican origin now live in the states than on the island, and that question is the only way the decennial census counts them. Without it, our communities in New York, Florida, Pennsylvania, Massachusetts, Connecticut, and elsewhere would disappear from the data used to enforce civil and voting rights and to plan services. I ask that Section 70.2(a) be withdrawn.

Section 60.2(a) says usual residence “should be consistent with, and evidenced by” tax records, but does not say which ones. Most Puerto Rico residents file with the Puerto Rico Department of the Treasury (Hacienda), our local tax authority, not with the IRS; employers issue Form 499R-2/W-2PR. I ask the Census Bureau to state in writing whether it would accept Hacienda returns and Form 499R-2/W-2PR as tax records in Puerto Rico, and how it would obtain and match them.

Even if the Bureau used Hacienda returns, a residence test based on tax records would leave many people in Puerto Rico out. An estimated one-third of the population doesn’t file and works in the informal economy (Caraballo-Cueto), and retirees and low-income households often file no return at all. Moreover, there is concern that a substantial share of the returns that are filed list a P.O. box or rural route as the address, which does not identify the home where the person lives. I ask that tax records not be made the proof of residence in Puerto Rico, and that self-response and field verification be accepted.

The Puerto Rico Community Survey and nearly all surveys are weighted to population estimates based on the decennial census. Section 70.4 says the ACS could still ask about race and origin, but without those data in the census there would be no reliable benchmark. Municipios, agencies, hospitals, universities, nonprofits, and businesses depend on these data, as does the distribution of federal funds for health, nutrition, education, housing, and disaster recovery. I ask that Part 70 not be adopted.

For these reasons, I ask the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that everyone in Puerto Rico and in the diaspora is counted, once, and in the right place.

Thank you for considering this comment.

Comment:

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Examples of these uses include: . 

* Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. This is highly necessary in my district where many children are going hungry even though their parents are working.

* Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

* Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

* Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

* Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

* Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

* Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

* Determining state higher education funding formulas 

* Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

* Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

* Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

First, to ensure a fair and accurate census,  the Census Bureau should  extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The Community Foundation of Greater Flint (CFGF) opposes the Census Bureau's proposed rule, "Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions." We ask the Bureau to withdraw both of its proposals in full, the new residence criteria and the restrictions on demographic questions. 

CFGF is a 501(c)3 public charity whose mission is to bring people together, connecting generosity to community-led solutions that help Genesee County thrive. For good. Forever. For everyone. Since 1988, CFGF has supported nonprofit organizations to assist in the building of a thriving community. CFGF serves Flint and all of Genesee County. 

In the lead up to the 2020 Census, CFGF partnered with peers and nonprofits across the state of Michigan to connect resources and education to Michigan communities to ensure an accurate and complete count. CFGF supported 38 local organizations and grassroots groups to increase census response rates in Flint and Genesee County. Those local partners directly engaged community in census education and outreach through hosting 366 in person and on-line events with more than 34,000 individuals being reached through these events.

CFGF relies on the census because it is the one data source designed to describe everyone who lives in the United States, while also providing local level data that shapes the way federal, state and philanthropic resources are allocated in our communities. When the data matches reality, government and organizations like ours can direct resources where they are needed. 

The Bureau’s yearly population estimates begin with the census count and build on it until the next census. An error made in 2030 is repeated in
every funding formula through 2040. When fewer households respond, the Bureau must send workers door to door, which is the most expensive part of any census, or fill the gaps with statistical guesses. 

Under the proposed rule, only U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents would count toward apportionment. Refugees, people granted asylum, people working or studying on visas, and undocumented immigrants would all be left out. This is unconstitutional. The Fourteenth Amendment requires the census to count “the whole number of persons in each State.” It was adopted after the Civil War to end the counting of enslaved people as three-fifths of a person, and it took away the government’s power to decide whose personhood counts. 
 
The proposed rule provides that “[n]o question about race, ethnicity, or sexual orientation shall appear on the short form decennial census questionnaire or any questionnaire used for the enumeration of the population.” The census has asked about race and ethnicity every decade since 1790. The Bureau now calls race an “immaterial personal characteristic.” It is not immaterial to the communities we serve, whose health, schooling, housing, and treatment under the law still differ in ways that can be addressed only if they can be measured. Privacy rationale fails, too. Statistical agencies have protected confidentiality for decades, and the Department of Commerce itself banned one of those safeguards in June 2026 before citing the resulting risk. 

The census is the only source that asks every person, in the same way, to state their own race and ethnicity. Other federal surveys and data systems are designed and checked against it. The Bureau suggests administrative files and the American Community Survey (ACS) can fill the gap. They cannot. Administrative files record race inconsistently or not at all, and they replace a person’s own answer with a label chosen by someone else. The ACS reaches only a sample of households; it cannot describe small areas or small populations with precision and is itself adjusted using decennial census results. The Voting Rights Act, Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, and the Fair Housing Act are all enforced with census data. If the census stops collecting it, States, cities, health systems, researchers, and organizations like ours would have to try to collect it at greater total cost and with results that cannot be compared from place to place. 

We urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule, to continue counting every resident where they live, to keep questions about citizenship and immigration status off the census form, and to use the updated SPD 15 race and ethnicity question on the 2030 Census. Please read our full comments in the attached document, where you will also find contact information for follow-up questions or comments.

Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

Determining the need for and funding health and social services

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I strongly oppose the Census Bureau’s proposed rule entitled, “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions,” published in the Federal Register on September 10, 2026, because the proposed changes eliminate the collection of information critical for health and human service providers to accurately plan for and effectively provide services that best meet the needs of their communities.  Further proposed changes are in violation of Amendment 14 to the US Constitution that mandates counting the “whole number of persons” in each state.
Effective services are built on accurate information.  The proposed changes limit our capacity to understand and serve our communities.  The Census helps us understand how many people live in a community, how community demographics change over time, and how we plan for the needs of a community.  Effective health and human service systems and public infrastructure are built on accurate knowledge about our population.  Artificially limiting information about our populations by not counting all persons and removing key demographic questions, such as race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation, limits our ability to provide effective services, including education, healthcare, roads, and other public infrastructure.
We can’t build solutions for disparities we don’t measure.  Health and human service providers routinely use demographic data to understand if our systems of care are equitably meeting the needs of different populations. Health and human service providers assess not only where disparities exist, but also the scope and scale of these disparities, and if our efforts are reducing disparities over time.  Failure to collect essential demographic information such as race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation prevents providers' capacity to understand, assess, and prevent disparities; it further eliminates our capacity to evaluate and respond to trends over time.
Not counting the entire population is not only unlawful, it ignores the realities of health and human service planning. The Fourteenth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution states that the “whole number of persons” in each state shall be counted for the purposes of apportioning representatives to government.   Decades of case law have affirmed that the “whole number of persons in each state” includes the total population, all residents, regardless of citizenship status. Not counting people living in our communities inaccurately apportions resources such as Federal funds for community development block grants and misses the true needs of local populations. It undercuts health and human service providers’ capacity to deliver necessary services to the full population and services that all community members are legally entitled to, regardless of citizenship status, such as public education and emergency medical treatment.  
The proposed US Census rule entitled, “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions,” irreparably harms health and human service providers’ capacity to accurately understand, plan for, and serve the needs of their communities.  It prevents health and human service providers from doing what they do best: strengthening the health and well-being of the communities that they serve.  We strongly recommend not enacting the U.S. Census Bureau’s proposed rule entitled, “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions.”

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am a researcher that has used census products in various projects over the last 6+ years, and I care about a fair and accurate census because this large of a shift in parameters would make quality control and comparison to previous instances tremendously hard, if not nearly impossible, and lead to higher levels of errors compared to current methods.

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, focusing on keeping methodology as consistent as possible for best comparison and best accuracy possible.

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.

Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-9005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). 
I am a lifelong resident of the State of Utah, working alongside a variety of businesses, Cities, and communities as a grant writer/funding consultant. I care deeply about a fair and accurate census, as it directly impacts my employment, the community I live in, the country as a whole, and as a student of history (BA - History, University of Utah). 

I oppose both part 60 and 70. I urge the Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

- Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The PURPOSE of the census is to COUNT ALL PEOPLE!

- Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred in the future. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples. 

-Count incarcerated individuals at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live. 

- Return to activity-based criteria for residences, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than the misleading and confusing “one hour” rule. 
As written, the proposed rule will exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans. 

Significant regulatory actions, such as this one, deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond. I ask the Census Bureau to extend the comment period to December 10, 2026.

Over my career and education, I have routinely used and relied on accurate census data. The proposed changes will ignore significant trends and information countrywide. How can we pinpoint the vast variety of needs, challenges, and successes when critical data is suppressed? How can accurate representation be assessed if all are not considered? This has been a source of concern and protest since before our country was born, and led to its founding. How can Federal agencies assess the impact of their efforts without an accurate, fully representative count and corresponding data?

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: US Census Bureau,I urge you to withdraw the proposed 2030 Census rule, including the requirement that a person’s usual residence be consistent with and evidenced by their tax records.This requirement could leave tens of millions of people out of the Census. Many people with low incomes are not required to file tax returns, and some do not have tax records that can be used to confirm their address. Children and other household members may also be missing from available tax records.Census Bureau researchers found that 11.5 percent of people in the 2020 Census had no record in the IRS data they examined. Everyone deserves to be counted, regardless of whether their address can be confirmed through a tax record.Please withdraw the entire proposed rule and protect a complete, accurate, and inclusive 2030 Census.Marlene Hayden [X], Washington 98444

Comment:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). 

I am a retired teacher of the Deaf/Hard of Hearing from California, and I care about a fair and accurate census because census data and other federal datasets based on the census are used to make key decisions that affect our nation’s students, educators, and schools.  

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Examples of these uses include:  [Early Childhood Education, sign language interpreters, speech/language pathologists, audiologists and paraprofessionals who are trained and fluent in sign language.

Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

Determining state higher education funding formulas

Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

Determining the need for and funding health and social services

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the Census Bureau, 
Comment Part 2
I’m writing to request that you withdraw both parts of this proposal. Docket No. USBC-2026-0628, Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions
On the Restrictions on the Inclusion of Certain Demographic Questions in the Decennial Census Operation
I’ll start with the part of this proposal that doesn’t add up. The notice says these questions should go because they raise privacy risk and lower response rates. Then it says the Bureau will keep getting the same information from administrative records and will keep asking the same questions on the American Community Survey. If the data is still being collected and published, the privacy concern hasn’t gone anywhere. It has only moved to a less accurate, less accountable source. If the data is still needed, the notice’s claim of “reduced need or usefulness” is unsupported. The Bureau doesn’t analyze how much the data is used, who uses it, or what would replace it.
The census checks itself with this data. After every census, the Bureau measures how many people it missed or double-counted, and it breaks that down by race and ethnicity. That is how we know that Black, Hispanic, and Native American communities have been undercounted, and that young children are undercounted too. Without race and ethnicity on the form, the Bureau loses the ability to measure its own mistakes, and the people most likely to be missed become the least visible.
Everything else builds on it. The American Community Survey and the Bureau’s other surveys are weighted to census population totals by race and ethnicity. Take those totals away, and the numbers behind school funding, hospital planning, transportation, and disaster response get less reliable for every community. The same data supports the redistricting files states receive under Public Law 94-171, Voting Rights Act enforcement, fair-lending and hiring investigations, and federal standards for how agencies report race and ethnicity. If a lender, a school district, or a health department wants to know whether a group is being left behind, this is where the answer comes from.
Administrative records can’t fill the gap. No federal record system holds complete, self-reported race and ethnicity for every resident. Existing records are partial, outdated, or based on narrower categories than people use to describe themselves. Where records are missing, the Bureau would have to guess. Those guesses will be least accurate for multiracial people, recent immigrants, and Hispanic and Middle Eastern or North African communities, whose identities don’t fit tidy boxes. People should be allowed to say who they are, not have it inferred for them from a tax file.
The response-rate argument is thin. The notice says more questions generally mean fewer responses. But the 2020 short form was already brief, and the notice offers no evidence that dropping these questions would measurably improve response. At the same time, the Bureau is floating a new question about legal status, the kind of question the Bureau’s own research shows can keep entire households from responding. The Bureau can’t claim that burden is the concern while considering the question is most likely to cause nonresponse.
On that same note, as far as I know, the decennial short form doesn’t ask about sexual orientation. There’s no question currently posed regarding sexual orientation. A ban on a question nobody is asking reads as a message, not a response to a problem. It makes it harder to believe the stated reasons are the real ones, and the Supreme Court has been clear that an agency’s explanation must be its actual reasoning.
The cited cases don’t say what the notice must include. The notice points to recent decisions describing the Constitution as “colorblind.” Those cases address when the government can make race-based decisions, like admissions or districting. None says the government can’t count and describe its own population. Measuring a problem isn’t the same as practicing discrimination. If we stop counting these critical points, we can’t show that discrimination has ended, and we can’t see it when it hasn’t. The notice also relies on an executive order on federal diversity programs, which states a policy preference rather than a statistical justification.
Congress already set up a process, and this skips it. Federal law requires the Secretary to tell Congress, years ahead of the census, which subjects and questions are planned so Congress and the public can weigh in. A standing regulation that permanently bars certain questions goes around that process and limits what future secretaries and Congresses can do. If the Bureau thinks these questions should be cut for 2030, it should make the case through that process, with evidence, not lock it in by rule.

Comment: US Census Bureau,I urge you to withdraw the proposed 2030 Census rule, including the requirement that a person’s usual residence be consistent with and evidenced by their tax records.This requirement could leave tens of millions of people out of the Census. Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the Census Bureau of the US Department of Commerce

RE: 15 CFR Parts 60 and 70 [Docket No. 260903-0005] RIN 0607-AA75

Niagara Pride, Inc. urges the Census Bureau to ensure LGBTQ+ people are fully counted in the 2030 Census, including through measures of sexual orientation and gender identity. To solve a health problem, you must first identify where it exists — and without a count, LGBTQ+ people are invisible for planning purposes.

Researchers link census data on income, education, housing, and neighborhood conditions with health records to track disparities in disease, disability, and premature death. Without LGBTQ+ data, those linkages break down, and real disparities go undocumented across health care, mental health, addiction, housing, and employment.

The disparities are stark across the lifespan. Among adults, 58% of LGBTQ+ adults postponed or skipped needed care in the past year, versus 38% of non-LGBTQ+ adults, and 22% forwent medications due to cost, versus 12% (KFF). Among youth, 65.7% of LGBQ+ high school students reported persistent sadness or hopelessness, versus 31.4% of heterosexual students, and 41.0% seriously considered suicide, versus 13.0% (CDC, 2023). Among seniors, 59% of LGBTQ+ elders report a lack of companionship, and 34% live alone, versus 21% of non-LGBT peers (SAGE).

The burden deepens for subgroups. The suicide rate among LGBTQ+ service members and veterans is 2.4 times the general veteran rate (82.5 vs. 34.7 per 100,000). Among Black LGBT adults, 35% have experienced homelessness, versus 22% of LGBT adults overall (KFF). LGBT adults report disability at nearly twice the rate of non-LGBT adults (18.6% vs. 10.8%, JAMA Network Open, 2025). In rural areas, 43% of LGBTQ+ youth considered suicide, versus 33% in large cities, and only 50% could access the mental health care they wanted, versus 59% (Trevor Project, 2025). Rural residents also face longer travel, fewer affirming providers, and less anonymity — so funding that follows only visible populations leaves them behind.

The census is the foundation for a decade of decisions: congressional apportionment, federal funding, and planning for hospitals, clinics, senior services, and schools. When a whole population is missing, every decision built on it tilts away from them for ten full years — not by deliberate exclusion, but by simple absence from the numbers.

We urge the Bureau to count LGBTQ+ residents fully and fairly, in accordance with constitutional principles and established norms. Strong communities are built on an accurate understanding of every person who lives there.

Niagara Pride, Inc.

Sources: KFF (2024); CDC Youth Risk Behavior Survey 2023; SAGE; JAMA Network Open (2025); Trevor Project (2025); U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs; Pennsylvania Department of Military and Veterans Affairs.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). 

As an educator, I care about a fair and accurate census because census data and other federal datasets based on the census are used to make key decisions that affect our nation’s students, educators, and schools.  

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Examples of these uses include: . 

* Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. 

* Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

* Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

* Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

* Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

* Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

* Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

* Determining state higher education funding formulas 

* Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

* Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

* Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

First, to ensure a fair and accurate census,  the Census Bureau should  extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. Second, I oppose both the proposed changes to the residence criteria and the proposed regulations regarding demographic questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. The Census Bureau should  withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The Constitution requires  counting all people living in the United States. 

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (including children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count. 

Revise the tax records language so that those whose mailing address differs from their residential address (servicemembers, those with a post office box) are not excluded.  

• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for civil rights enforcement, among other uses, and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The prohibition, as written, may also restrict the collection or publication of census data on same-sex couples that was asked in 2020. 

 The proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Sincerely,
Mrs. Carolyne Capizzano
Wayne, NJ

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Dear Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions,

I strongly oppose the proposed rule's changes to the residence criteria and demographic items for the 2030 Census. 

If adopted, this residence rule would have devastating impacts on all Americans — undermining the integrity of the count and excluding certain communities from being counted altogether, which would impact critical funding, apportionment, fair representation and more. 
To Whom It May Concern,

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed changes to the U.S. Census. The Census is one of the most important functions of our democracy, providing the data used to allocate federal resources, determine congressional representation, enforce civil rights protections, and guide planning for schools, hospitals, transportation, and emergency services.

The proposed changes raise serious concerns about the accuracy, fairness, and constitutionality of the Census process.

First, the proposal would exclude most noncitizens, including international students, work-visa holders, refugees, and other legal residents, from being counted. The Constitution requires an enumeration of the population, not merely citizens. Excluding millions of residents would produce inaccurate population counts and distort the data relied upon by governments, businesses, and community organizations. Communities with large populations of students, military families, refugees, and essential workers would be disproportionately affected.

Second, the proposal would eliminate the collection of race and ethnicity data. This information is critical for enforcing civil rights and anti-discrimination laws, including the Voting Rights Act and the Fair Housing Act. Without accurate demographic data, it becomes far more difficult to identify disparities, monitor discrimination, and ensure equal access to housing, employment, education, and public services.

Third, these changes could undermine fair political representation. Census data is used to draw legislative and congressional districts and to ensure compliance with voting rights protections. Without accurate population counts and demographic information, redistricting efforts may fail to reflect the actual makeup of communities, leading to districts that are less representative of the people they serve.

More broadly, any policy that reduces the completeness or accuracy of the Census weakens public confidence in the process and risks misallocating resources that communities depend on every day. An accurate Census benefits everyone, regardless of political affiliation, because it ensures that decisions are based on reliable information rather than incomplete or distorted data.

I urge policymakers to reject these proposed changes and instead strengthen efforts to ensure a complete, accurate, and inclusive count of all people living in the United States. The Census should remain a nonpartisan tool dedicated to representing the nation's true population and protecting the principle of equal representation.


Please withdraw this proposed rule so the 2030 Census fairly and accurately counts our community.



Sincerely,
Ms. Barb Fitch

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I strongly oppose any proposed rule or residence criteria that would exclude noncitizens from the decennial census or from the population count used for congressional apportionment.

The Constitution does not say that representation is based only on citizens, registered voters, or people eligible to vote. Section 2 of the Fourteenth Amendment requires representatives to be apportioned among the states according to their respective numbers, counting the “whole number of persons in each State.” The word is persons, not citizens.

For generations, the Census Bureau has followed this constitutional principle by counting people according to where they usually live, regardless of citizenship or immigration status. Noncitizens live in our communities, raise families, work, pay taxes, attend schools, use roads and public services, and are represented by the governments where they reside. They are unquestionably part of the population that the census is supposed to count.

Attempting to remove millions of people from the census count would distort congressional representation, redistricting, federal funding, emergency planning, infrastructure decisions, and countless other governmental functions that depend upon an accurate population count. It would also undermine public confidence in the census and discourage participation in communities that are already difficult to count.

This proposal is especially troubling because the Constitution deliberately uses the broad term “persons.” An administration should not be permitted to rewrite that constitutional language through executive policy or administrative regulation. The census is a constitutional enumeration of the population, not a voter-registration list and not a citizenship test.

The Census Bureau itself has long recognized that all people with a usual residence in the United States, including citizens and noncitizens, are included in the resident population. Changing that principle for political purposes would represent a profound departure from the purpose and history of the census.

I urge the Department of Commerce and the Census Bureau to reject any proposal that excludes noncitizens from the population count and to preserve the longstanding principle that the census counts every person residing in the United States.

The Constitution says “persons.” The federal government should follow it.

Comment on Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions:  Eliminating census race and ethnicity questions would be the single greatest step toward realizing our Nation's Ideals, as set forth in the Declaration of Independence, since the 13th Amendment abolished slavery. The American "White Race," constructed by the English colonies in the 1670s specifically to bolster the separation of slaves from free subjects, is the most persistent curse we carried with us into our new Republic after 1776. I remember browsing the published statistics of the 2000 census and finding the section entitled "The Characteristics of White People." Such absurd self-deception!  I strongly encourage eliminating this relic of past American Apartheid practices from the next, and all future, censuses.

Comment on Proposed Residence Criteria: Leave the current rules alone. The tortured arguments to justify excluding illegal aliens from the constitutionally-mandated count of the US population seem more designed to identify immigration status than to count the population resident in our country. A few flaws in your argument:
     You argue that "illegal aliens (among others) should not be included in the apportionment count, as they are not true inhabitants, members of the body politic, or persons with a “usual residence” in the United States due to their lack of a sufficient tie and allegiance to the United States."  However, consider this historical antecedant: there were almost a half-million Free Persons of Color counted as free inhabitants in 1860, who were deemed by some state laws and by the U. S. Supreme Court's ill-reasoned Dred Scott decision in 1857 to be non-citizens and who COULD NEVER BE CITIZENS under existing laws -- and yet no-one proposed that they should not be counted among the inhabitants of the United States for apportionment purposes. Citizenship was never the criterion for being an inhabitant of the USA.
     Entering the United States illegally and remaining here is not proof of "lack of a sufficient tie and allegiance to the United States."  In some cases, long-time residence and economic and social activities can indicate the exact opposite.
     Your argument mentions that "Indians not taxed" were excluded from the count, but you do not explain why: Indians who retained allegiance and membership in their sovereign tribes were deemed to be separate nations-within-a-nation with whom the US could and did sign treaties. Indians who (in the words of the 1860 census instructions) "have renounced tribal rule, and who under State or Territorial laws exercise the rights of citizens," were to be counted (note that the elective franchise was not a universal right that indicated citizenship). Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am a Minnesotan, and I care about a fair and accurate census because I believe that the every person counts. 

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including:

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.
As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I live in Philadelphia and work in higher education, and I care deeply about a fair and accurate census because it affects federal funding and our representation. 

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.
As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). 

I am [add a description of who you are, such as your profession and/or state where you live], and I care about a fair and accurate census because census data and other federal datasets based on the census are used to make key decisions that affect our nation’s students, educators, and schools.  

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Examples of these uses include:  [keep any/all points you would like to include in your comment – see this site if you would like to add state-specific statistics about funding impacts: Census Matters: Why an Accurate Count Is Essential to Funding Our Communities | Project On Government Oversight]. 

Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. 

Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners 

Determining the need for resources for students living in poverty 

Determining the need for resources for students with disabilities 

Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

Determining state higher education funding formulas 

Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

To ensure a fair and accurate census, I first ask the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. Significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve more time for the public to review and respond. 

Second, I oppose both the proposed changes to the residence criteria and the proposed regulations regarding demographic questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: [keep any/all points you would like to include in your comment] 

• Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people living in the United States. 

• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care. 

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count. 


As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Sincerely,
Mr. Stephen Hayes
Van Buren, AR 72956

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: US Census Bureau,I urge you to withdraw the proposed 2030 Census rule, including the requirement that a person’s usual residence be consistent with and evidenced by their tax records.This requirement could leave tens of millions of people out of the Census. Many people with low incomes are not required to file tax returns, and some do not have tax records that can be used to confirm their address. Children and other household members may also be missing from available tax records.Census Bureau researchers found that 11.5 percent of people in the 2020 Census had no record in the IRS data they examined. That represents more than 38 million people who may not have the tax records needed to verify their address in the 2030 Census under this proposal.Tax records also do not always reflect where people actually live. Someone may have moved since filing a return or may use a post office box, a business address, or an accountant’s address. A tax return may omit relatives and others who share a household.These problems could cause people to be missed or counted in the wrong place, with especially harmful consequences for low-income communities. An inaccurate count would distort representation in Congress and state and local governments and affect the allocation of funding for essential programs and services.The Constitution requires congressional representation to be based on the whole number of persons in each state. Everyone deserves to be counted, regardless of whether their address can be confirmed through a tax record.Please withdraw the entire proposed rule and protect a complete, accurate, and inclusive 2030 Census.Tracy Gibbons[x]Los Altos, California 94024

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I oppose the proposed prohibition on collecting race and ethnicity information through the decennial census. My principal concern is that eliminating these questions could undermine the data used to allocate funding and assess the needs of American Indian and Alaska Native populations.

Accurate demographic information has practical consequences for communities. For example, HUD’s Indian Housing Block Grant formula expressly uses the number of American Indian and Alaska Native persons reported in the most recent decennial census, with adjustments for population changes and undercounts. The formula also considers income and housing needs. Removing a foundational data source could impair the calculation of allocations and leave communities with funding that does not accurately reflect the populations they serve. The precise effects should be evaluated before this change is adopted.

I recognize that the proposal would continue to allow demographic questions on the American Community Survey and the receipt of demographic information from administrative records. However, allowing those sources does not establish that they can adequately replace direct collection through the decennial census. The ACS surveys a sample of addresses, and its estimates are subject to sampling uncertainty. The Bureau should demonstrate whether replacement data would provide sufficient accuracy and geographic detail for small Tribal communities, Alaska Native villages, and American Indian and Alaska Native populations living outside Tribal lands.

A complete population total cannot, by itself, identify the American Indian and Alaska Native population within that total. Counting a person while losing the information necessary to include that person accurately in a funding formula could still leave their community underserved.

Privacy and respondent burden deserve careful attention. I urge the Bureau to address those concerns through tested safeguards and questionnaire improvements while preserving information needed to administer public programs. Any claimed savings should be weighed against the potential costs of inaccurate allocations, additional data collection, and challenges to funding determinations.

Before proceeding, I request that the Bureau:

1. Identify federal funding formulas and programs that depend on decennial race and ethnicity data, including programs serving American Indian and Alaska Native populations.
2. Publish a program-specific analysis of how the proposed changes could affect allocations, data quality, and communities’ ability to document unmet needs.
3. Demonstrate that any proposed replacement data provide comparable coverage, accuracy, timeliness, and geographic detail.
4. Complete meaningful government-to-government consultation with affected Tribal Nations and explain how their concerns informed the decision.
5. Retain race and ethnicity questions, including the ability to identify as American Indian or Alaska Native alone or in combination with other identities.

The federal government should preserve the information necessary to understand community needs and distribute funding accurately. I urge the Bureau to withdraw the proposed prohibition.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am a concerned citizen and healthcare worker of  the US and California and I care about a fair and accurate census because everyone deserves to be counted. 

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.
