Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I write to provide public comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

As an academic public and population health scholar and practitioner, I am deeply concerned about these proposed changes. The fundamental purpose of the census is to count all people accurately and fairly. Decisions about residence rules and demographic questions are not merely technical matters; they determine who is represented in our national statistics, who receives political representation and public resources, and whose needs are recognized in policy decisions.

My work focuses on understanding population health and addressing disproportionate health burdens experienced by specific groups. Census data are foundational to this work. They provide the population denominators needed to calculate disease rates, mortality rates, and health disparities, and they serve as the backbone for numerous federal surveys and administrative datasets. Changes to census definitions and demographic data collection would have far-reaching effects across the nation's statistical system, limiting our ability to identify inequities, evaluate interventions, and respond effectively to critical social, economic, and health challenges.

Given the significance of these proposed changes, I respectfully request that the public comment period be extended to December 10, 2026, providing a full 90 days for public review and comment.

I strongly oppose both Part 60 and Part 70 of the proposed rule and urge the Census Bureau to withdraw and substantially revise the proposal. Specifically, I recommend that the Bureau:

Maintain clear and inclusive residence criteria and revise the proposed enumeration-period rules. Residence standards should adequately capture people with complex living arrangements, including recent movers, children in foster care, individuals experiencing homelessness, residents of emergency shelters, military families, students, and seasonal workers.

Retain activity-based definitions of residence. People should be counted where they usually live and sleep. Replacing longstanding standards with a technical "one-hour" rule introduces unnecessary complexity and risks reducing accuracy.

Count incarcerated individuals at their home communities rather than correctional facilities. Doing otherwise artificially shifts representation and resources away from the communities where these individuals maintain social and family ties.

Reduce reliance on tax records as evidence of residence. Tax records often reflect mailing addresses rather than actual residences and may fail to accurately represent rural residents, military families, highly mobile households, non-filers, and dependent children.

Address the unique challenges facing rural communities. Small population errors can have substantial consequences for representation, planning, and access to federal funding in rural areas that rely heavily on census-derived data.

Ensure agricultural, temporary visa, and seasonal workers are accurately counted. Excluding these populations would reduce data quality and create distortions in population and workforce estimates, particularly in rural communities.

Preserve and modernize race and ethnicity data collection. These data are essential for civil rights enforcement, public health surveillance, resource allocation, and monitoring disparities. Rather than eliminating these questions, the Census Bureau should update them to align with the 2024 Statistical Policy Directive No. 15 (SPD-15) standards.

Avoid restrictions on future demographic data collection. The census should retain the flexibility to collect information needed to understand the nation's evolving population and support evidence-based policymaking.

These proposed changes would increase the risk of an inaccurate and inequitable census, with consequences lasting throughout the decade because annual population estimates and numerous federal datasets are built from decennial census benchmarks. Rural communities, historically undercounted populations, and groups experiencing health and social inequities would be particularly affected. This harm is both avoidable and unacceptable.

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and develop a revised approach that ensures all people are counted accurately and fairly and remain visible in the data that shape our nation's policies, resources, and future.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: US Census Bureau,I urge you to withdraw the proposed 2030 Census rule, including the requirement that a person’s usual residence be consistent with and evidenced by their tax records.This requirement could leave tens of millions of people out of the Census. Many people with low incomes are not required to file tax returns, and some do not have tax records that can be used to confirm their address. Children and other household members may also be missing from available tax records.Census Bureau researchers found that 11.5 percent of people in the 2020 Census had no record in the IRS data they examined. That represents more than 38 million people who may not have the tax records needed to verify their address in the 2030 Census under this proposal.Tax records also do not always reflect where people actually live. Someone may have moved since filing a return or may use a post office box, a business address, or an accountant’s address. A tax return may omit relatives and others who share a household.These problems could cause people to be missed or counted in the wrong place, with especially harmful consequences for low-income communities. An inaccurate count would distort representation in Congress and state and local governments and affect the allocation of funding for essential programs and services.The Constitution requires congressional representation to be based on the whole number of persons in each state. Everyone deserves to be counted, regardless of whether their address can be confirmed through a tax record.Please withdraw the entire proposed rule and protect a complete, accurate, and inclusive 2030 Census.Carl Prellwitz [x] Newmarket, New Hampshire 03857

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census. These changes will not only weaken the accuracy and integrity of our nation's most important population count, but they will also harm our communities, and I strongly urge the Bureau to reject them. 

First, removing questions of race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation erases the full scope of my identity when I participate in the Census survey. These data points are not optional. They are the tools we use to enforce civil rights laws, monitor discrimination, and measure the disparities that still affect millions of people. Excluding them from the count does not make them disappear from our society, but it does make our government less equipped to handle big issues when they arise. 

The Constitution is clear: the census must count ALL persons living in the United States, regardless of their immigration or citizenship status. The proposal to exclude non-citizens, including those residents with some type of lawful status, violates more than two centuries of legal precedent. Every person counted in this country contributes to our communities, and every person deserves to be fully seen. 

The consequences of these changes will negatively impact our daily lives. The census affects everything. It determines political representation and the drawing of voting districts. It guides how billions of dollars in federal funding are used to close persistent disparities in schools, hospitals, and other government programs that are designed to improve our lives.  

The census is the foundation of our democracy. It must reflect the complete yet nuanced reality of who we are as a nation. And it must reflect the lives of our friends and neighbors who may not look, think, or speak like we do. I ask the Bureau to withdraw these proposed changes and to preserve a count that includes everyone and represents everyone. 

Thank you for considering my comment.

Sincerely,
Nicole Estrella

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Proposed code changes to the residency criteria should not be altered to try and account for "removable aliens" as proposed.   Other data noted in the announcement gained by agreements with HHS and DHS allows the census to - "utilizing its enormously broad access to administrative records to determine an individual's legal status". Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: US Census Bureau,I urge the Census Bureau and Department of Commerce to withdraw the proposed rule changing residence criteria for the decennial Census and restricting demographic questions.The proposal would exclude foreign citizens from the population used for congressional apportionment unless they are also U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents. The Census proposes to only include people if their address is confirmed by tax records -- which could mean millions, particularly low-income families, could be missed in the decennial Census. Overall, this would leave out people who actually live in our community, including many people who are lawfully present in the United States.For all past Census counts, including the 2020 Census, foreign citizens living in the United States were generally counted where they lived and slept most of the time. That approach recognizes the basic purpose of a Census: accurately counting the people who live in our communities. The 14th Amendment requires congressional representation to be apportioned according to the “whole number of persons in each State.”I am also deeply concerned by the proposal to prohibit race and ethnicity questions, along with sexual orientation, on the decennial Census enumeration questionnaire. The Census Bureau itself recognizes the importance of race data for civil rights protections, legislative redistricting, equal employment opportunities, and identifying disparities.The 2030 Census will determine congressional, state, and local representation for the decade that follows. It must be complete, accurate, and protected from political manipulation.Please withdraw this proposed rule and preserve a Census that fairly and accurately counts our community.Kathryn [X] Longview, Washington 98632

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). 

As an educator, I care about a fair and accurate census because census data and other federal datasets based on the census are used to make key decisions that affect our nation’s students, educators, and schools.  

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Examples of these uses include: . 

* Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. 

* Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

* Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

* Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

* Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

* Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

* Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

* Determining state higher education funding formulas 

* Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

* Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

* Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

First, to ensure a fair and accurate census,  the Census Bureau should  extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. Second, I oppose both the proposed changes to the residence criteria and the proposed regulations regarding demographic questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. The Census Bureau should  withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The Constitution requires  counting all people living in the United States. 

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (including children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count. 

Revise the tax records language so that those whose mailing address differs from their residential address (servicemembers, those with a post office box) are not excluded.  

• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for civil rights enforcement, among other uses, and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The prohibition, as written, may also restrict the collection or publication of census data on same-sex couples that was asked in 2020. 

 The proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Sincerely,
Ms. Linda Heath
Senecaville, OH

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am against including a citizenship question on the decennial census.  There is no need for it since the constitution says the congressional apportionment numbers must include the whole number of persons for each state.  Adding a citizenship question to the decennial census could decrease the response rate to the census altogether.  In addition, if the response rate to the citizenship question is low, that would require more imputations for missing responses. That would be bad because the quality of imputed values decreases as the nonresponse to a question increases.

I favor retaining race and ethnicity in the decennial census of population and housing to assist with fighting diseases in the country.  When, or if a disease (e.g., covid) affects the country, it is helpful in fighting the disease to know where populations of races or ethnicities are located who are more affected.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: US Census Bureau,I urge you to withdraw the proposed 2030 Census rule, including the requirement that a person’s usual residence be consistent with and evidenced by their tax records.This requirement could leave tens of millions of people out of the Census. Many people with low incomes are not required to file tax returns, and some do not have tax records that can be used to confirm their address. Children and other household members may also be missing from available tax records.Census Bureau researchers found that 11.5 percent of people in the 2020 Census had no record in the IRS data they examined. That represents more than 38 million people who may not have the tax records needed to verify their address in the 2030 Census under this proposal.Tax records also do not always reflect where people actually live. Someone may have moved since filing a return or may use a post office box, a business address, or an accountant’s address. A tax return may omit relatives and others who share a household.These problems could cause people to be missed or counted in the wrong place, with especially harmful consequences for low-income communities. An inaccurate count would distort representation in Congress and state and local governments and affect the allocation of funding for essential programs and services.The Constitution requires congressional representation to be based on the whole number of persons in each state. Everyone deserves to be counted, regardless of whether their address can be confirmed through a tax record.Please withdraw the entire proposed rule and protect a complete, accurate, and inclusive 2030 Census.Tomer Stinson[x]California 92377

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Since 1944, Citizens’ Committee for Children of New York has served as an independent child advocacy organization. CCC does not accept or receive public resources, provide direct services, or represent a sector or workforce; our priority is improving outcomes for children and families through research, advocacy, and civic engagement. We document the facts, engage and mobilize New Yorkers, and advocate for solutions to ensure every child is healthy, housed, educated, and safe. 

As a data-driven child advocacy organization, we staunchly oppose the proposed changes to the Census. Accurate and timely data is essential for illustrating the strengths and shortcomings in the well-being experienced by New York children, families, and communities. We use data to further public knowledge and inform legislative, budgetary, and administrative actions that can improve child and family outcomes.  

How CCC uses Census data 

Census data underpins almost all of CCC’s analytic products and resources including: our flagship publication Keeping Track of New York City’s Children, our data site with hundreds of indicators on child and family well-being, and our NY city and state well-being indices. The proposed changes would weaken our work in two ways, they would distort the population counts our neighborhood-level estimates are built on, and they would eliminate the demographic detail we need to see how different communities are faring.  

Inaccurate counts would distort local level data 

New York City’s community districts are the geography that residents, community boards, and city agencies use to plan local services. Many of the data sources we rely on, including the American Community Survey (ACS) and its Public Use Microdata Sample (PUMS), are released for Public Use Microdata Areas (PUMAs), which do not line up with community districts. CCC uses population data from the decennial census to convert PUMA-level data to community districts. We use decennial counts to determine population ratios for community districts that are split across PUMAs, share a PUMA with another community district, or are otherwise not directly geographically aligned. 

These ratios are only as accurate as the decennial count behind them. The proposal to count only lawful permanent residents would exclude international students, asylum applicants, visa holders, and others. This change would shift the ratios we use to allocate data across districts leading to an undercount in districts with large immigrant populations.  

 The proposal to count people where they spent the most days between January 3 and April 1 would misplace groups such as seasonal workers, college students, and people with more than one house or residence. This would change population counts and ratios at the local level even if total counts were correct. Thus, errors in the decennial count would carry into every community-district estimate built on it, for the entire decade.  

Removing race and ethnicity would erase the differences we need to see 

By using disaggregated data, we shed light on the unique experiences across different communities, as well as by age, race, and gender, ensuring that our data analysis captures the complete demographic nature of New York City. Race and ethnicity have been asked on the census since 1790. Removing these questions would leave policymakers unable to identify where disparities exist, target resources to the communities that need them, or measure whether policies are closing gaps.

I am [add a description of who you are, such as your profession and/or state where you live], and I care about a fair and accurate census because census data and other federal datasets based on the census are used to make key decisions that affect our nation’s students, educators, and schools.  

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Examples of these uses include:  [keep any/all points you would like to include in your comment – see this site if you would like to add state-specific statistics about funding impacts: Census Matters: Why an Accurate Count Is Essential to Funding Our Communities | Project On Government Oversight]. 

Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. 

Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners 

Determining the need for resources for students living in poverty 

Determining the need for resources for students with disabilities 

Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

Determining state higher education funding formulas 

Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

To ensure a fair and accurate census, I first ask the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. Significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve more time for the public to review and respond. 

Second, I oppose both the proposed changes to the residence criteria and the proposed regulations regarding demographic questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: [keep any/all points you would like to include in your comment] 

• Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people living in the United States. 

• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care. 

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count. 


As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:

It guides how billions of dollars in federal funding are used to close persistent disparities in schools, hospitals, and other government programs that are designed to improve our lives.  

The census is the foundation of our democracy. It must reflect the complete yet nuanced reality of who we are as a nation. I ask the Bureau to withdraw these proposed changes and to preserve a count that includes everyone and represents everyone. 

Thank you for considering my comment.

Sincerely,
Lori Martin

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to oppose the proposed new rules for the Decennial Census (docket USBC-2026-0628). Each of the proposed changes are misguided and will lead to an incomplete and inaccurate Census count. This will be especially important as trillions of tax dollars are distributed to states over the 2030s.

First, the US Constitution makes clear that ALL residents are to be counted. Limiting the count to only citizens and green card holders will miss a significant number of people, people who still participate in society, who go to schools, drive on roads, need clean air and water, etc. Here is Arkansas, we have the largest population of Marshallese in the country, and about 15,000 of them would not be counted according to the proposed changes. And yet they are here in the US legally.

Second, the change from "Census Day" to the look-back period does not make sense. This will not ensure that everyone is counted in their usual residence. For example, "snow birds" might be counted in their winter location, even though they spend the majority of their time in their summer location.

Related, using tax records to indentify location will not lead to more accurate locations while adding uncessary administration burden and cost. I think of my own children. They spend almost all of their time at their universities out-of-state, even as their tax forms list their parents' address. They would be counted in the wrong location, or even worse, counted twice or not at all.

Not only would these changes affect the distribution of federal tax dollars, they would also make it difficult for local and state government, businesses, and hospitals to plan. These entities rely on a complete and accurate count to accomplish their goals.

Third, it is not at all true that race and ethnicity are "immaterial personal characteristics." These factors are very important for understanding public heatlh, conducting market research, and bolserting workforce development. If we can't establish a baseline, we are unable to design programs, services, and products, and we certainly are not able to measure progress. The Walmart headquarters are located here in Arkansas. Walmart designs and locates rapid fulfillment centers across the country according to accurate census information, including race information. Arkansas hospitals design emergency room services based on race and population data. It is hard to imagine activities which will not be detrimentally affected by these proposed changes.

To argue that these changes will only affect the Decennnial Census is simply not true. The Decennial Census serves at the baseline or "demominator" for all other surveys, such as the American Community Survey or the Current Population Survey. Experts within the Census Bureau have made this clear. The same experts have developed appropriate strategies to safeguard individual Census data as we have strong and effective federal laws in place. Race has been asked in every Decennial Census dating back to 1790.

I am a researcher who relies on Census data for many of my projects. But more importantly, I am an American that is very concerned that we will not longer have an accurate Census so important to all aspects of American life. I ask that you reject these proposed changes.

The U.S. Census Bureau's proposed rule to strengthen the US Census is critical to fair representation and the future of America.  

The U.S. Census should not include distorted data in its count of Americans.  By including overly generalized ethnic demographic categories, we obscure the true goal of the census and hinder its constitutionally mandated purpose: an accurate count of Americans.  

Additionally, illegal aliens and other non-legal permanent residents should not be included for apportionment. Census data is used for the apportionment of congressional seats. Non-citizens cannot legally vote and should not be used to decrease the voting power of Americans. I support the Census Bureau in advancing the correct understanding of usual residence to recognize an element of allegiance that is antithetical to the inclusion of those not legally present in our country.  

This Census Bureau should also consider adding a citizenship question to the Census survey. The Supreme Court has already held that the Constitution lawfully permits the Census Bureau to at least inquire about citizenship on the census questionnaire. "The census should absolutely include questions related to citizenship and legal presence. 

These changes would strengthen the census in its core purpose of attaining an accurate count of Americans and have my full support. 

Thank you,  

Tate Coy

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: 91 FR 57524  Public Comment,Re: Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions (Docket No. USBC-2026-0628).I am writing to oppose the Census Bureau's proposed rule, "Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions," Docket No. USBC-2026-0628, because it would produce an inaccurate count of the people living in this country.Every ten years, the census gives the country one reliable picture of who lives here. Congress, states, cities, and businesses use it to divide representation, distribute federal funds, and plan for the next decade. This rule would distort that picture. Fewer people would be counted, and some communities would disappear from the data altogether. The errors would affect the entire country, but they would be heaviest in immigrant, minority, and low-income households and in the states and towns where they live.The undercount would come from several directions. The rule would stop counting many immigrants who live here, even though the Constitution requires counting every person. It also invites a question about legal status, which would keep many people in immigrant and mixed-status households from answering at all, whatever their own status. And it would decide where people live using tax records, even though many people are not required to file and the rule says nothing about how to count people such as those without stable housing, foster children, or people in shelters and nursing homes.The invisibility would come from banning the race and ethnicity question and from households afraid to respond. Without that information, it is much harder to show where needs are greatest, enforce civil rights laws, check whether voting maps are fair, or catch health problems that hit some communities harder. States, local governments, and health systems would have to collect it themselves, adding cost and producing less reliable numbers.This is a poor use of public money. More than $2.8 trillion a year in federal funding follows census numbers. When the count is wrong, that money goes to the wrong places for at least ten years, and schools, clinics, roads, and emergency plans are built for a population that does not match reality. Lower response rates also mean more costly follow-up work, paid for by taxpayers.A bad count in 2030 cannot be corrected until at least 2040. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw this rule.Kristin Laytons.kristin3@gmail.com1805 Merrit StOld Hickory, Tennessee 37138

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am a mom and proud patriot, and I care about a fair and accurate census because our country is comprised of a multitude of humans by design, it is our superpower.

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. Significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, as written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans. I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including:

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.

• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.

• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.

• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.

• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person’s “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer’s address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.

• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census. These changes will not only weaken the accuracy and integrity of our nation's most important population count, but they will also harm our communities, and I strongly urge the Bureau to reject them. 

First, removing questions of race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation erases the full scope of my identity when I participate in the Census survey. These data points are not optional. They are the tools we use to enforce civil rights laws, monitor discrimination, and measure the disparities that still affect millions of people. Excluding them from the count does not make them disappear from our society, but it does make our government less equipped to handle big issues when they arise. 

The Constitution is clear: the census must count ALL persons living in the United States, regardless of their immigration or citizenship status. The proposal to exclude non-citizens, including those residents with some type of lawful status, violates more than two centuries of legal precedent. Every person counted in this country contributes to our communities, and every person deserves to be fully seen. 

The consequences of these changes will negatively impact our daily lives. The census affects everything. It determines political representation and the drawing of voting districts. It guides how billions of dollars in federal funding are used to close persistent disparities in schools, hospitals, and other government programs that are designed to improve our lives.  

The census is the foundation of our democracy. It must reflect the complete yet nuanced reality of who we are as a nation. Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). I am a social worker and student at the University of Pittsburgh as a candidate for a master's degree in social work. I care about a fair and accurate census as in both my education and practice, I frequently engage with clients whose access to desperately needed social services could change as a result of the proposed changes.
I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond. More time is warranted given that the Secretary of Commerce terminated the Census Bureau’s advisory committees in 2025, which no longer are a pathway that people can use to make their voice heard. Providing adequate time to respond to these proposed changes will promote public trust in the census.
I am especially concerned about the following issues: 
Excluding noncitizens without lawful permanent residence from census apportionment data is unconstitutional and would deprive our communities of their fair share of resources and representation. The Constitution, statutes, and settled law clearly provide that all persons residing in the United States must be counted for the apportionment of Congressional seats. Research has also shown that adding a question on citizenship to the decennial census form would have a chilling effect on census participation. If the census does not count all residents, our communities will lose resources to support their schools, hospitals, transportation infrastructure, emergency services, and more. This would harm our community because many residents rely on educational & childcare programs such as free/reduced lunch and headstart, as well as wider reaching programs such as SNAP and Medicaid. The fear in these communities is pervasive as their existence is threatened by increasingly unjust detention and excluding them from the census only forces these communities further in the shadows, despite their contributions to the economy and community. 
Additionally, the proposed rule would radically redefine the concept of “usual residence,” making certain groups more likely to be missed or counted in the wrong place. The proposed rule would tie enumeration to tax records and “lawful” residence rather than to where people actually live, and establish a new three-month enumeration period rather than the usual April 1 “census day.” These unprecedented and untested changes would increase the risk that some groups (seasonal workers, foster youth, people with second homes, shelter residents, and others) will be missed or counted somewhere other than where they actually live most of the time. This will affect my community because low-income individuals move much more frequently. For seasonal workers, those who live in shelters or on the streets due to a lack of affordable housing, incarcerated individuals, or kids bouncing around the foster system at no fault of their own, the risk of not being included in the census is increased. This will, once again, put vulnerable people at risk by a lack of documentation of their existence, threatening the funding of programs needed to keep people alive and safe. 
I strongly oppose the changes in the proposed rule. I urge the Census Bureau and Department of Commerce to: 
Count all people residing in the United States in the 2030 Census, without regard to immigration status. Excluding noncitizens from census apportionment data violates the constitution and established legal precedent. It would suppress the count of many communities, effectively erasing them from critical datasets and depriving them of resources and Congressional representation. 
Withdraw other proposed changes to residence criteria, including tying place of residence to tax records and “lawful residence,” and the adoption of a three month enumeration period. The Census Bureau must extensively research and consult with stakeholders about the potential effects of such changes before proposing their implementation in a decennial census. 
Halt the practice of prison gerrymandering by counting incarcerated individuals in their home communities. This will yield more accurate census data and ensure that communities receive the Congressional representation to which they are entitled.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

Re: Docket No. 260903-0005, RIN 0607-AA75, USBC-2026-0628. “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions”

I am a resident of Puerto Rico (Trujillo Alto). I submit this comment to express my opposition to proposed Parts 60 and 70 of Title 15 of the Code of Federal Regulations, for the harm they would cause to a complete and correct count of Puerto Rico and Puerto Ricans.

The proposal does not mention Puerto Rico once, although the decennial Census counts more than 3.2 million U.S. citizens on the island and produces the data with which our legislative districts are redrawn. Sections 60.5 and 70.3 speak of the "stateside census" and the "national or state" level without defining "United States." I request that the Census Bureau explain in writing how Parts 60 and 70 would apply in Puerto Rico and not adopt a final rule without doing so.

Section 70.2(a) would prohibit the Hispanic origin question, which includes the "Puerto Rican" box. Today, more people of Puerto Rican origin live in states than in Puerto Rico, and that question is the only way the decennial Census counts them. Without it, our communities in New York, Florida, Pennsylvania, Massachusetts, Connecticut, and other states would disappear from the data used to enforce civil and voting rights and to plan services. I request that section 70.2(a) be eliminated.

Section 60.2(a) says that habitual residence "must be consistent with" tax records, but does not say which ones. Most residents of Puerto Rico file returns with the Department of Revenue, our local taxing authority, and not with the IRS; employers issue Form 499R-2/W-2PR. I request that the Census Bureau clarify in writing whether it would accept tax returns and Form 499R-2/W-2PR as tax records in Puerto Rico, and how it would obtain and record them.

Even if the Bureau were to use IRS returns, proof of residency based on tax records would leave out many people in Puerto Rico. It is estimated that about one-third of the population does not file a return and is in the informal economy (Caraballo-Cueto), and retirees and low-income households often do not file any. In addition, it is a concern that a substantial portion of the returns that do file use a P.O. Box or a rural route as an address, which does not identify the home where the person lives. I request that tax records not be made proof of residence in Puerto Rico and that auto-response and field verification be accepted.

For these reasons, I request that the Census Bureau withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all people in Puerto Rico and in the diaspora are counted, once and in the right place.

Thank you for considering this comment.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census. These changes will not only weaken the accuracy and integrity of our nation's most important population count, but they will also harm our communities, and I strongly urge the Bureau to reject them. 

First, removing questions of race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation erases the full scope of my identity when I participate in the Census survey. These data points are not optional. They are the tools we use to enforce civil rights laws, monitor discrimination, and measure the disparities that still affect millions of people. Excluding them from the count does not make them disappear from our society, but it does make our government less equipped to handle big issues when they arise. 

The Constitution is clear: the census must count ALL persons living in the United States, regardless of their immigration or citizenship status. The proposal to exclude non-citizens, including those residents with some type of lawful status, violates more than two centuries of legal precedent. Every person counted in this country contributes to our communities, and every person deserves to be fully seen. 

The consequences of these changes will negatively impact our daily lives. The census affects everything. It determines political representation and the drawing of voting districts. It guides how billions of dollars in federal funding are used to close persistent disparities in schools, hospitals, and other government programs that are designed to improve our lives.  

The census is the foundation of our democracy. It must reflect the complete yet nuanced reality of who we are as a nation. And it must reflect the lives of our friends and neighbors who may not look, think, or speak like we do. I ask the Bureau to withdraw these proposed changes and to preserve a count that includes everyone and represents everyone. 

Thank you for considering my comment.

Sincerely,
Robert Robinson

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). 

As a retired public school educator, I care about a fair and accurate census because census data and other federal datasets based on the census are used to make key decisions that affect our nation’s students, educators, and schools and more importantly, small, rural communities like my own.  

In 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Accurate census data is essential to our community beyond what the federal government "provides." This data drives decision making at the local level for county government services.

* Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. The federal governemtn has yet to fulfill its promise to fully fund their own portion of special education funding.  

* Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

* Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

* Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

* Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

* Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

* Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

* Determining state higher education funding formulas 

* Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

* Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

* Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

First, to ensure a fair and accurate census,  the Census Bureau should  extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. Second, I oppose both the proposed changes to the residence criteria and the proposed regulations regarding demographic questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation.  The Census Bureau should  withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The Constitution requires counting all people living in the United States. 

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (including children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count. 

Revise the tax records language so that those whose mailing address differs from their residential address (service members, those with a post office box) are not excluded.  

• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for civil rights enforcement, among other uses, and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The prohibition, as written, may also restrict the collection or publication of census data on same-sex couples that was asked in 2020. 

 The proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Sincerely,
Ms. Mary Bracken
Monte Rio, CA

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
A la Oficina del Censo de los Estados Unidos:

Re: Docket No. 260903-0005, RIN 0607-AA75, USBC-2026-0628. “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions”

Soy residente de Puerto Rico (Hatillo). Someto este comentario para expresar mi oposición a las Partes 60 y 70 propuestas del Título 15 del Código de Regulaciones Federales, por el daño que causarían a un conteo completo y correcto de Puerto Rico y de los puertorriqueños.

La propuesta no menciona a Puerto Rico ni una sola vez, aunque el Censo decenal cuenta a más de 3.2 millones de ciudadanos estadounidenses en la Isla y produce los datos con que se redibujan nuestros distritos legislativos. Las secciones 60.5 y 70.3 hablan del “stateside census” y del nivel “nacional o estatal” sin definir “Estados Unidos”. Solicito que la Oficina del Censo explique por escrito cómo aplicarían las Partes 60 y 70 en Puerto Rico y que no adopte una regla final sin hacerlo.

La sección 70.2(a) prohibiría la pregunta de origen hispano, que incluye el encasillado “puertorriqueño”. Hoy viven más personas de origen puertorriqueño en los estados que en Puerto Rico, y esa pregunta es la única forma en que el Censo decenal las cuenta. Sin ella, nuestras comunidades en Nueva York, Florida, Pensilvania, Massachusetts, Connecticut y otros estados desaparecerían de los datos que se usan para hacer cumplir los derechos civiles y electorales y para planificar servicios. Solicito que se elimine la sección 70.2(a).

La sección 60.2(a) dice que la residencia habitual “debe ser consistente con” los récords contributivos, pero no dice cuáles. La mayoría de los residentes de Puerto Rico rinde planilla ante el Departamento de Hacienda, nuestra autoridad contributiva local, y no ante el IRS; los patronos emiten el Formulario 499R-2/W-2PR. Solicito que la Oficina del Censo aclare por escrito si aceptaría las planillas de Hacienda y el Formulario 499R-2/W-2PR como récords contributivos en Puerto Rico, y cómo los obtendría y parearía.

Aun si la Oficina usara las planillas de Hacienda, una prueba de residencia basada en récords contributivos dejaría fuera a muchas personas en Puerto Rico. Se estima que cerca de un tercio de la población no rinde planilla y está en la economía informal (Caraballo-Cueto), y jubilados y hogares de bajos ingresos con frecuencia no rinden ninguna. Además, preocupa que una porción sustancial de las planillas que sí se rinden use un apartado postal o una ruta rural como dirección, que no identifica la vivienda donde vive la persona. Solicito que no se haga de los récords contributivos la prueba de residencia en Puerto Rico y que se acepten la autorespuesta y la verificación en el campo.

Se estima que entre el 40% y el 60% de las estructuras en Puerto Rico no tienen una dirección física de calle y número (city-style), el estándar que usan los sistemas federales, así que no se pueden validar, parear ni ubicar en un mapa. Muchas familias reciben su correspondencia en apartados postales o rutas rurales, no donde viven, y nuestras direcciones usan el campo “Urbanización” y acentos que los sistemas nacionales no parean bien. Un récord con dirección postal no prueba dónde vive una persona. Solicito que la Oficina publique las tasas de pareo de direcciones en Puerto Rico de cada fuente administrativa y que mantenga la enumeración en persona donde las direcciones no se puedan parear.

La Oficina pide comentarios sobre añadir una pregunta de estatus legal al cuestionario. Me opongo. Puerto Rico tiene comunidades inmigrantes arraigadas y muchos hogares de estatus mixto en los que viven ciudadanos estadounidenses. El temor provocado por una pregunta así reduciría la respuesta de familias completas y empeoraría el subconteo de los barrios y municipios donde viven.

La Constitución de Puerto Rico exige revisar los 40 distritos representativos y los 8 senatoriales después de cada censo, a partir de datos por bloque y barrio. El mismo conteo es la base de fondos federales para salud, nutrición, educación, vivienda y recuperación de desastres en los 78 municipios. Si la regla deja fuera hogares o los ubica en su dirección postal, los mapas y los fondos de la próxima década se distorsionan. Solicito que la Oficina publique un análisis del efecto de la regla en la base poblacional de Puerto Rico antes de adoptarla.

Por estas razones, solicito que la Oficina del Censo retire la regla propuesta y garantice que todas las personas en Puerto Rico y en la diáspora sean contadas, una vez y en el lugar correcto.

Gracias por considerar este comentario.

Ivan A Gonzalez Legarreta

The proposal to exclude non-citizens, including those residents with some type of lawful status, violates more than two centuries of legal precedent. Every person counted in this country contributes to our communities, and every person deserves to be fully seen.

It guides how billions of dollars in federal funding are used to close persistent disparities in schools, hospitals, and other government programs that are designed to improve our lives.  

The census is the foundation of our democracy. It must reflect the complete yet nuanced reality of who we are as a nation. And it must reflect the lives of our friends and neighbors who may not look, think, or speak like we do. I ask the Bureau to withdraw these proposed changes and to preserve a count that includes everyone and represents everyone. 

Thank you for considering my comment.

Sincerely,

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

Re: Docket No. 260903-0005, RIN 0607-AA75, USBC-2026-0628. “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions”

I am a resident of Puerto Rico (Patillas). I submit this comment to oppose proposed 15 CFR Parts 60 and 70 because of the harm they would cause to a complete and accurate count of Puerto Rico and of Puerto Ricans.

Section 70.2(a) would prohibit the Hispanic-origin question, which includes the “Puerto Rican” checkbox. More people of Puerto Rican origin now live in the states than on the island, and that question is the only way the decennial census counts them. Without it, our communities in New York, Florida, Pennsylvania, Massachusetts, Connecticut, and elsewhere would disappear from the data used to enforce civil and voting rights and to plan services. I ask that Section 70.2(a) be withdrawn.

Even if the Bureau used Hacienda returns, a residence test based on tax records would leave many people in Puerto Rico out. An estimated one-third of the population doesn’t file and works in the informal economy (Caraballo-Cueto), and retirees and low-income households often file no return at all. Moreover, there is concern that a substantial share of the returns that are filed list a P.O. box or rural route as the address, which does not identify the home where the person lives. I ask that tax records not be made the proof of residence in Puerto Rico, and that self-response and field verification be accepted.

An estimated 40% to 60% of structures in Puerto Rico have no physical street-and-number (city-style) address, the standard federal systems use, so they cannot be validated, matched, or placed on a map. Many families receive mail at P.O. boxes or rural routes rather than where they live, and our addresses use an “Urbanización” line and accents that national systems don’t match well. A record with a mailing address does not prove where a person lives. I ask the Bureau to publish Puerto Rico address-match rates for every administrative source and to keep in-person enumeration wherever addresses cannot be matched.

The Puerto Rico Community Survey and nearly all surveys are weighted to population estimates based on the decennial census. Section 70.4 says the ACS could still ask about race and origin, but without those data in the census there would be no reliable benchmark. Municipios, agencies, hospitals, universities, nonprofits, and businesses depend on these data, as does the distribution of federal funds for health, nutrition, education, housing, and disaster recovery. I ask that Part 70 not be adopted.

Puerto Rico’s Constitution requires its 40 house and 8 senate districts to be revised after each census, using block- and barrio-level data. The same count is the base for federal funds for health, nutrition, education, housing, and disaster recovery in all 78 municipios. If the rule drops households or places them at a mailing address, the next decade’s maps and funding are distorted. I ask the Bureau to publish an analysis of the rule’s effect on Puerto Rico’s population base before finalizing it.

These are the most sweeping changes proposed to the census in generations. Even extended to November 2, 2026, the comment period is not enough time for Puerto Rico’s communities to evaluate them. I ask for a further extension, public hearings in Spanish in Puerto Rico, and formal consultation with the Government of Puerto Rico and its municipios.

For these reasons, I ask the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that everyone in Puerto Rico and in the diaspora is counted, once, and in the right place.

Thank you for considering this comment.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census. These changes will not only weaken the accuracy and integrity of our nation's most important population count, but they will also harm our communities, and I strongly urge the Bureau to reject them. 

First, removing questions of race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation erases the full scope of my identity when I participate in the Census survey. These data points are not optional. They are the tools we use to enforce civil rights laws, monitor discrimination, and measure the disparities that still affect millions of people. Excluding them from the count does not make them disappear from our society, but it does make our government less equipped to handle big issues when they arise. 

The Constitution is clear: the census must count ALL persons living in the United States, regardless of their immigration or citizenship status. The proposal to exclude non-citizens, including those residents with some type of lawful status, violates more than two centuries of legal precedent. Every person counted in this country contributes to our communities, and every person deserves to be fully seen. 

The consequences of these changes will negatively impact our daily lives. The census affects everything. It determines political representation and the drawing of voting districts. It guides how billions of dollars in federal funding are used to close persistent disparities in schools, hospitals, and other government programs that are designed to improve our lives.  

The census is the foundation of our democracy. It must reflect the complete yet nuanced reality of who we are as a nation. And it must reflect the lives of our friends and neighbors who may not look, think, or speak like we do. I ask the Bureau to withdraw these proposed changes and to preserve a count that includes everyone and represents everyone. 

Thank you for considering my comment.

Sincerely,
Kate Horton

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
A la Oficina del Censo de los Estados Unidos:

Re: Docket No. 260903-0005, RIN 0607-AA75, USBC-2026-0628. “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions”

Soy puertorriqueño/a y vivo en los Estados Unidos (Massachusetts). Someto este comentario para expresar mi oposición a las Partes 60 y 70 propuestas del Título 15 del Código de Regulaciones Federales, por el daño que causarían a un conteo completo y correcto de Puerto Rico y de los puertorriqueños.

Vivo en Massachusetts y soy originaria de Arecibo PR, y debido al huracán María tuve que salir de la isla.

La propuesta no menciona a Puerto Rico ni una sola vez, aunque el Censo decenal cuenta a más de 3.2 millones de ciudadanos estadounidenses en la Isla y produce los datos con que se redibujan nuestros distritos legislativos. Las secciones 60.5 y 70.3 hablan del “stateside census” y del nivel “nacional o estatal” sin definir “Estados Unidos”. Solicito que la Oficina del Censo explique por escrito cómo aplicarían las Partes 60 y 70 en Puerto Rico y que no adopte una regla final sin hacerlo.

La sección 70.2(a) prohibiría la pregunta de origen hispano, que incluye el encasillado “puertorriqueño”. Hoy viven más personas de origen puertorriqueño en los estados que en Puerto Rico, y esa pregunta es la única forma en que el Censo decenal las cuenta. Sin ella, nuestras comunidades en Nueva York, Florida, Pensilvania, Massachusetts, Connecticut y otros estados desaparecerían de los datos que se usan para hacer cumplir los derechos civiles y electorales y para planificar servicios. Solicito que se elimine la sección 70.2(a).

La Oficina pide comentarios sobre añadir una pregunta de estatus legal al cuestionario. Me opongo. Puerto Rico tiene comunidades inmigrantes arraigadas y muchos hogares de estatus mixto en los que viven ciudadanos estadounidenses. El temor provocado por una pregunta así reduciría la respuesta de familias completas y empeoraría el subconteo de los barrios y municipios donde viven.

La Encuesta sobre la Comunidad de Puerto Rico y casi todas las encuestas se ajustan a estimados de población basados en el Censo decenal. La sección 70.4 dice que la ACS aún podría preguntar sobre raza y origen, pero sin esos datos en el Censo no habría punto de referencia confiable. Municipios, agencias, hospitales, universidades, organizaciones sin fines de lucro y negocios dependen de estos datos, igual que la distribución de fondos federales para salud, alimentos, educación, vivienda y recuperación de desastres. Solicito que no se adopte la Parte 70.

La Constitución de Puerto Rico exige revisar los 40 distritos representativos y los 8 senatoriales después de cada censo, a partir de datos por bloque y barrio. El mismo conteo es la base de fondos federales para salud, nutrición, educación, vivienda y recuperación de desastres en los 78 municipios. Si la regla deja fuera hogares o los ubica en su dirección postal, los mapas y los fondos de la próxima década se distorsionan. Solicito que la Oficina publique un análisis del efecto de la regla en la base poblacional de Puerto Rico antes de adoptarla.

Por estas razones, solicito que la Oficina del Censo retire la regla propuesta y garantice que todas las personas en Puerto Rico y en la diáspora sean contadas, una vez y en el lugar correcto.

Gracias por considerar este comentario.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

Re: Docket No. 260903-0005, RIN 0607-AA75, USBC-2026-0628. “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions”

I am Puerto Rican and live in the United States (Massachusetts). I submit this comment to oppose proposed 15 CFR Parts 60 and 70 because of the harm they would cause to a complete and accurate count of Puerto Rico and of Puerto Ricans.

Vivo en Massachusetts desde el huracán María, pero soy originaria de Arecibo, PR.

The proposed rule does not mention Puerto Rico a single time, even though the decennial census counts more than 3.2 million U.S. citizens on the island and produces the data used to redraw our legislative districts. Sections 60.5 and 70.3 refer to the “stateside census” and to the “national or state level” without defining “United States.” I ask the Census Bureau to explain in writing how Parts 60 and 70 would apply in Puerto Rico, and not to finalize any rule without doing so.

Section 70.2(a) would prohibit the Hispanic-origin question, which includes the “Puerto Rican” checkbox. More people of Puerto Rican origin now live in the states than on the island, and that question is the only way the decennial census counts them. Without it, our communities in New York, Florida, Pennsylvania, Massachusetts, Connecticut, and elsewhere would disappear from the data used to enforce civil and voting rights and to plan services. I ask that Section 70.2(a) be withdrawn.

The Bureau invites comments on adding a legal-status question to the questionnaire. I oppose it. Puerto Rico has long-established immigrant communities and many mixed-status households that include U.S. citizens. The fear such a question creates would suppress response from entire households and worsen undercounts in the barrios and municipios where they live.

The Puerto Rico Community Survey and nearly all surveys are weighted to population estimates based on the decennial census. Section 70.4 says the ACS could still ask about race and origin, but without those data in the census there would be no reliable benchmark. Municipios, agencies, hospitals, universities, nonprofits, and businesses depend on these data, as does the distribution of federal funds for health, nutrition, education, housing, and disaster recovery. I ask that Part 70 not be adopted.

Puerto Rico’s Constitution requires its 40 house and 8 senate districts to be revised after each census, using block- and barrio-level data. The same count is the base for federal funds for health, nutrition, education, housing, and disaster recovery in all 78 municipios. If the rule drops households or places them at a mailing address, the next decade’s maps and funding are distorted. I ask the Bureau to publish an analysis of the rule’s effect on Puerto Rico’s population base before finalizing it.

For these reasons, I ask the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that everyone in Puerto Rico and in the diaspora is counted, once, and in the right place.

Thank you for considering this comment.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:
I write to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). I oppose those provisions in part 60 and part 70 that change residence criteria and demographic items. 
I am a demographer, and in my research capacity I have used US census data, particularly the decennial census, over many years to examine patterns and trends in social and housing conditions.  As a resident of Rhode Island, I have also consulted census data for local area statistics, in some cases to aid or inform work by others, such as local service organizations.  A fair and accurate census is of utmost concern, because census data have extraordinarily broad reach and application.  Accuracy is needed to inform policy, including the allocation of government funds.  An accurate census gives the best snapshot of who we are and where we are going. A fair and accurate census also reinforces confidence in government at all levels, especially federal.  
As the Census Bureau itself has stated, the goal of the census is “Counting Everyone Once, Only Once and in the Right Place”.   That includes all residents, as is consistent with the Constitution and with historical census practice.  
The census should retain demographic questions. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public policy, including patterns of residence and access to resources. 
Census planning should not pre-emptively ban questions about sexual orientation.  This would be ill-informed and unwise.  Such questions should be considered and carefully reviewed by knowledgeable panels.
The Census Bureau should reaffirm its goal to count all US residents in a manner consistent with past practice and goals. The proposed revision regarding “usual residence” is ill-advised and is likely to decrease accuracy for science and policy. The proposed “reference period” is likely to inject confusion in the data collection and reduce accuracy.  These proposed actions should be withdrawn.  
In sum, the proposed rule would exclude residents, diminish accuracy, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. The proposed changes would not produce any appreciable enhancements to efficiency, but they would harm the ability of the Census Bureau to be the nation’s fact finder and pre-eminent government statistical agency.   I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule.
I submit this comment in my individual capacity and not on behalf of any organization.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to express opposition to the proposed changes of both parts 60 and 70 of federal regulations related to the United States Census. Both sections would have significant impacts on me and other residents of Minnesota, as well as citizens of our nation.

1) Part 60, Residence: The changes to part 60 include changing how a person's normal residence is determined. Historically, this has been the place where a person resides most of the year. This is also the place where someone has their primary residence, votes, and identifies for payment of income and property taxes. The proposed change would define a person's normal residence based on where they spent most of their time between January 3 and April 3 of the Census year. There are many Minnesota residents who spend significant parts of the winter in places other than Minnesota, either as temporary resident or on vacation. In addition, there are students on study abroad trips in their spring semester of college, working people on longer term temporary job assignments or training away from their home, and relocating to or from Minnesota late in this period. Each scenario presents a situation in which the count of people in Minnesota, and other states, will not accurately reflect the number of people represented by a member of Congress, and that requires government services. The approach to determining a person's residence for purpose of the census, and subsequently for allocation of federal funding and apportionment of congressional representation, should be based on what a person's identified as their "normal residence" as of April 1.

The guidance for determining residence is extremely cumbersome and likely to be confusing to people responding to the census. For example, the proposed rules include counting the hours in a day that someone is at one residence of another. This also creates confusion for members of the military. If a service member is deployed overseas or to a part of their U.S. which is not their "normal residence", the proposed rules would not accurately account for their residence for apportionment and federal funding.

The proposal to not include noncitizens residents who do not have legal permanent residence for apportionment is inconsistent with this treatment of noncitizen inclusion for apportionment since the country's founding.

2) Part 70: The proposed regulatory change to remove demographic information will create significant challenges with applying federal and state requirements for voting rights and providing resources and assistance to eligible voters with language challenges. In addition, state and local governments, as well as businesses across the country, rely on census demographic data to plan services and resources, as well as business development based on the demographic information. Demographic information has been collected with the census since the country's founding. The proposed change for collection of demographic information will be a significant impediment to implementing federal, state, and local government statutory requirements and programs.

I ask that the Department of Commerce and U.S. Census Bureau retract the proposed changes to Part 60 and Part 70 in their entirety to ensure the population of each state and local jurisdiction is accurately represented, consistent with the U.S. Constitution and history and tradition of the Census since the nation’s founding, and to ensure federal, state and local governments, as well as the business community, have information they need to meet the needs of their residents and their legal obligations.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am a bedside hospital Registered Nurse, who has cared for my community for over 13 years in Las vegas Nv and I care about a fair and accurate census because very person matters and every person should be counted. 

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions,

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.
