Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census. These changes will not only weaken the accuracy and integrity of our nation's most important population count, but they will also harm our communities, and I strongly urge the Bureau to reject them. 

First, removing questions of race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation erases the full scope of my identity when I participate in the Census survey. These data points are not optional. They are the tools we use to enforce civil rights laws, monitor discrimination, and measure the disparities that still affect millions of people. Excluding them from the count does not make them disappear from our society, but it does make our government less equipped to handle big issues when they arise. 

The Constitution is clear: the census must count ALL persons living in the United States, regardless of their immigration or citizenship status. The proposal to exclude non-citizens, including those residents with some type of lawful status, violates more than two centuries of legal precedent. Every person counted in this country contributes to our communities, and every person deserves to be fully seen. 

The consequences of these changes will negatively impact our daily lives. The census affects everything. It determines political representation and the drawing of voting districts. It guides how billions of dollars in federal funding are used to close persistent disparities in schools, hospitals, and other government programs that are designed to improve our lives.  

The census is the foundation of our democracy. It must reflect the complete yet nuanced reality of who we are as a nation. And it must reflect the lives of our friends and neighbors who may not look, think, or speak like we do. I ask the Bureau to withdraw these proposed changes and to preserve a count that includes everyone and represents everyone. 

Thank you for considering my comment.

Sincerely,
Susan Malphurs

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census. These changes will not only weaken the accuracy and integrity of our nation's most important population count, but they will also harm our communities, and I strongly urge the Bureau to reject them. 

First, removing questions of race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation erases the full scope of my identity when I participate in the Census survey. These data points are not optional. They are the tools we use to enforce civil rights laws, monitor discrimination, and measure the disparities that still affect millions of people. Excluding them from the count does not make them disappear from our society, but it does make our government less equipped to handle big issues when they arise.

The proposal to exclude non-citizens, including those residents with some type of lawful status, violates more than two centuries of legal precedent. Every person counted in this country contributes to our communities, and every person deserves to be fully seen. 

The consequences of these changes will negatively impact our daily lives. The census affects everything. It determines political representation and the drawing of voting districts. It guides how billions of dollars in federal funding are used to close persistent disparities in schools, hospitals, and other government programs that are designed to improve our lives.  

The census is the foundation of our democracy. It must reflect the complete yet nuanced reality of who we are as a nation. And it must reflect the lives of our friends and neighbors who may not look, think, or speak like we do. I ask the Bureau to withdraw these proposed changes and to preserve a count that includes everyone and represents everyone. 

Thank you for considering my comment.

Sincerely,
Quanetta McNeal

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: 91 FR 57524  Public Comment,Re: Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions (Docket No. USBC-2026-0628).I am writing to oppose the Census Bureau's proposed rule, "Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions," Docket No. USBC-2026-0628, because it would produce an inaccurate count of the people living in this country.Every ten years, the census gives the country one reliable picture of who lives here. Congress, states, cities, and businesses use it to divide representation, distribute federal funds, and plan for the next decade. This rule would distort that picture. Fewer people would be counted, and some communities would disappear from the data altogether. The errors would affect the entire country, but they would be heaviest in immigrant, minority, and low-income households and in the states and towns where they live.The undercount would come from several directions. The rule would stop counting many immigrants who live here, even though the Constitution requires counting every person. It also invites a question about legal status, which would keep many people in immigrant and mixed-status households from answering at all, whatever their own status. And it would decide where people live using tax records, even though many people are not required to file and the rule says nothing about how to count people such as those without stable housing, foster children, or people in shelters and nursing homes.The invisibility would come from banning the race and ethnicity question and from households afraid to respond. Without that information, it is much harder to show where needs are greatest, enforce civil rights laws, check whether voting maps are fair, or catch health problems that hit some communities harder. States, local governments, and health systems would have to collect it themselves, adding cost and producing less reliable numbers.This is a poor use of public money. More than $2.8 trillion a year in federal funding follows census numbers. When the count is wrong, that money goes to the wrong places for at least ten years, and schools, clinics, roads, and emergency plans are built for a population that does not match reality. Lower response rates also mean more costly follow-up work, paid for by taxpayers.A bad count in 2030 cannot be corrected until at least 2040. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw this rule.Fadi BANYALMAR [X] Kansas city, Missouri 64134

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule, “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions.”

For more than two centuries, the census has counted residents for purposes of congressional apportionment regardless of immigration status. Article I, Section 2, Clause 3 of the U.S. Constitution requires an “actual Enumeration” of the population, while the Fourteenth Amendment provides that representatives be apportioned among the states based on the “whole number of persons” in each state.

Historically, the census has included native-born and naturalized U.S. citizens, non-citizen U.S. nationals, lawful permanent residents, and other residents, including foreign students, refugees, asylum seekers, and undocumented immigrants. Immigration status has not been the basis for excluding residents from the population count.

An accurate and comprehensive census is essential to ensuring that communities receive appropriate representation and resources. Census data informs the allocation of funding and planning for schools, hospitals, roads, fire departments, and other critical public services. Excluding individuals from the population count risks leaving communities without resources proportionate to the number of people they serve.

The proposed rule would undermine the goal of achieving a complete and accurate count of the population and could have significant consequences for communities across the country. For these reasons, I strongly oppose the proposed rule and respectfully urge the U.S. Census Bureau not to adopt it.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). 

As an educator, I care about a fair and accurate census because census data and other federal datasets based on the census are used to make key decisions that affect our nation’s students, educators, and schools.  

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Examples of these uses include: . 

* Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. 

* Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

* Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

* Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

* Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

* Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

* Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

* Determining state higher education funding formulas 

* Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

* Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

* Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

First, to ensure a fair and accurate census,  the Census Bureau should  extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. Second, I oppose both the proposed changes to the residence criteria and the proposed regulations regarding demographic questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. The Census Bureau should  withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The Constitution requires  counting all people living in the United States. 

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (including children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count. 

Revise the tax records language so that those whose mailing address differs from their residential address (servicemembers, those with a post office box) are not excluded.  

• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for civil rights enforcement, among other uses, and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The prohibition, as written, may also restrict the collection or publication of census data on same-sex couples that was asked in 2020. 

 The proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Sincerely,
Mrs. Kathleen Nielsen
Brookfield, WI

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481

They are the tools we use to enforce civil rights laws, monitor discrimination, and measure the disparities that still affect millions of people. Excluding them from the count does not make them disappear from our society, but it does make our government less equipped to handle big issues when they arise.

Every person counted in this country contributes to our communities, and every person deserves to be fully seen. 

The consequences of these changes will negatively impact our daily lives. The census affects everything. It determines political representation and the drawing of voting districts. It guides how billions of dollars in federal funding are used to close persistent disparities in schools, hospitals, and other government programs that are designed to improve our lives.  

The census is the foundation of our democracy. It must reflect the complete yet nuanced reality of who we are as a nation. And it must reflect the lives of our friends and neighbors who may not look, think, or speak like we do. I ask the Bureau to withdraw these proposed changes and to preserve a count that includes everyone and represents everyone.

Comment: 91 FR 57524  Public Comment,Re: Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions (Docket No. USBC-2026-0628).I am writing to oppose the Census Bureau's proposed rule, "Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions," Docket No. USBC-2026-0628, because it would produce an inaccurate count of the people living in this country.Every ten years, the census gives the country one reliable picture of who lives here. And it would decide where people live using tax records, even though many people are not required to file and the rule says nothing about how to count people such as those without stable housing, foster children, or people in shelters and nursing homes.The invisibility would come from banning the race and ethnicity question and from households afraid to respond. Without that information, it is much harder to show where needs are greatest, enforce civil rights laws, check whether voting maps are fair, or catch health problems that hit some communities harder. States, local governments, and health systems would have to collect it themselves, adding cost and producing less reliable numbers.This is a poor use of public money. Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
A la Oficina del Censo de los Estados Unidos:

Re: Docket No. 260903-0005, RIN 0607-AA75, USBC-2026-0628. “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions”

Soy residente de Puerto Rico (San Juan). Someto este comentario para expresar mi oposición a las Partes 60 y 70 propuestas del Título 15 del Código de Regulaciones Federales, por el daño que causarían a un conteo completo y correcto de Puerto Rico y de los puertorriqueños.

La sección 60.2(a) dice que la residencia habitual “debe ser consistente con” los récords contributivos, pero no dice cuáles. La mayoría de los residentes de Puerto Rico rinde planilla ante el Departamento de Hacienda, nuestra autoridad contributiva local, y no ante el IRS; los patronos emiten el Formulario 499R-2/W-2PR. Solicito que la Oficina del Censo aclare por escrito si aceptaría las planillas de Hacienda y el Formulario 499R-2/W-2PR como récords contributivos en Puerto Rico, y cómo los obtendría y parearía.

Aun si la Oficina usara las planillas de Hacienda, una prueba de residencia basada en récords contributivos dejaría fuera a muchas personas en Puerto Rico. Se estima que cerca de un tercio de la población no rinde planilla y está en la economía informal (Caraballo-Cueto), y jubilados y hogares de bajos ingresos con frecuencia no rinden ninguna. Además, preocupa que una porción sustancial de las planillas que sí se rinden use un apartado postal o una ruta rural como dirección, que no identifica la vivienda donde vive la persona. Solicito que no se haga de los récords contributivos la prueba de residencia en Puerto Rico y que se acepten la autorespuesta y la verificación en el campo.

Se estima que entre el 40% y el 60% de las estructuras en Puerto Rico no tienen una dirección física de calle y número (city-style), el estándar que usan los sistemas federales, así que no se pueden validar, parear ni ubicar en un mapa. Muchas familias reciben su correspondencia en apartados postales o rutas rurales, no donde viven, y nuestras direcciones usan el campo “Urbanización” y acentos que los sistemas nacionales no parean bien. Un récord con dirección postal no prueba dónde vive una persona. Solicito que la Oficina publique las tasas de pareo de direcciones en Puerto Rico de cada fuente administrativa y que mantenga la enumeración en persona donde las direcciones no se puedan parear.

La Oficina pide comentarios sobre añadir una pregunta de estatus legal al cuestionario. Me opongo. Puerto Rico tiene comunidades inmigrantes arraigadas y muchos hogares de estatus mixto en los que viven ciudadanos estadounidenses. El temor provocado por una pregunta así reduciría la respuesta de familias completas y empeoraría el subconteo de los barrios y municipios donde viven.

La Encuesta sobre la Comunidad de Puerto Rico y casi todas las encuestas se ajustan a estimados de población basados en el Censo decenal. La sección 70.4 dice que la ACS aún podría preguntar sobre raza y origen, pero sin esos datos en el Censo no habría punto de referencia confiable. Municipios, agencias, hospitales, universidades, organizaciones sin fines de lucro y negocios dependen de estos datos, igual que la distribución de fondos federales para salud, alimentos, educación, vivienda y recuperación de desastres. Solicito que no se adopte la Parte 70.

La Constitución de Puerto Rico exige revisar los 40 distritos representativos y los 8 senatoriales después de cada censo, a partir de datos por bloque y barrio. El mismo conteo es la base de fondos federales para salud, nutrición, educación, vivienda y recuperación de desastres en los 78 municipios. Si la regla deja fuera hogares o los ubica en su dirección postal, los mapas y los fondos de la próxima década se distorsionan. Solicito que la Oficina publique un análisis del efecto de la regla en la base poblacional de Puerto Rico antes de adoptarla.

Estos cambios son los más profundos que se han propuesto al Censo en generaciones. El periodo de comentarios, aun extendido al 2 de noviembre de 2026, no basta para que las comunidades de Puerto Rico los evalúen. Solicito una extensión adicional, audiencias públicas en español en Puerto Rico y consulta formal con el gobierno de Puerto Rico y sus municipios.

Por estas razones, solicito que la Oficina del Censo retire la regla propuesta y garantice que todas las personas en Puerto Rico y en la diáspora sean contadas, una vez y en el lugar correcto.

Gracias por considerar este comentario.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Public Comment Opposing Proposed 15 CFR Parts 60 and 70

To: U.S. Census Bureau, U.S. Department of Commerce
Re: Docket No. 260903-0005 | RIN 0607-AA75 | USBC-2026-0628

I am a resident of Toa Alta, Puerto Rico, and strongly oppose proposed 15 CFR Parts 60 and 70. The proposal fails to address Puerto Rico's distinct circumstances despite its potential impact on millions of Island residents and Puerto Ricans throughout the United States.

1. Puerto Rico must be explicitly addressed.

Sections 60.5 and 70.3 refer to the "stateside census" and "national or state level" without explaining their application to U.S. territories. Puerto Rico's legal, administrative, geographic, and demographic circumstances cannot be assumed to fit a framework designed for the 50 states. Although Puerto Rico is not included in congressional apportionment, census data are essential to local legislative representation, public planning, and federal funding. The Bureau should clarify how these provisions apply before adopting a final rule.

2. Retain race and ethnicity questions.

Proposed § 70.2(a) would eliminate race and ethnicity questions from the decennial census. The Hispanic-origin question is essential to identifying Puerto Rican communities. Approximately 6.1 million people of Puerto Rican origin live in the 50 states and D.C., more than on the Island. Eliminating this question would weaken data needed for civil rights enforcement, Voting Rights Act protections, public policy, and resource allocation.

Although § 70.4 preserves demographic questions in the American Community Survey (ACS), a sample survey cannot provide the same coverage and geographic detail as a complete census. The Bureau should also clarify how § 70.3(b) would affect geographically detailed demographic data.

3. Tax records cannot determine usual residence.

Proposed § 60.2(a) relies on tax records to establish usual residence but overlooks Puerto Rico's separate tax system. Many residents file with the Puerto Rico Department of Treasury (Hacienda), rather than the IRS. Employers issue Form 499R-2/W-2PR. The proposal does not clarify whether these records would be accepted or how they would be matched.

Tax records also omit low-income individuals, retirees, and people in the informal economy. Returns may contain post office boxes or rural mailing addresses rather than actual residences. Making tax records a controlling test risks undercounting residents. Direct self-response, in-person enumeration, and field verification must remain available.

4. Puerto Rico's addressing system requires special consideration.

The Census Bureau has acknowledged that approximately 30% of Puerto Rico's dwellings lack a formal address. Many addresses rely on urbanización names, barrios, rural routes, kilometer markers, and post office boxes. These limitations complicate address matching and can cause households to be missed, duplicated, or assigned to the wrong community.

The Bureau should publish Puerto Rico-specific address-matching success rates and preserve in-person verification when administrative records cannot establish a household's location reliably.

5. Protect legislative representation and public planning.

Article III, Section 4 of the Constitution of Puerto Rico requires legislative district review after each decennial census. Accurate data are essential to fair representation across 40 representative and eight senatorial districts and resource allocation across all 78 municipalities. An inaccurate count or geographic assignment could undermine both.

Requested Actions

I respectfully request that the Census Bureau:

1. Withdraw Parts 60 and 70 or publish a Puerto Rico-specific impact assessment before final adoption.
2. Explain how each provision applies to Puerto Rico.
3. Retain race and ethnicity questions and clarify § 70.3(b)'s effects.
4. Reject tax records as a controlling residence test and preserve direct enumeration.
5. Clarify acceptance and treatment of Hacienda returns and Form 499R-2/W-2PR.
6. Publish Puerto Rico-specific address-matching data and recognize local addressing conventions.
7. Consult Puerto Rico's government, municipalities, and statistical agencies before adopting revised regulations.

Conclusion

A reliable census cannot depend on administrative records created for other purposes or eliminate demographic information essential to civil rights and public planning. Puerto Rico's distinct tax system, addressing conventions, and constitutional framework must be considered.

The people of Puerto Rico deserve the same commitment to an accurate and complete census as every other community under U.S. jurisdiction. I urge the Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule or address these concerns before adopting final regulations.

Respectfully submitted,

Toa Alta, Puerto Rico

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: As a sociologist of race and ethnicity (and gender), I strongly opposed the attempt to remove census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. These data provide an important window into understanding our society and the complexities of our national population. When I began my career almost 20 years ago, as a scholar of Mexico I have seen the problematic consequences of not having data on race and ethnicity and always supported a model of intricate and complex data collection. The United States has long been a model of such data collection on these issues and it would be a step back to remove those data from our census measures. At the global level, the move has been to recognize the increasing diversity and complexities of our societies, not ignore or evade them. The elimination of such questions would make it so we are operating in the dark on social issues, as opposed to understanding and confronting them head on.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census. These changes will not only weaken the accuracy and integrity of our nation's most important population count, but they will also harm our communities, and I strongly urge the Bureau to reject them. 

First, removing questions of race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation erases the full scope of my identity when I participate in the Census survey. These data points are not optional. They are the tools we use to enforce civil rights laws, monitor discrimination, and measure the disparities that still affect millions of people. Excluding them from the count does not make them disappear from our society, but it does make our government less equipped to handle big issues when they arise. 

The Constitution is clear: the census must count ALL persons living in the United States, regardless of their immigration or citizenship status. The proposal to exclude non-citizens, including those residents with some type of lawful status, violates more than two centuries of legal precedent. Every person counted in this country contributes to our communities, and every person deserves to be fully seen. 

The consequences of these changes will negatively impact our daily lives. The census affects everything. It determines political representation and the drawing of voting districts. It guides how billions of dollars in federal funding are used to close persistent disparities in schools, hospitals, and other government programs that are designed to improve our lives.  

The census is the foundation of our democracy. It must reflect the complete yet nuanced reality of who we are as a nation. And it must reflect the lives of our friends and neighbors who may not look, think, or speak like we do. I ask the Bureau to withdraw these proposed changes and to preserve a count that includes everyone and represents everyone. 

Thank you for considering my comment.

Sincerely,
Rex Grubb

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket number USBC-2026-0628, Docket No 260903-1005, Document 2006-18481, published Sept. 10, 2026 and extended October 5, 2026

First, I ask the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026.  Significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve more time for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70.  I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including 
:

The census should count ALL people/residents.  Do NOT exclude visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count.

Residence should be based on where someone usually lives and sleeps. What does the “one hour” rule even mean?

The guidelines for the “enumeration period” are unclear.  I worry that seasonal workers and recent movers will not be counted in the right place on Census Day.  I am also concerned that people in shelters or children in foster care will not be counted.  

I also believe that incarcerated people should be counted in their home, not in the facility.  This proposal would shift money to districts where prisons are built from the communities where people live.

The language on tax records is very confusing! Tax records reflect mailing addresses, not home addresses (e.g. P.O. Boxes, business addresses or tax preparers. They are inconsistent with residence addresses for many: e.g. military personnel and their families.  Extreme reliance on tax records risks not counting many dependent children in the court.  

Demographic questions need to be asked!  We have collected information about race since our first in 1790, for heaven’s sake.  Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement.  Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked should not be banned from future censuses

The proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count and prohibit collection of important data about our population.  This is unacceptable.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the decennial census, particularly the elimination of race and ethnicity questions and the proposed restrictions on determining who qualifies as a resident of the United States.

The decennial census is more than a population count. It is a critical tool for ensuring fair representation, equitable distribution of federal resources, and accountability in addressing the needs of communities throughout our nation.

1. Retain Race and Ethnicity Questions

Removing race and ethnicity questions from the decennial census would be a significant step backward.

Accurate demographic information is essential to understanding the composition of our nation's population and identifying disparities in education, healthcare, housing, employment, economic opportunities, and other areas affecting American communities.

Without reliable and consistent racial and ethnic data, government agencies, researchers, community organizations, and policymakers will have fewer tools to identify discrimination, measure progress, and develop effective solutions.

The absence of data does not mean the absence of inequality. Eliminating the ability to measure racial disparities will not eliminate those disparities. Instead, it risks making longstanding inequities more difficult to identify, document, and address.

2. Protect Fair Representation for All Residents

I oppose changes to census residency criteria that would exclude individuals from the population count based on immigration status.

The Constitution calls for an enumeration of the population. Communities are made up of people who live, work, attend school, contribute to local economies, and depend on public infrastructure and services.

Excluding individuals from the population count could distort the actual population of states and communities, potentially affecting congressional representation and resource distribution.

Every person who ordinarily resides in a community contributes to its population and should be appropriately accounted for in determining its needs.

3. Protect Communities That Depend on Accurate Census Data

Census information is used to guide decisions involving schools, hospitals, transportation, housing, economic development, and numerous federal programs.

Undercounting communities can have lasting consequences, particularly for historically underserved populations and communities with limited economic resources.

Accurate population and demographic information allow government agencies and community leaders to make informed decisions and direct resources where they are needed most.

4. Preserve Transparency and Public Accountability

The federal government should be committed to improving the accuracy, reliability, and usefulness of census information, not limiting the information available to understand the population.

If privacy and response burden are concerns, the appropriate response should be stronger confidentiality protections, improved questionnaire design, and greater public education—not the elimination of valuable demographic information.

The Census Bureau should also provide clear evidence demonstrating that these proposed changes will improve census accuracy without creating disproportionate harm to particular communities.

Conclusion

I strongly urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed restrictions on race and ethnicity questions and reconsider the proposed changes to residency criteria.

The 2030 Census must remain an accurate, inclusive, and reliable representation of the people who make up our nation.

We cannot address problems we refuse to measure, ensure equitable representation by excluding people from the count, or make informed public policy decisions without reliable information.

Every community deserves to be counted, represented, and recognized.

I urge the Census Bureau to preserve the integrity of the decennial census and ensure that the 2030 Census serves all communities fairly and accurately.My Additional Recommendations
I would encourage you to include these three points in your comments because they are particularly important:

Protect future generations. Census data helps establish the historical record future generations use to understand population changes, discrimination, economic progress, and social inequalities.
Protect HBCUs and underserved communities. Reliable demographic information helps institutions, including Historically Black Colleges and Universities, researchers, and community organizations understand educational and economic disparities and advocate for resources.
Protect voting rights. Population data is important for redistricting and evaluating whether communities have fair political representation. Removing demographic information could make certain voting-rights violations harder to identify.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am a resident of Massachusetts, a teacher, and I care about a fair and accurate census because the census count should depend on who is actually in the state, not how people are counted on their tax returns.

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including the need to count all persons residing.

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
RE: Public Comment on Proposed Rule — Decennial Census of the Population of Americans (Docket No. USBC-2026-0628)

To the U.S. Department of Commerce and Census Bureau:

I am submitting this comment to express my serious concerns regarding the proposed changes to the decennial census residence criteria and the collection of demographic information.

For 20 years, I have served in the nonprofit sector, working alongside communities, families, and individuals navigating poverty, housing instability, educational inequities, unemployment, and barriers to economic mobility. Throughout my career, I have witnessed how public policy decisions, particularly those concerning population data and resource allocation, directly influence the well-being of communities and the capacity of organizations to respond effectively to their needs.

The fundamental responsibility of the census must remain to count people accurately and comprehensively. The Fourteenth Amendment establishes representation based on the whole number of persons in each state. A person's presence in a community is not made less significant by their immigration status, economic circumstances, housing situation, or demographic identity.

I am particularly concerned about three aspects of the proposed regulations.

First, excluding certain residents from congressional apportionment risks undermining fair representation. Communities are shaped by everyone who lives, works, raises families, attends schools, and contributes to their local economies. Excluding residents who are physically present creates the potential for a population count that fails to reflect the communities our elected officials are responsible for serving.

Second, the proposed residence criteria may disproportionately disadvantage economically vulnerable populations. Individuals experiencing homelessness, housing transitions, informal living arrangements, or inconsistent employment may not have the conventional tax records or documentation contemplated by the proposal. In my experience, these are often the very individuals whose circumstances make accurate enumeration both more challenging and more important.

Third, restricting the collection of race and ethnicity information threatens our ability to understand and address persistent disparities. For decades, nonprofit organizations, researchers, policymakers, and community leaders have relied on reliable demographic data to identify inequities, develop targeted interventions, evaluate outcomes, and advocate for appropriate resources. We cannot effectively address disparities that we are no longer able to adequately measure.

In communities like Pontiac and Detroit, Michigan, where historic disinvestment and economic disparities remain significant challenges, accurate population and demographic data are essential tools for community development, educational planning, housing policy, and economic opportunity.

I recognize the importance of maintaining an efficient, secure, and constitutionally sound census. However, efficiency should never come at the expense of accuracy, and administrative convenience should not outweigh the responsibility to ensure communities are fully and fairly represented.

I respectfully urge the Census Bureau to reconsider the proposed exclusions under §60.4, carefully evaluate the potential for undercounting under §60.2, and retain the collection of race and ethnicity information under §70.2. I further encourage the Bureau to engage directly with community-based organizations and populations historically at risk of being undercounted before adopting changes of this magnitude.

After two decades of working to strengthen communities and expand opportunities for individuals and families, I remain convinced of one principle: Good public policy begins with an accurate understanding of the people it is intended to serve.

Every community deserves to be accurately counted, meaningfully represented, and equipped with reliable information to build a stronger future.

Thank you for considering my comments.

Antoine Jackson
Nonprofit Executive | Community Development Professional
20 Years of Experience in the Nonprofit Sector
Detroit, Michigan

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
am writing to express strong opposition to the sweeping changes proposed by the U.S. Census Bureau on September 10, 2026, regarding the 2030 Decennial Census. The proposed rule to alter long-standing residence criteria and eliminate vital demographic questions threatens the accuracy, constitutional compliance, and core integrity of the upcoming count.
An accurate census is essential for the equitable distribution of billions of dollars in federal funding and the lawful apportionment of congressional representation. The proposed changes would severely disrupt this balance in several critical ways:
• Unconstitutional Exclusion of Residents from Apportionment Counts: The proposal to exclude non-U.S. citizens without a green card—such as international students, H-1B visa holders, refugees, and undocumented immigrants—flatly violates the Fourteenth Amendment. The Constitution requires a count of the "whole number of persons in each State," not a count of citizens or legal permanent residents alone.
• Erasure of Critical Race and Ethnicity Data: For the first time since 1790, the Census Bureau proposes to eliminate race and ethnicity questions from the decennial questionnaire. Stripping this data makes it impossible to understand demographic shifts, properly enforce civil rights laws, track public health disparities, or allocate localized community resources effectively.
• Ban on Future SOGI Data Collection: Prohibiting the future collection of sexual orientation and gender identity (SOGI) data deliberately keeps vulnerable and marginalized LGBTQ+ communities invisible within federal data ecosystems.
• Flawed Residence Criteria and Data Inaccuracy: Shifting the mechanism of residency tracking to tax and administrative records, rather than relying on where individuals actually live and sleep, will lead to mass undercounts. This flawed methodology threatens to miss or miscount individuals in fluid housing situations, including foster youth, college students, individuals living in shelters, and nursing home residents.
By the Census Bureau’s own admissions in its impact analysis, these structural changes will disproportionately harm and suppress the count of specific groups, creating deeply flawed and unreliable data that will degrade our democracy for the next decade.
Because of the vast ramifications of these rules, the 60-day public comment period ending on November 2, 2026, is entirely insufficient for stakeholders to evaluate the long-term impacts. We urge the Bureau to immediately withdraw this proposed rule, maintain the constitutional standard of counting every individual, and formally extend the public comment window until at least December 10, 2026, to allow for transparent, data-driven public oversight.
Thank you for your attention to these critical matters.

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census. These changes will not only weaken the accuracy and integrity of our nation's most important population count, but they will also harm our communities, and I strongly urge the Bureau to reject them. 

First, removing questions of race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation erases the full scope of my identity when I participate in the Census survey. These data points are not optional. The census is the foundation of our democracy. It must reflect the complete yet nuanced reality of who we are as a nation. And it must reflect the lives of our friends and neighbors who may not look, think, or speak like we do. I ask the Bureau to withdraw these proposed changes and to preserve a count that includes everyone and represents everyone. 

The proposed changes are totally unacceptable. 

Thank you for considering my comment.

Sincerely,
Patricia Trisko

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

Re: Docket No. 260903-0005, RIN 0607-AA75, USBC-2026-0628. “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions”

I am a resident of Puerto Rico (Guaynabo). I submit this comment to oppose proposed 15 CFR Parts 60 and 70 because of the harm they would cause to a complete and accurate count of Puerto Rico and of Puerto Ricans.

The proposed rule does not mention Puerto Rico a single time, even though the decennial census counts more than 3.2 million U.S. citizens on the island and produces the data used to redraw our legislative districts. Sections 60.5 and 70.3 refer to the “stateside census” and to the “national or state level” without defining “United States.” I ask the Census Bureau to explain in writing how Parts 60 and 70 would apply in Puerto Rico, and not to finalize any rule without doing so.

Section 70.2(a) would prohibit the Hispanic-origin question, which includes the “Puerto Rican” checkbox. More people of Puerto Rican origin now live in the states than on the island, and that question is the only way the decennial census counts them. Without it, our communities in New York, Florida, Pennsylvania, Massachusetts, Connecticut, and elsewhere would disappear from the data used to enforce civil and voting rights and to plan services. I ask that Section 70.2(a) be withdrawn.

Section 60.2(a) says usual residence “should be consistent with, and evidenced by” tax records, but does not say which ones. Most Puerto Rico residents file with the Puerto Rico Department of the Treasury (Hacienda), our local tax authority, not with the IRS; employers issue Form 499R-2/W-2PR. I ask the Census Bureau to state in writing whether it would accept Hacienda returns and Form 499R-2/W-2PR as tax records in Puerto Rico, and how it would obtain and match them.

Even if the Bureau used Hacienda returns, a residence test based on tax records would leave many people in Puerto Rico out. An estimated one-third of the population doesn’t file and works in the informal economy (Caraballo-Cueto), and retirees and low-income households often file no return at all. Moreover, there is concern that a substantial share of the returns that are filed list a P.O. box or rural route as the address, which does not identify the home where the person lives. I ask that tax records not be made the proof of residence in Puerto Rico, and that self-response and field verification be accepted.

An estimated 40% to 60% of structures in Puerto Rico have no physical street-and-number (city-style) address, the standard federal systems use, so they cannot be validated, matched, or placed on a map. Many families receive mail at P.O. boxes or rural routes rather than where they live, and our addresses use an “Urbanización” line and accents that national systems don’t match well. A record with a mailing address does not prove where a person lives. I ask the Bureau to publish Puerto Rico address-match rates for every administrative source and to keep in-person enumeration wherever addresses cannot be matched.

The Puerto Rico Community Survey and nearly all surveys are weighted to population estimates based on the decennial census. Section 70.4 says the ACS could still ask about race and origin, but without those data in the census there would be no reliable benchmark. Municipios, agencies, hospitals, universities, nonprofits, and businesses depend on these data, as does the distribution of federal funds for health, nutrition, education, housing, and disaster recovery. I ask that Part 70 not be adopted.

Puerto Rico’s Constitution requires its 40 house and 8 senate districts to be revised after each census, using block- and barrio-level data. The same count is the base for federal funds for health, nutrition, education, housing, and disaster recovery in all 78 municipios. If the rule drops households or places them at a mailing address, the next decade’s maps and funding are distorted. I ask the Bureau to publish an analysis of the rule’s effect on Puerto Rico’s population base before finalizing it.

For these reasons, I ask the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that everyone in Puerto Rico and in the diaspora is counted, once, and in the right place.

Thank you for considering this comment.

luis

The U.S. Census Bureau's proposed rule to strengthen the US Census is critical to fair representation and the future of America.  

The U.S. Census should not include distorted data in its count of Americans.  By including overly generalized ethnic demographic categories, we obscure the true goal of the census and hinder its constitutionally mandated purpose: an accurate count of Americans.  

Additionally, illegal aliens and other non-legal permanent residents should not be included for apportionment. Census data is used for the apportionment of congressional seats. Non-citizens cannot legally vote and should not be used to decrease the voting power of Americans. I support the Census Bureau in advancing the correct understanding of usual residence to recognize an element of allegiance that is antithetical to the inclusion of those not legally present in our country.  

This Census Bureau should also consider adding a citizenship question to the Census survey. The Supreme Court has already held that the Constitution lawfully permits the Census Bureau to at least inquire about citizenship on the census questionnaire. "The census should absolutely include questions related to citizenship and legal presence. 

These changes would strengthen the census in its core purpose of attaining an accurate count of Americans and have my full support. 

Thank you,  

Kaye Watson

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census. These changes will not only weaken the accuracy and integrity of our nation's most important population count, but they will also harm our communities, and I strongly urge the Bureau to reject them. 

First, removing questions of race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation erases the full scope of my identity when I participate in the Census survey. These data points are not optional. They are the tools we use to enforce civil rights laws, monitor discrimination, and measure the disparities that still affect millions of people. Excluding them from the count does not make them disappear from our society, but it does make our government less equipped to handle big issues when they arise. 

The Constitution is clear: the census must count ALL persons living in the United States, regardless of their immigration or citizenship status. The proposal to exclude non-citizens, including those residents with some type of lawful status, violates more than two centuries of legal precedent. Every person counted in this country contributes to our communities, and every person deserves to be fully seen. 

The consequences of these changes will negatively impact our daily lives. The census affects everything. It determines political representation and the drawing of voting districts. It guides how billions of dollars in federal funding are used to close persistent disparities in schools, hospitals, and other government programs that are designed to improve our lives.  

The census is the foundation of our democracy. It must reflect the complete yet nuanced reality of who we are as a nation. And it must reflect the lives of our friends and neighbors who may not look, think, or speak like we do. I ask the Bureau to withdraw these proposed changes and to preserve a count that includes everyone and represents everyone. 

Thank you for considering my comment.

Sincerely,
Darlene Collier

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am a professor of Social Work in New York City and I care about a fair and accurate census. 

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: [keep any/all points you would like to include in your comment]

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.
As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I write to oppose the proposed rule and urge the Census Bureau to withdraw proposed 15 C.F.R. Parts 60 and 70 in their entirety. [Optional: one sentence on who you are.]
1. Part 60 violates the Constitution and federal law. The Fourteenth Amendment requires apportionment by "counting the whole number of persons in each State, excluding Indians not taxed." Its only exclusion is not noncitizens. Section 1 of the same Amendment separates "citizens" from "persons," and in 1866 Congress rejected basing apportionment on voters or citizens (see Evenwel v. Abbott, 578 U.S. 54 (2016)). 2 U.S.C. 2a and 13 U.S.C. 141 likewise require the "whole number of persons in each State." Every census since 1790 has counted residents regardless of citizenship.
2. The rule misuses "usual residence." Franklin v. Massachusetts used enduring ties to add federal workers posted abroad, not to subtract people who live here. Proposed 60.4(b) excludes refugees, asylees, TPS holders who have lived here for decades, students, and visa workers in one sentence. The rule never defines when a day is spent "lawfully," offers no way to correct errors, and does not say how U.S.-citizen children of excluded parents are counted.
3. It will reduce accuracy for everyone. Using administrative records or a legal-status question to sort residents will deter mixed-status households, including citizens, from responding. The 2020 Census already undercounted Black residents by about 3.3% and Hispanic residents by about 5%. Lost residents mean lost House seats, Electoral College votes, and federal funding for every community.
4. Part 70 eliminates data essential to civil rights enforcement. Race has been asked since 1790. Block-level race and ethnicity counts in the redistricting data are how courts and States assess vote dilution and racial gerrymandering, claims that still require proof after Louisiana v. Callais. The ACS cannot substitute: it is a sample, produces no block-level data, and is itself weighted to census race counts. Administrative records are incomplete and not self-reported, contrary to OMB's SPD 15, which the notice ignores. The new MENA category would disappear before its first use.
5. The stated reasons do not hold up. The race question takes seconds, and proposed 70.2(c) already makes demographic answers voluntary. Disclosure risk has long been managed without a ban. Yet the same notice invites a legal-status question, which is far more burdensome and sensitive. That inconsistency fails the reasoned-explanation requirement of State Farm and the genuine-reasons requirement of Department of Commerce v. New York. The notice also ignores the reliance interests of States, localities, courts, and researchers (DHS v. Regents), claims no federalism effects despite shifting representation among States, proposes before tribal consultation, and preempts the subject and question reports Congress requires under 13 U.S.C. 141(f).
Please withdraw the rule. At minimum, extend the comment period to 90 days, hold public hearings, and publish a full impact analysis.

Respectfully,
Sahar Al-Gazzali

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

Re: Docket No. 260903-0005, RIN 0607-AA75, USBC-2026-0628. “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions”

I am a resident of Puerto Rico. I submit this comment to oppose proposed 15 CFR Parts 60 and 70 because of the harm they would cause to a complete and accurate count of Puerto Rico and of Puerto Ricans.

The proposed rule does not mention Puerto Rico a single time, even though the decennial census counts more than 3.2 million U.S. citizens on the island and produces the data used to redraw our legislative districts. Sections 60.5 and 70.3 refer to the “stateside census” and to the “national or state level” without defining “United States.” I ask the Census Bureau to explain in writing how Parts 60 and 70 would apply in Puerto Rico, and not to finalize any rule without doing so.

Section 70.2(a) would prohibit the Hispanic-origin question, which includes the “Puerto Rican” checkbox. More people of Puerto Rican origin now live in the states than on the island, and that question is the only way the decennial census counts them. Without it, our communities in New York, Florida, Pennsylvania, Massachusetts, Connecticut, and elsewhere would disappear from the data used to enforce civil and voting rights and to plan services. I ask that Section 70.2(a) be withdrawn.

Section 60.2(a) says usual residence “should be consistent with, and evidenced by” tax records, but does not say which ones. Most Puerto Rico residents file with the Puerto Rico Department of the Treasury (Hacienda), our local tax authority, not with the IRS; employers issue Form 499R-2/W-2PR. I ask the Census Bureau to state in writing whether it would accept Hacienda returns and Form 499R-2/W-2PR as tax records in Puerto Rico, and how it would obtain and match them.

Even if the Bureau used Hacienda returns, a residence test based on tax records would leave many people in Puerto Rico out. An estimated one-third of the population doesn’t file and works in the informal economy (Caraballo-Cueto), and retirees and low-income households often file no return at all. Moreover, there is concern that a substantial share of the returns that are filed list a P.O. box or rural route as the address, which does not identify the home where the person lives. I ask that tax records not be made the proof of residence in Puerto Rico, and that self-response and field verification be accepted.

The Bureau invites comments on adding a legal-status question to the questionnaire. I oppose it. Puerto Rico has long-established immigrant communities and many mixed-status households that include U.S. citizens. The fear such a question creates would suppress response from entire households and worsen undercounts in the barrios and municipios where they live.

The Puerto Rico Community Survey and nearly all surveys are weighted to population estimates based on the decennial census. Section 70.4 says the ACS could still ask about race and origin, but without those data in the census there would be no reliable benchmark. Municipios, agencies, hospitals, universities, nonprofits, and businesses depend on these data, as does the distribution of federal funds for health, nutrition, education, housing, and disaster recovery. I ask that Part 70 not be adopted.

For these reasons, I ask the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that everyone in Puerto Rico and in the diaspora is counted, once, and in the right place.

Thank you for considering this comment.

* Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

* Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools

* Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

* Planning transportation, including roads and public transit

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481

It guides how billions of dollars in federal funding are distributed to improve local  schools, hospitals, and other government programs that benefit all Americans.  

The census is the foundation of our democracy. It must reflect the complete yet nuanced reality of who we are as a nation. And it must reflect the lives of our friends and neighbors who may not look, think, or speak like we do. I ask the Bureau to withdraw these proposed changes and to preserve a count that includes everyone and represents everyone. 

Thank you for considering my comment.

Sincerely,
Bruce Bridwell

Count every U.S. resident, including visa-holders, refugees, and asylum seekers.
Establish detailed  guidelines for complex residential situations such as recent movers, people in temporary situations, and children in foster care.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: 91 FR 57524  Public Comment,Re: Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions (Docket No. USBC-2026-0628).I am writing to oppose the Census Bureau's proposed rule, "Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions," Docket No. USBC-2026-0628, because it would produce an inaccurate count of the people living in this country.Every ten years, the census gives the country one reliable picture of who lives here. Without that information, it is much harder to show where needs are greatest, enforce civil rights laws, check whether voting maps are fair, or catch health problems that hit some communities harder. States, local governments, and health systems would have to collect it themselves, adding cost and producing less reliable numbers.This is a poor use of public money. More than $2.8 trillion a year in federal funding follows census numbers. When the count is wrong, that money goes to the wrong places for at least ten years, and schools, clinics, roads, and emergency plans are built for a population that does not match reality. Lower response rates also mean more costly follow-up work, paid for by taxpayers.A bad count in 2030 cannot be corrected until at least 2040. Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
RE: Opposition to Proposed 2030 Census Rule
Docket No. USBC-2026-0628

Dear U.S. Census Bureau,

I am writing as a resident of Taylor, Texas, a mother, grandmother, and someone who cares deeply about the future of my community and the people who call it home.

I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census.

The Fourteenth Amendment requires congressional representation to be based on the "whole number of persons in each State." Our census has long counted residents regardless of citizenship or immigration status. This proposal would change that fundamental principle by excluding millions of people, including some who are here legally, from the population count used to determine congressional representation.

But my concerns go beyond who gets counted. They extend to who gets seen, who gets heard, and whose needs are recognized.

Here in Taylor, I have witnessed residents of historically underserved neighborhoods, particularly Black residents in District 1, struggle to have their voices heard on decisions affecting their homes, neighborhoods, parks, and environment.

These are families who have lived, worked, raised children, and contributed to our community for generations. Yet too often, they must fight simply to be included in discussions about decisions that will affect their quality of life.

Removing race and ethnicity questions from the census threatens to make these inequalities even harder to identify and address.

How can we recognize disparities in education, housing, health care, environmental conditions, or public investment if we stop collecting the information that helps reveal them?

How can communities demonstrate unequal treatment or challenge unfair congressional districts without reliable demographic data?

We cannot correct inequalities we refuse to measure.

I am equally concerned about excluding residents based on immigration status and the increased reliance on government records to classify people. Such changes could undermine trust in the census and discourage families from participating.

And when families are afraid to participate, the consequences can extend to entire neighborhoods, including American citizens.

Our schools still need teachers. Our children still need services. Our neighborhoods still need safe roads, clean air, and reliable infrastructure. Excluding people from congressional apportionment doesn't make those needs disappear.

An accurate census is essential to fair representation and informed decisions about the resources our communities need.

The census should reflect the people who live in our communities—not redefine who matters within them.

I strongly urge the Census Bureau to withdraw this proposed rule, continue counting all usual residents for congressional apportionment, and preserve the collection of race and ethnicity information needed to protect civil rights and identify disparities.

Every community deserves to be counted accurately. Every community deserves to be seen.

And no community should become invisible simply because its residents have too little political power to demand otherwise.

Thank you for considering my comments.

Respectfully,
A concerned resident of Taylor, Texas

Comment: US Census Bureau,I urge you to withdraw the proposed 2030 Census rule, including the requirement that a person’s usual residence be consistent with and evidenced by their tax records.This requirement could leave tens of millions of people out of the Census. Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am a college professor who lives in Boston, Massachusetts, and I care about a fair and accurate census because my students spend most of their time in Boston, most of them vote locally, and their lives are affected by the quality of Boston's services which in turn depend on funding..

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: keeping the old rules about residency, where students and others who spend most of their time in a place count as living there.

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.
