Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to oppose Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions (Document ID: USBC-2026-0628-0001) for multiple reasons.
1.	I oppose the inclusion of a legal status question on the short-form decennial census questionnaire (or any census questionnaire) because it will reduce response rates and result in underrepresentation from mixed citizenship status households.
a.	Just because the court ruled that the enumeration clause allows a question on citizenship status, does not mean adding such a question is a good idea. As many experts observed during the court cases on this issue, asking about citizenship on the U.S. census short form will likely have a chilling effect on mixed citizenship status households and reduce overall response rates. For example, even if someone is a U.S. citizen entitled to enumeration and U.S. House representation, they may be afraid to respond to the census if they live in a household with people of varying citizenship status. This chilling effect would disproportionally suppress enumeration needed for apportionment of House seats and defeat the stated enumeration purpose of the census itself. 
b.	I also oppose asking about citizenship because there is a history of this kind of census information being used against U.S. citizens, such as the information-sharing used to identify and detain Japanese Americans during World War II, a shame on our nation’s history that should not be repeated.
2.	I oppose using tax records to count and enumerate people in the Census because it will result in the underrepresentation of low income people who do not file taxes.
a.	Limiting enumeration for the U.S. Census to people who file their taxes is counterproductive to the stated goals of this proposed rule, which is to count everyone who is eligible for political representation in the U.S. House. Many low-income people, including young people and seniors, do not file taxes. For 2025, the minimum income for Single filing status for filers under age 65 is $15,750. Limiting enumeration to people who file taxes would thus disproportionately undercount people in populations and communities that do not file taxes, resulting under-enumeration and underrepresentation in Congress. Given that U.S. Census data is used to allocate funding for Medicaid and hundreds of federal programs, the exclusion of low-income people who do not file taxes from the U.S. Census is especially problematic. 
3.	I oppose exclusion of demographic questions because it has the potential to result in the reduction of funding and resource allocations to low income communities.
a.	The proposed rule states that small governments will not be harmed by the exclusion of demographic questions from the short form census because this information can be obtained from other sources. However, the U.S. Census is the only source of census-tract level data used for hundreds of funding formulas and allocations—so this information cannot necessarily be obtained from other sources. Thus, small businesses, local and state governments, and many communities will be harmed by the exclusion of demographic questions proposed in this draft rule. I oppose this change because it has the potential to cut funding to low-income communities.

While the distortion of census data to prevent reidentification is a problem, this rule (including its proposed use of multiple data sources to violate people's confidentiality by identifying their citizenship status through other sources!) is not the solution. Please rescind this misguided rule in its entirety. Thank you for your consideration.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
ME/CFS San Diego opposes the proposed changes to the 2030 Census and urges the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule.

Accurate population data are essential to public health, healthcare planning, research, and the equitable distribution of resources. Organizations working with underserved patient populations depend on reliable data to understand community needs, identify disparities, plan services, and advocate for appropriate resources.

People living with ME/CFS and other poorly understood, underfunded chronic illnesses already face substantial barriers to healthcare, research participation, and adequate support. These populations are often overlooked in healthcare planning and resource allocation. Policies that further compromise the accuracy and completeness of population data risk making underserved communities even less visible.

We are particularly concerned about:

Excluding residents from population counts: Every person living in a community contributes to its needs and should be reflected in the population data used for representation and resource allocation. Excluding entire categories of residents will produce an inaccurate picture of communities and their needs.
Eliminating race and ethnicity data: These data are important for identifying health disparities, understanding unequal access to healthcare, and ensuring that research and public health initiatives address the needs of diverse populations. Removing them would make it harder to identify and respond to inequities.
Restricting future demographic data collection: Prohibiting questions about sexual orientation limits the ability to collect information that may be important for understanding health disparities and the needs of underserved populations.
Reliable data are fundamental to effective public health policy. We cannot adequately identify disparities, allocate resources, or address unmet healthcare needs when the underlying population data are incomplete or systematically exclude people.

ME/CFS San Diego urges the Census Bureau to withdraw this proposed rule and preserve a fair, accurate, inclusive, and comprehensive census that reflects the people who actually live in our communities.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
PUBLIC COMMENT
Docket No. USBC-2026-0628
RE: Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions

I am submitting this comment in opposition to the proposed rule changing the residence criteria used for congressional apportionment and restricting demographic questions on the decennial census.

1. The proposed residence criteria conflict with 230 years of practice and the Constitution's own text.

Every census since the first one in 1790 has counted everyone living in the United States for purposes of apportionment, citizens and noncitizens alike. The Fourteenth Amendment requires apportionment to be based on "the whole number of persons in each State," not "citizens" and not "lawful residents." That word choice was not accidental, and the rule's own preamble acknowledges as much. The proposed rule nonetheless asks the public to accept that "persons" secretly meant the narrower, allegiance-based category of "inhabitants" the agency now prefers. No court has adopted that reading for the purpose of congressional apportionment. Franklin v. Massachusetts examined "usual residence" only in the narrow context of overseas federal personnel, not as a basis for excluding entire categories of people who live, work, and raise families in this country every day.

2. The rule concedes it does not know its own impact.

The preamble includes no estimate of how many House seats or Electoral College votes would shift under this rule. That omission matters. This proposal reaches further than any prior version of this policy. Past attempts targeted undocumented immigrants specifically; this one also excludes people who are legally present on work visas, student visas, and pending asylum or refugee applications. An agency proposing to redraw the basis of political representation for the next decade should be able to say, at a minimum, what the proposal actually does. This one does not.

3. Removing race and ethnicity questions removes the tool used to enforce voting rights.

Block-level race and ethnicity data from the census is the evidentiary foundation for Voting Rights Act claims and redistricting challenges nationwide, including the 2022 ruling that struck down Maryland's own congressional map as an extreme partisan gerrymander. Eliminating this data does not make redistricting colorblind. It makes racial discrimination in redistricting harder to prove and therefore harder to stop.

4. States with large immigrant populations would bear a disproportionate cost.

Roughly one in six Maryland residents is foreign-born. Because congressional apportionment divides a fixed total of 435 seats, any reduction in one state's counted population does not just cost that state, it hands a windfall to states with smaller immigrant populations, regardless of how many people actually live in either state. The same dynamic applies to the $2.8 trillion in annual federal funding tied to census counts, funding for schools, hospitals, and infrastructure that serves entire communities regardless of any individual resident's immigration status.

5. This rule compresses a decade-defining decision into a 30-day comment window, and does so through unilateral regulation rather than the public process the Census Bureau itself has historically used to set residence criteria.

For these reasons, I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw both proposed changes and retain the residence and demographic-question criteria used for the 2020 census until a change of this magnitude can be considered through Congress or a longer, fully transparent rulemaking process.

Hilary Hershey
Chester, MD

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). 

As an educator, I care about a fair and accurate census because census data and other federal datasets based on the census are used to make key decisions that affect our nation’s students, educators, and schools.  

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Examples of these uses include: . 

* Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. 

* Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

* Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

* Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

* Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

* Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

* Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

* Determining state higher education funding formulas 

* Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

* Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

* Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

First, to ensure a fair and accurate census,  the Census Bureau should  extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. Second, I oppose both the proposed changes to the residence criteria and the proposed regulations regarding demographic questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. The Census Bureau should  withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The Constitution requires  counting all people living in the United States. 

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (including children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count. 

Revise the tax records language so that those whose mailing address differs from their residential address (servicemembers, those with a post office box) are not excluded.  

• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for civil rights enforcement, among other uses, and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The prohibition, as written, may also restrict the collection or publication of census data on same-sex couples that was asked in 2020. 

 The proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Sincerely,
Mrs. Tami Porter
Nampa, ID

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). 

As an educator, I care about a fair and accurate census because census data and other federal datasets based on the census are used to make key decisions that affect our nation’s students, educators, and schools.  

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Examples of these uses include: . 

* Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. 

* Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

* Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

* Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

* Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

* Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

* Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

* Determining state higher education funding formulas 

* Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

* Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

* Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

First, to ensure a fair and accurate census,  the Census Bureau should  extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. Second, I oppose both the proposed changes to the residence criteria and the proposed regulations regarding demographic questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. The Census Bureau should  withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The Constitution requires  counting all people living in the United States. 

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (including children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count. 

Revise the tax records language so that those whose mailing address differs from their residential address (servicemembers, those with a post office box) are not excluded.  

• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for civil rights enforcement, among other uses, and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The prohibition, as written, may also restrict the collection or publication of census data on same-sex couples that was asked in 2020. 

 The proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Sincerely,
Penny Abstetar, PhD

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including:
• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Dear Deputy General Sweeney,
I submit these comments in OPPOSITION to the proposed changes to the Decennial Census (Docket ID USBC-2026-0628).
As a Pacific Islander working alongside Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander (NHPI) communities, I am deeply concerned about how these changes would affect our people, our families, and future generations.
Protect the collection of race, ethnicity, and disaggregated NHPI data.
Native Hawaiians and Pacific Islanders are not one homogeneous population. Our communities include Native Hawaiians, Samoans, Tongans, Chamorros, Marshallese, Chuukese, Palauans, Yapese, Fijians, and many other distinct Pacific peoples, each with our own histories, languages, cultures, and experiences.
For decades, our communities have fought to be recognized in federal data rather than grouped into broader racial categories that make our needs invisible. Eliminating race and ethnicity data would reverse that progress.
Accurate, disaggregated data helps us understand disparities in maternal and infant health, chronic disease, education, housing, employment, and access to healthcare. It allows community organizations, researchers, and policymakers to identify needs, direct resources, and determine whether programs are reaching our people.
Without this information, inequities do not disappear. We simply lose the ability to document them and hold systems accountable.
Respect the distinct histories and political relationships of our Pacific peoples.
Native Hawaiians have a unique political and historical relationship with the United States, including federal trust responsibilities that must be honored. The Census Bureau must meaningfully consult with Native Hawaiian Organizations before making changes that affect their communities.
Other Pacific Islanders also have distinct relationships with the United States, including the peoples of American Samoa, Guam, the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, and citizens of the Federated States of Micronesia, the Republic of the Marshall Islands, and the Republic of Palau living in the United States under the Compacts of Free Association.
These relationships are not interchangeable. Federal policies must recognize our different political statuses, histories, and circumstances while ensuring every community is accurately represented.
Maintain residency criteria that support an accurate and complete count.
Our Pacific families are connected across islands, states, and nations. Many move for education, employment, military service, medical care, and family responsibilities. Others live in multigenerational households or experience housing instability.
Changes to residency criteria must not create additional barriers for these families or for people who are incarcerated, displaced, or temporarily living away from home.
The Census Bureau must preserve residency standards that support an accurate count and carefully consider how changes would affect NHPI communities.
Protect equitable representation and federal resources.
Census data informs decisions affecting healthcare, education, housing, infrastructure, and public services. For our rural, neighboring island, and underserved Pacific communities, these decisions have lasting consequences.
Community health workers, cultural practitioners, healthcare providers, and grassroots organizations depend on accurate information to understand community needs and advocate for appropriate resources.
When our people are undercounted or their identities disappear from federal data, the consequences go beyond statistics. They affect whether families receive services, whether communities receive investments, and whether our voices are represented in decisions affecting our future.
Extend the comment period and engage our communities.
I urge the Census Bureau to extend the public comment period through December 10, 2026, and provide meaningful opportunities for NHPI participation, including language-accessible outreach and engagement with community-based organizations.
Our people deserve sufficient time and information to understand and respond to decisions that will affect generations.
For our Pacific communities, being counted is about more than numbers. It is about recognizing our existence, honoring our distinct identities, understanding the conditions our families live in, and ensuring our communities have a voice.
We have spent generations advocating to be seen, heard, and counted. Federal policy should strengthen that progress, not erase it.
I respectfully urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed changes that would eliminate demographic data collection, preserve detailed race and ethnicity data, maintain residency criteria that support an accurate count, and meaningfully engage NHPI communities.
Our people count. Our identities matter. Our data matters. Our future generations deserve to be seen.
Respectfully,
Chantelle Eseta Matagi
Executive Director, Tagata Moana Hui Foundation
Oʻahu, Hawaiʻi

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Dear Director Cook, 

As a citizen of the United states of America, I appreciate the opportunity to comment on the Census Bureau's proposed rule governing residence criteria and demographic questions for the 2030 decennial census. The census is the foundation for distributing political representation and federal resources. Accurate census ensures communities receive fair funding for infrastructure, housing, education, public safety, emergency response and other essential services. Because census data guide funding and planning decision for the next decade, accuracy is critical.  

We are concerned that several provisions of the proposed rule could reduce the accuracy of our community's population count and affect our access to federal and state resources. 

Concerns about the Proposed Changes 

Apportionment and population count: The proposed rule would limit the population counted toward apportionment to U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents for the first time. Although this change applies only to apportionment, it may create confusion or fear among residents and discourage participation. We request additional information on how full population data would be collected, reported and communicated, to ensure that all residents are counted for the broader data set. 

Legal-status question: The proposed rule also raises the possibility of adding a legal-status question to the census questionnaire. Similar proposals considered for the 2020 Census were not adopted following concerns that it could reduce participation, particularly among immigrant and mixed-status households. Any decline in response rates would undermine the accuracy of our community's population count as a whole and could impact the resources available to young children and families specifically. 

Usual residence and the enumeration period: The proposed shift to counting residents based on where they spend the most time during a January 3-April 1 period, rather than their usual residence throughout the year, could affect our population count [of seasonal residents such as snowbirds/ students / part-time workers / other mobile populations]. We ask the Bureau to further evaluate the operational and data-accuracy impacts of this change and explain the rationale supporting it.  

Reliance on administrative records: Increased reliance on tax, immigration, health and other administrative records raises concerns about the potential undercount of populations in our community that may not be consistently represented in those records, including low-income households, college students, non-filers and children. We request additional information regarding when these records will be used and how the Bureau will ensure accurate counts for populations with less reliable administrative data.  

Demographic questions: The proposal would eliminate race and ethnicity questions, while making most other demographic questions optional. Accurate demographic data is essential to municipal planning and service delivery. Understanding who lives in our community gives local governments the ability to plan for our current population and take into consideration our future population's needs.  This data has many uses with huge implications and repercussions that will last for ten years. For example monitoring equitable service deliverables, administering  specific programs, public health planning, economic development targeting, etc. The loss or reduction in the quality of this data could affect our ability to provide much needed services to our residents and accurately plan for our future.  

Funding impact: Census data inform funding for other programs including Community Development Block Grants (CDBG), transit formula funding, and Title I education funding. An undercount of any portion of our population reduces resources available to the entire community — not just the households or individuals who go uncounted. Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Public Comment Opposing the Removal of Race and Ethnicity Questions from the U.S. Census

I strongly oppose the proposed removal of questions concerning race and ethnicity from the decennial U.S. Census. Collecting comprehensive demographic information is essential to understanding the composition of the U.S. population, tracking changes over time, evaluating economic and social progress, and informing government policy and resource allocation.

1. Race and ethnicity data are essential to accurately measuring demographic and economic trends.
The Census is one of the federal government's most important tools for understanding the population it serves. Collecting information about race and ethnicity allows the government to identify where different populations live, monitor changes in population composition, and evaluate disparities in economic opportunity, housing, education, employment, healthcare, and other areas of public life. These data are particularly important when comparing demographic and economic trends across census cycles. They allow policymakers, researchers, and public institutions to assess whether particular populations are experiencing economic advancement, stagnation, or declining opportunities. Without consistent racial and ethnic demographic data, the government would lose an essential means of measuring these changes and identifying which populations are benefiting from, or being excluded by, public policies. Furthermore, demographic information is critical to understanding domestic migration which is not static. Over the next 10, 20, or 30 years, migration patterns, regional population growth, and the racial and ethnic composition of communities across the country will continue to change. The Northeast Corridor, the West Coast, the Southwest, and the Southern border states are already experiencing distinct demographic shifts. Maintaining consistent census data is necessary to understand these developments and make informed projections about the country's future population.

2. Retaining racial and ethnic data serves the government's own institutional and policy interests, regardless of its political priorities.
There is also an important institutional consideration that shouldn’t be overlooked: the federal government has a vested interest in knowing the racial and ethnic composition of the population, regardless of the political ideology or policy objectives of the administration in power. Demographic data allow governments to understand which populations are growing, where they are concentrated, how their economic circumstances are changing, and how public policies affect different racial and ethnic groups. They inform decisions about federal funding, infrastructure investment, public services, regulatory oversight, and the distribution of government resources.
Even an administration pursuing policies intended to advantage particular racial or ethnic populations would have an institutional interest in retaining this information. Without reliable demographic data, how would the government measure whether its policies are achieving their intended demographic outcomes? How would it determine where particular populations are concentrated, whether their economic standing is changing, or how migration patterns are reshaping the communities in which they live? How would it evaluate whether its funding priorities are benefiting the populations it intends to prioritize? Eliminating the collection of racial and ethnic information would undermine the government's own capacity to measure the demographic consequences of its policies. This is true regardless of whether those policies are intended to reduce racial disparities, maintain existing inequalities, or advantage particular populations. The collection of race and ethnicity data is therefore not inherently tied to any particular political philosophy. It is an essential instrument of governance, accountability, and policy evaluation. Maintaining these questions ensures that the federal government retains the ability to understand the population it governs and measure the consequences of its decisions.

I urge the Census Bureau to retain the collection of race and ethnicity information in the decennial Census. The ability to measure demographic change accurately is in the government's own long-term institutional interest, regardless of which administration is in power or what political objectives it seeks to advance.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am a resident of Ohio, demographer, and former president of Population Association of America, and I care about a fair and accurate census because I want to ensure people in the U.S. are accurately counted and I use Census data for social science research.

First, please extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. Significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions.

• Given the purpose of the Census is count all people, please abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. 

• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.

• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.

• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.

• Revise the language on tax records because tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.

• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The Census is used to weight other surveys and the exclusion of demographic measures will make this impossible. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Best, Wendy Manning

Re: Docket No. 260903-0005, RIN 0607-AA75, USBC-2026-0628. “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions”

Soy puertorriqueño/a y vivo en los Estados Unidos (Florida). Someto este comentario para expresar mi oposición a las Partes 60 y 70 propuestas del Título 15 del Código de Regulaciones Federales, por el daño que causarían a un conteo completo y correcto de Puerto Rico y de los puertorriqueños.

Como puertorriqueña, profesional de la psicología, la consejería y el case management, y como ciudadana responsable que trabaja y paga sus contribuciones, me preocupa profundamente cualquier iniciativa que pretenda eliminar el renglón específico que nos identifica como puertorriqueños en el Censo.

La categoría de «hispanos» es amplia y diversa. Aunque compartimos raíces lingüísticas y culturales con otros pueblos, los puertorriqueños tenemos una identidad histórica, cultural y social particular, con nuestras propias tradiciones, costumbres, circunstancias políticas y una relación jurídica única con Estados Unidos. Nuestra identidad no debe diluirse en una categoría general que no refleje plenamente quiénes somos ni nuestras realidades particulares.

Esto no es solamente un asunto de identidad; también puede tener consecuencias concretas para nuestra gente. La manera en que se recopilan y clasifican los datos poblacionales puede influir en la planificación, la distribución de recursos y la justificación de fondos destinados a programas y servicios esenciales. Necesitamos que se evalúe cuidadosamente cómo cualquier cambio podría afectar a los niños que reciben servicios educativos y ayudas, las personas con discapacidades, los estudiantes con necesidades especiales y nuestros adultos mayores, entre otras poblaciones vulnerables de Puerto Rico.

Aunque actualmente resido en la diáspora, mi compromiso con Puerto Rico sigue intacto. Mi padre es un adulto mayor y veterano del Ejército; mi hermano pertenece a la Fuerza Aérea de Estados Unidos, y mi hermana es maestra de niños con discapacidades y necesidades especiales. Desde mi experiencia profesional y familiar, conozco la importancia de proteger a quienes dependen de servicios, apoyos y recursos para vivir con dignidad. No podemos permitir que una decisión administrativa termine invisibilizando nuestras particularidades o dificultando que se identifiquen y atiendan adecuadamente las necesidades de nuestra población. Nuestros niños, las personas con discapacidades y nuestros envejecientes merecen ser contados, reconocidos y considerados en las decisiones que afectan su bienestar.

Defender el renglón de los puertorriqueños no significa separarnos de nuestros hermanos hispanos; significa reconocer que la diversidad también requiere precisión, representación y respeto por las identidades particulares.

La Encuesta sobre la Comunidad de Puerto Rico y casi todas las encuestas se ajustan a estimados de población basados en el Censo decenal. La sección 70.4 dice que la ACS aún podría preguntar sobre raza y origen, pero sin esos datos en el Censo no habría punto de referencia confiable. Municipios, agencias, hospitales, universidades, organizaciones sin fines de lucro y negocios dependen de estos datos, igual que la distribución de fondos federales para salud, alimentos, educación, vivienda y recuperación de desastres. Solicito que no se adopte la Parte 70.

La Constitución de Puerto Rico exige revisar los 40 distritos representativos y los 8 senatoriales después de cada censo, a partir de datos por bloque y barrio. El mismo conteo es la base de fondos federales para salud, nutrición, educación, vivienda y recuperación de desastres en los 78 municipios. Si la regla deja fuera hogares o los ubica en su dirección postal, los mapas y los fondos de la próxima década se distorsionan. Solicito que la Oficina publique un análisis del efecto de la regla en la base poblacional de Puerto Rico antes de adoptarla.

Por estas razones, solicito que la Oficina del Censo retire la regla propuesta y garantice que todas las personas en Puerto Rico y en la diáspora sean contadas, una vez y en el lugar correcto.

Gracias por considerar este comentario.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census. These changes will not only weaken the accuracy and integrity of our nation's most important population count, but they will also harm our communities, and I strongly urge the Bureau to reject them. 

First, removing questions of race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation erases the full scope of my identity when I participate in the Census survey. These data points are not optional. They are the tools we use to enforce civil rights laws, monitor discrimination, and measure the disparities that still affect millions of people. Excluding them from the count does not make them disappear from our society, but it does make our government less equipped to handle big issues when they arise. 

The Constitution is clear: the census must count ALL persons living in the United States, regardless of their immigration or citizenship status. The proposal to exclude non-citizens, including those residents with some type of lawful status, violates more than two centuries of legal precedent. Every person counted in this country contributes to our communities, and every person deserves to be fully seen. 

The consequences of these changes will negatively impact our daily lives. The census affects everything. It determines political representation and the drawing of voting districts. It guides how billions of dollars in federal funding are used to close persistent disparities in schools, hospitals, and other government programs that are designed to improve our lives.  

The census is the foundation of our democracy. It must reflect the complete yet nuanced reality of who we are as a nation. And it must reflect the lives of our friends and neighbors who may not look, think, or speak like we do. I ask the Bureau to withdraw these proposed changes and to preserve a count that includes everyone and represents everyone. 

Thank you for considering my comment.

Sincerely,
Anita Brown

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Re: Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026. 
Dear U.S. Census Bureau:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions.” 
I am a native-born US citizen who cares about our constitution and our nation. I am deeply concerned about the proposal to radically change the U.S. census.  In light of the possible change to a process which has informed our nation since its founding, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but not enough. Significant regulatory actions like this deserve a full 90 days for the public to learn of the proposal, consider it, and express their opinions.
I oppose both parst 60 and 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions. I would suggest the following:
• Abandon all criteria that would exclude non-U.S. citizens who reside in the United States, including Lawful Permanent Residents, refugees, asylum seekers, workers, long-term students, TPS holders, undocumented immigrants and others present in the United States except for tourists and casual visitors.  The purpose of the census is to count all people residing in the U.S.
• Clarify guidelines for the range of residence such as for people who have recently moved, individuals and families in temporary shelters, children in foster care, etc. 
• Reinstate the activity-based standard for determining residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps.
• Ensure as complete a count as possible, setting procedures which will capture individuals such as seasonal workers, homeless people, and individuals who have recently changed residence in the correct locality on census day.  
• Stop including incarcerated people as “residing” in the jurisdiction where they are detained or imprisoned, and count them at the residence where they lived before incarceration. The current system improperly gives inflated representation to localities which have a prison industry, and deprives localities where those individuals actually lived and will likely return to.
• Change  the language on tax records. The following verbiage is unhelpful: “A person's ‘usual residence’ should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms).”  This ignores the particularities of tax records, which may reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Include and improve demographic questions on race and ethnicity. I was a census enumerator. Many individuals wanted to select “Latino” as their race, and could not do so. Many individuals wanted to select multiple races, and could not do so.  The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is important for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be improved. 
As written, the proposed rule would undercount residents, count some in the wrong jurisdiction, and decrease the usefulness of the data collected.  
Sincerely,
Toni Maschler

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: 91 FR 57524  Public Comment,I am submitting this comment in opposition to the Census Bureau's proposed rule on residence criteria and demographic questions for the decennial census, 91 FR 57524 (Sept. 10, 2026). This proposed rule makes significant changes to the 2030 Census, including leaving noncitizens without green cards out of the count used to divide seats in Congress, removing race and ethnicity questions, and possibly adding a citizenship or immigration status question. The Census determines congressional representation and guides planning for health, education, housing, and infrastructure, along with the distribution of more than $2.8 trillion a year across roughly 350 federal programs. When communities are miscounted or left out in the decennial Census, they lose their fair share of representation and resources for an entire decade. This rule violates the Constitution and federal law, which both count the "whole number of persons" in each state, not just citizens. Congress chose "persons" over "citizens" on purpose, and counting only some residents revives the logic of the three-fifths clause. Changing who counts would require a constitutional amendment, not a census rule. The Supreme Court recognized in 2016 that representation serves all residents, including children and noncitizens, not only voters. Under this rule, millions of people who live, work, pay taxes, and raise families here would no longer count, weakening the voting power of the communities they belong to, including the citizens who live alongside them. A citizenship question would make this worse. The success of the Census depends on public trust. Every person must feel confident that answering is safe, confidential, and separate from immigration enforcement. It would suppress participation among immigrant families, including naturalized citizens and citizen children, and increase fear and confusion about how Census information will be used. That means less accurate data for apportionment, redistricting, and funding formulas, higher costs as the Bureau chases households that did not respond, and resources directed away from Black and Brown communities. Removing race and ethnicity questions would also take away data that federal law requires to protect civil rights. This data helps reveal discrimination in housing, jobs, and voting, and shows whether district lines split up or pack a community to weaken its vote. Without them, unfair treatment becomes much harder to prove and solve. Lauren GarcesLauren@sdapicoalition.org10232 Maya Linda RdSan Diego, California 92126

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Re: Docket USBC-2026-0628 — Proposed Census Residence Criteria and Demographic Questions

I am a Snoqualmie Tribal citizen and a member of the Snoqualmie Tribal Council. I am submitting these comments in my individual capacity, not on behalf of the Snoqualmie Indian Tribe.

Through my work on our Tribe’s Census efforts, I have seen how much care, communication and trust it takes to reach people and help them understand why being counted matters. A count is not just a number on a page. It affects how communities are seen and the information governments have when planning for the people they serve.

I am concerned about the proposal to prohibit race and ethnicity questions on the decennial enumeration questionnaire. If the federal government does not ask people how they identify, it risks making Native people and other communities harder to see in the data used to understand their circumstances. I am also concerned about the proposed exclusion of certain noncitizens from the apportionment count. People live, work and raise families in our communities regardless of citizenship status. A census should give us an accurate picture of the people who are here. Changes that cause people to fear participating or leave residents out of the count can weaken that picture and the trust needed to obtain it.

Before moving forward, I urge the Census Bureau to engage in meaningful government-to-government consultation with Tribal Nations, explain the likely effects on Tribal data and communities, and consider alternatives that protect privacy while preserving an accurate count and useful information. Tribal Nations should have a real opportunity to understand and influence decisions that affect our people.

Respectfully,
Christina Sparling
Snoqualmie Tribal citizen
Submitted in my individual capacity

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I submit this comment in opposition to the proposed changes to the rules governing the 2030 Census.
1. The Constitution requires counting "the whole number of persons", not citizens.  Section 1 of the 14th Amendment defines citizenship; Section 2 deliberately uses different language -- "the whole number of persons in each State."  A rule that tallies only some persons, and then asks who qualifies, is not the enumeration the Constitution requires.  If every person is required to complete a census form, then every person must be counted, regardless of citizenship.
2. A legal-status question endangers human life.  Given the enforcement actions of the past year and the absence of accountability for them, requiring households to document who is and is not a citizen puts people at risk, including citizens.  This is a moral matter.  My conscience compels me to oppose any requirement to report immigration status when doing so could become a death sentence for our neighbors.
3. Participation will fall, and citizens will be harmed along with noncitizens.  Mixed-status households -- including those with citizen children -- are the least likely to respond to a questionnaire that asks about legal status.  Every nonresponse is an undercount of real people, including U.S. citizens.  Census Bureau leadership itself has acknowledged that a citizenship question "would dampen participation".
4.  Residence cannot be established by a snapshot or by tax paperwork.  A single Census Day cannot capture "usual residence," and neither can a fixed window such as January through April, which biases the count against northern states whose residents spend those months elsewhere.  Tax records reflect mailing addresses, not where people actually live; they are often stale, incomplete, and frequently nonresidential (like P.O. boxes).  Tax records also do not cover everyone, and processing schedules do not align with the census calendar, meaning millions could be missed or counted in the wrong place.
5. These proposals do not exist in a vacuum, and their stated rationale does not survive scrutiny. The removal of race and ethnicity questions while adding a legal-status question would have opposite effects on response rates, so accuracy and completion cannot be the true objective.  What these changes share is a mechanism for categorizing and excluding people from the political count -- one that makes noncitizens easier to surveil, target, and intimidate, while rendering minority populations statistically invisible so their needs can be disregarded when services and funding are allocated. A census designed this way would serve enforcement objectives rather than statistical ones, and the Bureau's statutory duty is to the latter.
6. Undercounts punish communities that already receive the least. Census data drive the distributions of federal funds for health care, schools, roads, food assistance, and housing. An undercount means fewer resources for services that citizens depend on.
For these reasons I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposal to exclude noncitizens from the apportionment count, to remove any legal-status question from the decennial instrument, to retain race and ethnicity questions, and to preserve a respondent-based definition of usual residence.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Why Noncitizens Should Not Be Included in the Census for Political Representation

The U.S. Census plays a fundamental role in determining political representation, the distribution of federal resources, and the balance of power among states. While every person living in America deserves basic human consideration and access to necessary public services, there is a legitimate argument that noncitizens should not be included in the population figures used to determine congressional representation.

The Constitution guarantees representation to the people of this country, but including noncitizens in the apportionment process allows individuals who cannot vote in federal elections to increase a state's political influence. This creates an imbalance between states and raises questions about whether American citizens' voting power is being diluted.

Consider that two states could have identical populations, yet one could have substantially fewer citizens because of its noncitizen population. Both would receive comparable congressional representation, despite having significantly different numbers of eligible voters. Citizens in states with larger noncitizen populations could therefore have less political influence per eligible voter.

There is also a question of fairness to American taxpayers. Census population figures influence the distribution of hundreds of billions of dollars in federal funding. Although noncitizens contribute to the overall economy and pay limited taxes, citizens have a particular stake in how their government is structured and how political power is allocated.

A reasonable alternative would be to count everyone for demographic purposes and the distribution of essential public services, while using the citizen population as a separate measure for congressional apportionment.

America should recognize the needs of everyone living within its borders. However, recognizing those needs does not necessarily require treating citizenship as irrelevant when determining political power. The census should provide an accurate picture of our population while preserving the principle that American citizens should have a meaningful and equitable voice in their government.

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am a resident of Pennsylvania, and I care about a fair and accurate census because these data from the census is crucial to understanding who is where and therefore how we should be represented and where resources need to be directed. Understanding where there is a need for more hospitals for instance. 

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.

Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.
As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

Re: Docket No. 260903-0005, RIN 0607-AA75, USBC-2026-0628. “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions”

I am a resident of Puerto Rico (Aguadilla). I submit this comment to oppose proposed 15 CFR Parts 60 and 70 because of the harm they would cause to a complete and accurate count of Puerto Rico and of Puerto Ricans.

The PR and US Governments have a PO BOX ADDRESS, I want my family and me counted in the census report. The canvass has to be door to door. Accuracy is paramount.

The proposed rule does not mention Puerto Rico a single time, even though the decennial census counts more than 3.2 million U.S. citizens on the island and produces the data used to redraw our legislative districts. Sections 60.5 and 70.3 refer to the “stateside census” and to the “national or state level” without defining “United States.” I ask the Census Bureau to explain in writing how Parts 60 and 70 would apply in Puerto Rico, and not to finalize any rule without doing so.

Section 70.2(a) would prohibit the Hispanic-origin question, which includes the “Puerto Rican” checkbox. More people of Puerto Rican origin now live in the states than on the island, and that question is the only way the decennial census counts them. Without it, our communities in New York, Florida, Pennsylvania, Massachusetts, Connecticut, and elsewhere would disappear from the data used to enforce civil and voting rights and to plan services. I ask that Section 70.2(a) be withdrawn.

Section 60.2(a) says usual residence “should be consistent with, and evidenced by” tax records, but does not say which ones. Most Puerto Rico residents file with the Puerto Rico Department of the Treasury (Hacienda), our local tax authority, not with the IRS; employers issue Form 499R-2/W-2PR. I ask the Census Bureau to state in writing whether it would accept Hacienda returns and Form 499R-2/W-2PR as tax records in Puerto Rico, and how it would obtain and match them.

Even if the Bureau used Hacienda returns, a residence test based on tax records would leave many people in Puerto Rico out. An estimated one-third of the population doesn’t file and works in the informal economy (Caraballo-Cueto), and retirees and low-income households often file no return at all. Moreover, there is concern that a substantial share of the returns that are filed list a P.O. box or rural route as the address, which does not identify the home where the person lives. I ask that tax records not be made the proof of residence in Puerto Rico, and that self-response and field verification be accepted.

An estimated 40% to 60% of structures in Puerto Rico have no physical street-and-number (city-style) address, the standard federal systems use, so they cannot be validated, matched, or placed on a map. Many families receive mail at P.O. boxes or rural routes rather than where they live, and our addresses use an “Urbanización” line and accents that national systems don’t match well. A record with a mailing address does not prove where a person lives. I ask the Bureau to publish Puerto Rico address-match rates for every administrative source and to keep in-person enumeration wherever addresses cannot be matched.

Section 60.2 would replace the long-standing concept of where a person lives and sleeps most of the time with a count of days between January 3 and April 1. Circular migration is common in Puerto Rico: students, seasonal farmworkers, people caring for relatives, and families displaced by hurricanes and earthquakes. This rule would place them in the wrong location or miss them entirely. I ask that the Bureau keep the usual-residence standard used in prior censuses.

The Puerto Rico Community Survey and nearly all surveys are weighted to population estimates based on the decennial census. Section 70.4 says the ACS could still ask about race and origin, but without those data in the census there would be no reliable benchmark. Municipios, agencies, hospitals, universities, nonprofits, and businesses depend on these data, as does the distribution of federal funds for health, nutrition, education, housing, and disaster recovery. I ask that Part 70 not be adopted.

These are the most sweeping changes proposed to the census in generations. Even extended to November 2, 2026, the comment period is not enough time for Puerto Rico’s communities to evaluate them. I ask for a further extension, public hearings in Spanish in Puerto Rico, and formal consultation with the Government of Puerto Rico and its municipios.

For these reasons, I ask the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that everyone in Puerto Rico and in the diaspora is counted, once, and in the right place.

Thank you for considering this comment.

Felix Chico Resto

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I write in support of the Census Bureau's proposed rule, "Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions" (Docket No. USBC-2026-0628; RIN 0607-AA75).

The Constitution calls for an "actual Enumeration" every ten years so that representation can be fairly apportioned among the states. The decennial census is meant to be a count, not a survey or a statistical estimate. Americans' voice in Congress depends on that count being right.

In 2020, the Bureau intentionally introduced statistical noise into the population data used to draw congressional and legislative districts. Data that determine political representation should never be deliberately altered. I support proposed  70.3, which directs the Bureau to prioritize the accuracy of the population count and prohibits publishing demographic data when doing so would introduce uncertainty into national or state population counts.

I also support the proposed residence criteria. Being counted at one's "usual residence" has never meant mere physical presence on Census Day. It reflects a lasting connection to a place, which is why service members stationed abroad are still counted in their home states. Counting citizens and lawful permanent residents, and excluding foreign nationals who are here unlawfully or temporarily, follows that principle.

I support keeping the enumeration questionnaire focused on the count itself. The Bureau can continue to produce demographic and statistical information through the American Community Survey and other tools, but those products should remain separate from the constitutional headcount.

To make these reforms durable, I urge the Bureau to state clearly in the final rule that the constitutional enumeration, and the counts used for apportionment and redistricting, are fundamentally distinct from routine federal statistical products and may not be adjusted to serve other statistical purposes.

Please finalize this rule so that the 2030 Census delivers an accurate count and restores Americans' trust in how they are represented.

Respectfully,
Sandra Racaniello
Queens, NY

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To whom it may concern,

I am a resident of Puerto Rico (Cayey). I submit this comment to oppose proposed 15 CFR Parts 60 and 70 because of the harm they would cause to a complete and accurate count of Puerto Rico and of Puerto Ricans.

I was born in New York and have been a resident of the center of the Island for the past 35 years, which is one of the humblest areas in Puerto Rico. As many families, my two daughters and I live together in a small house with limited resources and many medical conditions among the three of us, including among others several kinds of cancer, heart and mobility issues, neuropathy and ashtma.

The proposed rule does not mention Puerto Rico a single time, even though the decennial census counts more than 3.2 million U.S. citizens on the island and produces the data used to redraw our legislative districts. Sections 60.5 and 70.3 refer to the “stateside census” and to the “national or state level” without defining “United States.” I ask the Census Bureau to explain in writing how Parts 60 and 70 would apply in Puerto Rico, and not to finalize any rule without doing so.

Section 70.2(a) would prohibit the Hispanic-origin question, which includes the “Puerto Rican” checkbox. More people of Puerto Rican origin now live in the states than on the island, and that question is the only way the decennial census counts them. Without it, our communities in New York, Florida, Pennsylvania, Massachusetts, Connecticut, and elsewhere would disappear from the data used to enforce civil and voting rights and to plan services. I ask that Section 70.2(a) be withdrawn.

Section 60.2(a) says usual residence “should be consistent with, and evidenced by” tax records, but does not say which ones. Most Puerto Rico residents file with the Puerto Rico Department of the Treasury (Hacienda), our local tax authority, not with the IRS; employers issue Form 499R-2/W-2PR. I ask the Census Bureau to state in writing whether it would accept Hacienda returns and Form 499R-2/W-2PR as tax records in Puerto Rico, and how it would obtain and match them.

Even if the Bureau used Hacienda returns, a residence test based on tax records would leave many people in Puerto Rico out. An estimated one-third of the population doesn’t file and works in the informal economy (Caraballo-Cueto), and retirees and low-income households often file no return at all. Moreover, there is concern that a substantial share of the returns that are filed list a P.O. box or rural route as the address, which does not identify the home where the person lives. I ask that tax records not be made the proof of residence in Puerto Rico, and that self-response and field verification be accepted.

An estimated 40% to 60% of structures in Puerto Rico have no physical street-and-number (city-style) address, the standard federal systems use, so they cannot be validated, matched, or placed on a map. Many families receive mail at P.O. boxes or rural routes rather than where they live, and our addresses use an “Urbanización” line and accents that national systems don’t match well. A record with a mailing address does not prove where a person lives. I ask the Bureau to publish Puerto Rico address-match rates for every administrative source and to keep in-person enumeration wherever addresses cannot be matched.

Section 60.2 would replace the long-standing concept of where a person lives and sleeps most of the time with a count of days between January 3 and April 1. Circular migration is common in Puerto Rico: students, seasonal farmworkers, people caring for relatives, and families displaced by hurricanes and earthquakes. This rule would place them in the wrong location or miss them entirely. I ask that the Bureau keep the usual-residence standard used in prior censuses.

The Bureau invites comments on adding a legal-status question to the questionnaire. I oppose it. Puerto Rico has long-established immigrant communities and many mixed-status households that include U.S. citizens. The fear such a question creates would suppress response from entire households and worsen undercounts in the barrios and municipios where they live.

Puerto Rico’s Constitution requires its 40 house and 8 senate districts to be revised after each census, using block- and barrio-level data. The same count is the base for federal funds for health, nutrition, education, housing, and disaster recovery in all 78 municipios. If the rule drops households or places them at a mailing address, the next decade’s maps and funding are distorted. I ask the Bureau to publish an analysis of the rule’s effect on Puerto Rico’s population base before finalizing it.

For these reasons, I ask the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that everyone in Puerto Rico and in the diaspora is counted, once, and in the right place.

Thank you for considering this comment.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
As a citizen of the United States of America and a resident of the State of Arizona, I strongly oppose the proposal to exclude noncitizens who do not have lawful permanent residence from the population used for congressional apportionment.

The Fourteenth Amendment of the Constitution expressly requires apportionment based on the “whole number of persons in each State.” The apportionment base is not limited to citizens and lawful permanent residents. People who live in our communities should not be excluded from the population count based on their immigration status. Any attempt to change the Fourteenth Amendement of the Constitution should be subject to the requirements of submitting to the process and procedures of amending our Constitution.

Residents who live in a state are part of its population regardless of immigration status. Excluding them from the apportionment base would therefore risk replacing the Constitutional standard with an immigration-status-based standard, which has direct consequences for congressional representation and the Electoral College.

Further, I feel that these proposed changes are so ill-conceived and poorly constructed that the comment period due date should be delayed at least 60 days to allow for proper consideration of the harmful (and perhaps illegal) effects of the proposed changes and for deliberated response.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census. These changes will not only weaken the accuracy and integrity of our nation's most important population count, but they will also harm our communities, and I strongly urge the Bureau to reject them.

The Constitution is clear: the census must count ALL persons living in the United States, regardless of their immigration or citizenship status. Every person counted in this country contributes to our communities, and every person deserves to be fully seen. 

The consequences of these changes will negatively impact our daily lives. The census affects everything. It determines political representation and the drawing of voting districts. It guides how billions of dollars in federal funding are used to close persistent disparities in schools, hospitals, and other government programs that are designed to improve our lives.  

The census is the foundation of our democracy. It must reflect the complete yet nuanced reality of who we are as a nation. And it must reflect the lives of our friends and neighbors who may not look, think, or speak like we do. I ask the Bureau to withdraw these proposed changes and to preserve a count that includes everyone and represents everyone. 

Thank you for considering my comment.

Sincerely,
d'Anne MacNeil

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am a professor in NY state, working at a community college, and I care about a fair and accurate census because my students and I use data from government sources to help us understand the world we live in better. Without accurate counts, and with drastic changes to so many regulations about census, we would not be able to compare data across time to learn about important changes in our communities.

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 
• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people. These numbers may help set community budgets, and we need accurate numbers for who uses public resources like roads and hospitals, whether they're long-term residents or recently arrived.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.
Thank you for your time and consideration,
Virginia Shank, PhD
