Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To whoever at the Census Bureau is reading this, hello.

I am writing because I am a resident and citizen of the United States and I have concerns on the proposed rule changes listed in “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am a young adult who lives in Washington State and works in a freelance career. A fair and accurate census is critical to our ability to be able to respond to natural disasters (which are growing more and more frequent) as well as for allocating resources both within cities, states, but also within our country.

My first ask of the Census Bureau is to further extend the comment period. I am asking you to give residents and citizens- who will be directly effected by these changes- until December 10, 2026 to comment. The extension to November 2, 2026 is appreciated, but this is a significant regulatory action and it deserves a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose two parts of this new proposed regulation: part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw these proposed rules and come back with substantial revisions. Specifically focused on including the following:

-Abandoning any criteria that could exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The Census' goal is to count everyone. The data collected from this is critical for our functioning society and working to continue to improve our country for all.

-Return to activity-based criteria for what counts as someone's residence. Things such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than this new confusing “one hour” rule. As a young adult who went to college away from home, having clear rules that help establish where people really are based is important. There's lots of people who fall in weird places.

-Substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period”. We need to have guidelines that work to make sure people who are seasonal workers or recently movers are counted in the right place on Census Day. We also need to make sure that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not excluded from the count. Their voices and locations matter.

-Return to counting incarcerated people at their home address, rather than the facility they are in. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live. This could hurt those communities as they try to get resources and funds.
 
-No longer include the ban on demographic questions. The goal of the census is to count everyone, and then use that data to help make our country better. Understanding where different races and genders live is important for making sure we are working to help all communities. Similarly, while sexual orientation is not currently asked in the census, it should not be barred from future censuses.

I do not support the proposed rule as written. It would currently exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count of people in the US, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our diverse population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am Kwame Blake, an North Carolina citizen,aged 24 who works at Target, and I care about a fair and accurate census because a proper census gauges population growth and decline, changes in health and development in our communities, as well as showing what groups of people make up our country as a whole.

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including:

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
COMMENT OF STATE REPRESENTATIVE JIM SHAW, OKLAHOMA HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES, MEMBER OF THE OKLAHOMA FREEDOM CAUCUS
Docket No. USBC-2026-0628; RIN 0607-AA75

My full comment, with complete citations, is attached. This summary gives its main points.

I represent House District 32, which covers all of Lincoln County as well as Perkins and Meridian, and I serve as Vice Chair of the House State Powers Committee. In 2026 I filed House Bill 3725 to require E-Verify and House Bill 1454 to raise the fee on foreign wire transfers. After the 2030 census, the Legislature will redraw Oklahoma's congressional and legislative districts using the Bureau's numbers. I support the proposed residence criteria because that count should measure the American political community and nothing else.

1. The text requires it. The apportionment provision the Convention first approved used "inhabitants." That was a legal term requiring domicile and membership in the political community, and it "imports citizenship." Potter v. Ross, 23 N.J.L. 517, 520 (1852); Bas v. Steele, 2 F. Cas. 988, 993 (1818). The Framers wrote "persons" because the original formula counted enslaved people, not to credit every foreign national physically present. The Fourteenth Amendment's "whole number of persons" ended the Three-Fifths Compromise. It did not enlarge the political community.

2. The people are the political community. The Supreme Court reads "the people" as "members of the political community." District of Columbia v. Heller, 554 U.S. 570, 580 (2008). Apportionment allocates political power, which the community reserves to its members. Sugarman v. Dougall, 413 U.S. 634, 647 (1973); Bluman v. FEC, 800 F. Supp. 2d 281, 288 (D.D.C. 2011), aff'd, 565 U.S. 1104 (2012). The Bureau already excludes foreign tourists and diplomats and counts troops stationed overseas. "Usual residence" has always turned on a person's connection to the community.

3. The current count rewards illegal immigration. Illegal immigration shifted two House seats and two electoral votes in 2020, and the shift may reach seven by 2030 (Center for Immigration Studies, 2024). Apportionment is zero-sum, so those seats come from States that enforce the law. Oklahoma taxpayers paid an estimated $782.9 million for illegal immigration in 2023 (FAIR) and then lose representation on top of that.

4. It dilutes citizens' votes. Districts equalized on total population can hold very different numbers of citizens, so a citizen's vote counts for more in one district than in another. Wesberry v. Sanders and Reynolds v. Sims condemn that dilution. Evenwel v. Abbott, 578 U.S. 54 (2016), left open whether States may equalize on eligible voters, but States can't make that choice without reliable citizenship data.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am a Black woman, a lesbian, and a resident of St. Louis, Missouri. I am also a learning and development facilitator, a career and executive coach, and a small business owner. My work has focused on helping women develop skills, advance their careers, and build greater economic stability. I am submitting this comment in my personal capacity.

I care about an accurate census because I want decisions about representation, resources, and community needs to reflect the people who actually live here. That includes people whose housing, family arrangements, or immigration status do not fit a narrow definition of who belongs.

First, I ask the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2 is welcome, but a proposal with consequences this substantial deserves at least 90 days for public review and meaningful participation.

Second, I oppose both proposed part 60 and proposed part 70. I urge the Bureau to withdraw the rule and make substantial revisions that address the following concerns:

* Count all U.S. residents for apportionment. Residents should not be excluded simply because they are not citizens or lawful permanent residents. Visa holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and other people who live in our communities should be included.
* Restore clear guidance for varied living arrangements, including recent moves, temporary shelters, and foster care. The rules should help people understand where they belong in the count and help census workers count them accurately.
* Determine usual residence based on where someone ordinarily lives and sleeps. The proposed standard allowing one hour of presence to count as a day at a residence introduces confusion about what it means to live somewhere.
* Revise the proposed enumeration-period criteria so that seasonal workers, recent movers, children in foster care, and people in emergency shelters are counted in the appropriate place on Census Day. Changes in someone’s circumstances should not cause them to disappear from the count.
* Count incarcerated people in their home communities rather than at correctional facilities. I oppose assigning their population to the communities where prisons are located while their home communities lose that representation.
* Revise the reliance on tax records as evidence of residence. A mailing address on a tax document may differ from where someone actually lives. The Bureau needs safeguards that account for those differences and ensure that dependent children and people with less straightforward documentation are counted.
* Remove the prohibition on questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Race and ethnicity data are necessary to understand disparities, inform public health decisions, and support civil rights enforcement. Those questions should follow the 2024 Statistical Policy Directive No. 15 standards. The Bureau should also preserve the ability to consider sexual orientation questions in future censuses and collect and publish accurate information about same-sex couples.

As someone whose work centers on helping people move toward greater opportunity, I believe public institutions need reliable information about both who lives in our communities and the conditions affecting their lives. Excluding residents or restricting demographic information would undermine that understanding.

Please withdraw the proposed rule and return with a proposal that supports a complete, accurate count and meaningful public participation.

Sincerely,

AB
St. Louis, Missouri

The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.

Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. I oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census because a fair and accurate census is critical to ensuring every community is counted, fairly represented, and able to get the resources people need to live healthy lives — including sexual and reproductive healthcare. An inaccurate or incomplete census can deepen existing inequities, particularly for communities that already face disenfranchisement and barriers to healthcare.

The Census Bureau must extensively research and consult with stakeholders about the potential effects of such changes before proposing their implementation in a decennial census.

There are 3 types of people within the country as far as the Census is concerned; Citizens, Residents, and Visitors. Citizens are those who are born here, born to Citizens, or completed the naturalization process. Residents are those who have officially announced their intent to relocate to the United Stated on a permanent basis utilizing the visa system, who have not become Citizens. Visitors are those who have not officially announced their intent to relocate on a permanent basis. Of those groups, only the first two can be counted within the body of “We the People OF the United States”, whereas the last can only be accurately called “people IN the United States.”
As the duty of the Census is to generate population data to inform the process of apportionment for the House of Representatives, it would be both logical and sensible to collect data only on those who are actually Represented by that House. Temporary visitors to the country are represented to the government by the ambassadors and embassies of their home nation. They do not need, nor should have, an impact of the representation in Congress any more than a dinner guest at one’s house should impact what color to paint the bedrooms.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am a mother, wife, foster care nonprofit professional, and community volunteer in Colorado Springs, Colorado. Our son joined our family through adoption from Ethiopia as a baby, and he is nearly 19. When he was small, we could shield him from discrimination. As he becomes an adult, we can't. He will apply for jobs, rent apartments, and seek loans as a young Black man. If he faces discrimination, he will need data showing the patterns are real. Without it, unfair treatment is far easier to dismiss as coincidence.

For this reason, I oppose both parts of this proposed rule and ask the Bureau to withdraw them.

Banning race and ethnicity questions (70.2(a)). The notice cites general research on questionnaire length but no evidence that removing these questions would improve response. Redistricting, Voting Rights Act enforcement, fair housing, and civil rights analysis all depend on this data. Administrative records and the American Community Survey are not substitutes. Records capture self-identification poorly, and the survey has wide margins of error for small areas. The Bureau should also explain how section 70.3(b) would limit publication of demographic data.


Excluding noncitizens without green cards (60.4(b)). The Fourteenth Amendment apportions representatives by "the whole number of persons in each State." The Bureau concedes its 2020 criteria made no distinction by legal status. Section 60.4(b) also excludes people who are lawfully here, including workers, students, and those with humanitarian status.

Determining status (60.2, 60.4). Using tax, DHS, and other records, or adding a legal-status question, invites errors and will discourage participation, including among citizens in mixed-status households.

Discrimination doesn't end when it stops being measured. It becomes harder to see, prove, and challenge.

I urge the Bureau to withdraw both proposals and publish a full analysis of their effects on accuracy, participation, and civil rights enforcement.

Respectfully,
Michele Heath
Colorado Springs, Colorado

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Public Comment of the North Carolina Military Affairs Commission

Docket No. USBC-2026-0628 | RIN 0607-AA75

The North Carolina Military Affairs Commission (NCMAC) opposes the proposed changes to military residence criteria for the 2030 Decennial Census and urges the U.S. Census Bureau to retain the military-specific rules used in the 2020 Census. The proposed regulations, published September 10, 2026 (91 Fed. Reg. 57524), risk inaccurately attributing military personnel and their dependents to locations other than the communities where they ordinarily reside and receive public services.

Preserving the 2020 Census Standards

The 2020 Census established clear residence criteria recognizing the unique circumstances of military service. Personnel assigned to barracks or dormitories were counted at those facilities; service members and dependents residing in ordinary housing were generally counted where they lived and slept most of the time; and personnel temporarily deployed overseas remained associated with their usual U.S. residence. These standards appropriately distinguished physical residence from legal domicile, voting residence, and home of record.

Problems with the Proposed Regulations

Proposed 15 C.F.R. § 60.2 establishes residence based on the greatest number of days lawfully spent at a location between January 3 and April 1, with reference to tax records. The proposal also counts a day at a residence after as little as one hour of presence.

These standards fail to account adequately for military assignments, temporary duty (TDY), training exercises, permanent change of station (PCS) transitions, and deployments. A service member temporarily away from an installation during the prescribed 89-day period could be attributed to a location that does not reflect their ordinary residence.

Additionally, military personnel frequently maintain legal domicile or tax residency in states other than their assigned duty stations. Although the proposal does not expressly require counting personnel at their tax domicile, reliance on tax records creates a risk of inconsistent or inaccurate residence determinations.

Consequences for Military Communities

The proposed regulations also eliminate the explicit 2020 requirement to count personnel assigned to military barracks and dormitories at those facilities. This change could disproportionately affect communities surrounding major military installations, including Fort Bragg, Camp Lejeune, and Marine Corps Air Station Cherry Point.

Census population figures influence congressional apportionment, redistricting, federal funding formulas, infrastructure planning, and public services. Incorrectly attributing military populations could disadvantage installation communities despite continued demand for schools, roads, utilities, emergency services, housing, and healthcare.

While the precise number of potentially affected personnel has not been established, even modest systematic population shifts could have meaningful consequences for military-hosting states and localities.

Requested Actions

NCMAC urges the Census Bureau to:

Retain the 2020 requirement that military personnel assigned to barracks and dormitories be counted at those facilities.

Preserve the usual stateside residence of personnel temporarily deployed overseas from U.S. duty stations.

Explicitly clarify that legal domicile, tax residence, voting residence, and home of record do not independently determine census residence.

Protect the separate residence determinations of military dependents, including geographically separated families.

Establish specific residence criteria for PCS transitions, TDY assignments, training, shipboard assignments, and military treatment facilities.

Conduct and publish a comparative impact assessment identifying potential population shifts by installation, state, and military assignment category, and consult affected military departments and state and local governments.

Conclusion

NCMAC supports the Census Bureau's objective of counting every person once and in the correct location. However, the proposed residence criteria do not sufficiently recognize the compulsory, temporary, and geographically complex nature of military service.

The Commission strongly recommends retaining the 2020 military-specific residence standards for the 2030 Census. The Census Bureau should not finalize the proposed military provisions without first demonstrating through transparent analysis that the changes will not systematically misattribute military personnel and their dependents or disadvantage the communities supporting America's Armed Forces.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Re: Docket USBC-2026-0628, RIN 0607-AA75, Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions

I am an Associate Professor of sociology at the University of Utah, and I study how state public policies relate to population health. I submit this comment as an individual researcher, and my views do not represent those of my university. I ask the Census Bureau to substantially revise proposed 15 CFR Parts 60 and 70, as recommended by the Population Association of America (PAA) and the Association of Population Centers (APC) in their joint comment dated September 29, 2026. In particular, I support their requests that any final rule preserve the collection of race and ethnicity information in the decennial census, restore coherent residence rules, and avoid unnecessary limits on disclosure avoidance methods.

Because I study how state-level conditions relate to premature mortality, morbidity, and mental health, my work depends on population data that remain comparable over time. I have three concerns about how the proposed rule would affect the validity of this research.

First, health rates hinge on population denominators, and population estimates begin with the decennial census. Section 60.4 would exclude many residents from the apportionment count, but the Federal Register notice does not explain whether they would be enumerated and retained in the base for population estimates. If they were dropped from denominators while their deaths and illnesses remained in numerators, rates would be inflated, particularly in states with more excluded residents.

Second, the January 3 to April 1 enumeration period and the tax record language in Section 60.2 could change where people are counted, and those changes would likely not be distributed evenly across states and age groups. Residence in vital and health records may not follow the same rule, so numerators and denominators could become misaligned. A one-time shift in 2030 that differs across states would not be removed by standard adjustments for stable state differences (state fixed effects), and it could be mistaken for a real change in population health.

Third, Section 70.4 preserves demographic questions on the American Community Survey, but its weighting relies on population controls by race and Hispanic origin that are built from the decennial census. The same estimates also supply the denominators for rates such as mortality and cancer. As PAA and APC note, administrative records are not currently an adequate substitute because they can lack this information, contain incomplete information, or rely on race and ethnicity assigned by a third party. The Census Bureau itself acknowledges this problem in its Preliminary Regulatory Impact Analysis, which states that no other source is comparably accurate and that omitting these questions would require estimates built from outdated or less accurate data. The Census Bureau cites response burden, but PAA and APC point out that the decennial census uses an extremely short questionnaire and respondents have shown they are willing and able to answer these questions. That reduction in burden is hard to justify without evidence from the Census Bureau of strong gains that outweigh the data quality losses described in its own impact analysis.

I ask that, before implementing any changes, the Census Bureau test them, publish their expected effects on population estimates and survey weights, and explain how continuity with prior censuses will be maintained, as the Society for Epidemiologic Research also recommends in its comment.
Megan Reynolds, PhD

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

Re: Docket No. 260903-0005, RIN 0607-AA75, USBC-2026-0628. "Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions"

As a resident of Guaynabo, Puerto Rico, I oppose proposed 15 CFR Parts 60 and 70. If adopted, these rules would undermine a full and accurate count of Puerto Rico's residents and of Puerto Ricans living in the states.

1. Puerto Rico is left out. The proposal never mentions Puerto Rico. Yet the decennial census counts over 3.2 million U.S. citizens on the island and supplies the data used to redraw our legislative districts. Sections 60.5 and 70.3 refer to the "stateside census" and the "national or state level," but they leave "United States" undefined. The Bureau should explain in writing how Parts 60 and 70 would work in Puerto Rico, and it should not adopt a final rule until it does.

2. The diaspora would vanish from the data. Section 70.2(a) would eliminate the Hispanic-origin question and, with it, the "Puerto Rican" checkbox. More people of Puerto Rican descent now live in the states than on the island, and that question is the only way the decennial census identifies them. Without it, communities in New York, Florida, Pennsylvania, Massachusetts, Connecticut, and beyond would disappear from the data used to enforce civil and voting rights and to plan services. Section 70.2(a) should be withdrawn.

3. "Tax records" is undefined. Section 60.2(a) provides that usual residence "should be consistent with, and evidenced by" tax records, but it does not say which records. Most island residents file with the Puerto Rico Department of the Treasury (Hacienda), not the IRS, and their employers issue Form 499R-2/W-2PR. The Bureau should state in writing whether Hacienda returns and Form 499R-2/W-2PR qualify, and how it would obtain and match them.

4. A tax-based test would exclude many residents. Even with Hacienda data, many people would fall outside a tax-record standard. Roughly one-third of the population does not file and works in the informal economy (Caraballo-Cueto). Many retirees and low-income households file no return. There is also concern that a large share of filed returns list a P.O. box or rural route, which does not show where the filer lives. Tax records should not serve as proof of residence in Puerto Rico, and self-response and field verification must remain valid.

5. Island addresses don't fit federal systems. An estimated 40% to 60% of structures in Puerto Rico have no city-style street-and-number address. Federal systems depend on that format, so these structures cannot be reliably validated, matched, or mapped. Many households get mail at a P.O. box or rural route rather than at home. Local addresses also include an "Urbanización" line and accented characters that national databases handle poorly. A mailing address is not evidence of residence. The Bureau should publish Puerto Rico address-match rates for each administrative source and keep in-person enumeration wherever addresses cannot be matched.

6. Redistricting and funding are at stake. Puerto Rico's Constitution requires that its 40 House and 8 Senate districts be revised after every census, using block- and barrio-level data. Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

Re: “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions”

I am a resident of San Juan, P.R. I submit this comment to oppose proposed 15 CFR Parts 60 and 70 because of the harm they would cause to a complete and accurate count of Puerto Rico and of Puerto Ricans.

The proposed rule does not mention Puerto Rico a single time, even though the decennial census counts more than 3.2 million U.S. citizens on the island and produces the data used to redraw our legislative districts. Sections 60.5 and 70.3 refer to the “stateside census” and to the “national or state level” without defining “United States.” I ask the Census Bureau to explain in writing how Parts 60 and 70 would apply in Puerto Rico, and not to finalize any rule without doing so.

Section 70.2(a) would prohibit the Hispanic-origin question, which includes the “Puerto Rican” checkbox. More people of Puerto Rican origin now live in the states than on the island, and that question is the only way the decennial census counts them. Without it, our communities in U.S. would disappear from the data used to enforce civil and voting rights and to plan services. I ask that Section 70.2(a) be withdrawn.

Section 60.2(a) says usual residence “should be consistent with and evidenced by” tax records. Most Puerto Rico residents file with our local tax authority (Hacienda), not with the IRS. I ask the Census Bureau to state in writing whether it would accept Hacienda returns and Form 499R-2/W-2PR as tax records in Puerto Rico, and how it would obtain and match them.

Even if the Bureau used Hacienda returns, a residence test based on tax records would leave many people in Puerto Rico out. An estimated one-third of the population doesn’t file and works in the informal economy (Caraballo-Cueto), and retirees and low-income households often file no return at all. Moreover, there is concern that a substantial share of the returns that are filed list a P.O. box or rural route as the address, which does not identify the home where the person lives. I ask that tax records not be made the proof of residence in Puerto Rico, and that self-response and field verification be accepted.

An estimated 40% to 60% of structures in Puerto Rico have no physical street-and-number (city-style) address, the standard federal systems use, so they cannot be validated, matched, or placed on a map. Many families receive mail at P.O. boxes or rural routes rather than where they live, and our addresses use an “Urbanización” line and accents that national systems don’t match well. I ask the Bureau to publish Puerto Rico address-match rates for every administrative source and to keep in-person enumeration wherever addresses cannot be matched.

Section 60.2 would replace the long-standing concept of where a person lives and sleeps most of the time with a count of days between January 3 and April 1. Circular migration is common in Puerto Rico: students, seasonal farmworkers, people caring for relatives, and families displaced by hurricanes and earthquakes. This rule would place them in the wrong location or miss them entirely. I ask that the Bureau keep the usual-residence standard used in prior censuses.

I am opposing to a legal-status question. Puerto Rico has long-established immigrant communities and many mixed-status households that include U.S. citizens. The fear such a question creates would suppress response from entire households and worsen undercounts in the barrios and municipios where they live.

The Puerto Rico Community Survey and nearly all surveys are weighted to population estimates based on the decennial census. Section 70.4 says the ACS could still ask about race and origin, but without those data in the census there would be no reliable benchmark. Municipios, agencies, hospitals, universities, nonprofits, and businesses depend on these data, as does the distribution of federal funds for health, nutrition, education, housing, and disaster recovery. I ask that Part 70 not be adopted.

Puerto Rico use block-and barrio-level data to revised 40 house and 8 senate districts to be revised after each census, for federal funds for health, nutrition, education, housing, and disaster recovery. If the rule drops households or places them at a mailing address, the next decade’s maps and funding are distorted. I ask the Bureau to publish an analysis of the rule’s effect on Puerto Rico’s population base before finalizing it.

These are the most sweeping changes proposed to the census in generations. I ask for a further extension, public hearings in Spanish in Puerto Rico, and formal consultation with the Government of Puerto Rico and its municipios.

For these reasons, I ask the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that everyone in Puerto Rico and in the diaspora is counted, once, and in the right place.

Thank you.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including:

• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Dear Director Cook,

As a private citizen, I appreciate the opportunity to comment on the Census Bureau's proposed rule governing residence criteria and demographic questions for the 2030 decennial census. The census is the foundation for distributing political representation and federal resources. Accurate census ensures communities receive fair funding for infrastructure, housing, education, public safety, emergency response and other essential services. Because census data guide funding and planning decision for the next decade, accuracy is critical.  

We are concerned that several provisions of the proposed rule could reduce the accuracy of our community's population count and affect our access to federal and state resources. 

Concerns about the Proposed Changes 
Apportionment and population count: The proposed rule would limit the population counted toward apportionment to U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents for the first time. Although this change applies only to apportionment, it may create confusion or fear among residents and discourage participation. We request additional information on how full population data would be collected, reported and communicated, to ensure that all residents are counted for the broader data set. 

Legal-status question: The proposed rule also raises the possibility of adding a legal-status question to the census questionnaire. Similar proposals considered for the 2020 Census were not adopted following concerns that it could reduce participation, particularly among immigrant and mixed-status households. Any decline in response rates would undermine the accuracy of our community's population count as a whole and could impact the resources available to young children and families specifically. 

Usual residence and the enumeration period: The proposed shift to counting residents based on where they spend the most time during a January 3-April 1 period, rather than their usual residence throughout the year, could affect our population count [of seasonal residents such as snowbirds/ students / part-time workers / other mobile populations]. We ask the Bureau to further evaluate the operational and data-accuracy impacts of this change and explain the rationale supporting it.  

Reliance on administrative records: Increased reliance on tax, immigration, health and other administrative records raises concerns about the potential undercount of populations in our community that may not be consistently represented in those records, including low-income households, college students, non-filers and children. We request additional information regarding when these records will be used and how the Bureau will ensure accurate counts for populations with less reliable administrative data.  

Demographic questions: The proposal would eliminate race and ethnicity questions, while making most other demographic questions optional. Accurate demographic data is essential to municipal planning and service delivery. Understanding who lives in our community gives local governments the ability to plan for our current population and take into consideration our future population's needs. [Private citizen uses this data for...e.g., monitoring equitable service delivery, administering a specific program, public health planning, economic development targeting, etc]. The loss or reduction in the quality of this data could affect our ability to provide much needed services to our residents and accurately plan for our future.  

Funding impact: Census data inform funding for other programs including Community Development Block Grants (CDBG), transit formula funding, and Title I education funding. An undercount of any portion of our population reduces resources available to the entire community  not just the households or individuals who go uncounted. State funding allocations depend, in many cases, on accurate census data. While the Bureau distinguishes between apportionment and funding distribution, changes that discourage participation risk reducing the quality of data used for both purposes.  

We respectfully ask the Census Bureau to withdraw these proposed changes. Any changes to residence criteria, data collection methods or demographic questions must not compromise the accuracy of the population counts that Private citizen and communities like ours rely on. 

We appreciate the opportunity to comment on this proposal and would welcome the chance to provide additional information or answer any questions the Bureau may have. 

Sincerely, 
Louise Seeley
Private Citizen

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481

Summary: 

The American College of Epidemiology opposes the Census Bureau's proposed rule on residence criteria and demographic questions (15 CFR Parts 60 and 70) and urges its withdrawal. As a national society of epidemiologists across academia, government, healthcare, and industry, it warns that the rule would degrade census data quality. Census counts supply the denominators for disease, mortality, and health-utilization rates, and systematically excluding, misclassifying, or misplacing populations would bias those rates in ways that can't be fixed with larger samples or routine adjustment. It would also make comparisons across years and places unreliable.

The College makes two requests. First, it asks for the comment period to be extended to December 10, 2026, to allow a full 90 days of review for a rule of this significance. Second, it asks the Bureau to withdraw the rule and return with substantial revisions. Chief among these: drop the ban on demographic questions (race and ethnicity questions should instead follow the 2024 SPD 15 standards), and don't exclude visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, or other residents from the apportionment count.

The College also calls for restoring detailed residence guidelines for people who recently moved, live in temporary shelters, or are in foster care, and for returning to activity-based criteria (where someone usually lives and sleeps) in place of the "one hour" rule. It asks the Bureau to revise the enumeration-period guidelines so seasonal workers, recent movers, foster children, and shelter residents are counted correctly. It would also count incarcerated people at their home addresses rather than at prisons, and it objects to leaning on tax records, which often show mailing rather than residential addresses and could miss military families and dependent children. Finally, it opposes barring sexual orientation questions from future censuses.

The letter concludes that these changes risk undercounts that can't easily be corrected later, and urges the Bureau to work with public health, demographic, state, local, and community stakeholders to build criteria that maximize accuracy, transparency, and public trust.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
On behalf of the undersigned education and community organizations, we are writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (FDMS Docket No. USBC-2026-0628, published September 10, 2026) (the “proposed rule”). We strongly oppose the proposed rule’s changes to the residence criteria and demographic questions for the 2030 Census. It would deny communities fair representation and seriously compromise the data needed to advance the well-being and prosperity of all our nation’s residents.

Accurate census data is critical to educational organizations’ ability to ensure students are given the support and services they need to succeed in life, postsecondary education, and career. Census data is used to determine the distribution of billions of dollars in vital education funding to states and schools. Census data also determines the share of elected representation serving our schools and providing important constituent services to our community members.

As a threshold matter, despite the recent three-week extension, we believe the current comment period is inappropriate for changes of this scale, which would affect the apportionment of congressional seats, the questions asked of every household, and the data on which countless decisions depend. The Department of Commerce and the Census Bureau should immediately extend the comment period by at least 60 days to allow meaningful public input.

The proposed rule would undermine the fairness, accuracy, and integrity of the 2030 Census. We are particularly concerned about the following issues: 

1.	Excluding immigrants from the apportionment count violates the 14th Amendment and would dilute fair representation in Congress. The 14th Amendment requires that apportionment be based on the “whole number of persons in each state.” Since at least 1990, “usual residence” has generally meant the place where a person lives and sleeps most of the time. The proposed rule distorts that concept to exclude immigrants other than lawful permanent residents from the apportionment count. States with large immigrant populations, such as California, Florida, and Texas, would gain fewer congressional seats or lose more, and their districts would hold more residents, making it harder for members of Congress to serve them. Everyone in these districts loses. In California, more than 200,000 immigrant students are enrolled statewide; artificially diminished representation in the 2030 Census would dilute the resources available to all students by allocating fewer resources to schools serving the same number of students.

2.	The proposed rule creates a vague and confusing standard for who counts and when. It counts lawful permanent residents but excludes noncitizens whose status is “less durable and indefinite in length,” without defining that standard. It is unclear whether refugees, asylees, recipients of Temporary Protected Status and Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals, and people with pending green card or asylum applications, who live and work here lawfully, would be counted. The rule also replaces the April 1 reference date used since 1930 with a test that assigns people to the place they spent the most days between January 3 and April 1, counts one hour of lawful presence as a day, and allows a day to count at more than one residence. This is far harder to explain than “where you live on April 1.” It would confuse families and make it significantly more difficult for our community members to be informed about census participation. 

3.	The rule lays the foundation for citizenship and immigration status questions that would deter responses and worsen the undercount. The proposed rule expressly asks for comment on adding a legal status question to the questionnaire. Extensive research shows that such questions deter populations such as Latinos from responding, including U.S.-born citizens and members of mixed-status households. The 2020 Census undercounted Latinos by a historic net 4.99 percent – a significant increase from the population’s 1.54 percent undercount in 2010. Aggressive immigration enforcement and data-sharing have since deepened the climate of fear, which could result in an even higher undercount for the 2030 Census. 

For these reasons, we strongly oppose the changes proposed in this rule and urge the Census Bureau and the Department of Commerce to withdraw it. At a minimum, we call on the Department to extend the comment period by at least 60 days and, if the Department moves forward, conduct the rigorous testing and meaningful stakeholder consultation that changes of this scale require.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am a Research Scientist and I care about a fair and accurate census because the census is critical for public health and influences the distribution of power through government representation, allocation of federal, state, and local resources, and public health planning and surveillance.

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
COMMENT OF STATE LEGISLATOR R. JOSIAH MAGNUSON, SOUTH CAROLINA HOUSE, MEMBER OF THE SOUTH CAROLINA FREEDOM CAUCUS

Docket No. USBC-2026-0628; RIN 0607-AA75 Decennial Census of the Population of Americans: Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions

I am Roy Josiah Magnuson, a member of the South Carolina House of Representatives representing House District 38 and a member of the SC Freedom Caucus. I have served in the State House since 2016. The Constitution assigns me, and the legislators of every state, the duty to draw districts that give equal representation to the American citizens who elect us. Every map I draw begins with the Bureau’s count. I submit this comment in support of the proposed residence criteria because that count should measure the American political community and nothing else.

The Constitution creates a government of, by, and for the American people. It apportions seats in the House, and with them votes in the Electoral College, among the States according to a count of “persons,” a word the Framers used interchangeably with “inhabitants” and “the people.” Those words describe the members of the American political community, the citizens who vote, serve on juries, and bear the obligations of self-government. They do not describe foreign nationals, and least of all those who entered or remain in this country in violation of its laws. The Bureau’s rule restores that understanding. The Commenter urges its permanent adoption for five major reasons :

1. The text compels it. “Inhabitant” was a legal term of art that required domicile, intent to remain, and membership in the political community, a status that “imports citizenship.” Potter v. Ross, 23 N.J.L. 517, 520 (Sup. Ct. 1852). A foreign national is a stranger to that community, and the Constitution does not apportion representation to strangers.

2. The people are the political community. The Supreme Court reads “the people” as “members of the political community.” District of Columbia v. Heller, 554 U.S. 570, 580 (2008). Foreign nationals are outside it, and the apportionment clauses cannot sensibly extend further than the community they exist to represent.

3. The current count rewards illegal immigration. States that tolerate illegal immigration gain House seats and electoral votes at the expense of states that enforce the law. No legislature should be forced to defend that result, and no State should be given a political incentive to disregard immigration law.

4. The current count dilutes the votes of citizens. Districts equalized on a count that includes illegal aliens give the citizens of those districts more weight than citizens elsewhere.

5. The Bureau has the authority. Congress delegated the census to the Secretary of Commerce, and the Supreme Court has repeatedly upheld his discretion over how to take it.

Illegal immigration should not be rewarded with political power. Apart from the citizenship point, illegal entry violates federal law. A census that nevertheless credits their presence with congressional seats and electoral votes tells every State that tolerates illegal immigration that it will be paid in representation. States that enforce federal law and bear the costs of doing so are penalized. Illegal immigration shifted two House seats, and two electoral votes, in 2020, and the shift is projected to reach as many as seven seats by 2030. Steven A. Camarota & Karen Zeigler, Tilting the Balance, Ctr. for Immigr. Stud. (Oct. 31, 2024). Apportionment is zero-sum, and the seats are taken from States whose citizens followed the law.

Further, states that follow the law pay twice. State taxpayers already bear the costs of illegal immigration in schools, hospitals, and law enforcement. I have heard this directly from people in my district, for example at Spartanburg School District 2. A census that then credits those same populations to other States’ representation takes political power from the States that kept faith with federal law. State legislators answer to citizens who ask why obeying the law should cost them seats in Congress and votes in the Electoral College. The Bureau’s rule gives us the answer they deserve.

The Commenter asks the Bureau to adopt the proposed rule to restrict apportionment to American citizen only population. The Commenter also supports proposed 15 C.F.R. § 70.2, which removes questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation from the decennial questionnaire and makes responses to the remaining demographic questions voluntary. A citizen-based count and a colorblind questionnaire serve the same goal: a census that counts Americans as Americans.

Respectfully submitted,

R. Josiah Magnuson
State Representative - South Carolina House
Member, SC Freedom Caucus

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Submitted on behalf of the Sisters of St. Joseph Neighborhood Network (SSJNN)
Erie County, Pennsylvania 

SSJNN respectfully urges the federal government to preserve the established methodology of the decennial census and refrain from implementing changes that could compromise the accuracy, completeness, or integrity of the population count.

Our work is grounded in the belief that every person has dignity, every neighborhood matters, and every individual deserves the opportunity to live in a safe, healthy, and thriving community. Through our commitment to neighborhood revitalization, community engagement, relationship building, and addressing the needs of individuals and families, we see firsthand how federal, state, and local resources affect the well-being of our communities. An accurate census is essential to this work.

The decennial census is the foundation upon which decisions are made about political representation, federal funding, public services, and community investments. Census data help determine resources for affordable housing, healthcare, education, transportation, food assistance, infrastructure, and programs that support children, families, older adults, and individuals experiencing poverty.

For Erie, an inaccurate population count could have serious and lasting consequences. An undercount could mean fewer federal resources in our community at a time when the needs of residents remain significant. It could undermine the work of nonprofit organizations, neighborhood-based initiatives, local governments, schools, and community partners who work every day to strengthen neighborhoods and improve quality of life.

For SSJNN, the consequences would be felt directly by the people we serve.

When communities are undercounted, their needs can become invisible in the decisions that determine where resources are directed. Fewer resources can mean greater challenges in addressing housing instability, food insecurity, access to healthcare, educational opportunities, transportation barriers, and the many interconnected issues that affect families and neighborhood stability.

Changes to the census that discourage participation, create fear, or exclude individuals could compromise our ability to advocate effectively for the communities we serve. Those who are already experiencing economic hardship or social vulnerability could be disproportionately affected.

We are also deeply concerned about any effort to limit the census population count to U.S. citizens.

The Constitution's requirement for a decennial enumeration is based on counting persons, not exclusively citizens. We believe that every person living in the United States must be counted for purposes of congressional apportionment and representation, regardless of citizenship or immigration status.

Every person has needs. Every person is affected by decisions involving schools, housing, healthcare, transportation, public safety, and community resources. Excluding individuals from the population count would distort the true makeup of our communities and could diminish their representation and access to resources.

An accurate census gives communities visibility. It provides the information necessary to identify needs, advocate for resources, and ensure that public decisions reflect the actual population.

We therefore respectfully ask the federal government to:

Preserve the established decennial census methodology and avoid changes that could jeopardize an accurate and complete population count.

Count every person living in the United States, regardless of citizenship or immigration status, for purposes of congressional apportionment and representation.

Protect the integrity and confidentiality of census participation so people can respond without fear or intimidation.

Ensure that historically undercounted and economically vulnerable populations are fully represented in the census.

Recognize the direct impact of census undercounts on Erie County, including the potential loss of federal resources that support essential services, neighborhood revitalization, and community development.

We believe strong neighborhoods are built when people are seen, heard, valued, and included. An accurate census is fundamental to that vision.

We cannot effectively address the needs of our neighborhoods if the people who live in them are not counted. We cannot advocate for adequate resources if our communities are underrepresented in the data used to make funding and policy decisions.

The consequences of an inaccurate census will extend well beyond the counting process. They will affect the resources available to our neighborhoods, the services our residents depend upon, and the opportunities available to future generations.

Every person matters. Every neighborhood matters. Every person deserves to be counted.

Respectfully,

Sisters of St. Joseph Neighborhood Network
Erie County, Pennsylvania

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am a young American and I care about a fair and accurate census because of the impacts it’ll have on my and future generations.

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including:

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.
As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
A la Oficina del Censo de los Estados Unidos:

Re: Docket No. 260903-0005, RIN 0607-AA75, USBC-2026-0628. “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions”

Soy residente de Puerto Rico (Humacao). Someto este comentario para expresar mi oposición a las Partes 60 y 70 propuestas del Título 15 del Código de Regulaciones Federales, por el daño que causarían a un conteo completo y correcto de Puerto Rico y de los puertorriqueños.

Soy residente de Humacao y me preocupa, como las medidas propuestas al CENSO 2030 pueden afectar la disponibilidad de fondos federales a Puerto Rico.

La propuesta no menciona a Puerto Rico ni una sola vez, aunque el Censo decenal cuenta a más de 3.2 millones de ciudadanos estadounidenses en la Isla y produce los datos con que se redibujan nuestros distritos legislativos. Las secciones 60.5 y 70.3 hablan del “stateside census” y del nivel “nacional o estatal” sin definir “Estados Unidos”. Solicito que la Oficina del Censo explique por escrito cómo aplicarían las Partes 60 y 70 en Puerto Rico y que no adopte una regla final sin hacerlo.

La sección 70.2(a) prohibiría la pregunta de origen hispano, que incluye el encasillado “puertorriqueño”. Hoy viven más personas de origen puertorriqueño en los estados que en Puerto Rico, y esa pregunta es la única forma en que el Censo decenal las cuenta. Sin ella, nuestras comunidades en Nueva York, Florida, Pensilvania, Massachusetts, Connecticut y otros estados desaparecerían de los datos que se usan para hacer cumplir los derechos civiles y electorales y para planificar servicios. Solicito que se elimine la sección 70.2(a).

La sección 60.2(a) dice que la residencia habitual “debe ser consistente con” los récords contributivos, pero no dice cuáles. La mayoría de los residentes de Puerto Rico rinde planilla ante el Departamento de Hacienda, nuestra autoridad contributiva local, y no ante el IRS; los patronos emiten el Formulario 499R-2/W-2PR. Solicito que la Oficina del Censo aclare por escrito si aceptaría las planillas de Hacienda y el Formulario 499R-2/W-2PR como récords contributivos en Puerto Rico, y cómo los obtendría y parearía.

Aun si la Oficina usara las planillas de Hacienda, una prueba de residencia basada en récords contributivos dejaría fuera a muchas personas en Puerto Rico. Se estima que cerca de un tercio de la población no rinde planilla y está en la economía informal (Caraballo-Cueto), y jubilados y hogares de bajos ingresos con frecuencia no rinden ninguna. Además, preocupa que una porción sustancial de las planillas que sí se rinden use un apartado postal o una ruta rural como dirección, que no identifica la vivienda donde vive la persona. Solicito que no se haga de los récords contributivos la prueba de residencia en Puerto Rico y que se acepten la autorespuesta y la verificación en el campo.

Se estima que entre el 40% y el 60% de las estructuras en Puerto Rico no tienen una dirección física de calle y número (city-style), el estándar que usan los sistemas federales, así que no se pueden validar, parear ni ubicar en un mapa. Muchas familias reciben su correspondencia en apartados postales o rutas rurales, no donde viven, y nuestras direcciones usan el campo “Urbanización” y acentos que los sistemas nacionales no parean bien. Un récord con dirección postal no prueba dónde vive una persona. Solicito que la Oficina publique las tasas de pareo de direcciones en Puerto Rico de cada fuente administrativa y que mantenga la enumeración en persona donde las direcciones no se puedan parear.

La sección 60.2 sustituiría el concepto de dónde una persona vive y duerme la mayor parte del tiempo por un conteo de días entre el 3 de enero y el 1 de abril. En Puerto Rico la migración circular es común: estudiantes, trabajadores agrícolas temporeros, personas que cuidan a familiares y familias desplazadas por huracanes y terremotos. Esta regla las ubicaría en el lugar equivocado o las dejaría fuera. Solicito que se mantenga el estándar de residencia habitual usado en censos anteriores.

Por estas razones, solicito que la Oficina del Censo retire la regla propuesta y garantice que todas las personas en Puerto Rico y en la diáspora sean contadas, una vez y en el lugar correcto.

Gracias por considerar este comentario.

Gerardo Vicéns

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
My name is [Your Name] and I am your constituent from [City/Zip Code]. As Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander (AANHPI) Heritage Month comes to a close, I write to urge you to support AANHPI students by cosponsoring the All Students Count Act.

To the U.S. Census Bureau: 

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule titled “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005). Eliminating the collection of race and ethnic data, prohibiting the collection of sexual orientation, and leaving non-citizens out of the apportionment would significantly harm the Southeast Asian American (SEAA) and broader Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander (AANHPI) communities. I respectfully request that the Census Bureau withdraw the proposed rule and extend the comment period to December 10, 2026. 

This proposed rule would significantly harm the SEAA and AANHPI communities. The AANHPI community is not a homogenous population; it encompasses over 50 different ethnic groups and 100 languages and dialects. There are vast socioeconomic disparities within the AANHPI population, often related to their migratory and historical experience. SEAAs, such as the Cambodian, Hmong, Laotian, and Mien populations, often have higher rates of poverty and lower educational attainment rates than both the broader AANHPI and American populations. 

For SEAAs, this disparity is generally tied to their experiences escaping their countries of origin and resettlement in the United States after the Vietnam War, Secret War in Laos, and Khmer Rouge genocide in Cambodia. For example, because of the 2020 Census, we now know that the Mien population has lower educational attainment rates compared to the general American and AANHPI populations. Additionally, the data also show that Mien men have a lower educational attainment rate compared to women. Such information could only be obtained because of the census, which is the primary source for data collection and reporting of small ethnic groups. These data cannot be replicated by other surveys, including the American Community Survey. 

Accurate data, reflective of race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation, help our elected officials properly identify and address the unique needs and challenges of our communities. Prohibiting the collection of this demographic data would prevent our government officials from passing informed public policy; hamper the ability of community-based organizations to demonstrate data narratives for fundraising purposes; and inhibit the ability of students and academics studying our communities from accessing the most robust source of information on SEAAs and the broader AANHPI community. 

Thank you for taking my comment into consideration. I reiterate my request that the US Census Bureau withdraws the proposed rule; preserves the collection of race and ethnic data; and keeps its commitment to count everyone once, only once, and in the right place.

I also ask the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. Changes of this scope deserve more time for the public to review and respond.

Sincerely,
Nam Tien
Long Beach, CA 90805

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
1. The proposal to change census rules to collect information on immigration status. The justification is that this is needed to exclude immigrants of questionable status from the population counts used to determine apportionment of representatives in Congress. Methods would include mining other federal data and including questions on immigration status in the census questionnaires. Both are extremely problematic. The first violates many rights to privacy. The second- in our current anti-immigrant climate- will have a chilling effect on households with recent legal immigrants and on households with mixed immigration status. Many will not respond truthfully (or at all) to census questionnaires. Thus, all residents within such households, both legal and illegal, will be undercounted in the census. 

Under the old census rules, systemic undercounting was corrected using statistical models based on demographic data. Under the new rules such demographic data will not be collected, so there will be no way to correct for systemic undercounts driven by questions involving immigration status. The net effect will be a real but unmeasurable undercount of citizens and legal residents whose ethnicity or families link them to recent immigrants.

This undercounting will create a terrible inequity for apportionment of representatives. States and communities with higher immigrant populations will be under-represented at all levels of government. 

Undercounting populations linked to immigrants will also create terrible problems for everyone else who use census data for its many other current uses. Impacts will range from poor public health decisions to increased traffic. Funding will go to the wrong places. Schools won't have enough seats for incoming students. Public safety decisions will be based on inaccurate crime rates. Wait times will get longer for healthcare. Business decisions will be based on faulty information. And evacuating people during an emergency will be more difficult

The most egregious criticism of these proposed rule changes is that there is nothing within constitutional or congressional mandates that justifies collecting data on immigration status. The mandate for the census is only to count the number of persons and their usual residence. Any arguments that immigration status can or should be considered in apportioning representation in Congress are specious wishful thinking. 

2. The proposed rule changes on re-defining residency by an enumeration period from Jan3-April1. This will create terrible confusion. What happens to the millions of snowbirds and seasonal workers, who winter in southern states but return to their primary domicile when spring arrives? How to count those who winter out-of-country? They will be mis-counted to southern states, or even excluded entirely. 

3.Trying to use tax records to determine residency is even more problematic. What happens with college students or overseas military personnel whose tax records do NOT represent their primary domicile? To all those who do not appear at all in the tax records?

4.. These proposed rule changes are not following the proper process for “significant regulatory action”. Regulatory meetings that are statutorily-required under the Convening of interested parties under the Negotiated Rulemaking Act have not been held. The interval between release of the proposal and the closing date for public comments is far too short- only 53 days. Moreover, the comment period is completely overshadowed by the impending midterm elections, so that the it has been ignored by the press and concerned parties and citizens are completely unaware of these momentous proposed rule changes.
