Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

Re: Docket No. 260903-0005, RIN 0607-AA75, USBC-2026-0628. “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions”

I am a resident of Puerto Rico. I submit this comment to oppose proposed 15 CFR Parts 60 and 70 because of the harm they would cause to a complete and accurate count of Puerto Rico and of Puerto Ricans.

The proposed rule does not mention Puerto Rico a single time, even though the decennial census counts more than 3.2 million U.S. citizens on the island and produces the data used to redraw our legislative districts. Sections 60.5 and 70.3 refer to the “stateside census” and to the “national or state level” without defining “United States.” I ask the Census Bureau to explain in writing how Parts 60 and 70 would apply in Puerto Rico, and not to finalize any rule without doing so.

Section 70.2(a) would prohibit the Hispanic-origin question, which includes the “Puerto Rican” checkbox. More people of Puerto Rican origin now live in the states than on the island, and that question is the only way the decennial census counts them. Without it, our communities in New York, Florida, Pennsylvania, Massachusetts, Connecticut, and elsewhere would disappear from the data used to enforce civil and voting rights and to plan services. I ask that Section 70.2(a) be withdrawn.

Section 60.2(a) says usual residence “should be consistent with, and evidenced by” tax records, but does not say which ones. Most Puerto Rico residents file with the Puerto Rico Department of the Treasury (Hacienda), our local tax authority, not with the IRS; employers issue Form 499R-2/W-2PR. I ask the Census Bureau to state in writing whether it would accept Hacienda returns and Form 499R-2/W-2PR as tax records in Puerto Rico, and how it would obtain and match them.

Even if the Bureau used Hacienda returns, a residence test based on tax records would leave many people in Puerto Rico out. An estimated one-third of the population doesn’t file and works in the informal economy (Caraballo-Cueto), and retirees and low-income households often file no return at all. Moreover, there is concern that a substantial share of the returns that are filed list a P.O. box or rural route as the address, which does not identify the home where the person lives. I ask that tax records not be made the proof of residence in Puerto Rico, and that self-response and field verification be accepted.

For these reasons, I ask the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that everyone in Puerto Rico and in the diaspora is counted, once, and in the right place.

Thank you for considering this comment.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am a Minnesota based public health researcher. I care about a fair and accurate census because it is essential for a functioning democracy and plays a foundational role in many of the survey-based data sources we use to monitor public health and health policy in this country and across states.  

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).  These changes will severely impact the quality and usefulness of the Census data.



First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.
As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481

I strongly oppose the proposed rules changes to the residence criteria and demographic questions for the 2030 Census.

As an initial matter, I urge the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. 30 days is not enough time for members of the public to review and respond to the proposed rule given the scope of the prospective changes. 

I oppose the proposed rule because I am concerned it will undermine the accuracy and usefulness of census data, particularly for marginalized Americans. Census counts are used for a wide variety of important purposes, from planning and funding critical infrastructure to understanding patterns of discrimination. By leading to a census that only counts part of the population and contains limited demographic data, the proposed rule will make it harder for policy makers to make evidence-based decisions that affect Americans everyday lives. Underrepresented groups, including women, people of color, and LGBTQ+ people, among others, will be most negatively impacted. 

If the proposed residence criteria are finalized, the U.S. will lose a complete and accurate count of the population and its distribution and stray from the Constitutions mandate to count all persons. The proposed rule would, for the first time, exclude many U.S. residents from the apportionment count, including international students, work visa-holders, and refugees and asylum seekers. Robust demographic data is necessary to enforce civil rights laws and ensure equal opportunity for all Americans. If finalized, the proposed rule would make it harder to identify and address issues like workplace discrimination, public health discrepancies, and more. 

Census data needs to accurately represent all Americans. For the reasons stated above, I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw and revise the proposed rule, especially part 60 and 70. Thank you for your consideration.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

**Re: Docket No. 260903-0005, RIN 0607-AA75, USBC-2026-0628 — “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions”**

I live in Guaynabo, Puerto Rico, and submit this comment to oppose the proposed 15 CFR Parts 60 and 70.

I am a Certified Public Accountant with nearly 20 years of experience in federal grants management, compliance, and program implementation. My work with Puerto Rico municipalities, government agencies, and nonprofit organizations has shown me how essential reliable Census data are to delivering federally funded services. These data do more than inform funding formulas: local governments use them to identify underserved populations, establish priorities, prepare grant applications, develop action plans, justify investments, and measure whether programs reach the people they are intended to serve.

Consider a municipality seeking funding for services for older adults. It needs credible information about how many older residents live in each community, where they live, and the economic and housing conditions they face. Without reliable, geographically detailed data, the municipality may struggle to demonstrate need, target services, or support a competitive grant application. These are practical problems I worry about because I work with municipalities that must turn limited resources into actual services.

Yet the proposed rule does not expressly address Puerto Rico, where the decennial census counts more than 3.2 million residents and provides data used for legislative redistricting. Sections 60.5 and 70.3 refer to the “stateside census” and “national or state level” without clearly explaining the rule’s territorial application. I ask the Bureau to explain specifically how Parts 60 and 70 would operate in Puerto Rico before any rule is finalized.

Section 70.2(a) would prohibit the Hispanic-origin question, including the “Puerto Rican” identification option. This would undermine the ability to identify Puerto Rican communities across the states and assess their needs. I request that Section 70.2(a) be withdrawn.

Section 60.2(a) would make usual residence consistent with, and evidenced by, tax records, without identifying which records would be used. Puerto Rico has a distinct tax system: many residents file with the Puerto Rico Department of the Treasury rather than the IRS, and employers issue Form 499R-2/W-2PR. The Bureau should explain whether these records would be accepted, how they would be obtained and matched, and how individuals without relevant tax filings would be counted.

Tax records alone cannot adequately establish residence for all Puerto Rico residents. Older adults, low-income households, and people working outside the formal economy may not file income tax returns. Mailing addresses also do not necessarily identify physical residences. Many households rely on post office boxes, rural routes, and local address conventions that are not reliably matched in national databases. I urge the Bureau not to treat tax records or automated address matching as substitutes for self-response and in-person verification. It should publish Puerto Rico-specific address-match results and establish safeguards for residents whose records cannot be matched.

My central concern is that an inaccurate or incomplete count would compound existing challenges for municipalities trying to plan services and document community needs. A community poorly represented in the data can also be overlooked when governments decide where to invest. These consequences could persist throughout the decade.

I ask the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule, clearly address its application to Puerto Rico, preserve the ability to identify Puerto Rican origin, and maintain reliable methods of counting residents regardless of tax-filing status or address format. Every person must be counted once, in the right place.

Thank you for considering my comment.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am a certified Oncology Data Specialist (formerly Certified Tumor Registrar), a concerned United States Citizen, and I care about a fair and accurate census because this information is critical to providing informed cancer surveillance data to ensure the integrity and accuracy of cancer registry data within the cancer surveillance field.

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including:
• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.
As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am a Ph.D. Candidate in the Department of Political Science at UCLA, and I care about a fair and accurate census because concise data is necessary for a better society.

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including:

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

My name is Skylar Bergeron, and I live in Portland, Maine where I work as a health promotion specialist. My community of Portland would be particularly impacted by the proposed changes.

A large number of Greater Portland residents or “snowbirds” live in warmer states during the winter months. According to American Community Survey 5-year estimates, 15% of all homes in Maine were seasonally vacant in 2024. Snowbirds tend to be older adults. Consequently, excluding non-U.S. citizens or permanent residents from the Census would egregiously misrepresent Maine’s workforce and economic contributions.

The ban on collecting race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation in the census will degrade public health services, as public health practitioners rely on this data for understanding who lives in the community. When practitioners understand who is in the community, they can better understand the community’s needs and how to work towards the effective and equitable delivery of services. Healthcare providers, public health agencies, and policymakers won’t be able to accurately identify population-level health differences without a baseline of who is in the community. Without focused public health and medical interventions, the community will likely experience increased rates of chronic illness, maternal morbidity and mortality, and infectious diseases. This would affect many communities in Portland, but would disproportionately affect the  roughly 23% of the population that belongs to a racial or ethnic minority group (U.S. Census Bureau). These groups often already experience disruptions in their health care services or experience lower quality of care.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Re: Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026

To Whom It May Concern:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions”. 

I am an American citizen living in Pennsylvania with a professional history of leading entrepreneur support organizations and supporting the city of Pittsburgh in workforce and community issues through government.  I care about a fair and accurate census because data allows us to track what we are doing well and what we need to improve. Statistical accuracy and comprehensive information will also help us see patterns that affect what resources we need, what we no longer need, and how to improve people's quality of life. 

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count everyone to accurately represent who is here.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. Thank you for reviewing my comment. 

Warmly,
Nadyli

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: I work as a public health data analyst at a county health department in Colorado, overseeing a large, random-sample household based community health survey (CHS). Dozens of nonprofits, healthcare and service organizations use the information we produce for program planning and needs assessments. For the past two decades, the accuracy and utility of our survey has depended on demographic benchmarks produced by the U.S. Census Bureau. The proposed rule changes governing the census undermine our county’s efforts to collect and trend representative data on our population’s health: Removing questions on race and ethnicity from the decennial census would substantially disrupt our long-established weighting methodology, rendering data collected after the 2030 census incompatible with all previous years of the CHS. We know that Hispanic/Latino residents in our county experience higher rates of diabetes and a lack of access to health care. We also know that they are underrepresented among respondents to our survey, and that without census data on race and ethnicity our assessment of health issues would be increasingly vulnerable to bias. This proposed change would leave us unable to measure the success of our efforts to address these issues and unable to identify emerging disparities so as to best allocate our resources.  Historically, changes to the census have been carefully tested at length before implementation. The proposed changes to the 2030 U.S. Census methodology, includingchanges to the enumeration period and reliance on tax records to validate residencehave not been tested at all and local public health agencies such as ours will be left in the dark as to how these changes misrepresent our population. In particular, these changes threaten to undercount residents with multiple residences, recent movers, students, and others whose living situations may not align neatly with administrative records. The potential undercount resulting from these untested changes will disrupt the CHS, our most important source of local data on the health and wellbeing of our residents and leave us with less confidence that we understand the health-related needs of our residents. Were these changes to take effect, they would create a discontinuity in the data we have spent 20 years collecting, breaking our ability to make comparisons before and after the 2030 census.   As someone whose work relies on the continuity and sanctity of the decennial census, I respectfully request that the Census Bureau withdraw the proposed changes to the 2030 U.S. Census.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
**Public Comment Opposing the Proposed 2030 Census Residence Criteria and Citizenship/Legal-Status Question**  
**Docket No. 260903-0005 | RIN 0607-AA75**

I strongly oppose the Census Bureau's proposed changes to the 2030 Census residence criteria and any inclusion of a citizenship or immigration legal-status question. Specifically, I oppose excluding individuals from the apportionment count based on their immigration or citizenship status. Every person residing in the United States should be counted, regardless of whether they are U.S. citizens, lawful permanent residents, temporary visa holders, asylum seekers, refugees, or undocumented immigrants.

The purpose of the decennial Census is to count the people who live in our communities. The Constitution calls for an enumeration of the "whole number of persons in each State," not simply citizens or individuals with a particular immigration classification. A person's contribution to their community, presence in a household, or need for public services does not depend on citizenship status.

**1. Every person deserves to be counted.**

I strongly disagree with redefining usual residence in a way that excludes undocumented individuals and other noncitizens who do not hold lawful permanent resident status. Immigrants are an integral part of our communities, workforce, economy, and society. They work in agriculture, construction, healthcare, food service, and countless other industries that sustain our nation.

Excluding people based on immigration status creates an incomplete and distorted picture of the population. It also undermines fair political representation by reducing the population counts of communities with significant immigrant populations. Representation should reflect the people who live in a community, not be determined by the legal status of its residents.

**2. A citizenship or immigration-status question will discourage participation.**

I oppose adding a citizenship or legal-status question to the Census questionnaire. Such a question would create fear, distrust, and confusion, particularly among immigrant families, mixed-status households, and communities already hesitant to interact with government agencies.

The chilling effect would extend beyond undocumented individuals. Entire households, including U.S. citizen children and adults, could avoid participating out of concern that their information might expose relatives to immigration enforcement or other consequences.

The Census must remain a trusted, confidential process. It should never be perceived as an extension of immigration enforcement.

**3. The proposed changes will disproportionately harm underserved communities.**

This proposal is particularly concerning for rural communities and agricultural regions such as California's Central Valley, where immigrant and farmworker families are essential to the local economy and community infrastructure.

An undercount would have lasting consequences for access to healthcare, schools, transportation, housing, nutrition programs, emergency preparedness, and other federally supported services. Census data informs funding and policy decisions for an entire decade. When people are excluded, their communities lose visibility, representation, and the resources needed to address their needs.

**4. Protect confidentiality and community trust.**

I am also concerned about proposals to use administrative records from federal, state, local, and commercial sources to determine individuals' immigration or legal status. Expanding the use of personal information in this manner risks further eroding public trust and discouraging participation.

The Census Bureau should prioritize confidentiality, transparency, and meaningful protections against the use of Census information for immigration enforcement.

**Recommendations**

I urge the Census Bureau to:

1. Reject the proposed exclusion of undocumented immigrants and other noncitizens from the apportionment count.
2. Count every person residing in the United States, regardless of citizenship or immigration status.
3. Reject the inclusion of citizenship or immigration legal-status questions on the 2030 Census questionnaire.
4. Reject the use of Census responses and expanded administrative data matching to identify or classify individuals for immigration-related purposes.
5. Invest in trusted community-based organizations, bilingual outreach workers, and culturally appropriate education to ensure historically undercounted communities can participate safely and confidently.

The Census is intended to count people, not determine who deserves to be counted. Every person living in the United States contributes to the needs, workforce, and fabric of our communities. Every person deserves to be represented.

I urge the Census Bureau to reject these proposed changes and preserve a complete, inclusive, and accurate count of everyone residing in the United States.

I am a Decolonial Social Scientist, a community advocate, and a person whose existence this government is proposing to render statistically invisible. I am writing because silence here is complicity.

Calling race and ethnicity "immaterial personal characteristics" is not neutral administrative language. It is epistemicide written into federal regulation. Epistemicide is the deliberate destruction of knowledge systems and the erasure of communities from the official record. It is a governance strategy with a documented global history, and the United States is proposing to deploy it right now through a regulatory filing most people will never hear about.

You cannot enforce civil rights protections for communities you have erased from the data. You cannot address health disparities you have made statistically invisible. You cannot redistribute resources to people the government has decided do not need to be counted. Erasure from the archive is not colorblindness. It is the removal of the evidentiary infrastructure that makes accountability possible.

This is not a new strategy. It is the oldest colonial playbook in existence. The colonial instrument was never simply counting or not counting. It was control of the archive. Spain built the sistema de castas and used it to govern who owned land, who could be enslaved, and who held legal rights across the Americas. Britain manufactured and codified caste and religion into rigid legal categories across colonized India through census, categories that still structure Indian politics today. Belgium buried the death toll of ten million Congolese people under the paperwork of a private colonial corporation. Italy suppressed the documented record of chemical warfare and mass civilian slaughter in Libya and Ethiopia. Portugal controlled the archive of what extraction actually cost the people who survived it across Africa and Brazil.

These empires counted race meticulously when counting served domination. They destroyed or suppressed the record when documentation would have evidenced the crime. Same hand on the ledger, both directions.

The United States counted race for 230 years to enforce slavery, segregation, redlining, and systematic exclusion from wealth, housing, education, and political power. It is proposing to stop now, precisely when that data is finally being used for remedy instead of control. Same instrument. Opposite direction. Identical function.

The proposed exclusion of non-citizens without green cards from the apportionment base compounds this harm with surgical precision. The Legal Defense Fund has already warned that this will directly diminish Black political representation. Apportionment determines congressional seats and billions of dollars in federal funding. Removing entire communities from that count is not an administrative adjustment. It is the deliberate engineering of political invisibility for communities that are already targeted by every other mechanism of state power.

An undocumented harm is a harm that legally did not occur. An uncounted community is a community the government has granted itself permission to ignore. That is the function of this proposal. Not colorblindness. Not neutrality. Permission to harm without accountability.

I am demanding the full retention of race and ethnicity questions in the 2030 Census. I am demanding the inclusion of all residents in the apportionment base regardless of citizenship status. I am demanding that this held to the evidentiary standard that civil rights enforcement requires.

The public has a right to know this comment period exists. Most people do not. That is not an accident.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Eliminating decennial census race data would severely inhibit funding to Native American Tribes, citizens, and communities
Public comment by Robert Maxim, Gwynne Evans-Lomayesva, and Saundra Mitrovich

We are Native American Tribal citizens who are experts in Census Bureau data and federal funding flows to Indian Country. Robert Maxim is a citizen of the Mashpee Wampanoag Tribe and a fellow at the Brookings Institution. Gwynne Evans-Lomayesva is a citizen of the Hopi Tribal Nation and a PhD candidate in Demography at the University of Pennsylvania. Saundra Mitrovich is a citizen of the Tyme Maidu Tribe of the Berry Creek Rancheria and a descendant of the Yahmonee Maidu Tribe, and serves as census consultant at the Native American Rights Fund and co-lead of the Natives Count Coalition.

We are writing in response to the Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions for the Decennial Census of the Population of Americans, Docket ID USBC-2026-0628.

In September the Trump Administration announced plans to eliminate questions related to race and ethnicity on the 2030 decennial census. This policy change would have significant negative effects across many areas of American life, including weakening civil rights and voting rights enforcement, as well as making it more difficult to understand economic and social disparities across different groups in the United States. Further, these census changes would have compounding downstream impacts on other federal data, limiting our ability as a nation to understand basic population changes in mortality, fertility, and domestic migration patterns, which vary by race and ethnicity. 

For Native Americans, this change would have multiple negative effects, including undermining civil and voting rights, limiting the ability of government agencies to track economic development and social disparities, and disrupting billions of dollars in federal funding flows to Tribal nations, citizens, and communities. Cumulatively, these impacts would significantly disrupt Tribal governance and undermine Tribal sovereignty. 

While Native Americans are unique among populations in the U.S., in that they are classified as both a racial group and a political group, most of the data that informs federal programs for Indian Country are based on census race data. Eliminating the race and ethnicity question from the decennial census questionnaire would therefore make it impossible for the U.S. to continue operating many critical federal funding streams for Indian Country.

The attached comment explains the role that decennial census data plays in allocating funding to Native American Tribes and people, overviews the existing shortcomings of federal census data for Indian Country, explains why proposed alternatives to census data are nonetheless inadequate, and proposes ideas for how the federal government can instead make census data collection more effective for Native Americans.

In addition to its role in voting rights enforcement, Census Bureau data plays an important role in distributing federal funding to Indian Country. A 2023 analysis by Census Bureau staff member Ceci Villa Ross found that over 350 federal programs used decennial census data to allocate $2.8 trillion in funding.

Of those programs, at least 13 explicitly target Native Americans and Native Hawaiians. Based on Census Bureau data, these programs distributed $8.5 billion in federal funding in FY 2021. 

What is needed is not an abolition of census race data, which would make it nearly impossible to administer federal programs serving Indian Country, but a strengthening of Census Bureau data collection to make it more accurate for and representative of Indian Country. To do so, policymakers should keep the existing race and ethnicity questions for the 2030 decennial census and conduct national content tests to determine the scientific robustness of any suggested or planned changes. 

One option for Census Bureau officials to explore would be the current practice in place in other countries with shared histories of English colonization, including Canada, Australia, and New Zealand. These countries have a question about ethnicity or ancestry, comparable to the current U.S. question about race or ethnicity, but then also incorporate a separate question about Indigenous identity.

Policymakers can also take steps to help improve the quality of data on Indian Country, such as by providing greater funding for Tribes to do their own data work. Policymakers should also pursue a more dedicated effort to build trust and create pathways for voluntary, mutually beneficial data sharing agreements between Tribes and other levels of government, which maintain data ownership with the partner Tribal nation. One of the best examples of this type of work is the 2024 Census Bureau-Osage Nation data sharing agreement.

Please see the attached comment for additional historical context, data, and recommendations.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am concerned about the proposed revisions to current regulations and practices of the Bureau of the Census.  With regard to the first proposed change as to who would be included in future census counts, the Constitution states that "Representatives and direct taxes shall be apportioned among the several states...according to their respective numbers, which shall be determined by adding to the whole number of free Persons, including those bound to service for a term of years,..."  Article 1, Section 2.  The Fourteenth Amendment, Section 2, states "Representatives shall be apportioned among the several states according to their respective numbers, counting the whole number of persons in each state..."  The clear meaning of both these was all persons living in a state + those temporarily absent, are to be included.  No citizenship requirement was included.  This is the only legitimate reading or interpretation of "whole number of persons".  States and local governments must provide essential public services to all living in their respective states, and resources available to them are frequently based on population.  To change the reading of the Constitution to allow the elimination of some residents in the Census counts would be a vast disservice to all and create a hardship disproportionately on states and local governments.  These changes will severely distort population counts and create inaccurate representation of states and communities.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am 22 years old, live in Washington, DC, and work in strategic communications. I care about a fair and accurate census because it affects apportionment and decisions about federal funding, which affects all of us. 

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is appreciated, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond accurately,

Second, I oppose both Part 60 and Part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions:

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.
As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit the collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Census data help federal agencies, state, and local community organizations identify language-access needs and determine where translated materials and interpretation services are necessary. A la Oficina del Censo de los Estados Unidos:

Re: Docket No. 260903-0005, RIN 0607-AA75, USBC-2026-0628. “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions”

Soy residente de Puerto Rico. Someto este comentario para expresar mi oposición a las Partes 60 y 70 propuestas del Título 15 del Código de Regulaciones Federales, por el daño que causarían a un conteo completo y correcto de Puerto Rico y de los puertorriqueños.

La propuesta no menciona a Puerto Rico ni una sola vez, aunque el Censo decenal cuenta a más de 3.2 millones de ciudadanos estadounidenses en la Isla y produce los datos con que se redibujan nuestros distritos legislativos. Las secciones 60.5 y 70.3 hablan del “stateside census” y del nivel “nacional o estatal” sin definir “Estados Unidos”. Solicito que la Oficina del Censo explique por escrito cómo aplicarían las Partes 60 y 70 en Puerto Rico y que no adopte una regla final sin hacerlo.

La sección 70.2(a) prohibiría la pregunta de origen hispano, que incluye el encasillado “puertorriqueño”. Hoy viven más personas de origen puertorriqueño en los estados que en Puerto Rico, y esa pregunta es la única forma en que el Censo decenal las cuenta. Sin ella, nuestras comunidades en Nueva York, Florida, Pensilvania, Massachusetts, Connecticut y otros estados desaparecerían de los datos que se usan para hacer cumplir los derechos civiles y electorales y para planificar servicios. Solicito que se elimine la sección 70.2(a).

La sección 60.2(a) dice que la residencia habitual “debe ser consistente con” los récords contributivos, pero no dice cuáles. La mayoría de los residentes de Puerto Rico rinde planilla ante el Departamento de Hacienda, nuestra autoridad contributiva local, y no ante el IRS; los patronos emiten el Formulario 499R-2/W-2PR. Solicito que la Oficina del Censo aclare por escrito si aceptaría las planillas de Hacienda y el Formulario 499R-2/W-2PR como récords contributivos en Puerto Rico, y cómo los obtendría y parearía.

Aun si la Oficina usara las planillas de Hacienda, una prueba de residencia basada en récords contributivos dejaría fuera a muchas personas en Puerto Rico. Se estima que cerca de un tercio de la población no rinde planilla y está en la economía informal (Caraballo-Cueto), y jubilados y hogares de bajos ingresos con frecuencia no rinden ninguna. Además, preocupa que una porción sustancial de las planillas que sí se rinden use un apartado postal o una ruta rural como dirección, que no identifica la vivienda donde vive la persona. Solicito que no se haga de los récords contributivos la prueba de residencia en Puerto Rico y que se acepten la autorespuesta y la verificación en el campo.

Por estas razones, solicito que la Oficina del Censo retire la regla propuesta y garantice que todas las personas en Puerto Rico y en la diáspora sean contadas, una vez y en el lugar correcto.

Gracias por considerar este comentario.

An estimated one-third of the population doesn’t file and works in the informal economy (Caraballo-Cueto), and retirees and low-income households often file no return at all. Moreover, there is concern that a substantial share of the returns that are filed list a P.O. box or rural route as the address, which does not identify the home where the person lives. I ask that tax records not be made the proof of residence in Puerto Rico, and that self-response and field verification be accepted.

An estimated 40% to 60% of structures in Puerto Rico have no physical street-and-number (city-style) address, the standard federal systems use, so they cannot be validated, matched, or placed on a map. Many families receive mail at P.O. boxes or rural routes rather than where they live, and our addresses use an “Urbanización” line and accents that national systems don’t match well. A record with a mailing address does not prove where a person lives. I ask the Bureau to publish Puerto Rico address-match rates for every administrative source and to keep in-person enumeration wherever addresses cannot be matched.

The Puerto Rico Community Survey and nearly all surveys are weighted to population estimates based on the decennial census. A la Oficina del Censo de los Estados Unidos:

Re: Docket No. 260903-0005, RIN 0607-AA75, USBC-2026-0628. “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions”

Soy puertorriqueño/a y vivo en los Estados Unidos (Mayagüez). Someto este comentario para expresar mi oposición a las Partes 60 y 70 propuestas del Título 15 del Código de Regulaciones Federales, por el daño que causarían a un conteo completo y correcto de Puerto Rico y de los puertorriqueños.

Vivo en New Hampshire pero tengo propiedad en Mayaguez, por razones de trabajo tuve que emigrar a EU.

La propuesta no menciona a Puerto Rico ni una sola vez, aunque el Censo decenal cuenta a más de 3.2 millones de ciudadanos estadounidenses en la Isla y produce los datos con que se redibujan nuestros distritos legislativos. Las secciones 60.5 y 70.3 hablan del “stateside census” y del nivel “nacional o estatal” sin definir “Estados Unidos”. Solicito que la Oficina del Censo explique por escrito cómo aplicarían las Partes 60 y 70 en Puerto Rico y que no adopte una regla final sin hacerlo.

La sección 70.2(a) prohibiría la pregunta de origen hispano, que incluye el encasillado “puertorriqueño”. Hoy viven más personas de origen puertorriqueño en los estados que en Puerto Rico, y esa pregunta es la única forma en que el Censo decenal las cuenta. Sin ella, nuestras comunidades en Nueva York, Florida, Pensilvania, Massachusetts, Connecticut y otros estados desaparecerían de los datos que se usan para hacer cumplir los derechos civiles y electorales y para planificar servicios. Solicito que se elimine la sección 70.2(a).

La sección 60.2(a) dice que la residencia habitual “debe ser consistente con” los récords contributivos, pero no dice cuáles. La mayoría de los residentes de Puerto Rico rinde planilla ante el Departamento de Hacienda, nuestra autoridad contributiva local, y no ante el IRS; los patronos emiten el Formulario 499R-2/W-2PR. Solicito que la Oficina del Censo aclare por escrito si aceptaría las planillas de Hacienda y el Formulario 499R-2/W-2PR como récords contributivos en Puerto Rico, y cómo los obtendría y parearía.

Aun si la Oficina usara las planillas de Hacienda, una prueba de residencia basada en récords contributivos dejaría fuera a muchas personas en Puerto Rico. Se estima que cerca de un tercio de la población no rinde planilla y está en la economía informal (Caraballo-Cueto), y jubilados y hogares de bajos ingresos con frecuencia no rinden ninguna. Además, preocupa que una porción sustancial de las planillas que sí se rinden use un apartado postal o una ruta rural como dirección, que no identifica la vivienda donde vive la persona. Solicito que no se haga de los récords contributivos la prueba de residencia en Puerto Rico y que se acepten la autorespuesta y la verificación en el campo.

Se estima que entre el 40% y el 60% de las estructuras en Puerto Rico no tienen una dirección física de calle y número (city-style), el estándar que usan los sistemas federales, así que no se pueden validar, parear ni ubicar en un mapa. Muchas familias reciben su correspondencia en apartados postales o rutas rurales, no donde viven, y nuestras direcciones usan el campo “Urbanización” y acentos que los sistemas nacionales no parean bien. Un récord con dirección postal no prueba dónde vive una persona. Solicito que la Oficina publique las tasas de pareo de direcciones en Puerto Rico de cada fuente administrativa y que mantenga la enumeración en persona donde las direcciones no se puedan parear.

La sección 60.2 sustituiría el concepto de dónde una persona vive y duerme la mayor parte del tiempo por un conteo de días entre el 3 de enero y el 1 de abril. En Puerto Rico la migración circular es común: estudiantes, trabajadores agrícolas temporeros, personas que cuidan a familiares y familias desplazadas por huracanes y terremotos. Esta regla las ubicaría en el lugar equivocado o las dejaría fuera. Solicito que se mantenga el estándar de residencia habitual usado en censos anteriores.

La Oficina pide comentarios sobre añadir una pregunta de estatus legal al cuestionario. Me opongo. Puerto Rico tiene comunidades inmigrantes arraigadas y muchos hogares de estatus mixto en los que viven ciudadanos estadounidenses. El temor provocado por una pregunta así reduciría la respuesta de familias completas y empeoraría el subconteo de los barrios y municipios donde viven.La Encuesta sobre la Comunidad de Puerto Rico y casi todas las encuestas se ajustan a estimados de población basados en el Censo decenal.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the U.S. Census Bureau’s proposed rule published on September 10, 2026, regarding modifications to the 2030 Decennial Census. I urge the Bureau to withdraw these proposed changes immediately.

The proposed rule threatens the core constitutional and democratic integrity of the nation by seeking to alter the historical and lawful definitions of population enumeration. My specific objections focus on the following critical points:

1. Undermining Constitutional Apportionment
The proposal to narrow the definition of "usual residence" to exclude noncitizens without lawful permanent resident status contradicts the plain text and historical precedent of the U.S. Constitution. Article I, Section 2, and the Fourteenth Amendment mandate an apportionment based on the "whole number of persons" in each state. By intentionally undercounting millions of residents, this rule would directly and unfairly reduce the number of U.S. House seats and electoral votes for numerous states, distorting democratic representation.

2. Inaccurate Allocation of Federal Resources
Federal funding for infrastructure, healthcare, education, and emergency services relies directly on accurate decennial census data to meet the actual needs of communities. Excluding portions of the local population from the headcount does not eliminate those individuals from the community; it simply deprives states and municipalities of the resources required to support everyone living there. This would lead to severe, long-term underfunding of essential public services.

3. Unprecedented Shifts in Residence Criteria
The proposed shifts to evaluate residence based on a narrow window (January 3 to April 1) and cross-referencing tax records present significant operational risks. These complex, unvetted criteria are likely to increase undercounts among highly mobile populations, seasonal workers, students, and low-income individuals, further degrading the quality and accuracy of the data.

An accurate census is a non-partisan, foundational requirement for fair representation and equitable distribution of public funds. The proposed rule would actively result in an incomplete and flawed headcount with severe consequences for communities nationwide. I strongly oppose these changes and request that the Census Bureau maintain the established, inclusive standards for the 2030 Census.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I strongly oppose all aspects of this proposed rule. These changes would undermine centuries of standard practices that have defined the decennial census and jeopardize the quality and accuracy of its data. I am particularly concerned about changes regarding who is counted (and where) and the removal of race and ethnicity questions.  If finalized and implemented, the changes in this proposed rule would mark the first time that race and ethnicity data are not collected in the decennial census and would also be the first time that millions of noncitizen immigrants, including those who are lawfully present but who lack LPR status, are excluded from U.S. population counts. 
As an epidemiologist for a local government, I rely on the accuracy of census data to conduct my job duties. When we calculate rates of disease and death (e.g. cancer death and incidence rates), population counts from the census are our denominators. When the population counts are not accurate, then our rates are not accurate. Furthermore, when race and ethnicity data are removed, we are unable to calculate rates of disease and death by specific races and ethnicities, effectively removing these populations from health statistics. This jeopardizes investment in health-related research and programs for minority communities. When populations become invisible in the data, they become invisible to funders. 
The proposed rule also has broader implications for the allocation of funds and representation across populations. The exclusion of millions of noncitizen immigrants from apportionment counts could lead to decreased federal funding and resources for states and localities with higher shares of immigrants. This includes funding for health programs that millions of people rely on, such as Medicaid and the Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP). Additionally, the proposed changes could impact the redistricting process and lead to shifts in political representation, including potentially reallocating congressional seats in ways that would reduce political representation for states with large immigrant populations.
We are a nation of immigrants, and everyone should be counted. This proposed rule goes against everything this county was built on.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am a small business owner who lives in the State of Virginia. I care about a fair and accurate census because it provides the statistical foundation for good democratic governance. I also want to ensure that all current U.S. residents are accurately counted in the proper location, per the U.S. Constitution.

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Re-establish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Thank you for considering my and the many other comments being provided. I hope that you will take them seriously, and act in accordance with good democratic governance and principled public policy.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Re: Docket USBC-2026-0628; RIN 0607-AA75 
Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed 
Regulations for Demographic Questions 
Dear Director of the U.S. Census Bureau: 
I submit this comment on behalf of Central Jersey Alumnae Chapter to raise serious concerns 
regarding proposed changes to the 2030 Census and their potential consequences for Black 
communities and other racial and ethnic populations, including residents of Piscataway 
Township and Middlesex County. 
The Constitution requires an “actual Enumeration” every ten years, and the Fourteenth 
Amendment provides for congressional representation based on the “whole number of persons 
in each State.” U.S. Const. art. I, § 2; amend. XIV, § 2. Congress further directs the Secretary of 
Commerce to conduct the decennial census and report state population totals for 
apportionment. 13 U.S.C. § 141. 
Changes to the population used for apportionment require careful constitutional and statutory 
scrutiny. Any change excluding people who ordinarily reside within a state could affect 
representation and should be supported by a clear legal basis and rigorous methodological 
analysis. 
Removing race and ethnicity questions from the decennial census questionnaire could impair 
data used for redistricting, voting-rights analysis, civil-rights enforcement, research, and 
identification of racial disparities in the distribution of federal resources. Census race data are 
based on self-identification, allowing individuals to identify their own racial and ethnic 
backgrounds rather than relying exclusively on administrative records or statistical assignments. 
These concerns are particularly significant because racial and ethnic communities have different 
population patterns that must be accurately represented. The Census Bureau found a 
statistically significant 3.30% national undercount of the Black or African American alone or in
combination population in the 2020 Census. 
Piscataway Township demonstrates why preserving accurate race and ethnicity data is critical. 
According to the 2020 Census, Piscataway Township had 60,804 residents. Of those residents, 
11,771 identified as Black or African American alone, 23,973 as Asian alone, 130 as American 
Indian or Alaska Native alone, 21 as Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander alone, 834 as 
some other race alone, and 1,548 as two or more races. Piscataway Township also had 
approximately 8,276 Hispanic or Latino residents according to Census Bureau demographic 
data. 
Middlesex County is similarly diverse. Current Census Bureau QuickFacts indicate that 
approximately 20.1% of county residents are Black, 39.6% Asian, 0.4% American Indian or 
Alaska Native, 7% identify with two or more races, and 13.6% are Hispanic or Latino. The 2020 
Census counted 12,208 Black residents, 24,048 Asian residents, 252 American Indian or Alaska 
Native residents, 28 Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander residents, 4,349 residents 
identifying as some other race, and 4,282 residents identifying with two or more races in 
Middlesex County. 
These populations are not statistically interchangeable. Accurate self-reported demographic 
information is necessary to understand where communities live, how populations are changing, 
whether electoral districts provide equitable representation, and whether disparities exist in 
housing, health, education, employment, transportation, and access to public services. 
Proposed changes to “usual residence” also require rigorous testing. Piscataway Township is 
home to college students, renters, immigrants, multigenerational households, individuals 
experiencing housing instability, families with shared living arrangements, and residents who 
move during the year. Residence rules must be designed and tested so these populations are 
neither omitted nor counted in the wrong location. 
Any collection or use of legal-status information should likewise be evaluated for its effect on 
census participation. Before adopting such a change, the Census Bureau should publicly 
demonstrate whether it could affect response rates, household omissions, public confidence, or 
participation among immigrant and mixed-status households. 
Before finalizing substantial changes to the 2030 Census, the Bureau should provide 
transparent legal analysis, field testing, coverage-error analysis, and publicly available evidence 
addressing impacts on historically undercounted populations and racial and ethnic communities. 
The governing objective of the 2030 Census should remain clear: every person should be 
counted accurately, once, and in the appropriate place, while preserving reliable demographic 
data necessary to understand and represent communities such as Piscataway Township and 
Middlesex County. 
Thank you for your consideration. 
Sincerely, 
Central Jersey Alumnae Chapter 
South Plainfield, New Jersey

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am commenting on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am the grandchild of refugees, a parent, and a social scientist.  I live in Massachusetts.  I care about a fair and accurate census because census data directly affects representation in our government, and every American deserves to be represented.

I have two requests:
1) Please extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

2) Please withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including:

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all of the people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied reality of actual living arrangements in the United States, including for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. Tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Eliminate the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Re: Docket USBC-2026-0628; RIN 0607-AA75 
Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed 
Regulations for Demographic Questions 
Dear Director of the U.S. Census Bureau: 
I submit this comment on behalf of Central Jersey Alumnae Chapter to raise serious concerns 
regarding proposed changes to the 2030 Census and their potential consequences for Black 
communities and other racial and ethnic populations, including residents of City of Plainfield and 
Union County. 
The Constitution requires an “actual Enumeration” every ten years, and the Fourteenth 
Amendment provides for congressional representation based on the “whole number of persons 
in each State.” U.S. Const. art. I, § 2; amend. XIV, § 2. Congress further directs the Secretary of 
Commerce to conduct the decennial census and report state population totals for 
apportionment. 13 U.S.C. § 141. 
Changes to the population used for apportionment require careful constitutional and statutory 
scrutiny. Any change excluding people who ordinarily reside within a state could affect 
representation and should be supported by a clear legal basis and rigorous methodological 
analysis. 
Removing race and ethnicity questions from the decennial census questionnaire could impair 
data used for redistricting, voting-rights analysis, civil-rights enforcement, research, and 
identification of racial disparities in the distribution of federal resources. Census race data are 
based on self-identification, allowing individuals to identify their own racial and ethnic 
backgrounds rather than relying exclusively on administrative records or statistical assignments. 
These concerns are particularly significant because racial and ethnic communities have different 
population patterns that must be accurately represented. The Census Bureau found a 
statistically significant 3.30% national undercount of the Black or African American alone or in
combination population in the 2020 Census. 
City of Plainfield demonstrates why preserving accurate race and ethnicity data is critical. 
According to the 2020 Census, City of Plainfield had 54,586 residents. Of those residents, 
19,611 identified as Black or African American alone, 523 as Asian alone, 1,063 as American 
Indian or Alaska Native alone, 30 as Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander alone, 21,061 as 
some other race alone, and 6,843 as two or more races. City of Plainfield also had 
approximately 29,792 Hispanic or Latino residents according to Census Bureau demographic 
data. 
Union County is similarly diverse. Current Census Bureau QuickFacts indicate that 
approximately 20.4% of county residents are Black, 5.6% Asian, 0.7% American Indian or 
Alaska Native, 13.8% identify with two or more races, and 34% are Hispanic or Latino. The 
2020 Census counted 117,306 Black residents, 32,434 Asian residents, 4,022 American Indian 
or Alaska Native residents, 200 Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander residents, 105,583 
residents identifying as some other race, and 79,211 residents identifying with two or more 
races in Union County. 
These populations are not statistically interchangeable. Accurate self-reported demographic 
information is necessary to understand where communities live, how populations are changing, 
whether electoral districts provide equitable representation, and whether disparities exist in 
housing, health, education, employment, transportation, and access to public services. 
Proposed changes to “usual residence” also require rigorous testing. City of Plainfield is home 
to college students, renters, immigrants, multigenerational households, individuals experiencing 
housing instability, families with shared living arrangements, and residents who move during the 
year. Residence rules must be designed and tested so these populations are neither omitted 
nor counted in the wrong location. 
Any collection or use of legal-status information should likewise be evaluated for its effect on 
census participation. Before adopting such a change, the Census Bureau should publicly 
demonstrate whether it could affect response rates, household omissions, public confidence, or 
participation among immigrant and mixed-status households. 
Before finalizing substantial changes to the 2030 Census, the Bureau should provide 
transparent legal analysis, field testing, coverage-error analysis, and publicly available evidence 
addressing impacts on historically undercounted populations and racial and ethnic communities. 
The governing objective of the 2030 Census should remain clear: every person should be 
counted accurately, once, and in the appropriate place, while preserving reliable demographic 
data necessary to understand and represent communities such as City of Plainfield and Union 
County. 
Thank you for your consideration. 
Sincerely, 
Central Jersey Alumnae Chapter 
South Plainfield, New Jersey 
Delta Sigma Theta Sorority, Inc.
