Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

Re: Docket No. 260903-0005, RIN 0607-AA75, USBC-2026-0628. “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions”

I am a resident of Puerto Rico (Gurabo). I submit this comment to oppose proposed 15 CFR Parts 60 and 70 because of the harm they would cause to a complete and accurate count of Puerto Rico and of Puerto Ricans.

Soy una adulta puertorriqueña con un hijo adolescente. Me preocupa el impacto de los cambios propuestos y el impacto que esto puede causar. Trabajo en unas sin fines de lucro y me parece que estos cambios pudieran afectar los fondos que recibimos para atender poblaciones desventajadas.

The proposed rule does not mention Puerto Rico a single time, even though the decennial census counts more than 3.2 million U.S. citizens on the island and produces the data used to redraw our legislative districts. Sections 60.5 and 70.3 refer to the “stateside census” and to the “national or state level” without defining “United States.” I ask the Census Bureau to explain in writing how Parts 60 and 70 would apply in Puerto Rico, and not to finalize any rule without doing so.

Section 70.2(a) would prohibit the Hispanic-origin question, which includes the “Puerto Rican” checkbox. More people of Puerto Rican origin now live in the states than on the island, and that question is the only way the decennial census counts them. Without it, our communities in New York, Florida, Pennsylvania, Massachusetts, Connecticut, and elsewhere would disappear from the data used to enforce civil and voting rights and to plan services. I ask that Section 70.2(a) be withdrawn.

Section 60.2(a) says usual residence “should be consistent with, and evidenced by” tax records, but does not say which ones. Most Puerto Rico residents file with the Puerto Rico Department of the Treasury (Hacienda), our local tax authority, not with the IRS; employers issue Form 499R-2/W-2PR. I ask the Census Bureau to state in writing whether it would accept Hacienda returns and Form 499R-2/W-2PR as tax records in Puerto Rico, and how it would obtain and match them.

Even if the Bureau used Hacienda returns, a residence test based on tax records would leave many people in Puerto Rico out. An estimated one-third of the population doesn’t file and works in the informal economy (Caraballo-Cueto), and retirees and low-income households often file no return at all. Moreover, there is concern that a substantial share of the returns that are filed list a P.O. box or rural route as the address, which does not identify the home where the person lives. I ask that tax records not be made the proof of residence in Puerto Rico, and that self-response and field verification be accepted.

An estimated 40% to 60% of structures in Puerto Rico have no physical street-and-number (city-style) address, the standard federal systems use, so they cannot be validated, matched, or placed on a map. Many families receive mail at P.O. boxes or rural routes rather than where they live, and our addresses use an “Urbanización” line and accents that national systems don’t match well. A record with a mailing address does not prove where a person lives. I ask the Bureau to publish Puerto Rico address-match rates for every administrative source and to keep in-person enumeration wherever addresses cannot be matched.

Section 60.2 would replace the long-standing concept of where a person lives and sleeps most of the time with a count of days between January 3 and April 1. Circular migration is common in Puerto Rico: students, seasonal farmworkers, people caring for relatives, and families displaced by hurricanes and earthquakes. This rule would place them in the wrong location or miss them entirely. I ask that the Bureau keep the usual-residence standard used in prior censuses.

The Bureau invites comments on adding a legal-status question to the questionnaire. I oppose it. Puerto Rico has long-established immigrant communities and many mixed-status households that include U.S. citizens. The fear such a question creates would suppress response from entire households and worsen undercounts in the barrios and municipios where they live.

The Puerto Rico Community Survey and nearly all surveys are weighted to population estimates based on the decennial census. Section 70.4 says the ACS could still ask about race and origin, but without those data in the census there would be no reliable benchmark. Municipios, agencies, hospitals, universities, nonprofits, and businesses depend on these data, as does the distribution of federal funds for health, nutrition, education, housing, and disaster recovery. 

Thank you for considering this comment.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am a public health professional working in Minnesota, and I care about a fair and accurate census because this count impacts funding, resources, and representation in our communities. Inaccurate information will harm our public health and make it harder to support our community. 

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.
As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:

Ariel Lugo, President
Brianna Davis, Social Action Chair

Re: Docket USBC-2026-0628; RIN 0607-AA75
Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions
 
Dear Director of the U.S. Census Bureau:
 
I submit this comment on behalf of Xi Beta to raise serious concerns regarding proposed changes to the 2030 Census and their potential consequences for Black communities and other racial and ethnic populations, including residents of Rock Hill and York County.
 
The Constitution requires an “actual Enumeration” every ten years, and the Fourteenth Amendment provides for congressional representation based on the “whole number of persons in each State.” U.S. Const. art. I, § 2; amend. XIV, § 2. Congress further directs the Secretary of Commerce to conduct the decennial census and report state population totals for apportionment. 13 U.S.C. § 141.
 
Changes to the population used for apportionment require careful constitutional and statutory scrutiny. Any change excluding people who ordinarily reside within a state could affect representation and should be supported by a clear legal basis and rigorous methodological analysis.
 
Removing race and ethnicity questions from the decennial census questionnaire could impair data used for redistricting, voting-rights analysis, civil-rights enforcement, research, and identification of racial disparities in the distribution of federal resources. Census race data are based on self-identification, allowing individuals to identify their own racial and ethnic backgrounds rather than relying exclusively on administrative records or statistical assignments.
 
These concerns are particularly significant because racial and ethnic communities have different population patterns that must be accurately represented. The Census Bureau found a statistically significant 3.30% national undercount of the Black or African American alone or in-combination population in the 2020 Census.
 
Rock Hill demonstrates why preserving accurate race and ethnicity data is critical. According to the 2020 Census, Rock Hill had 74,345 residents. Of those residents, 38.3%  identified as Black or African American alone, 1.8% as Asian alone, 0.6% as American Indian or Alaska Native alone, 0.0%  as Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander alone, 49.2%  as some other race alone, and 6.5% as two or more races. Rock Hill also had approximately 6.9% Hispanic or Latino residents according to Census Bureau demographic data.
 
York County is similarly diverse. Current Census Bureau QuickFacts indicate that approximately 18.4 % of county residents are Black, 3.1% Asian, 0.9% American Indian or Alaska Native, 6.6% identify with two or more races, and 8.5% are Hispanic or Latino. The 2020 Census counted 51,898 Black residents, 8,825 Asian residents, 2,284 American Indian or Alaska Native residents, 128 Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander residents, 8,346 residents identifying as some other race, and 18,760 residents identifying with two or more races in York County.
 
These populations are not statistically interchangeable. Accurate self-reported demographic information is necessary to understand where communities live, how populations are changing, whether electoral districts provide equitable representation, and whether disparities exist in housing, health, education, employment, transportation, and access to public services.
 
Proposed changes to “usual residence” also require rigorous testing. Rock Hill is home to college students, renters, immigrants, multigenerational households, individuals experiencing housing instability, families with shared living arrangements, and residents who move during the year. Residence rules must be designed and tested so these populations are neither omitted nor counted in the wrong location.
 
Any collection or use of legal-status information should likewise be evaluated for its effect on census participation. Before adopting such a change, the Census Bureau should publicly demonstrate whether it could affect response rates, household omissions, public confidence, or participation among immigrant and mixed-status households.
 
Before finalizing substantial changes to the 2030 Census, the Bureau should provide transparent legal analysis, field testing, coverage-error analysis, and publicly available evidence addressing impacts on historically undercounted populations and racial and ethnic communities.
 
The governing objective of the 2030 Census should remain clear: every person should be counted accurately, once, and in the appropriate place, while preserving reliable demographic data necessary to understand and represent communities such as Rock Hill and York County.
 
Thank you for your consideration.
 
Sincerely,
Xi Beta 
Rock Hill, South Carolina
Delta Sigma Theta Sorority, Inc.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am a past foster parent, current adoptive parent, teacher, and Christian in Central Texas, and I care about a fair and accurate census because accurate data helps protect our representative democracy and our constitutional rights.

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including:

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.
As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Thank you,
Will Slade

Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.
As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

 The proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. I am very concerned that the proposed residence criteria and changes to demographic questions would undermine the accuracy, integrity, and usefulness of census data. 
As a recent graduate with a Master of Science in Economics, I know that comprehensive and accurate data are essential. Our policymakers, businesses and organizations rely on data to craft legislation, make business investments, and understand the critical issues of society.

Therefore, I urge you to continue collecting race and ethnicity data and implement the 2024 OMB SPD 15 standards.

I thank you for your consideration as you work to implement the best policies for people the United States.

Kind regards,

Comment:
I am vehemently opposed to the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). The proposed changes are harmful to data democracy. It goes against historical precedent and threatens the integrity of census data. I oppose both part 60 and part 70 and urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule. I also ask that the comment period be extended to the full 90 day period as the American people deserve more time to review and respond to these unlawful changes. 

I am a researcher and user of U.S. Census data. I have conducted various data analyses using Census Bureau data. These analyses require the use of accurate and comprehensive data and were used to help answer both scientific and applied research questions. I am very concerned about the proposed changes to the 2030 Census and future surveys. The purpose of the census is to count all people in the United States: both citizens and non-citizens alike. Only counting some people would not result in a fair or accurate count. All people deserve representation, not just some select individuals. Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am a community member in Illinois and I care about a fair and accurate census because without it we cannot provide the appropriate aid to our communities. A proper census ensures that everyone is taken into account and resources can be allocated appropriately. Our nation has collected race and ethnicity data in every census since 1790, and we should continue through and past 2030.  There are a multitude of factors that contribute to health outcomes and disparities, and excluding any of them greatly alters the efficacy of census data.

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including:

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.
As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am a citizen of the United States of America, and I am commenting as an individual.  I am addressing sections 60.4 and 70.2 of the NPRM.  I support the proposed language of section 60.4 as published.  I further support the language of section 70.2 also as published.  The reasons for my support are as follows:

The census data are used for apportionment, which specifies the number of representatives each state will send to the United States House of Representatives.  Members of that body are elected by American citizens--people who by definition owe allegiance to America--to act on our behalf and in our interest.  Skewing the numbers of representatives states send to Congress to execute that sacred duty with inflated numbers deriving from people who are not American citizens, and do not owe their allegiance to America, is unconscionable.  More than just the injustice of overrepresentation for states that allowed themselves to be overrun with illegal aliens, there is the attendant blatant unfairness of underrepresentation of the citizens of states that did not. 
Even more fundamentally, the citizens of foreign countries should no more have a voice in American governance than should we in theirs.  The notion is nonsensical on its very face.  Whatever can be done to safeguard the integrity of our Representative Republic should be done, and this proposed language is a step in that direction.

Regarding the second section specifically, it is wholly inappropriate for the U.S. government to inquire about Americans' race, ethnicity, or sexual orientation in the context of the census.  The purpose of the census is literally to count Americans, as discussed above, and these "categories" have nothing whatsoever to do with that objective.  Americans are all free and equal citizens of this country regardless of the color of our skin or whom we choose as partners, and our right to representation is unaffected (or should be) by those irrelevant individual traits.  Moreover, any information gathering that could be used by bad actors to further divide rather than unite Americans violates the fundamental meaning of our citizenship and exposes the nefarious motivations of the people behind it.  American citizens are American citizens.  That statement of fact is simple and straightforward, and it must be left at that.

I am submitting anonymously because of the harms, up to and including violence, that people who have a different viewpoint have tended to cause of late.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
My name is [Your Name] and I am your constituent from [City/Zip Code]. As Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander (AANHPI) Heritage Month comes to a close, I write to urge you to support AANHPI students by cosponsoring the All Students Count Act.

To the U.S. Census Bureau: 

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule titled “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005). Eliminating the collection of race and ethnic data, prohibiting the collection of sexual orientation, and leaving non-citizens out of the apportionment would significantly harm the Southeast Asian American (SEAA) and broader Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander (AANHPI) communities. I respectfully request that the Census Bureau withdraw the proposed rule and extend the comment period to December 10, 2026. 

This proposed rule would significantly harm the SEAA and AANHPI communities. The AANHPI community is not a homogenous population; it encompasses over 50 different ethnic groups and 100 languages and dialects. There are vast socioeconomic disparities within the AANHPI population, often related to their migratory and historical experience. SEAAs, such as the Cambodian, Hmong, Laotian, and Mien populations, often have higher rates of poverty and lower educational attainment rates than both the broader AANHPI and American populations. 

For SEAAs, this disparity is generally tied to their experiences escaping their countries of origin and resettlement in the United States after the Vietnam War, Secret War in Laos, and Khmer Rouge genocide in Cambodia. For example, because of the 2020 Census, we now know that the Mien population has lower educational attainment rates compared to the general American and AANHPI populations. Additionally, the data also show that Mien men have a lower educational attainment rate compared to women. Such information could only be obtained because of the census, which is the primary source for data collection and reporting of small ethnic groups. These data cannot be replicated by other surveys, including the American Community Survey. 

Accurate data, reflective of race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation, help our elected officials properly identify and address the unique needs and challenges of our communities. Prohibiting the collection of this demographic data would prevent our government officials from passing informed public policy; hamper the ability of community-based organizations to demonstrate data narratives for fundraising purposes; and inhibit the ability of students and academics studying our communities from accessing the most robust source of information on SEAAs and the broader AANHPI community. 

Thank you for taking my comment into consideration. I reiterate my request that the US Census Bureau withdraws the proposed rule; preserves the collection of race and ethnic data; and keeps its commitment to count everyone once, only once, and in the right place.

I also ask the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. Changes of this scope deserve more time for the public to review and respond.

Sincerely,
Pouelinna Chhey
Norwalk, CA 90650-4735

Comment:
September 28, 2026 

Re: Docket No. 260903-0005, RIN 0607-AA75, Department of Commerce, Census Bureau, Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions 

To Whom It May Concern, 

Thank you for the opportunity to provide comments on the proposal to revise several parts of the proposed regulation Docket No. 260903-0005, RIN 0607-AA75, Department of Commerce, Census Bureau, Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions. 

My name is James White. I am the executive director of the Nonprofit Association of Oregon. We represent over 1,700 nonprofits and individuals across Oregon in urban, suburban, rural, frontier, and coastal communities.

Executive Director

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: US Census Bureau,I urge the Census Bureau and Department of Commerce to withdraw the proposed rule changing residence criteria for the decennial Census and restricting demographic questions.The proposal would exclude foreign citizens from the population used for congressional apportionment unless they are also U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents. The Census proposes to only include people if their address is confirmed by tax records -- which could mean millions, particularly low-income families, could be missed in the decennial Census. Overall, this would leave out people who actually live in our community, including many people who are lawfully present in the United States.For all past Census counts, including the 2020 Census, foreign citizens living in the United States were generally counted where they lived and slept most of the time. That approach recognizes the basic purpose of a Census: accurately counting the people who live in our communities. The 14th Amendment requires congressional representation to be apportioned according to the “whole number of persons in each State.”I am also deeply concerned by the proposal to prohibit race and ethnicity questions, along with sexual orientation, on the decennial Census enumeration questionnaire. The Census Bureau itself recognizes the importance of race data for civil rights protections, legislative redistricting, equal employment opportunities, and identifying disparities.The 2030 Census will determine congressional, state, and local representation for the decade that follows. It must be complete, accurate, and protected from political manipulation.Please withdraw this proposed rule and preserve a Census that fairly and accurately counts our community.Douglas  [X] Bellmead, Ohio 44107

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: US Census Bureau,I urge the Census Bureau and Department of Commerce to withdraw the proposed rule changing residence criteria for the decennial Census and restricting demographic questions.The proposal would exclude foreign citizens from the population used for congressional apportionment unless they are also U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents. The Census proposes to only include people if their address is confirmed by tax records -- which could mean millions, particularly low-income families, could be missed in the decennial Census. Overall, this would leave out people who actually live in our community, including many people who are lawfully present in the United States.For all past Census counts, including the 2020 Census, foreign citizens living in the United States were generally counted where they lived and slept most of the time. That approach recognizes the basic purpose of a Census: accurately counting the people who live in our communities. The 14th Amendment requires congressional representation to be apportioned according to the “whole number of persons in each State.”I am also deeply concerned by the proposal to prohibit race and ethnicity questions, along with sexual orientation, on the decennial Census enumeration questionnaire. The Census Bureau itself recognizes the importance of race data for civil rights protections, legislative redistricting, equal employment opportunities, and identifying disparities.The 2030 Census will determine congressional, state, and local representation for the decade that follows. It must be complete, accurate, and protected from political manipulation.Please withdraw this proposed rule and preserve a Census that fairly and accurately counts our community.Dr. Robert  [X] Bethlehem, Pennsylvania 18017

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: US Census Bureau,I urge the Census Bureau and Department of Commerce to withdraw the proposed rule changing residence criteria for the decennial Census and restricting demographic questions.The proposal would exclude foreign citizens from the population used for congressional apportionment unless they are also U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents. The Census proposes to only include people if their address is confirmed by tax records -- which could mean millions, particularly low-income families, could be missed in the decennial Census. Overall, this would leave out people who actually live in our community, including many people who are lawfully present in the United States.For all past Census counts, including the 2020 Census, foreign citizens living in the United States were generally counted where they lived and slept most of the time. That approach recognizes the basic purpose of a Census: accurately counting the people who live in our communities. Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: US Census Bureau,I urge the Census Bureau and Department of Commerce to withdraw the proposed rule changing residence criteria for the decennial Census and restricting demographic questions.The proposal would exclude foreign citizens from the population used for congressional apportionment unless they are also U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents. The Census proposes to only include people if their address is confirmed by tax records -- which could mean millions, particularly low-income families, could be missed in the decennial Census. Overall, this would leave out people who actually live in our community, including many people who are lawfully present in the United States.For all past Census counts, including the 2020 Census, foreign citizens living in the United States were generally counted where they lived and slept most of the time. That approach recognizes the basic purpose of a Census: accurately counting the people who live in our communities. The 14th Amendment requires congressional representation to be apportioned according to the “whole number of persons in each State.”I am also deeply concerned by the proposal to prohibit race and ethnicity questions, along with sexual orientation, on the decennial Census enumeration questionnaire. The Census Bureau itself recognizes the importance of race data for civil rights protections, legislative redistricting, equal employment opportunities, and identifying disparities.The 2030 Census will determine congressional, state, and local representation for the decade that follows. It must be complete, accurate, and protected from political manipulation.Please withdraw this proposed rule and preserve a Census that fairly and accurately counts our community.Rachel  [X] Essex Junction, Vermont 05452

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: US Census Bureau,I urge the Census Bureau and Department of Commerce to withdraw the proposed rule changing residence criteria for the decennial Census and restricting demographic questions.The proposal would exclude foreign citizens from the population used for congressional apportionment unless they are also U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents. It must be complete, accurate, and protected from political manipulation.Please withdraw this proposed rule and preserve a Census that fairly and accurately counts our community.Robert  [X] Granger , Washington 98932

Comment: US Census Bureau,I urge the Census Bureau and Department of Commerce to withdraw the proposed rule changing residence criteria for the decennial Census and restricting demographic questions.The proposal would exclude foreign citizens from the population used for congressional apportionment unless they are also U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents. The Census proposes to only include people if their address is confirmed by tax records -- which could mean millions, particularly low-income families, could be missed in the decennial Census. Overall, this would leave out people who actually live in our community, including many people who are lawfully present in the United States.For all past Census counts, including the 2020 Census, foreign citizens living in the United States were generally counted where they lived and slept most of the time. That approach recognizes the basic purpose of a Census: accurately counting the people who live in our communities. The 14th Amendment requires congressional representation to be apportioned according to the “whole number of persons in each State.”I am also deeply concerned by the proposal to prohibit race and ethnicity questions, along with sexual orientation, on the decennial Census enumeration questionnaire. The Census Bureau itself recognizes the importance of race data for civil rights protections, legislative redistricting, equal employment opportunities, and identifying disparities.The 2030 Census will determine congressional, state, and local representation for the decade that follows. It must be complete, accurate, and protected from political manipulation.Please withdraw this proposed rule and preserve a Census that fairly and accurately counts our community.Rosemary Seifert- [X] Cummington, Massachusetts 01026

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). 

I live in Pasadena, California and as a former educator I care about a fair and accurate census because census data and other federal datasets based on the census are used to make key decisions that affect our nation’s students, educators, and schools.  

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Examples of these uses include:  

Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. 

Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

Determining state higher education funding formulas 

Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

First, to ensure a fair and accurate census,  the Census Bureau should  extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. Second, I oppose both the proposed changes to the residence criteria and the proposed regulations regarding demographic questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. The Census Bureau should  withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 



• Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The Constitution requires  counting all people living in the United States. 

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (including children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count. 

Revise the tax records language so that those whose mailing address differs from their residential address (servicemembers, those with a post office box) are not excluded.  

• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for civil rights enforcement, among other uses, and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The prohibition, as written, may also restrict the collection or publication of census data on same-sex couples that was asked in 2020. 

 The proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Sincerely,
Jennie Cohen

Overall, this would leave out people who actually live in our community, including many people who are lawfully present in the United States.For all past Census counts, including the 2020 Census, foreign citizens living in the United States were generally counted where they lived and slept most of the time. That approach recognizes the basic purpose of a Census: accurately counting the people who live in our communities. The 14th Amendment requires congressional representation to be apportioned according to the “whole number of persons in each State.”I am also deeply concerned by the proposal to prohibit race and ethnicity questions, along with sexual orientation, on the decennial Census enumeration questionnaire. The Census Bureau itself recognizes the importance of race data for civil rights protections, legislative redistricting, equal employment opportunities, and identifying disparities.The 2030 Census will determine congressional, state, and local representation for the decade that follows. It must be complete, accurate, and protected from political manipulation.Please withdraw this proposed rule and preserve a Census that fairly and accurately counts our community.Georgeann  [X] Portland , Oregon 97202

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). 

I am [add a description of who you are and/or state where you live], and I care about a fair and accurate census because census data and other federal datasets based on the census are used to make key decisions that affect our nation’s students, educators, and schools.  

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Examples of these uses include:  [keep any/all points you would like to include in your comment – see this site if you would like to add state-specific statistics about funding impacts]. 

Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. 

Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

Determining state higher education funding formulas 

Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

First, to ensure a fair and accurate census,  the Census Bureau should  extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. Second, I oppose both the proposed changes to the residence criteria and the proposed regulations regarding demographic questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. The Census Bureau should  withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: [keep any/all points you would like to include in your comment] 

• Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The Constitution requires  counting all people living in the United States. 

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (including children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count. 

Revise the tax records language so that those whose mailing address differs from their residential address (servicemembers, those with a post office box) are not excluded.  

• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for civil rights enforcement, among other uses, and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The prohibition, as written, may also restrict the collection or publication of census data on same-sex couples that was asked in 2020. 

 The proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Sincerely,
Ms Carolyn Polak
Cleveland, OH 44134

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: US Census Bureau,I urge the Census Bureau and Department of Commerce to withdraw the proposed rule changing residence criteria for the decennial Census and restricting demographic questions.The proposal would exclude foreign citizens from the population used for congressional apportionment unless they are also U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents. The Census proposes to only include people if their address is confirmed by tax records -- which could mean millions, particularly low-income families, could be missed in the decennial Census. Overall, this would leave out people who actually live in our community, including many people who are lawfully present in the United States.For all past Census counts, including the 2020 Census, foreign citizens living in the United States were generally counted where they lived and slept most of the time. That approach recognizes the basic purpose of a Census: accurately counting the people who live in our communities. The 14th Amendment requires congressional representation to be apportioned according to the “whole number of persons in each State.”I am also deeply concerned by the proposal to prohibit race and ethnicity questions, along with sexual orientation, on the decennial Census enumeration questionnaire. The Census Bureau itself recognizes the importance of race data for civil rights protections, legislative redistricting, equal employment opportunities, and identifying disparities.The 2030 Census will determine congressional, state, and local representation for the decade that follows. It must be complete, accurate, and protected from political manipulation.Please withdraw this proposed rule and preserve a Census that fairly and accurately counts our community.Marianna  [X] Lopez Island, Washington 98261

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
My name is [Your Name] and I am your constituent from [City/Zip Code]. As Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander (AANHPI) Heritage Month comes to a close, I write to urge you to support AANHPI students by cosponsoring the All Students Count Act.

To the U.S. Census Bureau: 

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule titled “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005). Eliminating the collection of race and ethnic data, prohibiting the collection of sexual orientation, and leaving non-citizens out of the apportionment would significantly harm the Southeast Asian American (SEAA) and broader Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander (AANHPI) communities. I respectfully request that the Census Bureau withdraw the proposed rule and extend the comment period to December 10, 2026. 

This proposed rule would significantly harm the SEAA and AANHPI communities. The AANHPI community is not a homogenous population; it encompasses over 50 different ethnic groups and 100 languages and dialects. There are vast socioeconomic disparities within the AANHPI population, often related to their migratory and historical experience. SEAAs, such as the Cambodian, Hmong, Laotian, and Mien populations, often have higher rates of poverty and lower educational attainment rates than both the broader AANHPI and American populations. 

For SEAAs, this disparity is generally tied to their experiences escaping their countries of origin and resettlement in the United States after the Vietnam War, Secret War in Laos, and Khmer Rouge genocide in Cambodia. For example, because of the 2020 Census, we now know that the Mien population has lower educational attainment rates compared to the general American and AANHPI populations. Additionally, the data also show that Mien men have a lower educational attainment rate compared to women. Such information could only be obtained because of the census, which is the primary source for data collection and reporting of small ethnic groups. These data cannot be replicated by other surveys, including the American Community Survey. 

Accurate data, reflective of race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation, help our elected officials properly identify and address the unique needs and challenges of our communities. Prohibiting the collection of this demographic data would prevent our government officials from passing informed public policy; hamper the ability of community-based organizations to demonstrate data narratives for fundraising purposes; and inhibit the ability of students and academics studying our communities from accessing the most robust source of information on SEAAs and the broader AANHPI community. 

Thank you for taking my comment into consideration. I reiterate my request that the US Census Bureau withdraws the proposed rule; preserves the collection of race and ethnic data; and keeps its commitment to count everyone once, only once, and in the right place.

I also ask the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. Changes of this scope deserve more time for the public to review and respond.

Sincerely,
Jenny Korn
Rainbow City, AL 35906-6230

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: US Census Bureau,I urge the Census Bureau and Department of Commerce to withdraw the proposed rule changing residence criteria for the decennial Census and restricting demographic questions.The proposal would exclude foreign citizens from the population used for congressional apportionment unless they are also U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents. Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: US Census Bureau,I urge the Census Bureau and Department of Commerce to withdraw the proposed rule changing residence criteria for the decennial Census and restricting demographic questions.The proposal would exclude foreign citizens from the population used for congressional apportionment unless they are also U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents. The Census proposes to only include people if their address is confirmed by tax records -- which could mean millions, particularly low-income families, could be missed in the decennial Census. Overall, this would leave out people who actually live in our community, including many people who are lawfully present in the United States.For all past Census counts, including the 2020 Census, foreign citizens living in the United States were generally counted where they lived and slept most of the time. That approach recognizes the basic purpose of a Census: accurately counting the people who live in our communities. The 14th Amendment requires congressional representation to be apportioned according to the “whole number of persons in each State.”I am also deeply concerned by the proposal to prohibit race and ethnicity questions, along with sexual orientation, on the decennial Census enumeration questionnaire. The Census Bureau itself recognizes the importance of race data for civil rights protections, legislative redistricting, equal employment opportunities, and identifying disparities.The 2030 Census will determine congressional, state, and local representation for the decade that follows. It must be complete, accurate, and protected from political manipulation.Please withdraw this proposed rule and preserve a Census that fairly and accurately counts our community.Cynthia Radfordrichardradford@comcast.net51 Magnolia DrCalistoga, California 94515

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: US Census Bureau,I urge the Census Bureau and Department of Commerce to withdraw the proposed rule changing residence criteria for the decennial Census and restricting demographic questions.The proposal would exclude foreign citizens from the population used for congressional apportionment unless they are also U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents. It must be complete, accurate, and protected from political manipulation.Please withdraw this proposed rule and preserve a Census that fairly and accurately counts our community.Richard Guierrsguier444@msn.com255 W 108th St New YorkNew York, New York 10025

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Hello,
I am writing to express my opposition to the proposed changes for the census in 2030 and moving forward. Do not change the criteria for the census which has been in place since 1970. The purpose of a census is to determine the current population of all peoples, regardless of citizenship or immigration status, residing in the United States of America at that time. The current changes that are proposed in preparation for the 2030 census will grossly misrepresent the US population and deny resources and representation to thousands of citizens.
First of all, citizenship/legal status has no place on the census. If a person cannot legally vote then they will be unable to register to vote, but they are still a member of the community and their voice must be heard by lawmakers. I listen to them and so should you. Also, using federal databases to determine legal status is an invasion of privacy and, as we have seen since 2025, has been detrimental in allowing individuals to become citizens but that is a different discussion. Again, the purpose of the census is to get an accurate picture of the population and their needs, and that leads me to my next point: race and ethnicity. Claiming "color blindness" helps no one, not even white people. And many studies show that People of Color recieve less medical care and less education opportunities (Shah, N. Anti-racism in Education: A Conceptual Map. Urban Rev 58, 73 (2026). https://doi.org/10.1007/s11256-026-00856-x). Race and ethinicity is important to understanding the needs of a community, which trickles up to the benefit of the state and country as a whole. The original plan for the 2030 census was going to include more subgroups to race and ethnicity and I request that you expand on that question rather than remove it entirely. I will also say that listing sexual orientation as an optional response is also important if our country is to provide the best healthcare and education to her people.
Another concern I have is the use of tax records to determine a person's residence. This affects people who frequently move or do not have a set residence such as college students, nurses, long-term care facilities, unhoused persons (they need to be counted too!), military persons, and people who split their time between two residences. This last one especially applies to me as a seasonal biologist. I bounce between locations--often between states or counties--based on the seasonal jobs. The 2020 census criteria accounted for 30 living situations, but the 2030 criteria is going to account for 10 situations. Once again, that will result in an inaccurate count of America's population and lead to gross misrepresentation of the people's needs in the House.
In conclusion, I urge you to count every person residing in America regardless of citizenship status, retain the questions on race and ethnicity, and take into account the citizens that have unique living situations. Thank you for your time.

Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. 

Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

Determining state higher education funding formulas 

Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

First, to ensure a fair and accurate census,  the Census Bureau should  extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. • Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The Constitution requires  counting all people living in the United States. 

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (including children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.

Valley Park, MO 63088

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: US Census Bureau,I urge the Census Bureau and Department of Commerce to withdraw the proposed rule changing residence criteria for the decennial Census and restricting demographic questions.The proposal would exclude foreign citizens from the population used for congressional apportionment unless they are also U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents. The Census proposes to only include people if their address is confirmed by tax records -- which could mean millions, particularly low-income families, could be missed in the decennial Census. Overall, this would leave out people who actually live in our community, including many people who are lawfully present in the United States.For all past Census counts, including the 2020 Census, foreign citizens living in the United States were generally counted where they lived and slept most of the time. That approach recognizes the basic purpose of a Census: accurately counting the people who live in our communities. The 14th Amendment requires congressional representation to be apportioned according to the “whole number of persons in each State.”I am also deeply concerned by the proposal to prohibit race and ethnicity questions, along with sexual orientation, on the decennial Census enumeration questionnaire. The Census Bureau itself recognizes the importance of race data for civil rights protections, legislative redistricting, equal employment opportunities, and identifying disparities.The 2030 Census will determine congressional, state, and local representation for the decade that follows. It must be complete, accurate, and protected from political manipulation.Please withdraw this proposed rule and preserve a Census that fairly and accurately counts our community.Kay Samson [X] Green Bay , Wisconsin 54303

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am a social worker in St. Louis, Missouri, and I care about a fair and accurate census because so many important decisions about resource allocation, trends in disease burden, social determinants of health, and other critically important areas are based on results from the U.S. Census.  I see this play out in my professional world (I've been a social worker for 20 years) as well as in my personal life.

First, I ask the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. Significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve more time for the public to review and respond.  There is no valid reason to rush to make such sweeping changes without sufficient time for the public to be made aware and to have a chance to give input.  

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: allowing asylum seekers,  visa holders, DACA recipients, and Temporary Protected Status (TPS) holders to be counted towards representation as well as maintaining questions about race and ethnicity.  Questions about race and ethnicity are not, as the proposal indicates, sensitive in nature -- they provide us with valuable information about the composition of communities, the income level and many other associated factors, and help inform where and how resources are allocated.  In an ideal state, there wouldn't be such enormous health and wealth disparities across race and ethnicity -- but that is very far from reality.  We need these questions to be included in the U.S. Census as a continued benchmark for dozens of key data sets that rely on Census data.  I also urge you to:

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am commenting in strong opposition to the proposed rule: Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions. Article I, Section 2, Clause 3 of the U.S. Constitution mandates that an "actual Enumeration" of the population. This proposal undermines that mandate. First, the new regulations would exclude millions of immigrants. DACA holders, international students, work-visa holders, refugees, asylees, and other residents from the Census. This would be the first time in 260 years that the Census has excluded people based on immigration status and would thus significantly undercount the actual US population. This would then affect funding, services, and our fundamental understanding of our country and communities.
Eliminating significant demographic information such as race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation also weakens the Census and its utlilty. This policy would effectively render vulnerable and marginalized communities and groups invisible making it extremely difficult to address inequities. 
Finally, the majority of other government and non-government surveys are weighted to U.S. Census counts, so the loss of this data and resulting erasure would have immense downstream effects on public opinion, public health, public education, and civil rights.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: US Census Bureau,I urge the Census Bureau and Department of Commerce to withdraw the proposed rule changing residence criteria for the decennial Census and restricting demographic questions.The proposal would exclude foreign citizens from the population used for congressional apportionment unless they are also U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents. The Census proposes to only include people if their address is confirmed by tax records -- which could mean millions, particularly low-income families, could be missed in the decennial Census. Overall, this would leave out people who actually live in our community, including many people who are lawfully present in the United States.For all past Census counts, including the 2020 Census, foreign citizens living in the United States were generally counted where they lived and slept most of the time. That approach recognizes the basic purpose of a Census: accurately counting the people who live in our communities. The 14th Amendment requires congressional representation to be apportioned according to the “whole number of persons in each State.”I am also deeply concerned by the proposal to prohibit race and ethnicity questions, along with sexual orientation, on the decennial Census enumeration questionnaire. The Census Bureau itself recognizes the importance of race data for civil rights protections, legislative redistricting, equal employment opportunities, and identifying disparities.The 2030 Census will determine congressional, state, and local representation for the decade that follows. It must be complete, accurate, and protected from political manipulation.Please withdraw this proposed rule and preserve a Census that fairly and accurately counts our community.Deidre [X] Lake City, Pennsylvania 16423

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing in opposition to the Census Bureau's proposed rule: "Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions" (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I strongly object to a change that would radically alter who is counted for congressional apportionment, which local communities are resourced, and whether we can track progress on civil rights protections without race and ethnicity questions from the decennial census.

1. The Census Must Count Everyone Who Lives Here

The Constitution requires representation to be based on the "whole number of persons in each State," not citizens specifically. This rule would exclude international students, work visa holders, refugees, and asylum seekers from the count for the first time, even though they live in our communities, work, pay taxes, and use the same roads and schools as everyone else. Attempting to sort people by legal status also creates fear that keeps entire households, including U.S. citizens, from responding at all.

2. Counting People by Administrative Record Will Distort Representation

The rule would place people based on tax records and other administrative data rather than where they actually live. Tax records often list an old address, a P.O. box, or a preparer's office, which fails students, seasonal workers, service members, and anyone who moved recently. Federal law has always set a single fixed date, April 1, for the census. This rule replaces that with a shifting three-month window, adding complexity without adding accuracy.

3. Race and Ethnicity Data Are Essential

The census has asked about race in some form since the very first census in 1790. This data is what allows the country to track discrimination, enforce voting rights, and direct public health and civil rights resources. The American Community Survey cannot replace it, since it only produces estimates and itself relies on the decennial census for accuracy. The rule would also make nearly every demographic question voluntary, despite a federal law requiring people to answer census questions. And it would bar any future question on sexual orientation, though the more significant risk is a new provision giving the Bureau broad discretion to withhold published data on smaller communities, including same-sex households.

4. Communities Without Accurate Data Get Left Behind

Arab Americans have historically been undercounted because no census category captured them. The 2030 Census is set to be the first with a dedicated Middle Eastern or North African (MENA) category, a change advocates spent years securing to improve data collection on people from the MENA region. This rule would eliminate that progress along with all race and ethnicity data collection. Any community without accurate data becomes harder to serve, harder to protect, and easier to overlook.

I urge the Census Bureau and the Department of Commerce to withdraw these proposed changes and to count everyone who lives here, accurately and in the right place.

Sincerely,
Z Haider

The Constitution requires counting every resident to ensure fair representation and funding for our communities. Manipulating the headcount undermines our democracy. Please preserve an accurate, inclusive 2030 Census.EllenPennsylvania

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: US Census Bureau,I urge the Census Bureau and Department of Commerce to withdraw the proposed rule changing residence criteria for the decennial Census and restricting demographic questions.The proposal would exclude foreign citizens from the population used for congressional apportionment unless they are also U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents. The Census proposes to only include people if their address is confirmed by tax records -- which could mean millions, particularly low-income families, could be missed in the decennial Census. Overall, this would leave out people who actually live in our community, including many people who are lawfully present in the United States.For all past Census counts, including the 2020 Census, foreign citizens living in the United States were generally counted where they lived and slept most of the time. That approach recognizes the basic purpose of a Census: accurately counting the people who live in our communities. The 14th Amendment requires congressional representation to be apportioned according to the “whole number of persons in each State.”I am also deeply concerned by the proposal to prohibit race and ethnicity questions, along with sexual orientation, on the decennial Census enumeration questionnaire. The Census Bureau itself recognizes the importance of race data for civil rights protections, legislative redistricting, equal employment opportunities, and identifying disparities.The 2030 Census will determine congressional, state, and local representation for the decade that follows. It must be complete, accurate, and protected from political manipulation.Please withdraw this proposed rule and preserve a Census that fairly and accurately counts our community.Kurt  [X] Overland Park, Kansas 66207

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). 

I am [add a description of who you are and/or state where you live], and I care about a fair and accurate census because census data and other federal datasets based on the census are used to make key decisions that affect our nation’s students, educators, and schools.  

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Examples of these uses include:  [keep any/all points you would like to include in your comment – see this site if you would like to add state-specific statistics about funding impacts]. 

Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. 

Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

Determining state higher education funding formulas 

Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

First, to ensure a fair and accurate census,  the Census Bureau should  extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. Second, I oppose both the proposed changes to the residence criteria and the proposed regulations regarding demographic questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. The Census Bureau should  withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: [keep any/all points you would like to include in your comment] 

• Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The Constitution requires  counting all people living in the United States. 

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (including children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count. 

Revise the tax records language so that those whose mailing address differs from their residential address (servicemembers, those with a post office box) are not excluded.  

• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for civil rights enforcement, among other uses, and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The prohibition, as written, may also restrict the collection or publication of census data on same-sex couples that was asked in 2020. 

 The proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Sincerely,
Ms. Debbie Farber
Bridgewater, NJ 08807
