Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am concerned citizen living and working in Los Osos CA and I care about a fair and accurate census.

First, I ask the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. Significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve more time for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with the following:

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.
As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

It must be complete, accurate, and protected from political manipulation.Please withdraw this proposed rule and preserve a Census that fairly and accurately counts our community.Esther [X] Massachusetts 02148-8148

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Census Bureau's proposed rule to strengthen the US Census is critical to fair representation and the future of America.  

The U.S. Census should not include distorted data in its count of Americans.  By including overly generalized ethnic demographic categories, we obscure the true goal of the census and hinder its constitutionally mandated purpose: an accurate count of Americans.  

Additionally, illegal aliens and other non-legal permanent residents should not be included for apportionment. Census data is used for the apportionment of congressional seats. Non-citizens cannot legally vote and should not be used to decrease the voting power of Americans. I support the Census Bureau in advancing the correct understanding of usual residence to recognize an element of allegiance that is antithetical to the inclusion of those not legally present in our country.  

This Census Bureau should also consider adding a citizenship question to the Census survey. The Supreme Court has already held that the Constitution lawfully permits the Census Bureau to at least inquire about citizenship on the census questionnaire. "The census should absolutely include questions related to citizenship and legal presence. 

These changes would strengthen the census in its core purpose of attaining an accurate count of Americans and have my full support. 

Thank you,  

Sue Black

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). 

I am [add a description of who you are and/or state where you live], and I care about a fair and accurate census because census data and other federal datasets based on the census are used to make key decisions that affect our nation’s students, educators, and schools.  

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Examples of these uses include:  [keep any/all points you would like to include in your comment – see this site if you would like to add state-specific statistics about funding impacts]. 

Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. 

Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

Determining state higher education funding formulas 

Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

First, to ensure a fair and accurate census,  the Census Bureau should  extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. Second, I oppose both the proposed changes to the residence criteria and the proposed regulations regarding demographic questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. The Census Bureau should  withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: [keep any/all points you would like to include in your comment] 

• Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The Constitution requires  counting all people living in the United States. 

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (including children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count. 

Revise the tax records language so that those whose mailing address differs from their residential address (servicemembers, those with a post office box) are not excluded.  

• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for civil rights enforcement, among other uses, and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The prohibition, as written, may also restrict the collection or publication of census data on same-sex couples that was asked in 2020. 

 The proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Sincerely,
Mr. Marc Silverman
Los Angeles, CA 90068

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: US Census Bureau,I urge the Census Bureau and Department of Commerce to withdraw the proposed rule changing residence criteria for the decennial Census and restricting demographic questions.The proposal would exclude foreign citizens from the population used for congressional apportionment unless they are also U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents. The Census proposes to only include people if their address is confirmed by tax records -- which could mean millions, particularly low-income families, could be missed in the decennial Census. Overall, this would leave out people who actually live in our community, including many people who are lawfully present in the United States.For all past Census counts, including the 2020 Census, foreign citizens living in the United States were generally counted where they lived and slept most of the time. That approach recognizes the basic purpose of a Census: accurately counting the people who live in our communities. The 14th Amendment requires congressional representation to be apportioned according to the “whole number of persons in each State.”I am also deeply concerned by the proposal to prohibit race and ethnicity questions, along with sexual orientation, on the decennial Census enumeration questionnaire. The Census Bureau itself recognizes the importance of race data for civil rights protections, legislative redistricting, equal employment opportunities, and identifying disparities.The 2030 Census will determine congressional, state, and local representation for the decade that follows. It must be complete, accurate, and protected from political manipulation.Please withdraw this proposed rule and preserve a Census that fairly and accurately counts our community.Kim [X] North Carolina 27597

Comment:

Thank you!

Comment:
Re: Docket No. USBC-2026-0628, Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions

​I am a resident of St Charles, Illinois, and I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw this proposed rule.

Firstly, and most importantly, keep race and ethnicity questions on the 2030 Census. This data is essential for drawing fair voting districts, enforcing the Voting Rights Act (to whatever degree its hollowed-out corpse remains in effect, or might yet be resurrected in the future), and making sure federal resources reach the communities that need them. Removing it would make it harder for communities like mine, and those immediately surrounding, to be seen, served, and fairly represented.

Secondly, count every person. The 14th Amendment requires apportionment based on "the whole number of persons in each state." Excluding people based on immigration status would undercount communities, distort representation, and shortchange local governments that serve everyone who lives here. While there is a separate debate to be had regarding the services which illegal immigrants currently or ought to receive, regardless, this is clearly spelled out in the Constitution.
​
Finally, a 30-day comment period is not enough for changes that will shape representation and funding for the next decade. At a bare minimum, the comment period should be extended until November 13th, 2026, for a total of 60 days, or ideally until December 13th, 2026, for a total of 90 days.

As my children start to enter the school system over the next few years, it will be critical to ensure that our schools receive the level of funding necessary to serve every pupil, not just those whom the current administration would prefer to consider.

Ben
St. Charles, IL

The decennial census has significant consequences for congressional representation, redistricting, federal policy, and the distribution of federal resources. Americans should have confidence that the process is accurate, transparent, consistent, and faithful to federal law.

Cynthia Love

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:

Excluding people who actually reside in the United States would create an incomplete picture of the population and could distort decisions involving federal funding, infrastructure, emergency preparedness, health care, education, and other public services.

These data are critical for evaluating disparities, monitoring compliance with civil rights laws, identifying inequities in access to services, and understanding whether government programs are reaching the populations they are intended to serve. Removing these questions would not make disparities disappear; it would make them more difficult to identify, measure, and address.

These changes could have particularly serious consequences for states and communities with large immigrant populations or significant racial and ethnic diversity. If census data no longer accurately reflects the people who live in a community, policymakers and public agencies may be making major decisions using incomplete information.

The strength of the census depends on producing an accurate, comprehensive, and consistent count of the population. I urge the Census Bureau to preserve residence standards and demographic data collection practices that support a complete count and reliable data for public decision-making.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: 91 FR 57524  Public Comment,I am submitting this comment in opposition to the Census Bureau's proposed rule on residence criteria and demographic questions for the decennial census, 91 FR 57524 (Sept. 10, 2026). This proposed rule makes significant changes to the 2030 Census, including leaving noncitizens without green cards out of the count used to divide seats in Congress, removing race and ethnicity questions, and possibly adding a citizenship or immigration status question. The Census determines congressional representation and guides planning for health, education, housing, and infrastructure, along with the distribution of more than $2.8 trillion a year across roughly 350 federal programs. When communities are miscounted or left out in the decennial Census, they lose their fair share of representation and resources for an entire decade. This rule violates the Constitution and federal law, which both count the "whole number of persons" in each state, not just citizens. Congress chose "persons" over "citizens" on purpose, and counting only some residents revives the logic of the three-fifths clause. Changing who counts would require a constitutional amendment, not a census rule. The Supreme Court recognized in 2016 that representation serves all residents, including children and noncitizens, not only voters. Under this rule, millions of people who live, work, pay taxes, and raise families here would no longer count, weakening the voting power of the communities they belong to, including the citizens who live alongside them. A citizenship question would make this worse. The success of the Census depends on public trust. Every person must feel confident that answering is safe, confidential, and separate from immigration enforcement. It would suppress participation among immigrant families, including naturalized citizens and citizen children, and increase fear and confusion about how Census information will be used. That means less accurate data for apportionment, redistricting, and funding formulas, higher costs as the Bureau chases households that did not respond, and resources directed away from Black and Brown communities. Removing race and ethnicity questions would also take away data that federal law requires to protect civil rights. This data helps reveal discrimination in housing, jobs, and voting, and shows whether district lines split up or pack a community to weaken its vote. Without them, unfair treatment becomes much harder to prove and solve. Mary [X] Milford, Michigan 48381

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am concerned about, and object to, the changes related to “usual resident” and “demographic information”. My concerns are grounded in my professional background in public health.

For public health, the notion of a person is not a legal abstraction, but a measure of actual people. It is important to know the number of actual people in order to address: infectious disease diseases; assure access to health services; and have an accurate denominator for determining sentinel indicators of population health like infant and maternal mortality. 

Infectious diseases is possibly the easiest to understand reason that we need the type of information currently provided by the census. Infectious organisms spread throughout the human population, irrespective of a person‘s political standing, legal status in a country, or any other legalistic indication of personhood. All humans are susceptible to getting infected. We all benefit from accurate surveillance of diseases. In order to combat the spread of an infectious agent, clear information needs to reach all people at risk. Communication is best when culturally tailored and delivered by trusted messengers. Knowledge about race and other demographics within geographic areas is instrumental in developing and delivering effective communications about an infectious agent. The same is true for delivering services such as screening, vaccination and provision of protective equipment and tools. 

Demographic information, such as race and income are critical for understanding the disproportionate impact of policies, economic development, and pollution - and the resulting impact on human health. 

For both of these measures, it is not only federal resources that are allocated based on the findings of each census. State governments, local governments and non-government organizations use this data on a regular basis to allocate funding and human resources and to evaluate their programs’ effectiveness.

I urge the Census Bureau and Department of Commerce to withdraw the proposed rule changing residence criteria for the decennial Census and restricting demographic questions. The proposal excludes foreign citizens from the population used for congressional apportionment unless they are also U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents. The who point of the Census is to accurately record the data of all the individuals living in our country. This proposal seeks to only include people if their address is confirmed by tax records -- which means millions, specifically low-income families, could be missed in the decennial Census. This proposal would leave out people who actually live in our community, including many people who are lawfully present in the United States.

All past Census counts included foreign citizens living in the United States, recognizing the basic purpose of a Census: accurately counting the people who live in our communities. The 14th Amendment requires congressional representation to be apportioned according to the “whole number of persons in each State.” It does not allow the people in government to just pick and choose the data that shows who lives in our communities. It shows accurate data and to do otherwise would be a lie. This proposal genuinely disgusts me and terrifies me. It is a blatant attack on our democracy by a group of individuals who seek to throw us into the dark ages by disenfranchising people they deem lesser.

This proposal seeks to prohibit race and ethnicity questions, along with sexual orientation, on the decennial Census enumeration questionnaire which for years had been used to gather data that helped with civil rights protections, legislative redistricting, equal employment opportunities, and identifying disparities. The Census Bureau itself recognizes the importance of race data. Without this accurate data so many people will not be represented and many states may lose funding to help these people.

The 2030 Census will determine congressional, state, and local representation for the decade that follows. It must be complete, accurate, and protected from political manipulation.

You must do the right thing and withdraw this proposed rule and preserve a Census that fairly and accurately counts our communities. -- Rachael, Colorado

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: Demographic data is not immaterial. A country as diverse as the United States cannot effectively understand or address the needs of its communities by treating the population as though we are all the same. Race, ethnicity, age, income, and other demographic factors can reveal significant differences in needs and help policymakers anticipate unintended consequences rather than addressing problems in a vacuum. Communities in Florida do not necessarily have the same needs as communities in Ohio, nor do people across different socioeconomic and cultural backgrounds. Collecting this information does not diminish our shared citizenship; it gives government the information necessary to serve its people more effectively and equitably.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: 91 FR 57524  Public Comment,I am submitting this comment in opposition to the Census Bureau's proposed rule on residence criteria and demographic questions for the decennial census, 91 FR 57524 (Sept. 10, 2026). This proposed rule makes significant changes to the 2030 Census, including leaving noncitizens without green cards out of the count used to divide seats in Congress, removing race and ethnicity questions, and possibly adding a citizenship or immigration status question. The Census determines congressional representation and guides planning for health, education, housing, and infrastructure, along with the distribution of more than $2.8 trillion a year across roughly 350 federal programs. When communities are miscounted or left out in the decennial Census, they lose their fair share of representation and resources for an entire decade. This rule violates the Constitution and federal law, which both count the "whole number of persons" in each state, not just citizens. Congress chose "persons" over "citizens" on purpose, and counting only some residents revives the logic of the three-fifths clause. Changing who counts would require a constitutional amendment, not a census rule. The Supreme Court recognized in 2016 that representation serves all residents, including children and noncitizens, not only voters. Under this rule, millions of people who live, work, pay taxes, and raise families here would no longer count, weakening the voting power of the communities they belong to, including the citizens who live alongside them. A citizenship question would make this worse. The success of the Census depends on public trust. Every person must feel confident that answering is safe, confidential, and separate from immigration enforcement. It would suppress participation among immigrant families, including naturalized citizens and citizen children, and increase fear and confusion about how Census information will be used. That means less accurate data for apportionment, redistricting, and funding formulas, higher costs as the Bureau chases households that did not respond, and resources directed away from Black and Brown communities. Removing race and ethnicity questions would also take away data that federal law requires to protect civil rights. This data helps reveal discrimination in housing, jobs, and voting, and shows whether district lines split up or pack a community to weaken its vote. Without them, unfair treatment becomes much harder to prove and solve. Kym [X] Lake Orion, Michigan 48362

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I oppose proposed § 70.2(a), which would prohibit race and ethnicity questions from appearing on the decennial census questionnaire.

Race and ethnicity data from the decennial census have important and concrete uses. States rely on Census data when drawing congressional and state legislative districts, and race, Hispanic origin, and voting-age population data have historically been included in redistricting data. These data also support voting-rights and civil-rights analysis and allow governments, researchers, nonprofits, and communities to identify disparities and understand whether populations are being adequately represented and served.

Accurate demographic data also have significant economic value. Businesses use Census demographic information to understand local markets, identify potential customers, evaluate where to locate or expand stores and services, and make investment decisions. Census itself provides tools such as Census Business Builder specifically to help businesses analyze demographic and economic characteristics of communities. Race and ethnicity are also important dimensions of federal business statistics, including data on business ownership and economic activity.

This matters to me personally because underrepresented populations are particularly affected when demographic data become less complete or less precise. If we do not accurately measure who lives in our communities, it becomes harder to identify disparities, understand changing populations, allocate resources effectively, and determine whether institutions and public programs are reaching the people they are intended to serve.

I am also concerned that the American Community Survey and administrative records are not equivalent substitutes for information collected directly through the decennial census. Survey estimates and administrative records may differ in geographic precision, completeness, and the ability of individuals to self-identify. Before eliminating direct collection, the Census Bureau should demonstrate that alternative sources can provide comparable accuracy, geographic detail, reliability, and continuity.

The proposed change is especially difficult to understand given the Census Bureau's extensive recent work to improve race and ethnicity measurement. Following years of research and public engagement, federal statistical standards were updated in 2024 to use a combined race/ethnicity question and add a Middle Eastern or North African category. Census subsequently prepared to implement the improved question in the 2030 Census and reported that its research found the combined format reduced missing responses and improved reporting in established race and ethnicity categories.

Before abandoning that work, the Bureau should provide clear empirical evidence that removing race and ethnicity questions would materially improve enumeration and explain how equivalent demographic information would be produced.

Collecting race and ethnicity information does not determine whether someone should be counted. It allows the country to understand who is being counted and how our population is changing.

I respectfully urge the Census Bureau not to finalize proposed § 70.2(a) and to retain a scientifically tested, self-reported race and ethnicity question on the 2030 Census.

Thank you for considering my comment.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I support the Census Bureau’s effort to clarify residence criteria for the 2030 decennial census so that the apportionment base better reflects durable ties to the United States. I offer the following comments:

Citizenship question
I strongly support the restoration of a citizenship (or legal-status) question on the 2030 census short-form questionnaire. Including this question will help the Bureau accurately determine who should be included in the apportionment count and will improve the reliability of the data collected.

Actual enumeration
The Constitution requires an “actual Enumeration.” I urge the Bureau to prioritize a direct, real-world count of people and to minimize the use of algorithms, statistical estimates, or imputation wherever possible. Administrative records may be useful as supporting evidence, but they should not replace actual enumeration.

Apportionment base limited to U.S. citizens
I recommend that the final rule go further than the current proposal. Only U.S. citizens should be counted toward the apportionment of House seats. Lawful permanent residents should not be included in the apportionment base. Restricting the count to citizens best aligns the census with the constitutional purpose.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To Whom It May Concern:

I am submitting this comment to express concern that adding a citizenship question and altering race/ethnicity categories in the decennial census will unintentionally harm Republican political representation and resource allocation for the next decade.

According to reporting from NPR (September 9, 2026), experts warn that adding a citizenship question is likely to depress response rates among mixed‑status households, including many U.S. citizens who fear government misuse of personal data. The Census Bureau’s own research during the 2020 cycle found that the proposed citizenship question at that time was projected to reduce self‑response rates by 5.8% in households with noncitizens, with spillover effects on citizen respondents in those same communities (source: U.S. Census Bureau, 2019 analysis; cited by NPR).

This undercount would not be limited to Democratic‑leaning urban centers. Rural counties with high numbers of Latino citizens — many of which voted Republican in 2016, 2020, and 2024 — would also lose population counts, directly reducing their share of federal funding and potentially their congressional representation. States such as Texas, Florida, Arizona, and even Kansas and Nebraska have Republican‑leaning districts with significant Latino citizen populations. Undercounting these areas would shrink their political influence for the next ten years.

Additionally, the proposed changes to race categories risk misclassifying or fragmenting demographic groups whose accurate enumeration is essential for redistricting. The Census Bureau has repeatedly emphasized that sudden shifts in category structure reduce data continuity and increase respondent confusion, which leads to higher item‑nonresponse rates and lower overall accuracy (source: Census Bureau Race/Ethnicity Research Working Group reports, 2023–2025).

From a purely strategic standpoint, Republicans rely on precise census data to maintain rural representation, allocate resources to aging communities, and protect district boundaries in states they currently control. Any policy that reduces participation among conservative‑leaning demographic groups — including Hispanic citizens, multiracial rural families, and immigrant‑adjacent agricultural communities — directly weakens Republican political power.

For these reasons, I urge the administration to reconsider these changes. The long‑term consequence will not be improved accuracy or fairness, but rather a measurable reduction in representation for Republican districts, diminished federal funding for conservative‑leaning counties, and avoidable instability in the redistricting process.

Thank you for your consideration.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
My name is [Your Name] and I am your constituent from [City/Zip Code]. As Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander (AANHPI) Heritage Month comes to a close, I write to urge you to support AANHPI students by cosponsoring the All Students Count Act.

To the U.S. Census Bureau: 

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule titled “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005). Eliminating the collection of race and ethnic data, prohibiting the collection of sexual orientation, and leaving non-citizens out of the apportionment would significantly harm the Southeast Asian American (SEAA) and broader Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander (AANHPI) communities. This proposed rule would significantly harm the SEAA and AANHPI communities. The AANHPI community is not a homogenous population; it encompasses over 50 different ethnic groups and 100 languages and dialects. There are vast socioeconomic disparities within the AANHPI population, often related to their migratory and historical experience. SEAAs, such as the Cambodian, Hmong, Laotian, and Mien populations, often have higher rates of poverty and lower educational attainment rates than both the broader AANHPI and American populations. 

For SEAAs, this disparity is generally tied to their experiences escaping their countries of origin and resettlement in the United States after the Vietnam War, Secret War in Laos, and Khmer Rouge genocide in Cambodia. For example, because of the 2020 Census, we now know that the Mien population has lower educational attainment rates compared to the general American and AANHPI populations. Additionally, the data also show that Mien men have a lower educational attainment rate compared to women. Such information could only be obtained because of the census, which is the primary source for data collection and reporting of small ethnic groups. These data cannot be replicated by other surveys, including the American Community Survey. 

Accurate data, reflective of race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation, help our elected officials properly identify and address the unique needs and challenges of our communities. Prohibiting the collection of this demographic data would prevent our government officials from passing informed public policy; hamper the ability of community-based organizations to demonstrate data narratives for fundraising purposes; and inhibit the ability of students and academics studying our communities from accessing the most robust source of information on SEAAs and the broader AANHPI community.

I also ask the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. Changes of this scope deserve more time for the public to review and respond.

Sincerely,
UyenMy Nguyen
Stockton, CA 95209-2620

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). 

As and educator, and I care about a fair and accurate census because census data and other federal datasets based on the census are used to make key decisions that affect our nation’s students, educators, and schools.  

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Examples of these uses include: . 

* Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. 

* Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

* Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

* Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

* Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

* Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

* Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

* Determining state higher education funding formulas 

* Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

* Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

* Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

First, to ensure a fair and accurate census,  the Census Bureau should  extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. Second, I oppose both the proposed changes to the residence criteria and the proposed regulations regarding demographic questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. The Census Bureau should  withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The Constitution requires  counting all people living in the United States. 

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (including children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count. 

Revise the tax records language so that those whose mailing address differs from their residential address (servicemembers, those with a post office box) are not excluded.  

• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for civil rights enforcement, among other uses, and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The prohibition, as written, may also restrict the collection or publication of census data on same-sex couples that was asked in 2020. 

 The proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Sincerely,
Mr. Paul Mallery
Ballwin, MO

Additionally, illegal aliens and other non-legal permanent residents should not be included for apportionment. Census data is used for the apportionment of congressional seats. This Census Bureau should also consider adding a citizenship question to the Census survey. The Supreme Court has already held that the Constitution lawfully permits the Census Bureau to at least inquire about citizenship on the census questionnaire. "The census should absolutely include questions related to citizenship and legal presence. 

These changes would strengthen the census in its core purpose of attaining an accurate count of Americans and have my full support. 

Thank you,  

Jan Schaefer

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). 

As and educator, and I care about a fair and accurate census because census data and other federal datasets based on the census are used to make key decisions that affect our nation’s students, educators, and schools.  

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Examples of these uses include: . 

* Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. 

* Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

* Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

* Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

* Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

* Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

* Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

* Determining state higher education funding formulas 

* Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

* Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

* Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

First, to ensure a fair and accurate census,  the Census Bureau should  extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. Second, I oppose both the proposed changes to the residence criteria and the proposed regulations regarding demographic questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. The Census Bureau should  withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The Constitution requires  counting all people living in the United States. 

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (including children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count. 

Revise the tax records language so that those whose mailing address differs from their residential address (servicemembers, those with a post office box) are not excluded.  

• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for civil rights enforcement, among other uses, and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The prohibition, as written, may also restrict the collection or publication of census data on same-sex couples that was asked in 2020. 

 The proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Sincerely,
Mr. r j
Shawano, WI

Dear Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions,

Subject: Re: Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions (Docket No. 260903-0005; RIN 0607-AA75) 

I strongly oppose the proposed rules for the census and changes to its residence rule. Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Re: Proposed Census Regulation.

To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am Beth Hope, a voter and resident of Oregon since 1977. For the past 12 years, I have worked for agencies that support survivors of sexual and physical violence, including many folks who do not yet have legal permanent residence or citizenship but have children who are citizens of our country. These people are often the most hardworking and responsible folks I know. 

I care about a fair and accurate census because not counting the people who live and work in our country but have not obtained LPR or citizenship deserve to be counted as well as their citizen children. In addition, not counting such a major population of our country will reduce benefits and funding for too many agencies and nonprofits who serve survivors of crime and violence as well as those already under-represented folks who live in poverty due to situations not in their control.

First, I ask the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. Significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve more time for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including:

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.

• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.

• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.

• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.

• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Sincerely,

Beth (Bethany) A. Hope

Sincerely,
Ms. Beth Hope
Rockaway Beach, OR 97136-9547

This proposed rule would significantly harm the SEAA and AANHPI communities. The AANHPI community is not a homogenous population; it encompasses over 50 different ethnic groups and 100 languages and dialects. There are vast socioeconomic disparities within the AANHPI population, often related to their migratory and historical experience. SEAAs, such as the Cambodian, Hmong, Laotian, and Mien populations, often have higher rates of poverty and lower educational attainment rates than both the broader AANHPI and American populations. 

For SEAAs, this disparity is generally tied to their experiences escaping their countries of origin and resettlement in the United States after the Vietnam War, Secret War in Laos, and Khmer Rouge genocide in Cambodia. For example, because of the 2020 Census, we now know that the Mien population has lower educational attainment rates compared to the general American and AANHPI populations. Additionally, the data also show that Mien men have a lower educational attainment rate compared to women. Such information could only be obtained because of the census, which is the primary source for data collection and reporting of small ethnic groups. These data cannot be replicated by other surveys, including the American Community Survey. 

Accurate data, reflective of race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation, help our elected officials properly identify and address the unique needs and challenges of our communities. Prohibiting the collection of this demographic data would prevent our government officials from passing informed public policy; hamper the ability of community-based organizations to demonstrate data narratives for fundraising purposes; and inhibit the ability of students and academics studying our communities from accessing the most robust source of information on SEAAs and the broader AANHPI community. 

Thank you for taking my comment into consideration. I reiterate my request that the US Census Bureau withdraws the proposed rule; preserves the collection of race and ethnic data; and keeps its commitment to count everyone once, only once, and in the right place.

I also ask the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. Changes of this scope deserve more time for the public to review and respond.

Sincerely,
Andrea Reeve
Fort Collins, CO 80528-4463

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). 

As and educator, and I care about a fair and accurate census because census data and other federal datasets based on the census are used to make key decisions that affect our nation’s students, educators, and schools.  

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Examples of these uses include: . 

* Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. 

* Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

* Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

* Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

* Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

* Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

* Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

* Determining state higher education funding formulas 

* Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

* Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

* Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

First, to ensure a fair and accurate census,  the Census Bureau should  extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. Second, I oppose both the proposed changes to the residence criteria and the proposed regulations regarding demographic questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. The Census Bureau should  withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The Constitution requires  counting all people living in the United States. 

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (including children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count. 

Revise the tax records language so that those whose mailing address differs from their residential address (servicemembers, those with a post office box) are not excluded.  

• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for civil rights enforcement, among other uses, and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The prohibition, as written, may also restrict the collection or publication of census data on same-sex couples that was asked in 2020. 

 The proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Sincerely,
Dr. Ruth Chaffee
Minneapolis, MN

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Excluding noncitizens from the 2030 census would be both unconstitutional and harmful to every community in the country.
The 14th Amendment requires that House seats be apportioned by counting the whole number of persons in each state, not just citizens or legal residents. Courts have upheld that reading, and Justice Departments under administrations of both parties have concluded that immigrants, including those in the country illegally, cannot be left out of the apportionment count. Congress, not the executive branch, holds final authority over how the census is conducted, so experts expect this proposal to face serious legal challenges.
The practical damage would reach well beyond noncitizens. If people fear that their citizenship information could be misused, many will simply not respond, and that erodes accuracy for everyone. Census data underpins annual population estimates, health statistics, and federal survey benchmarks, and it is how we identify disparities between communities. Weakening it means losing the ability to see those gaps.
The financial stakes are just as high. Census figures steer trillions of dollars in federal funding for transportation, schools, hospitals, and housing. An undercount gets locked into funding formulas and can shortchange communities for a full decade. Changing who is counted would also reshape political representation and power for years to come.
A census works only when it counts everyone who lives here. We should protect that principle rather than gamble with our Constitution, our data, and our communities.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). 

As and educator, and I care about a fair and accurate census because census data and other federal datasets based on the census are used to make key decisions that affect our nation’s students, educators, and schools.  

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Examples of these uses include: . 

* Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. 

* Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

* Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

* Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

* Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

* Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

* Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

* Determining state higher education funding formulas 

* Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

* Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

* Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

First, to ensure a fair and accurate census,  the Census Bureau should  extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. Second, I oppose both the proposed changes to the residence criteria and the proposed regulations regarding demographic questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. The Census Bureau should  withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The Constitution requires  counting all people living in the United States. 

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (including children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count. 

Revise the tax records language so that those whose mailing address differs from their residential address (servicemembers, those with a post office box) are not excluded.  

• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for civil rights enforcement, among other uses, and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The prohibition, as written, may also restrict the collection or publication of census data on same-sex couples that was asked in 2020. 

 The proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Sincerely,
Mr. Kent Minault
Knoxville, TN

The U.S. Census Bureau's proposed rule to strengthen the US Census is critical to fair representation and the future of America.  

The U.S. Census should not include distorted data in its count of Americans.  By including overly generalized ethnic demographic categories, we obscure the true goal of the census and hinder its constitutionally mandated purpose: an accurate count of Americans.  

Additionally, illegal aliens and other non-legal permanent residents should not be included for apportionment. Census data is used for the apportionment of congressional seats. Non-citizens cannot legally vote and should not be used to decrease the voting power of Americans. I support the Census Bureau in advancing the correct understanding of usual residence to recognize an element of allegiance that is antithetical to the inclusion of those not legally present in our country.  

This Census Bureau should also consider adding a citizenship question to the Census survey. The Supreme Court has already held that the Constitution lawfully permits the Census Bureau to at least inquire about citizenship on the census questionnaire. "The census should absolutely include questions related to citizenship and legal presence. 

These changes would strengthen the census in its core purpose of attaining an accurate count of Americans and have my full support. 

Thank you,  
}}Gilbert W Vierra

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: The proposed change to the census is unconstitutional; the 14th Amendment says that the census is not meant to count citizens but EVERY person living in the US--regardless of legal status. It is important to know who is living within our borders--not just the citizens, EVERYONE. The framers of the Constitution were not idiots; if they had meant "citizens" they would have said "citizens." They said "persons." In the age of big data it is more vital than ever that the census provide a complete and accurate count of the population, including all relevant demographic information. This includes asking questions about race, ethnicity, and other factors that affect peoples' lives! If the census is not complete, accurate, and containing all the major demographic categories, then it is useless--and then elected officials and government workers will not be able to make informed decisions.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: US Census Bureau,It would appear that the current administration would like to gerrymander the census by excluding those who have been traditionally been counted in previous census counts. This is unacceptable. Proper representation is essential to our country and should not be engineered by this administration to suit its own prejudiced  purposes. I urge the Census Bureau and Department of Commerce to withdraw the proposed rule changing residence criteria for the decennial Census and restricting demographic questions.The proposal would exclude foreign citizens from the population used for congressional apportionment unless they are also U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents. The Census proposes to only include people if their address is confirmed by tax records -- which could mean millions, particularly low-income families, could be missed in the decennial Census. Overall, this would leave out people who actually live in our community, including many people who are lawfully present in the United States.For all past Census counts, including the 2020 Census, foreign citizens living in the United States were generally counted where they lived and slept most of the time. That approach recognizes the basic purpose of a Census: accurately counting the people who live in our communities. The 14th Amendment requires congressional representation to be apportioned according to the “whole number of persons in each State.”I am also deeply concerned by the proposal to prohibit race and ethnicity questions, along with sexual orientation, on the decennial Census enumeration questionnaire. The Census Bureau itself recognizes the importance of race data for civil rights protections, legislative redistricting, equal employment opportunities, and identifying disparities.The 2030 Census will determine congressional, state, and local representation for the decade that follows. It must be complete, accurate, and protected from political manipulation.Please withdraw this proposed rule and preserve a Census that fairly and accurately counts our community.Geraldine[x]Livonia, Michigan 48154

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
My name is [Your Name] and I am your constituent from [City/Zip Code]. As Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander (AANHPI) Heritage Month comes to a close, I write to urge you to support AANHPI students by cosponsoring the All Students Count Act.

To the U.S. Census Bureau: 

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule titled “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005). Eliminating the collection of race and ethnic data, prohibiting the collection of sexual orientation, and leaving non-citizens out of the apportionment would significantly harm the Southeast Asian American (SEAA) and broader Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander (AANHPI) communities. I respectfully request that the Census Bureau withdraw the proposed rule and extend the comment period to December 10, 2026. 

This proposed rule would significantly harm the SEAA and AANHPI communities. The AANHPI community is not a homogenous population; it encompasses over 50 different ethnic groups and 100 languages and dialects. There are vast socioeconomic disparities within the AANHPI population, often related to their migratory and historical experience. SEAAs, such as the Cambodian, Hmong, Laotian, and Mien populations, often have higher rates of poverty and lower educational attainment rates than both the broader AANHPI and American populations. 

For SEAAs, this disparity is generally tied to their experiences escaping their countries of origin and resettlement in the United States after the Vietnam War, Secret War in Laos, and Khmer Rouge genocide in Cambodia. For example, because of the 2020 Census, we now know that the Mien population has lower educational attainment rates compared to the general American and AANHPI populations. Additionally, the data also show that Mien men have a lower educational attainment rate compared to women. Such information could only be obtained because of the census, which is the primary source for data collection and reporting of small ethnic groups. These data cannot be replicated by other surveys, including the American Community Survey. 

Accurate data, reflective of race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation, help our elected officials properly identify and address the unique needs and challenges of our communities. Prohibiting the collection of this demographic data would prevent our government officials from passing informed public policy; hamper the ability of community-based organizations to demonstrate data narratives for fundraising purposes; and inhibit the ability of students and academics studying our communities from accessing the most robust source of information on SEAAs and the broader AANHPI community. 

Thank you for taking my comment into consideration. I reiterate my request that the US Census Bureau withdraws the proposed rule; preserves the collection of race and ethnic data; and keeps its commitment to count everyone once, only once, and in the right place.

I also ask the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. Changes of this scope deserve more time for the public to review and respond.

Sincerely,
Sky Bloomer
Silver Spring, MD 20910-5111

There are vast socioeconomic disparities within the AANHPI population, often related to their migratory and historical experience. SEAAs, such as the Cambodian, Hmong, Laotian, and Mien populations, often have higher rates of poverty and lower educational attainment rates than both the broader AANHPI and American populations.

Sincerely,
Akari Brown

Comment:
My name is [Your Name] and I am your constituent from [City/Zip Code]. As Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander (AANHPI) Heritage Month comes to a close, I write to urge you to support AANHPI students by cosponsoring the All Students Count Act.

To the U.S. Census Bureau: 

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule titled “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005). Eliminating the collection of race and ethnic data, prohibiting the collection of sexual orientation, and leaving non-citizens out of the apportionment would significantly harm the Southeast Asian American (SEAA) and broader Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander (AANHPI) communities. I respectfully request that the Census Bureau withdraw the proposed rule and extend the comment period to December 10, 2026. 

This proposed rule would significantly harm the SEAA and AANHPI communities. The AANHPI community is not a homogenous population; it encompasses over 50 different ethnic groups and 100 languages and dialects. There are vast socioeconomic disparities within the AANHPI population, often related to their migratory and historical experience. SEAAs, such as the Cambodian, Hmong, Laotian, and Mien populations, often have higher rates of poverty and lower educational attainment rates than both the broader AANHPI and American populations. 

For SEAAs, this disparity is generally tied to their experiences escaping their countries of origin and resettlement in the United States after the Vietnam War, Secret War in Laos, and Khmer Rouge genocide in Cambodia. For example, because of the 2020 Census, we now know that the Mien population has lower educational attainment rates compared to the general American and AANHPI populations. Additionally, the data also show that Mien men have a lower educational attainment rate compared to women. Such information could only be obtained because of the census, which is the primary source for data collection and reporting of small ethnic groups. These data cannot be replicated by other surveys, including the American Community Survey. 

Accurate data, reflective of race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation, help our elected officials properly identify and address the unique needs and challenges of our communities. Prohibiting the collection of this demographic data would prevent our government officials from passing informed public policy; hamper the ability of community-based organizations to demonstrate data narratives for fundraising purposes; and inhibit the ability of students and academics studying our communities from accessing the most robust source of information on SEAAs and the broader AANHPI community.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I strongly oppose the Trump administration's proposed rule change for the 2030 Census that would eliminate questions on race and ethnicity and exclude noncitizens without green cards from population counts. The Census is one of our nation's most important tools for understanding who lives in our communities and what our communities need. As a public health professional, I rely on accurate population data to understand health needs, identify disparities, plan programs, and ensure that services reach the people who need them.
Removing this race/ethnicity data makes it nearly impossible to track racial disparities in healthcare, housing, employment, and education. This is a massive setback of civil rights progress. Without reliable race and ethnicity data, we will have greater difficulty identifying disparities, understanding who is being underserved, evaluating whether policies are producing equitable outcomes, and directing resources where they are most needed. The decennial census provides a uniquely comprehensive picture of the population, and replacing direct self-reported information with administrative data will never be a substitute for asking people how they identify as part of a reliable, comprehensive, standard assessment. 
The removal of noncitizen data is also particularly concerning from a public health perspective. People who live in a community use its roads, schools, hospitals, emergency services, public health programs, and other infrastructure regardless of their citizenship status. Their status doesn’t change their presence in our communities, and their presence is what has impact. We need accurate information about the people who actually live in our communities in order to plan effectively and respond to needs.
These changes will result in immense waste of precious resources (time, money, and strategic thought), and they will greatly reduce the impact of good work being done across the country.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Dear Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions,

Subject: Re: Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions (Docket No. 260903-0005; RIN 0607-AA75) 

I strongly oppose the proposed rules for the census and changes to its residence rule. All persons in the United States have a right to be counted, as the 14th Amendment of the Constitution plainly establishes. This proposed rule will weaken our democracy, our systems of representation, and the doctrine of “one person, one vote.” Without an accurate count, people will not be fairly represented in Congress or state legislatures. 

By generating inaccurate and unreliable data, this change would also make it harder for my state and local officials to properly plan for the services we need and the emergencies we may face. Furthermore, the exclusion of questions about race and ethnicity will exacerbate the degradation of data quality, and it will lead to undercounts of Black and brown communities that are already undercounted in past censuses. If we don't know who is living in our communities, we cannot prepare for the challenges we may face, and we will not receive adequate funds from federal programs. 

Additionally, the lack of transparency and sufficient opportunity for the public to comment on this incredibly consequential rule is concerning. I urge you to both extend the comment period to a full 90 days until December 9th, and to reject this proposed rule. 
Stop trying to turn the Census Bureau into a political action arm of the Administration!  The Census Bureau should collect accurate information on which to base decisions.  If the Administration then wants to make political decisions, it will have the solid information on which to base its actions.

Candis Harbison,
[X]

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Census Bureau's proposed rule to strengthen the US Census is critical to fair representation and the future of America.  

The U.S. Census should not include distorted data in its count of Americans.  By including overly generalized ethnic demographic categories, we obscure the true goal of the census and hinder its constitutionally mandated purpose: an accurate count of Americans.

These changes would strengthen the census in its core purpose of attaining an accurate count of Americans and have my full support. 

Thank you,  

Richard E. Shoemaker

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). 

As and educator, and I care about a fair and accurate census because census data and other federal datasets based on the census are used to make key decisions that affect our nation’s students, educators, and schools.  

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Examples of these uses include: . 

* Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. 

* Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

* Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

* Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

* Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

* Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

* Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

* Determining state higher education funding formulas 

* Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

* Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

* Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

First, to ensure a fair and accurate census,  the Census Bureau should  extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. Second, I oppose both the proposed changes to the residence criteria and the proposed regulations regarding demographic questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. The Census Bureau should  withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The Constitution requires  counting all people living in the United States. 

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (including children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count. 

Revise the tax records language so that those whose mailing address differs from their residential address (servicemembers, those with a post office box) are not excluded.  

• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for civil rights enforcement, among other uses, and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The prohibition, as written, may also restrict the collection or publication of census data on same-sex couples that was asked in 2020. 

 The proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Sincerely,
Ms. Linda Kitchen
Oak Park, IL
