The Census proposes to only include people if their address is confirmed by tax records -- which could mean millions, particularly low-income families, could be missed in the decennial Census. Overall, this would leave out people who actually live in our community, including many people who are lawfully present in the United States.For all past Census counts, including the 2020 Census, foreign citizens living in the United States were generally counted where they lived and slept most of the time. That approach recognizes the basic purpose of a Census: accurately counting the people who live in our communities. The 14th Amendment requires congressional representation to be apportioned according to the “whole number of persons in each State.”I am also deeply concerned by the proposal to prohibit race and ethnicity questions, along with sexual orientation, on the decennial Census enumeration questionnaire. The Census Bureau itself recognizes the importance of race data for civil rights protections, legislative redistricting, equal employment opportunities, and identifying disparities.The 2030 Census will determine congressional, state, and local representation for the decade that follows. It must be complete, accurate, and protected from political manipulation.Please withdraw this proposed rule and preserve a Census that fairly and accurately counts our community.Jimmy [X] Costa Mesa, California 92627

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:

Subject: Re: Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions (Docket No. 260903-0005; RIN 0607-AA75)

Please withdraw the proposed changes to the census.  It will affect voters very negatively and there has not been time for the public to respond.
Sincerely, 
Kate McIntire

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Dear Census Bureau staff,

Re: Docket No. 260903-0005 (Document 2026-18481), "Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions," published September 10, 2026

I have spent more than 30 years in industry, working in mechanical engineering, operations, product management, sales operations and general management. I now teach business process improvement and technology strategy at the university level. My comments come from a principle I have practiced and taught for decades: change how you measure something and you change the answer. A measurement system should be judged by how well it captures reality, not by how easy it is to run.

The proposed rule does not meet that standard. I ask the Bureau to withdraw parts 60 and 70 and come back with a substantially revised proposal. At a minimum, please extend the comment period to December 10, 2026. A rule that will shape apportionment, redistricting and federal funding for the next decade needs more public review than the current window allows.

Count everyone who lives here. The Fourteenth Amendment calls for counting "the whole number of persons in each State." Leaving visa holders, refugees, asylum seekers and other residents out of the apportionment count does not remove them from their communities. They still attend local schools, drive local roads and use local hospitals. Leaving them out of the count only makes the data wrong about the places they live.

Define residence by where people live and sleep. Lean and Six Sigma practice depends on operational definitions that are clear, observable and repeatable. The proposed "one hour" standard is none of those, and respondents and enumerators will apply it inconsistently. The Bureau should return to activity-based "usual residence" criteria. It should also restore its detailed guidance for harder cases, such as people who recently moved, people in temporary shelters and children in foster care. A measurement system usually fails at its edge cases. Removing the guidance doesn't remove those cases; it hands the judgment to respondents with no instructions.

Fix the enumeration period. As written, it risks counting seasonal workers and recent movers in the wrong place on Census Day. It could also drop children in foster care and people in emergency shelters from the count entirely. The census is a snapshot taken on one day, and the rules should make that snapshot accurate. Eliminate this provision or substantially revise it.

Count incarcerated people at their home address. The proposal moves population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from the communities people come from and usually return to. In Wisconsin, as in many states, correctional facilities are often far from those home communities.

Don't use tax records as a stand-in for residence. Tax records were built for a different purpose. They often show a mailing address, such as a post office box, a business address or a tax preparer's office, rather than where someone lives. That is especially common for military personnel and their families. Many people are not required to file at all, and dependent children are easy to miss. Using a measure validated for one purpose to answer a different question is a classic data-quality error. The language saying "usual residence" should be "consistent with, and evidenced by" tax records should be revised.

Keep demographic questions. The census has asked about race in every count since 1790. Public health agencies and civil rights enforcement depend on race and ethnicity data. Businesses rely on census demographics too: I have used them for market sizing, site selection and workforce planning, and I teach students to do the same. Sexual orientation is not asked today, but the rule should not bar it from future censuses or limit the collection or publication of data on same-sex couples.

As written, the proposed rule would leave out residents, produce an inaccurate count and block the collection of basic data about who we are. Leaders in government, business and public health depend on these data, and every American is affected when the data are wrong. Please withdraw the rule and revise it.

Sincerely,

David, Wisconsin

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Census Bureau's proposed rule to strengthen the US Census is critical to fair representation and the future of America.  

The U.S. Census should not include distorted data in its count of Americans.  By including overly generalized ethnic demographic categories, we obscure the true goal of the census and hinder its constitutionally mandated purpose: an accurate count of Americans.  

Additionally, illegal aliens and other non-legal permanent residents should not be included for apportionment. Census data is used for the apportionment of congressional seats. Non-citizens cannot legally vote and should not be used to decrease the voting power of Americans. I support the Census Bureau in advancing the correct understanding of usual residence to recognize an element of allegiance that is antithetical to the inclusion of those not legally present in our country.  

This Census Bureau should also consider adding a citizenship question to the Census survey. The Supreme Court has already held that the Constitution lawfully permits the Census Bureau to at least inquire about citizenship on the census questionnaire. "The census should absolutely include questions related to citizenship and legal presence. 

These changes would strengthen the census in its core purpose of attaining an accurate count of Americans and have my full support. 

Thank you,  

Melinda Akowski

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. I oppose this proposed rule because it departs from that constitutional mandate, risking severe harm to my community. Excluding noncitizens from the population count used for congressional apportionment and federal funding, while adding a citizenship question designed to deter participation, will suppress response rates across immigrant communities and mixed-status families who fear being targeted. An undercount here would directly strip my community of appropriate congressional representation and our fair share of federal funding for essential safety-net programs like SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, CHIP, and Title I education grants. As someone who cares about fairness and the rule of law, I urge the Bureau to withdraw this proposal and count every person living in our communities, as the Constitution requires. 

I am also concerned that the proposed rule erases vital Census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Decades of demographic data serve as the baseline that public and private institutions rely on to identify inequalities and direct resources where they are needed most. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities.  

Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.  

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Sincerely,
Linda Sader
Waukesha, WI

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. I oppose this proposed rule because it departs from that constitutional mandate, risking severe harm to my community. Excluding noncitizens from the population count used for congressional apportionment and federal funding, while adding a citizenship question designed to deter participation, will suppress response rates across immigrant communities and mixed-status families who fear being targeted. An undercount here would directly strip my community of appropriate congressional representation and our fair share of federal funding for essential safety-net programs like SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, CHIP, and Title I education grants. As someone who cares about fairness and the rule of law, I urge the Bureau to withdraw this proposal and count every person living in our communities, as the Constitution requires. 

I am also concerned that the proposed rule erases vital Census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Decades of demographic data serve as the baseline that public and private institutions rely on to identify inequalities and direct resources where they are needed most. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities.  

Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.  

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Sincerely,
Kevin Agee
Hyattsville, MD

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:

I strongly oppose the proposed rules for the census and changes to its residence rule. Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I respectfully submit this comment in opposition to the proposed changes to the United States Census under the Trump administration.
What concerns me most is not simply the policy itself, but the message behind it. The growing hostility toward non-citizens in this country has got to stop. Our government seems to forget that the people who founded this great nation were not born as United States citizens. They came here seeking freedom, opportunity, and the ability to live without fear of persecution for their faith, speech, and beliefs. Those principles are the foundation of America.
Do I support illegal immigration? No. Do I believe our current immigration system is working as it should? Also no. However, those beliefs do not change my conviction that every person living in this country should be counted in the Census.
The Census is not about rewarding or encouraging illegal immigration. It is about accurately counting the people who live in our communities. Schools, hospitals, roads, emergency services, and countless other resources depend on accurate population data. When people are intentionally excluded or made afraid to participate, everyone suffers from inaccurate representation and funding.
America is a nation built by immigrants. It is a nation that has long served as a refuge for people fleeing persecution, violence, oppression, poverty, and hopelessness. People come here because they want the opportunity to build a better life and contribute to something greater than themselves. That has been true throughout our history and remains true today.
I believe the voices of future Americans matter just as much as the voices of current Americans. Their lives, families, and contributions are part of our communities, and they deserve to be counted. A complete Census ensures fair representation, responsible funding decisions, and a government that understands the people it serves.
I strongly oppose these proposed changes because I believe they are part of a broader effort by the Trump administration to spread fear, divide communities, and make certain groups feel unwelcome in a country that has always drawn strength from its diversity. Policies built on fear and exclusion do not make America stronger. They undermine the very values that have made this nation a beacon of hope for generations.
I support having all voices heard, all people counted, and all communities represented. I urge others to oppose these changes and stand up for a Census that reflects everyone living in the United States.
We are one nation, united not by fear or hatred, but by our shared commitment to freedom, opportunity, liberty, and justice for all.
In God We Trust, and may we continue striving to be a nation that truly provides liberty and justice for all.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). 

As and educator, and I care about a fair and accurate census because census data and other federal datasets based on the census are used to make key decisions that affect our nation’s students, educators, and schools.  

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Examples of these uses include: . 

* Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. 

* Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

* Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

* Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

* Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

* Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

* Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

* Determining state higher education funding formulas 

* Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

* Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

* Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

First, to ensure a fair and accurate census,  the Census Bureau should  extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. Second, I oppose both the proposed changes to the residence criteria and the proposed regulations regarding demographic questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. The Census Bureau should  withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The Constitution requires  counting all people living in the United States. 

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (including children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count. 

Revise the tax records language so that those whose mailing address differs from their residential address (servicemembers, those with a post office box) are not excluded.  

• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for civil rights enforcement, among other uses, and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The prohibition, as written, may also restrict the collection or publication of census data on same-sex couples that was asked in 2020. 

 The proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Sincerely,
Ms. Laurie Dare
Oak Park, MI

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Census Bureau's proposed rule to strengthen the US Census is critical to fair representation and the future of America.  

The U.S. Census should not include distorted data in its count of Americans.  By including overly generalized ethnic demographic categories, we obscure the true goal of the census and hinder its constitutionally mandated purpose: an accurate count of Americans.  

Additionally, illegal aliens and other non-legal permanent residents should not be included for apportionment. Census data is used for the apportionment of congressional seats. Non-citizens cannot legally vote and should not be used to decrease the voting power of Americans. I support the Census Bureau in advancing the correct understanding of usual residence to recognize an element of allegiance that is antithetical to the inclusion of those not legally present in our country.  

This Census Bureau should also consider adding a citizenship question to the Census survey. The Supreme Court has already held that the Constitution lawfully permits the Census Bureau to at least inquire about citizenship on the census questionnaire. "The census should absolutely include questions related to citizenship and legal presence. 

These changes would strengthen the census in its core purpose of attaining an accurate count of Americans and have my full support. 

Thank you,  

Judy Shoemaker

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Dear Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions,

Subject: Re: Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions (Docket No. 260903-0005; RIN 0607-AA75) 

I strongly oppose the proposed rules for the census and changes to its residence rule. All persons in the United States have a right to be counted, as the 14th Amendment of the Constitution plainly establishes. This proposed rule will weaken our democracy, our systems of representation, and the doctrine of “one person, one vote.” Without an accurate count, people will not be fairly represented in Congress or state legislatures. 

By generating inaccurate and unreliable data, this change would also make it harder for my state and local officials to properly plan for the services we need and the emergencies we may face. Furthermore, the exclusion of questions about race and ethnicity will exacerbate the degradation of data quality, and it will lead to undercounts of Black and brown communities that are already undercounted in past censuses. If we don't know who is living in our communities, we cannot prepare for the challenges we may face, and we will not receive adequate funds from federal programs. 

Additionally, the lack of transparency and sufficient opportunity for the public to comment on this incredibly consequential rule is concerning. I urge you to both extend the comment period to a full 90 days until December 9th, and to reject this proposed rule. 


Phoenix Muchowski,

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: US Census Bureau,I urge the Census Bureau and Department of Commerce to withdraw the proposed rule changing residence criteria for the decennial Census and restricting demographic questions.The proposal would exclude foreign citizens from the population used for congressional apportionment unless they are also U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents. Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: US Census Bureau,I urge the Census Bureau and Department of Commerce to withdraw the proposed rule changing residence criteria for the decennial Census and restricting demographic questions.The proposal would exclude foreign citizens from the population used for congressional apportionment unless they are also U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents. It must be complete, accurate, and protected from political manipulation.Please withdraw this proposed rule and preserve a Census that fairly and accurately counts our community.Nyla  [X]Prairie Farm, Wisconsin 54762

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Dear Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions,

Subject: Re: Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions (Docket No. 260903-0005; RIN 0607-AA75) 

I strongly oppose the proposed rules for the census and changes to its residence rule. All persons in the United States have a right to be counted, as the 14th Amendment of the Constitution plainly establishes. This proposed rule will weaken our democracy, our systems of representation, and the doctrine of “one person, one vote.” Without an accurate count, people will not be fairly represented in Congress or state legislatures. 

By generating inaccurate and unreliable data, this change would also make it harder for my state and local officials to properly plan for the services we need and the emergencies we may face. Furthermore, the exclusion of questions about race and ethnicity will exacerbate the degradation of data quality, and it will lead to undercounts of Black and brown communities that are already undercounted in past censuses. If we don't know who is living in our communities, we cannot prepare for the challenges we may face, and we will not receive adequate funds from federal programs. 

Additionally, the lack of transparency and sufficient opportunity for the public to comment on this incredibly consequential rule is concerning. I urge you to both extend the comment period to a full 90 days until December 9th, and to reject this proposed rule. 
Thank you for your attention to this matter.
Cathrine Greene

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: US Census Bureau,I urge the Census Bureau and Department of Commerce to withdraw the proposed rule changing residence criteria for the decennial Census and restricting demographic questions.The proposal would exclude foreign citizens from the population used for congressional apportionment unless they are also U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents. Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Dear Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions,

Subject: Re: Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions (Docket No. 260903-0005; RIN 0607-AA75) 

I strongly oppose the proposed rules for the census and changes to its residence rule. All persons in the United States have a right to be counted, as the 14th Amendment of the Constitution plainly establishes. This proposed rule will weaken our democracy, our systems of representation, and the doctrine of “one person, one vote.” Without an accurate count, people will not be fairly represented in Congress or state legislatures. 

By generating inaccurate and unreliable data, this change would also make it harder for my state and local officials to properly plan for the services we need and the emergencies we may face. Furthermore, the exclusion of questions about race and ethnicity will exacerbate the degradation of data quality, and it will lead to undercounts of Black and brown communities that are already undercounted in past censuses. If we don't know who is living in our communities, we cannot prepare for the challenges we may face, and we will not receive adequate funds from federal programs. 

Additionally, the lack of transparency and sufficient opportunity for the public to comment on this incredibly consequential rule is concerning. I urge you to both extend the comment period to a full 90 days until December 9th, and to reject this proposed rule. 
I oppose the quashing of accurate accounting of our population.  It distorts the truth.

Josephine Foote,
[x]

Comment:
The U.S. Census is a count of persons, not of partisans. Please see to it that it remains that way. Count people, not only the ones you want.

The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. I oppose this proposed rule because it departs from that constitutional mandate, risking severe harm to my community. Excluding noncitizens from the population count used for congressional apportionment and federal funding, while adding a citizenship question designed to deter participation, will suppress response rates across immigrant communities and mixed-status families who fear being targeted. An undercount here would directly strip my community of appropriate congressional representation and our fair share of federal funding for essential safety-net programs like SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, CHIP, and Title I education grants. As someone who cares about fairness and the rule of law, I urge the Bureau to withdraw this proposal and count every person living in our communities, as the Constitution requires. 

I am also concerned that the proposed rule erases vital Census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Decades of demographic data serve as the baseline that public and private institutions rely on to identify inequalities and direct resources where they are needed most. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities.  

Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.  

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Sincerely,
Annemarie Carr
Newark, DE

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Dear Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions,

Subject: Re: Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions (Docket No. 260903-0005; RIN 0607-AA75) 

I strongly oppose the proposed rules for the census and changes to its residence rule. All persons in the United States have a right to be counted, as the 14th Amendment of the Constitution plainly establishes. This proposed rule will weaken our democracy, our systems of representation, and the doctrine of “one person, one vote.” Without an accurate count, people will not be fairly represented in Congress or state legislatures. 

By generating inaccurate and unreliable data, this change would also make it harder for my state and local officials to properly plan for the services we need and the emergencies we may face. Furthermore, the exclusion of questions about race and ethnicity will exacerbate the degradation of data quality, and it will lead to undercounts of Black and brown communities that are already undercounted in past censuses. If we don't know who is living in our communities, we cannot prepare for the challenges we may face, and we will not receive adequate funds from federal programs. 

Additionally, the lack of transparency and sufficient opportunity for the public to comment on this incredibly consequential rule is concerning. I urge you to both extend the comment period to a full 90 days until December 9th, and to reject this proposed rule. 


Lorraine Thompson,
[X]
Saline
MI



Sincerely,
Dr. Lorraine Thompson

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: US Census Bureau,I urge the Census Bureau and Department of Commerce to withdraw the proposed rule changing residence criteria for the decennial Census and restricting demographic questions.The proposal would exclude foreign citizens from the population used for congressional apportionment unless they are also U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents. The Census proposes to only include people if their address is confirmed by tax records -- which could mean millions, particularly low-income families, could be missed in the decennial Census. Overall, this would leave out people who actually live in our community, including many people who are lawfully present in the United States.For all past Census counts, including the 2020 Census, foreign citizens living in the United States were generally counted where they lived and slept most of the time. That approach recognizes the basic purpose of a Census: accurately counting the people who live in our communities. The 14th Amendment requires congressional representation to be apportioned according to the “whole number of persons in each State.”I am also deeply concerned by the proposal to prohibit race and ethnicity questions, along with sexual orientation, on the decennial Census enumeration questionnaire. The Census Bureau itself recognizes the importance of race data for civil rights protections, legislative redistricting, equal employment opportunities, and identifying disparities.The 2030 Census will determine congressional, state, and local representation for the decade that follows. It must be complete, accurate, and protected from political manipulation.Please withdraw this proposed rule and preserve a Census that fairly and accurately counts our community.Carolyn  [X]Portage, Michigan 49024

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Dear Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions,

Subject: Re: Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions (Docket No. 260903-0005; RIN 0607-AA75)

Additionally, the lack of transparency and sufficient opportunity for the public to comment on this incredibly consequential rule is concerning. I urge you to both extend the comment period to a full 90 days until December 9th, and to reject this proposed rule.

Hazelhurst
WI

David Barnhill

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Census Bureau's proposed rule to strengthen the US Census is critical to fair representation and the future of America.  

The U.S. Census should not include distorted data in its count of Americans.  By including overly generalized ethnic demographic categories, we obscure the true goal of the census and hinder its constitutionally mandated purpose: an accurate count of Americans.

Thank you,  

Larry Disbrow

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). 

As and educator, and I care about a fair and accurate census because census data and other federal datasets based on the census are used to make key decisions that affect our nation’s students, educators, and schools.  

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Examples of these uses include: . 

* Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. 

* Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

* Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

* Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

* Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

* Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

* Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

* Determining state higher education funding formulas 

* Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

* Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

* Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

First, to ensure a fair and accurate census,  the Census Bureau should  extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. Second, I oppose both the proposed changes to the residence criteria and the proposed regulations regarding demographic questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. The Census Bureau should  withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The Constitution requires  counting all people living in the United States. 

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (including children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count. 

Revise the tax records language so that those whose mailing address differs from their residential address (servicemembers, those with a post office box) are not excluded.  

• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for civil rights enforcement, among other uses, and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The prohibition, as written, may also restrict the collection or publication of census data on same-sex couples that was asked in 2020. 

 The proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Sincerely,
Ms. Shellie Rodgers
Pleasant Hill, MO

Comment:
Dear Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions,

Subject: Re: Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions (Docket No. 260903-0005; RIN 0607-AA75)

MN

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Census Bureau's proposed rule to strengthen the US Census is critical to fair representation and the future of America.  

The U.S. Census should not include distorted data in its count of Americans.  By including overly generalized ethnic demographic categories, we obscure the true goal of the census and hinder its constitutionally mandated purpose: an accurate count of Americans.  

Additionally, illegal aliens and other non-legal permanent residents should not be included for apportionment. Census data is used for the apportionment of congressional seats. Non-citizens cannot legally vote and should not be used to decrease the voting power of Americans. I support the Census Bureau in advancing the correct understanding of usual residence to recognize an element of allegiance that is antithetical to the inclusion of those not legally present in our country.  

This Census Bureau should also consider adding a citizenship question to the Census survey. The Supreme Court has already held that the Constitution lawfully permits the Census Bureau to at least inquire about citizenship on the census questionnaire. "The census should absolutely include questions related to citizenship and legal presence. 

These changes would strengthen the census in its core purpose of attaining an accurate count of Americans and have my full support. 

Thank you,  
Anthony DANDREA
Anthony D'Andrea

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: US Census Bureau,I urge the Census Bureau and Department of Commerce to withdraw the proposed rule changing residence criteria for the decennial Census and restricting demographic questions.The proposal would exclude foreign citizens from the population used for congressional apportionment unless they are also U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents. Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: US Census Bureau,I urge the Census Bureau and Department of Commerce to withdraw the proposed rule changing residence criteria for the decennial Census and restricting demographic questions.The proposal would exclude foreign citizens from the population used for congressional apportionment unless they are also U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents. It must be complete, accurate, and protected from political manipulation.Please withdraw this proposed rule and preserve a Census that fairly and accurately counts our community.Robert Anthonyranthony154@gmail.com712 E 4th StWeatherford, Texas 76086-1844

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Dear Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions,

Subject: Re: Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions (Docket No. 260903-0005; RIN 0607-AA75) 

I strongly oppose the proposed rules for the census and changes to its residence rule. All persons in the United States have a right to be counted, as the 14th Amendment of the Constitution plainly establishes. This proposed rule will weaken our democracy, our systems of representation, and the doctrine of “one person, one vote.” Without an accurate count, people will not be fairly represented in Congress or state legislatures. 

By generating inaccurate and unreliable data, this change would also make it harder for my state and local officials to properly plan for the services we need and the emergencies we may face. Furthermore, the exclusion of questions about race and ethnicity will exacerbate the degradation of data quality, and it will lead to undercounts of Black and brown communities that are already undercounted in past censuses. If we don't know who is living in our communities, we cannot prepare for the challenges we may face, and we will not receive adequate funds from federal programs. 

Additionally, the lack of transparency and sufficient opportunity for the public to comment on this incredibly consequential rule is concerning. I urge you to both extend the comment period to a full 90 days until December 9th, and to reject this proposed rule. 
I urge you to keep the Census Constitutionally correct.

Robin Ballard,
[X]
BELLINGHAM
WA



Sincerely,
Ms. Robin Ballard

The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. I oppose this proposed rule because it departs from that constitutional mandate, risking severe harm to my community. Excluding noncitizens from the population count used for congressional apportionment and federal funding, while adding a citizenship question designed to deter participation, will suppress response rates across immigrant communities and mixed-status families who fear being targeted. An undercount here would directly strip my community of appropriate congressional representation and our fair share of federal funding for essential safety-net programs like SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, CHIP, and Title I education grants. As someone who cares about fairness and the rule of law, I urge the Bureau to withdraw this proposal and count every person living in our communities, as the Constitution requires. 

I am also concerned that the proposed rule erases vital Census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Decades of demographic data serve as the baseline that public and private institutions rely on to identify inequalities and direct resources where they are needed most. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities.  

Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.  

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Sincerely,
Leighton Clark
Fort Worth, TX

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: US Census Bureau,I urge the Census Bureau and Department of Commerce to withdraw the proposed rule changing residence criteria for the decennial Census and restricting demographic questions.The proposal would exclude foreign citizens from the population used for congressional apportionment unless they are also U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents. The Census proposes to only include people if their address is confirmed by tax records -- which could mean millions, particularly low-income families, could be missed in the decennial Census. Overall, this would leave out people who actually live in our community, including many people who are lawfully present in the United States.For all past Census counts, including the 2020 Census, foreign citizens living in the United States were generally counted where they lived and slept most of the time. That approach recognizes the basic purpose of a Census: accurately counting the people who live in our communities. The 14th Amendment requires congressional representation to be apportioned according to the “whole number of persons in each State.”I am also deeply concerned by the proposal to prohibit race and ethnicity questions, along with sexual orientation, on the decennial Census enumeration questionnaire. The Census Bureau itself recognizes the importance of race data for civil rights protections, legislative redistricting, equal employment opportunities, and identifying disparities.The 2030 Census will determine congressional, state, and local representation for the decade that follows. It must be complete, accurate, and protected from political manipulation.Please withdraw this proposed rule and preserve a Census that fairly and accurately counts our community.Christie  [x] Slidell , Louisiana 70460

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). 

As and educator, and I care about a fair and accurate census because census data and other federal datasets based on the census are used to make key decisions that affect our nation’s students, educators, and schools.  

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Examples of these uses include: . 

* Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. 

* Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

* Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

* Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

* Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

* Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

* Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

* Determining state higher education funding formulas 

* Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

* Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

* Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

First, to ensure a fair and accurate census,  the Census Bureau should  extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. Second, I oppose both the proposed changes to the residence criteria and the proposed regulations regarding demographic questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. The Census Bureau should  withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The Constitution requires  counting all people living in the United States. 

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (including children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count. 

Revise the tax records language so that those whose mailing address differs from their residential address (servicemembers, those with a post office box) are not excluded.  

• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for civil rights enforcement, among other uses, and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The prohibition, as written, may also restrict the collection or publication of census data on same-sex couples that was asked in 2020. 

 The proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Sincerely,
Mrs. Lori Moniz
Woodbury Heights, NJ

Comment:

Thank you for listening to citizens of this country and following the law rather than biased ideology.

Sharen Barboza,

NY

Sharen Barboza

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. I oppose this proposed rule because it departs from that constitutional mandate, risking severe harm to my community. Excluding noncitizens from the population count used for congressional apportionment and federal funding, while adding a citizenship question designed to deter participation, will suppress response rates across immigrant communities and mixed-status families who fear being targeted. An undercount here would directly strip my community of appropriate congressional representation and our fair share of federal funding for essential safety-net programs like SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, CHIP, and Title I education grants. As someone who cares about fairness and the rule of law, I urge the Bureau to withdraw this proposal and count every person living in our communities, as the Constitution requires. 

I am also concerned that the proposed rule erases vital Census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Decades of demographic data serve as the baseline that public and private institutions rely on to identify inequalities and direct resources where they are needed most. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities.  

Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.  

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Sincerely,
richard Houle
Hugo, MN

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Census Bureau's proposed rule to strengthen the US Census is critical to fair representation and the future of America.  

The U.S. Census should not include distorted data in its count of Americans.  By including overly generalized ethnic demographic categories, we obscure the true goal of the census and hinder its constitutionally mandated purpose: an accurate count of Americans.  

Additionally, illegal aliens and other non-legal permanent residents should not be included for apportionment. Census data is used for the apportionment of congressional seats. Non-citizens cannot legally vote and should not be used to decrease the voting power of Americans. I support the Census Bureau in advancing the correct understanding of usual residence to recognize an element of allegiance that is antithetical to the inclusion of those not legally present in our country.  

This Census Bureau should also consider adding a citizenship question to the Census survey. The Supreme Court has already held that the Constitution lawfully permits the Census Bureau to at least inquire about citizenship on the census questionnaire. "The census should absolutely include questions related to citizenship and legal presence. 

These changes would strengthen the census in its core purpose of attaining an accurate count of Americans and have my full support. 

Thank you,  

Sandra Hodgins

The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. I oppose this proposed rule because it departs from that constitutional mandate, risking severe harm to my community. Excluding noncitizens from the population count used for congressional apportionment and federal funding, while adding a citizenship question designed to deter participation, will suppress response rates across immigrant communities and mixed-status families who fear being targeted. An undercount here would directly strip my community of appropriate congressional representation and our fair share of federal funding for essential safety-net programs like SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, CHIP, and Title I education grants. As someone who cares about fairness and the rule of law, I urge the Bureau to withdraw this proposal and count every person living in our communities, as the Constitution requires. 

I am also concerned that the proposed rule erases vital Census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Decades of demographic data serve as the baseline that public and private institutions rely on to identify inequalities and direct resources where they are needed most. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities.  

Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.  

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Sincerely,
Dawn Petry
Hague, NY

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: US Census Bureau,I urge the Census Bureau and Department of Commerce to withdraw the proposed rule changing residence criteria for the decennial Census and restricting demographic questions.The proposal would exclude foreign citizens from the population used for congressional apportionment unless they are also U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents. The Census proposes to only include people if their address is confirmed by tax records -- which could mean millions, particularly low-income families, could be missed in the decennial Census. Overall, this would leave out people who actually live in our community, including many people who are lawfully present in the United States.For all past Census counts, including the 2020 Census, foreign citizens living in the United States were generally counted where they lived and slept most of the time. That approach recognizes the basic purpose of a Census: accurately counting the people who live in our communities. The 14th Amendment requires congressional representation to be apportioned according to the “whole number of persons in each State.”I am also deeply concerned by the proposal to prohibit race and ethnicity questions, along with sexual orientation, on the decennial Census enumeration questionnaire. The Census Bureau itself recognizes the importance of race data for civil rights protections, legislative redistricting, equal employment opportunities, and identifying disparities.The 2030 Census will determine congressional, state, and local representation for the decade that follows. It must be complete, accurate, and protected from political manipulation.Please withdraw this proposed rule and preserve a Census that fairly and accurately counts our community.Sincerely,  Zane C. Woods 3635[x]Portland, Oregon 97202

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Dear Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions,

Subject: Re: Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions (Docket No. 260903-0005; RIN 0607-AA75) 

I strongly oppose the proposed rules for the census and changes to its residence rule. All persons in the United States have a right to be counted, as the 14th Amendment of the Constitution plainly establishes. This proposed rule will weaken our democracy, our systems of representation, and the doctrine of “one person, one vote.” Without an accurate count, people will not be fairly represented in Congress or state legislatures. 

By generating inaccurate and unreliable data, this change would also make it harder for my state and local officials to properly plan for the services we need and the emergencies we may face. Furthermore, the exclusion of questions about race and ethnicity will exacerbate the degradation of data quality, and it will lead to undercounts of Black and brown communities that are already undercounted in past censuses. If we don't know who is living in our communities, we cannot prepare for the challenges we may face, and we will not receive adequate funds from federal programs. 

Additionally, the lack of transparency and sufficient opportunity for the public to comment on this incredibly consequential rule is concerning. I urge you to both extend the comment period to a full 90 days until December 9th, and to reject this proposed rule. 


Jane Lyon,
[x]

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. I oppose this proposed rule because it departs from that constitutional mandate, risking severe harm to my community. Excluding noncitizens from the population count used for congressional apportionment and federal funding, while adding a citizenship question designed to deter participation, will suppress response rates across immigrant communities and mixed-status families who fear being targeted. An undercount here would directly strip my community of appropriate congressional representation and our fair share of federal funding for essential safety-net programs like SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, CHIP, and Title I education grants. As someone who cares about fairness and the rule of law, I urge the Bureau to withdraw this proposal and count every person living in our communities, as the Constitution requires. 

I am also concerned that the proposed rule erases vital Census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Decades of demographic data serve as the baseline that public and private institutions rely on to identify inequalities and direct resources where they are needed most. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities.  

Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.  

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Sincerely,
Donna Munro
Bremerton, WA

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). 

As and educator, and I care about a fair and accurate census because census data and other federal datasets based on the census are used to make key decisions that affect our nation’s students, educators, and schools.  

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Examples of these uses include: . 

* Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. 

* Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

* Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

* Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

* Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

* Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

* Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

* Determining state higher education funding formulas 

* Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

* Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

* Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

First, to ensure a fair and accurate census,  the Census Bureau should  extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. Second, I oppose both the proposed changes to the residence criteria and the proposed regulations regarding demographic questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. The Census Bureau should  withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The Constitution requires  counting all people living in the United States. 

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (including children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count. 

Revise the tax records language so that those whose mailing address differs from their residential address (servicemembers, those with a post office box) are not excluded.  

• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for civil rights enforcement, among other uses, and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The prohibition, as written, may also restrict the collection or publication of census data on same-sex couples that was asked in 2020. 

 The proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Sincerely,
Mrs. DELIA VAN BRUNT
Olympia, WA

Overall, this would leave out people who actually live in our community, including many people who are lawfully present in the United States.For all past Census counts, including the 2020 Census, foreign citizens living in the United States were generally counted where they lived and slept most of the time. That approach recognizes the basic purpose of a Census: accurately counting the people who live in our communities. The 14th Amendment requires congressional representation to be apportioned according to the “whole number of persons in each State.”I am also deeply concerned by the proposal to prohibit race and ethnicity questions, along with sexual orientation, on the decennial Census enumeration questionnaire. The Census Bureau itself recognizes the importance of race data for civil rights protections, legislative redistricting, equal employment opportunities, and identifying disparities.The 2030 Census will determine congressional, state, and local representation for the decade that follows. It must be complete, accurate, and protected from political manipulation.Please withdraw this proposed rule and preserve a Census that fairly and accurately counts our community.Gina  [X] ARCATA, California 95521-6947

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. I oppose this proposed rule because it departs from that constitutional mandate, risking severe harm to my community. Excluding noncitizens from the population count used for congressional apportionment and federal funding, while adding a citizenship question designed to deter participation, will suppress response rates across immigrant communities and mixed-status families who fear being targeted. An undercount here would directly strip my community of appropriate congressional representation and our fair share of federal funding for essential safety-net programs like SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, CHIP, and Title I education grants. As someone who cares about fairness and the rule of law, I urge the Bureau to withdraw this proposal and count every person living in our communities, as the Constitution requires. 

I am also concerned that the proposed rule erases vital Census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Decades of demographic data serve as the baseline that public and private institutions rely on to identify inequalities and direct resources where they are needed most. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities.  

Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.  

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Sincerely,
Steve Wasil
Stamford, CT

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Census Bureau's proposed rule to strengthen the US Census is critical to fair representation and the future of America.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. I oppose this proposed rule because it departs from that constitutional mandate, risking severe harm to my community. Excluding noncitizens from the population count used for congressional apportionment and federal funding, while adding a citizenship question designed to deter participation, will suppress response rates across immigrant communities and mixed-status families who fear being targeted. An undercount here would directly strip my community of appropriate congressional representation and our fair share of federal funding for essential safety-net programs like SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, CHIP, and Title I education grants. I am also concerned that the proposed rule erases vital Census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities.

Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.  

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Sincerely,

Malvern, PA

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Dear Director Cook,

I appreciate the opportunity to comment on the Census Bureau's proposed rule governing residence criteria and demographic questions for the 2030 decennial census.

Please be aware that you may receive a large number of pre-written form responses. Information was provided by Virginia Municipal League to their member organizations based on leadership preferences and with provided wording.  These responses were fed through the webpage https://nlc.quorum.us/campaign/170324.

I appreciate several provisions of the proposed rule, while I and am simultaneously concerned that one provision could reduce the accuracy of our community's population count and affect our access to federal and state resources. 


Appreciation for the Proposed Changes:

Apportionment and population count: The proposed rule would apportion Congressional representation based on U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents. In a very similar concept as with the broadly-maligned "two-thirds" provisions, it may seem unfair on the surface, but on deeper consideration, one realizes that the provision quite reasonably shifts the focus of vote weight to those who are legally entitled to vote, and away from those being used and potentially misused by the vote of others while having no say themselves.

Legal-status question: The proposed rule also raises the possibility of adding a legal-status question to the census questionnaire. This proposal is a logical counterbalance to the proposed change of apportionment, providing consideration for those who may be here without legal status without counting them towards votes in which they cannot legally participate.

Reliance on administrative records: This topic was presented as a concern by the Virginia Municipal League, however, they provided no details of the concern. My initial impression in the face of lack of facts is that greater use of tax, immigration, health, and other administrative records will improve accuracy of the census as a whole, which is critical to the census' core mission and purpose, contrasted with the concerns of potentially undercounting populations who have taken deliberate efforts to avoid being recorded. 

Demographic questions: The proposal would eliminate race and ethnicity questions, and make most other demographic questions optional. These improvements will help to reduce decisions illegally and immorally based on race and other factors which are Constitutionally protected from preferential treatment. Some express concerns of the loss of this data, but the use of such factors in decision-making is largely contrary to law.


Concerns about the Proposed Changes:

Usual residence and the enumeration period: My one concern in the proposals as presented by VML is the proposed shift to counting residents based on where they spend the most time during a January 3-April 1 period, rather than their usual residence throughout the year. This change could affect our population count, particular concerning seasonal residents such as snowbirds/ students / part-time workers / other mobile populations. I ask the Bureau to further evaluate the operational and data-accuracy impacts of this change and explain the rationale supporting it.


While others would clearly prefer to broadly criticize recommendations, I would respectfully ask the Census Bureau to support the proposed changes with data and rationale.  

I appreciate the opportunity to comment on this proposal and would welcome the chance to provide additional information or answer any questions the Bureau may have. 

Sincerely, 
Michael Pollard
Bristol Virginia City Council

I oppose this proposed rule because it departs from that constitutional mandate, risking severe harm to my community. Excluding noncitizens from the population count used for congressional apportionment and federal funding, while adding a citizenship question designed to deter participation, will suppress response rates across immigrant communities and mixed-status families who fear being targeted. An undercount here would directly strip my community of appropriate congressional representation and our fair share of federal funding for essential safety-net programs like SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, CHIP, and Title I education grants. As someone who cares about fairness and the rule of law, I urge the Bureau to withdraw this proposal and count every person living in our communities, as the Constitution requires. 

I am also concerned that the proposed rule erases vital Census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Decades of demographic data serve as the baseline that public and private institutions rely on to identify inequalities and direct resources where they are needed most. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities.  

Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.  

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Sincerely,
Veronica Noechel
Raleigh, NC
