The Census proposes to only include people if their address is confirmed by tax records -- which could mean millions, particularly low-income families, could be missed in the decennial Census. Overall, this would leave out people who actually live in our community, including many people who are lawfully present in the United States.For all past Census counts, including the 2020 Census, foreign citizens living in the United States were generally counted where they lived and slept most of the time. That approach recognizes the basic purpose of a Census: accurately counting the people who live in our communities. The 14th Amendment requires congressional representation to be apportioned according to the “whole number of persons in each State.”I am also deeply concerned by the proposal to prohibit race and ethnicity questions, along with sexual orientation, on the decennial Census enumeration questionnaire. The Census Bureau itself recognizes the importance of race data for civil rights protections, legislative redistricting, equal employment opportunities, and identifying disparities.The 2030 Census will determine congressional, state, and local representation for the decade that follows. It must be complete, accurate, and protected from political manipulation.Please withdraw this proposed rule and preserve a Census that fairly and accurately counts our community.Jennifer[X] Massapequa Park, New York 11762

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Census Bureau's proposed rule to strengthen the US Census is critical to fair representation and the future of America.  

The U.S. Census should not include distorted data in its count of Americans.  By including overly generalized ethnic demographic categories, we obscure the true goal of the census and hinder its constitutionally mandated purpose: an accurate count of Americans.  

Additionally, illegal aliens and other non-legal permanent residents should not be included for apportionment. Census data is used for the apportionment of congressional seats. Non-citizens cannot legally vote and should not be used to decrease the voting power of Americans. I support the Census Bureau in advancing the correct understanding of usual residence to recognize an element of allegiance that is antithetical to the inclusion of those not legally present in our country.  

This Census Bureau should also consider adding a citizenship question to the Census survey. The Supreme Court has already held that the Constitution lawfully permits the Census Bureau to at least inquire about citizenship on the census questionnaire. "The census should absolutely include questions related to citizenship and legal presence. 

These changes would strengthen the census in its core purpose of attaining an accurate count of Americans and have my full support. 

Thank you,  

Susan Grover

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. I oppose this proposed rule because it departs from that constitutional mandate, risking severe harm to my community. Excluding noncitizens from the population count used for congressional apportionment and federal funding, while adding a citizenship question designed to deter participation, will suppress response rates across immigrant communities and mixed-status families who fear being targeted. An undercount here would directly strip my community of appropriate congressional representation and our fair share of federal funding for essential safety-net programs like SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, CHIP, and Title I education grants. As someone who cares about fairness and the rule of law, I urge the Bureau to withdraw this proposal and count every person living in our communities, as the Constitution requires. 

I am also concerned that the proposed rule erases vital Census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Decades of demographic data serve as the baseline that public and private institutions rely on to identify inequalities and direct resources where they are needed most. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities.  

Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.  

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Sincerely,
Wilma Win
Honolulu, HI

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: US Census Bureau,I urge the Census Bureau and Department of Commerce to withdraw the proposed rule changing residence criteria for the decennial Census and restricting demographic questions.The proposal would exclude foreign citizens from the population used for congressional apportionment unless they are also U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents. It must be complete, accurate, and protected from political manipulation.Please withdraw this proposed rule and preserve a Census that fairly and accurately counts our community.Rosalie [X]  Bakersfield , California 93311

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. I oppose this proposed rule because it departs from that constitutional mandate, risking severe harm to my community. Excluding noncitizens from the population count used for congressional apportionment and federal funding, while adding a citizenship question designed to deter participation, will suppress response rates across immigrant communities and mixed-status families who fear being targeted. An undercount here would directly strip my community of appropriate congressional representation and our fair share of federal funding for essential safety-net programs like SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, CHIP, and Title I education grants. As someone who cares about fairness and the rule of law, I urge the Bureau to withdraw this proposal and count every person living in our communities, as the Constitution requires. 

I am also concerned that the proposed rule erases vital Census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Decades of demographic data serve as the baseline that public and private institutions rely on to identify inequalities and direct resources where they are needed most. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities.  

Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.  

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Sincerely,
Carol Miller
Richardson, TX

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). 

As and educator, and I care about a fair and accurate census because census data and other federal datasets based on the census are used to make key decisions that affect our nation’s students, educators, and schools.  

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Examples of these uses include: . 

* Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. 

* Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

* Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

* Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

* Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

* Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

* Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

* Determining state higher education funding formulas 

* Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

* Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

* Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

First, to ensure a fair and accurate census,  the Census Bureau should  extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. Second, I oppose both the proposed changes to the residence criteria and the proposed regulations regarding demographic questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. The Census Bureau should  withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The Constitution requires  counting all people living in the United States. 

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (including children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count. 

Revise the tax records language so that those whose mailing address differs from their residential address (servicemembers, those with a post office box) are not excluded.  

• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for civil rights enforcement, among other uses, and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The prohibition, as written, may also restrict the collection or publication of census data on same-sex couples that was asked in 2020. 

 The proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Sincerely,
Mrs Anastasia Alley
South Thomaston, ME

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). 

As and educator, and I care about a fair and accurate census because census data and other federal datasets based on the census are used to make key decisions that affect our nation’s students, educators, and schools.  

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Examples of these uses include: . 

* Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. 

* Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

* Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

* Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

* Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

* Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

* Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

* Determining state higher education funding formulas 

* Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

* Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

* Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

First, to ensure a fair and accurate census,  the Census Bureau should  extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. Second, I oppose both the proposed changes to the residence criteria and the proposed regulations regarding demographic questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. The Census Bureau should  withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The Constitution requires  counting all people living in the United States. 

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (including children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count. 

Revise the tax records language so that those whose mailing address differs from their residential address (servicemembers, those with a post office box) are not excluded.  

• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for civil rights enforcement, among other uses, and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The prohibition, as written, may also restrict the collection or publication of census data on same-sex couples that was asked in 2020. 

 The proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Sincerely,
Mr. Larry Rolfe
Sunfield, MI

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: US Census Bureau,I urge the Census Bureau and Department of Commerce to withdraw the proposed rule changing residence criteria for the decennial Census and restricting demographic questions.The proposal would exclude foreign citizens from the population used for congressional apportionment unless they are also U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents. The Census proposes to only include people if their address is confirmed by tax records -- which could mean millions, particularly low-income families, could be missed in the decennial Census. Overall, this would leave out people who actually live in our community, including many people who are lawfully present in the United States.For all past Census counts, including the 2020 Census, foreign citizens living in the United States were generally counted where they lived and slept most of the time. That approach recognizes the basic purpose of a Census: accurately counting the people who live in our communities. The 14th Amendment requires congressional representation to be apportioned according to the “whole number of persons in each State.”I am also deeply concerned by the proposal to prohibit race and ethnicity questions, along with sexual orientation, on the decennial Census enumeration questionnaire. The Census Bureau itself recognizes the importance of race data for civil rights protections, legislative redistricting, equal employment opportunities, and identifying disparities.The 2030 Census will determine congressional, state, and local representation for the decade that follows. It must be complete, accurate, and protected from political manipulation.Please withdraw this proposed rule and preserve a Census that fairly and accurately counts our community.Sincerely, Robert Kreimeyer[X] Adair , Iowa 50002

* Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

* Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

* Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

* Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

* Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

* Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

* Determining state higher education funding formulas 

* Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

* Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

* Determining the need for and funding health and social services

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. I oppose this proposed rule because it departs from that constitutional mandate, risking severe harm to my community. Excluding noncitizens from the population count used for congressional apportionment and federal funding, while adding a citizenship question designed to deter participation, will suppress response rates across immigrant communities and mixed-status families who fear being targeted. An undercount here would directly strip my community of appropriate congressional representation and our fair share of federal funding for essential safety-net programs like SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, CHIP, and Title I education grants. As someone who cares about fairness and the rule of law, I urge the Bureau to withdraw this proposal and count every person living in our communities, as the Constitution requires. 

I am also concerned that the proposed rule erases vital Census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Decades of demographic data serve as the baseline that public and private institutions rely on to identify inequalities and direct resources where they are needed most. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities.  

Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.  

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Sincerely,
Gloria Burd
Sunnyvale, CA

Comment:
Dear Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions,

Subject: Re: Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions (Docket No. 260903-0005; RIN 0607-AA75)

So, the American people expect you to do your job seriously and legally by administering the upcoming census fully. Count all people residing in the U.S. at the time of the upcoming census and record all requisite information, as clearly expressed in the 14th Amendment and the Enumeration Clause. You must not go forward with these ill-conceived, shortsighted, unconscionable democracy-destroying proposed changes.

* Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

* Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

* Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

* Determining state higher education funding formulas 

* Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

* Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

* Determining the need for and funding health and social services

As and educator, and I care about a fair and accurate census because census data and other federal datasets based on the census are used to make key decisions that affect our nation’s students, educators, and schools.  

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Examples of these uses include: . 

* Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. 

* Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

* Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

* Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

* Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

* Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

* Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

* Determining state higher education funding formulas 

* Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

* Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

* Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

First, to ensure a fair and accurate census,  the Census Bureau should  extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. Second, I oppose both the proposed changes to the residence criteria and the proposed regulations regarding demographic questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. The Census Bureau should  withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The Constitution requires  counting all people living in the United States. 

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (including children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count. 

Revise the tax records language so that those whose mailing address differs from their residential address (servicemembers, those with a post office box) are not excluded.  

• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for civil rights enforcement, among other uses, and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The prohibition, as written, may also restrict the collection or publication of census data on same-sex couples that was asked in 2020. 

 The proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Sincerely,
Ms. Sue Hanson

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Re: Docket No. USBC-2026-0628, Proposed Residence Criteria and Demographic Question Restrictions for the 2030 Census

I oppose this proposed rule and ask the Census Bureau to withdraw it.

I live in Peoria, Maricopa County in Arizona. My community depends on census data for Peoria Unified School District's Title I funding and Valleywise Hospital's Medicaid reimbursements. This funding ensures that our most vulnerable children can receive an equitable education, and our local hospital can continue to support our most vulnerable citizens with the medical care they can't afford. 

The rule would stop counting millions of people who live here lawfully, including workers on visas, students, and people with temporary protected status or pending asylum claims, along with undocumented residents. The Fourteenth Amendment requires “counting the whole number of persons in each State.” Every census since 1790 has counted everyone who lives here, regardless of citizenship. The rule does not say whether the people it excludes will be counted for any purpose, or whether they will appear in the population totals that decide federal funding for my state. I ask the Bureau to answer that on the record. The Bureau’s own 2019 research found that asking about citizenship would cut responses from noncitizen households by 8 percent. This rule goes further than that question did, and it will keep families in my community, including citizen children, from answering at all.

The rule also removes race and ethnicity from the census for the first time since 1790. Every measure of whether this country treats its people equally starts with that count. We know how much shorter Black and Native American lives are, how much lower Black homeownership is, which neighborhoods banks have redlined, and which children the last census missed, because the census asks. Take the question away and the disparities do not end. They become impossible to prove, and impossible to fix. The Bureau’s own analysis, posted with this docket, admits there are “no other comparably accurate, comprehensive, and reliable sources” for this data. A government that stops counting harm by race is choosing not to see it.

The Bureau’s own analysis admits it “cannot quantify” any cost or benefit of this rule. A rule the agency cannot evaluate should not be adopted. 

Sincerely, 
Anonymous Concerned Citizen

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). 

As and educator, and I care about a fair and accurate census because census data and other federal datasets based on the census are used to make key decisions that affect our nation’s students, educators, and schools.  

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Examples of these uses include: . 

* Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. 

* Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

* Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

* Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

* Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

* Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

* Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

* Determining state higher education funding formulas 

* Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

* Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

* Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

First, to ensure a fair and accurate census,  the Census Bureau should  extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. Second, I oppose both the proposed changes to the residence criteria and the proposed regulations regarding demographic questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. The Census Bureau should  withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The Constitution requires  counting all people living in the United States. 

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (including children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count. 

Revise the tax records language so that those whose mailing address differs from their residential address (servicemembers, those with a post office box) are not excluded.  

• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for civil rights enforcement, among other uses, and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The prohibition, as written, may also restrict the collection or publication of census data on same-sex couples that was asked in 2020. 

 The proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Sincerely,
Mrs. Barbara SANSONETTI
Haverstraw, NY

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: 91 FR 57524  Public Comment,I am submitting this comment in opposition to the Census Bureau's proposed rule on residence criteria and demographic questions for the decennial census, 91 FR 57524 (Sept. 10, 2026). This proposed rule makes significant changes to the 2030 Census, including leaving noncitizens without green cards out of the count used to divide seats in Congress, removing race and ethnicity questions, and possibly adding a citizenship or immigration status question. The Census determines congressional representation and guides planning for health, education, housing, and infrastructure, along with the distribution of more than $2.8 trillion a year across roughly 350 federal programs. When communities are miscounted or left out in the decennial Census, they lose their fair share of representation and resources for an entire decade. This rule violates the Constitution and federal law, which both count the "whole number of persons" in each state, not just citizens. Congress chose "persons" over "citizens" on purpose, and counting only some residents revives the logic of the three-fifths clause. Changing who counts would require a constitutional amendment, not a census rule. The Supreme Court recognized in 2016 that representation serves all residents, including children and noncitizens, not only voters. Under this rule, millions of people who live, work, pay taxes, and raise families here would no longer count, weakening the voting power of the communities they belong to, including the citizens who live alongside them. A citizenship question would make this worse. The success of the Census depends on public trust. Every person must feel confident that answering is safe, confidential, and separate from immigration enforcement. It would suppress participation among immigrant families, including naturalized citizens and citizen children, and increase fear and confusion about how Census information will be used. That means less accurate data for apportionment, redistricting, and funding formulas, higher costs as the Bureau chases households that did not respond, and resources directed away from Black and Brown communities. Removing race and ethnicity questions would also take away data that federal law requires to protect civil rights. This data helps reveal discrimination in housing, jobs, and voting, and shows whether district lines split up or pack a community to weaken its vote. Without them, unfair treatment becomes much harder to prove and solve. Baneen Aljaberi [X] Dearborn, Michigan 48128

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Dear Director Cook,

Town of Wheatland Senior Center appreciates the opportunity to comment on the Census Bureau's proposed rule governing residence criteria and demographic questions for the 2030 decennial census. The census is the foundation for distributing political representation and federal resources. Accurate census ensures communities receive fair funding for infrastructure, housing, education, public safety, emergency response and other essential services. Because census data guide funding and planning decision for the next decade, accuracy is critical.  

We are concerned that several provisions of the proposed rule could reduce the accuracy of our community's population count and affect our access to federal and state resources. 

Concerns about the Proposed Changes 

Apportionment and population count: The proposed rule would limit the population counted toward apportionment to U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents for the first time. Although this change applies only to apportionment, it may create confusion or fear among residents and discourage participation. We request additional information on how full population data would be collected, reported and communicated, to ensure that all residents are counted for the broader data set. 

Legal-status question: The proposed rule also raises the possibility of adding a legal-status question to the census questionnaire. Similar proposals considered for the 2020 Census were not adopted following concerns that it could reduce participation, particularly among immigrant and mixed-status households. Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). 

As and educator, and I care about a fair and accurate census because census data and other federal datasets based on the census are used to make key decisions that affect our nation’s students, educators, and schools.  

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Examples of these uses include: . 

* Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. 

* Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

* Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

* Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

* Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

* Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

* Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

* Determining state higher education funding formulas 

* Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

* Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

* Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

First, to ensure a fair and accurate census,  the Census Bureau should  extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. Second, I oppose both the proposed changes to the residence criteria and the proposed regulations regarding demographic questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. The Census Bureau should  withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The Constitution requires  counting all people living in the United States. 

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (including children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count. 

Revise the tax records language so that those whose mailing address differs from their residential address (servicemembers, those with a post office box) are not excluded.  

• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for civil rights enforcement, among other uses, and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The prohibition, as written, may also restrict the collection or publication of census data on same-sex couples that was asked in 2020. 

 The proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Sincerely,
Ms. Grace Gutierrez
Buckeye, AZ

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. I oppose this proposed rule because it departs from that constitutional mandate, risking severe harm to my community. Excluding noncitizens from the population count used for congressional apportionment and federal funding, while adding a citizenship question designed to deter participation, will suppress response rates across immigrant communities and mixed-status families who fear being targeted. An undercount here would directly strip my community of appropriate congressional representation and our fair share of federal funding for essential safety-net programs like SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, CHIP, and Title I education grants. As someone who cares about fairness and the rule of law, I urge the Bureau to withdraw this proposal and count every person living in our communities, as the Constitution requires. 

I am also concerned that the proposed rule erases vital Census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Decades of demographic data serve as the baseline that public and private institutions rely on to identify inequalities and direct resources where they are needed most. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities.  

Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.  

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Sincerely,
Mary Kay Nicholson
Mountain View, MO

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). 

As and educator, and I care about a fair and accurate census because census data and other federal datasets based on the census are used to make key decisions that affect our nation’s students, educators, and schools.  

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Examples of these uses include: . 

* Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. 

* Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

* Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

* Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

* Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

* Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

* Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

* Determining state higher education funding formulas 

* Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

* Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

* Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

First, to ensure a fair and accurate census,  the Census Bureau should  extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. Second, I oppose both the proposed changes to the residence criteria and the proposed regulations regarding demographic questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. The Census Bureau should  withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The Constitution requires  counting all people living in the United States. 

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (including children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count. 

Revise the tax records language so that those whose mailing address differs from their residential address (servicemembers, those with a post office box) are not excluded.  

• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for civil rights enforcement, among other uses, and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The prohibition, as written, may also restrict the collection or publication of census data on same-sex couples that was asked in 2020. 

 The proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Sincerely,
Mr. A. Ramerman
Mountlake Terrace, WA

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. I oppose this proposed rule because it departs from that constitutional mandate, risking severe harm to my community. Excluding noncitizens from the population count used for congressional apportionment and federal funding, while adding a citizenship question designed to deter participation, will suppress response rates across immigrant communities and mixed-status families who fear being targeted. An undercount here would directly strip my community of appropriate congressional representation and our fair share of federal funding for essential safety-net programs like SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, CHIP, and Title I education grants. As someone who cares about fairness and the rule of law, I urge the Bureau to withdraw this proposal and count every person living in our communities, as the Constitution requires. 

I am also concerned that the proposed rule erases vital Census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Decades of demographic data serve as the baseline that public and private institutions rely on to identify inequalities and direct resources where they are needed most. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities.  

Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.  

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Sincerely,
Meredith Box
Aurora, CO

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I oppose the proposed rule and urge the Bureau to withdraw it. The Constitution calls for an "actual Enumeration" of the "whole number of persons in each State." The proposal would narrow who is counted and limit the questions that make census data useful. Both changes would make the count less accurate.

Residence criteria. The proposal would count only U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents for apportionment and would solicit comment on adding a legal-status question. The Constitution's text refers to persons, not citizens, and the Bureau has long counted every resident. Asking about legal status for the first time on the full-population form would likely depress response among immigrant households and mixed-status families, including their citizen children and relatives. The resulting undercount would fall hardest on communities already difficult to reach, and it would distort both congressional representation and the population-based formulas that distribute federal funds to states and counties. This could have consequences for public school funding. 
The proposal would also define "usual residence" by where a person lawfully spent the most days between January 3 and April 1, with administrative records as supporting evidence. This is a significant departure from current practice. It adds complexity and makes it hard for some people to fill out accurately.

Demographic questions. Barring questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation, and making most other demographic questions voluntary, would weaken the data that businesses, researchers, local governments, and civil rights enforcement depend on. Responses to census questions are currently mandatory under 13 U.S.C. § 221, and making them voluntary would reduce response rates and data quality. Race and ethnicity data are essential for enforcing the Voting Rights Act, drawing fair districts, and identifying disparities in health, education, and housing. Consistent, comparable data across decades is one of the census's greatest strengths, and this proposal would break that continuity.

For these reasons, I urge the Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and continue counting every person residing in the United States using the established, tested methods that produce the most complete count possible.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. I oppose this proposed rule because it departs from that constitutional mandate, risking severe harm to my community. Excluding noncitizens from the population count used for congressional apportionment and federal funding, while adding a citizenship question designed to deter participation, will suppress response rates across immigrant communities and mixed-status families who fear being targeted. An undercount here would directly strip my community of appropriate congressional representation and our fair share of federal funding for essential safety-net programs like SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, CHIP, and Title I education grants. As someone who cares about fairness and the rule of law, I urge the Bureau to withdraw this proposal and count every person living in our communities, as the Constitution requires. 

I am also concerned that the proposed rule erases vital Census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Decades of demographic data serve as the baseline that public and private institutions rely on to identify inequalities and direct resources where they are needed most. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities.  

Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.  

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Sincerely,
Jack Parker
San Luis Obispo, CA

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. I oppose this proposed rule because it departs from that constitutional mandate, risking severe harm to my community. Excluding noncitizens from the population count used for congressional apportionment and federal funding, while adding a citizenship question designed to deter participation, will suppress response rates across immigrant communities and mixed-status families who fear being targeted. An undercount here would directly strip my community of appropriate congressional representation and our fair share of federal funding for essential safety-net programs like SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, CHIP, and Title I education grants. As someone who cares about fairness and the rule of law, I urge the Bureau to withdraw this proposal and count every person living in our communities, as the Constitution requires. 

I am also concerned that the proposed rule erases vital Census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Decades of demographic data serve as the baseline that public and private institutions rely on to identify inequalities and direct resources where they are needed most. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities.  

Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.  

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Sincerely,
Jesse MacDonald
Brooklyn, NY

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). 

A fair and accurate census capturing U.S. Census Data used for other federal datasets based on the census are used to make key decisions that affect our nation’s students, educators, and schools.  

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Examples of these uses include: 

* Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. 

* Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

* Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

* Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

* Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

* Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

* Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

* Determining state higher education funding formulas 

* Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

* Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

* Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

First, to ensure a fair and accurate census,  the Census Bureau should  extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. Second, I oppose both the proposed changes to the residence criteria and the proposed regulations regarding demographic questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. The Census Bureau should  withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The Constitution requires  counting all people living in the United States. 

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (including children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count. 

Revise the tax records language so that those whose mailing address differs from their residential address (servicemembers, those with a post office box) are not excluded.  

• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for civil rights enforcement, among other uses, and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The prohibition, as written, may also restrict the collection or publication of census data on same-sex couples that was asked in 2020. 

 The proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Sincerely,
Ms. Michelle Santantonio
Bellport, NY

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Constitution requires our nation to undertake a census every 10 years to count all people living in the United States. The data collected by the decennial census determines the number of seats each state has in the U.S. House of Representatives and is used to distribute hundreds of billions of dollars in federal funds to local communities. I am commenting to urge that these proposed changed regulations not be implemented. Thank you for your time and attention.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
If anything in this country should be non-partisan, it is the count of people who live here.  Using the census for political purposes invalidates any results.

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). 

As and educator, and I care about a fair and accurate census because census data and other federal datasets based on the census are used to make key decisions that affect our nation’s students, educators, and schools.  

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Examples of these uses include: . 

* Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. 

* Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

* Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

* Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

* Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

* Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

* Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

* Determining state higher education funding formulas 

* Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

* Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

* Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

First, to ensure a fair and accurate census,  the Census Bureau should  extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. Second, I oppose both the proposed changes to the residence criteria and the proposed regulations regarding demographic questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. The Census Bureau should  withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The Constitution requires  counting all people living in the United States. 

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (including children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count. 

Revise the tax records language so that those whose mailing address differs from their residential address (servicemembers, those with a post office box) are not excluded.  

• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for civil rights enforcement, among other uses, and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The prohibition, as written, may also restrict the collection or publication of census data on same-sex couples that was asked in 2020. 

 The proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Sincerely,
Mr. John Duggan
Jacksonville, OR

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. I oppose this proposed rule because it departs from that constitutional mandate, risking severe harm to my community. Excluding noncitizens from the population count used for congressional apportionment and federal funding, while adding a citizenship question designed to deter participation, will suppress response rates across immigrant communities and mixed-status families who fear being targeted. An undercount here would directly strip my community of appropriate congressional representation and our fair share of federal funding for essential safety-net programs like SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, CHIP, and Title I education grants. As someone who cares about fairness and the rule of law, I urge the Bureau to withdraw this proposal and count every person living in our communities, as the Constitution requires.

This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities.  

Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.  

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). 

As and educator, and I care about a fair and accurate census because census data and other federal datasets based on the census are used to make key decisions that affect our nation’s students, educators, and schools.  

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Examples of these uses include: . 

* Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. 

* Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

* Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

* Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

* Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

* Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

* Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

* Determining state higher education funding formulas 

* Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

* Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

* Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

First, to ensure a fair and accurate census,  the Census Bureau should  extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. Second, I oppose both the proposed changes to the residence criteria and the proposed regulations regarding demographic questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. The Census Bureau should  withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The Constitution requires  counting all people living in the United States. 

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (including children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count. 

Revise the tax records language so that those whose mailing address differs from their residential address (servicemembers, those with a post office box) are not excluded.  

• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for civil rights enforcement, among other uses, and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The prohibition, as written, may also restrict the collection or publication of census data on same-sex couples that was asked in 2020. 

 The proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Sincerely,
Keith Kreger

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am Professor at the University of Puerto Rico and Director of the Center for Development Studies where we use Census data regularly. 
I write to oppose the proposed rule as drafted and to ask the Bureau to address its effects on Puerto Rico before finalizing it. The rule does not mention Puerto Rico or the territories. Yet Puerto Rico's count is taken under the same Title 13 authority, and Part 60's residence test and tax-record evidence standard would govern how the more than 3.2 million people living on the island are counted. That count sets Puerto Rico's base for federal formula funding.
Because many Puerto Rico residents do not file federal tax returns with the IRS, using federal tax records as the sole proof of residence will systematically undercount eligible working families, shrinking the database used to justify federal family-support allocations.
1. Direct Impact on Major Federal Healthcare and Assistance Programs:
Decennial census population and poverty counts form the foundational baseline for federal allocations, survey sample weights (PRCS), and administrative benchmarks that determine funding for Puerto Rico’s key safety-net programs. Undercounting Puerto Rico’s population or dropping unverified tax-record households will severely impact:
Healthcare (Medicare & Medicaid): Census population estimates dictate annual growth projections and statutory caps for Medicare baseline calculations and Medicaid block grants/FMAP distributions.
Nutrition Assistance: Federal funding allocations and caseload planning for the Nutrition Assistance Program (NAP) and WIC rely directly on census-derived poverty and child population benchmarks.

2. The tax-record evidence standard (§ 60.2(a)) does not fit Puerto Rico. The rule says residence "should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)." Bona fide residents of Puerto Rico generally file income tax with the Puerto Rico Department of Treasury (Hacienda), not the IRS, and are generally not required to file a federal return on Puerto Rico-source income. Employers issue Form 499R-2/W-2PR through Hacienda. The rule does not say whether Hacienda returns, W-2PRs, or other territorial records count as evidence.

3. Puerto Rico's addresses often cannot be matched to a dwelling. Address structure reports that about 40% of Puerto Rico addresses are "non-city style" (rural routes, post office boxes, physical descriptions), against well under 1% nationally. Tax and benefit records carry mailing addresses, which in Puerto Rico often differ from where people live. A records-based test will drop households or place them at the wrong block or municipio.
4. Puerto Rico's informal economy leaves many residents with no tax trace. Published estimates place roughly a third of Puerto Rico's labor market activity outside formal reporting. Informal workers, older adults, and households living on public transfers are the residents least likely to hold any tax record.
5. The publication limit (§ 70.3) threatens vital local data for small areas. Disaster recovery and municipal planning in Puerto Rico depend on detailed census tract and block data across all 78 municipios. Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Dear Director Cook,

an Individual appreciates the opportunity to comment on the Census Bureau's proposed rule governing residence criteria and demographic questions for the 2030 decennial census. The census is the foundation for distributing political representation and federal resources. Accurate census ensures communities receive fair funding for infrastructure, housing, education, public safety, emergency response and other essential services. Because census data guide funding and planning decision for the next decade, accuracy is critical.  

We are concerned that several provisions of the proposed rule could reduce the accuracy of our community's population count and affect our access to federal and state resources. 

Concerns about the Proposed Changes 

Apportionment and population count: The proposed rule would limit the population counted toward apportionment to U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents for the first time. Although this change applies only to apportionment, it may create confusion or fear among residents and discourage participation. We request additional information on how full population data would be collected, reported and communicated, to ensure that all residents are counted for the broader data set. 

Legal-status question: The proposed rule also raises the possibility of adding a legal-status question to the census questionnaire. Similar proposals considered for the 2020 Census were not adopted following concerns that it could reduce participation, particularly among immigrant and mixed-status households. Any decline in response rates would undermine the accuracy of our community's population count as a whole and could impact the resources available to young children and families specifically. 

Usual residence and the enumeration period: The proposed shift to counting residents based on where they spend the most time during a January 3-April 1 period, rather than their usual residence throughout the year, could affect our population count [of seasonal residents such as snowbirds/ students / part-time workers / other mobile populations]. We ask the Bureau to further evaluate the operational and data-accuracy impacts of this change and explain the rationale supporting it.  

Reliance on administrative records: Increased reliance on tax, immigration, health and other administrative records raises concerns about the potential undercount of populations in our community that may not be consistently represented in those records, including low-income households, college students, non-filers and children. We request additional information regarding when these records will be used and how the Bureau will ensure accurate counts for populations with less reliable administrative data.  

Demographic questions: The proposal would eliminate race and ethnicity questions, while making most other demographic questions optional. Accurate demographic data is essential to municipal planning and service delivery. Understanding who lives in our community gives local governments the ability to plan for our current population and take into consideration our future population's needs. [an Individual uses this data for...e.g., monitoring equitable service delivery, administering a specific program, public health planning, economic development targeting, etc]. The loss or reduction in the quality of this data could affect our ability to provide much needed services to our residents and accurately plan for our future.  

Funding impact: Census data inform funding for other programs including Community Development Block Grants (CDBG), transit formula funding, and Title I education funding. An undercount of any portion of our population reduces resources available to the entire community  not just the households or individuals who go uncounted. State funding allocations depend, in many cases, on accurate census data. While the Bureau distinguishes between apportionment and funding distribution, changes that discourage participation risk reducing the quality of data used for both purposes.  

We respectfully ask the Census Bureau to withdraw these proposed changes. Any changes to residence criteria, data collection methods or demographic questions must not compromise the accuracy of the population counts that an Individual and communities like ours rely on. 

We appreciate the opportunity to comment on this proposal and would welcome the chance to provide additional information or answer any questions the Bureau may have. 

Sincerely, 
Karen Redden
an US Citizen
