Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I teach in the MA in Constitutional Government, Civics and Law. One of my graduate students answered works incredible detail:
I respectfully submit this comment regarding the Census Bureau’s proposed residence criteria for the decennial census. I urge the Bureau not to adopt the proposed criteria insofar as they would exclude from the congressional apportionment population persons who actually reside in a state based on their citizenship or immigration status.
My concern is constitutional and historical. The proposed rule presents its interpretation as one that restores fidelity to the Constitution’s original understanding of “persons,” “inhabitants,” and “usual residence.” But the historical record surrounding both Article I, Section 2 and Section 2 of the Fourteenth Amendment points strongly in the opposite direction.
The Constitution’s history repeatedly distinguishes among persons, inhabitants, voters, and citizens. Most importantly, the historical record indicates that the people represented in Congress were understood to constitute a broader population than those entitled to participate politically.
I. The Founding-Era Understanding Was Representation Based on Inhabitants, Not Voters or Citizens
The original Constitution did not make citizenship or eligibility to vote the basis of congressional apportionment. Article I, Section 2 instead apportioned representatives according to numbers of “Persons.”
The distinction was understood at the Founding.
In Federalist No. 54, James Madison described what he called a “fundamental principle of the proposed Constitution”: the number of representatives allocated to each state was to be “founded on the aggregate number of inhabitants,” while the states could determine which portion of those inhabitants could actually vote.
Madison then made the distinction explicit. He observed that every state contained inhabitants who were denied the right of suffrage but nevertheless “will be included in the census by which the federal Constitution apportions the representatives.”
That is an important statement of the constitutional theory underlying apportionment. Representation was not limited to the electorate.
Madison further described nonvoting inhabitants as persons “not admitted to all the rights of citizens.” Nevertheless, they remained part of the population used to determine representation.
The Supreme Court recognized this history in Evenwel v. Abbott, 578 U.S. 54 (2016). Quoting Federalist No. 54, the Court explained that “the basis of representation in the House was to include all inhabitants” even though states could deny many of those inhabitants participation in selecting their representatives.
The constitutional text reinforces the distinction. Article I, Section 2 requires a member of the House to have been a citizen of the United States for seven years. Yet when the Constitution turns to determining how many representatives each state receives, it uses persons, not citizens.
The Framers therefore knew how to impose citizenship as a constitutional qualification when they intended to do so.
II. The Fourteenth Amendment Makes the Distinction Even Clearer
The history of the Fourteenth Amendment provides even more direct evidence because the Thirty-Ninth Congress specifically reconsidered the constitutional basis of representation after slavery was abolished.
The Thirteenth Amendment made the original Three-Fifths Compromise obsolete. Congress therefore had to determine how representation would work in a nation in which formerly enslaved persons were now free.
Congress considered alternatives that would have based representation upon citizens or voters.
It rejected them.
Representative Roscoe Conkling, a member of the Joint Committee on Reconstruction, explained the choice directly:
“‘Persons,’ and not ‘citizens,’ have always constituted the basis.”
Cong. Globe, 39th Cong., 1st Sess. 359 (1866).
This statement is especially significant because Conkling explained that his own original draft had actually used “citizens.” He nevertheless concluded that the appropriate word was “persons,” and the committee agreed.
Even more importantly for the present rulemaking, Conkling expressly discussed aliens while explaining that decision. He observed that “the number of aliens in some of the States is very large” and that states already held representation “in part by reason of their aliens.”
Thus, the distinction between persons and citizens was not merely theoretical. The committee understood that retaining persons meant retaining aliens in the population upon which representation was based.
Other members of the Thirty-Ninth Congress made the same point.
Representative John Bingham stated that “the entire immigrant population of this country is included in the basis of representation.” Cong. Globe, 39th Cong., 1st Sess. 432

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). 

As and educator, and I care about a fair and accurate census because census data and other federal datasets based on the census are used to make key decisions that affect our nation’s students, educators, and schools.  

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Examples of these uses include: . 

* Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. 

* Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

* Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

* Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

* Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

* Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

* Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

* Determining state higher education funding formulas 

* Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

* Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

* Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

First, to ensure a fair and accurate census,  the Census Bureau should  extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. Second, I oppose both the proposed changes to the residence criteria and the proposed regulations regarding demographic questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. The Census Bureau should  withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The Constitution requires  counting all people living in the United States. 

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (including children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count. 

Revise the tax records language so that those whose mailing address differs from their residential address (servicemembers, those with a post office box) are not excluded.  

• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for civil rights enforcement, among other uses, and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The prohibition, as written, may also restrict the collection or publication of census data on same-sex couples that was asked in 2020. 

 The proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Sincerely,
Mr. and Ms Joe And Fran Frain Aguirre
Denver, CO

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Re: Docket No. USBC-2026-0628, Proposed Residence Criteria and Demographic Question Restrictions for the 2030 Census

I oppose this proposed rule and ask the Census Bureau to withdraw it.

I live in McKinney, Collin County,TX. My community depends on census data for McKinneyIndependentSchool District, Baylor Hospital's Medicaid reimbursement, Collin County’s road and transit funding. These programs are vital to our community and need to be continued at optimum levels. 

The rule would stop counting millions of people who live here lawfully, including workers on visas, students, and people with temporary protected status or pending asylum claims, along with undocumented residents. The Fourteenth Amendment requires “counting the whole number of persons in each State.” Every census since 1790 has counted everyone who lives here, regardless of citizenship. The rule does not say whether the people it excludes will be counted for any purpose, or whether they will appear in the population totals that decide federal funding for my state. I ask the Bureau to answer that on the record. The Bureau’s own 2019 research found that asking about citizenship would cut responses from noncitizen households by 8 percent. This rule goes further than that question did, and it will keep families in my community, including citizen children, from answering at all.

The rule also removes race and ethnicity from the census for the first time since 1790. Every measure of whether this country treats its people equally starts with that count. We know how much shorter Black and Native American lives are, how much lower Black homeownership is, which neighborhoods banks have redlined, and which children the last census missed, because the census asks. Take the question away and the disparities do not end. They become impossible to prove, and impossible to fix. The Bureau’s own analysis, posted with this docket, admits there are “no other comparably accurate, comprehensive, and reliable sources” for this data. A government that stops counting harm by race is choosing not to see it, and the people it stops seeing are [name your community, if you choose].

The Bureau’s own analysis admits it “cannot quantify” any cost or benefit of this rule. A rule the agency cannot evaluate should not be adopted.

Robert S. Guy

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). 

As and educator, and I care about a fair and accurate census because census data and other federal datasets based on the census are used to make key decisions that affect our nation’s students, educators, and schools.  

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Examples of these uses include: . 

* Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. 

* Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

* Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

* Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

* Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

* Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

* Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

* Determining state higher education funding formulas 

* Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

* Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

* Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

First, to ensure a fair and accurate census,  the Census Bureau should  extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. Second, I oppose both the proposed changes to the residence criteria and the proposed regulations regarding demographic questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. The Census Bureau should  withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The Constitution requires  counting all people living in the United States. 

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (including children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count. 

Revise the tax records language so that those whose mailing address differs from their residential address (servicemembers, those with a post office box) are not excluded.  

• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for civil rights enforcement, among other uses, and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The prohibition, as written, may also restrict the collection or publication of census data on same-sex couples that was asked in 2020. 

 The proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Sincerely,
mx AJ cho
San Leandro, CA

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. I oppose this proposed rule because it departs from that constitutional mandate, risking severe harm to my community. Excluding noncitizens from the population count used for congressional apportionment and federal funding, while adding a citizenship question designed to deter participation, will suppress response rates across immigrant communities and mixed-status families who fear being targeted. An undercount here would directly strip my community of appropriate congressional representation and our fair share of federal funding for essential safety-net programs like SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, CHIP, and Title I education grants. As someone who cares about fairness and the rule of law, I urge the Bureau to withdraw this proposal and count every person living in our communities, as the Constitution requires. I am also concerned that the proposed rule erases vital Census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Decades of demographic data serve as the baseline that public and private institutions rely on to identify inequalities and direct resources where they are needed most. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities. Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). 

As and educator, and I care about a fair and accurate census because census data and other federal datasets based on the census are used to make key decisions that affect our nation’s students, educators, and schools.  

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Examples of these uses include: . 

* Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. 

* Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

* Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

* Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

* Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

* Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

* Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

* Determining state higher education funding formulas 

* Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

* Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

* Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

First, to ensure a fair and accurate census,  the Census Bureau should  extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. Second, I oppose both the proposed changes to the residence criteria and the proposed regulations regarding demographic questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. The Census Bureau should  withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The Constitution requires  counting all people living in the United States. 

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (including children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count. 

Revise the tax records language so that those whose mailing address differs from their residential address (servicemembers, those with a post office box) are not excluded.  

• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for civil rights enforcement, among other uses, and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The prohibition, as written, may also restrict the collection or publication of census data on same-sex couples that was asked in 2020. 

 The proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Sincerely,
Mr. Richard Hofman
Rockville, MD

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am work in public service in Washington, and I care about a fair and accurate census because the my agency uses the decennial counts in our work in environmental health.

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including:

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans. Thank you.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: 91 FR 57524  Public Comment,I am submitting this comment in opposition to the Census Bureau's proposed rule on residence criteria and demographic questions for the decennial census, 91 FR 57524 (Sept. 10, 2026). This proposed rule makes significant changes to the 2030 Census, including leaving noncitizens without green cards out of the count used to divide seats in Congress, removing race and ethnicity questions, and possibly adding a citizenship or immigration status question. The Census determines congressional representation and guides planning for health, education, housing, and infrastructure, along with the distribution of more than $2.8 trillion a year across roughly 350 federal programs. When communities are miscounted or left out in the decennial Census, they lose their fair share of representation and resources for an entire decade. This rule violates the Constitution and federal law, which both count the "whole number of persons" in each state, not just citizens. Congress chose "persons" over "citizens" on purpose, and counting only some residents revives the logic of the three-fifths clause. Changing who counts would require a constitutional amendment, not a census rule. The Supreme Court recognized in 2016 that representation serves all residents, including children and noncitizens, not only voters. Under this rule, millions of people who live, work, pay taxes, and raise families here would no longer count, weakening the voting power of the communities they belong to, including the citizens who live alongside them. A citizenship question would make this worse. The success of the Census depends on public trust. Every person must feel confident that answering is safe, confidential, and separate from immigration enforcement. It would suppress participation among immigrant families, including naturalized citizens and citizen children, and increase fear and confusion about how Census information will be used. That means less accurate data for apportionment, redistricting, and funding formulas, higher costs as the Bureau chases households that did not respond, and resources directed away from Black and Brown communities. Removing race and ethnicity questions would also take away data that federal law requires to protect civil rights. This data helps reveal discrimination in housing, jobs, and voting, and shows whether district lines split up or pack a community to weaken its vote. Without them, unfair treatment becomes much harder to prove and solve. Lena Mansour Poles[x]Farmington Hills , Michigan 48331

To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am a long-term voter and taxpayer, and I care about a fair and accurate census because it is what makes our country great.

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026, is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Dear Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions,

Subject: Re: Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions (Docket No. 260903-0005; RIN 0607-AA75) 

I strongly oppose the proposed rules for the census and changes to its residence rule. All persons in the United States have a right to be counted, as the 14th Amendment of the Constitution plainly establishes. This proposed rule will weaken our democracy, our systems of representation, and the doctrine of “one person, one vote.” Without an accurate count, people will not be fairly represented in Congress or state legislatures. 

By generating inaccurate and unreliable data, this change would also make it harder for my state and local officials to properly plan for the services we need and the emergencies we may face. Furthermore, the exclusion of questions about race and ethnicity will exacerbate the degradation of data quality, and it will lead to undercounts of Black and brown communities that are already undercounted in past censuses. If we don't know who is living in our communities, we cannot prepare for the challenges we may face, and we will not receive adequate funds from federal programs. 

Additionally, the lack of transparency and sufficient opportunity for the public to comment on this incredibly consequential rule is concerning. I urge you to both extend the comment period to a full 90 days until December 9th, and to reject this proposed rule. 


Christina Roe,
[X]
Fresno
CA



Sincerely,
Ms. Christina Roe

Thank you.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. I oppose this proposed rule because it departs from that constitutional mandate, risking severe harm to my community. Excluding noncitizens from the population count used for congressional apportionment and federal funding, while adding a citizenship question designed to deter participation, will suppress response rates across immigrant communities and mixed-status families who fear being targeted. An undercount here would directly strip my community of appropriate congressional representation and our fair share of federal funding for essential safety-net programs like SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, CHIP, and Title I education grants. As someone who cares about fairness and the rule of law, I urge the Bureau to withdraw this proposal and count every person living in our communities, as the Constitution requires. 

I am also concerned that the proposed rule erases vital Census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Decades of demographic data serve as the baseline that public and private institutions rely on to identify inequalities and direct resources where they are needed most. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities.  

Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.  

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Sincerely,
Raymond Mihm
Waynesboro, PA

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
My name is [Your Name] and I am your constituent from [City/Zip Code]. As Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander (AANHPI) Heritage Month comes to a close, I write to urge you to support AANHPI students by cosponsoring the All Students Count Act.

To the U.S. Census Bureau: 

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule titled “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005). Eliminating the collection of race and ethnic data, prohibiting the collection of sexual orientation, and leaving non-citizens out of the apportionment would significantly harm the Southeast Asian American (SEAA) and broader Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander (AANHPI) communities. I respectfully request that the Census Bureau withdraw the proposed rule and extend the comment period to December 10, 2026. 

This proposed rule would significantly harm the SEAA and AANHPI communities. The AANHPI community is not a homogenous population; it encompasses over 50 different ethnic groups and 100 languages and dialects. There are vast socioeconomic disparities within the AANHPI population, often related to their migratory and historical experience. SEAAs, such as the Cambodian, Hmong, Laotian, and Mien populations, often have higher rates of poverty and lower educational attainment rates than both the broader AANHPI and American populations. 

For SEAAs, this disparity is generally tied to their experiences escaping their countries of origin and resettlement in the United States after the Vietnam War, Secret War in Laos, and Khmer Rouge genocide in Cambodia. For example, because of the 2020 Census, we now know that the Mien population has lower educational attainment rates compared to the general American and AANHPI populations. Additionally, the data also show that Mien men have a lower educational attainment rate compared to women. Such information could only be obtained because of the census, which is the primary source for data collection and reporting of small ethnic groups. These data cannot be replicated by other surveys, including the American Community Survey. 

Accurate data, reflective of race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation, help our elected officials properly identify and address the unique needs and challenges of our communities. Prohibiting the collection of this demographic data would prevent our government officials from passing informed public policy; hamper the ability of community-based organizations to demonstrate data narratives for fundraising purposes; and inhibit the ability of students and academics studying our communities from accessing the most robust source of information on SEAAs and the broader AANHPI community. 

Thank you for taking my comment into consideration. I reiterate my request that the US Census Bureau withdraws the proposed rule; preserves the collection of race and ethnic data; and keeps its commitment to count everyone once, only once, and in the right place.

I also ask the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. Changes of this scope deserve more time for the public to review and respond.

Sincerely,
Jacinda Tran
Brooklyn, NY 11225

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: 91 FR 57524  Public Comment,I am submitting this comment in opposition to the Census Bureau's proposed rule on residence criteria and demographic questions for the decennial census, 91 FR 57524 (Sept. 10, 2026). This proposed rule makes significant changes to the 2030 Census, including leaving noncitizens without green cards out of the count used to divide seats in Congress, removing race and ethnicity questions, and possibly adding a citizenship or immigration status question. The Census determines congressional representation and guides planning for health, education, housing, and infrastructure, along with the distribution of more than $2.8 trillion a year across roughly 350 federal programs. When communities are miscounted or left out in the decennial Census, they lose their fair share of representation and resources for an entire decade. This rule violates the Constitution and federal law, which both count the "whole number of persons" in each state, not just citizens. Congress chose "persons" over "citizens" on purpose, and counting only some residents revives the logic of the three-fifths clause. Changing who counts would require a constitutional amendment, not a census rule. The Supreme Court recognized in 2016 that representation serves all residents, including children and noncitizens, not only voters. Under this rule, millions of people who live, work, pay taxes, and raise families here would no longer count, weakening the voting power of the communities they belong to, including the citizens who live alongside them. A citizenship question would make this worse. The success of the Census depends on public trust. Every person must feel confident that answering is safe, confidential, and separate from immigration enforcement. It would suppress participation among immigrant families, including naturalized citizens and citizen children, and increase fear and confusion about how Census information will be used. That means less accurate data for apportionment, redistricting, and funding formulas, higher costs as the Bureau chases households that did not respond, and resources directed away from Black and Brown communities. Removing race and ethnicity questions would also take away data that federal law requires to protect civil rights. This data helps reveal discrimination in housing, jobs, and voting, and shows whether district lines split up or pack a community to weaken its vote. Without them, unfair treatment becomes much harder to prove and solve. Tanya [X]Des Plaines, Illinois 60016

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am a local government employee that calls North Carolina home. I care about a fair and accurate census because it impacts both my work and I believe an equitable, fair census is key to our democracy, especially as this affects Congressional apportionment. I also am someone whose mailing address and physical address does not match, through no fault of my own, as I live in a more rural area. Many parts of this regulation seem meant to obfuscate while not coming to terms with the practical implications arising from this and how to resolve them, like these address mismatches. 

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people, per the United States Constitution.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am a molecular biologist, and an immigrant with naturalized citizen status that lives in Rhode Island. I care about a fair and accurate census because I think all people living in US should be counted accurately and without discrimination.

I ask the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026.

I oppose both parts 60 and 70 and urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including:

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.

• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.

• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.

• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.

• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.

• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census. The proposal would fundamentally alter the census in ways that are unprecedented in modern history, undermine the constitutional principle of counting all persons, and jeopardize the accuracy and usefulness of the nation's most important source of population data. 

For more than two centuries, the Census Bureau has operated under the principle of counting every person once, only once, and in the right place. I strongly oppose the proposal to exclude broad categories of residents from the apportionment count, including international students, refugees, asylum seekers, visa holders, and other individuals who live, work, and contribute to communities across the country. Excluding residents from the census would create an intentional undercount and depart from longstanding census practice and understanding of the Constitution's enumeration requirement. 

An accurate census is critical to all levels of government. Census data informs representation, funding sources, school planning, transportation investments, emergency preparedness, housing policy, public health programs, and countless other decisions that affect our communities. 

I also oppose the inclusion of a citizenship or immigration status question. Such a question has not been adequately tested and risks reducing participation and public trust in the census. Major methodological changes to the decennial census should only occur after extensive research, testing, and evaluation. The proposal includes numerous significant changes, including new residence criteria, increased reliance on administrative records, and the potential addition of citizenship-related questions, none of which have undergone the level of testing traditionally required for the census. 

I further oppose the proposal to eliminate race and ethnicity questions from the decennial census. Race and ethnicity data are essential for understanding community needs, enforcing civil rights protections, identifying disparities, targeting services, and evaluating whether programs are reaching underserved populations. Removing these questions would diminish the nation's ability to understand demographic change and address inequities. 

The Framers established the census to count the population for representation, and for nearly 250 years the nation has worked to improve the accuracy and completeness of that count. This proposal moves in the opposite direction by excluding residents who have long been counted, reducing critical demographic data, and advancing changes that have not been substantially tested.

I respectfully urge the Census Bureau to preserve the longstanding commitment to counting everyone once, only once, and in the right place, and to reject the proposed changes.

The Census proposes to only include people if their address is confirmed by tax records -- which could mean millions, particularly low-income families, could be missed in the decennial Census. Overall, this would leave out people who actually live in our community, including many people who are lawfully present in the United States.For all past Census counts, including the 2020 Census, foreign citizens living in the United States were generally counted where they lived and slept most of the time. That approach recognizes the basic purpose of a Census: accurately counting the people who live in our communities. The 14th Amendment requires congressional representation to be apportioned according to the “whole number of persons in each State.”I am also deeply concerned by the proposal to prohibit race and ethnicity questions, along with sexual orientation, on the decennial Census enumeration questionnaire. The Census Bureau itself recognizes the importance of race data for civil rights protections, legislative redistricting, equal employment opportunities, and identifying disparities.The 2030 Census will determine congressional, state, and local representation for the decade that follows. It must be complete, accurate, and protected from political manipulation.Please withdraw this proposed rule and preserve a Census that fairly and accurately counts our community.Claire  [X] Burien, Washington 98166

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. I oppose this proposed rule because it departs from that constitutional mandate, risking severe harm to my community. Excluding noncitizens from the population count used for congressional apportionment and federal funding, while adding a citizenship question designed to deter participation, will suppress response rates across immigrant communities and mixed-status families who fear being targeted. An undercount here would directly strip my community of appropriate congressional representation and our fair share of federal funding for essential safety-net programs like SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, CHIP, and Title I education grants. As someone who cares about fairness and the rule of law, I urge the Bureau to withdraw this proposal and count every person living in our communities, as the Constitution requires. 

I am also concerned that the proposed rule erases vital Census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Decades of demographic data serve as the baseline that public and private institutions rely on to identify inequalities and direct resources where they are needed most. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities.  

Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.  

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Sincerely,
Elizabeth Watts
Boynton Beach, FL

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). 

As and educator, and I care about a fair and accurate census because census data and other federal datasets based on the census are used to make key decisions that affect our nation’s students, educators, and schools.  

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Examples of these uses include: . 

* Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. 

* Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

* Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

* Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

* Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

* Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

* Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

* Determining state higher education funding formulas 

* Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

* Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

* Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

First, to ensure a fair and accurate census,  the Census Bureau should  extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. Second, I oppose both the proposed changes to the residence criteria and the proposed regulations regarding demographic questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. The Census Bureau should  withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The Constitution requires  counting all people living in the United States. 

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (including children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count. 

Revise the tax records language so that those whose mailing address differs from their residential address (servicemembers, those with a post office box) are not excluded.  

• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for civil rights enforcement, among other uses, and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The prohibition, as written, may also restrict the collection or publication of census data on same-sex couples that was asked in 2020. 

 The proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Sincerely,
Dr. Kerri McGoldrick
Castro Valley, CA

To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am a retired educator and I care about a fair and accurate census because it is vital that we have accurate data for critical planning for many aspects of our civic life, including education.

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 
• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.
As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Census Bureaus proposed rule to strengthen the decennial census is critical to ensuring fair representation and protecting the future of America.

The census should not rely on distorted or overly generalized demographic categories that obscure the true purpose of the count. Data should be collected and reported in a way that supports the Constitutions mandate: an accurate count of the people residing in the United States.

Additionally, individuals who are unlawfully present, as well as other non-legal permanent residents, should not be included when congressional seats are apportioned. These changes would strengthen the censuss core purpose of achieving an accurate count of Americans, and they have my full support.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Docket No. 260903-0005 / RIN 0607-AA75  
FDMS Docket No. USBC-2026-0628

I oppose substantial portions of the proposed rule governing residence criteria and demographic questions for the decennial census. I submit this in my personal capacity as a rural Missouri resident, small-business owner working with healthcare and EMS agencies, and local public-service board member. Please consider my attached Supplemental Comment and Technical/Legal Basis as part of this submission.

My concern is not partisan. In my work, population figures and demographic denominators are not abstract statistics; they inform needs assessments, grant opportunities, service-area planning, workforce decisions, and decisions about where limited resources should be directed. I want the Census to produce the most accurate, stable, and useful population data possible.

1. Apportionment and legal status. Proposed Sec. 60.4 would count foreign citizens who are also U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents while excluding all other foreign citizens from apportionment. The Fourteenth Amendment directs apportionment according to the "whole number of persons in each State" and uses "citizens" elsewhere when citizenship is intended. I recognize that "in each State" requires a residence rule, but the Bureau should explain why a person actually residing in a State can be excluded solely because the person's status is neither citizenship nor lawful permanent residence. Franklin v. Massachusetts involved federal personnel physically overseas who retained enduring ties to a State; it did not decide this different question.

The Bureau asks whether other legal statuses are materially similar to lawful permanent residence. My primary objection precedes that inquiry: the Bureau has not adequately established that apportionment should turn on whether an immigration classification is sufficiently LPR-like. I therefore do not endorse additional status-based lines unless the Bureau first establishes their legal basis, operational accuracy, and representational consequences.

2. Residence methodology. Proposed Sec. 60.2 would replace the familiar "lives and sleeps most of the time" principle with a January 3-April 1 period, count as little as one hour of lawful presence at a residence as a day, permit the same day to count at multiple residences, and state that residence should be consistent with and evidenced by tax records. Before adopting this method, the Bureau should publish validation comparing it with the existing approach, including coverage, duplication, geolocation, and record-linkage error and procedures for conflicting, stale, or incomplete records.

3. Legal-status question. The Bureau also asks whether a legal-status question should be included on the short-form decennial questionnaire. I oppose adding such a question on the present record. Before considering it, the Bureau should demonstrate necessity and test effects on item and unit nonresponse, proxy response, differential response, record linkage, and overall coverage.

4. Race, ethnicity, and trade-offs. I oppose proposed Part 70's categorical prohibition on race and ethnicity questions on questionnaires used for the decennial enumeration. I recognize legitimate interests in reducing respondent burden, disclosure risk, and operational cost, and that ACS and administrative sources would remain available. But those sources do not necessarily preserve a decennial benchmark. The Bureau's own impact analysis identifies potential deterioration in ACS and other federal estimates without updated decennial race and ethnicity counts.

The Bureau seeks comment on respondent-burden reduction estimates. I do not have an empirical basis for a reliable numerical estimate and do not believe one should be invented. The final analysis should quantify the expected burden and response-rate improvement and compare those benefits with the statistical cost of losing the benchmark. A better alternative to a categorical prohibition is to preserve the Bureau's authority to determine, based on testing, legal requirements, statistical need, privacy protections, and future conditions, which demographic questions are warranted for each census.

I urge the Bureau to withdraw or substantially revise proposed Parts 60 and 70, publish the empirical testing, error analysis, alternatives analysis, and downstream-impact analysis supporting any final changes, and extend the comment period through December 10, 2026. The decennial Census is too consequential to redesign on assumptions that have not been adequately demonstrated in the rulemaking record.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). 

As and educator, and I care about a fair and accurate census because census data and other federal datasets based on the census are used to make key decisions that affect our nation’s students, educators, and schools.  

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Examples of these uses include: . 

* Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. 

* Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

* Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

* Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

* Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

* Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

* Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

* Determining state higher education funding formulas 

* Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

* Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

* Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

First, to ensure a fair and accurate census,  the Census Bureau should  extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. Second, I oppose both the proposed changes to the residence criteria and the proposed regulations regarding demographic questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. The Census Bureau should  withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The Constitution requires  counting all people living in the United States. 

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (including children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count. 

Revise the tax records language so that those whose mailing address differs from their residential address (servicemembers, those with a post office box) are not excluded.  

• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for civil rights enforcement, among other uses, and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The prohibition, as written, may also restrict the collection or publication of census data on same-sex couples that was asked in 2020. 

 The proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Sincerely,
Ms. Jennifer McGrath
Pawtucket, RI

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Re: Docket No. USBC-2026-0628, Proposed Residence Criteria and Demographic Question Restrictions for the 2030 Census

I oppose this proposed rule and ask the Census Bureau to withdraw it.

I live in Grosse Pointe, Wayne county, Michigan. My community depends on census data for our hospitals Medicaid reimbursements. This is vitally important for our neighbors, old and young, to access affordable and life saving healthcare. 

The rule would stop counting millions of people who live here lawfully, including workers on visas, students, and people with temporary protected status or pending asylum claims, along with undocumented residents. The Fourteenth Amendment requires “counting the whole number of persons in each State.” Every census since 1790 has counted everyone who lives here, regardless of citizenship. The rule does not say whether the people it excludes will be counted for any purpose, or whether they will appear in the population totals that decide federal funding for my state. I ask the Bureau to answer that on the record. The Bureau’s own 2019 research found that asking about citizenship would cut responses from noncitizen households by 8 percent. This rule goes further than that question did, and it will keep families in my community, including citizen children, from answering at all.

The rule also removes race and ethnicity from the census for the first time since 1790. Every measure of whether this country treats its people equally starts with that count. We know how much shorter Black and Native American lives are, how much lower Black homeownership is, which neighborhoods banks have redlined, and which children the last census missed, because the census asks. Take the question away and the disparities do not end. They become impossible to prove, and impossible to fix. The Bureau’s own analysis, posted with this docket, admits there are “no other comparably accurate, comprehensive, and reliable sources” for this data. A government that stops counting harm by race is choosing not to see it, and the people it stops seeing are in Wayne County, Michigan. 

The Bureau’s own analysis admits it “cannot quantify” any cost or benefit of this rule. A rule the agency cannot evaluate should not be adopted. Respect humanity!

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. I oppose this proposed rule because it departs from that constitutional mandate, risking severe harm to my community. Excluding noncitizens from the population count used for congressional apportionment and federal funding, while adding a citizenship question designed to deter participation, will suppress response rates across immigrant communities and mixed-status families who fear being targeted. An undercount here would directly strip my community of appropriate congressional representation and our fair share of federal funding for essential safety-net programs like SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, CHIP, and Title I education grants. As someone who cares about fairness and the rule of law, I urge the Bureau to withdraw this proposal and count every person living in our communities, as the Constitution requires. 

I am also concerned that the proposed rule erases vital Census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Decades of demographic data serve as the baseline that public and private institutions rely on to identify inequalities and direct resources where they are needed most. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities.  

Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.  

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Sincerely,
J. Huston
Crockett, CA

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the Department of Commerce: 

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). 

I am a teacher, a veteran of the US Navy, and I live in Ohio, and I care about a fair and accurate census because census data and other federal datasets based on the census are used to make key decisions that affect our nation's students, educators, and schools.  

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. 

Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. 

Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

Determining state higher education funding formulas 

Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

First, to ensure a fair and accurate census, the Census Bureau should  extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. Second, I oppose both the proposed changes to the residence criteria and the proposed regulations regarding demographic questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. The Census Bureau should  withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions. 

Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The Constitution requires  counting all people living in the United States. 
Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (including children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count. 
Revise the tax records language so that those whose mailing address differs from their residential address (servicemembers, those with a post office box) are not excluded.  
Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for civil rights enforcement, among other uses, and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The prohibition, as written, may also restrict the collection or publication of census data on same-sex couples that was asked in 2020. 
 The proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans. 

Sincerely,
(Form signed below)
