Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census. These changes will not only weaken the accuracy and integrity of our nation's most important population count, but they will also harm our communities, and I strongly urge the Bureau to reject them. 

First, removing questions of race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation erases the full scope of my identity when I participate in the Census survey. These data points are not optional. They are the tools we use to enforce civil rights laws, monitor discrimination, and measure the disparities that still affect millions of people. Excluding them from the count does not make them disappear from our society, but it does make our government less equipped to handle big issues when they arise. 

The Constitution is clear: the census must count ALL persons living in the United States, regardless of their immigration or citizenship status. The proposal to exclude non-citizens, including those residents with some type of lawful status, violates more than two centuries of legal precedent. Every person counted in this country contributes to our communities, and every person deserves to be fully seen. 

The consequences of these changes will negatively impact our daily lives. The census affects everything. It determines political representation and the drawing of voting districts. It guides how billions of dollars in federal funding are used to close persistent disparities in schools, hospitals, and other government programs that are designed to improve our lives.  

The census is the foundation of our democracy. It must reflect the complete yet nuanced reality of who we are as a nation. And it must reflect the lives of our friends and neighbors who may not look, think, or speak like we do. I ask the Bureau to withdraw these proposed changes and to preserve a count that includes everyone and represents everyone. 

Thank you for considering my comment.

Sincerely,
Rachel Boyd

I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census. These changes will not only weaken the accuracy and integrity of our nation's most important population count, but they will also harm our communities, and I strongly urge the Bureau to reject them. 

First, removing questions of race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation erases the full scope of my identity when I participate in the Census survey. These data points are not optional. They are the tools we use to enforce civil rights laws, monitor discrimination, and measure the disparities that still affect millions of people. Excluding them from the count does not make them disappear from our society, but it does make our government less equipped to handle big issues when they arise. 

The Constitution is clear: the census must count ALL persons living in the United States, regardless of their immigration or citizenship status. The proposal to exclude non-citizens, including those residents with some type of lawful status, violates more than two centuries of legal precedent. Every person counted in this country contributes to our communities, and every person deserves to be fully seen. 

The consequences of these changes will negatively impact our daily lives. The census affects everything. It determines political representation and the drawing of voting districts. It guides how billions of dollars in federal funding are used to close persistent disparities in schools, hospitals, and other government programs that are designed to improve our lives.  

The census is the foundation of our democracy. It must reflect the complete yet nuanced reality of who we are as a nation. And it must reflect the lives of our friends and neighbors who may not look, think, or speak like we do. I ask the Bureau to withdraw these proposed changes and to preserve a count that includes everyone and represents everyone. 

Thank you for considering my comment.

Sincerely,
karen casavnt

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Dear Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions,

Subject: Re: Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions (Docket No. 260903-0005; RIN 0607-AA75) 

I strongly oppose the proposed rules for the census and changes to its residence rule. Additionally, the lack of transparency and sufficient opportunity for the public to comment on this incredibly consequential rule is concerning. I urge you to both extend the comment period to a full 90 days until December 9th, and to reject this proposed rule. 
I am asking for this new rule regarding the census be withdrawn.  If the rule is implemented it will result in significantly skewed and incorrect data.  It will affect countless state and local activities which rely on accurate census data.

I oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census because a fair and accurate census is critical to ensuring every community is counted, fairly represented, and able to get the resources people need to live healthy lives — including sexual and reproductive healthcare. An inaccurate or incomplete census can deepen existing inequities, particularly for communities that already face disenfranchisement and barriers to healthcare.

When communities are undercounted or excluded, they risk losing both resources and political representation. 

The Census Bureau and Department of Commerce must:

1. Count all people residing in the United States in the 2030 Census, without regard to immigration status. Excluding noncitizens from census apportionment data violates the Constitution and established legal precedent. It would suppress the count of many communities, effectively erasing them from critical datasets and depriving them of resources and congressional representation –— including resources and political representation that support access to healthcare.

2. Continue collecting race and ethnicity data and implement the 2024 OMB SPD 15 standards. Census race and ethnicity data are essential for important research across many sectors, for upholding civil rights, and for growing the economy. Extensive Census Bureau research and engagement with expert stakeholders shows that implementing the modernized 2024 OMB SPD 15 standards for race and ethnicity data collection will yield data that more accurately represent the nation’s increasingly diverse population.

3. Remove the clause banning the addition of future questions on sexual orientation. Proposed changes to demographic items should be based on research and guided by a deliberative and transparent process, including extensive stakeholder consultation.

4. Withdraw other proposed changes to residence criteria, including tying place of residence to tax records and "lawful residence," and the adoption of a three month enumeration period. The Census Bureau must extensively research and consult with stakeholders about the potential effects of such changes before proposing their implementation in a decennial census.

5. Halt the practice of prison gerrymandering by counting incarcerated individuals in their home communities. This will yield more accurate census data and ensure that communities receive the congressional representation to which they are entitled.

Comment: 91 FR 57524  Public Comment,Re: Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions (Docket No. USBC-2026-0628).I am writing to oppose the Census Bureau's proposed rule, "Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions," Docket No. USBC-2026-0628, because it would produce an inaccurate count of the people living in this country.Every ten years, the census gives the country one reliable picture of who lives here. Congress, states, cities, and businesses use it to divide representation, distribute federal funds, and plan for the next decade. This rule would distort that picture. Fewer people would be counted, and some communities would disappear from the data altogether. The errors would affect the entire country, but they would be heaviest in immigrant, minority, and low-income households and in the states and towns where they live.The undercount would come from several directions. The rule would stop counting many immigrants who live here, even though the Constitution requires counting every person. It also invites a question about legal status, which would keep many people in immigrant and mixed-status households from answering at all, whatever their own status. And it would decide where people live using tax records, even though many people are not required to file and the rule says nothing about how to count people such as those without stable housing, foster children, or people in shelters and nursing homes.The invisibility would come from banning the race and ethnicity question and from households afraid to respond. Without that information, it is much harder to show where needs are greatest, enforce civil rights laws, check whether voting maps are fair, or catch health problems that hit some communities harder. States, local governments, and health systems would have to collect it themselves, adding cost and producing less reliable numbers.This is a poor use of public money. More than $2.8 trillion a year in federal funding follows census numbers. When the count is wrong, that money goes to the wrong places for at least ten years, and schools, clinics, roads, and emergency plans are built for a population that does not match reality. Lower response rates also mean more costly follow-up work, paid for by taxpayers.A bad count in 2030 cannot be corrected until at least 2040. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw this rule.Robert [x]

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
My name is [Your Name] and I am your constituent from [City/Zip Code]. As Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander (AANHPI) Heritage Month comes to a close, I write to urge you to support AANHPI students by cosponsoring the All Students Count Act.

To the U.S. Census Bureau: 

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule titled “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005). Eliminating the collection of race and ethnic data, prohibiting the collection of sexual orientation, and leaving non-citizens out of the apportionment would significantly harm the Southeast Asian American (SEAA) and broader Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander (AANHPI) communities. I respectfully request that the Census Bureau withdraw the proposed rule and extend the comment period to December 10, 2026. 

This proposed rule would significantly harm the SEAA and AANHPI communities. The AANHPI community is not a homogenous population; it encompasses over 50 different ethnic groups and 100 languages and dialects. There are vast socioeconomic disparities within the AANHPI population, often related to their migratory and historical experience. SEAAs, such as the Cambodian, Hmong, Laotian, and Mien populations, often have higher rates of poverty and lower educational attainment rates than both the broader AANHPI and American populations. 

For SEAAs, this disparity is generally tied to their experiences escaping their countries of origin and resettlement in the United States after the Vietnam War, Secret War in Laos, and Khmer Rouge genocide in Cambodia. For example, because of the 2020 Census, we now know that the Mien population has lower educational attainment rates compared to the general American and AANHPI populations. Additionally, the data also show that Mien men have a lower educational attainment rate compared to women. Such information could only be obtained because of the census, which is the primary source for data collection and reporting of small ethnic groups. These data cannot be replicated by other surveys, including the American Community Survey. 

Accurate data, reflective of race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation, help our elected officials properly identify and address the unique needs and challenges of our communities. Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census. These changes will not only weaken the accuracy and integrity of our nation's most important population count, but they will also harm our communities, and I strongly urge the Bureau to reject them. 

First, removing questions of race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation erases the full scope of my identity when I participate in the Census survey. These data points are not optional. Excluding them from the count does not make them disappear from our society, but it does make our government less equipped to handle big issues when they arise. 

The Constitution is clear: the census must count ALL persons living in the United States, regardless of their immigration or citizenship status. The proposal to exclude non-citizens, including those residents with some type of lawful status, violates more than two centuries of legal precedent. Every person counted in this country contributes to our communities, and every person deserves to be fully seen. 

The consequences of these changes will negatively impact our daily lives. The census affects everything. It determines political representation and the drawing of voting districts. It guides how billions of dollars in federal funding are used to close persistent disparities in schools, hospitals, and other government programs that are designed to improve our lives.  

The census is the foundation of our democracy. It must reflect the complete yet nuanced reality of who we are as a nation. And it must reflect the lives of our friends and neighbors who may not look, think, or speak like we do. I ask the Bureau to withdraw these proposed changes and to preserve a count that includes everyone and represents everyone. 

Thank you for considering my comment.

Sincerely,
Eric Lamar HENRY

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).
I am a public health analyst that lives in Missouri and works in Kansas, and I care about a fair and accurate census because an accurate count of our population helps people who work in public health better serve communities in need. We rely on Census data to identify public health issues in our communities and accurate data helps us to better use resources to develop plans to address those issues.
First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.
Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including:
• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.
As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: 91 FR 57524  Public Comment,I am submitting this comment in opposition to the Census Bureau's proposed rule on residence criteria and demographic questions for the decennial census, 91 FR 57524 (Sept. 10, 2026). This proposed rule makes significant changes to the 2030 Census, including leaving noncitizens without green cards out of the count used to divide seats in Congress, removing race and ethnicity questions, and possibly adding a citizenship or immigration status question. The Census determines congressional representation and guides planning for health, education, housing, and infrastructure, along with the distribution of more than $2.8 trillion a year across roughly 350 federal programs. When communities are miscounted or left out in the decennial Census, they lose their fair share of representation and resources for an entire decade. This rule violates the Constitution and federal law, which both count the "whole number of persons" in each state, not just citizens. Congress chose "persons" over "citizens" on purpose, and counting only some residents revives the logic of the three-fifths clause. Changing who counts would require a constitutional amendment, not a census rule. The Supreme Court recognized in 2016 that representation serves all residents, including children and noncitizens, not only voters. Under this rule, millions of people who live, work, pay taxes, and raise families here would no longer count, weakening the voting power of the communities they belong to, including the citizens who live alongside them. A citizenship question would make this worse. The success of the Census depends on public trust. Every person must feel confident that answering is safe, confidential, and separate from immigration enforcement. It would suppress participation among immigrant families, including naturalized citizens and citizen children, and increase fear and confusion about how Census information will be used. That means less accurate data for apportionment, redistricting, and funding formulas, higher costs as the Bureau chases households that did not respond, and resources directed away from Black and Brown communities. Removing race and ethnicity questions would also take away data that federal law requires to protect civil rights. This data helps reveal discrimination in housing, jobs, and voting, and shows whether district lines split up or pack a community to weaken its vote. Without them, unfair treatment becomes much harder to prove and solve. Da [X]West Bloomfield, Michigan 48324-2108

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: 91 FR 57524  Public Comment,Re: Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions (Docket No. USBC-2026-0628).I am writing to oppose the Census Bureau's proposed rule, "Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions," Docket No. USBC-2026-0628, because it would produce an inaccurate count of the people living in this country.Every ten years, the census gives the country one reliable picture of who lives here. Congress, states, cities, and businesses use it to divide representation, distribute federal funds, and plan for the next decade. This rule would distort that picture. Fewer people would be counted, and some communities would disappear from the data altogether. The errors would affect the entire country, but they would be heaviest in immigrant, minority, and low-income households and in the states and towns where they live.The undercount would come from several directions. The rule would stop counting many immigrants who live here, even though the Constitution requires counting every person. It also invites a question about legal status, which would keep many people in immigrant and mixed-status households from answering at all, whatever their own status. And it would decide where people live using tax records, even though many people are not required to file and the rule says nothing about how to count people such as those without stable housing, foster children, or people in shelters and nursing homes.The invisibility would come from banning the race and ethnicity question and from households afraid to respond. Without that information, it is much harder to show where needs are greatest, enforce civil rights laws, check whether voting maps are fair, or catch health problems that hit some communities harder. States, local governments, and health systems would have to collect it themselves, adding cost and producing less reliable numbers. As a researcher, it would lead to policy decisions that are rash and shortsighted.This is a poor use of public money. More than $2.8 trillion a year in federal funding follows census numbers. When the count is wrong, that money goes to the wrong places for at least ten years, and schools, clinics, roads, and emergency plans are built for a population that does not match reality. Lower response rates also mean more costly follow-up work, paid for by taxpayers.A bad count in 2030 cannot be corrected until at least 2040. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw this rule.Tarek  [X]

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
My name is [Your Name] and I am your constituent from [City/Zip Code]. As Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander (AANHPI) Heritage Month comes to a close, I write to urge you to support AANHPI students by cosponsoring the All Students Count Act.

To the U.S. Census Bureau: 

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule titled “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005). Eliminating the collection of race and ethnic data, prohibiting the collection of sexual orientation, and leaving non-citizens out of the apportionment would significantly harm the Southeast Asian American (SEAA) and broader Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander (AANHPI) communities. I respectfully request that the Census Bureau withdraw the proposed rule and extend the comment period to December 10, 2026. 

This proposed rule would significantly harm the SEAA and AANHPI communities. The AANHPI community is not a homogenous population; it encompasses over 50 different ethnic groups and 100 languages and dialects. There are vast socioeconomic disparities within the AANHPI population, often related to their migratory and historical experience. SEAAs, such as the Cambodian, Hmong, Laotian, and Mien populations, often have higher rates of poverty and lower educational attainment rates than both the broader AANHPI and American populations. 

For SEAAs, this disparity is generally tied to their experiences escaping their countries of origin and resettlement in the United States after the Vietnam War, Secret War in Laos, and Khmer Rouge genocide in Cambodia. For example, because of the 2020 Census, we now know that the Mien population has lower educational attainment rates compared to the general American and AANHPI populations. Additionally, the data also show that Mien men have a lower educational attainment rate compared to women. Such information could only be obtained because of the census, which is the primary source for data collection and reporting of small ethnic groups. These data cannot be replicated by other surveys, including the American Community Survey. 

Accurate data, reflective of race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation, help our elected officials properly identify and address the unique needs and challenges of our communities. Prohibiting the collection of this demographic data would prevent our government officials from passing informed public policy; hamper the ability of community-based organizations to demonstrate data narratives for fundraising purposes; and inhibit the ability of students and academics studying our communities from accessing the most robust source of information on SEAAs and the broader AANHPI community. 

Thank you for taking my comment into consideration. I reiterate my request that the US Census Bureau withdraws the proposed rule; preserves the collection of race and ethnic data; and keeps its commitment to count everyone once, only once, and in the right place.

I also ask the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. Changes of this scope deserve more time for the public to review and respond.

Sincerely,
Brandon Lee
Saint Paul, MN 55106

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. I oppose this proposed rule because it departs from that constitutional mandate, risking severe harm to my community. Excluding noncitizens from the population count used for congressional apportionment and federal funding, while adding a citizenship question designed to deter participation, will suppress response rates across immigrant communities and mixed-status families who fear being targeted. An undercount here would directly strip my community of appropriate congressional representation and our fair share of federal funding for essential safety-net programs like SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, CHIP, and Title I education grants. As someone who cares about fairness and the rule of law, I urge the Bureau to withdraw this proposal and count every person living in our communities, as the Constitution requires. 

I am also concerned that the proposed rule erases vital Census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Decades of demographic data serve as the baseline that public and private institutions rely on to identify inequalities and direct resources where they are needed most. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities.  

Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.  

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Sincerely,
Kenji Granberry
Chicago, IL

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). 

As an educator, I care about a fair and accurate census because census data and other federal datasets based on the census are used to make key decisions that affect our nation’s students, educators, and schools.  

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Examples of these uses include: . 

* Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. 

* Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

* Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

* Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

* Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

* Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

* Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

* Determining state higher education funding formulas 

* Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

* Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

* Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

First, to ensure a fair and accurate census,  the Census Bureau should  extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. Second, I oppose both the proposed changes to the residence criteria and the proposed regulations regarding demographic questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. The Census Bureau should  withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The Constitution requires  counting all people living in the United States. 

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (including children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count. 

Revise the tax records language so that those whose mailing address differs from their residential address (servicemembers, those with a post office box) are not excluded.  

• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for civil rights enforcement, among other uses, and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The prohibition, as written, may also restrict the collection or publication of census data on same-sex couples that was asked in 2020. 

 The proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Sincerely,
Lynne Teplin

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. I oppose this proposed rule because it departs from that constitutional mandate, risking severe harm to my community. Excluding noncitizens from the population count used for congressional apportionment and federal funding, while adding a citizenship question designed to deter participation, will suppress response rates across immigrant communities and mixed-status families who fear being targeted. An undercount here would directly strip my community of appropriate congressional representation and our fair share of federal funding for essential safety-net programs like SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, CHIP, and Title I education grants. As someone who cares about fairness and the rule of law, I urge the Bureau to withdraw this proposal and count every person living in our communities, as the Constitution requires. 

I am also concerned that the proposed rule erases vital Census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Decades of demographic data serve as the baseline that public and private institutions rely on to identify inequalities and direct resources where they are needed most. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities.  

Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.  

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Sincerely,
Sandra Cole
Portage, IN

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). 

As an educator, I care about a fair and accurate census because census data and other federal datasets based on the census are used to make key decisions that affect our nation’s students, educators, and schools.  

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Examples of these uses include: . 

* Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. 

* Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

* Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

* Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

* Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

* Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

* Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

* Determining state higher education funding formulas 

* Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

* Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

* Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

First, to ensure a fair and accurate census,  the Census Bureau should  extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. Second, I oppose both the proposed changes to the residence criteria and the proposed regulations regarding demographic questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. The Census Bureau should  withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The Constitution requires  counting all people living in the United States. 

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (including children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count. 

Revise the tax records language so that those whose mailing address differs from their residential address (servicemembers, those with a post office box) are not excluded.  

• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for civil rights enforcement, among other uses, and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The prohibition, as written, may also restrict the collection or publication of census data on same-sex couples that was asked in 2020. 

 The proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Sincerely,
Mrs. Paulette Bannec
Gary, IN

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:

Census counts are used for a wide variety of important purposes, from planning and funding critical infrastructure to understanding patterns of discrimination. By leading to a census that only counts part of the population and contains limited demographic data, the proposed rule will make it harder for policy makers to make evidence-based decisions that affect Americans everyday lives. Underrepresented groups, including women, people of color, and LGBTQ+ people, among others, will be most negatively impacted. 

If the proposed residence criteria are finalized, the U.S. will lose a complete and accurate count of the population and its distribution and stray from the Constitutions mandate to count all persons. The proposed rule would, for the first time, exclude many U.S. residents from the apportionment count, including international students, work visa-holders, and refugees and asylum seekers. The proposed changes would also increase the likelihood that residents are counted in the wrong location, such as by defining usual residence based on tax records that may not reflect the physical address where someone primarily lives, pays taxes, and votes. The census strives to count everyone once, only once, and in the right place so that resources can be distributed based on need and public services can be accurately planned. If finalized, the proposed rule would make it harder to identify and address issues like workplace discrimination, public health discrepancies, and more.

Roosevelt, NY

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). 

As an educator, I care about a fair and accurate census because census data and other federal datasets based on the census are used to make key decisions that affect our nation’s students, educators, and schools.  

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Examples of these uses include: . 

* Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. 

* Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

* Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

* Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

* Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

* Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

* Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

* Determining state higher education funding formulas 

* Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

* Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

* Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

First, to ensure a fair and accurate census,  the Census Bureau should  extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. • Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The Constitution requires  counting all people living in the United States. 

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (including children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count. 

Revise the tax records language so that those whose mailing address differs from their residential address (servicemembers, those with a post office box) are not excluded.  

• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for civil rights enforcement, among other uses, and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The prohibition, as written, may also restrict the collection or publication of census data on same-sex couples that was asked in 2020. 

 The proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Sincerely,
Ms. Allison Eagle
Lafayette, CA

The U.S. Census should not include distorted data in its count of Americans.  By including overly generalized ethnic demographic categories, we obscure the true goal of the census and hinder its constitutionally mandated purpose: an accurate count of Americans.

This Census Bureau should also consider adding a citizenship question to the Census survey. The Supreme Court has already held that the Constitution lawfully permits the Census Bureau to at least inquire about citizenship on the census questionnaire. "The census should absolutely include questions related to citizenship and legal presence. 

These changes would strengthen the census in its core purpose of attaining an accurate count of Americans and have my full support. 

Thank you,  

Larry Cirignano

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
As a stakeholder, I demand that the Census Bureau and Department of Commerce withdraw the proposed rule changing residence criteria for the decennial Census and restricting demographic questions.

The proposal would exclude foreign citizens from the population used for congressional apportionment unless they are also U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents. Overall, this would leave out people who actually live in our community, including many people who are lawfully present in the United States.

For all past Census counts, including the 2020 Census, foreign citizens living in the United States were generally counted where they lived and slept most of the time. That approach recognizes the basic purpose of a Census: accurately counting the people who live in our communities. The 14th Amendment requires congressional representation to be apportioned according to the “whole number of persons in each State.”

I am also deeply concerned by the proposal to prohibit race and ethnicity questions, along with sexual orientation, on the decennial Census enumeration questionnaire. The Census Bureau itself recognizes the importance of race data for civil rights protections, legislative redistricting, equal employment opportunities, and identifying disparities.

The 2030 Census will determine congressional, state, and local representation for the decade that follows. It must be complete, accurate, and protected from political manipulation.

Please withdraw this proposed rule and preserve a Census that fairly and accurately counts our community.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: U.S. Census Bureau,I am writing to oppose the Census Bureau's proposal to remove race and ethnicity questions from the 2030 Census (Docket No. USBC-2026-0628).For decades, federal standards counted Middle Eastern and North African (MENA) Americans as White. This made our communities invisible in the data. In 2024, after years of advocacy and research by the Census Bureau itself, federal standards finally added a "Middle Eastern or North African" category. This proposal would erase that progress before the MENA category is ever used on the census.The Bureau has also decided not to use the updated standards in the 2027 American Community Survey. As a result, no federal survey would count MENA Americans using the MENA category. Without accurate counts, we cannot document the health, education, and economic gaps we face, or the discrimination our communities report.Accurate, detailed data also helps the government spend public dollars wisely. When agencies know who lives where and what they need, they can direct funding and services to the places they will do the most good. Removing these questions would make public spending less efficient, not more.I urge the Census Bureau to:1. Keep race and ethnicity questions on the 2030 Census, including the MENA category required by the 2024 standards.2. Recommit to full implementation of the 2024 revision to Statistical Policy Directive No. 15 (SPD 15), including on the American Community Survey.3. Extend the comment period by 60 days. A proposal of this importance deserves more time for public review.4. Re-engage with community organizations, researchers, and state and local governments in a collaborative process to use more detailed data for the public good, including to direct resources more efficiently to the communities that need them most.Thank you for considering my comment.Elijah Sanchez [X] Colorado Springs, Colorado 80904

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
My name is [Your Name] and I am your constituent from [City/Zip Code]. As Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander (AANHPI) Heritage Month comes to a close, I write to urge you to support AANHPI students by cosponsoring the All Students Count Act.

To the U.S. Census Bureau: 

As a member of the Filipino community, I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw its proposed rule, “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions,” and extend the public comment period to December 10, 2026.

My community knows why detailed race and ethnicity data matter. During COVID-19, Filipino nurses experienced a devastating share of deaths. In its March 2021 report, National Nurses United found that Filipinos made up just 4% of registered nurses nationwide, yet accounted for more than 26% of the nurse deaths it documented. Without data identifying Filipinos separately, this unequal toll would have been hidden within the broader “Asian” category.

This example shows why we need more detailed information about our communities. Many Filipino Americans work in health care, where caring for others can expose them to serious risks. Data that distinguish Filipino Americans from other Asian populations help identify when our community needs stronger workplace protections or health services. While the census does not track COVID-19 deaths, its population counts provide a foundation for understanding who lives in our communities and assessing unequal outcomes. Other surveys, including the American Community Survey, provide valuable information but do not replace the census’s effort to count every resident.

Removing race and ethnicity questions would take away information that Filipino, Southeast Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander communities rely on to show their needs. Local organizations use these data to seek funding, researchers use them to identify disparities, and public officials use them to plan services. Prohibiting questions about sexual orientation would also limit efforts to understand and address the needs of LGBTQ+ people within our communities.

I also oppose excluding residents who are not citizens or green card holders from the population count used to allocate seats in the US House of Representatives. Filipino immigrants with temporary statuses live and work here and contribute to their neighborhoods. Excluding them could reduce representation for the states they call home, weakening the political voice of everyone living there.

The Census Bureau should preserve demographic data, count every resident, and give the public more time to respond. Our communities deserve information that makes their needs visible and representation that reflects everyone who lives here.

I also ask the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. Changes of this scope deserve more time for the public to review and respond.

Sincerely,
Elaine Sanchez Wilson
Philadelphia, PA 19128

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census. These changes will not only weaken the accuracy and integrity of our nation's most important population count, but they will also harm our communities, and I strongly urge the Bureau to reject them. 

First, removing questions of race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation erases the full scope of my identity when I participate in the Census survey. These data points are not optional. They are the tools we use to enforce civil rights laws, monitor discrimination, and measure the disparities that still affect millions of people. Excluding them from the count does not make them disappear from our society, but it does make our government less equipped to handle big issues when they arise. 

The Constitution is clear: the census must count ALL persons living in the United States, regardless of their immigration or citizenship status. The proposal to exclude non-citizens, including those residents with some type of lawful status, violates more than two centuries of legal precedent. Every person counted in this country contributes to our communities, and every person deserves to be fully seen. 

The consequences of these changes will negatively impact our daily lives. The census affects everything. It determines political representation and the drawing of voting districts. It guides how billions of dollars in federal funding are used to close persistent disparities in schools, hospitals, and other government programs that are designed to improve our lives.  

The census is the foundation of our democracy. It must reflect the complete yet nuanced reality of who we are as a nation. And it must reflect the lives of our friends and neighbors who may not look, think, or speak like we do. I ask the Bureau to withdraw these proposed changes and to preserve a count that includes everyone and represents everyone. 

Thank you for considering my comment.

Sincerely,
Fred Read

Subject: Re: Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions (Docket No. 260903-0005; RIN 0607-AA75) 

I strongly oppose the proposed rules for the census and changes to its residence rule. All persons in the United States have a right to be counted, as the 14th Amendment of the Constitution plainly establishes. Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. I oppose this proposed rule because it departs from that constitutional mandate, risking severe harm to my community. Excluding noncitizens from the population count used for congressional apportionment and federal funding, while adding a citizenship question designed to deter participation, will suppress response rates across immigrant communities and mixed-status families who fear being targeted. An undercount here would directly strip my community of appropriate congressional representation and our fair share of federal funding for essential safety-net programs like SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, CHIP, and Title I education grants. As someone who cares about fairness and the rule of law, I urge the Bureau to withdraw this proposal and count every person living in our communities, as the Constitution requires. I am also concerned that the proposed rule erases vital Census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Decades of demographic data serve as the baseline that public and private institutions rely on to identify inequalities and direct resources where they are needed most. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities. Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). 

As an educator, I care about a fair and accurate census because census data and other federal datasets based on the census are used to make key decisions that affect our nation’s students, educators, and schools.  

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Examples of these uses include: . 

* Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. 

* Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

* Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

* Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

* Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

* Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

* Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

* Determining state higher education funding formulas 

* Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

* Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

* Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

First, to ensure a fair and accurate census,  the Census Bureau should  extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. Second, I oppose both the proposed changes to the residence criteria and the proposed regulations regarding demographic questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. The Census Bureau should  withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The Constitution requires  counting all people living in the United States. 

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (including children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count. 

Revise the tax records language so that those whose mailing address differs from their residential address (servicemembers, those with a post office box) are not excluded.  

• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for civil rights enforcement, among other uses, and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The prohibition, as written, may also restrict the collection or publication of census data on same-sex couples that was asked in 2020. 

 The proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Sincerely,
Mr. John Lorona
Aptos, CA

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. I oppose this proposed rule because it departs from that constitutional mandate, risking severe harm to my community. Excluding noncitizens from the population count used for congressional apportionment and federal funding, while adding a citizenship question designed to deter participation, will suppress response rates across immigrant communities and mixed-status families who fear being targeted. An undercount here would directly strip my community of appropriate congressional representation and our fair share of federal funding for essential safety-net programs like SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, CHIP, and Title I education grants. As someone who cares about fairness and the rule of law, I urge the Bureau to withdraw this proposal and count every person living in our communities, as the Constitution requires. 

I am also concerned that the proposed rule erases vital Census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Decades of demographic data serve as the baseline that public and private institutions rely on to identify inequalities and direct resources where they are needed most. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities.  

Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.  

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Sincerely,
Gabrielle Schapira
New York, NY

Comment:

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am a concerned American writing to comment on the proposed rule Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). I strongly oppose the proposed rules changes to the residence criteria and demographic questions for the 2030 Census.

As an initial matter, I urge the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. 30 days is not enough time for members of the public to review and respond to the proposed rule given the scope of the prospective changes. 

I oppose the proposed rule because I am concerned it will undermine the accuracy and usefulness of census data, particularly for marginalized Americans. Census counts are used for a wide variety of important purposes, from planning and funding critical infrastructure to understanding patterns of discrimination. By leading to a census that only counts part of the population and contains limited demographic data, the proposed rule will make it harder for policy makers to make evidence-based decisions that affect Americans everyday lives. Underrepresented groups, including women, people of color, and LGBTQ+ people, among others, will be most negatively impacted. 

If the proposed residence criteria are finalized, the U.S. will lose a complete and accurate count of the population and its distribution and stray from the Constitutions mandate to count all persons. The proposed rule would, for the first time, exclude many U.S. residents from the apportionment count, including international students, work visa-holders, and refugees and asylum seekers. The proposed changes would also increase the likelihood that residents are counted in the wrong location, such as by defining usual residence based on tax records that may not reflect the physical address where someone primarily lives, pays taxes, and votes. The census strives to count everyone once, only once, and in the right place so that resources can be distributed based on need and public services can be accurately planned. The proposed rule would undermine this stated goal. 

By prohibiting questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation, the proposed rule would also cause the U.S. to lose critical, reliable demographic data. Every U.S. census has collected race and ethnicity data in some form since the first in 1790. These data are the foundation for a wide variety of population-based surveys and studies that allow researchers to gain important understanding of national issues and inequities. Although sexual orientation is not currently asked about in the census, barring these questions from future censuses will similarly restrict data on LGBTQ+ Americans. Robust demographic data is necessary to enforce civil rights laws and ensure equal opportunity for all Americans. If finalized, the proposed rule would make it harder to identify and address issues like workplace discrimination, public health discrepancies, and more. 

Census data needs to accurately represent all Americans. For the reasons stated above, I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw and revise the proposed rule, especially part 60 and 70. Thank you for your consideration. 

Sincerely, 
Mrs. Tracey Smallwood Katsouros
Waldorf, MD

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am a concerned American writing to comment on the proposed rule Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). I strongly oppose the proposed rules changes to the residence criteria and demographic questions for the 2030 Census.

As an initial matter, I urge the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. 30 days is not enough time for members of the public to review and respond to the proposed rule given the scope of the prospective changes. 

I oppose the proposed rule because I am concerned it will undermine the accuracy and usefulness of census data, particularly for marginalized Americans. Census counts are used for a wide variety of important purposes, from planning and funding critical infrastructure to understanding patterns of discrimination. By leading to a census that only counts part of the population and contains limited demographic data, the proposed rule will make it harder for policy makers to make evidence-based decisions that affect Americans everyday lives. Underrepresented groups, including women, people of color, and LGBTQ+ people, among others, will be most negatively impacted. 

If the proposed residence criteria are finalized, the U.S. will lose a complete and accurate count of the population and its distribution and stray from the Constitutions mandate to count all persons. The proposed rule would, for the first time, exclude many U.S. residents from the apportionment count, including international students, work visa-holders, and refugees and asylum seekers. The proposed changes would also increase the likelihood that residents are counted in the wrong location, such as by defining usual residence based on tax records that may not reflect the physical address where someone primarily lives, pays taxes, and votes. The census strives to count everyone once, only once, and in the right place so that resources can be distributed based on need and public services can be accurately planned. The proposed rule would undermine this stated goal. 

By prohibiting questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation, the proposed rule would also cause the U.S. to lose critical, reliable demographic data. Every U.S. census has collected race and ethnicity data in some form since the first in 1790. These data are the foundation for a wide variety of population-based surveys and studies that allow researchers to gain important understanding of national issues and inequities. Although sexual orientation is not currently asked about in the census, barring these questions from future censuses will similarly restrict data on LGBTQ+ Americans. Robust demographic data is necessary to enforce civil rights laws and ensure equal opportunity for all Americans. If finalized, the proposed rule would make it harder to identify and address issues like workplace discrimination, public health discrepancies, and more. 

Census data needs to accurately represent all Americans. For the reasons stated above, I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw and revise the proposed rule, especially part 60 and 70. Thank you for your consideration. 

Sincerely, 
Bill Wood
Mount Shasta, CA

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I write in support of the Census Bureau's proposed rule, "Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions" (Docket No. USBC-2026-0628; RIN 0607-AA75).

The Constitution calls for an "actual Enumeration" every ten years so that representation can be fairly apportioned among the states. The decennial census is meant to be a count, not a survey or a statistical estimate. Americans' voice in Congress depends on that count being right.

In 2020, the Bureau intentionally introduced statistical noise into the population data used to draw congressional and legislative districts. Data that determine political representation should never be deliberately altered. I support proposed  70.3, which directs the Bureau to prioritize the accuracy of the population count and prohibits publishing demographic data when doing so would introduce uncertainty into national or state population counts.

I also support the proposed residence criteria. Being counted at one's "usual residence" has never meant mere physical presence on Census Day. It reflects a lasting connection to a place, which is why service members stationed abroad are still counted in their home states. Counting citizens and lawful permanent residents, and excluding foreign nationals who are here unlawfully or temporarily, follows that principle.

I support keeping the enumeration questionnaire focused on the count itself. The Bureau can continue to produce demographic and statistical information through the American Community Survey and other tools, but those products should remain separate from the constitutional headcount.

To make these reforms durable, I urge the Bureau to state clearly in the final rule that the constitutional enumeration, and the counts used for apportionment and redistricting, are fundamentally distinct from routine federal statistical products and may not be adjusted to serve other statistical purposes.

Please finalize this rule so that the 2030 Census delivers an accurate count and restores Americans' trust in how they are represented.

Respectfully,
Joshua Mercer
Petoskey, MI

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
See attached file for full public comment.

Lane County, a continuously operating local government in the State of Oregon since 1851, respectfully submits the following comment on the proposed rule governing residence criteria and demographic questions for the decennial census.

15 CFR Part 60: Residence Rules
Lane County opposes the proposed residence rule changes as written because they impose new federal requirements without accounting for local operational realities. Replacing the long‑standing “most of the time” standard with a rigid January 3–April 1 enumeration period does not reflect how residents actually live and work in Lane County’s rural, agricultural, university, and tourism dependent communities. Seasonal population fluctuations are well documented and predictable. A rigid federal measurement period will produce miscounts that local governments will have no ability to correct, despite bearing the consequences in state and federal program formulas.

The newly proposed “dependents” category raises further concerns about federal level decisions affecting state mandated child welfare responsibilities. Children in foster care, youth in kinship care, or shared custody could be counted outside the jurisdiction that is legally and financially responsible for their placement. Counties must have clear guidance so federal counting rules do not interfere with Title IV E reimbursement or child welfare caseload accuracy.

The exclusion of non‑citizens, including lawful non‑permanent residents, from the enumeration will shift both fiscal and administrative burdens onto counties, which must continue to serve all residents regardless of federal counting decisions. This will create an artificially low benchmark of population served, while reducing congressional representation and federal funding formula allocations. The resulting population undercount would create a mismatch between statutory responsibilities and federal formula funding.

15 CFR Part 70: Demographic Questions and Data Disclosure
Lane County cannot support changes limiting demographic questions on the decennial census, as written, as they would weaken the data counties are legally required to use while increasing administrative challenges at the local level. Race and ethnicity data are required for compliance with the Voting Rights Act, Section 203 language assistance, redistricting defense, and civil rights obligations. Removing these questions from the census short form, while offering no alternative source of equivalent data collection or reliability, shifts compliance risk from the federal government onto counties. Local governments do not have the authority or resources to generate the demographic data that multiple federal laws require.

Age‑based data such as biological sex, date of birth, and household relationship are critical for administering federal programs for seniors, childcare assistance, and other statutory requirements. Making demographic responses optional introduces nonresponse bias that counties cannot fix but must still absorb operationally. Counties need clear guidance on how optional responses will affect official population totals and which data will be used in federal program formulas.

Finally, Lane County requests clarity on how demographic data from the American Community Survey and the Population Estimates Program will align with apportionment counts. Federal funding streams rely on consistent population bases; shifting methodologies between federal programs will increase administrative burden at the local level and introduce fiscal uncertainty that affects long‑term planning.

Accurate Census data is essential for tracking population changes, migration patterns, school enrollment, public safety statistics, genealogical research, and economic activity in our predominantly rural region. Reducing the reliability of taxpayer‑funded data undermines public trust and makes it harder for counties to meet statutory obligations.

Reliance on administrative records: Increased reliance on tax, immigration, health and other administrative records raises concerns about the potential undercount of populations in our community that may not be consistently represented in those records, including low-income households, college students, non-filers and children. We request additional information regarding when these records will be used and how the Bureau will ensure accurate counts for populations with less reliable administrative data.  

Demographic questions: The proposal would eliminate race and ethnicity questions, while making most other demographic questions optional. Accurate demographic data is essential to municipal planning and service delivery. Understanding who lives in our community gives local governments the ability to plan for our current population and take into consideration our future population's needs. Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The Census Bureau’s proposed 2030 reforms move the count back toward its constitutional purpose: an actual enumeration for political representation, not a statistical product shaped for other ends.
Article I requires an “actual Enumeration” of the population, conducted in the manner Congress directs, to apportion representation. In recent decades that mandate was stretched. Usual residence lost a clear tie to lawful presence and allegiance. Disclosure methods such as differential privacy injected noise into the very counts states use to draw districts. Demographic questions that are not needed for apportionment were treated as part of the enumeration itself. The result was a census pulled away from representation and toward policy and statistical uses.
The 2030 proposals correct that course. They restore meaning to residence by counting U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents at their usual residence and excluding foreign citizens whose status is less durable than permanent residence from the apportionment base. They put representation first, and they treat the decennial count as a constitutional enumeration rather than a general-purpose survey. Ending differential privacy would reinforce that same principle: the numbers used for apportionment and redistricting should be enumerated counts, not noise-adjusted estimates.
I strongly support these reforms. An accurate count for political representation is the Census’s first duty. The Bureau should finalize rules that restore actual enumeration, residence that means something, and a count fit for apportionment.
