Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). 

As an educator, I care about a fair and accurate census because census data and other federal datasets based on the census are used to make key decisions that affect our nation’s students, educators, and schools.  

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Examples of these uses include: . 

* Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. 

* Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

* Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

* Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

* Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

* Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

* Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

* Determining state higher education funding formulas 

* Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

* Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

* Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

First, to ensure a fair and accurate census,  the Census Bureau should  extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. Second, I oppose both the proposed changes to the residence criteria and the proposed regulations regarding demographic questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. The Census Bureau should  withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The Constitution requires  counting all people living in the United States. 

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (including children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count. 

Revise the tax records language so that those whose mailing address differs from their residential address (servicemembers, those with a post office box) are not excluded.  

• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for civil rights enforcement, among other uses, and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The prohibition, as written, may also restrict the collection or publication of census data on same-sex couples that was asked in 2020. 

 The proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Sincerely,
Ms. Maria Venegas
Los Angeles, CA

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I write in support of the Census Bureau's proposed rule, "Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions" (Docket No. USBC-2026-0628; RIN 0607-AA75).

The Constitution calls for an "actual Enumeration" every ten years so that representation can be fairly apportioned among the states. The decennial census is meant to be a count, not a survey or a statistical estimate. Americans' voice in Congress depends on that count being right.

In 2020, the Bureau intentionally introduced statistical noise into the population data used to draw congressional and legislative districts. Data that determine political representation should never be deliberately altered. I support proposed  70.3, which directs the Bureau to prioritize the accuracy of the population count and prohibits publishing demographic data when doing so would introduce uncertainty into national or state population counts.

I also support the proposed residence criteria. Being counted at one's "usual residence" has never meant mere physical presence on Census Day. It reflects a lasting connection to a place, which is why service members stationed abroad are still counted in their home states. Counting citizens and lawful permanent residents, and excluding foreign nationals who are here unlawfully or temporarily, follows that principle.

I support keeping the enumeration questionnaire focused on the count itself. The Bureau can continue to produce demographic and statistical information through the American Community Survey and other tools, but those products should remain separate from the constitutional headcount.

To make these reforms durable, I urge the Bureau to state clearly in the final rule that the constitutional enumeration, and the counts used for apportionment and redistricting, are fundamentally distinct from routine federal statistical products and may not be adjusted to serve other statistical purposes.

Please finalize this rule so that the 2030 Census delivers an accurate count and restores Americans' trust in how they are represented.

Respectfully,
Patrick Schreck
Lake Oswego, OR

Comment:

I oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census because a fair and accurate census is critical to ensuring every community is counted, fairly represented, and able to get the resources people need to live healthy lives — including sexual and reproductive healthcare. An inaccurate or incomplete census can deepen existing inequities, particularly for communities that already face disenfranchisement and barriers to healthcare. 

A fair and accurate census is essential to our health and rights. 

Census data help determine access to programs patients and their families rely on, including important programs like Medicaid, SNAP, WIC, and TANF. Accurate census data also shape political representation by determining how seats in the U.S. House of Representatives are apportioned among states and providing data used for redistricting. When communities are undercounted or excluded, they risk losing both resources and political representation. 

The Census Bureau and Department of Commerce must:

1. Count all people residing in the United States in the 2030 Census, without regard to immigration status. Excluding noncitizens from census apportionment data violates the Constitution and established legal precedent. It would suppress the count of many communities, effectively erasing them from critical datasets and depriving them of resources and congressional representation –— including resources and political representation that support access to healthcare.

2. Continue collecting race and ethnicity data and implement the 2024 OMB SPD 15 standards. Census race and ethnicity data are essential for important research across many sectors, for upholding civil rights, and for growing the economy. Extensive Census Bureau research and engagement with expert stakeholders shows that implementing the modernized 2024 OMB SPD 15 standards for race and ethnicity data collection will yield data that more accurately represent the nation’s increasingly diverse population.

3. Remove the clause banning the addition of future questions on sexual orientation. Proposed changes to demographic items should be based on research and guided by a deliberative and transparent process, including extensive stakeholder consultation.

4. Withdraw other proposed changes to residence criteria, including tying place of residence to tax records and "lawful residence," and the adoption of a three month enumeration period. The Census Bureau must extensively research and consult with stakeholders about the potential effects of such changes before proposing their implementation in a decennial census.

5. Halt the practice of prison gerrymandering by counting incarcerated individuals in their home communities. This will yield more accurate census data and ensure that communities receive the congressional representation to which they are entitled.

Add introduction text here. If introduction text is not needed, uncheck the above checkbox "Include Introduction". This text is NOT editable by the supporter.

I oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census because a fair and accurate census is critical to ensuring every community is counted, fairly represented, and able to get the resources people need to live healthy lives — including sexual and reproductive healthcare. An inaccurate or incomplete census can deepen existing inequities, particularly for communities that already face disenfranchisement and barriers to healthcare. 

A fair and accurate census is essential to our health and rights. 

Census data help determine access to programs patients and their families rely on, including important programs like Medicaid, SNAP, WIC, and TANF. Accurate census data also shape political representation by determining how seats in the U.S. House of Representatives are apportioned among states and providing data used for redistricting. When communities are undercounted or excluded, they risk losing both resources and political representation. 

The Census Bureau and Department of Commerce must:

1. Count all people residing in the United States in the 2030 Census, without regard to immigration status. Excluding noncitizens from census apportionment data violates the Constitution and established legal precedent. It would suppress the count of many communities, effectively erasing them from critical datasets and depriving them of resources and congressional representation –— including resources and political representation that support access to healthcare.

2. Continue collecting race and ethnicity data and implement the 2024 OMB SPD 15 standards. Census race and ethnicity data are essential for important research across many sectors, for upholding civil rights, and for growing the economy. Extensive Census Bureau research and engagement with expert stakeholders shows that implementing the modernized 2024 OMB SPD 15 standards for race and ethnicity data collection will yield data that more accurately represent the nation’s increasingly diverse population.

3. Remove the clause banning the addition of future questions on sexual orientation. Proposed changes to demographic items should be based on research and guided by a deliberative and transparent process, including extensive stakeholder consultation.

4. Withdraw other proposed changes to residence criteria, including tying place of residence to tax records and "lawful residence," and the adoption of a three month enumeration period. The Census Bureau must extensively research and consult with stakeholders about the potential effects of such changes before proposing their implementation in a decennial census.

5. Halt the practice of prison gerrymandering by counting incarcerated individuals in their home communities. This will yield more accurate census data and ensure that communities receive the congressional representation to which they are entitled.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I write in support of the Census Bureau's proposed rule, "Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions" (Docket No. USBC-2026-0628; RIN 0607-AA75).

The Constitution calls for an "actual Enumeration" every ten years so that representation can be fairly apportioned among the states. The decennial census is meant to be a count, not a survey or a statistical estimate. Americans' voice in Congress depends on that count being right.

In 2020, the Bureau intentionally introduced statistical noise into the population data used to draw congressional and legislative districts. Data that determine political representation should never be deliberately altered. I support proposed  70.3, which directs the Bureau to prioritize the accuracy of the population count and prohibits publishing demographic data when doing so would introduce uncertainty into national or state population counts.

I also support the proposed residence criteria. Being counted at one's "usual residence" has never meant mere physical presence on Census Day. It reflects a lasting connection to a place, which is why service members stationed abroad are still counted in their home states. Counting citizens and lawful permanent residents, and excluding foreign nationals who are here unlawfully or temporarily, follows that principle.

I support keeping the enumeration questionnaire focused on the count itself. The Bureau can continue to produce demographic and statistical information through the American Community Survey and other tools, but those products should remain separate from the constitutional headcount.

To make these reforms durable, I urge the Bureau to state clearly in the final rule that the constitutional enumeration, and the counts used for apportionment and redistricting, are fundamentally distinct from routine federal statistical products and may not be adjusted to serve other statistical purposes.

Please finalize this rule so that the 2030 Census delivers an accurate count and restores Americans' trust in how they are represented.

Respectfully,
Jennifer Browner
Tecumseh, MI

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I write in support of the Census Bureau's proposed rule, "Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions" (Docket No. USBC-2026-0628; RIN 0607-AA75).

The Constitution calls for an "actual Enumeration" every ten years so that representation can be fairly apportioned among the states. The decennial census is meant to be a count, not a survey or a statistical estimate. Americans' voice in Congress depends on that count being right.

In 2020, the Bureau intentionally introduced statistical noise into the population data used to draw congressional and legislative districts. Data that determine political representation should never be deliberately altered. I support proposed  70.3, which directs the Bureau to prioritize the accuracy of the population count and prohibits publishing demographic data when doing so would introduce uncertainty into national or state population counts.

I also support the proposed residence criteria. Being counted at one's "usual residence" has never meant mere physical presence on Census Day. It reflects a lasting connection to a place, which is why service members stationed abroad are still counted in their home states. Counting citizens and lawful permanent residents, and excluding foreign nationals who are here unlawfully or temporarily, follows that principle.

I support keeping the enumeration questionnaire focused on the count itself. The Bureau can continue to produce demographic and statistical information through the American Community Survey and other tools, but those products should remain separate from the constitutional headcount.

To make these reforms durable, I urge the Bureau to state clearly in the final rule that the constitutional enumeration, and the counts used for apportionment and redistricting, are fundamentally distinct from routine federal statistical products and may not be adjusted to serve other statistical purposes.

Please finalize this rule so that the 2030 Census delivers an accurate count and restores Americans' trust in how they are represented.

Respectfully,
{Genny Jones}
{Gilbert, AZ}

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am a concerned American writing to comment on the proposed rule Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). I strongly oppose the proposed rules changes to the residence criteria and demographic questions for the 2030 Census.

As an initial matter, I urge the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. 30 days is not enough time for members of the public to review and respond to the proposed rule given the scope of the prospective changes. 

I oppose the proposed rule because I am concerned it will undermine the accuracy and usefulness of census data, particularly for marginalized Americans. Census counts are used for a wide variety of important purposes, from planning and funding critical infrastructure to understanding patterns of discrimination. By leading to a census that only counts part of the population and contains limited demographic data, the proposed rule will make it harder for policy makers to make evidence-based decisions that affect Americans everyday lives. Underrepresented groups, including women, people of color, and LGBTQ+ people, among others, will be most negatively impacted. 

If the proposed residence criteria are finalized, the U.S. will lose a complete and accurate count of the population and its distribution and stray from the Constitutions mandate to count all persons. The proposed rule would, for the first time, exclude many U.S. residents from the apportionment count, including international students, work visa-holders, and refugees and asylum seekers. The proposed changes would also increase the likelihood that residents are counted in the wrong location, such as by defining usual residence based on tax records that may not reflect the physical address where someone primarily lives, pays taxes, and votes. The census strives to count everyone once, only once, and in the right place so that resources can be distributed based on need and public services can be accurately planned. The proposed rule would undermine this stated goal. 

By prohibiting questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation, the proposed rule would also cause the U.S. to lose critical, reliable demographic data. Every U.S. census has collected race and ethnicity data in some form since the first in 1790. These data are the foundation for a wide variety of population-based surveys and studies that allow researchers to gain important understanding of national issues and inequities. Although sexual orientation is not currently asked about in the census, barring these questions from future censuses will similarly restrict data on LGBTQ+ Americans. Robust demographic data is necessary to enforce civil rights laws and ensure equal opportunity for all Americans. If finalized, the proposed rule would make it harder to identify and address issues like workplace discrimination, public health discrepancies, and more. 

Census data needs to accurately represent all Americans. For the reasons stated above, I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw and revise the proposed rule, especially part 60 and 70. Thank you for your consideration. 

Sincerely, 
Gloria Fooks
Saint Clair, MO

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am an American citizen and a parent, and I care about a fair and accurate census on behalf of everyone living in the United States.

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including:

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.
As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I write in support of the Census Bureau's proposed rule, "Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions" (Docket No. USBC-2026-0628; RIN 0607-AA75).

The Constitution calls for an "actual Enumeration" every ten years so that representation can be fairly apportioned among the states. The decennial census is meant to be a count, not a survey or a statistical estimate. Americans' voice in Congress depends on that count being right.

In 2020, the Bureau intentionally introduced statistical noise into the population data used to draw congressional and legislative districts. Data that determine political representation should never be deliberately altered. I support proposed  70.3, which directs the Bureau to prioritize the accuracy of the population count and prohibits publishing demographic data when doing so would introduce uncertainty into national or state population counts.

I also support the proposed residence criteria. Being counted at one's "usual residence" has never meant mere physical presence on Census Day. It reflects a lasting connection to a place, which is why service members stationed abroad are still counted in their home states. Counting citizens and lawful permanent residents, and excluding foreign nationals who are here unlawfully or temporarily, follows that principle.

I support keeping the enumeration questionnaire focused on the count itself. The Bureau can continue to produce demographic and statistical information through the American Community Survey and other tools, but those products should remain separate from the constitutional headcount.

To make these reforms durable, I urge the Bureau to state clearly in the final rule that the constitutional enumeration, and the counts used for apportionment and redistricting, are fundamentally distinct from routine federal statistical products and may not be adjusted to serve other statistical purposes.

Please finalize this rule so that the 2030 Census delivers an accurate count and restores Americans' trust in how they are represented.

Respectfully,
Ronald M Chrismer
Laurel, MD

I oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census because a fair and accurate census is critical to ensuring every community is counted, fairly represented, and able to get the resources people need to live healthy lives — including sexual and reproductive healthcare. An inaccurate or incomplete census can deepen existing inequities, particularly for communities that already face disenfranchisement and barriers to healthcare. 

A fair and accurate census is essential to our health and rights. 

Census data help determine access to programs patients and their families rely on, including important programs like Medicaid, SNAP, WIC, and TANF. Accurate census data also shape political representation by determining how seats in the U.S. House of Representatives are apportioned among states and providing data used for redistricting. When communities are undercounted or excluded, they risk losing both resources and political representation. 

The Census Bureau and Department of Commerce must:

1. Count all people residing in the United States in the 2030 Census, without regard to immigration status. Excluding noncitizens from census apportionment data violates the Constitution and established legal precedent. It would suppress the count of many communities, effectively erasing them from critical datasets and depriving them of resources and congressional representation –— including resources and political representation that support access to healthcare.

2. Continue collecting race and ethnicity data and implement the 2024 OMB SPD 15 standards. Census race and ethnicity data are essential for important research across many sectors, for upholding civil rights, and for growing the economy. Extensive Census Bureau research and engagement with expert stakeholders shows that implementing the modernized 2024 OMB SPD 15 standards for race and ethnicity data collection will yield data that more accurately represent the nation’s increasingly diverse population.

3. Remove the clause banning the addition of future questions on sexual orientation. Proposed changes to demographic items should be based on research and guided by a deliberative and transparent process, including extensive stakeholder consultation.

4. Withdraw other proposed changes to residence criteria, including tying place of residence to tax records and "lawful residence," and the adoption of a three month enumeration period. The Census Bureau must extensively research and consult with stakeholders about the potential effects of such changes before proposing their implementation in a decennial census.

5. Halt the practice of prison gerrymandering by counting incarcerated individuals in their home communities. This will yield more accurate census data and ensure that communities receive the congressional representation to which they are entitled.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing as a citizen, a physical therapist, and a volunteer in a Catholic ministry to people experiencing homelessness. I oppose any changes to the census that would remove racial information or leave people without stable housing uncounted.

Through my ministry, I meet neighbors who sleep in cars, shelters, and encampments, and who are too often treated as invisible. My faith teaches that every person has inherent dignity and that we are called to care for "the least of these." Being counted is a basic form of recognition. A census that skips people because they lack an address tells them, and everyone else, that they do not count. An undercount would also reduce the funding for shelters, outreach, and health services that organizations like mine depend on, and it would hide the true scale of the housing crisis from the policymakers responsible for addressing it.

My clinical work has shown me the same thing from another angle. Evidence-based care starts with accurate data, and so does evidence-based policy. Racial data on the census is how we identify health and economic disparities, enforce the Voting Rights Act and other civil rights protections, and direct resources to communities that have long been underserved. Removing it would make discrimination harder to detect and easier to ignore. We cannot fix what we have stopped measuring.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:

I oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census because a fair and accurate census is critical to ensuring every community is counted, fairly represented, and able to get the resources people need to live healthy lives — including sexual and reproductive healthcare. An inaccurate or incomplete census can deepen existing inequities, particularly for communities that already face disenfranchisement and barriers to healthcare. 

A fair and accurate census is essential to our health and rights. 

Census data help determine access to programs patients and their families rely on, including important programs like Medicaid, SNAP, WIC, and TANF. Accurate census data also shape political representation by determining how seats in the U.S. House of Representatives are apportioned among states and providing data used for redistricting. When communities are undercounted or excluded, they risk losing both resources and political representation. 

The Census Bureau and Department of Commerce must:

1. Count all people residing in the United States in the 2030 Census, without regard to immigration status. Excluding noncitizens from census apportionment data violates the Constitution and established legal precedent. It would suppress the count of many communities, effectively erasing them from critical datasets and depriving them of resources and congressional representation –— including resources and political representation that support access to healthcare.

2. Continue collecting race and ethnicity data and implement the 2024 OMB SPD 15 standards. Census race and ethnicity data are essential for important research across many sectors, for upholding civil rights, and for growing the economy. Extensive Census Bureau research and engagement with expert stakeholders shows that implementing the modernized 2024 OMB SPD 15 standards for race and ethnicity data collection will yield data that more accurately represent the nation’s increasingly diverse population.

3. Remove the clause banning the addition of future questions on sexual orientation. Proposed changes to demographic items should be based on research and guided by a deliberative and transparent process, including extensive stakeholder consultation.

4. Withdraw other proposed changes to residence criteria, including tying place of residence to tax records and "lawful residence," and the adoption of a three month enumeration period. The Census Bureau must extensively research and consult with stakeholders about the potential effects of such changes before proposing their implementation in a decennial census.

5. Halt the practice of prison gerrymandering by counting incarcerated individuals in their home communities. This will yield more accurate census data and ensure that communities receive the congressional representation to which they are entitled.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am a concerned American writing to comment on the proposed rule Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). I strongly oppose the proposed rules changes to the residence criteria and demographic questions for the 2030 Census.

As an initial matter, I urge the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. 30 days is not enough time for members of the public to review and respond to the proposed rule given the scope of the prospective changes. 

I oppose the proposed rule because I am concerned it will undermine the accuracy and usefulness of census data, particularly for marginalized Americans. Census counts are used for a wide variety of important purposes, from planning and funding critical infrastructure to understanding patterns of discrimination. By leading to a census that only counts part of the population and contains limited demographic data, the proposed rule will make it harder for policy makers to make evidence-based decisions that affect Americans everyday lives. Underrepresented groups, including women, people of color, and LGBTQ+ people, among others, will be most negatively impacted. 

If the proposed residence criteria are finalized, the U.S. will lose a complete and accurate count of the population and its distribution and stray from the Constitutions mandate to count all persons. The proposed rule would, for the first time, exclude many U.S. residents from the apportionment count, including international students, work visa-holders, and refugees and asylum seekers. The proposed changes would also increase the likelihood that residents are counted in the wrong location, such as by defining usual residence based on tax records that may not reflect the physical address where someone primarily lives, pays taxes, and votes. The census strives to count everyone once, only once, and in the right place so that resources can be distributed based on need and public services can be accurately planned. The proposed rule would undermine this stated goal. 

By prohibiting questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation, the proposed rule would also cause the U.S. to lose critical, reliable demographic data. Every U.S. census has collected race and ethnicity data in some form since the first in 1790. These data are the foundation for a wide variety of population-based surveys and studies that allow researchers to gain important understanding of national issues and inequities. Although sexual orientation is not currently asked about in the census, barring these questions from future censuses will similarly restrict data on LGBTQ+ Americans. Robust demographic data is necessary to enforce civil rights laws and ensure equal opportunity for all Americans. If finalized, the proposed rule would make it harder to identify and address issues like workplace discrimination, public health discrepancies, and more. 

Census data needs to accurately represent all Americans. For the reasons stated above, I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw and revise the proposed rule, especially part 60 and 70. Thank you for your consideration. 

Sincerely, 
Ms. Karen Kirschling
San Francisco, CA

I oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census because a fair and accurate census is critical to ensuring every community is counted, fairly represented, and able to get the resources people need to live healthy lives — including sexual and reproductive healthcare. An inaccurate or incomplete census can deepen existing inequities, particularly for communities that already face disenfranchisement and barriers to healthcare.

When communities are undercounted or excluded, they risk losing both resources and political representation. 

The Census Bureau and Department of Commerce must:

1. Count all people residing in the United States in the 2030 Census, without regard to immigration status. Excluding noncitizens from census apportionment data violates the Constitution and established legal precedent. It would suppress the count of many communities, effectively erasing them from critical datasets and depriving them of resources and congressional representation –— including resources and political representation that support access to healthcare.

2. Continue collecting race and ethnicity data and implement the 2024 OMB SPD 15 standards. Census race and ethnicity data are essential for important research across many sectors, for upholding civil rights, and for growing the economy. Extensive Census Bureau research and engagement with expert stakeholders shows that implementing the modernized 2024 OMB SPD 15 standards for race and ethnicity data collection will yield data that more accurately represent the nation’s increasingly diverse population.

3. Remove the clause banning the addition of future questions on sexual orientation. Proposed changes to demographic items should be based on research and guided by a deliberative and transparent process, including extensive stakeholder consultation.

4. Withdraw other proposed changes to residence criteria, including tying place of residence to tax records and "lawful residence," and the adoption of a three month enumeration period. The Census Bureau must extensively research and consult with stakeholders about the potential effects of such changes before proposing their implementation in a decennial census.

5. Halt the practice of prison gerrymandering by counting incarcerated individuals in their home communities. This will yield more accurate census data and ensure that communities receive the congressional representation to which they are entitled.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I write in support of the Census Bureau's proposed rule, "Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions" (Docket No. USBC-2026-0628; RIN 0607-AA75).

The Constitution calls for an "actual Enumeration" every ten years so that representation can be fairly apportioned among the states. The decennial census is meant to be a count, not a survey or a statistical estimate. Americans' voice in Congress depends on that count being right.

In 2020, the Bureau intentionally introduced statistical noise into the population data used to draw congressional and legislative districts. Data that determine political representation should never be deliberately altered. I support proposed  70.3, which directs the Bureau to prioritize the accuracy of the population count and prohibits publishing demographic data when doing so would introduce uncertainty into national or state population counts.

I also support the proposed residence criteria. Being counted at one's "usual residence" has never meant mere physical presence on Census Day. It reflects a lasting connection to a place, which is why service members stationed abroad are still counted in their home states. Counting citizens and lawful permanent residents, and excluding foreign nationals who are here unlawfully or temporarily, follows that principle.

I support keeping the enumeration questionnaire focused on the count itself. The Bureau can continue to produce demographic and statistical information through the American Community Survey and other tools, but those products should remain separate from the constitutional headcount.

To make these reforms durable, I urge the Bureau to state clearly in the final rule that the constitutional enumeration, and the counts used for apportionment and redistricting, are fundamentally distinct from routine federal statistical products and may not be adjusted to serve other statistical purposes.

Please finalize this rule so that the 2030 Census delivers an accurate count and restores Americans' trust in how they are represented.

Respectfully,
Molly Breaux
Shelbyville, KY

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).
I am an educator with nearly 30 years of experience serving public school students, families, and communities in California. I care deeply about a fair and accurate census because public education relies directly on complete demographic data and accurate population counts. Decennial census data determines the fair distribution of federal education dollars—including Title I funding for low-income schools, special education resources, school lunch programs, and local community infrastructure—ensuring that every child gets the support they deserve.
First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.
Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including:
•	Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
•	Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
•	Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
•	Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
•	Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
•	Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
•	Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health, education planning, and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.
As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am a concerned American writing to comment on the proposed rule Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). I strongly oppose the proposed rules changes to the residence criteria and demographic questions for the 2030 Census.

As an initial matter, I urge the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. 30 days is not enough time for members of the public to review and respond to the proposed rule given the scope of the prospective changes. 

I oppose the proposed rule because I am concerned it will undermine the accuracy and usefulness of census data, particularly for marginalized Americans. Census counts are used for a wide variety of important purposes, from planning and funding critical infrastructure to understanding patterns of discrimination. By leading to a census that only counts part of the population and contains limited demographic data, the proposed rule will make it harder for policy makers to make evidence-based decisions that affect Americans everyday lives. Underrepresented groups, including women, people of color, and LGBTQ+ people, among others, will be most negatively impacted. 

If the proposed residence criteria are finalized, the U.S. will lose a complete and accurate count of the population and its distribution and stray from the Constitutions mandate to count all persons. The proposed rule would, for the first time, exclude many U.S. residents from the apportionment count, including international students, work visa-holders, and refugees and asylum seekers. The proposed changes would also increase the likelihood that residents are counted in the wrong location, such as by defining usual residence based on tax records that may not reflect the physical address where someone primarily lives, pays taxes, and votes. The census strives to count everyone once, only once, and in the right place so that resources can be distributed based on need and public services can be accurately planned. The proposed rule would undermine this stated goal. 

By prohibiting questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation, the proposed rule would also cause the U.S. to lose critical, reliable demographic data. Every U.S. census has collected race and ethnicity data in some form since the first in 1790. These data are the foundation for a wide variety of population-based surveys and studies that allow researchers to gain important understanding of national issues and inequities. Although sexual orientation is not currently asked about in the census, barring these questions from future censuses will similarly restrict data on LGBTQ+ Americans. Robust demographic data is necessary to enforce civil rights laws and ensure equal opportunity for all Americans. If finalized, the proposed rule would make it harder to identify and address issues like workplace discrimination, public health discrepancies, and more. 

Census data needs to accurately represent all Americans. For the reasons stated above, I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw and revise the proposed rule, especially part 60 and 70. Thank you for your consideration. 

Sincerely, 
Jackie Gray
Carrboro, NC

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I write in support of the Census Bureau's proposed rule, "Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions" (Docket No. USBC-2026-0628; RIN 0607-AA75).

The Constitution calls for an "actual Enumeration" every ten years so that representation can be fairly apportioned among the states. The decennial census is meant to be a count, not a survey or a statistical estimate. Americans' voice in Congress depends on that count being right.

In 2020, the Bureau intentionally introduced statistical noise into the population data used to draw congressional and legislative districts. Data that determine political representation should never be deliberately altered. I support proposed  70.3, which directs the Bureau to prioritize the accuracy of the population count and prohibits publishing demographic data when doing so would introduce uncertainty into national or state population counts.

I also support the proposed residence criteria. Being counted at one's "usual residence" has never meant mere physical presence on Census Day. It reflects a lasting connection to a place, which is why service members stationed abroad are still counted in their home states. Counting citizens and lawful permanent residents, and excluding foreign nationals who are here unlawfully or temporarily, follows that principle.

I support keeping the enumeration questionnaire focused on the count itself. The Bureau can continue to produce demographic and statistical information through the American Community Survey and other tools, but those products should remain separate from the constitutional headcount.

To make these reforms durable, I urge the Bureau to state clearly in the final rule that the constitutional enumeration, and the counts used for apportionment and redistricting, are fundamentally distinct from routine federal statistical products and may not be adjusted to serve other statistical purposes.

Please finalize this rule so that the 2030 Census delivers an accurate count and restores Americans' trust in how they are represented.

Respectfully,
Kathleen Gualtieri
Morton, PA

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Examples of these uses include: . 

* Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. 

* Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

* Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

* Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

* Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

* Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

* Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

* Determining state higher education funding formulas 

* Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

* Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

* Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

First, to ensure a fair and accurate census,  the Census Bureau should  extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. Second, I oppose both the proposed changes to the residence criteria and the proposed regulations regarding demographic questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. The Census Bureau should  withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The Constitution requires  counting all people living in the United States. 

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (including children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count. 

Revise the tax records language so that those whose mailing address differs from their residential address (servicemembers, those with a post office box) are not excluded.  

• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for civil rights enforcement, among other uses, and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The prohibition, as written, may also restrict the collection or publication of census data on same-sex couples that was asked in 2020. 

 The proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Sincerely,
Ms. thalia lubin
Redwood City, CA

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am an educator, an education researcher, and a citizen. I object to both the US Census Bureau’s proposed new residence criteria and the proposed regulations for reducing the collection of demographic information on upcoming censuses. 

As for the Residence Criteria: As described in the regulatory text, the census has never been merely a count of citizens, but of the people who live in each state and congressional district – its inhabitants. Political representation is based on these inhabitants, not merely those who have the vote. Children have always been counted despite being too young to vote. Women were counted before they gained suffrage in 1920. Even in the antebellum South, enslaved people counted towards political representation even though this increased the power of their enslavers. Citizenship and even personhood were not relevant criteria in these counts. We should be counting every person living in each area for purposes of congressional apportionment.

But census counts are used not only for congressional apportionment – their initial political function – but also, importantly, by custom and statute, for distributing funds and resources to specific areas based on need. A wide variety of public services – public transportation and highways, housing, food safety services, policing, educational resources, the electric grid, internet infrastructure, health care, and so on are used by both citizens and non-citizens; by those living in each area legally and permanently, as well as those living there temporarily or illegally. By failing to count these temporary or undocumented but very real people – that is, those who do not fit the restrictions proposed by the Census Bureau but who put demands on the systems providing these essential services – funds and supports for systems and services will not be distributed based on the needs of the population, as intended by Congress. Some areas with proportionately fewer temporary or undocumented people will get more resources than their populations require; others with proportionately more temporary or undocumented people will get fewer resources than are needed to support the health and well-being of their populations. This will have an impact not only on the uncounted, but also on their neighbors and citizens. 

Furthermore, the rule seems to limit counting of people who do not have a permanent domicile, excluding unhoused people living on the streets, or temporarily sharing space with relatives or friends, as well as those who are itinerant and persistently on the road for their work. These are important groups for policymakers and citizens to know about and should be included in the census count. 

The proposed residency rule attempts to impose a restricted view of who counts as a person in our understanding of the US population, a restricted view that is at odds with Congressional intent for use of Census data in policy-making and resource distribution, and at odds with the views of many people, myself included, and should be rejected. 

I also object to the proposed removal of demographic questions about race, ethnicity and sexual orientation. I use these demographic variables in my work with students through the Census-at-School database, and they are important to help students understand changes in discrimination over time. In addition, this administration seems to believe that by not paying attention to racial or ethnic differences, that they are somehow being more equitable or fair. But when we don’t collect this information, we lose our ability to tell whether there are persistent differences in impact by racial and ethnic, or sexual orientation identities, and whether any policy efforts to reduce negative race-/ ethnicity-/ sexual-orientation-based differences have been effective. Racial and ethnic differences in health care, education, housing, equitable pay, experiences of violent crime, equitable legal protections, and on and on are well-documented over many decades. If we stop collecting these data, the differences don’t just go away – but we won’t know whether any efforts to assure equity are being effective. Racially motivated housing, education and wage discrimination (among others) will persist, but we will be blind to these differences and so limited in our capacity to address them. Continuity of collection of these data, especially in an increasingly multi-racial and multi-ethnic society, is essential for citizens and their governments to understand the impacts of policies intended to improve the quality of life of everyone.

The Census proposes to only include people if their address is confirmed by tax records -- which could mean millions, particularly low-income families, could be missed in the decennial Census. Overall, this would leave out people who actually live in our community, including many people who are lawfully present in the United States.For all past Census counts, including the 2020 Census, foreign citizens living in the United States were generally counted where they lived and slept most of the time. That approach recognizes the basic purpose of a Census: accurately counting the people who live in our communities. The 14th Amendment requires congressional representation to be apportioned according to the “whole number of persons in each State.”I am also deeply concerned by the proposal to prohibit race and ethnicity questions, along with sexual orientation, on the decennial Census enumeration questionnaire. The Census Bureau itself recognizes the importance of race data for civil rights protections, legislative redistricting, equal employment opportunities, and identifying disparities.The 2030 Census will determine congressional, state, and local representation for the decade that follows. It must be complete, accurate, and protected from political manipulation.Please withdraw this proposed rule and preserve a Census that fairly and accurately counts our community.Michele  [X] Syracuse , New York 13207

Comment:

I oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census because a fair and accurate census is critical to ensuring every community is counted, fairly represented, and able to get the resources people need to live healthy lives — including sexual and reproductive healthcare. An inaccurate or incomplete census can deepen existing inequities, particularly for communities that already face disenfranchisement and barriers to healthcare. 

A fair and accurate census is essential to our health and rights. 

Census data help determine access to programs patients and their families rely on, including important programs like Medicaid, SNAP, WIC, and TANF. Accurate census data also shape political representation by determining how seats in the U.S. House of Representatives are apportioned among states and providing data used for redistricting. When communities are undercounted or excluded, they risk losing both resources and political representation. 

The Census Bureau and Department of Commerce must:

1. Count all people residing in the United States in the 2030 Census, without regard to immigration status. Excluding noncitizens from census apportionment data violates the Constitution and established legal precedent. It would suppress the count of many communities, effectively erasing them from critical datasets and depriving them of resources and congressional representation –— including resources and political representation that support access to healthcare.

2. Continue collecting race and ethnicity data and implement the 2024 OMB SPD 15 standards. Census race and ethnicity data are essential for important research across many sectors, for upholding civil rights, and for growing the economy. Extensive Census Bureau research and engagement with expert stakeholders shows that implementing the modernized 2024 OMB SPD 15 standards for race and ethnicity data collection will yield data that more accurately represent the nation’s increasingly diverse population.

3. Remove the clause banning the addition of future questions on sexual orientation. Proposed changes to demographic items should be based on research and guided by a deliberative and transparent process, including extensive stakeholder consultation.

4. Withdraw other proposed changes to residence criteria, including tying place of residence to tax records and "lawful residence," and the adoption of a three month enumeration period. The Census Bureau must extensively research and consult with stakeholders about the potential effects of such changes before proposing their implementation in a decennial census.

5. Halt the practice of prison gerrymandering by counting incarcerated individuals in their home communities. This will yield more accurate census data and ensure that communities receive the congressional representation to which they are entitled.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I write in support of the Census Bureau's proposed rule, "Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions" (Docket No. USBC-2026-0628; RIN 0607-AA75).

The Constitution calls for an "actual Enumeration" every ten years so that representation can be fairly apportioned among the states. The decennial census is meant to be a count, not a survey or a statistical estimate. Americans' voice in Congress depends on that count being right.

In 2020, the Bureau intentionally introduced statistical noise into the population data used to draw congressional and legislative districts. Data that determine political representation should never be deliberately altered. I support proposed  70.3, which directs the Bureau to prioritize the accuracy of the population count and prohibits publishing demographic data when doing so would introduce uncertainty into national or state population counts.

I also support the proposed residence criteria. Being counted at one's "usual residence" has never meant mere physical presence on Census Day. It reflects a lasting connection to a place, which is why service members stationed abroad are still counted in their home states. Counting citizens and lawful permanent residents, and excluding foreign nationals who are here unlawfully or temporarily, follows that principle.

I support keeping the enumeration questionnaire focused on the count itself. The Bureau can continue to produce demographic and statistical information through the American Community Survey and other tools, but those products should remain separate from the constitutional headcount.

To make these reforms durable, I urge the Bureau to state clearly in the final rule that the constitutional enumeration, and the counts used for apportionment and redistricting, are fundamentally distinct from routine federal statistical products and may not be adjusted to serve other statistical purposes.

Please finalize this rule so that the 2030 Census delivers an accurate count and restores Americans' trust in how they are represented.

Respectfully,
Gary Lamons
Clayton, CA

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census. These changes will not only weaken the accuracy and integrity of our nation's most important population count, but they will also harm our communities, and I strongly urge the Bureau to reject them. 

First, removing questions of race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation erases the full scope of my identity when I participate in the Census survey. These data points are not optional. They are the tools we use to enforce civil rights laws, monitor discrimination, and measure the disparities that still affect millions of people. Excluding them from the count does not make them disappear from our society, but it does make our government less equipped to handle big issues when they arise. 

The Constitution is clear: the census must count ALL persons living in the United States, regardless of their immigration or citizenship status. The proposal to exclude non-citizens, including those residents with some type of lawful status, violates more than two centuries of legal precedent. Every person counted in this country contributes to our communities, and every person deserves to be fully seen. 

The consequences of these changes will negatively impact our daily lives. The census affects everything. It determines political representation and the drawing of voting districts. It guides how billions of dollars in federal funding are used to close persistent disparities in schools, hospitals, and other government programs that are designed to improve our lives.  

The census is the foundation of our democracy. It must reflect the complete yet nuanced reality of who we are as a nation. And it must reflect the lives of our friends and neighbors who may not look, think, or speak like we do. I ask the Bureau to withdraw these proposed changes and to preserve a count that includes everyone and represents everyone. 

Thank you for considering my comment.

Sincerely,
Larry Barbee

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). 

As an educator, I care about a fair and accurate census because census data and other federal datasets based on the census are used to make key decisions that affect our nation’s students, educators, and schools.  

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Examples of these uses include: . 

* Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. 

* Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

* Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

* Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

* Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

* Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

* Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

* Determining state higher education funding formulas 

* Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

* Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

* Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

First, to ensure a fair and accurate census,  the Census Bureau should  extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. Second, I oppose both the proposed changes to the residence criteria and the proposed regulations regarding demographic questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. The Census Bureau should  withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The Constitution requires  counting all people living in the United States. 

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (including children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count. 

Revise the tax records language so that those whose mailing address differs from their residential address (servicemembers, those with a post office box) are not excluded.  

• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for civil rights enforcement, among other uses, and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The prohibition, as written, may also restrict the collection or publication of census data on same-sex couples that was asked in 2020. 

 The proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Sincerely,
Mr. John Sheppeck
Guilderland, NY

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I write in support of the Census Bureau's proposed rule, "Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions" (Docket No. USBC-2026-0628; RIN 0607-AA75).

The Constitution calls for an "actual Enumeration" every ten years so that representation can be fairly apportioned among the states. The decennial census is meant to be a count, not a survey or a statistical estimate. Americans' voice in Congress depends on that count being right.

In 2020, the Bureau intentionally introduced statistical noise into the population data used to draw congressional and legislative districts. Data that determine political representation should never be deliberately altered. I support proposed  70.3, which directs the Bureau to prioritize the accuracy of the population count and prohibits publishing demographic data when doing so would introduce uncertainty into national or state population counts.

I also support the proposed residence criteria. Being counted at one's "usual residence" has never meant mere physical presence on Census Day. It reflects a lasting connection to a place, which is why service members stationed abroad are still counted in their home states. Counting citizens and lawful permanent residents, and excluding foreign nationals who are here unlawfully or temporarily, follows that principle.

I support keeping the enumeration questionnaire focused on the count itself. The Bureau can continue to produce demographic and statistical information through the American Community Survey and other tools, but those products should remain separate from the constitutional headcount.

To make these reforms durable, I urge the Bureau to state clearly in the final rule that the constitutional enumeration, and the counts used for apportionment and redistricting, are fundamentally distinct from routine federal statistical products and may not be adjusted to serve other statistical purposes.

Please finalize this rule so that the 2030 Census delivers an accurate count and restores Americans' trust in how they are represented.

Respectfully,
Katherine Marron
Havre de Grace, MD

I oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census because a fair and accurate census is critical to ensuring every community is counted, fairly represented, and able to get the resources people need to live healthy lives — including sexual and reproductive healthcare. An inaccurate or incomplete census can deepen existing inequities, particularly for communities that already face disenfranchisement and barriers to healthcare. 

A fair and accurate census is essential to our health and rights. 

Census data help determine access to programs patients and their families rely on, including important programs like Medicaid, SNAP, WIC, and TANF. Accurate census data also shape political representation by determining how seats in the U.S. House of Representatives are apportioned among states and providing data used for redistricting. When communities are undercounted or excluded, they risk losing both resources and political representation. 

The Census Bureau and Department of Commerce must:

1. Count all people residing in the United States in the 2030 Census, without regard to immigration status. Excluding noncitizens from census apportionment data violates the Constitution and established legal precedent. It would suppress the count of many communities, effectively erasing them from critical datasets and depriving them of resources and congressional representation –— including resources and political representation that support access to healthcare.

2. Continue collecting race and ethnicity data and implement the 2024 OMB SPD 15 standards. Census race and ethnicity data are essential for important research across many sectors, for upholding civil rights, and for growing the economy. Extensive Census Bureau research and engagement with expert stakeholders shows that implementing the modernized 2024 OMB SPD 15 standards for race and ethnicity data collection will yield data that more accurately represent the nation’s increasingly diverse population.

3. Remove the clause banning the addition of future questions on sexual orientation. Proposed changes to demographic items should be based on research and guided by a deliberative and transparent process, including extensive stakeholder consultation.

4. Withdraw other proposed changes to residence criteria, including tying place of residence to tax records and "lawful residence," and the adoption of a three month enumeration period. The Census Bureau must extensively research and consult with stakeholders about the potential effects of such changes before proposing their implementation in a decennial census.

5. Halt the practice of prison gerrymandering by counting incarcerated individuals in their home communities. This will yield more accurate census data and ensure that communities receive the congressional representation to which they are entitled.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I live in Seattle, King County, WA. I live with my spouse and use a mailing address for most things.

Census counts shape my community schools, our roads, hospitals, local emergency planning, and more.

I am concerned that:

    The rule would leave many residents of my community out of the apportionment count, and the fear it creates would lower response in households with citizens, too.
    *Tying “usual residence” to tax records would misplace people who file taxes from a P.O. box, a parent's home, or a tax preparer's office.
    *Prohibiting race and ethnicity questions would end data my community relies on.
    *The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.

I ask the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and keep its commitment to count everyone once, only once, and in the right place as the Constitution requires.

I also ask the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. Changes of this scope deserve more time for the public to review and respond.

Edward Caffee 
Seattle, Washington

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am mother of two young children in Overland Park, Kansas, and I care about a fair and accurate census because I want my children to grow up in a country where all people are treated equally and counted.

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Thank you.
