Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
My name is [Your Name] and I am your constituent from [City/Zip Code]. As Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander (AANHPI) Heritage Month comes to a close, I write to urge you to support AANHPI students by cosponsoring the All Students Count Act.

To the U.S. Census Bureau: 

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule titled “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005). Eliminating the collection of race and ethnic data, prohibiting the collection of sexual orientation, and leaving non-citizens out of the apportionment would significantly harm the Southeast Asian American (SEAA) and broader Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander (AANHPI) communities. I respectfully request that the Census Bureau withdraw the proposed rule and extend the comment period to December 10, 2026. 

I am deeply concerned that excluding refugees, asylum seekers, and other U.S. residents from being counted will be an inaccurate representation of Americans. The purpose of the census is to count all people, and decisions using taxpayer money and government funds will be made without factual information. The rule would also bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.

This proposed rule would significantly harm the SEAA and AANHPI communities. The AANHPI community is not a homogenous population; it encompasses over 50 different ethnic groups and 100 languages and dialects. There are vast socioeconomic disparities within the AANHPI population, often related to their migratory and historical experience. SEAAs, such as the Cambodian, Hmong, Laotian, and Mien populations, often have higher rates of poverty and lower educational attainment rates than both the broader AANHPI and American populations. 

For SEAAs, this disparity is generally tied to their experiences escaping their countries of origin and resettlement in the United States after the Vietnam War, Secret War in Laos, and Khmer Rouge genocide in Cambodia. For example, because of the 2020 Census, we now know that the Mien population has lower educational attainment rates compared to the general American and AANHPI populations. Additionally, the data also show that Mien men have a lower educational attainment rate compared to women. Such information could only be obtained because of the census, which is the primary source for data collection and reporting of small ethnic groups. These data cannot be replicated by other surveys, including the American Community Survey. 

Accurate data, reflective of race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation, help our elected officials properly identify and address the unique needs and challenges of our communities. Prohibiting the collection of this demographic data would prevent our government officials from passing informed public policy; hamper the ability of community-based organizations to demonstrate data narratives for fundraising purposes; and inhibit the ability of students and academics studying our communities from accessing the most robust source of information on SEAAs and the broader AANHPI community. 

Thank you for taking my comment into consideration. I reiterate my request that the US Census Bureau withdraws the proposed rule; preserves the collection of race and ethnic data; and keeps its commitment to count everyone once, only once, and in the right place.

I also ask the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. Changes of this scope deserve more time for the public to review and respond.

Sincerely,
Akemi Chan-Imai
Martinez, CA 94553

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Re: Docket No. USBC-2026-0628, Proposed Residence Criteria and Demographic Question Restrictions for the 2030 Census

I oppose this proposed rule and ask the Census Bureau to withdraw it.

I live in Seattle, King County, Washington. My community depends on census data for our county’s road and transit funding. As someone who uses public transit, this is very important to me. Without proper funding our region cannot continue to expand public transit in the Greater Seattle Area.

The rule would stop counting millions of people who live here lawfully, including workers on visas, students, and people with temporary protected status or pending asylum claims, along with undocumented residents. The Fourteenth Amendment requires “counting the whole number of persons in each State.” Every census since 1790 has counted everyone who lives here, regardless of citizenship. The rule does not say whether the people it excludes will be counted for any purpose, or whether they will appear in the population totals that decide federal funding for my state. I ask the Bureau to answer that on the record. The Bureau’s own 2019 research found that asking about citizenship would cut responses from noncitizen households by 8 percent. This rule goes further than that question did, and it will keep families in my community, including citizen children, from answering at all.

The rule also removes race and ethnicity from the census for the first time since 1790. Every measure of whether this country treats its people equally starts with that count. We know how much shorter Black and Native American lives are, how much lower Black homeownership is, which neighborhoods banks have redlined, and which children the last census missed, because the census asks. Take the question away and the disparities do not end. They become impossible to prove, and impossible to fix. The Bureau’s own analysis, posted with this docket, admits there are “no other comparably accurate, comprehensive, and reliable sources” for this data. A government that stops counting harm by race is choosing not to see it.

The Bureau’s own analysis admits it “cannot quantify” any cost or benefit of this rule. A rule the agency cannot evaluate should not be adopted.

Anonymous Taxpayer and Regular Voter

The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities.

Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Re: Docket USBC-2026-0628, Strong Support for Proposed 15 CFR § 60.4

To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I strongly support proposed 15 CFR § 60.4 and urge its adoption without weakening its eligibility requirements. ONLY U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents should be included in the population used to allocate seats in the U.S. House of Representatives. All other foreign citizens, including illegal aliens, must be excluded from that apportionment count. This distinction must be explicit and applied consistently nationwide.

Congressional apportionment distributes political power among the states for an entire decade. With a fixed total of 435 House seats, representation gained by one state affects the representation available to others. Who is included in that calculation has consequences for Americans throughout the country.

I consider it fundamentally unfair to American citizens, who have a vested interest in this country and its future, for their congressional representation to be weakened because other states count foreign citizens who possess neither U.S. citizenship nor lawful permanent resident status. Citizens should not lose political influence because another jurisdiction includes those populations in its apportionment count. The proposed standard recognizes citizenship and permanent lawful residence as meaningful, enduring connections to the United States.

I am particularly concerned about the political incentive the current system creates for Democratic-led cities and states that adopt policies accommodating illegal immigration. When illegal aliens are included in the apportionment population, their presence can help a state gain additional House seats or retain seats it might otherwise lose. That creates an opportunity to pursue political advantage through population growth driven by illegal immigration. I strongly object to a system that leaves room for elected officials to use that incentive to preserve or expand their power.

No government or political party should be rewarded with greater congressional representation for accommodating illegal immigration. American citizens deserve an apportionment standard that protects fair representation and prevents unlawful residence from becoming a source of congressional power.

The need for population information for public services and planning should be addressed separately. The Bureau states that it expects to continue maintaining and publishing statistics apart from those used for apportionment. Those statistical needs do not justify abandoning a clear eligibility standard for distributing House seats.

I urge the Bureau to verify eligibility through reliable administrative records and apply the same requirements in every state.

Please adopt proposed § 60.4 without diluting its central distinction. Count U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents for congressional apportionment. Exclude other foreign citizens. Protect fair representation and public confidence through a clear national standard.

Thank you for considering my comments.

Sincerely,
Michael Bowe

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing in opposition to the Census Bureau's proposed rule: "Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions" (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I strongly object to a change that would radically alter who is counted for congressional apportionment, which local communities are resourced, and whether we can track progress on civil rights protections without race and ethnicity questions from the decennial census.

1. The Census Must Count Everyone Who Lives Here

The Constitution requires representation to be based on the "whole number of persons in each State," not citizens specifically. This rule would exclude international students, work visa holders, refugees, and asylum seekers from the count for the first time, even though they live in our communities, work, pay taxes, and use the same roads and schools as everyone else. Attempting to sort people by legal status also creates fear that keeps entire households, including U.S. citizens, from responding at all.

2. Counting People by Administrative Record Will Distort Representation

The rule would place people based on tax records and other administrative data rather than where they actually live. Tax records often list an old address, a P.O. box, or a preparer's office, which fails students, seasonal workers, service members, and anyone who moved recently. Federal law has always set a single fixed date, April 1, for the census. This rule replaces that with a shifting three-month window, adding complexity without adding accuracy.

3. Race and Ethnicity Data Are Essential

The census has asked about race in some form since the very first census in 1790. This data is what allows the country to track discrimination, enforce voting rights, and direct public health and civil rights resources. The American Community Survey cannot replace it, since it only produces estimates and itself relies on the decennial census for accuracy. The rule would also make nearly every demographic question voluntary, despite a federal law requiring people to answer census questions. And it would bar any future question on sexual orientation, though the more significant risk is a new provision giving the Bureau broad discretion to withhold published data on smaller communities, including same-sex households.

4. Communities Without Accurate Data Get Left Behind

Arab Americans have historically been undercounted because no census category captured them. The 2030 Census is set to be the first with a dedicated Middle Eastern or North African (MENA) category, a change advocates spent years securing to improve data collection on people from the MENA region. This rule would eliminate that progress along with all race and ethnicity data collection. Any community without accurate data becomes harder to serve, harder to protect, and easier to overlook.

I urge the Census Bureau and the Department of Commerce to withdraw these proposed changes and to count everyone who lives here, accurately and in the right place.

Sincerely,
Laura

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). 

As an educator, I care about a fair and accurate census because census data and other federal datasets based on the census are used to make key decisions that affect our nation’s students, educators, and schools.  

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Examples of these uses include: . 

* Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. 

* Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

* Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

* Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

* Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

* Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

* Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

* Determining state higher education funding formulas 

* Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

* Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

* Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

First, to ensure a fair and accurate census,  the Census Bureau should  extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. Second, I oppose both the proposed changes to the residence criteria and the proposed regulations regarding demographic questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. The Census Bureau should  withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The Constitution requires  counting all people living in the United States. 

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (including children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count. 

Revise the tax records language so that those whose mailing address differs from their residential address (servicemembers, those with a post office box) are not excluded.  

• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for civil rights enforcement, among other uses, and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The prohibition, as written, may also restrict the collection or publication of census data on same-sex couples that was asked in 2020. 

 The proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Sincerely,
Mr Ed Fiedler
Austin, TX

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I write in support of the Census Bureau's proposed rule, "Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions" (Docket No. USBC-2026-0628; RIN 0607-AA75).

The Constitution calls for an "actual Enumeration" every ten years so that representation can be fairly apportioned among the states. The decennial census is meant to be a count, not a survey or a statistical estimate. Americans' voice in Congress depends on that count being right.

In 2020, the Bureau intentionally introduced statistical noise into the population data used to draw congressional and legislative districts. Data that determine political representation should never be deliberately altered. I support proposed  70.3, which directs the Bureau to prioritize the accuracy of the population count and prohibits publishing demographic data when doing so would introduce uncertainty into national or state population counts.

I also support the proposed residence criteria. Being counted at one's "usual residence" has never meant mere physical presence on Census Day. It reflects a lasting connection to a place, which is why service members stationed abroad are still counted in their home states. Counting citizens and lawful permanent residents, and excluding foreign nationals who are here unlawfully or temporarily, follows that principle.

I support keeping the enumeration questionnaire focused on the count itself. The Bureau can continue to produce demographic and statistical information through the American Community Survey and other tools, but those products should remain separate from the constitutional headcount.

To make these reforms durable, I urge the Bureau to state clearly in the final rule that the constitutional enumeration, and the counts used for apportionment and redistricting, are fundamentally distinct from routine federal statistical products and may not be adjusted to serve other statistical purposes.

Please finalize this rule so that the 2030 Census delivers an accurate count and restores Americans' trust in how they are represented.

Respectfully,
Bennett Robichaux
LaPlace, LA

I oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census because a fair and accurate census is critical to ensuring every community is counted, fairly represented, and able to get the resources people need to live healthy lives — including sexual and reproductive healthcare. An inaccurate or incomplete census can deepen existing inequities, particularly for communities that already face disenfranchisement and barriers to healthcare. 

A fair and accurate census is essential to our health and rights. 

Census data help determine access to programs patients and their families rely on, including important programs like Medicaid, SNAP, WIC, and TANF. Accurate census data also shape political representation by determining how seats in the U.S. House of Representatives are apportioned among states and providing data used for redistricting. When communities are undercounted or excluded, they risk losing both resources and political representation. 

The Census Bureau and Department of Commerce must:

1. Count all people residing in the United States in the 2030 Census, without regard to immigration status. Excluding noncitizens from census apportionment data violates the Constitution and established legal precedent. It would suppress the count of many communities, effectively erasing them from critical datasets and depriving them of resources and congressional representation –— including resources and political representation that support access to healthcare.

2. Continue collecting race and ethnicity data and implement the 2024 OMB SPD 15 standards. Census race and ethnicity data are essential for important research across many sectors, for upholding civil rights, and for growing the economy. Extensive Census Bureau research and engagement with expert stakeholders shows that implementing the modernized 2024 OMB SPD 15 standards for race and ethnicity data collection will yield data that more accurately represent the nation’s increasingly diverse population.

3. Remove the clause banning the addition of future questions on sexual orientation. Proposed changes to demographic items should be based on research and guided by a deliberative and transparent process, including extensive stakeholder consultation.

4. Withdraw other proposed changes to residence criteria, including tying place of residence to tax records and "lawful residence," and the adoption of a three month enumeration period. The Census Bureau must extensively research and consult with stakeholders about the potential effects of such changes before proposing their implementation in a decennial census.

5. Halt the practice of prison gerrymandering by counting incarcerated individuals in their home communities. This will yield more accurate census data and ensure that communities receive the congressional representation to which they are entitled.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census. These changes will not only weaken the accuracy and integrity of our nation's most important population count, but they will also harm our communities, and I strongly urge the Bureau to reject them. 

First, removing questions of race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation erases the full scope of my identity when I participate in the Census survey. These data points are not optional. They are the tools we use to enforce civil rights laws, monitor discrimination, and measure the disparities that still affect millions of people. Excluding them from the count does not make them disappear from our society, but it does make our government less equipped to handle big issues when they arise. 

The Constitution is clear: the census must count ALL persons living in the United States, regardless of their immigration or citizenship status. The proposal to exclude non-citizens, including those residents with some type of lawful status, violates more than two centuries of legal precedent. Every person counted in this country contributes to our communities, and every person deserves to be fully seen. 

The consequences of these changes will negatively impact our daily lives. The census affects everything. It determines political representation and the drawing of voting districts. It guides how billions of dollars in federal funding are used to close persistent disparities in schools, hospitals, and other government programs that are designed to improve our lives.  

The census is the foundation of our democracy. It must reflect the complete yet nuanced reality of who we are as a nation. And it must reflect the lives of our friends and neighbors who may not look, think, or speak like we do. I ask the Bureau to withdraw these proposed changes and to preserve a count that includes everyone and represents everyone. 

Thank you for considering my comment.

Sincerely,
Bessie Pierce

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule: Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions.
The census has counted all residents for apportionment regardless of legal status for 230 years. Article I, Section 2, Clause 3 of the U.S. Constitution mandates that an "actual Enumeration" of the population be conducted within three years of the first Congress meeting and every subsequent term of ten years. The 14th Amendment further clarifies that representatives are apportioned by counting the "whole number of persons" in each state.
We have always counted native-born U.S. citizens, naturalized U.S. citizens, non-citizen U.S. nationals, lawful permanent residents and temporary migrants, such as foreign students, refugees, asylum seekers and undocumented immigrants. The census has never left out residents because of their immigration status.
The census determines the funding and representation of our communities. By not counting all people, communities will not get the resources they need for schools, hospitals, roads, firefighters and other critical services. It is very important to me that each and EVERY person be counted, so that monies can be fairly distributed.
This proposal would mean there would no longer be a complete and accurate count of our population. I strongly oppose this rule and encourage the census bureau not to enact it.

Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule: Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions.
The census has counted all residents for apportionment regardless of legal status for 230 years. Article I, Section 2, Clause 3 of the U.S. Constitution mandates that an "actual Enumeration" of the population be conducted within three years of the first Congress meeting and every subsequent term of ten years. This proposal would mean there would no longer be a complete and accurate count of our population. I strongly oppose this rule and encourage the census bureau not to enact it.

Comment:
My name is [Your Name] and I am your constituent from [City/Zip Code]. As Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander (AANHPI) Heritage Month comes to a close, I write to urge you to support AANHPI students by cosponsoring the All Students Count Act.

To the U.S. Census Bureau: 

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule titled “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005). Eliminating the collection of race and ethnic data, prohibiting the collection of sexual orientation, and leaving non-citizens out of the apportionment would significantly harm the Southeast Asian American (SEAA) and broader Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander (AANHPI) communities. I respectfully request that the Census Bureau withdraw the proposed rule and extend the comment period to December 10, 2026. 

This proposed rule would significantly harm the SEAA and AANHPI communities. The AANHPI community is not a homogenous population; it encompasses over 50 different ethnic groups and 100 languages and dialects. There are vast socioeconomic disparities within the AANHPI population, often related to their migratory and historical experience. SEAAs, such as the Cambodian, Hmong, Laotian, and Mien populations, often have higher rates of poverty and lower educational attainment rates than both the broader AANHPI and American populations. 

For SEAAs, this disparity is generally tied to their experiences escaping their countries of origin and resettlement in the United States after the Vietnam War, Secret War in Laos, and Khmer Rouge genocide in Cambodia. For example, because of the 2020 Census, we now know that the Mien population has lower educational attainment rates compared to the general American and AANHPI populations. Additionally, the data also show that Mien men have a lower educational attainment rate compared to women. Such information could only be obtained because of the census, which is the primary source for data collection and reporting of small ethnic groups. These data cannot be replicated by other surveys, including the American Community Survey. 

Accurate data, reflective of race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation, help our elected officials properly identify and address the unique needs and challenges of our communities. Prohibiting the collection of this demographic data would prevent our government officials from passing informed public policy; hamper the ability of community-based organizations to demonstrate data narratives for fundraising purposes; and inhibit the ability of students and academics studying our communities from accessing the most robust source of information on SEAAs and the broader AANHPI community. 

Thank you for taking my comment into consideration. I reiterate my request that the US Census Bureau withdraws the proposed rule; preserves the collection of race and ethnic data; and keeps its commitment to count everyone once, only once, and in the right place.

I also ask the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. Changes of this scope deserve more time for the public to review and respond.

Portland, ME 04102

The Constitution calls for an "actual Enumeration" every ten years so that representation can be fairly apportioned among the states. The decennial census is meant to be a count, not a survey or a statistical estimate. Americans' voice in Congress depends on that count being right.

In 2020, the Bureau intentionally introduced statistical noise into the population data used to draw congressional and legislative districts. Data that determine political representation should never be deliberately altered. I support proposed  70.3, which directs the Bureau to prioritize the accuracy of the population count and prohibits publishing demographic data when doing so would introduce uncertainty into national or state population counts.

I also support the proposed residence criteria. Being counted at one's "usual residence" has never meant mere physical presence on Census Day. It reflects a lasting connection to a place, which is why service members stationed abroad are still counted in their home states. Counting citizens and lawful permanent residents, and excluding foreign nationals who are here unlawfully or temporarily, follows that principle.

I support keeping the enumeration questionnaire focused on the count itself. The Bureau can continue to produce demographic and statistical information through the American Community Survey and other tools, but those products should remain separate from the constitutional headcount.

To make these reforms durable, I urge the Bureau to state clearly in the final rule that the constitutional enumeration, and the counts used for apportionment and redistricting, are fundamentally distinct from routine federal statistical products and may not be adjusted to serve other statistical purposes.

Please finalize this rule so that the 2030 Census delivers an accurate count and restores Americans' trust in how they are represented.

Respectfully,
Dawn Kelly
St. Augustine, Fl 32086

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
A fair and accurate U.S. Census is both a constitutional mandate and an imperative to a functioning democracy. The data collected determines apportionment counts (including the Electoral College), supports redistricting efforts, and informs policymakers at local, state, and federal levels. The data is also critical to the annual distribution of more than $1.5 trillion through hundreds of federal programs. Schools, roads, hospitals, emergency preparedness, and more are reliant on accurate data provided by the Census so that towns, cities, and states can function well for all residents. A new proposed rule by the Department of Commerce would change the way the Census is conducted in two extremely harmful ways.

First, it would change the residence criteria by calling for an unprecedented exclusion of non-citizens who are not green card holders, clearly running afoul of the 14th Amendment to the Constitution. This would mean that international students, work visa holders, recognized refugees, asylum seekers, and undocumented individuals would all lose representation. The Pew Research Center estimates that this represents a staggering 16 million individuals in total.

Second, it would eliminate questions about race and ethnicity from the Census. Without these critical data, it would be far more difficult to track disparities in everything from from healthcare to the environment, making it nearly impossible to enforce civil rights laws. It would also skew the distribution of federal funding away from communities that need it the most and from programs that were designed to protect them.

The whole point of the census is to count everyone who lives in this country so we can fairly divide representation and make sure communities get the resources they need. That’s how it’s worked for more than two centuries. The Constitution requires an “actual Enumeration” every ten years, and the 14th Amendment makes it clear that apportionment is based on the “whole number of persons” in each state — not just certain categories of people.

For 230 years, the census has counted all residents, no matter their immigration status. That includes native‑born citizens, naturalized citizens, non‑citizen nationals, permanent residents, foreign students, refugees, asylum seekers, and undocumented immigrants. This proposal would break with long‑standing practice and undermine the accuracy of the census. I strongly oppose it and urge the Census Bureau not to move forward with this rule.

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

As written, the proposed rule would seriously compromise the quality of the research in my field. I urge the Census Bureau to reconsider these changes so that the census can continue to be a rich and accurate source of data for my research.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
As a research scientist specializing in epidemiology and public health, I am concerned about the potential implications of the proposed changes to the 2030 Census for scientific research, public health planning, healthcare resource allocation, and evidence-based policymaking.

Specifically, the proposed changes to Section 60, which would exclude certain individuals from population counts and introduce a residency reference period rather than enumerating individuals based on where they usually live and sleep as of Census Day, could significantly affect our ability to characterize population health and environmental exposures accurately. In epidemiological research, including studies examining the neural exposome and environmental determinants of cognitive health, knowing where people actually reside is essential. Residential location influences environmental exposures, access to healthcare, availability of community resources, and other social determinants of health. Accurate population counts, regardless of immigration status, are therefore critical for understanding disease patterns, identifying community needs, and preparing public health systems.

I am equally concerned about the proposed elimination of race and ethnicity questions. These demographic data are fundamental to identifying and monitoring health disparities, particularly among populations that experience disproportionate burdens of chronic diseases. For example, research consistently documents a greater burden of Alzheimer's disease and related dementias among certain racial and ethnic populations, including Black/African American, Hispanic, and some Indigenous communities. Without reliable, geographically detailed demographic information, researchers and public health agencies would face substantial challenges in estimating disease burden, identifying underserved populations, evaluating health disparities, and anticipating future healthcare needs.

These concerns extend beyond scientific research. Census data inform decisions about healthcare infrastructure, federal and state resource allocation, community health services, and long-term policy planning. Population counts that do not adequately reflect the individuals living in a community may underestimate service demand, potentially leaving local healthcare systems and public health agencies with insufficient resources to serve their populations. These consequences could be particularly significant in rural, economically disadvantaged, and historically underserved communities, where healthcare resources are already limited.

Regardless of differing perspectives on immigration policy or federal spending priorities, accurately understanding where people live and the demographic characteristics of our communities is essential for responsible public health planning. Population measurement and policy decisions regarding eligibility for specific publicly funded services are distinct issues. Comprehensive population data allow policymakers to make informed decisions about infrastructure, disease prevention, emergency preparedness, and healthcare capacity based on the needs of the communities they serve.

The decennial census is more than a population count; it is a foundational resource for scientific research, public health surveillance, and evidence-based decision-making. Changes that reduce the completeness, comparability, or demographic detail of census data could have consequences extending well beyond 2030, affecting our ability to anticipate population needs and respond effectively to emerging public health challenges.

I respectfully urge the Census Bureau to reconsider the proposed changes to Section 60 and the elimination of race and ethnicity questions, and to carefully evaluate their potential effects on population data quality, public health research, healthcare planning, and resource allocation. Maintaining accurate, comprehensive, and representative census data is essential to ensuring that our nation's public health policies and investments are informed by the populations they are intended to serve.

Thank you for considering these concerns and for the opportunity to provide public comment.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Department of Commerce
Census Bureau

5123 N NC HWY 119
Mebane NC 27302

Tuesday, October 6, 2026

Re: Docket USBC-2026-0628, RIN 0607-AA75 – Comment in Opposition

I am Dr. Crystal Cavalier, a citizen of the Occaneechi Band of the Saponi Nation, a state-recognized tribe in North Carolina, and Co-Founder of 7 Directions of Service. I strongly oppose this proposed rule. It would erase American Indian and Alaska Native (AIAN) people from the census, the most important source of data about our communities.

1. Banning race and ethnicity questions removes AIAN self-identification.
Proposed Section 70.2(a) bans race and ethnicity questions from the census. Today, the race question is the only place on the census where a person can identify as American Indian or Alaska Native and write in their tribe. The Bureau notes (footnote 11) that tribal membership is "not necessarily" a question about race, yet the rule adds no tribal question to replace what it removes. As a result, the census would no longer count Native people as Native.

2. Tribes depend on these data for funding, health, housing, and voting rights.
Federal agencies, tribes, and states use census AIAN counts to distribute funding for Indian housing, health care, education, and nutrition programs; measure health disparities; and draw fair districts under the Voting Rights Act. Without these data, Native communities become statistically invisible, and resources meant for us will be misdirected or lost.

3. Administrative records will not find us.
The Bureau plans to replace self-response with federal administrative records. Those records do not reliably identify Native people, especially members of state-recognized tribes, tribes without federal recognition, and the majority of Native people who live off reservations and in cities. The proposed "usual residence" test in Section 60.2, tied to tax records, also disadvantages rural, low-income, and multigenerational Native households and people without traditional addresses. AIAN people living on reservations were already undercounted by an estimated 5.6 percent in 2020. This rule would worsen that undercount.

4. The American Community Survey is not a substitute.
Section 70.4 points to the ACS, but the ACS is a sample survey. It is too small to produce reliable numbers for small tribal communities and rural areas, and its estimates depend on decennial census counts as a baseline.

5. Expanded data sharing will discourage participation.
The rule describes linking census records with Homeland Security, Treasury, State Department, and commercial data. Native communities have a long, painful history with government record-keeping being used against us. This expanded surveillance will deepen distrust and lower response rates in the communities that are already hardest to count.

6. Tribal consultation must come first.
The notice says the Bureau "plans to" consult tribes. Under Executive Order 13175, meaningful consultation must happen before a policy is developed, not after it has been proposed. A 30-day comment period, with consultation still to come, does not meet that standard. State-recognized tribes must also be included.

7. The rule undermines tribal sovereignty and the trust responsibility.
Accurate data are a tool of self-determination. Tribes use census data to plan for our citizens, protect our lands, and hold governments accountable. Removing our ability to be counted as Native peoples conflicts with the federal government's trust responsibility to tribal nations.

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw Part 70 in its entirety, keep the race and ethnicity question with the AIAN category and tribal write-in, withdraw the residence criteria that depend on tax and immigration records, and carry out full, good-faith consultation with federally and state-recognized tribes before any further action.

Respectfully,


Dr. Crystal Cavalier
Co-Founder, 7 Directions of Service
Occaneechi Band of the Saponi Nation
North Carolina

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I write comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am a professional living in Chicago, Illinois, and I care about a fair and accurate census because it is imperative to count accurately and thoroughly all voices, especially as we determine how to allocate our precious resources and focus our time and attention of populations in need.

I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 
• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people. Again - we need a full and accurate account of people living in the United States.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations to properly include the variety of living arrangements in the United States, such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Revise the language on tax records to avoid extreme reliance on tax records data that risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude people who actually reside in the US, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

I oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census because a fair and accurate census is critical to ensuring every community is counted, fairly represented, and able to get the resources people need to live healthy lives — including sexual and reproductive healthcare. An inaccurate or incomplete census can deepen existing inequities, particularly for communities that already face disenfranchisement and barriers to healthcare. 

A fair and accurate census is essential to our health and rights. 

Census data help determine access to programs patients and their families rely on, including important programs like Medicaid, SNAP, WIC, and TANF. Accurate census data also shape political representation by determining how seats in the U.S. House of Representatives are apportioned among states and providing data used for redistricting. When communities are undercounted or excluded, they risk losing both resources and political representation. 

The Census Bureau and Department of Commerce must:

1. Count all people residing in the United States in the 2030 Census, without regard to immigration status. Excluding noncitizens from census apportionment data violates the Constitution and established legal precedent. It would suppress the count of many communities, effectively erasing them from critical datasets and depriving them of resources and congressional representation –— including resources and political representation that support access to healthcare.

2. Continue collecting race and ethnicity data and implement the 2024 OMB SPD 15 standards. Census race and ethnicity data are essential for important research across many sectors, for upholding civil rights, and for growing the economy. Extensive Census Bureau research and engagement with expert stakeholders shows that implementing the modernized 2024 OMB SPD 15 standards for race and ethnicity data collection will yield data that more accurately represent the nation’s increasingly diverse population.

3. Remove the clause banning the addition of future questions on sexual orientation. Proposed changes to demographic items should be based on research and guided by a deliberative and transparent process, including extensive stakeholder consultation.

4. Withdraw other proposed changes to residence criteria, including tying place of residence to tax records and "lawful residence," and the adoption of a three month enumeration period. The Census Bureau must extensively research and consult with stakeholders about the potential effects of such changes before proposing their implementation in a decennial census.

5. Halt the practice of prison gerrymandering by counting incarcerated individuals in their home communities. This will yield more accurate census data and ensure that communities receive the congressional representation to which they are entitled.

This proposal would mean there would no longer be a complete and accurate count of our population. I strongly oppose this rule and encourage the census bureau not to enact it.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am strongly opposed to the proposed census changes.

Section 60: the enumeration requirements for residency have been consistent over time and are being misguidedly dragged into political fields which will directly prevent the census from being useful to local, state, and national governments, as well as researchers and other policy actors. By taking residency on census day exactly, we create a clear picture of a moment in time, which would be much more difficult to interpret under proposed changes. There are many reasons someone may not be a full time resident of the place where they live on census day: consider college students, workers with seasonal jobs, or service members. It would be foolish to collect the census data in a way that ignores how these factors shape populations. 

Section 70: Even more so in this case, it is unwise and unnecessary to let politics remove common-sense features of the census. It is baffling to me that this would even be proposed. Race and ethnicity are simple and obvious descriptions about the nature of a population. It would be much more difficult to describe, for example, my hometown (Arlington, VA) without noting its mix of white residents in the north and latinos in the south, with a minority black population interspersed.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Subject: Comment on Proposed Residence Criteria and Demographic Questions — Docket USBC-2026-0628

I am submitting this comment as a Pennsylvania resident and as someone who has spent many years working in health policy and teaching consumers about how government data and policy decisions affect their access to health care and other essential services.

I am concerned about the proposed changes to the rules governing the 2030 Census. The Census is more than a population count. Census data are used for congressional apportionment and are an important source of information for communities, researchers, health systems, and governments as they plan for services and resources.

The Census Bureau’s own historical materials explain that the concept of “usual residence” has been used since the first census in 1790 and that the 2020 Census counted foreign citizens living in the United States at the residence where they lived and slept most of the time, without distinguishing between those who were legally or illegally present.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I write in support of the Census Bureau's proposed rule, "Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions" (Docket No. USBC-2026-0628; RIN 0607-AA75).

The Constitution calls for an "actual Enumeration" every ten years so that representation can be fairly apportioned among the states. The decennial census is meant to be a count, not a survey or a statistical estimate. Americans' voice in Congress depends on that count being right.

In 2020, the Bureau intentionally introduced statistical noise into the population data used to draw congressional and legislative districts. Data that determine political representation should never be deliberately altered. I support proposed  70.3, which directs the Bureau to prioritize the accuracy of the population count and prohibits publishing demographic data when doing so would introduce uncertainty into national or state population counts.

I also support the proposed residence criteria. Being counted at one's "usual residence" has never meant mere physical presence on Census Day. It reflects a lasting connection to a place, which is why service members stationed abroad are still counted in their home states. Counting citizens and lawful permanent residents, and excluding foreign nationals who are here unlawfully or temporarily, follows that principle.

I support keeping the enumeration questionnaire focused on the count itself. The Bureau can continue to produce demographic and statistical information through the American Community Survey and other tools, but those products should remain separate from the constitutional headcount.

To make these reforms durable, I urge the Bureau to state clearly in the final rule that the constitutional enumeration, and the counts used for apportionment and redistricting, are fundamentally distinct from routine federal statistical products and may not be adjusted to serve other statistical purposes.

Please finalize this rule so that the 2030 Census delivers an accurate count and restores Americans' trust in how they are represented.

Respectfully,
Robert Collins
Glendale, AZ

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:

I oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census because a fair and accurate census is critical to ensuring every community is counted, fairly represented, and able to get the resources people need to live healthy lives — including sexual and reproductive healthcare. An inaccurate or incomplete census can deepen existing inequities, particularly for communities that already face disenfranchisement and barriers to healthcare. 

A fair and accurate census is essential to our health and rights. 

Census data help determine access to programs patients and their families rely on, including important programs like Medicaid, SNAP, WIC, and TANF. Accurate census data also shape political representation by determining how seats in the U.S. House of Representatives are apportioned among states and providing data used for redistricting. When communities are undercounted or excluded, they risk losing both resources and political representation. 

The Census Bureau and Department of Commerce must:

1. Count all people residing in the United States in the 2030 Census, without regard to immigration status. Excluding noncitizens from census apportionment data violates the Constitution and established legal precedent. It would suppress the count of many communities, effectively erasing them from critical datasets and depriving them of resources and congressional representation –— including resources and political representation that support access to healthcare.

2. Continue collecting race and ethnicity data and implement the 2024 OMB SPD 15 standards. Census race and ethnicity data are essential for important research across many sectors, for upholding civil rights, and for growing the economy. Extensive Census Bureau research and engagement with expert stakeholders shows that implementing the modernized 2024 OMB SPD 15 standards for race and ethnicity data collection will yield data that more accurately represent the nation’s increasingly diverse population.

3. Remove the clause banning the addition of future questions on sexual orientation. Proposed changes to demographic items should be based on research and guided by a deliberative and transparent process, including extensive stakeholder consultation.

4. Withdraw other proposed changes to residence criteria, including tying place of residence to tax records and "lawful residence," and the adoption of a three month enumeration period. The Census Bureau must extensively research and consult with stakeholders about the potential effects of such changes before proposing their implementation in a decennial census.

5. Halt the practice of prison gerrymandering by counting incarcerated individuals in their home communities. This will yield more accurate census data and ensure that communities receive the congressional representation to which they are entitled.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule: Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions.
The census has counted all residents for apportionment regardless of legal status for 230 years. Article I, Section 2, Clause 3 of the U.S. Constitution mandates that an "actual Enumeration" of the population be conducted within three years of the first Congress meeting and every subsequent term of ten years. The 14th Amendment further clarifies that representatives are apportioned by counting the "whole number of persons" in each state.

This proposal would mean there would no longer be a complete and accurate count of our population. I strongly oppose this rule and encourage the census bureau not to enact it.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Docket USBC-2026-0628, Strong Support for Proposed 15 CFR § 60.4

To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I strongly support proposed 15 CFR § 60.4 and urge its adoption without weakening its eligibility requirements. ONLY U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents should be included in the population used to allocate seats in the U.S. House of Representatives. All other foreign citizens, including illegal aliens, must be excluded from that apportionment count. This distinction must be explicit and applied consistently nationwide.

I consider it fundamentally unfair to American citizens, who have a vested interest in this country and its future, for their congressional representation to be weakened because other states count foreign citizens who possess neither U.S. citizenship nor lawful permanent resident status. Citizens should not lose political influence because another jurisdiction includes those populations in its apportionment count. The proposed standard recognizes citizenship and permanent lawful residence as meaningful, enduring connections to the United States.

I am particularly concerned about the political incentive the current system creates for Democratic-led cities and states that adopt policies accommodating illegal immigration. When illegal aliens are included in the apportionment population, their presence can help a state gain additional House seats or retain seats it might otherwise lose. That creates an opportunity to pursue political advantage through population growth driven by illegal immigration. 

No government or political party should be rewarded with greater congressional representation for accommodating illegal immigration. American citizens deserve an apportionment standard that protects fair representation and prevents unlawful residence from becoming a source of congressional power.

I urge the Bureau to verify eligibility through reliable administrative records and apply the same requirements in all fifty states.

Please adopt proposed § 60.4 without diluting its central distinction. Count U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents for congressional apportionment. Exclude other foreign citizens. Protect fair representation and public confidence through a clear national standard.

Thank you for your time.

Sincerely,

Mario P. Basile

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I oppose the proposed Sections 60 and 70 because they risk undermining the accuracy, continuity, and usefulness of the decennial census. As an economist conducting research on educational mobility, socioeconomic inequality, and public policy, I rely on high-quality demographic data to understand disparities across populations and geographic areas and to evaluate policies intended to improve economic opportunity.

Changes to residence rules under Section 60 could result in individuals being excluded from the census or counted in locations that do not reflect where they actually live. This would compromise population estimates and distort analyses of local economic and social conditions. The proposed restrictions on collecting race and ethnicity data under Section 70 would further limit researchers’ ability to measure disparities, assess whether public policies are reaching different communities, and monitor changes in inequality over time.

The decennial census is a foundational source of information for research, public administration, and evidence-based policymaking. I urge the Census Bureau to retain residence rules that accurately reflect where people live and to preserve the collection of essential demographic information. Reliable, comprehensive, and consistent census data are critical to understanding the U.S. population and ensuring that public policies are informed by the needs of the communities they serve.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. I oppose this proposed rule because it departs from that constitutional mandate, risking severe harm to my community. Excluding noncitizens from the population count used for congressional apportionment and federal funding, while adding a citizenship question designed to deter participation, will suppress response rates across immigrant communities and mixed-status families who fear being targeted. An undercount here would directly strip my community of appropriate congressional representation and our fair share of federal funding for essential safety-net programs like SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, CHIP, and Title I education grants. As someone who cares about fairness and the rule of law, I urge the Bureau to withdraw this proposal and count every person living in our communities, as the Constitution requires. 

I am also concerned that the proposed rule erases vital Census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Decades of demographic data serve as the baseline that public and private institutions rely on to identify inequalities and direct resources where they are needed most. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities.  

Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.  

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Sincerely,
Nora  [X]

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I disagree with the September 10th, 2026, proposed rule to prohibit questions about race,
ethnicity, and sexual orientation on the 2030 U.S. Census because I believe these questions
provide visibility and representation for the different communities that make up our country. The
census should not only count how many people live in America but also help us understand who
they are. Removing these questions could make minority communities less visible and cause
their needs to be overlooked. For example, LGBTQ+ and Latino communities could lose
important representation in government statistics, affecting how resources are distributed and
discrimination is identified. I believe recognizing our differences is just as important as
recognizing what makes us equal, and removing these questions would be a step backward for
representation in America.
Collecting racial data is important because it allows the government to better understand
and represent the different communities living in America. Although race may be socially
constructed, it still plays a significant role in our society. Completely removing racial categories
from the census without providing an alternative could do more harm than good. For example,
removing racial data could make it harder to identify schools in predominantly Black
communities that are underfunded and need additional support. Without this information,
educational inequalities could become less visible, potentially causing institutions that already
lack resources to be overlooked.1 Removing racial information would not eliminate inequality
but could instead make it harder for the government to recognize and address the challenges
facing minority communities.
In addition to race, ethnicity is another important part of a person's identity that deserves
recognition on the census. Even though two people might identify as the same race, their cultural
backgrounds and needs can be different. For example, someone from Brazil might speak
Portuguese, while someone from Mexico might speak Spanish. Although both countries are in
Latin America, they have different languages and cultures. 2 Keeping ethnicity questions on the
census is important because it allows us to recognize our cultural differences while finding better
ways to help the communities that make up America.
Another important reason the census should keep demographic questions is to ensure the
LGBTQ+ community is accurately represented. The government can better understand how
many people identify as part of this community and recognize their needs through statistics.
Although the 2020 census did not directly ask about sexual orientation, it identified about 3
million people living in same-sex couple households.3 If I were part of the LGBTQ+
1 U.S. Census Bureau, “Race,” American Community Survey, https://www.census.gov/acs/www/about/why-we-
ask-each-question/race/.
2 U.S. Census Bureau, “Hispanic or Latino Origin,” American Community Survey,
https://www.census.gov/acs/www/about/why -we -ask-each-question/ethnicity/.
3 U.S. Census Bureau, "About 3 million People in Same-Sex Couple Households", September 19th, 2024
https://www.census.gov/library/stories/2024/09/sdhc -coupled-households.html
community, I would want my sexual orientation recognized because everyone deserves to be
counted. Including these questions is not about dividing Americans, but ensuring no community
is overlooked.
I understand that some people have privacy concerns about the census, but I believe those
concerns are addressed by federal laws that protect individual responses. The Census Bureau
does not make people's personal answers public. Instead, it uses that information to understand
the whole country. I believe collecting this information is important because it helps the
government recognize and serve different communities better.
I also understand that some people might be discouraged from completing the census
because they feel uncomfortable answering personal questions. However, I do not believe
removing these questions is the right solution. Instead, the government should do a better job
explaining why this information is collected and how people's privacy is protected. I believe
educating people about the purpose of the census would be more beneficial than removing questions that help represent different communities keeping questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation on the
census strengthens our country by ensuring different communities are recognized and supported.
Our government institutions are here to serve the people. Rather than removing these questions, I
believe the Census Bureau should continue collecting this information to ensure that all
Americans have a voice and no community is overlooked. Although these questions might seem
invasive, they help us better understand one another and promote equality and visibility for all.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I write in support of the Census Bureau's proposed rule, "Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions" (Docket No. USBC-2026-0628; RIN 0607-AA75).

The Constitution calls for an "actual Enumeration" every ten years so that representation can be fairly apportioned among the states. The decennial census is meant to be a count, not a survey or a statistical estimate. Americans' voice in Congress depends on that count being right.

In 2020, the Bureau intentionally introduced statistical noise into the population data used to draw congressional and legislative districts. Data that determine political representation should never be deliberately altered. I support proposed  70.3, which directs the Bureau to prioritize the accuracy of the population count and prohibits publishing demographic data when doing so would introduce uncertainty into national or state population counts.

I also support the proposed residence criteria. Being counted at one's "usual residence" has never meant mere physical presence on Census Day. It reflects a lasting connection to a place, which is why service members stationed abroad are still counted in their home states. Counting citizens and lawful permanent residents, and excluding foreign nationals who are here unlawfully or temporarily, follows that principle.

I support keeping the enumeration questionnaire focused on the count itself. The Bureau can continue to produce demographic and statistical information through the American Community Survey and other tools, but those products should remain separate from the constitutional headcount.

To make these reforms durable, I urge the Bureau to state clearly in the final rule that the constitutional enumeration, and the counts used for apportionment and redistricting, are fundamentally distinct from routine federal statistical products and may not be adjusted to serve other statistical purposes.

Please finalize this rule so that the 2030 Census delivers an accurate count and restores Americans' trust in how they are represented.

Respectfully,
Paula McDonald
Kelseyville, CA

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I write today to strongly oppose the proposed rule: Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions.

The constitutional basis for the census is clear. Article I, Section 2, Clause 3 requires an "actual Enumeration" of the population. The 14th Amendment clearly states that representatives be apportioned by counting the "whole number of persons" in each state. Neither clause makes a distinction based on immigration status or citizenship. This proposed rule is in direct conflict with both.

The census has counted all residents, regardless of legal status, in every decennial count since 1790. That includes native-born citizens, naturalized citizens, lawful permanent residents, temporary migrants, and undocumented immigrants. Excluding any portion of the population would produce an incomplete count. An incomplete count is not an enumeration.

The consequences of this proposal are serious. Census data determines federal funding for schools, hospitals, roads, emergency services. Communities where residents go uncounted will receive fewer resources, not because they are in less need, but because they weren't even counted.

I urge the Census Bureau to reject this proposal. It directly conflicts with the Bureau's constitutional mandate.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Dear Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions,

Subject: Re: Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions (Docket No. 260903-0005; RIN 0607-AA75) 

I strongly oppose the proposed rules for the census and changes to its residence rule. All persons in the United States have a right to be counted, as the 14th Amendment of the Constitution plainly establishes. This proposed rule will weaken our democracy, our systems of representation, and the doctrine of “one person, one vote.” Without an accurate count, people will not be fairly represented in Congress or state legislatures. 

By generating inaccurate and unreliable data, this change would also make it harder for my state and local officials to properly plan for the services we need and the emergencies we may face. Furthermore, the exclusion of questions about race and ethnicity will exacerbate the degradation of data quality, and it will lead to undercounts of Black and brown communities that are already undercounted in past censuses. If we don't know who is living in our communities, we cannot prepare for the challenges we may face, and we will not receive adequate funds from federal programs. 

I urge you to reject this proposed rule. 


Jean [X]

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: US Census Bureau,I urge the Census Bureau and Department of Commerce to withdraw the proposed rule changing residence criteria for the decennial Census and restricting demographic questions.The proposal would exclude foreign citizens from the population used for congressional apportionment unless they are also U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents. The Census proposes to only include people if their address is confirmed by tax records -- which could mean millions, particularly low-income families, could be missed in the decennial Census. Overall, this would leave out people who actually live in our community, including many people who are lawfully present in the United States.For all past Census counts, including the 2020 Census, foreign citizens living in the United States were generally counted where they lived and slept most of the time. That approach recognizes the basic purpose of a Census: accurately counting the people who live in our communities. The 14th Amendment requires congressional representation to be apportioned according to the “whole number of persons in each State.”I am also deeply concerned by the proposal to prohibit race and ethnicity questions, along with sexual orientation, on the decennial Census enumeration questionnaire. The Census Bureau itself recognizes the importance of race data for civil rights protections, legislative redistricting, equal employment opportunities, and identifying disparities.The 2030 Census will determine congressional, state, and local representation for the decade that follows. It must be complete, accurate, and protected from political manipulation.Please withdraw this proposed rule and preserve a Census that fairly and accurately counts our community.Jazmine [X] Claymont, Delaware 19703

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to voice my strong opposition to the proposed changes to the 2030 Census. These changes would weaken the accuracy and integrity of our nation's most important population count, and I urge the Bureau to reject them.

The Constitution is clear: the census must count all persons living in the United States, regardless of immigration status. The proposal to exclude non-citizens, including residents with lawful status, breaks with more than two centuries of precedent. Every person counted here contributes to our communities, and every person deserves to be seen.

I also oppose the removal of demographic questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. This data is not optional. It is the tool we use to enforce civil rights laws, monitor discrimination, and measure the disparities that still affect millions of people. Strip it away, and we lose the ability to hold our institutions accountable.

The consequences reach into every corner of American life. The census determines political representation and the drawing of voting districts. It guides how billions of dollars in federal funding reach schools, hospitals, and programs designed to close persistent gaps. An undercount does not simply erase numbers on a page. It erases people, silences communities, and undermines the promise of equal representation.

The census is the foundation of our democracy. It must reflect the full and diverse reality of who we are as a nation. I ask the Bureau to withdraw these proposed changes and to preserve a count that includes everyone and represents everyone.

Thank you for considering my comment.

Sincerely,
Wisdom Cole

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: I am writing to oppose the changes proposed in Section 70. I am a social scientist with a Ph.D. in economics from Yale, and my empirical work depends on the decennial census as the benchmark for the entire federal statistical system. The census is the only full-count source of population by race and ethnicity. Removing race and ethnicity from the questionnaire would not eliminate a single variable; it would degrade the accuracy of every survey-based estimate of wages, employment, poverty, and health across groups, because those estimates are calibrated to census counts. It would also break comparability with every census since 1790 and make it impossible to assess whether public policy is narrowing or widening disparities. Prohibiting a question on sexual orientation likewise forecloses data that the research community has long asked for. I urge the Bureau to retain the race and ethnicity questions and withdraw Section 70.
