Comment:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). 

As an educator, I care about a fair and accurate census because census data and other federal datasets based on the census are used to make key decisions that affect our nation’s students, educators, and schools.  

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Examples of these uses include: . 

* Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. 

* Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

* Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

* Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

* Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

* Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

* Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

* Determining state higher education funding formulas 

* Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

* Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

* Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

First, to ensure a fair and accurate census,  the Census Bureau should  extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. Second, I oppose both the proposed changes to the residence criteria and the proposed regulations regarding demographic questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. The Census Bureau should  withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The Constitution requires  counting all people living in the United States. 

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (including children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count. 

Revise the tax records language so that those whose mailing address differs from their residential address (servicemembers, those with a post office box) are not excluded.  

• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for civil rights enforcement, among other uses, and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The prohibition, as written, may also restrict the collection or publication of census data on same-sex couples that was asked in 2020. 

 The proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Sincerely,
Ms. Teresa Sophia Barut
Easthampton, MA

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am a resident of Minnesota and work with communities of all races and backgrounds across the Great Lakes region to protect their clean water. I care about a fair and accurate census because I care about consistent data collection and the accurate representation of our nation's residents.

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: [keep any/all points you would like to include in your comment]

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Comment:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). 

As an educator, I care about a fair and accurate census because census data and other federal datasets based on the census are used to make key decisions that affect our nation’s students, educators, and schools.  

In FY 2023, $129.8 billion in education spending was guided by census data. Census-driven programs support primary education, special education, and higher education, as well as training and education for community members. Examples of these uses include: . 

* Federal education funding allocations, including money for Title I, IDEA, Head Start and other early childhood education programs, and School Nutrition Programs. 

* Forecasting changes in the size and demographics of student populations and thus the need for educators and school facilities 

* Determining the need for resources for emergent multilingual learners, students living in poverty, and students with disabilities  

* Identifying disparities and enforcing federal, state, and local civil rights statutes 

* Informing outreach and support programs for first-generation college students 

* Planning and funding for community colleges and technical/vocational schools 

* Aligning higher education programming with regional labor market demands 

* Determining state higher education funding formulas 

* Determining student loan repayment models and income-driven repayment thresholds 

* Planning transportation, including roads and public transit 

* Determining the need for and funding health and social services 

First, to ensure a fair and accurate census,  the Census Bureau should  extend the comment period until December 10, 2026 as the public needs more time to review and respond. Second, I oppose both the proposed changes to the residence criteria and the proposed regulations regarding demographic questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. • Eliminate any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The Constitution requires  counting all people living in the United States. 

• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (including children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count. 

Revise the tax records language so that those whose mailing address differs from their residential address (servicemembers, those with a post office box) are not excluded.  

• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for civil rights enforcement, among other uses, and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses.  The proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Ms. Alex Player
Elma, WA

As someone preparing for a career in business, I see reliable demographic data as essential to understanding the population businesses serve, anticipating future needs, and making informed decisions. I encourage the Census Bureau to reconsider restricting these questions on the short-form decennial census and instead continue working to balance privacy protections with the need for representative, useful data.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. I oppose this proposed rule because it departs from that constitutional mandate, risking severe harm to my community. Excluding noncitizens from the population count used for congressional apportionment and federal funding, while adding a citizenship question designed to deter participation, will suppress response rates across immigrant communities and mixed-status families who fear being targeted. An undercount here would directly strip my community of appropriate congressional representation and our fair share of federal funding for essential safety-net programs like SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, CHIP, and Title I education grants. As someone who cares about fairness and the rule of law, I urge the Bureau to withdraw this proposal and count every person living in our communities, as the Constitution requires. 

I am also concerned that the proposed rule erases vital Census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Decades of demographic data serve as the baseline that public and private institutions rely on to identify inequalities and direct resources where they are needed most. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities.  

Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.  

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Sincerely,
Deborah  [X]

The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. I oppose this proposed rule because it departs from that constitutional mandate, risking severe harm to my community. Excluding noncitizens from the population count used for congressional apportionment and federal funding, while adding a citizenship question designed to deter participation, will suppress response rates across immigrant communities and mixed-status families who fear being targeted. An undercount here would directly strip my community of appropriate congressional representation and our fair share of federal funding for essential safety-net programs like SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, CHIP, and Title I education grants. As someone who cares about fairness and the rule of law, I urge the Bureau to withdraw this proposal and count every person living in our communities, as the Constitution requires. 

I am also concerned that the proposed rule erases vital Census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Decades of demographic data serve as the baseline that public and private institutions rely on to identify inequalities and direct resources where they are needed most. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities.  

Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.  

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Sincerely,
Gloria [X]

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: US Census Bureau,I urge the Census Bureau and Department of Commerce to withdraw the proposed rule changing residence criteria for the decennial Census and restricting demographic questions.The proposal would exclude foreign citizens from the population used for congressional apportionment unless they are also U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents. The Census proposes to only include people if their address is confirmed by tax records -- which could mean millions, particularly low-income families, could be missed in the decennial Census. Overall, this would leave out people who actually live in our community, including many people who are lawfully present in the United States.For all past Census counts, including the 2020 Census, foreign citizens living in the United States were generally counted where they lived and slept most of the time. That approach recognizes the basic purpose of a Census: accurately counting the people who live in our communities. The 14th Amendment requires congressional representation to be apportioned according to the “whole number of persons in each State.”I am also deeply concerned by the proposal to prohibit race and ethnicity questions, along with sexual orientation, on the decennial Census enumeration questionnaire. The Census Bureau itself recognizes the importance of race data for civil rights protections, legislative redistricting, equal employment opportunities, and identifying disparities.The 2030 Census will determine congressional, state, and local representation for the decade that follows. It must be complete, accurate, and protected from political manipulation.Please withdraw this proposed rule and preserve a Census that fairly and accurately counts our community.R Gary  [X] t. Collins, Colorado 80521

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule: Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions.

The census has counted all residents for apportionment regardless of legal status for 230 years. Article I, Section 2, Clause 3 of the U.S. Constitution mandates that an "actual Enumeration" of the population be conducted within three years of the first Congress meeting and every subsequent term of ten years. The 14th Amendment further clarifies that representatives are apportioned by counting the "whole number of persons" in each state.

We have always counted native-born U.S. citizens, naturalized U.S. citizens, non-citizen U.S. nationals, lawful permanent residents and temporary migrants, such as foreign students, refugees, asylum seekers and undocumented immigrants. The census has never left out residents because of their immigration status.
The census determines the funding and representation of our communities. By not counting all people, communities will not get the resources they need for schools, hospitals, roads, firefighters and other critical services. These changes are yet another way for the current administration to destroy the fabric of American communities and must not be enacted. 

This proposal would mean there would no longer be a complete and accurate count of our population. Who, I might ask, does this benefit? I strongly oppose this rule and encourage the census bureau not to enact it.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am a citizen, a veteran, a retired Federal careerist and a senior citizen who resides in Lake Orion, Michigan and I care about a fair and accurate census because I have served the US all of my 81 years of life.

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: US Census Bureau,I urge the Census Bureau and Department of Commerce to withdraw the proposed rule changing residence criteria for the decennial Census and restricting demographic questions.The proposal would exclude foreign citizens from the population used for congressional apportionment unless they are also U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents. It must be complete, accurate, and protected from political manipulation.Please withdraw this proposed rule and preserve a Census that fairly and accurately counts our community.Ann[X] Hingham, Massachusetts 02043

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
How on earth can entire groups of people be excluded from the Census?! That's so egregiously racist, xenophobic, and bigoted, and it amounts to taxation without representation, none of which are founding principles of this nation or part of the oath I swore to when I volunteered to serve my once great--and now rapidly deteriorating, under Trump--country. 

I strongly oppose the proposed rule, Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions.
The census has counted all residents for apportionment regardless of legal status for 230 years. Article I, Section 2, Clause 3 of the U.S. Constitution mandates that an "actual Enumeration" of the population be conducted within three years of the first Congress meeting and every subsequent term of ten years. The 14th Amendment further clarifies that representatives are apportioned by counting the "whole number of persons" in each state.
We have always counted native-born U.S. citizens, naturalized U.S. citizens, non-citizen U.S. nationals, lawful permanent residents and temporary migrants, such as foreign students, refugees, asylum seekers and undocumented immigrants. The census has never left out residents because of their immigration status.
The census determines the funding and representation of our communities. By not counting all people, communities will not get the resources they need for schools, hospitals, roads, firefighters and other critical services.
This proposal would mean there would no longer be a complete and accurate count of our population. I strongly oppose this rule and encourage the census bureau not to enact it.

I oppose this proposed rule because it departs from that constitutional mandate, risking severe harm to my community. Excluding noncitizens from the population count used for congressional apportionment and federal funding, while adding a citizenship question designed to deter participation, will suppress response rates across immigrant communities and mixed-status families who fear being targeted. An undercount here would directly strip my community of appropriate congressional representation and our fair share of federal funding for essential safety-net programs like SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, CHIP, and Title I education grants. As someone who cares about fairness and the rule of law, I urge the Bureau to withdraw this proposal and count every person living in our communities, as the Constitution requires. 

I am also concerned that the proposed rule erases vital Census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Decades of demographic data serve as the baseline that public and private institutions rely on to identify inequalities and direct resources where they are needed most. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities.  

Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.  

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Sincerely,
Kathryn Thacker
Colonia, NJ

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: US Census Bureau,I urge the Census Bureau and Department of Commerce to withdraw the proposed rule changing residence criteria for the decennial Census and restricting demographic questions.The proposal would exclude foreign citizens from the population used for congressional apportionment unless they are also U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents. The Census proposes to only include people if their address is confirmed by tax records -- which could mean millions, particularly low-income families, could be missed in the decennial Census. Overall, this would leave out people who actually live in our community, including many people who are lawfully present in the United States.For all past Census counts, including the 2020 Census, foreign citizens living in the United States were generally counted where they lived and slept most of the time. That approach recognizes the basic purpose of a Census: accurately counting the people who live in our communities. The 14th Amendment requires congressional representation to be apportioned according to the “whole number of persons in each State.”I am also deeply concerned by the proposal to prohibit race and ethnicity questions, along with sexual orientation, on the decennial Census enumeration questionnaire. The Census Bureau itself recognizes the importance of race data for civil rights protections, legislative redistricting, equal employment opportunities, and identifying disparities.The 2030 Census will determine congressional, state, and local representation for the decade that follows. It must be complete, accurate, and protected from political manipulation.Please withdraw this proposed rule and preserve a Census that fairly and accurately counts our community.Nancy [X] Spokane, Washington 99224

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: I am a physician and health services researcher who focuses on improving the care of people who use drugs and alcohol. As a nationally-recognized expert, the data that the Census provides is of the utmost importance to informing public health and clinical interventions. It is my strongest recommendation that detailed data be collected about the population, included detailed demographic information - specifically race and ethnicity, which is imperative to providing an accurate representation of the population. My second recommendation is that all people have the opportunity to be counted regardless of their housing status. Indeed, sheltered and unsheltered homelessness occurs in about 1-2% of the population annually (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40615-023-01521-9) and therefore lifetime prevalence is much larger. Not counting these folks as part of the Census will limit their representation and therefore researchers, public health practitioners, regulators, policymakers, politicians, and more cannot make informed decisions.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am submitting this comment in response to Docket USBC-2026-0628, the proposed rule eliminating race and ethnicity questions from the 2030 Decennial Census.

I am a tribal member, and I'm concerned about how this proposal would affect Native families like mine. A significant share of tribal and federal program funding is calculated based on the number of people who actually reside in a village or community — not on total tribal enrollment. I've watched this play out unfairly for my own relatives, who are enrolled members but don't live in the community and end up excluded from funding and services that residency-based formulas are built around.

This isn't unique to one tribe. It's common for tribal governance to exclude nonresident members from running for council or having any say in decisions, even though those decisions affect how they're counted and represented. When only a small pool of resident members controls those decisions, there's little internal accountability for whether funding and services actually reach the people they're intended for — including people who are enrolled but live elsewhere. Accurate, community-level race and tribal-affiliation data from the census is one of the few independent tools available to expose these gaps, regardless of how any individual tribe chooses to spend its funding.

This concern is made worse by the fact that tribal members are sometimes coached on how to self-identify for census purposes, which further muddies the data needed to hold this system accountable.

I urge the Census Bureau to retain race, ethnicity, and tribal affiliation questions on the 2030 census questionnaire. This data isn't about giving any tribe more money — it's about whether the federal government, researchers, and Native people themselves can even see where the gaps and inequities are. Tillila Beetus - Native Village of Hughes tribal member

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Dear Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions,

Subject: Re: Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions (Docket No. 260903-0005; RIN 0607-AA75) 

I strongly oppose the proposed rules for the census and changes to its residence rule. All persons in the United States have a right to be counted, as the 14th Amendment of the Constitution plainly establishes. This proposed rule will weaken our democracy, our systems of representation, and the doctrine of “one person, one vote.” Without an accurate count, people will not be fairly represented in Congress or state legislatures.

Furthermore, the exclusion of questions about race and ethnicity will exacerbate the degradation of data quality, and it will lead to undercounts of Black and brown communities that are already undercounted in past censuses. If we don't know who is living in our communities, we cannot prepare for the challenges we may face, and we will not receive adequate funds from federal programs. 

I urge you to reject this proposed rule. 
The Trump regime must not be allowed to dumb-down the data needed to serve ALL the people.

Tom Parsons,
[x]
San Diego
CA



Sincerely,
Mr. Tom Parsons

Count every U.S. resident, including visa-holders, refugees, and asylum seekers.

Count incarcerated people at home, not at the facility.

Sincerely,

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
As a statistician and decision support analyst for local government, I am alarmed at the current proposal to change how people are counted and omit certain data from collection in the upcoming 2030 census. We rely on accurate counts of resident population to plan our activities and match resources to need across our jurisdiction. Collection of data on race and ethnicity - something that has occurred since Thomas Jefferson led the first US census in 1790 - is crucial to many local government activities, from program planning to anticipating where the risk of disease introduction may be highest during global health crises. While questions on sexual orientation have not been included in any census to date, their prohibition on ideological grounds does not align with the duty of governments to understand, serve, and protect the populations under their jurisdiction. 

If these proposed changes are adopted, it will mark a shameful chapter in our nation's history. It will bring us closer in nature to regimes like the People's Republic of China or DPRK, where truth is molded to serve the interests and ideologies of the few instead of sought with clear eyes to best serve the nation. Let's not put narrative over objective facts. It never works out in the long run.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I’m writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

As a person who cares about people and our planet, I know how important this data is, and as such, we need a fair and accurate Census. 

First, I ask the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. Significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve more time for members of the public — people like me — to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70 of the proposed rule. I urge you to withdraw the rule for substantial revisions, including:

Count every U.S. resident, including visa-holders, refugees, and asylum seekers.
Establish detailed  guidelines for complex residential situations such as recent movers, people in temporary situations, and children in foster care.
Go back to activity-based residence, not a “one hour” rule.
Drop the January-to-April enumeration period.
Count incarcerated people at home, not at the facility.
Revise the tax records language. Extreme reliance on tax records risks creating inconsistencies in the count.
Drop the ban on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation questions.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of communities like mine. Furthermore, the data collected by the Census determines how billions of dollars of environmental funding is distributed across the country. This includes funding for water and waste disposal systems, public transportation infrastructure, and disaster relief on which we all rely. The data collected will also inform research to identify and address environmental injustices. 

Moving forward with this proposed rule would harm all Americans. Our democracy works best when all people that live within our borders are fully represented in the data collected by the Census.

Sincerely,
Sarah Hunnewell

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: I think both questions are appropriate to add. A question about race for demographic purposes is not racist. It is just data, and the data should be complete. Additionally, I do not think illegal aliens should be counted for the purpose of the census. Removing this loophole would remove the basis for the support of unchecked illegal migration by the Democratic Party, the Red Cross, and others who are using it as a political tool to change the balance of the house. I do believe, however, that people that are born in a state but are not citizens of the federal United States which is incorporated in DC should still be counted on the census for representation, as they are following their reading of the original text of the constitution, either correctly or incorrectly. So the question should allow for the distinction. When the 14th amendment was created, it was understood that “United States citizen” was an additional class that it applied to, and not equivalent to a citizen of a state. See Justice Wards comments in the Susan B Anthony case regarding 14th amendment protected citizens of the United States vs citizens of one or several states and how their protections are derived from different places in the constitution. (United States v. Anthony, 24 F. Cas. 829 (C.C.N.D.N.Y. 1873) (No. 14,459) (June 18, 1873)

The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. I oppose this proposed rule because it departs from that constitutional mandate, risking severe harm to my community. Excluding noncitizens from the population count used for congressional apportionment and federal funding, while adding a citizenship question designed to deter participation, will suppress response rates across immigrant communities and mixed-status families who fear being targeted. An undercount here would directly strip my community of appropriate congressional representation and our fair share of federal funding for essential safety-net programs like SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, CHIP, and Title I education grants. As someone who cares about fairness and the rule of law, I urge the Bureau to withdraw this proposal and count every person living in our communities, as the Constitution requires. 

I am also concerned that the proposed rule erases vital Census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Decades of demographic data serve as the baseline that public and private institutions rely on to identify inequalities and direct resources where they are needed most. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities.  

Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.  

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Sincerely,
MJ Cooper
Union City, GA

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: US Census Bureau,I urge the Census Bureau and Department of Commerce to withdraw the proposed rule changing residence criteria for the decennial Census and restricting demographic questions.The proposal would exclude foreign citizens from the population used for congressional apportionment unless they are also U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents. The Census proposes to only include people if their address is confirmed by tax records -- which could mean millions, particularly low-income families, could be missed in the decennial Census. Overall, this would leave out people who actually live in our community, including many people who are lawfully present in the United States.For all past Census counts, including the 2020 Census, foreign citizens living in the United States were generally counted where they lived and slept most of the time. That approach recognizes the basic purpose of a Census: accurately counting the people who live in our communities. The 14th Amendment requires congressional representation to be apportioned according to the “whole number of persons in each State.”I am also deeply concerned by the proposal to prohibit race and ethnicity questions, along with sexual orientation, on the decennial Census enumeration questionnaire. The Census Bureau itself recognizes the importance of race data for civil rights protections, legislative redistricting, equal employment opportunities, and identifying disparities.The 2030 Census will determine congressional, state, and local representation for the decade that follows. It must be complete, accurate, and protected from political manipulation.Please withdraw this proposed rule and preserve a Census that fairly and accurately counts our community.Sam [x]

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I’m writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

As a person who cares about people and our planet, I know how important this data is, and as such, we need a fair and accurate Census. 

First, I ask the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. Significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve more time for members of the public — people like me — to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70 of the proposed rule. I urge you to withdraw the rule for substantial revisions, including:

Count every U.S. resident, including visa-holders, refugees, and asylum seekers.
Establish detailed  guidelines for complex residential situations such as recent movers, people in temporary situations, and children in foster care.
Go back to activity-based residence, not a “one hour” rule.
Drop the January-to-April enumeration period.
Count incarcerated people at home, not at the facility.
Revise the tax records language. Extreme reliance on tax records risks creating inconsistencies in the count.
Drop the ban on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation questions.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of communities like mine. Furthermore, the data collected by the Census determines how billions of dollars of environmental funding is distributed across the country. This includes funding for water and waste disposal systems, public transportation infrastructure, and disaster relief on which we all rely. The data collected will also inform research to identify and address environmental injustices. 

Moving forward with this proposed rule would harm all Americans. Our democracy works best when all people that live within our borders are fully represented in the data collected by the Census.

Sincerely,
Hugh McDowell

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:

Drop the January-to-April enumeration period.
Count incarcerated people at home, not at the facility.

Moving forward with this proposed rule would harm all Americans. Our democracy works best when all people that live within our borders are fully represented in the data collected by the Census.

Sincerely,
Michael Daus

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule: Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions.
The census has counted all residents for apportionment regardless of legal status for 230 years. Article I, Section 2, Clause 3 of the U.S. Constitution mandates that an "actual Enumeration" of the population be conducted within three years of the first Congress meeting and every subsequent term of ten years. The 14th Amendment further clarifies that representatives are apportioned by counting the "whole number of persons" in each state.
We have always counted native-born U.S. citizens, naturalized U.S. citizens, non-citizen U.S. nationals, lawful permanent residents and temporary migrants, such as foreign students, refugees, asylum seekers and undocumented immigrants. The census has never left out residents because of their immigration status.
The census determines the funding and representation of our communities. By not counting all people, communities will not get the resources they need for schools, hospitals, roads, firefighters and other critical services.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Dear Census Bureau,

There have been huge changes during COVID. The 2030 Census could provide our government with insights that cannot come from any other source.

I write in support of the Census Bureau's proposed rule, "Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions" (Docket No. USBC-2026-0628; RIN 0607-AA75).

The Constitution calls for an "actual Enumeration" every ten years so that representation can be fairly apportioned among the states. The decennial census is meant to be a count, not a survey or a statistical estimate. Americans' voice in Congress depends on that count being right.

I support proposed  70.3, which directs the Bureau to prioritize the accuracy of the population count and prohibits publishing demographic data when doing so would introduce uncertainty into national or state population counts.

I also support the proposed residence criteria. Being counted at one's "usual residence" has never meant mere physical presence on Census Day. It reflects a lasting connection to a place, which is why service members stationed abroad are still counted in their home states. Counting citizens and lawful permanent residents, and excluding foreign nationals who are here unlawfully or temporarily, follows that principle.

To make these reforms durable, I urge the Bureau to state clearly in the final rule that the constitutional enumeration, and the counts used for apportionment and redistricting, are fundamentally distinct from routine federal statistical products and may not be adjusted to serve other statistical purposes.

Please finalize this rule so that the 2030 Census delivers an accurate count and restores Americans' trust in how they are represented.

Respectfully,
Patrick Sullivan
Fountain Valley, CA

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Census data help inform congressional representation, federal funding, public services, infrastructure planning, emergency preparedness, research and community development. Changes to Census methodology could affect the accuracy and availability of population and demographic data used by governments and communities. I ask the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. Significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve more time for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 
Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than confusing "one hour" rule.
Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the "enumeration period" so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
Revise the language on tax records. The text, "A person's 'usual residence', should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms" ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many tax payers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.
As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:

I strongly oppose this rule and encourage the census bureau not to enact it.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I’m writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

As a person who cares about people and our planet, I know how important this data is, and as such, we need a fair and accurate Census. 

First, I ask the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. Significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve more time for members of the public — people like me — to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70 of the proposed rule. I urge you to withdraw the rule for substantial revisions, including:

Count every U.S. resident, including visa-holders, refugees, and asylum seekers.
Establish detailed  guidelines for complex residential situations such as recent movers, people in temporary situations, and children in foster care.
Go back to activity-based residence, not a “one hour” rule.
Drop the January-to-April enumeration period.
Count incarcerated people at home, not at the facility.
Revise the tax records language. Extreme reliance on tax records risks creating inconsistencies in the count.
Drop the ban on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation questions.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of communities like mine. Furthermore, the data collected by the Census determines how billions of dollars of environmental funding is distributed across the country. This includes funding for water and waste disposal systems, public transportation infrastructure, and disaster relief on which we all rely. The data collected will also inform research to identify and address environmental injustices. 

Moving forward with this proposed rule would harm all Americans. Our democracy works best when all people that live within our borders are fully represented in the data collected by the Census.

Sincerely,
Andy Tuggle

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am aghast to hear that there is a proposed rule to block certain people living in America from being counted in the 2030 census.  The census was established in the Constitution (Article I, Section 2, Clause 3) and mandates that an "actual Enumeration" of the population be conducted. The 14th Amendment further clarifies that representatives are apportioned by counting the "whole number of persons" in each state.

We have always counted ALL people living in a place: native-born U.S. citizens, naturalized U.S. citizens, non-citizen U.S. nationals, lawful permanent residents and temporary migrants, such as foreign students, refugees, asylum seekers and undocumented immigrants. The census has NEVER left out residents because of their immigration status.

The United States uses this census to apportion resources for schools, hospitals, firefighters, and so much more, as well as the number of representatives.  Without a correct census counting ALL people, places will be denied the resources they need to provide services for residents.  Just because someone is not an American citizen does not mean their home cannot catch on fire and need the fire department to respond, or that such a fire wouldn't spread to the homes of anyone else in the area.

I strongly oppose this proposed rule, and ask that the census bureau not enact it.

The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities.  

Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.  

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Sincerely,
Lenore Martin
Chapel Hill, NC

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I’m writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

As a person who cares about people and our planet, I know how important this data is, and as such, we need a fair and accurate Census. 

First, I ask the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. Significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve more time for members of the public — people like me — to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70 of the proposed rule. I urge you to withdraw the rule for substantial revisions, including:

Count every U.S. resident, including visa-holders, refugees, and asylum seekers.
Establish detailed  guidelines for complex residential situations such as recent movers, people in temporary situations, and children in foster care.
Go back to activity-based residence, not a “one hour” rule.
Drop the January-to-April enumeration period.
Count incarcerated people at home, not at the facility.
Revise the tax records language. Extreme reliance on tax records risks creating inconsistencies in the count.
Drop the ban on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation questions.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of communities like mine. Furthermore, the data collected by the Census determines how billions of dollars of environmental funding is distributed across the country. This includes funding for water and waste disposal systems, public transportation infrastructure, and disaster relief on which we all rely. The data collected will also inform research to identify and address environmental injustices. 

Moving forward with this proposed rule would harm all Americans. Our democracy works best when all people that live within our borders are fully represented in the data collected by the Census.

Sincerely,
anthony spratford

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am against the proposed rule: Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions.

Article I, Section 2, Clause 3 of the U.S. Constitution mandates that an "actual Enumeration" of the population be conducted within three years of the first Congress meeting and every subsequent term of ten years. The 14th Amendment further clarifies that representatives are apportioned by counting the "whole number of persons" in each state.

“Whole number of persons” has included native-born U.S. citizens, naturalized U.S. citizens, non-citizen U.S. nationals, lawful permanent residents and temporary migrants, such as foreign students, refugees, asylum seekers and undocumented immigrants. The census has never left out residents because of their immigration status.

By not counting all people who live in our country, funding for resources like schools, hospitals, roads, firefighters and other critical services may be wrong, which will be a problem for all people who live in these communities.

This proposal would mean there would no longer be a complete and accurate count of our population. I strongly oppose this rule and encourage the census bureau not to enact it.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I’m writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

As a person who cares about people and our planet, I know how important this data is, and as such, we need a fair and accurate Census. 

First, I ask the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. Significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve more time for members of the public — people like me — to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70 of the proposed rule. I urge you to withdraw the rule for substantial revisions, including:

Count every U.S. resident, including visa-holders, refugees, and asylum seekers.
Establish detailed  guidelines for complex residential situations such as recent movers, people in temporary situations, and children in foster care.
Go back to activity-based residence, not a “one hour” rule.
Drop the January-to-April enumeration period.
Count incarcerated people at home, not at the facility.
Revise the tax records language. Extreme reliance on tax records risks creating inconsistencies in the count.
Drop the ban on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation questions.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of communities like mine. Furthermore, the data collected by the Census determines how billions of dollars of environmental funding is distributed across the country. This includes funding for water and waste disposal systems, public transportation infrastructure, and disaster relief on which we all rely. The data collected will also inform research to identify and address environmental injustices. 

Moving forward with this proposed rule would harm all Americans. Our democracy works best when all people that live within our borders are fully represented in the data collected by the Census.

Sincerely,
Amanda Griffin

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing in opposition to the Census Bureau's proposed rule: "Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions" (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I strongly object to a change that would radically alter who is counted for congressional apportionment, which local communities are resourced, and whether we can track progress on civil rights protections without race and ethnicity questions from the decennial census.

1. The Census Must Count Everyone Who Lives Here

The Constitution requires representation to be based on the "whole number of persons in each State," not citizens specifically. This rule would exclude international students, work visa holders, refugees, and asylum seekers from the count for the first time, even though they live in our communities, work, pay taxes, and use the same roads and schools as everyone else. Attempting to sort people by legal status also creates fear that keeps entire households, including U.S. citizens, from responding at all.

2. Counting People by Administrative Record Will Distort Representation

The rule would place people based on tax records and other administrative data rather than where they actually live. Tax records often list an old address, a P.O. box, or a preparer's office, which fails students, seasonal workers, service members, and anyone who moved recently. Federal law has always set a single fixed date, April 1, for the census. This rule replaces that with a shifting three-month window, adding complexity without adding accuracy.

3. Race and Ethnicity Data Are Essential

The census has asked about race in some form since the very first census in 1790. This data is what allows the country to track discrimination, enforce voting rights, and direct public health and civil rights resources. The American Community Survey cannot replace it, since it only produces estimates and itself relies on the decennial census for accuracy. The rule would also make nearly every demographic question voluntary, despite a federal law requiring people to answer census questions. And it would bar any future question on sexual orientation, though the more significant risk is a new provision giving the Bureau broad discretion to withhold published data on smaller communities, including same-sex households.

4. Communities Without Accurate Data Get Left Behind

Arab Americans have historically been undercounted because no census category captured them. The 2030 Census is set to be the first with a dedicated Middle Eastern or North African (MENA) category, a change advocates spent years securing to improve data collection on people from the MENA region. This rule would eliminate that progress along with all race and ethnicity data collection. Any community without accurate data becomes harder to serve, harder to protect, and easier to overlook.

I urge the Census Bureau and the Department of Commerce to withdraw these proposed changes and to count everyone who lives here, accurately and in the right place.

Sincerely,

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I’m writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

As a person who cares about people and our planet, I know how important this data is, and as such, we need a fair and accurate Census. 

First, I ask the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. Significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve more time for members of the public — people like me — to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70 of the proposed rule. I urge you to withdraw the rule for substantial revisions, including:

Count every U.S. resident, including visa-holders, refugees, and asylum seekers.
Establish detailed  guidelines for complex residential situations such as recent movers, people in temporary situations, and children in foster care.
Go back to activity-based residence, not a “one hour” rule.
Drop the January-to-April enumeration period.
Count incarcerated people at home, not at the facility.
Revise the tax records language. Extreme reliance on tax records risks creating inconsistencies in the count.
Drop the ban on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation questions.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of communities like mine. Furthermore, the data collected by the Census determines how billions of dollars of environmental funding is distributed across the country. This includes funding for water and waste disposal systems, public transportation infrastructure, and disaster relief on which we all rely. The data collected will also inform research to identify and address environmental injustices. 

Moving forward with this proposed rule would harm all Americans. Our democracy works best when all people that live within our borders are fully represented in the data collected by the Census.

Sincerely,
Janet Jan Schachter

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I’m writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

As a person who cares about people and our planet, I know how important this data is, and as such, we need a fair and accurate Census. 

First, I ask the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. Significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve more time for members of the public — people like me — to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70 of the proposed rule. I urge you to withdraw the rule for substantial revisions, including:

Count every U.S. resident, including visa-holders, refugees, and asylum seekers.
Establish detailed  guidelines for complex residential situations such as recent movers, people in temporary situations, and children in foster care.
Go back to activity-based residence, not a “one hour” rule.
Drop the January-to-April enumeration period.
Count incarcerated people at home, not at the facility.
Revise the tax records language. Extreme reliance on tax records risks creating inconsistencies in the count.
Drop the ban on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation questions.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of communities like mine. Furthermore, the data collected by the Census determines how billions of dollars of environmental funding is distributed across the country. This includes funding for water and waste disposal systems, public transportation infrastructure, and disaster relief on which we all rely. The data collected will also inform research to identify and address environmental injustices. 

Moving forward with this proposed rule would harm all Americans. Our democracy works best when all people that live within our borders are fully represented in the data collected by the Census.

Sincerely,
Sandra Brown

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: I am a county government employee who uses census data extensively in my work as a geographic information systems analyst. I work for a northern, rural county that has a large seasonal population, including a substantial population that travels south for the winter months. The proposed changes to residence rules will likely have the effect of significantly miscounting our actual population, since we have a large number of residents who return to the area in late March or early April after living the "snowbird" months down south. These residents live locally for the majority of the year aside from the proposed new "Census Period" of January - April 1, which coincide with the "snowbird" months. I strongly urge the Census Bureau to use its historic count method of counting people where they are residing on April 1.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I’m writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

Moving forward with this proposed rule would harm all Americans. Our democracy works best when all people that live within our borders are fully represented in the data collected by the Census.

Sincerely,
cynthia strout

Comment:
To think that I have to leave this message is very upsetting to me.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The proposed rule: Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions, is abhorrent, unconstitutional, un-American, and appallingly racist. Article I, Section 2, Clause 3 of the U.S. Constitution mandates that an "actual Enumeration" of the population be conducted within three years of the first Congress meeting and every subsequent term of ten years. The 14th Amendment further clarifies that representatives are apportioned by counting the "whole number of persons" in each state. This means counting ALL residents regardless of legal status. 

For 230 years the United States has counted all native-born U.S. citizens, naturalized U.S. citizens, non-citizen U.S. nationals, lawful permanent residents and temporary migrants, such as foreign students, refugees, asylum seekers and undocumented immigrants. The census has NEVER left out residents because of their immigration status.

The census determines the funding and representation of our communities. By not counting all of the people who live there, communities will not get the resources they need for schools, hospitals, roads, firefighters and other critical services.

This proposal would mean there would no longer be a complete and accurate count of our population. I strongly oppose this rule. The census bureau should not enact it.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I’m writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

As a person who cares about people and our planet, I know how important this data is, and as such, we need a fair and accurate Census. 

First, I ask the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. Significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve more time for members of the public — people like me — to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70 of the proposed rule. I urge you to withdraw the rule for substantial revisions, including:

Count every U.S. resident, including visa-holders, refugees, and asylum seekers.
Establish detailed  guidelines for complex residential situations such as recent movers, people in temporary situations, and children in foster care.
Go back to activity-based residence, not a “one hour” rule.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. I oppose this proposed rule because it departs from that constitutional mandate, risking severe harm to my community. Excluding noncitizens from the population count used for congressional apportionment and federal funding, while adding a citizenship question designed to deter participation, will suppress response rates across immigrant communities and mixed-status families who fear being targeted. An undercount here would directly strip my community of appropriate congressional representation and our fair share of federal funding for essential safety-net programs like SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, CHIP, and Title I education grants. As someone who cares about fairness and the rule of law, I urge the Bureau to withdraw this proposal and count every person living in our communities, as the Constitution requires. 

I am also concerned that the proposed rule erases vital Census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Decades of demographic data serve as the baseline that public and private institutions rely on to identify inequalities and direct resources where they are needed most. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities.  

Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.  

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Sincerely,
Ron Welch
Nashville, TN

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:

This proposal would mean there would no longer be a complete and accurate count of our population. I strongly oppose this rule and encourage the census bureau not to enact it.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I’m writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

As a person who cares about people and our planet, I know how important this data is, and as such, we need a fair and accurate Census. 

First, I ask the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. Significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve more time for members of the public — people like me — to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70 of the proposed rule. I urge you to withdraw the rule for substantial revisions, including:

Count every U.S. resident, including visa-holders, refugees, and asylum seekers.
Establish detailed  guidelines for complex residential situations such as recent movers, people in temporary situations, and children in foster care.
Go back to activity-based residence, not a “one hour” rule.
Drop the January-to-April enumeration period.
Count incarcerated people at home, not at the facility.
Revise the tax records language. Extreme reliance on tax records risks creating inconsistencies in the count.
Drop the ban on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation questions.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of communities like mine. Furthermore, the data collected by the Census determines how billions of dollars of environmental funding is distributed across the country. This includes funding for water and waste disposal systems, public transportation infrastructure, and disaster relief on which we all rely. The data collected will also inform research to identify and address environmental injustices. 

Moving forward with this proposed rule would harm all Americans. Our democracy works best when all people that live within our borders are fully represented in the data collected by the Census.

Sincerely,
Nancy Helgeson

I oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census because a fair and accurate census is critical to ensuring every community is counted, fairly represented, and able to get the resources people need to live healthy lives — including sexual and reproductive healthcare.
