Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Dear Director Cook,

Florence , AZ appreciates the opportunity to comment on the Census Bureau's proposed rule governing residence criteria and demographic questions for the 2030 decennial census. The census is the foundation for distributing political representation and federal resources. Accurate census ensures communities receive fair funding for infrastructure, housing, education, public safety, emergency response and other essential services. Because census data guide funding and planning decision for the next decade, accuracy is critical.  

We are concerned that several provisions of the proposed rule could reduce the accuracy of our community's population count and affect our access to federal and state resources. 

Concerns about the Proposed Changes 

[Select and adapt the paragraphs below that apply to your community. Delete any that don't.] 

Apportionment and population count: The proposed rule would limit the population counted toward apportionment to U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents for the first time. Although this change applies only to apportionment, it may create confusion or fear among residents and discourage participation. We request additional information on how full population data would be collected, reported and communicated, to ensure that all residents are counted for the broader data set. 

Legal-status question: The proposed rule also raises the possibility of adding a legal-status question to the census questionnaire. Similar proposals considered for the 2020 Census were not adopted following concerns that it could reduce participation, particularly among immigrant and mixed-status households. Any decline in response rates would undermine the accuracy of our community's population count as a whole and could impact the resources available to young children and families specifically. 

Usual residence and the enumeration period: The proposed shift to counting residents based on where they spend the most time during a January 3-April 1 period, rather than their usual residence throughout the year, could affect our population count [of seasonal residents such as snowbirds/ students / part-time workers / other mobile populations]. We ask the Bureau to further evaluate the operational and data-accuracy impacts of this change and explain the rationale supporting it.  

Reliance on administrative records: Increased reliance on tax, immigration, health and other administrative records raises concerns about the potential undercount of populations in our community that may not be consistently represented in those records, including low-income households, college students, non-filers and children. We request additional information regarding when these records will be used and how the Bureau will ensure accurate counts for populations with less reliable administrative data.  

Demographic questions: The proposal would eliminate race and ethnicity questions, while making most other demographic questions optional. Accurate demographic data is essential to municipal planning and service delivery. Understanding who lives in our community gives local governments the ability to plan for our current population and take into consideration our future population's needs. [Florence , AZ uses this data for...e.g., monitoring equitable service delivery, administering a specific program, public health planning, economic development targeting, etc]. The loss or reduction in the quality of this data could affect our ability to provide much needed services to our residents and accurately plan for our future.  

Funding impact: Census data inform funding for eother programs including Community Development Block Grants (CDBG), transit formula funding, and Title I education funding. An undercount of any portion of our population reduces resources available to the entire community  not just the households or individuals who go uncounted. State funding allocations depend, in many cases, on accurate census data. While the Bureau distinguishes between apportionment and funding distribution, changes that discourage participation risk reducing the quality of data used for both purposes.  

We respectfully ask the Census Bureau to withdraw these proposed changes. Any changes to residence criteria, data collection methods or demographic questions must not compromise the accuracy of the population counts that Florence , AZ and communities like ours rely on. 

We appreciate the opportunity to comment on this proposal and would welcome the chance to provide additional information or answer any questions the Bureau may have. 

Sincerely, 
James Bencina
Town council Florence Az

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: US Census Bureau,I urge the Census Bureau and Department of Commerce to withdraw the proposed rule changing residence criteria for the decennial Census and restricting demographic questions.The proposal would exclude foreign citizens from the population used for congressional apportionment unless they are also U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents. Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. I oppose this proposed rule because it departs from that constitutional mandate, risking severe harm to my community. Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I’m writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

As a person who cares about people and our planet, I know how important this data is, and as such, we need a fair and accurate Census. 

First, I ask the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. Significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve more time for members of the public — people like me — to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70 of the proposed rule. I urge you to withdraw the rule for substantial revisions, including:

Count every U.S. resident, including visa-holders, refugees, and asylum seekers.
Establish detailed  guidelines for complex residential situations such as recent movers, people in temporary situations, and children in foster care.
Go back to activity-based residence, not a “one hour” rule.
Drop the January-to-April enumeration period.
Count incarcerated people at home, not at the facility.
Revise the tax records language. Extreme reliance on tax records risks creating inconsistencies in the count.
Drop the ban on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation questions.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of communities like mine. Furthermore, the data collected by the Census determines how billions of dollars of environmental funding is distributed across the country. This includes funding for water and waste disposal systems, public transportation infrastructure, and disaster relief on which we all rely. The data collected will also inform research to identify and address environmental injustices. 

Moving forward with this proposed rule would harm all Americans. Our democracy works best when all people that live within our borders are fully represented in the data collected by the Census.

Sincerely,
Stephen Christian-Michaels

The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. I oppose this proposed rule because it departs from that constitutional mandate, risking severe harm to my community. Excluding noncitizens from the population count used for congressional apportionment and federal funding, while adding a citizenship question designed to deter participation, will suppress response rates across immigrant communities and mixed-status families who fear being targeted. An undercount here would directly strip my community of appropriate congressional representation and our fair share of federal funding for essential safety-net programs like SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, CHIP, and Title I education grants. As someone who cares about fairness and the rule of law, I urge the Bureau to withdraw this proposal and count every person living in our communities, as the Constitution requires. 

I am also concerned that the proposed rule erases vital Census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Decades of demographic data serve as the baseline that public and private institutions rely on to identify inequalities and direct resources where they are needed most. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities.  

Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.  

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Sincerely,
Laura Chinofsky
Southampton, PA

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I’m writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

As a person who cares about people and our planet, I know how important this data is, and as such, we need a fair and accurate Census. 

First, I ask the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. Significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve more time for members of the public — people like me — to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70 of the proposed rule. I urge you to withdraw the rule for substantial revisions, including:

Count every U.S. resident, including visa-holders, refugees, and asylum seekers.
Establish detailed  guidelines for complex residential situations such as recent movers, people in temporary situations, and children in foster care.
Go back to activity-based residence, not a “one hour” rule.
Drop the January-to-April enumeration period.
Count incarcerated people at home, not at the facility.
Revise the tax records language. Extreme reliance on tax records risks creating inconsistencies in the count.
Drop the ban on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation questions.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of communities like mine. Furthermore, the data collected by the Census determines how billions of dollars of environmental funding is distributed across the country. This includes funding for water and waste disposal systems, public transportation infrastructure, and disaster relief on which we all rely. The data collected will also inform research to identify and address environmental injustices. 

Moving forward with this proposed rule would harm all Americans. Our democracy works best when all people that live within our borders are fully represented in the data collected by the Census.

Sincerely,
Patti Fink

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Comment Regarding Proposed Changes to Sections 60 and 70 of the Decennial Census

I strongly oppose the proposed changes contained in both Section 60 and Section 70.

The decennial census is one of the most important statistical undertakings conducted by the federal government. Its value extends far beyond congressional apportionment and redistricting. Census data serve as the foundation for economic research, business investment decisions, public health planning, educational resource allocation, infrastructure development, and countless government programs. The consequences of census design choices persist for an entire decade. Changes that reduce accuracy, completeness, or comparability will have lasting negative effects on the quality of information available to decision-makers across the nation.

Section 60: Residence Rules

I oppose the proposal to omit certain persons from the count and to replace the longstanding practice of counting individuals where they live and sleep most of the time as of Census Day with a residency reference period.

The current rule provides a clear, understandable, and historically consistent standard. A residency reference period would introduce unnecessary ambiguity, particularly for students, military personnel, seasonal workers, individuals experiencing housing instability, and children who divide time between households. Increased ambiguity increases the risk of undercounting and misclassification.

The most significant concern is the effect on data quality. Census-based population estimates are used by state and local governments to plan public services, transportation systems, and infrastructure investments. Hospitals rely on these data to assess community needs and plan future capacity. School systems use population data to forecast enrollment and allocate resources. Businesses use census information to evaluate labor markets, identify potential customers, and make investment decisions. Researchers depend on consistent census definitions to evaluate long-term demographic and economic trends.

Changing residence rules and omitting persons from the count would reduce comparability with prior censuses and weaken one of the nation's most valuable statistical resources. Decisions made using census data affect communities for years after each census is completed. Accuracy and consistency should therefore remain paramount considerations.

Section 70: Race and Ethnicity Data

I strongly oppose eliminating race and ethnicity questions from the decennial census.

Race and ethnicity data have been collected throughout the nation's history because they provide essential information for understanding demographic, economic, educational, and health outcomes. Eliminating these questions would create a substantial and permanent loss of information that cannot be easily replaced by other data sources.

As an economist, I am particularly concerned about the consequences for evidence-based policymaking and research. Census race and ethnicity data are routinely used to study labor markets, income mobility, educational attainment, housing outcomes, entrepreneurship, and health disparities. These analyses help policymakers, businesses, healthcare providers, and educators make informed decisions.

The consequences would extend well beyond academic research. Businesses rely on demographic information to assess markets and workforce needs. State and local governments use these data to plan services and evaluate programs. Hospitals and public health agencies depend on demographic data to identify and address health disparities. School systems use demographic information to anticipate educational needs and evaluate outcomes.

Most importantly, the loss would persist for decades. Once these data are omitted from a decennial census, they cannot be recovered later. Future researchers and policymakers would lose the ability to compare outcomes across demographic groups over time, creating a permanent break in one of the nation's most important longitudinal datasets.

Conclusion

The census is not merely a population count. It is critical national data infrastructure. Economists, businesses, state governments, hospitals, schools, researchers, and community organizations rely on census data for years after each enumeration. The proposed changes in Sections 60 and 70 would reduce the quality, completeness, and usefulness of that information, ultimately impairing decision-making across both the public and private sectors.

For these reasons, I urge the Census Bureau to reject the proposed changes and preserve the established residence rules and demographic data collection practices that have long supported accurate enumeration and high-quality statistical data for the nation.

José Fernandez
 Professor of Economics
 University of Louisville

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. I oppose this proposed rule because it departs from that constitutional mandate, risking severe harm to my community. Excluding noncitizens from the population count used for congressional apportionment and federal funding, while adding a citizenship question designed to deter participation, will suppress response rates across immigrant communities and mixed-status families who fear being targeted. An undercount here would directly strip my community of appropriate congressional representation and our fair share of federal funding for essential safety-net programs like SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, CHIP, and Title I education grants. As someone who cares about fairness and the rule of law, I urge the Bureau to withdraw this proposal and count every person living in our communities, as the Constitution requires. 

I am also concerned that the proposed rule erases vital Census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Decades of demographic data serve as the baseline that public and private institutions rely on to identify inequalities and direct resources where they are needed most. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities.  

Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.  

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Sincerely,
Andrea Lauren Brown
Wilmington, DE

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I’m writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

As a person who cares about people and our planet, I know how important this data is, and as such, we need a fair and accurate Census. 

First, I ask the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. Significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve more time for members of the public — people like me — to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70 of the proposed rule. I urge you to withdraw the rule for substantial revisions, including:

Count every U.S. resident, including visa-holders, refugees, and asylum seekers.
Establish detailed  guidelines for complex residential situations such as recent movers, people in temporary situations, and children in foster care.
Go back to activity-based residence, not a “one hour” rule.
Drop the January-to-April enumeration period.
Count incarcerated people at home, not at the facility.
Revise the tax records language. Extreme reliance on tax records risks creating inconsistencies in the count.
Drop the ban on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation questions.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of communities like mine. Furthermore, the data collected by the Census determines how billions of dollars of environmental funding is distributed across the country. This includes funding for water and waste disposal systems, public transportation infrastructure, and disaster relief on which we all rely. The data collected will also inform research to identify and address environmental injustices. 

Moving forward with this proposed rule would harm all Americans. Our democracy works best when all people that live within our borders are fully represented in the data collected by the Census.

Sincerely,
Jocelyn Stevenson

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. I oppose this proposed rule because it departs from that constitutional mandate, risking severe harm to my community. Excluding noncitizens from the population count used for congressional apportionment and federal funding, while adding a citizenship question designed to deter participation, will suppress response rates across immigrant communities and mixed-status families who fear being targeted. An undercount here would directly strip my community of appropriate congressional representation and our fair share of federal funding for essential safety-net programs like SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, CHIP, and Title I education grants. As someone who cares about fairness and the rule of law, I urge the Bureau to withdraw this proposal and count every person living in our communities, as the Constitution requires. 

I am also concerned that the proposed rule erases vital Census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Decades of demographic data serve as the baseline that public and private institutions rely on to identify inequalities and direct resources where they are needed most. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities.  

Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.  

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Sincerely,
Anne Brown
Vail, CO

Stanhope, NJ

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I’m writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

As a person who cares about people and our planet, I know how important this data is, and as such, we need a fair and accurate Census. 

First, I ask the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. Significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve more time for members of the public — people like me — to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70 of the proposed rule. I urge you to withdraw the rule for substantial revisions, including:

Count every U.S. resident, including visa-holders, refugees, and asylum seekers.
Establish detailed  guidelines for complex residential situations such as recent movers, people in temporary situations, and children in foster care.
Go back to activity-based residence, not a “one hour” rule.
Drop the January-to-April enumeration period.
Count incarcerated people at home, not at the facility.
Revise the tax records language. Extreme reliance on tax records risks creating inconsistencies in the count.
Drop the ban on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation questions.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of communities like mine. Furthermore, the data collected by the Census determines how billions of dollars of environmental funding is distributed across the country. This includes funding for water and waste disposal systems, public transportation infrastructure, and disaster relief on which we all rely. The data collected will also inform research to identify and address environmental injustices. 

Moving forward with this proposed rule would harm all Americans. Our democracy works best when all people that live within our borders are fully represented in the data collected by the Census.

Sincerely,
Patrick McGuffin

Comment:
The Bureau seeks to alter the people's power as the foundation of government by eliminating those it seeks to undercount - Deprive representation, as well as appropriations, to residents no longer deemed Congressional constituents. The Constitution, statutes, and settled law clearly provide that all persons residing in the United States must be counted for the apportionment of Congressional seats. If the census does not count all residents, our communities will lose resources to support their schools, hospitals, transportation infrastructure, emergency services, and more.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am Carol Poenisch from Northville, MI. I am a retired teacher and I care about a fair and accurate census because I knew someone who was a census taker and didn’t have enough time to finish her turf. 

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions. 
• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.
As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. I oppose this proposed rule because it departs from that constitutional mandate, risking severe harm to my community. Excluding noncitizens from the population count used for congressional apportionment and federal funding, while adding a citizenship question designed to deter participation, will suppress response rates across immigrant communities and mixed-status families who fear being targeted. An undercount here would directly strip my community of appropriate congressional representation and our fair share of federal funding for essential safety-net programs like SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, CHIP, and Title I education grants. As someone who cares about fairness and the rule of law, I urge the Bureau to withdraw this proposal and count every person living in our communities, as the Constitution requires. 

I am also concerned that the proposed rule erases vital Census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Decades of demographic data serve as the baseline that public and private institutions rely on to identify inequalities and direct resources where they are needed most. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities.  

Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.  

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Sincerely,
Catherine Williams
Tucson, AZ

Comment: US Census Bureau,I urge the Census Bureau and Department of Commerce to withdraw the proposed rule changing residence criteria for the decennial Census and restricting demographic questions.The proposal would exclude foreign citizens from the population used for congressional apportionment unless they are also U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents. Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
My name is [Your Name] and I am your constituent from [City/Zip Code]. As Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander (AANHPI) Heritage Month comes to a close, I write to urge you to support AANHPI students by cosponsoring the All Students Count Act.

To the U.S. Census Bureau: 

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule titled “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005). Eliminating the collection of race and ethnic data, prohibiting the collection of sexual orientation, and leaving non-citizens out of the apportionment would significantly harm the Southeast Asian American (SEAA) and broader Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander (AANHPI) communities. I respectfully request that the Census Bureau withdraw the proposed rule and extend the comment period to December 10, 2026. 

This proposed rule would significantly harm the SEAA and AANHPI communities. The AANHPI community is not a homogenous population; it encompasses over 50 different ethnic groups and 100 languages and dialects. There are vast socioeconomic disparities within the AANHPI population, often related to their migratory and historical experience. SEAAs, such as the Cambodian, Hmong, Laotian, and Mien populations, often have higher rates of poverty and lower educational attainment rates than both the broader AANHPI and American populations. 

For SEAAs, this disparity is generally tied to their experiences escaping their countries of origin and resettlement in the United States after the Vietnam War, Secret War in Laos, and Khmer Rouge genocide in Cambodia. For example, because of the 2020 Census, we now know that the Mien population has lower educational attainment rates compared to the general American and AANHPI populations. Additionally, the data also show that Mien men have a lower educational attainment rate compared to women. Such information could only be obtained because of the census, which is the primary source for data collection and reporting of small ethnic groups. These data cannot be replicated by other surveys, including the American Community Survey. 

Accurate data, reflective of race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation, help our elected officials properly identify and address the unique needs and challenges of our communities. Prohibiting the collection of this demographic data would prevent our government officials from passing informed public policy; hamper the ability of community-based organizations to demonstrate data narratives for fundraising purposes; and inhibit the ability of students and academics studying our communities from accessing the most robust source of information on SEAAs and the broader AANHPI community. 

Thank you for taking my comment into consideration. I reiterate my request that the US Census Bureau withdraws the proposed rule; preserves the collection of race and ethnic data; and keeps its commitment to count everyone once, only once, and in the right place.

I also ask the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. Changes of this scope deserve more time for the public to review and respond.

Sincerely,
Allison Anderson
Cottage Grove, MN 55016

As a person who cares about people and our planet, I know how important this data is, and as such, we need a fair and accurate Census. 

First, I ask the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. Significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve more time for members of the public — people like me — to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70 of the proposed rule. I urge you to withdraw the rule for substantial revisions, including:

Count every U.S. resident, including visa-holders, refugees, and asylum seekers.
Establish detailed  guidelines for complex residential situations such as recent movers, people in temporary situations, and children in foster care.
Go back to activity-based residence, not a “one hour” rule.
Drop the January-to-April enumeration period.
Count incarcerated people at home, not at the facility.
Revise the tax records language. Extreme reliance on tax records risks creating inconsistencies in the count.
Drop the ban on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation questions.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of communities like mine. Furthermore, the data collected by the Census determines how billions of dollars of environmental funding is distributed across the country. This includes funding for water and waste disposal systems, public transportation infrastructure, and disaster relief on which we all rely. The data collected will also inform research to identify and address environmental injustices. 

Moving forward with this proposed rule would harm all Americans. Our democracy works best when all people that live within our borders are fully represented in the data collected by the Census.

Sincerely,
Kwankisha Crawford

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: US Census Bureau,I urge the Census Bureau and Department of Commerce to withdraw the proposed rule changing residence criteria for the decennial Census and restricting demographic questions.The proposal would exclude foreign citizens from the population used for congressional apportionment unless they are also U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents. The Census proposes to only include people if their address is confirmed by tax records -- which could mean millions, particularly low-income families, could be missed in the decennial Census. Overall, this would leave out people who actually live in our community, including many people who are lawfully present in the United States.For all past Census counts, including the 2020 Census, foreign citizens living in the United States were generally counted where they lived and slept most of the time. That approach recognizes the basic purpose of a Census: accurately counting the people who live in our communities. The 14th Amendment requires congressional representation to be apportioned according to the “whole number of persons in each State.”I am also deeply concerned by the proposal to prohibit race and ethnicity questions, along with sexual orientation, on the decennial Census enumeration questionnaire. The Census Bureau itself recognizes the importance of race data for civil rights protections, legislative redistricting, equal employment opportunities, and identifying disparities.The 2030 Census will determine congressional, state, and local representation for the decade that follows. It must be complete, accurate, and protected from political manipulation.Please withdraw this proposed rule and preserve a Census that fairly and accurately counts our community.Kenneth  Bryan[X]Arab , Alabama 35016

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. I oppose this proposed rule because it departs from that constitutional mandate, risking severe harm to my community. Excluding noncitizens from the population count used for congressional apportionment and federal funding, while adding a citizenship question designed to deter participation, will suppress response rates across immigrant communities and mixed-status families who fear being targeted. An undercount here would directly strip my community of appropriate congressional representation and our fair share of federal funding for essential safety-net programs like SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, CHIP, and Title I education grants. As someone who cares about fairness and the rule of law, I urge the Bureau to withdraw this proposal and count every person living in our communities, as the Constitution requires. 

I am also concerned that the proposed rule erases vital Census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Decades of demographic data serve as the baseline that public and private institutions rely on to identify inequalities and direct resources where they are needed most. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities.  

Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.  

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Sincerely,
Donna Pope
Tampa, FL

I oppose this proposed rule because it departs from that constitutional mandate, risking severe harm to my community. Excluding noncitizens from the population count used for congressional apportionment and federal funding, while adding a citizenship question designed to deter participation, will suppress response rates across immigrant communities and mixed-status families who fear being targeted. An undercount here would directly strip my community of appropriate congressional representation and our fair share of federal funding for essential safety-net programs like SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, CHIP, and Title I education grants. As someone who cares about fairness and the rule of law, I urge the Bureau to withdraw this proposal and count every person living in our communities, as the Constitution requires. I am also concerned that the proposed rule erases vital Census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Decades of demographic data serve as the baseline that public and private institutions rely on to identify inequalities and direct resources where they are needed most. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities. Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I’m writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

As a person who cares about people and our planet, I know how important this data is, and as such, we need a fair and accurate Census. 

First, I ask the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. Significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve more time for members of the public — people like me — to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70 of the proposed rule. I urge you to withdraw the rule for substantial revisions, including:

Count every U.S. resident, including visa-holders, refugees, and asylum seekers.
Establish detailed  guidelines for complex residential situations such as recent movers, people in temporary situations, and children in foster care.
Go back to activity-based residence, not a “one hour” rule.
Drop the January-to-April enumeration period.
Count incarcerated people at home, not at the facility.
Revise the tax records language. Extreme reliance on tax records risks creating inconsistencies in the count.
Drop the ban on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation questions.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of communities like mine. Furthermore, the data collected by the Census determines how billions of dollars of environmental funding is distributed across the country. This includes funding for water and waste disposal systems, public transportation infrastructure, and disaster relief on which we all rely. The data collected will also inform research to identify and address environmental injustices. 

Moving forward with this proposed rule would harm all Americans. Our democracy works best when all people that live within our borders are fully represented in the data collected by the Census.

Sincerely,
D.G. Sifuentes

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule: Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions.
The census has counted all residents for apportionment regardless of legal status for 230 years. Article I, Section 2, Clause 3 of the U.S. Constitution mandates that an "actual Enumeration" of the population be conducted within three years of the first Congress meeting and every subsequent term of ten years. The 14th Amendment further clarifies that representatives are apportioned by counting the "whole number of persons" in each state.
We have always counted native-born U.S. citizens, naturalized U.S. citizens, non-citizen U.S. nationals, lawful permanent residents and temporary migrants, such as foreign students, refugees, asylum seekers and undocumented immigrants. The census has never left out residents because of their immigration status.
The point of the census is to determine funding and representation of our communities. By not counting all people, communities will not get the resources they need for schools, hospitals, roads, firefighters and other critical services. 
This proposal would mean there would no longer be a complete and accurate count of our population. I strongly oppose this rule and encourage the census bureau not to enact it.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to STRONGLY OPPOSE the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). I specifically oppose the proposals to:

-- restrict the count to US citizens
-- ban collection of data on race/ethnicity and to prohibit any collection of data on sexual orientation
-- make most demographic questions voluntary, except biological sex, date of birth, and household relationship, which is inconsistent with US law 
-- expand the time period for determining usual residence from April 1 (used since 1790) to instead January 3 – April 1
-- tie determination of usual residence to address used in tax returns
-- entrench the wrongful practice of counting incarcerated persons at the facility they are located, rather than their community from which they come

The basis of my STRONG OPPOSITION to ALL of these proposals is that I am a population health scientist, specifically an epidemiologist, and for the past 40 years I have relied extensively on US census data for my research. As I know well from my research, including extensive reliance on US decennial data counts, and on area-based metrics about the populations living in US census tracts, counties, and states, the decennial census data: 

(1) provide the population counts vital for the denominators for all mortality and morbidity rates (i.e., cases/count of relevant population) 

(2) provide the data necessary to weight the surveys that are critical for understanding patterns of population health (e.g., National Health Interview Survey, Household Pulse Survey,  and many many others)

(3) provide the data necessary to “paint a truer picture” of US population health, as per the words of Edgar Sydenstricker, the first statistician hired by the US Bureau of Commerce in the early 1900s, and who was key to the design of the Hagerstown morbidity surveys in the 1920s and the first national health survey in the 1930s (as quoted in my article at: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1449172/)  

-- obtaining data on race/ethnicity and sexuality is essential for understanding population health

-- preventing collection of these demographic data, and making provision of other sociodemographic data voluntary (except for age, sex, and household relation),  is thus substantively and methodologically flawed and dishonest 

(4) provide the data necessary for counts for political representation and also myriad allocation formula for disbursement of federal funds, determining the amount of federal aid provided to each and every US state, county, city/town, tribal area, and other relevant units of geography 

-- the proposed changes would also wrongly further entrench the practice US census “prison gerrymandering,” a policy widely criticized by US states, whereby incarcerated persons are counted as being part of the population where the facility is located thus wrongly inflating the population in the area including the facility, thereby wrongly inflating its political representation and allocation of resources, and, conversely, denying allocation of political representation and resources (as shaped by population counts) to the communities of residence of the incarcerated populations

The proposed changes are thus wrong and irresponsible. They will exacerbate – not reduce – problems of the US census undercount, and they will exacerbate problems in determining individual’s correct residence, especially since not all US persons file tax returns, and not all people live in solely one residence during the proposed expanded time frame. Nor does the proposal explain how the US census would deal with false-positive and false-negative matches induced by the reliance on tax records.

These proposed shocking (literally: shock to the system) and unjustified changes to counting the US population thus will HARM understanding of population health parameters AND make time trend analysis impossible for understanding if population health patterns are improving, staying stagnant, or getting worse. They will also HARM people’s health by wrongly altering the allocation of federal funds and political representation, via wrongful undercount and inflation of different area’s population counts.

Consequently, the proposed changes pose a grave threat to the US public’s health and well-being. They must NOT be implemented.

I accordingly demand that the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and to test any change to residence criteria or content through its established research and review process before adopting it. 

I also ask the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026, given the scope of changes proposed.

Nancy Krieger, PhD 
   Professor of Social Epidemiology
   American Cancer Society Clinical Research Professor 
   Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health (Boston, MA)

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: US Census Bureau,I urge the Census Bureau and Department of Commerce to withdraw the proposed rule changing residence criteria for the decennial Census and restricting demographic questions.The proposal would exclude foreign citizens from the population used for congressional apportionment unless they are also U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents. The Census proposes to only include people if their address is confirmed by tax records -- which could mean millions, particularly low-income families, could be missed in the decennial Census. Overall, this would leave out people who actually live in our community, including many people who are lawfully present in the United States.For all past Census counts, including the 2020 Census, foreign citizens living in the United States were generally counted where they lived and slept most of the time. The 14th Amendment requires congressional representation to be apportioned according to the “whole number of persons in each State.”I am also deeply concerned by the proposal to prohibit race and ethnicity questions, along with sexual orientation, on the decennial Census enumeration questionnaire. The Census Bureau itself recognizes the importance of race data for civil rights protections, legislative redistricting, equal employment opportunities, and identifying disparities.The 2030 Census will determine congressional, state, and local representation for the decade that follows. It must be complete, accurate, and protected from political manipulation.Please withdraw this proposed rule and preserve a Census that fairly and accurately counts our community.Kathy Pollock[X]Tewksbury, Massachusetts 01876

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule: Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions.

The census has counted *all* residents for apportionment regardless of legal status for 230 years. Article I, Section 2, Clause 3 of the U.S. Constitution mandates that an "actual Enumeration" of the population be conducted within three years of the first Congress meeting and every subsequent term of ten years. The 14th Amendment further clarifies that representatives are apportioned by counting the "whole number of persons" in each state.
We have always counted native-born U.S. citizens, naturalized U.S. citizens, non-citizen U.S. nationals, lawful permanent residents and temporary migrants, such as foreign students, refugees, asylum seekers and undocumented immigrants. The census has *never* left out residents because of their immigration status.
The census determines the funding and representation of our communities. By not counting all people, communities will not get the resources they need for schools, hospitals, roads, firefighters and other critical services.

This proposal would mean there would no longer be a complete and accurate count of our population. I strongly oppose this rule and encourage the census bureau not to enact it.

Thank you,
Kristin B. Webb

I oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census because a fair and accurate census is critical to ensuring every community is counted, fairly represented, and able to get the resources people need to live healthy lives — including sexual and reproductive healthcare. An inaccurate or incomplete census can deepen existing inequities, particularly for communities that already face disenfranchisement and barriers to healthcare.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. I oppose this proposed rule because it departs from that constitutional mandate, risking severe harm to my community. Excluding noncitizens from the population count used for congressional apportionment and federal funding, while adding a citizenship question designed to deter participation, will suppress response rates across immigrant communities and mixed-status families who fear being targeted. An undercount here would directly strip my community of appropriate congressional representation and our fair share of federal funding for essential safety-net programs like SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, CHIP, and Title I education grants. As someone who cares about fairness and the rule of law, I urge the Bureau to withdraw this proposal and count every person living in our communities, as the Constitution requires. I am also concerned that the proposed rule erases vital Census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Decades of demographic data serve as the baseline that public and private institutions rely on to identify inequalities and direct resources where they are needed most. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities. Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census. These changes will not only weaken the accuracy and integrity of our nation's most important population count, but they will also harm our communities, and I strongly urge the Bureau to reject them. 

First, removing questions of race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation erases the full scope of my identity when I participate in the Census survey. These data points are not optional. They are the tools we use to enforce civil rights laws, monitor discrimination, and measure the disparities that still affect millions of people. Excluding them from the count does not make them disappear from our society, but it does make our government less equipped to handle big issues when they arise. 

The Constitution is clear: the census must count ALL persons living in the United States, regardless of their immigration or citizenship status. The proposal to exclude non-citizens, including those residents with some type of lawful status, violates more than two centuries of legal precedent. Every person counted in this country contributes to our communities, and every person deserves to be fully seen. 

The consequences of these changes will negatively impact our daily lives. The census affects everything. It determines political representation and the drawing of voting districts. It guides how billions of dollars in federal funding are used to close persistent disparities in schools, hospitals, and other government programs that are designed to improve our lives.  

The census is the foundation of our democracy. It must reflect the complete yet nuanced reality of who we are as a nation. And it must reflect the lives of our friends and neighbors who may not look, think, or speak like we do. I ask the Bureau to withdraw these proposed changes and to preserve a count that includes everyone and represents everyone. 

Thank you for considering my comment.

Sincerely,
Yvette Wilds

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census. These changes will not only weaken the accuracy and integrity of our nation's most important population count, but they will also harm our communities, and I strongly urge the Bureau to reject them. 

First, removing questions of race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation erases the full scope of my identity when I participate in the Census survey. These data points are not optional. They are the tools we use to enforce civil rights laws, monitor discrimination, and measure the disparities that still affect millions of people. Excluding them from the count does not make them disappear from our society, but it does make our government less equipped to handle big issues when they arise. 

The Constitution is clear: the census must count ALL persons living in the United States, regardless of their immigration or citizenship status. The proposal to exclude non-citizens, including those residents with some type of lawful status, violates more than two centuries of legal precedent. Every person counted in this country contributes to our communities, and every person deserves to be fully seen. 

The consequences of these changes will negatively impact our daily lives. The census affects everything. It determines political representation and the drawing of voting districts. It guides how billions of dollars in federal funding are used to close persistent disparities in schools, hospitals, and other government programs that are designed to improve our lives.  

The census is the foundation of our democracy. It must reflect the complete yet nuanced reality of who we are as a nation. And it must reflect the lives of our friends and neighbors who may not look, think, or speak like we do. I ask the Bureau to withdraw these proposed changes and to preserve a count that includes everyone and represents everyone. 

Thank you for considering my comment.

Sincerely,
Ariel Dawkins

Comment:

I oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census because a fair and accurate census is critical to ensuring every community is counted, fairly represented, and able to get the resources people need to live healthy lives — including sexual and reproductive healthcare. An inaccurate or incomplete census can deepen existing inequities, particularly for communities that already face disenfranchisement and barriers to healthcare. 

A fair and accurate census is essential to our health and rights. 

Census data help determine access to programs patients and their families rely on, including important programs like Medicaid, SNAP, WIC, and TANF. Accurate census data also shape political representation by determining how seats in the U.S. House of Representatives are apportioned among states and providing data used for redistricting. When communities are undercounted or excluded, they risk losing both resources and political representation. 

The Census Bureau and Department of Commerce must:

1. Count all people residing in the United States in the 2030 Census, without regard to immigration status. Excluding noncitizens from census apportionment data violates the Constitution and established legal precedent. It would suppress the count of many communities, effectively erasing them from critical datasets and depriving them of resources and congressional representation –— including resources and political representation that support access to healthcare.

2. Continue collecting race and ethnicity data and implement the 2024 OMB SPD 15 standards. Census race and ethnicity data are essential for important research across many sectors, for upholding civil rights, and for growing the economy. Extensive Census Bureau research and engagement with expert stakeholders shows that implementing the modernized 2024 OMB SPD 15 standards for race and ethnicity data collection will yield data that more accurately represent the nation’s increasingly diverse population.

3. Remove the clause banning the addition of future questions on sexual orientation. Proposed changes to demographic items should be based on research and guided by a deliberative and transparent process, including extensive stakeholder consultation.

4. Withdraw other proposed changes to residence criteria, including tying place of residence to tax records and "lawful residence," and the adoption of a three month enumeration period. The Census Bureau must extensively research and consult with stakeholders about the potential effects of such changes before proposing their implementation in a decennial census.

5. Halt the practice of prison gerrymandering by counting incarcerated individuals in their home communities. This will yield more accurate census data and ensure that communities receive the congressional representation to which they are entitled.

This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities. Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census. The proposed changes are NOT in compliance with the US Constitution and should NOT be implemented.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am [add a description of who you are, such as your profession and/or state where you live], and I care about a fair and accurate census because [add a brief description of why you care].

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: [keep any/all points you would like to include in your comment]

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.
As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:

Regarding the proposed rule, “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026):
My name is Chandler Felt. I live with my wife in Seattle, King County, Washington.  I recently retired as Demographer for the King County Washington government. I am writing to request that the Census Bureau withdraw the proposed new rule, and retain its commitment to count the whole population of the United States, completely, counting everyone once, only once, and in the right place.
As Demographer for a county of more than 2,000,000 residents – not all of them citizens – I relied utterly on the accuracy and comprehensiveness of both the Decennial Census and the American Community Survey to perform my work. -	F. Chandler Felt

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. I oppose this proposed rule because it departs from that constitutional mandate, risking severe harm to my community. Excluding noncitizens from the population count used for congressional apportionment and federal funding, while adding a citizenship question designed to deter participation, will suppress response rates across immigrant communities and mixed-status families who fear being targeted. An undercount here would directly strip my community of appropriate congressional representation and our fair share of federal funding for essential safety-net programs like SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, CHIP, and Title I education grants. As someone who cares about fairness and the rule of law, I urge the Bureau to withdraw this proposal and count every person living in our communities, as the Constitution requires. 

I am also concerned that the proposed rule erases vital Census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Decades of demographic data serve as the baseline that public and private institutions rely on to identify inequalities and direct resources where they are needed most. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities.  

Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.  

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Sincerely,
Jackie Nelson
Springfield, MA
