Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
My name is [Your Name] and I am your constituent from [City/Zip Code]. As Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander (AANHPI) Heritage Month comes to a close, I write to urge you to support AANHPI students by cosponsoring the All Students Count Act.

To the U.S. Census Bureau: 

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule titled “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005). Eliminating the collection of race and ethnic data, prohibiting the collection of sexual orientation, and leaving non-citizens out of the apportionment would significantly harm the Southeast Asian American (SEAA) and broader Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander (AANHPI) communities. I respectfully request that the Census Bureau withdraw the proposed rule and extend the comment period to December 10, 2026. 

This proposed rule would significantly harm the SEAA and AANHPI communities. The AANHPI community is not a homogenous population; it encompasses over 50 different ethnic groups and 100 languages and dialects. There are vast socioeconomic disparities within the AANHPI population, often related to their migratory and historical experience. SEAAs, such as the Cambodian, Hmong, Laotian, and Mien populations, often have higher rates of poverty and lower educational attainment rates than both the broader AANHPI and American populations. 

For SEAAs, this disparity is generally tied to their experiences escaping their countries of origin and resettlement in the United States after the Vietnam War, Secret War in Laos, and Khmer Rouge genocide in Cambodia. For example, because of the 2020 Census, we now know that the Mien population has lower educational attainment rates compared to the general American and AANHPI populations. Additionally, the data also show that Mien men have a lower educational attainment rate compared to women. Such information could only be obtained because of the census, which is the primary source for data collection and reporting of small ethnic groups. These data cannot be replicated by other surveys, including the American Community Survey. 

Accurate data, reflective of race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation, help our elected officials properly identify and address the unique needs and challenges of our communities. Prohibiting the collection of this demographic data would prevent our government officials from passing informed public policy; hamper the ability of community-based organizations to demonstrate data narratives for fundraising purposes; and inhibit the ability of students and academics studying our communities from accessing the most robust source of information on SEAAs and the broader AANHPI community. 

Thank you for taking my comment into consideration. I reiterate my request that the US Census Bureau withdraws the proposed rule; preserves the collection of race and ethnic data; and keeps its commitment to count everyone once, only once, and in the right place.

I also ask the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. Changes of this scope deserve more time for the public to review and respond.

Sincerely,
Sron Devy
Buena Park, CA 90620

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. I oppose this proposed rule because it departs from that constitutional mandate, risking severe harm to my community. Excluding noncitizens from the population count used for congressional apportionment and federal funding, while adding a citizenship question designed to deter participation, will suppress response rates across immigrant communities and mixed-status families who fear being targeted. An undercount here would directly strip my community of appropriate congressional representation and our fair share of federal funding for essential safety-net programs like SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, CHIP, and Title I education grants. As someone who cares about fairness and the rule of law, I urge the Bureau to withdraw this proposal and count every person living in our communities, as the Constitution requires. 

I am also concerned that the proposed rule erases vital Census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Decades of demographic data serve as the baseline that public and private institutions rely on to identify inequalities and direct resources where they are needed most. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities.  

Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.  

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Sincerely,
Lana Couts
Alameda, CA

To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am a 36-year-old female teacher on Texas, and I care about a fair and accurate census because it should be a true representation of the people who make up/populate this country.

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including:

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. I oppose this proposed rule because it departs from that constitutional mandate, risking severe harm to my community. Excluding noncitizens from the population count used for congressional apportionment and federal funding, while adding a citizenship question designed to deter participation, will suppress response rates across immigrant communities and mixed-status families who fear being targeted. An undercount here would directly strip my community of appropriate congressional representation and our fair share of federal funding for essential safety-net programs like SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, CHIP, and Title I education grants. As someone who cares about fairness and the rule of law, I urge the Bureau to withdraw this proposal and count every person living in our communities, as the Constitution requires. 

I am also concerned that the proposed rule erases vital Census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Decades of demographic data serve as the baseline that public and private institutions rely on to identify inequalities and direct resources where they are needed most. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities.  

Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.  

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Sincerely,
Dorothy Brenn
Bouse, AZ

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: U.S. Census Bureau,I am writing to oppose the Census Bureau's proposal to remove race and ethnicity questions from the 2030 Census (Docket No. USBC-2026-0628).For decades, federal standards counted Middle Eastern and North African (MENA) Americans as White. This made our communities invisible in the data. In 2024, after years of advocacy and research by the Census Bureau itself, federal standards finally added a "Middle Eastern or North African" category. This proposal would erase that progress before the MENA category is ever used on the census.The Bureau has also decided not to use the updated standards in the 2027 American Community Survey. As a result, no federal survey would count MENA Americans using the MENA category. Without accurate counts, we cannot document the health, education, and economic gaps we face, or the discrimination our communities report.Accurate, detailed data also helps the government spend public dollars wisely. When agencies know who lives where and what they need, they can direct funding and services to the places they will do the most good. Removing these questions would make public spending less efficient, not more.I urge the Census Bureau to:1. Keep race and ethnicity questions on the 2030 Census, including the MENA category required by the 2024 standards.2. Recommit to full implementation of the 2024 revision to Statistical Policy Directive No. 15 (SPD 15), including on the American Community Survey.3. Extend the comment period by 60 days. A proposal of this importance deserves more time for public review.4. Re-engage with community organizations, researchers, and state and local governments in a collaborative process to use more detailed data for the public good, including to direct resources more efficiently to the communities that need them most.Thank you for considering my comment.Colette [X] San Diego, California 92126

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I write in support of the Census Bureau's proposed rule, "Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions" (Docket No. USBC-2026-0628; RIN 0607-AA75).

The Constitution calls for an "actual Enumeration" every ten years so that representation can be fairly apportioned among the states. The decennial census is meant to be a count, not a survey or a statistical estimate. Americans' voice in Congress depends on that count being right.

In 2020, the Bureau intentionally introduced statistical noise into the population data used to draw congressional and legislative districts. Data that determine political representation should never be deliberately altered. I support proposed  70.3, which directs the Bureau to prioritize the accuracy of the population count and prohibits publishing demographic data when doing so would introduce uncertainty into national or state population counts.

I also support the proposed residence criteria. Being counted at one's "usual residence" has never meant mere physical presence on Census Day. It reflects a lasting connection to a place, which is why service members stationed abroad are still counted in their home states. Counting citizens and lawful permanent residents, and excluding foreign nationals who are here unlawfully or temporarily, follows that principle.

I support keeping the enumeration questionnaire focused on the count itself. The Bureau can continue to produce demographic and statistical information through the American Community Survey and other tools, but those products should remain separate from the constitutional headcount.

To make these reforms durable, I urge the Bureau to state clearly in the final rule that the constitutional enumeration, and the counts used for apportionment and redistricting, are fundamentally distinct from routine federal statistical products and may not be adjusted to serve other statistical purposes.

Please finalize this rule so that the 2030 Census delivers an accurate count and restores Americans' trust in how they are represented.

Respectfully,
Ryan Husaynu
West Bloomfield, MI

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
As a member of the Clinton City Council representing Ward 3 in Clinton, Oklahoma, I am concerned about the potential impact of the Census Bureau’s proposed changes to the decennial census on communities like ours.

For a rural community, accurate census data is not simply a matter of statistics. It is information we rely upon to understand our community, plan for its future, pursue grants and resources, support economic development, and make informed decisions about infrastructure and public services.

Clinton is a diverse community, and that diversity is one of our strengths. Removing race and ethnicity questions from the decennial census could reduce the availability and precision of demographic information about communities like ours. The Census Bureau currently produces race and Hispanic-origin data at very small geographic levels from the decennial census, including data used for redistricting. Replacing direct decennial collection with other surveys or administrative data raises legitimate concerns about whether smaller and rural communities will have access to information of the same detail and reliability.

I am also concerned about proposed changes to the residence criteria that could exclude some people who actually live in our community from certain census population counts based on their immigration status. Regardless of an individual's citizenship status, people who live in Clinton use our streets and infrastructure, send children to schools, shop in our businesses, work for local employers, and are part of the population for which local governments must plan and provide services.

For cities like Clinton, knowing how many people actually live here matters.

The Census Bureau itself recognizes that census statistics influence decisions involving federal funding for schools, roads, health care, emergency services and other community needs. Small and rural communities already face challenges competing for limited resources. Changes that make our population or its characteristics less accurately represented could make those challenges greater.

I believe census policy should provide local governments with the most complete and accurate picture possible of the people who actually live in the communities we serve. As a city council member, I need reliable information about all of the residents of Clinton—not only some of them—to make responsible decisions about our city's future.

My concern is practical and local: Clinton should not become harder to understand, plan for, or adequately resource because the federal government has changed which residents or demographic characteristics are reflected in the nation's most important population count.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to strongly oppose the new rule being proposed: 
“Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions.”
The proposed rule would directly violate and undermine a major purpose of the census: namely, to determine the representation of our communities and the federal funding they receive, and to enable every level of government (local, county, state and federal) to both know and effectively serve the persons residing in its territory. By not counting all persons actually there, communities will not get the resources they need for police, schools, hospitals, roads, firefighters, nor have knowledge of the specific needs of different segments of each community.  Not every “person” is the same and not knowing the actual distinctions among them—by age, gender, & race—it will be impossible for elected officials to honor what the 14th Amendment of the U.S. Constitution requires: to give “equal protection of the laws” to “any person within its jurisdiction.”

As is well-known, for 230 years the census has counted all residents of each area, regardless of legal status, for the purpose of apportionment.  Yes, prior to the 13th and 14th Amendments, slaves and former slaves (“other Persons”) were counted as merely 2/3 of a human being, but those two Amendments abolished that.  That returned the census to the task of simply counting “the numbers” of persons, period. 
It is obvious why local, county, and state governments need to know exactly who is in their population “numbers”: even foreign students, refugees, asylum seekers and undocumented immigrants need to be serviced by the area’s police, fire departments, roads and transportation services, water and energy services, and in many cases hospitals and schools.  It is unfunctional and harmful to local, county and state administrations to leave out those who are actually resident, and using those services, simply because of their status as not yet being full citizens.

Since this proposal would mean there would no longer be a complete and accurate count of the U.S. population, at each and every level, I strongly oppose this rule and encourage the census bureau to not enact it.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. I oppose this proposed rule because it departs from that constitutional mandate, risking severe harm to my community. Excluding noncitizens from the population count used for congressional apportionment and federal funding, while adding a citizenship question designed to deter participation, will suppress response rates across immigrant communities and mixed-status families who fear being targeted. An undercount here would directly strip my community of appropriate congressional representation and our fair share of federal funding for essential safety-net programs like SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, CHIP, and Title I education grants. As someone who cares about fairness and the rule of law, I urge the Bureau to withdraw this proposal and count every person living in our communities, as the Constitution requires. 

I am also concerned that the proposed rule erases vital Census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Decades of demographic data serve as the baseline that public and private institutions rely on to identify inequalities and direct resources where they are needed most. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities.  

Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.  

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Sincerely,
GAYLA CREMIN
Collinsville, OK

I’m writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

As a person who cares about people and our planet, I know how important this data is, and as such, we need a fair and accurate Census. 

First, I ask the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. Significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve more time for members of the public — people like me — to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70 of the proposed rule. I urge you to withdraw the rule for substantial revisions, including:

Count every U.S. resident, including visa-holders, refugees, and asylum seekers.
Establish detailed  guidelines for complex residential situations such as recent movers, people in temporary situations, and children in foster care.
Go back to activity-based residence, not a “one hour” rule.
Drop the January-to-April enumeration period.
Count incarcerated people at home, not at the facility.
Revise the tax records language. Extreme reliance on tax records risks creating inconsistencies in the count.
Drop the ban on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation questions.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of communities like mine. Furthermore, the data collected by the Census determines how billions of dollars of environmental funding is distributed across the country. This includes funding for water and waste disposal systems, public transportation infrastructure, and disaster relief on which we all rely. The data collected will also inform research to identify and address environmental injustices. 

Moving forward with this proposed rule would harm all Americans. Our democracy works best when all people that live within our borders are fully represented in the data collected by the Census.

Sincerely,
Susan Adams

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. I oppose this proposed rule because it departs from that constitutional mandate, risking severe harm to my community. Excluding noncitizens from the population count used for congressional apportionment and federal funding, while adding a citizenship question designed to deter participation, will suppress response rates across immigrant communities and mixed-status families who fear being targeted. An undercount here would directly strip my community of appropriate congressional representation and our fair share of federal funding for essential safety-net programs like SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, CHIP, and Title I education grants. As someone who cares about fairness and the rule of law, I urge the Bureau to withdraw this proposal and count every person living in our communities, as the Constitution requires. 

I am also concerned that the proposed rule erases vital Census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Decades of demographic data serve as the baseline that public and private institutions rely on to identify inequalities and direct resources where they are needed most. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities.  

Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.  

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Sincerely,
Stan Kumiega
Aston, PA

Comment: 91 FR 57524  Public Comment,Re: Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions (Docket No. USBC-2026-0628).I am writing to oppose the Census Bureau's proposed rule, "Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions," Docket No. USBC-2026-0628, because it would produce an inaccurate count of the people living in this country.Every ten years, the census gives the country one reliable picture of who lives here. Congress, states, cities, and businesses use it to divide representation, distribute federal funds, and plan for the next decade. This rule would distort that picture. Fewer people would be counted, and some communities would disappear from the data altogether. The errors would affect the entire country, but they would be heaviest in immigrant, minority, and low-income households and in the states and towns where they live.The undercount would come from several directions. The rule would stop counting many immigrants who live here, even though the Constitution requires counting every person. It also invites a question about legal status, which would keep many people in immigrant and mixed-status households from answering at all, whatever their own status. And it would decide where people live using tax records, even though many people are not required to file and the rule says nothing about how to count people such as those without stable housing, foster children, or people in shelters and nursing homes.The invisibility would come from banning the race and ethnicity question and from households afraid to respond. Without that information, it is much harder to show where needs are greatest, enforce civil rights laws, check whether voting maps are fair, or catch health problems that hit some communities harder. States, local governments, and health systems would have to collect it themselves, adding cost and producing less reliable numbers.This is a poor use of public money. More than $2.8 trillion a year in federal funding follows census numbers. When the count is wrong, that money goes to the wrong places for at least ten years, and schools, clinics, roads, and emergency plans are built for a population that does not match reality. Lower response rates also mean more costly follow-up work, paid for by taxpayers.A bad count in 2030 cannot be corrected until at least 2040. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw this rule.Mary  [X]Dearborn, Michigan 48124

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am a concerned American writing to comment on the proposed rule Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). I strongly oppose the proposed rules changes to the residence criteria and demographic questions for the 2030 Census.

As an initial matter, I urge the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. 30 days is not enough time for members of the public to review and respond to the proposed rule given the scope of the prospective changes. 

I oppose the proposed rule because I am concerned it will undermine the accuracy and usefulness of census data, particularly for marginalized Americans. Census counts are used for a wide variety of important purposes, from planning and funding critical infrastructure to understanding patterns of discrimination. By leading to a census that only counts part of the population and contains limited demographic data, the proposed rule will make it harder for policy makers to make evidence-based decisions that affect Americans everyday lives. Underrepresented groups, including women, people of color, and LGBTQ+ people, among others, will be most negatively impacted. 

If the proposed residence criteria are finalized, the U.S. will lose a complete and accurate count of the population and its distribution and stray from the Constitutions mandate to count all persons. The proposed rule would, for the first time, exclude many U.S. residents from the apportionment count, including international students, work visa-holders, and refugees and asylum seekers. The proposed changes would also increase the likelihood that residents are counted in the wrong location, such as by defining usual residence based on tax records that may not reflect the physical address where someone primarily lives, pays taxes, and votes. The census strives to count everyone once, only once, and in the right place so that resources can be distributed based on need and public services can be accurately planned. The proposed rule would undermine this stated goal. 

By prohibiting questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation, the proposed rule would also cause the U.S. to lose critical, reliable demographic data. Every U.S. census has collected race and ethnicity data in some form since the first in 1790. These data are the foundation for a wide variety of population-based surveys and studies that allow researchers to gain important understanding of national issues and inequities. Although sexual orientation is not currently asked about in the census, barring these questions from future censuses will similarly restrict data on LGBTQ+ Americans. Robust demographic data is necessary to enforce civil rights laws and ensure equal opportunity for all Americans. If finalized, the proposed rule would make it harder to identify and address issues like workplace discrimination, public health discrepancies, and more. 

Census data needs to accurately represent all Americans. For the reasons stated above, I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw and revise the proposed rule, especially part 60 and 70. Thank you for your consideration. 

Sincerely, 
Donna Schneiderman
Brooklyn, NY

The Fourteenth Amendment requires “counting the whole number of persons in each State.” Every census since 1790 has counted everyone who lives here, regardless of citizenship. The rule does not say whether the people it excludes will be counted for any purpose, or whether they will appear in the population totals that decide federal funding for my state. I ask the Bureau to answer that on the record. The Bureau’s own 2019 research found that asking about citizenship would cut responses from noncitizen households by 8 percent. This rule goes further than that question did, and it will keep families in my community, including citizen children, from answering at all.
The rule also removes race and ethnicity from the census for the first time since 1790. Every measure of whether this country treats its people equally starts with that count. We know how much shorter Black and Native American lives are, how much lower Black homeownership is, which neighborhoods banks have redlined, and which children the last census missed, because the census asks. Take the question away and the disparities do not end. They become impossible to prove, and impossible to fix. The Bureau’s own analysis, posted with this docket, admits there are “no other comparably accurate, comprehensive, and reliable sources” for this data. A government that stops counting harm by race is choosing not to see it, and the people it stops seeing are Black people.
The Bureau’s own analysis admits it “cannot quantify” any cost or benefit of this rule. A rule the agency cannot evaluate should not be adopted.
Christy Ford

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481

I am also concerned that the proposed rule erases vital Census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Decades of demographic data serve as the baseline that public and private institutions rely on to identify inequalities and direct resources where they are needed most. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities.  

Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.  

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Sincerely,
Anne Miettinen

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Dear Director Cook,

The City of Ionia appreciates this opportunity to comment on the Census Bureau's proposed rule governing residence criteria and demographic questions for the 2030 decennial census. The census is the foundation for distributing political representation and federal resources. Accurate census ensures communities receive fair funding for infrastructure, housing, education, public safety, emergency response and other essential services. Because census data guide funding and planning decision for the next decade, accuracy is critical.  

We are concerned that several provisions of the proposed rule could reduce the accuracy of our community's population count and affect our access to federal and state resources. 

Concerns about the Proposed Changes 

Apportionment and population count: The proposed rule would limit the population counted toward apportionment to U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents for the first time. Although this change applies only to apportionment, it may create confusion or fear among residents and discourage participation. We request additional information on how full population data would be collected, reported and communicated, to ensure that all residents are counted for the broader data set. 

Legal-status question: The proposed rule also raises the possibility of adding a legal-status question to the census questionnaire. Similar proposals considered for the 2020 Census were not adopted following concerns that it could reduce participation, particularly among immigrant and mixed-status households. Any decline in response rates would undermine the accuracy of our community's population count as a whole and could impact the resources available to young children and families specifically. 

Usual residence and the enumeration period: The proposed shift to counting residents based on where they spend the most time during a January 3-April 1 period, rather than their usual residence throughout the year, could affect our population count of seasonal residents, such as snowbirds/ students / part-time workers / other mobile populations. We ask the Bureau to further evaluate the operational and data-accuracy impacts of this change and explain the rationale supporting it.  

Reliance on administrative records: Increased reliance on tax, immigration, health and other administrative records raises concerns about the potential undercount of populations in our community that may not be consistently represented in those records, including low-income households, college students, non-filers and children. We request additional information regarding when these records will be used and how the Bureau will ensure accurate counts for populations with less reliable administrative data.  

Demographic questions: The proposal would eliminate race and ethnicity questions, while making most other demographic questions optional. Accurate demographic data is essential to municipal planning and service delivery. Understanding who lives in our community gives local governments the ability to plan for our current population and take into consideration our future population's needs. The City of Ionia uses this data for monitoring equitable service delivery, particularly with our public transit department. The loss or reduction in the quality of this data could affect our ability to provide much needed services to our residents and accurately plan for our future.  

Funding impact: Census data inform funding for other programs including Community Development Block Grants (CDBG), transit formula funding, and Title I education funding. An undercount of any portion of our population reduces resources available to the entire community  not just the households or individuals who go uncounted. State funding allocations depend, in many cases, on accurate census data. While the Bureau distinguishes between apportionment and funding distribution, changes that discourage participation risk reducing the quality of data used for both purposes.  

We respectfully ask the Census Bureau to withdraw these proposed changes. Any changes to residence criteria, data collection methods or demographic questions must not compromise the accuracy of the population counts that the City of Ionia and communities like ours rely on. 

We appreciate the opportunity to comment on this proposal and would welcome the chance to provide additional information or answer any questions the Bureau may have. 

Sincerely, 
Precia L. Garland
City Manager
City of Ionia

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to oppose the proposed elimination of key demographic data described in Section 70. As a university researcher, I am particularly concerned about the consequences that reducing the demographic information collected through the decennial census would have for research.

Meaningful empirical research often depends not simply on knowing how many people live in the United States, but on understanding the characteristics of the population and how experiences and outcomes vary across groups. Removing demographic measures would constrain researchers' ability to examine these differences, identify changes over time, and develop a fuller understanding of economic and social phenomena.

The decennial census is an exceptionally important source of information about the U.S. population. Preserving high-quality demographic data will help ensure that researchers and other users can continue to develop evidence-based understanding of the country and its changing population. I therefore urge the Census Bureau not to eliminate these demographic questions from the 2030 Census.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the Census Bureau:

I strongly oppose the proposed changes to Census data collection for the 2030 Census that would (1) remove or prohibit collection of race and ethnicity data (and other demographic measures), (2) exclude millions of immigrants from the population used for apportionment and redistricting, and (3) condition counting on address confirmation through tax records or similar administrative sources. These changes would damage the accuracy and legitimacy of the Census, weaken civil rights enforcement, and distort political representation and federal funding—especially for Black, Brown, immigrant, and low-income communities.

The Constitution and longstanding practice require apportionment based on the “whole number of persons in each State.” Any rule that intentionally excludes categories of residents from the apportionment count is an attempt to manipulate representation rather than measure reality. The Census is not a tool for partisan advantage; it is the foundation of democratic representation. A distorted count undermines the principle of equal representation and harms states and localities whose residents are erased on paper.

Race and ethnicity data are not optional or symbolic. They are essential to
enforcing civil rights laws (including voting rights and anti-discrimination protections), ensuring fair redistricting and identifying vote dilution,
Targeting public health and education interventions, and understanding and addressing disparities in housing, employment, environmental exposure, and healthcare.

Removing these questions would make inequities easier to ignore and harder to prove. It would also reduce the government’s ability to allocate resources fairly and evaluate whether programs are working.

Millions of immigrants—documented and undocumented—live, work, pay taxes (including sales and payroll taxes), raise families, and contribute to local communities. Excluding them from the counts used to determine congressional representation and districting would shift political power away from the places where people actually live. It would also distort formulas used for federal funding, harming schools, hospitals, transportation, emergency preparedness, and community services in areas with large immigrant populations.

A rule that only counts people whose address is confirmed through tax records or similar administrative data will predictably undercount low-income households, people experiencing homelessness or housing instability, young adults and students, people in informal housing arrangements or multigenerational households, and communities with lower rates of tax filing.

This is not modernization—it is disenfranchisement by administrative exclusion. The Census must be designed to count everyone, ESPECIALLY those least connected to formal systems.

Per the US Constitution, the Census is only taken every 10 years. It is not easily corrected after the fact. Undercounts and data erasure would lock in unequal representation and unequal resources for an entire decade. That is unacceptable and contrary to the Census Bureau’s duty to produce an accurate, complete count.

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw this proposal and reaffirm its commitment to
counting all residents for apportionment consistent with the Constitution’s “whole number of persons” requirement; collecting race and ethnicity data (and other demographic data necessary for civil rights enforcement and public accountability); and avoiding administrative “verification” requirements that predictably undercount low-income and marginalized communities.

A democracy cannot function when the government chooses who counts. The Census must reflect the real population of the United States—not a politically engineered version of it.

Sincerely,
Shelly Arsneault, PhD
Whittier, CA 90603

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
My name is [Your Name] and I am your constituent from [City/Zip Code]. As Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander (AANHPI) Heritage Month comes to a close, I write to urge you to support AANHPI students by cosponsoring the All Students Count Act.

To the U.S. Census Bureau: 

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule titled “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005). Eliminating the collection of race and ethnic data, prohibiting the collection of sexual orientation, and leaving non-citizens out of the apportionment would significantly harm the Southeast Asian American (SEAA) and broader Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander (AANHPI) communities. I respectfully request that the Census Bureau withdraw the proposed rule and extend the comment period to December 10, 2026. 

This proposed rule would significantly harm the SEAA and AANHPI communities. The AANHPI community is not a homogenous population; it encompasses over 50 different ethnic groups and 100 languages and dialects. There are vast socioeconomic disparities within the AANHPI population, often related to their migratory and historical experience. SEAAs, such as the Cambodian, Hmong, Laotian, and Mien populations, often have higher rates of poverty and lower educational attainment rates than both the broader AANHPI and American populations. 

For SEAAs, this disparity is generally tied to their experiences escaping their countries of origin and resettlement in the United States after the Vietnam War, Secret War in Laos, and Khmer Rouge genocide in Cambodia. For example, because of the 2020 Census, we now know that the Mien population has lower educational attainment rates compared to the general American and AANHPI populations. Additionally, the data also show that Mien men have a lower educational attainment rate compared to women. Such information could only be obtained because of the census, which is the primary source for data collection and reporting of small ethnic groups. These data cannot be replicated by other surveys, including the American Community Survey. 

Accurate data, reflective of race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation, help our elected officials properly identify and address the unique needs and challenges of our communities. Prohibiting the collection of this demographic data would prevent our government officials from passing informed public policy; hamper the ability of community-based organizations to demonstrate data narratives for fundraising purposes; and inhibit the ability of students and academics studying our communities from accessing the most robust source of information on SEAAs and the broader AANHPI community. 

Thank you for taking my comment into consideration. I reiterate my request that the US Census Bureau withdraws the proposed rule; preserves the collection of race and ethnic data; and keeps its commitment to count everyone once, only once, and in the right place.

I also ask the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. Changes of this scope deserve more time for the public to review and respond.

Sincerely,
Alvina Yeh
Washington, DC 20011

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. An undercount here would directly strip my community of appropriate congressional representation and our fair share of federal funding for essential safety-net programs like SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, CHIP, and Title I education grants. As someone who cares about fairness and the rule of law, I urge the Bureau to withdraw this proposal and count every person living in our communities, as the Constitution requires. 

I am also concerned that the proposed rule erases vital Census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Decades of demographic data serve as the baseline that public and private institutions rely on to identify inequalities and direct resources where they are needed most. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities.

Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.  

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am a concerned American writing to comment on the proposed rule Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). I strongly oppose the proposed rules changes to the residence criteria and demographic questions for the 2030 Census.

As an initial matter, I urge the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. 30 days is not enough time for members of the public to review and respond to the proposed rule given the scope of the prospective changes. 

I oppose the proposed rule because I am concerned it will undermine the accuracy and usefulness of census data, particularly for marginalized Americans. Census counts are used for a wide variety of important purposes, from planning and funding critical infrastructure to understanding patterns of discrimination. By leading to a census that only counts part of the population and contains limited demographic data, the proposed rule will make it harder for policy makers to make evidence-based decisions that affect Americans everyday lives. Underrepresented groups, including women, people of color, and LGBTQ+ people, among others, will be most negatively impacted. 

If the proposed residence criteria are finalized, the U.S. will lose a complete and accurate count of the population and its distribution and stray from the Constitutions mandate to count all persons. The proposed rule would, for the first time, exclude many U.S. residents from the apportionment count, including international students, work visa-holders, and refugees and asylum seekers. The proposed changes would also increase the likelihood that residents are counted in the wrong location, such as by defining usual residence based on tax records that may not reflect the physical address where someone primarily lives, pays taxes, and votes. The census strives to count everyone once, only once, and in the right place so that resources can be distributed based on need and public services can be accurately planned. The proposed rule would undermine this stated goal. 

By prohibiting questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation, the proposed rule would also cause the U.S. to lose critical, reliable demographic data. Every U.S. census has collected race and ethnicity data in some form since the first in 1790. These data are the foundation for a wide variety of population-based surveys and studies that allow researchers to gain important understanding of national issues and inequities. Although sexual orientation is not currently asked about in the census, barring these questions from future censuses will similarly restrict data on LGBTQ+ Americans. Robust demographic data is necessary to enforce civil rights laws and ensure equal opportunity for all Americans. If finalized, the proposed rule would make it harder to identify and address issues like workplace discrimination, public health discrepancies, and more. 

Census data needs to accurately represent all Americans. For the reasons stated above, I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw and revise the proposed rule, especially part 60 and 70. Thank you for your consideration. 

Sincerely, 
Kristan Knierim
Price, UT

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. I oppose this proposed rule because it departs from that constitutional mandate, risking severe harm to my community. Excluding noncitizens from the population count used for congressional apportionment and federal funding, while adding a citizenship question designed to deter participation, will suppress response rates across immigrant communities and mixed-status families who fear being targeted. An undercount here would directly strip my community of appropriate congressional representation and our fair share of federal funding for essential safety-net programs like SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, CHIP, and Title I education grants. As someone who cares about fairness and the rule of law, I urge the Bureau to withdraw this proposal and count every person living in our communities, as the Constitution requires. 

I am also concerned that the proposed rule erases vital Census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Decades of demographic data serve as the baseline that public and private institutions rely on to identify inequalities and direct resources where they are needed most. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities.  

Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.  

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Sincerely,
Kristen Lightbody
Germansville, PA

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am a spatial data scientist working for a large survey research company which is based in Chicago, IL, and I care about a fair and accurate census because I work with census data on a daily basis. Consistent, accurate, up-to-date census products are the linchpin of my work (which is often on federal contract projects). Nearly every single day I am using data from the Decennial census or ACS along with TIGER spatial data to produce impactful and scientifically sound maps and data products. These changes to the census would make my work much more difficult, leading to less scientifically reproducible results for our clients from the federal government to local partners across the country.

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including:

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans. In addition, it makes data analysis and research using demographic data from the census unnecessarily difficult by reducing the ability to compare across years. One of the great advantages of the US census is its consistency for over 230 years. There is no reason to change what works merely for the sake of change.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am submitting this comment as a private citizen who believes that good decisions depend on good information. 

The Census Bureau's collection of race and ethnicity data serves purposes that extend far beyond the decennial census itself. These data help inform the American Community Survey, public health research, vital statistics, workforce analyses, educational planning, economic forecasting, and countless other efforts to understand our nation's changing population.

If we do not know who lives in the United States, we cannot effectively plan for our future. 

Race and ethnicity data are not collected simply for historical interest. They help policymakers, researchers, businesses, health systems, and communities understand demographic trends and respond to emerging needs. They allow us to measure change over time, evaluate outcomes, and make informed decisions based on evidence rather than assumptions.

The loss of these data would have consequences far beyond a single census cycle. It would disrupt long-standing data series that help us understand how the nation is changing and make it more difficult to compare future conditions to past trends. Once such information is no longer collected, it cannot easily be reconstructed.

The decisions we make today about data collection will also affect what future generations are able to know about the country they inherit. Our children and grandchildren should have access to reliable information about how the United States has evolved over time. Preserving the continuity of demographic data is an investment not only in today's decision-makers, but also in the ability of future Americans to understand their own history and prepare for their own future.

As someone who values evidence-based decision-making, I am concerned that eliminating race and ethnicity questions would reduce the quality and usefulness of one of the nation's most important statistical resources. A less complete understanding of the American population will not improve planning or policymaking. It will make both more difficult.

A country that chooses not to measure demographic change does not stop changing; it simply loses the ability to understand those changes and prepare for them.

For these reasons, I urge the Census Bureau to preserve the collection of race and ethnicity data and maintain the continuity of information that has long supported effective planning, research, and public decision-making.

I oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census because a fair and accurate census is critical to ensuring every community is counted, fairly represented, and able to get the resources people need to live healthy lives — including sexual and reproductive healthcare. An inaccurate or incomplete census can deepen existing inequities, particularly for communities that already face disenfranchisement and barriers to healthcare. 

A fair and accurate census is essential to our health and rights. 

Census data help determine access to programs patients and their families rely on, including important programs like Medicaid, SNAP, WIC, and TANF. Accurate census data also shape political representation by determining how seats in the U.S. House of Representatives are apportioned among states and providing data used for redistricting. When communities are undercounted or excluded, they risk losing both resources and political representation. 

The Census Bureau and Department of Commerce must:

1. Count all people residing in the United States in the 2030 Census, without regard to immigration status. Excluding noncitizens from census apportionment data violates the Constitution and established legal precedent. It would suppress the count of many communities, effectively erasing them from critical datasets and depriving them of resources and congressional representation –— including resources and political representation that support access to healthcare.

2. Continue collecting race and ethnicity data and implement the 2024 OMB SPD 15 standards. Census race and ethnicity data are essential for important research across many sectors, for upholding civil rights, and for growing the economy. Extensive Census Bureau research and engagement with expert stakeholders shows that implementing the modernized 2024 OMB SPD 15 standards for race and ethnicity data collection will yield data that more accurately represent the nation’s increasingly diverse population.

3. Remove the clause banning the addition of future questions on sexual orientation. Proposed changes to demographic items should be based on research and guided by a deliberative and transparent process, including extensive stakeholder consultation.

4. Withdraw other proposed changes to residence criteria, including tying place of residence to tax records and "lawful residence," and the adoption of a three month enumeration period. The Census Bureau must extensively research and consult with stakeholders about the potential effects of such changes before proposing their implementation in a decennial census.

5. Halt the practice of prison gerrymandering by counting incarcerated individuals in their home communities. This will yield more accurate census data and ensure that communities receive the congressional representation to which they are entitled.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am a concerned American writing to comment on the proposed rule Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). I strongly oppose the proposed rules changes to the residence criteria and demographic questions for the 2030 Census.

As an initial matter, I urge the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. 30 days is not enough time for members of the public to review and respond to the proposed rule given the scope of the prospective changes. 

I oppose the proposed rule because I am concerned it will undermine the accuracy and usefulness of census data, particularly for marginalized Americans. Census counts are used for a wide variety of important purposes, from planning and funding critical infrastructure to understanding patterns of discrimination. By leading to a census that only counts part of the population and contains limited demographic data, the proposed rule will make it harder for policy makers to make evidence-based decisions that affect Americans everyday lives. Underrepresented groups, including women, people of color, and LGBTQ+ people, among others, will be most negatively impacted. 

If the proposed residence criteria are finalized, the U.S. will lose a complete and accurate count of the population and its distribution and stray from the Constitutions mandate to count all persons. The proposed rule would, for the first time, exclude many U.S. residents from the apportionment count, including international students, work visa-holders, and refugees and asylum seekers. The proposed changes would also increase the likelihood that residents are counted in the wrong location, such as by defining usual residence based on tax records that may not reflect the physical address where someone primarily lives, pays taxes, and votes. The census strives to count everyone once, only once, and in the right place so that resources can be distributed based on need and public services can be accurately planned. The proposed rule would undermine this stated goal. 

By prohibiting questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation, the proposed rule would also cause the U.S. to lose critical, reliable demographic data. Every U.S. census has collected race and ethnicity data in some form since the first in 1790. These data are the foundation for a wide variety of population-based surveys and studies that allow researchers to gain important understanding of national issues and inequities. Although sexual orientation is not currently asked about in the census, barring these questions from future censuses will similarly restrict data on LGBTQ+ Americans. Robust demographic data is necessary to enforce civil rights laws and ensure equal opportunity for all Americans. If finalized, the proposed rule would make it harder to identify and address issues like workplace discrimination, public health discrepancies, and more. 

Census data needs to accurately represent all Americans. For the reasons stated above, I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw and revise the proposed rule, especially part 60 and 70. Thank you for your consideration. 

Sincerely, 
James Klein
Corpus Christi, TX

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule titled “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005). Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am an economist and I care about a fair and accurate census because it helps inform good policy and it’s important to have data that can be compared over time. 

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions that ensure every person in the country is counted once. 

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.
As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

I strongly oppose the proposed rules changes to the residence criteria and demographic questions for the 2030 Census.

As an initial matter, I urge the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. 30 days is not enough time for members of the public to review and respond to the proposed rule given the scope of the prospective changes. 

I oppose the proposed rule because I am concerned it will undermine the accuracy and usefulness of census data, particularly for marginalized Americans. Census counts are used for a wide variety of important purposes, from planning and funding critical infrastructure to understanding patterns of discrimination. By leading to a census that only counts part of the population and contains limited demographic data, the proposed rule will make it harder for policy makers to make evidence-based decisions that affect Americans everyday lives. Underrepresented groups, including women, people of color, and LGBTQ+ people, among others, will be most negatively impacted. 

If the proposed residence criteria are finalized, the U.S. will lose a complete and accurate count of the population and its distribution and stray from the Constitutions mandate to count all persons. The proposed rule would, for the first time, exclude many U.S. residents from the apportionment count, including international students, work visa-holders, and refugees and asylum seekers. The proposed changes would also increase the likelihood that residents are counted in the wrong location, such as by defining usual residence based on tax records that may not reflect the physical address where someone primarily lives, pays taxes, and votes. The census strives to count everyone once, only once, and in the right place so that resources can be distributed based on need and public services can be accurately planned. The proposed rule would undermine this stated goal. 

By prohibiting questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation, the proposed rule would also cause the U.S. to lose critical, reliable demographic data. Every U.S. census has collected race and ethnicity data in some form since the first in 1790. These data are the foundation for a wide variety of population-based surveys and studies that allow researchers to gain important understanding of national issues and inequities. Although sexual orientation is not currently asked about in the census, barring these questions from future censuses will similarly restrict data on LGBTQ+ Americans. Robust demographic data is necessary to enforce civil rights laws and ensure equal opportunity for all Americans. If finalized, the proposed rule would make it harder to identify and address issues like workplace discrimination, public health discrepancies, and more. 

Census data needs to accurately represent all Americans. For the reasons stated above, I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw and revise the proposed rule, especially part 60 and 70. Thank you for your consideration.

The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.  

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.
