Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. I oppose this proposed rule because it departs from that constitutional mandate, risking severe harm to my community. Excluding noncitizens from the population count used for congressional apportionment and federal funding, while adding a citizenship question designed to deter participation, will suppress response rates across immigrant communities and mixed-status families who fear being targeted. An undercount here would directly strip my community of appropriate congressional representation and our fair share of federal funding for essential safety-net programs like SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, CHIP, and Title I education grants. As someone who cares about fairness and the rule of law, I urge the Bureau to withdraw this proposal and count every person living in our communities, as the Constitution requires. 

I am also concerned that the proposed rule erases vital Census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Decades of demographic data serve as the baseline that public and private institutions rely on to identify inequalities and direct resources where they are needed most. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities.  

Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.  

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Sincerely,
Barri Rosenblum
Berkeley, CA

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am a concerned American writing to comment on the proposed rule Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). I strongly oppose the proposed rules changes to the residence criteria and demographic questions for the 2030 Census.

As an initial matter, I urge the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. 30 days is not enough time for members of the public to review and respond to the proposed rule given the scope of the prospective changes. 

I oppose the proposed rule because I am concerned it will undermine the accuracy and usefulness of census data, particularly for marginalized Americans. Census counts are used for a wide variety of important purposes, from planning and funding critical infrastructure to understanding patterns of discrimination. By leading to a census that only counts part of the population and contains limited demographic data, the proposed rule will make it harder for policy makers to make evidence-based decisions that affect Americans everyday lives. Underrepresented groups, including women, people of color, and LGBTQ+ people, among others, will be most negatively impacted. 

If the proposed residence criteria are finalized, the U.S. will lose a complete and accurate count of the population and its distribution and stray from the Constitutions mandate to count all persons. The proposed rule would, for the first time, exclude many U.S. residents from the apportionment count, including international students, work visa-holders, and refugees and asylum seekers. The proposed changes would also increase the likelihood that residents are counted in the wrong location, such as by defining usual residence based on tax records that may not reflect the physical address where someone primarily lives, pays taxes, and votes. The census strives to count everyone once, only once, and in the right place so that resources can be distributed based on need and public services can be accurately planned. The proposed rule would undermine this stated goal. 

By prohibiting questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation, the proposed rule would also cause the U.S. to lose critical, reliable demographic data. Every U.S. census has collected race and ethnicity data in some form since the first in 1790. These data are the foundation for a wide variety of population-based surveys and studies that allow researchers to gain important understanding of national issues and inequities. Although sexual orientation is not currently asked about in the census, barring these questions from future censuses will similarly restrict data on LGBTQ+ Americans. Robust demographic data is necessary to enforce civil rights laws and ensure equal opportunity for all Americans. If finalized, the proposed rule would make it harder to identify and address issues like workplace discrimination, public health discrepancies, and more. 

Census data needs to accurately represent all Americans. For the reasons stated above, I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw and revise the proposed rule, especially part 60 and 70. Thank you for your consideration. 

Sincerely, 
Elizabeth MacKelvie
Appleton, WI

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Dear Director Cook,

I appreciate the opportunity to comment on the Census Bureau's proposed rule governing residence criteria and demographic questions for the 2030 decennial census. The census is the foundation for distributing political representation and federal resources. Accurate census ensures communities receive fair funding for infrastructure, housing, education, public safety, emergency response and other essential services. Because census data guide funding and planning decision for the next decade, accuracy is critical.  

I am concerned that several provisions of the proposed rule could reduce the accuracy of our community's population count and affect our access to federal and state resources. 

Concerns about the Proposed Changes 

[Select and adapt the paragraphs below that apply to your community. Delete any that don't.] 

Apportionment and population count: The proposed rule would limit the population counted toward apportionment to U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents for the first time. Although this change applies only to apportionment, it may create confusion or fear among residents and discourage participation. We as Americans demand additional information on how full population data would be collected, reported and communicated, to ensure that all residents are counted for the broader data set. 

Legal-status question: The proposed rule also raises the possibility of adding a legal-status question to the census questionnaire. Similar proposals considered for the 2020 Census were not adopted following concerns that it could reduce participation, particularly among immigrant and mixed-status households. Any decline in response rates would undermine the accuracy of our community's population count as a whole and could impact the resources available to young children and families specifically. 

Usual residence and the enumeration period: The proposed shift to counting residents based on where they spend the most time during a January 3-April 1 period, rather than their usual residence throughout the year, could affect our population count [of seasonal residents such as snowbirds/ students / part-time workers / other mobile populations]. We ask the Bureau to further evaluate the operational and data-accuracy impacts of this change and explain the rationale supporting it.  

Reliance on administrative records: Increased reliance on tax, immigration, health and other administrative records raises concerns about the potential undercount of populations in our community that may not be consistently represented in those records, including low-income households, college students, non-filers and children. We request additional information regarding when these records will be used and how the Bureau will ensure accurate counts for populations with less reliable administrative data.  

Demographic questions: The proposal would eliminate race and ethnicity questions, while making most other demographic questions optional. Accurate demographic data is essential to municipal planning and service delivery. Understanding who lives in our community gives local governments the ability to plan for our current population and take into consideration our future population's needs. I use this date in my job to understand who are our users, what type of staffing may be needed and where there is more opportunity to tap into new communities. The loss or reduction in the quality of this data could affect my employers ability to provide much needed services to our residents and accurately plan for our future.  

Funding impact: Census data inform funding for other programs including Community Development Block Grants (CDBG), transit formula funding, and Title I education funding. An undercount of any portion of our population reduces resources available to the entire community  not just the households or individuals who go uncounted. State funding allocations depend, in many cases, on accurate census data. While the Bureau distinguishes between apportionment and funding distribution, changes that discourage participation risk reducing the quality of data used for both purposes.  

I respectfully ask the Census Bureau to withdraw these proposed changes. Any changes to residence criteria, data collection methods or demographic questions must not compromise the accuracy of the population counts. 

We as Americans appreciate the opportunity to comment on this proposal and would welcome the chance to provide additional information or answer any questions the Bureau may have. 

Sincerely, 
Christina Saenz
Concerned US Citizen and Data Specialist

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am a member of the public, and I care about a fair and accurate census because I care about our representation as citizens of the United States and proper recognition of those who live here as residents.

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including:

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people residing in the U.S. Data is just simply that: data, and it should be as accurate as possible. Failing to count individuals who are residing in the U.S. because of their legal status denies the public valuable data and fails to accurately measure all U.S. residents. This is poor research practice. It is also unclear how this policy benefits anyone. Lacking data on residents limits community's abilities to properly design policy around the reality of their populations. 
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care. People's residency in the U.S. is not dependent on their residential situation, as long as they reside on U.S. soil. 
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live. Population determines resources. Residential communities with high levels of incarceration in particular tend to be underresourced and denying them in favor of the prisons is harmful to the wider community.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count. Children are perhaps the most underserved population in the U.S., and ensuring their representation is paramount. 
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples. 

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans. Ultimately, regardless of whether certain groups of people may be seen as a deserving part of our political community or not, they are living here and they deserve recognition for that fact alone. The role of data is to describe reality. The decisions made based on that data should be a separate process made by elected officials. Failing to count groups of people who might be considered undesirable parts the political community by some does not change the fact that they are living here; it simply means that we lack information on them and thus lack the ability to generate data informed policy for our whole communities.

Eliminating the collection of race and ethnic data, prohibiting the collection of sexual orientation, and leaving non-citizens out of the apportionment would significantly harm the Southeast Asian American (SEAA) and broader Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander (AANHPI) communities. I respectfully request that the Census Bureau withdraw the proposed rule and extend the comment period to December 10, 2026. 

This proposed rule would significantly harm the SEAA and AANHPI communities. The AANHPI community is not a homogenous population; it encompasses over 50 different ethnic groups and 100 languages and dialects. There are vast socioeconomic disparities within the AANHPI population, often related to their migratory and historical experience. SEAAs, such as the Cambodian, Hmong, Laotian, and Mien populations, often have higher rates of poverty and lower educational attainment rates than both the broader AANHPI and American populations. 

For SEAAs, this disparity is generally tied to their experiences escaping their countries of origin and resettlement in the United States after the Vietnam War, Secret War in Laos, and Khmer Rouge genocide in Cambodia. For example, because of the 2020 Census, we now know that the Mien population has lower educational attainment rates compared to the general American and AANHPI populations. Additionally, the data also show that Mien men have a lower educational attainment rate compared to women. Such information could only be obtained because of the census, which is the primary source for data collection and reporting of small ethnic groups. These data cannot be replicated by other surveys, including the American Community Survey. 

Accurate data, reflective of race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation, help our elected officials properly identify and address the unique needs and challenges of our communities. Prohibiting the collection of this demographic data would prevent our government officials from passing informed public policy; hamper the ability of community-based organizations to demonstrate data narratives for fundraising purposes; and inhibit the ability of students and academics studying our communities from accessing the most robust source of information on SEAAs and the broader AANHPI community. 

Thank you for taking my comment into consideration. I reiterate my request that the US Census Bureau withdraws the proposed rule; preserves the collection of race and ethnic data; and keeps its commitment to count everyone once, only once, and in the right place.

I also ask the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. Changes of this scope deserve more time for the public to review and respond.

Sincerely,
Yen Marshall
Sacramento, CA 95831

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am submitting this comment as an applied researcher in Nebraska. My organization serves as the Nebraska liaison for the State Data Center program. Our work relies on Census data to examine the demographic, economic, and social characteristics of Nebraskans so that we can provide reliable information to local governments, nonprofit organizations, state agencies, and community decision-makers. The proposed changes raise significant concerns about the quality, continuity, comparability, and usefulness of Census data.

Race and ethnicity data are essential to understanding communities and how they change over time. Census data support community profiles, needs assessments, population analyses, strategic planning, and resource allocation. To be clear, the value of Census data extends beyond population counts to understanding the unique characteristics of communities. Removing race and ethnicity questions from the decennial census would reduce the availability of detailed demographic information and disrupt longitudinal comparisons that we are frequently asked to provide for Nebraska communities.

Additional concerns regarding the proposed changes to residence criteria will complicate comparisons across Census products. Changes in data collection methods, definitions, and population universes can also create breaks in statistical series, making it difficult to distinguish actual demographic change from changes in measurement. These issues warrant careful methodological evaluation and transparent documentation of their implications for data quality and comparability.

I strongly oppose the proposed regulations. Preserving the continuity, geographic detail, comparability, and integrity of Census data is essential to supporting research, planning, and evidence-based decision-making in communities across the country.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am a concerned American writing to comment on the proposed rule Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026). I strongly oppose the proposed rules changes to the residence criteria and demographic questions for the 2030 Census.

As an initial matter, I urge the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. 30 days is not enough time for members of the public to review and respond to the proposed rule given the scope of the prospective changes. 

I oppose the proposed rule because I am concerned it will undermine the accuracy and usefulness of census data, particularly for marginalized Americans. Census counts are used for a wide variety of important purposes, from planning and funding critical infrastructure to understanding patterns of discrimination. By leading to a census that only counts part of the population and contains limited demographic data, the proposed rule will make it harder for policy makers to make evidence-based decisions that affect Americans everyday lives. Underrepresented groups, including women, people of color, and LGBTQ+ people, among others, will be most negatively impacted. 

If the proposed residence criteria are finalized, the U.S. will lose a complete and accurate count of the population and its distribution and stray from the Constitutions mandate to count all persons. The proposed rule would, for the first time, exclude many U.S. residents from the apportionment count, including international students, work visa-holders, and refugees and asylum seekers. The proposed changes would also increase the likelihood that residents are counted in the wrong location, such as by defining usual residence based on tax records that may not reflect the physical address where someone primarily lives, pays taxes, and votes. The census strives to count everyone once, only once, and in the right place so that resources can be distributed based on need and public services can be accurately planned. The proposed rule would undermine this stated goal. 

By prohibiting questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation, the proposed rule would also cause the U.S. to lose critical, reliable demographic data. Every U.S. census has collected race and ethnicity data in some form since the first in 1790. These data are the foundation for a wide variety of population-based surveys and studies that allow researchers to gain important understanding of national issues and inequities. Although sexual orientation is not currently asked about in the census, barring these questions from future censuses will similarly restrict data on LGBTQ+ Americans. Robust demographic data is necessary to enforce civil rights laws and ensure equal opportunity for all Americans. If finalized, the proposed rule would make it harder to identify and address issues like workplace discrimination, public health discrepancies, and more. 

Census data needs to accurately represent all Americans. For the reasons stated above, I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw and revise the proposed rule, especially part 60 and 70. Thank you for your consideration. 

Sincerely,

Guilford, VT

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I’m writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

As a person who cares about people and our planet, I know how important this data is, and as such, we need a fair and accurate Census. 

First, I ask the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. Significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve more time for members of the public — people like me — to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70 of the proposed rule. I urge you to withdraw the rule for substantial revisions, including:

Count every U.S. resident, including visa-holders, refugees, and asylum seekers.
Establish detailed  guidelines for complex residential situations such as recent movers, people in temporary situations, and children in foster care.
Go back to activity-based residence, not a “one hour” rule.
Drop the January-to-April enumeration period.
Count incarcerated people at home, not at the facility.
Revise the tax records language. Extreme reliance on tax records risks creating inconsistencies in the count.
Drop the ban on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation questions.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of communities like mine. Furthermore, the data collected by the Census determines how billions of dollars of environmental funding is distributed across the country. This includes funding for water and waste disposal systems, public transportation infrastructure, and disaster relief on which we all rely. The data collected will also inform research to identify and address environmental injustices. 

Moving forward with this proposed rule would harm all Americans. Our democracy works best when all people that live within our borders are fully represented in the data collected by the Census.

Sincerely,
Kevin Karl

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am an undergraduate college student from Minnesota who is studying Public Health, and I care about a fair and accurate census because data is important to ensure we are addressing disparities in our country.

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am a researcher based in Chicago, and I care about a fair and accurate census because I know that accurate data is the key to a thriving society. The census data affects thousands of research projects across the country, and I am in utter disbelief and disgust that these proposals exist. If passed, there will be undercounts that will skew research takeaways and, in due time, wreak havoc on local communities across the country. And thus, I ask for the following: 

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: 

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• And last but certainly not least: Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau,

As a sociology student, I am concerned about the proposed changes to the decennial census and how they could affect the accuracy and usefulness of the data collected. The census is important not only for determining representation in Congress but also for helping researchers, policymakers, and communities understand the population and the challenges people face.

Excluding certain people based on their immigration status could leave communities underrepresented and from a research perspective, it is important that population data reflect the people who actually live in the United States. This could affect the quality of future research and make it harder to understand how communities are changing.

I understand that the Census Bureau may be trying to improve the census process, but I believe accuracy and representation should remain priorities. I encourage the Bureau to reconsider removing race and ethnicity questions and to conduct thorough research on the potential effects of the proposed residency and population-counting changes. The Bureau should also consult researchers and affected communities before making changes that could have long-term consequences.

The census should give an accurate picture of the population and help us better understand the society we live in. Changes that leave people out or make it harder to study inequality could reduce the value of this important resource. I urge the Census Bureau to protect the quality, fairness, and usefulness of census data for future generations.

Thank you for considering my comments.

Respectfully,

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. I oppose this proposed rule because it departs from that constitutional mandate, risking severe harm to my community. Excluding noncitizens from the population count used for congressional apportionment and federal funding, while adding a citizenship question designed to deter participation, will suppress response rates across immigrant communities and mixed-status families who fear being targeted. An undercount here would directly strip my community of appropriate congressional representation and our fair share of federal funding for essential safety-net programs like SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, CHIP, and Title I education grants. As someone who cares about fairness and the rule of law, I urge the Bureau to withdraw this proposal and count every person living in our communities, as the Constitution requires. 

I am also concerned that the proposed rule erases vital Census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Decades of demographic data serve as the baseline that public and private institutions rely on to identify inequalities and direct resources where they are needed most. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities.  

Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.  

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Sincerely,
Maria Gomez Murphy
Rio Rico, AZ

The Constitution calls for an "actual Enumeration" every ten years so that representation can be fairly apportioned among the states. The decennial census is meant to be a count, not a survey or a statistical estimate. Americans' voice in Congress depends on that count being right.

In 2020, the Bureau intentionally introduced statistical noise into the population data used to draw congressional and legislative districts. Counting citizens and lawful permanent residents, and excluding foreign nationals who are here unlawfully or temporarily, follows that principle.

I support keeping the enumeration questionnaire focused on the count itself. The Bureau can continue to produce demographic and statistical information through the American Community Survey and other tools, but those products should remain separate from the constitutional headcount.

To make these reforms durable, I urge the Bureau to state clearly in the final rule that the constitutional enumeration, and the counts used for apportionment and redistricting, are fundamentally distinct from routine federal statistical products and may not be adjusted to serve other statistical purposes.

Please finalize this rule so that the 2030 Census delivers an accurate count and restores Americans' trust in how they are represented.

Hamilton, Ohio

I write in support of the Census Bureau's proposed rule, "Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions" (Docket No. USBC-2026-0628; RIN 0607-AA75).

The Constitution calls for an "actual Enumeration" every ten years so that representation can be fairly apportioned among the states. The decennial census is meant to be a count, not a survey or a statistical estimate. Americans' voice in Congress depends on that count being right.

In 2020, the Bureau intentionally introduced statistical noise into the population data used to draw congressional and legislative districts. It reflects a lasting connection to a place, which is why service members stationed abroad are still counted in their home states. Counting citizens and lawful permanent residents, and excluding foreign nationals who are here unlawfully or temporarily, follows that principle.

I support keeping the enumeration questionnaire focused on the count itself. The Bureau can continue to produce demographic and statistical information through the American Community Survey and other tools, but those products should remain separate from the constitutional headcount.

To make these reforms durable, I urge the Bureau to state clearly in the final rule that the constitutional enumeration, and the counts used for apportionment and redistricting, are fundamentally distinct from routine federal statistical products and may not be adjusted to serve other statistical purposes.

Please finalize this rule so that the 2030 Census delivers an accurate count and restores Americans' trust in how they are represented.

Respectfully,

Queens, NY

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The decennial census has asked questions about race since the very first U.S. Census in 1790.  Collecting this information has clearly been considered valuable since the birth of the United States.  Understanding basic demographic information about the U.S. population is a hallmark of quality research and information.  Understanding overall proportions of different populations within the United States, not only by race or ethnicity, but age and gender, allow all health research to understand the denominator for any condition affecting the U.S. population.  It is not enough to know the sheer count of individuals with a particular condition, but how that count differs by and in relation to, the overall population for a particular demographic group. 

Recent improvements to the OMB standardized questions (SPD 15), developed with extensive input from the public and experts in statistical data, were set to shepherd in an era of even more rigorous self-reported race and ethnicity data.  By combining the race and ethnicity questions into a single question and adding a Middle Eastern North African category, the new standards support stronger response rates and more comprehensive data collection.  In addition, the Census has long set the standard for the demographic data we collect in this country. As the census degrades the quality of its collected data, others who collect demographic data will follow suit and ultimately degrade the overall quality of American demographic data.  We are moving in the wrong direction if we choose to remove these questions, which have been a fixture of the census since its inception.  The arguments put forth in the proposal are made in bad faith, misrepresenting issues like response rates and data privacy efforts.  One function of the census is to apportion representation, but it is not the ONLY function of the census.  Having a robust dataset on the U.S. population is the sign of a strong nation that prioritizes the best in data collection, statistical rigor, and information. 

There is also great value in collection sexual orientation demographic information on the U.S. Census.  While there isn’t as longstanding a precedent for collecting this information as the race and ethnicity questions, having data on sexual orientation would help better understand the demographics of the U.S. population.  Casting any and all information about race, gender, or sexual orientation as “DEI”, as this Administration has, is reckless and naive.  It is setting American research back decades and putting us far behind peer nations. Do not let these short sighted and misguided efforts to do away with “DEI” degrade the overall quality of one of the oldest American surveys, the U.S. Census. 

In addition, the proposal to change who is “counted” in the census based on permanent legal status would greatly negatively impact the ability of state programs, which are funded in relation to their populations, to serve the people living here. These changes would force states with larger immigrant populations to do much more with much less if Medicaid and CHIP funds are made to stretch even further than they already have been.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I’m writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

As a person who cares about people and our planet, I know how important this data is, and as such, we need a fair and accurate Census. 

First, I ask the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. Significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve more time for members of the public — people like me — to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70 of the proposed rule. I urge you to withdraw the rule for substantial revisions, including:

Count every U.S. resident, including visa-holders, refugees, and asylum seekers.
Establish detailed  guidelines for complex residential situations such as recent movers, people in temporary situations, and children in foster care.
Go back to activity-based residence, not a “one hour” rule.
Drop the January-to-April enumeration period.
Count incarcerated people at home, not at the facility.
Revise the tax records language. Extreme reliance on tax records risks creating inconsistencies in the count.
Drop the ban on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation questions.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of communities like mine. Furthermore, the data collected by the Census determines how billions of dollars of environmental funding is distributed across the country. This includes funding for water and waste disposal systems, public transportation infrastructure, and disaster relief on which we all rely. The data collected will also inform research to identify and address environmental injustices. 

Moving forward with this proposed rule would harm all Americans. Our democracy works best when all people that live within our borders are fully represented in the data collected by the Census.

Sincerely,
Michael IRELAND

Sincerely,

Sergio Quintanar

Lake in the Hills, Illinois

Please withdraw this proposed rule and preserve a Census that fairly and accurately counts our community.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Dear Director Cook,

I appreciate the opportunity to comment on the Census Bureau's proposed rule governing residence criteria and demographic questions for the 2030 decennial census. The census is the foundation for distributing political representation and federal resources. It must be accurate in order to ensure communities receive fair funding for infrastructure, housing, education, public safety, emergency response and other essential services. Because census data guide funding and planning decision for the next decade, accuracy is critical.  

I am concerned that several provisions of the proposed rule could reduce the accuracy of Amherst's population count and affect our access to federal and state resources. 

In particular, I am concerned about two of the proposed changes:  Apportionment and population count and the Usual Residence determination. 

Amherst, MA is the home to the flagship campus of the University of Massachusetts, as well as Amherst College. The proposed rule would limit the population counted toward apportionment to U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents for the first time. As a small town host to multiple higher education institutions, we have year round residents from all over the world, many on student visas and some on work visas. These residents make our economy strong. They also add costs to the Town. Those costs don't go away simply because they aren't citizens or permanent residents.  As a town councilor, I represent the needs of all residents, including those that aren't citizens. They presence in Amherst should count towards all parts of population determinations, including apportionment. 

The proposed shift to counting residents based on where they spend the most time during a January 3-April 1 period, rather than their usual residence throughout the year, could affect our population count, particularly with respect to the students who live here and study here 10 months of the year. 

The funding impact of these changes will be detrimental to towns that host higher education institutions. The institutions don't pay property taxes, so the funding we receive from programs including Community Development Block Grants (CDBG), transit formula funding, and Title I education funding, is vital to helping our community thrive. By removing students from the count (either because they are visa holders or through the change in "usual residence", we would face even more economic hardship from hosting education institutions that help the entire US economy thrive. 

An undercount of any portion of our population like this reduces resources available to the entire community  not just the households or individuals who go uncounted. State funding allocations depend, in many cases, on accurate census data. 

I respectfully ask the Census Bureau to withdraw these proposed changes. Any changes to residence criteria must not compromise the accuracy of the population counts that Amherst and communities like mine rely on. 

Sincerely, 
Mandi Jo Hanneke
President, Amherst, MA Town Council

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. I oppose this proposed rule because it departs from that constitutional mandate, risking severe harm to my community. Excluding noncitizens from the population count used for congressional apportionment and federal funding, while adding a citizenship question designed to deter participation, will suppress response rates across immigrant communities and mixed-status families who fear being targeted. An undercount here would directly strip my community of appropriate congressional representation and our fair share of federal funding for essential safety-net programs like SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, CHIP, and Title I education grants. As someone who cares about fairness and the rule of law, I urge the Bureau to withdraw this proposal and count every person living in our communities, as the Constitution requires. 

I am also concerned that the proposed rule erases vital Census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Decades of demographic data serve as the baseline that public and private institutions rely on to identify inequalities and direct resources where they are needed most. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities.  

Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.  

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Sincerely,
Christine Baker
Arvada, CO

Eliminating the collection of race and ethnic data, prohibiting the collection of sexual orientation, and leaving non-citizens out of the apportionment would significantly harm the Southeast Asian American (SEAA) and broader Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander (AANHPI) communities. I respectfully request that the Census Bureau withdraw the proposed rule and extend the comment period to December 10, 2026. 

This proposed rule would significantly harm the SEAA and AANHPI communities. The AANHPI community is not a homogenous population; it encompasses over 50 different ethnic groups and 100 languages and dialects. There are vast socioeconomic disparities within the AANHPI population, often related to their migratory and historical experience. SEAAs, such as the Cambodian, Hmong, Laotian, and Mien populations, often have higher rates of poverty and lower educational attainment rates than both the broader AANHPI and American populations. 

For SEAAs, this disparity is generally tied to their experiences escaping their countries of origin and resettlement in the United States after the Vietnam War, Secret War in Laos, and Khmer Rouge genocide in Cambodia. For example, because of the 2020 Census, we now know that the Mien population has lower educational attainment rates compared to the general American and AANHPI populations. Additionally, the data also show that Mien men have a lower educational attainment rate compared to women. Such information could only be obtained because of the census, which is the primary source for data collection and reporting of small ethnic groups. These data cannot be replicated by other surveys, including the American Community Survey. 

Accurate data, reflective of race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation, help our elected officials properly identify and address the unique needs and challenges of our communities. Prohibiting the collection of this demographic data would prevent our government officials from passing informed public policy; hamper the ability of community-based organizations to demonstrate data narratives for fundraising purposes; and inhibit the ability of students and academics studying our communities from accessing the most robust source of information on SEAAs and the broader AANHPI community. 

Thank you for taking my comment into consideration. I reiterate my request that the US Census Bureau withdraws the proposed rule; preserves the collection of race and ethnic data; and keeps its commitment to count everyone once, only once, and in the right place.

I also ask the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. Changes of this scope deserve more time for the public to review and respond.

Sincerely,
Jacqueline MAC FALLON
Chicago, IL 60625-1804

Comment:
The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. Moving forward with this proposed rule would harm all Americans. Our democracy works best when all people that live within our borders are fully represented in the data collected by the Census.

Sincerely,

Comment:
The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. I oppose this proposed rule because it departs from that constitutional mandate, risking severe harm to my community. Excluding noncitizens from the population count used for congressional apportionment and federal funding, while adding a citizenship question designed to deter participation, will suppress response rates across immigrant communities and mixed-status families who fear being targeted. An undercount here would directly strip my community of appropriate congressional representation and our fair share of federal funding for essential safety-net programs like SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, CHIP, and Title I education grants. As someone who cares about fairness and the rule of law, I urge the Bureau to withdraw this proposal and count every person living in our communities, as the Constitution requires. 

I am also concerned that the proposed rule erases vital Census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Decades of demographic data serve as the baseline that public and private institutions rely on to identify inequalities and direct resources where they are needed most. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities.  

Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.  

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Sincerely,
Ruth Ryan
Hilton Head Island, SC

Moving forward with this proposed rule would harm all Americans. Our democracy works best when all people that live within our borders are fully represented in the data collected by the Census.

Sincerely,

Respectfully,

Vicki Bermúdez

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. I oppose this proposed rule because it departs from that constitutional mandate, risking severe harm to my community. Excluding noncitizens from the population count used for congressional apportionment and federal funding, while adding a citizenship question designed to deter participation, will suppress response rates across immigrant communities and mixed-status families who fear being targeted. An undercount here would directly strip my community of appropriate congressional representation and our fair share of federal funding for essential safety-net programs like SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, CHIP, and Title I education grants. As someone who cares about fairness and the rule of law, I urge the Bureau to withdraw this proposal and count every person living in our communities, as the Constitution requires. 

I am also concerned that the proposed rule erases vital Census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Decades of demographic data serve as the baseline that public and private institutions rely on to identify inequalities and direct resources where they are needed most. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities.  

Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.  

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Sincerely,
JoEllen Rudolph
Petoskey, MI

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census. These changes will not only weaken the accuracy and integrity of our nation's most important population count, but they will also harm our communities, and I strongly urge the Bureau to reject them. 

First, removing questions of race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation erases the full scope of my identity when I participate in the Census survey. These data points are not optional. They are the tools we use to enforce civil rights laws, monitor discrimination, and measure the disparities that still affect millions of people. Excluding them from the count does not make them disappear from our society, but it does make our government less equipped to handle big issues when they arise. 

The Constitution is clear: the census must count ALL persons living in the United States, regardless of their immigration or citizenship status. The proposal to exclude non-citizens, including those residents with some type of lawful status, violates more than two centuries of legal precedent. Every person counted in this country contributes to our communities, and every person deserves to be fully seen. 

The consequences of these changes will negatively impact our daily lives. The census affects everything. It determines political representation and the drawing of voting districts. It guides how billions of dollars in federal funding are used to close persistent disparities in schools, hospitals, and other government programs that are designed to improve our lives.  

The census is the foundation of our democracy. It must reflect the complete yet nuanced reality of who we are as a nation. And it must reflect the lives of our friends and neighbors who may not look, think, or speak like we do. I ask the Bureau to withdraw these proposed changes and to preserve a count that includes everyone and represents everyone. 

Thank you for considering my comment.

Sincerely,
Carla Applegate

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
RE: Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions, Docket No. USBC-2026-0628 

I strongly oppose the U.S. Census Bureau's proposed rule to make unprecedented changes to the 2030 Census that would end data collection on race and ethnicity, exclude millions of U.S. residents, and result in an inaccurate count of our population. I ask the Census Bureau to extend the public comment period to December 26, 2026 to give the public a meaningful opportunity to share our input. 

Second, I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw this proposed rule for the harm it would cause to our communities. Data on race and ethnicity are essential to protecting our civil rights and ensuring equal opportunity for all Americans. Ending the centuries-long collection of this data would only make it harder to understand and address the needs of different communities.  

My representation at all levels of government and funding for local schools and hospitals, for example, also depend on census data. Excluding the millions of international students, temporary workers, refugees, and others living in the U.S. from the apportionment count would mean that communities like mine don't get fair representation or resources. 

Though the census does not currently ask about sexual orientation, this proposed rule would prohibit the Census Bureau from ever collecting that data in the future. That decision should be based on research, testing, and input from impacted communities, not on a political agenda. 

The Census Bureau should count all people living in the United States, regardless of immigration status, and continue to collect data on race and ethnicity. I urge the agency to withdraw this proposed rule. Thank you for considering this comment. 

Sincerely,
Elizabeth Haynes

To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I’m writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

Count every U.S. resident, including visa-holders, refugees, and asylum seekers.

Drop the January-to-April enumeration period.
Count incarcerated people at home, not at the facility.

This includes funding for water and waste disposal systems, public transportation infrastructure, and disaster relief on which we all rely. The data collected will also inform research to identify and address environmental injustices. 

Moving forward with this proposed rule would harm all Americans. Our democracy works best when all people that live within our borders are fully represented in the data collected by the Census.

Sincerely,
Al Gelina

Moving forward with this proposed rule would harm all Americans. Our democracy works best when all people that live within our borders are fully represented in the data collected by the Census.

Sincerely,

Martha Karmann

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I’m writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

As a person who cares about people and our planet, I know how important this data is, and as such, we need a fair and accurate Census. 

First, I ask the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. Significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve more time for members of the public — people like me — to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70 of the proposed rule. I urge you to withdraw the rule for substantial revisions, including:

Count every U.S. resident, including visa-holders, refugees, and asylum seekers.
Establish detailed  guidelines for complex residential situations such as recent movers, people in temporary situations, and children in foster care.
Go back to activity-based residence, not a “one hour” rule.
Drop the January-to-April enumeration period.
Count incarcerated people at home, not at the facility.
Revise the tax records language. Extreme reliance on tax records risks creating inconsistencies in the count.
Drop the ban on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation questions.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of communities like mine. Furthermore, the data collected by the Census determines how billions of dollars of environmental funding is distributed across the country. This includes funding for water and waste disposal systems, public transportation infrastructure, and disaster relief on which we all rely. The data collected will also inform research to identify and address environmental injustices. 

Moving forward with this proposed rule would harm all Americans. Our democracy works best when all people that live within our borders are fully represented in the data collected by the Census.

Sincerely,
Barbara Pray

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census because a fair and accurate census is critical to ensuring every community is counted, fairly represented, and able to get the resources people need to live healthy lives — including sexual and reproductive healthcare. An inaccurate or incomplete census can deepen existing inequities, particularly for communities that already face disenfranchisement and barriers to healthcare. 

A fair and accurate census is essential to our health and rights. 

Census data help determine access to programs patients and their families rely on, including important programs like Medicaid, SNAP, WIC, and TANF. Accurate census data also shape political representation by determining how seats in the U.S. House of Representatives are apportioned among states and providing data used for redistricting. When communities are undercounted or excluded, they risk losing both resources and political representation. 

The Census Bureau and Department of Commerce must:

1. Count all people residing in the United States in the 2030 Census, without regard to immigration status. Excluding noncitizens from census apportionment data violates the Constitution and established legal precedent. It would suppress the count of many communities, effectively erasing them from critical datasets and depriving them of resources and congressional representation –— including resources and political representation that support access to healthcare.

2. Continue collecting race and ethnicity data and implement the 2024 OMB SPD 15 standards. Census race and ethnicity data are essential for important research across many sectors, for upholding civil rights, and for growing the economy. Extensive Census Bureau research and engagement with expert stakeholders shows that implementing the modernized 2024 OMB SPD 15 standards for race and ethnicity data collection will yield data that more accurately represent the nation’s increasingly diverse population.

3. Remove the clause banning the addition of future questions on sexual orientation. Proposed changes to demographic items should be based on research and guided by a deliberative and transparent process, including extensive stakeholder consultation.

4. Withdraw other proposed changes to residence criteria, including tying place of residence to tax records and "lawful residence," and the adoption of a three month enumeration period. The Census Bureau must extensively research and consult with stakeholders about the potential effects of such changes before proposing their implementation in a decennial census.

5. Halt the practice of prison gerrymandering by counting incarcerated individuals in their home communities. This will yield more accurate census data and ensure that communities receive the congressional representation to which they are entitled.

Sincerely,
Dahlia V.
NJ 08876

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities. Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I write in support of the Census Bureau's proposed rule, "Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions" (Docket No. USBC-2026-0628; RIN 0607-AA75).

The Constitution calls for an "actual Enumeration" every ten years so that representation can be fairly apportioned among the states. The decennial census is meant to be a count, not a survey or a statistical estimate. Americans' voice in Congress depends on that count being right.

In 2020, the Bureau intentionally introduced statistical noise into the population data used to draw congressional and legislative districts. Data that determine political representation should never be deliberately altered. I support proposed  70.3, which directs the Bureau to prioritize the accuracy of the population count and prohibits publishing demographic data when doing so would introduce uncertainty into national or state population counts.

I also support the proposed residence criteria. Being counted at one's "usual residence" has never meant mere physical presence on Census Day. It reflects a lasting connection to a place, which is why service members stationed abroad are still counted in their home states. Counting citizens and lawful permanent residents, and excluding foreign nationals who are here unlawfully or temporarily, follows that principle.

I support keeping the enumeration questionnaire focused on the count itself. The Bureau can continue to produce demographic and statistical information through the American Community Survey and other tools, but those products should remain separate from the constitutional headcount.

To make these reforms durable, I urge the Bureau to state clearly in the final rule that the constitutional enumeration, and the counts used for apportionment and redistricting, are fundamentally distinct from routine federal statistical products and may not be adjusted to serve other statistical purposes.

Please finalize this rule so that the 2030 Census delivers an accurate count and restores Americans' trust in how they are represented.

Respectfully,
Sue Karl
Zephyrhills, FL

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:

If we don’t know who is living in our communities, we cannot prepare for the challenges we may face, and we will not receive adequate funds from federal programs. 
I urge you to both extend the comment period to a full 90 days until December 9th, and to reject this proposed rule.

Thank You for your Attention.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I’m writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

As a person who cares about people and our planet, I know how important this data is, and as such, we need a fair and accurate Census. 

First, I ask the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. Significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve more time for members of the public — people like me — to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70 of the proposed rule. I urge you to withdraw the rule for substantial revisions, including:

Count every U.S. resident, including visa-holders, refugees, and asylum seekers.
Establish detailed  guidelines for complex residential situations such as recent movers, people in temporary situations, and children in foster care.
Go back to activity-based residence, not a “one hour” rule.
Drop the January-to-April enumeration period.
Count incarcerated people at home, not at the facility.
Revise the tax records language. Extreme reliance on tax records risks creating inconsistencies in the count.
Drop the ban on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation questions.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of communities like mine. Furthermore, the data collected by the Census determines how billions of dollars of environmental funding is distributed across the country. This includes funding for water and waste disposal systems, public transportation infrastructure, and disaster relief on which we all rely. The data collected will also inform research to identify and address environmental injustices. 

Moving forward with this proposed rule would harm all Americans. Our democracy works best when all people that live within our borders are fully represented in the data collected by the Census.

Sincerely,
Sam Miller

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census because a fair and accurate census is critical to ensuring every community is counted, fairly represented, and able to get the resources people need to live healthy lives — including sexual and reproductive healthcare. An inaccurate or incomplete census can deepen existing inequities, particularly for communities that already face disenfranchisement and barriers to healthcare. 

A fair and accurate census is essential to our health and rights. 

Census data help determine access to programs patients and their families rely on, including important programs like Medicaid, SNAP, WIC, and TANF. Accurate census data also shape political representation by determining how seats in the U.S. House of Representatives are apportioned among states and providing data used for redistricting. When communities are undercounted or excluded, they risk losing both resources and political representation. 

The Census Bureau and Department of Commerce must:

1. Count all people residing in the United States in the 2030 Census, without regard to immigration status. Excluding noncitizens from census apportionment data violates the Constitution and established legal precedent. It would suppress the count of many communities, effectively erasing them from critical datasets and depriving them of resources and congressional representation –— including resources and political representation that support access to healthcare.

2. Continue collecting race and ethnicity data and implement the 2024 OMB SPD 15 standards. Census race and ethnicity data are essential for important research across many sectors, for upholding civil rights, and for growing the economy. Extensive Census Bureau research and engagement with expert stakeholders shows that implementing the modernized 2024 OMB SPD 15 standards for race and ethnicity data collection will yield data that more accurately represent the nation’s increasingly diverse population.

3. Remove the clause banning the addition of future questions on sexual orientation. Proposed changes to demographic items should be based on research and guided by a deliberative and transparent process, including extensive stakeholder consultation.

4. Withdraw other proposed changes to residence criteria, including tying place of residence to tax records and "lawful residence," and the adoption of a three month enumeration period. The Census Bureau must extensively research and consult with stakeholders about the potential effects of such changes before proposing their implementation in a decennial census.

5. Halt the practice of prison gerrymandering by counting incarcerated individuals in their home communities. This will yield more accurate census data and ensure that communities receive the congressional representation to which they are entitled.

Sincerely,
Margaux Ortiz
MD 21001
