Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to strongly oppose the proposed residence criteria and restrictions on demographic questions for the decennial census.

I believe the census should accurately reflect the people who live in our communities. The Constitution calls for representation based on the whole number of persons in each state. I am deeply concerned that excluding residents based on immigration status would undermine that principle and potentially distort political representation.

I also oppose the proposed prohibition on collecting race and ethnicity information through census enumeration questionnaires. As a Black woman, I understand that racial disparities do not disappear simply because we stop collecting information about them. Accurate demographic data helps us identify inequalities, understand community needs, enforce civil rights protections, and make informed decisions about public resources.

The Census Bureau should not sacrifice meaningful demographic information in the name of efficiency without demonstrating that alternative methods will provide equally accurate and useful data.

I am also concerned about the proposed reliance on government administrative records to determine legal status. The agency should thoroughly examine the potential for errors, privacy risks, and the consequences of incorrectly excluding people from population counts.

I recognize the importance of protecting privacy, simplifying participation, and improving census accuracy. However, those goals should be achieved through carefully evaluated methods that preserve public trust and ensure fair representation.

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed exclusionary residence criteria and reconsider the restrictions on demographic questions. Before adopting any changes, the agency should provide clear evidence of their effects on census accuracy, civil rights enforcement, community resources, and congressional representation.

Every person who lives in our communities matters. Our government cannot make informed decisions about the needs of its people if its policies result in incomplete counts or insufficient information about the populations it serves.

I respectfully oppose this proposed rule and request that the Census Bureau preserve an accurate, inclusive, and transparent census process.

Thank you for considering my comment.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. I oppose this proposed rule because it departs from that constitutional mandate, risking severe harm to my community. Excluding noncitizens from the population count used for congressional apportionment and federal funding, while adding a citizenship question designed to deter participation, will suppress response rates across immigrant communities and mixed-status families who fear being targeted. An undercount here would directly strip my community of appropriate congressional representation and our fair share of federal funding for essential safety-net programs like SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, CHIP, and Title I education grants. As someone who cares about fairness and the rule of law, I urge the Bureau to withdraw this proposal and count every person living in our communities, as the Constitution requires. 

I am also concerned that the proposed rule erases vital Census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Decades of demographic data serve as the baseline that public and private institutions rely on to identify inequalities and direct resources where they are needed most. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities.  

Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.  

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Sincerely,
Dan Blakey
East Lansing, MI

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I write in opposition to the proposals in this proposed regulation.  

The notion that people living ongoing in the US without legal status are somehow not "inhabitants" defies common sense and is solely constructed for a political purpose.  A nuanced rule might work to distinguish between travelers and residents, but this rule's simplistic formulation offers no such benefit.  

Meanwhile, the inclusion of a legal status question on the census form is a callous attempt to use an information gathering exercise as a means to immigration enforcement.  No one will answer "no."  This approach will not gather accurate information, and is likely to intimidate people to avoid the census.  This administration needs to separate immigration enforcement from other matters of law precisely because we need people to follow other aspects of the law even when they are unlawfully present.  

The prescriptive elimination of any questions regarding race, ethnicity, or sexual orientation is a similarly crude proposal, ignoring the very real demographic factors that continue to weigh in this country.  Perhaps there are questions that could be thoughtfully revised or removed, but a blanket "simplification" threatens a host of useful information, including but not limited to Tribal membership.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I believe taking an accurate census is essential to the workings of our representative government.  

Therefore, I write in support of the Census Bureau's proposed rule, "Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions" (Docket No. USBC-2026-0628; RIN 0607-AA75).

The Constitution calls for an "actual Enumeration" every ten years so that representation can be fairly apportioned among the states. The decennial census is meant to be a count, not a survey or a statistical estimate. Americans' voice in Congress depends on that count being right.

In 2020, the Bureau intentionally introduced statistical noise into the population data used to draw congressional and legislative districts. Data that determine political representation should never be deliberately altered. I support proposed  70.3, which directs the Bureau to prioritize the accuracy of the population count and prohibits publishing demographic data when doing so would introduce uncertainty into national or state population counts.

I also support the proposed residence criteria. Being counted at one's "usual residence" has never meant mere physical presence on Census Day. It reflects a lasting connection to a place, which is why service members stationed abroad are still counted in their home states. Counting citizens and lawful permanent residents, and excluding foreign nationals who are here unlawfully or temporarily, follows that principle.

I support keeping the enumeration questionnaire focused on the count itself. The Bureau can continue to produce demographic and statistical information through the American Community Survey and other tools, but those products should remain separate from the constitutional headcount.

To make these reforms durable, I urge the Bureau to state clearly in the final rule that the constitutional enumeration, and the counts used for apportionment and redistricting, are fundamentally distinct from routine federal statistical products and may not be adjusted to serve other statistical purposes.

Please finalize this rule so that the 2030 Census delivers an accurate count and restores Americans' trust in how they are represented.

Respectfully,
Rose Newcomer
York, PA

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
Crosswinds News strongly opposes the Census Bureau's proposal to eliminate race and ethnicity questions from the decennial census.

For Native American communities, accurate population data is not simply a matter of statistics. It is essential to our visibility, political representation, access to resources, and ability to document the needs of communities that have historically been displaced, excluded, and undercounted.

According to the 2024 American Community Survey 1-Year Estimates, California (1,321,675), Texas (781,735), and Oklahoma (588,301) have the three largest Native American populations. These figures reflect a history shaped by forced removal, displacement, and migration, as well as the continued presence and resilience of Native peoples across the United States.

Removing race and ethnicity questions from the decennial census threatens to make these communities less visible in the very data used to inform public policy, funding decisions, voting rights protections, and community development.

The Census Bureau should not eliminate direct, self-reported demographic information without demonstrating how equally accurate, reliable, and comprehensive Native population data will be maintained. Administrative records and smaller population surveys are not adequate substitutes without evidence that they can capture the full diversity of Native populations, particularly people living in urban communities and outside tribal jurisdictions.

I am also deeply concerned about the limited opportunity provided for meaningful tribal consultation. Tribal Nations received approximately two weeks' advance notice before the October 2 consultation, rather than the customary 30-day notice. A policy with such significant implications for tribal governments and Native communities deserves more than an expedited consultation process.

Tribal Nations are sovereign governments, not merely stakeholder groups. Their participation should be central to decisions about federal data collection practices that may affect their citizens, resources, and governmental responsibilities.

The proposal also fails to adequately address the distinction between racial identification and tribal citizenship. These are not interchangeable categories, and recognizing their legal differences does not eliminate the need for accurate data about Native populations.

We urge the Census Bureau to:

Withdraw the proposed restrictions on race and ethnicity questions in the decennial census.

Conduct additional, meaningful government-to-government consultations with Tribal Nations, providing adequate advance notice and time for review.

Publish a comprehensive assessment of how eliminating these questions would affect Native population data, including urban Native communities, redistricting, research, and federal funding.

Demonstrate how any proposed alternative data collection methods would preserve the accuracy, accessibility, and reliability of Native demographic information.

Protect the ability of individuals to self-identify rather than relying primarily on administrative records to determine demographic characteristics.

The federal government has a long history of making decisions about Native people without adequately including Native voices. This proposal risks continuing that pattern.

Native people should not have to fight to be visible in the federal government's own population data.

We at Crosswinds News strongly urge the Census Bureau to withdraw these proposed restrictions and work directly with Tribal Nations and Native communities to strengthen, rather than diminish, accurate and inclusive census data collection.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I’m writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

We need the census to be complete, including further details about people.

As a person who cares about people and our planet, I know how important this data is, and as such, we need a fair and accurate Census.

First, I ask the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. Significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve more time for members of the public — people like me — to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70 of the proposed rule. I urge you to withdraw the rule for substantial revisions, including:

Count every U.S. resident, including visa-holders, refugees, and asylum seekers.
Establish detailed  guidelines for complex residential situations such as recent movers, people in temporary situations, and children in foster care.
Go back to activity-based residence, not a “one hour” rule.
Drop the January-to-April enumeration period.
Count incarcerated people at home, not at the facility.
Revise the tax records language. Extreme reliance on tax records risks creating inconsistencies in the count.
Drop the ban on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation questions.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of communities like mine. Furthermore, the data collected by the Census determines how billions of dollars of environmental funding is distributed across the country. This includes funding for water and waste disposal systems, public transportation infrastructure, and disaster relief on which we all rely. 

Moving forward with this proposed rule would harm all Americans. Our democracy works best when all people that live within our borders are fully shown in the data collected by the Census.

Sincerely,
Catherine Moran

protections.

The Census exists to provide a complete and accurate count of the people who live in the United States. For more than two centuries, census data has been used to understand our nation’s population, allocate resources, guide public policy, and ensure fair representation. Any changes that diminish the accuracy or completeness of that count undermine the fundamental purpose of the Census.

First, excluding undocumented immigrants and certain noncitizens from population counts used for congressional representation and Electoral College apportionment would distort the true population of states and communities. Millions of people live, work, pay taxes, raise families, attend schools, and contribute to the social and economic life of this country. Representation should reflect the actual population residing in a community. Excluding groups of residents would reduce representation for areas where they live and create disparities in political power that do not reflect reality.

Second, eliminating questions regarding race and ethnicity would significantly impair our nation’s ability to understand demographic trends and address inequalities. Race and ethnicity data are essential for measuring disparities in health care, education, housing, employment, and economic opportunity. These data help policymakers, researchers, and community organizations identify needs and develop effective solutions. Removing them would make many persistent inequities more difficult to identify and address.

Third, eliminating demographic data used to enforce civil rights laws would weaken one of the country’s most important tools for protecting equal opportunity and combating discrimination. Reliable demographic information is critical for monitoring compliance with laws that prohibit discrimination in voting, housing, employment, lending, education, and other areas. Without these data, government agencies, courts, researchers, and communities would have fewer tools to detect and remedy unequal treatment.
The proposed changes would disproportionately affect Black, Latino, immigrant, and other historically underrepresented communities by reducing their visibility in federal data and potentially diminishing their political representation. The Census should strive to count everyone and provide policymakers with the information necessary to serve all communities fairly.

I urge the Census Bureau to reject these proposed changes and preserve a complete, inclusive, and accurate Census that counts all residents and continues to collect the demographic information necessary for representation, civil rights enforcement, and informed policymaking.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am a lifelong resident of NJ and mother of two, and I care about a fair and accurate census because it impacts emergency assistance in our communities and proper apportionment in our schools and government services.

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. 

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
**Subject: Support for a Citizenship Question and Citizen-Based Congressional Apportionment in the 2030 Census**

I support including a citizenship question on the 2030 Census questionnaire and urge the Census Bureau to provide accurate, transparent data that distinguishes U.S. citizens from noncitizens.

First, the 2030 Census questionnaire should ask every respondent to identify their U.S. citizenship status. Reliable citizenship data would help policymakers and the public understand the composition of the nation's population and provide the information needed to evaluate how population figures are used in determining political representation.

Second, I support apportioning seats in the U.S. House of Representatives based on the U.S. citizen population rather than including noncitizens in the apportionment count. Congressional representation is fundamental to our system of self-government, and I believe the allocation of congressional seats should reflect the citizen population of each state. I urge the Census Bureau and the appropriate federal policymakers to pursue this change through lawful means.

Third, the Census Bureau should prioritize an accurate, verifiable count based on actual responses and reliable, documented enumeration methods. Census results should not be altered by unsupported assumptions, speculative additions, or opaque statistical adjustments. Any use of estimates, administrative records, or other supplemental methods should be transparent, subject to rigorous quality controls, and clearly disclosed to the public. I urge the Bureau to maximize direct enumeration and explain how any supplemental methods affect the final results.

The 2030 Census will have lasting consequences for congressional representation and public policy. Americans deserve a census process that is accurate, transparent, and accountable to the public.

Please include a citizenship question on the 2030 Census, support citizen-based congressional apportionment through the appropriate lawful process, and ensure that census results are produced using verifiable and transparent methods.

Thank you for considering my comments.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census. These changes will not only weaken the accuracy and integrity of our nation's most important population count, but they will also harm our communities, and I strongly urge the Bureau to reject them. 

First, removing questions of race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation erases the full scope of my identity when I participate in the Census survey. These data points are not optional. They are the tools we use to enforce civil rights laws, monitor discrimination, and measure the disparities that still affect millions of people. Excluding them from the count does not make them disappear from our society, but it does make our government less equipped to handle big issues when they arise. 

The Constitution is clear: the census must count ALL persons living in the United States, regardless of their immigration or citizenship status. The proposal to exclude non-citizens, including those residents with some type of lawful status, violates more than two centuries of legal precedent. Every person counted in this country contributes to our communities, and every person deserves to be fully seen. 

The consequences of these changes will negatively impact our daily lives. The census affects everything. It determines political representation and the drawing of voting districts. It guides how billions of dollars in federal funding are used to close persistent disparities in schools, hospitals, and other government programs that are designed to improve our lives.  

The census is the foundation of our democracy. It must reflect the complete yet nuanced reality of who we are as a nation. And it must reflect the lives of our friends and neighbors who may not look, think, or speak like we do. I ask the Bureau to withdraw these proposed changes and to preserve a count that includes everyone and represents everyone. 

Thank you for considering my comment.

Sincerely,
Jenifer Strozier

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. I oppose this proposed rule because it departs from that constitutional mandate, risking severe harm to my community. Excluding noncitizens from the population count used for congressional apportionment and federal funding, while adding a citizenship question designed to deter participation, will suppress response rates across immigrant communities and mixed-status families who fear being targeted. An undercount here would directly strip my community of appropriate congressional representation and our fair share of federal funding for essential safety-net programs like SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, CHIP, and Title I education grants. As someone who cares about fairness and the rule of law, I urge the Bureau to withdraw this proposal and count every person living in our communities, as the Constitution requires. 

I am also concerned that the proposed rule erases vital Census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Decades of demographic data serve as the baseline that public and private institutions rely on to identify inequalities and direct resources where they are needed most. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities.  

Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.  

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Sincerely,
Catherine Mc Arthur
Milwaukee, WI

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

I am [add a description of who you are, such as your profession and/or state where you live], and I care about a fair and accurate census because [add a brief description of why you care].

First, I ask the Census Bureau to further extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. The extension to November 2, 2026 is welcome, but significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve a full 90 days for the public to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and return with substantial revisions, including: [keep any/all points you would like to include in your comment]

• Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
• Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
• Return to activity-based criteria for residence, such as where someone usually lives and sleeps, rather than a confusing “one hour” rule.
• Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (including seasonal workers and recent movers) are counted in the right place on Census Day and so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not accidentally excluded from the count.
• Count incarcerated people at their home rather than their facility. The current proposal shifts population toward the districts where prisons are built and away from communities where people live.
• Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count.
• Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm all Americans.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census. These changes will not only weaken the accuracy and integrity of our nation's most important population count, but they will also harm our communities, and I strongly urge the Bureau to reject them. 

First, removing questions of race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation erases the full scope of my identity when I participate in the Census survey. These data points are not optional. They are the tools we use to enforce civil rights laws, monitor discrimination, and measure the disparities that still affect millions of people. Excluding them from the count does not make them disappear from our society, but it does make our government less equipped to handle big issues when they arise. 

The Constitution is clear: the census must count ALL persons living in the United States, regardless of their immigration or citizenship status. The proposal to exclude non-citizens, including those residents with some type of lawful status, violates more than two centuries of legal precedent. Every person counted in this country contributes to our communities, and every person deserves to be fully seen. 

The consequences of these changes will negatively impact our daily lives. The census affects everything. It determines political representation and the drawing of voting districts. It guides how billions of dollars in federal funding are used to close persistent disparities in schools, hospitals, and other government programs that are designed to improve our lives.  

The census is the foundation of our democracy. It must reflect the complete yet nuanced reality of who we are as a nation. And it must reflect the lives of our friends and neighbors who may not look, think, or speak like we do. I ask the Bureau to withdraw these proposed changes and to preserve a count that includes everyone and represents everyone. 

Thank you for considering my comment.

Sincerely,
Dallas Windham

Comment:
I write in support of the Census Bureau's proposed rule, "Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions" (Docket No. USBC-2026-0628; RIN 0607-AA75).

The Constitution calls for an "actual Enumeration" every ten years so that representation can be fairly apportioned among the states. The decennial census is meant to be a count, not a survey or a statistical estimate. Americans' voice in Congress depends on that count being right.

In 2020, the Bureau intentionally introduced statistical noise into the population data used to draw congressional and legislative districts. Data that determine political representation should never be deliberately altered. I support proposed  70.3, which directs the Bureau to prioritize the accuracy of the population count and prohibits publishing demographic data when doing so would introduce uncertainty into national or state population counts.

I also support the proposed residence criteria. Being counted at one's "usual residence" has never meant mere physical presence on Census Day. It reflects a lasting connection to a place, which is why service members stationed abroad are still counted in their home states. Counting citizens and lawful permanent residents, and excluding foreign nationals who are here unlawfully or temporarily, follows that principle.

I support keeping the enumeration questionnaire focused on the count itself. The Bureau can continue to produce demographic and statistical information through the American Community Survey and other tools, but those products should remain separate from the constitutional headcount.

To make these reforms durable, I urge the Bureau to state clearly in the final rule that the constitutional enumeration, and the counts used for apportionment and redistricting, are fundamentally distinct from routine federal statistical products and may not be adjusted to serve other statistical purposes.

Please finalize this rule so that the 2030 Census delivers an accurate count and restores Americans' trust in how they are represented.

Respectfully,

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the 2030 Census. These changes will not only weaken the accuracy and integrity of our nation's most important population count, but they will also harm our communities, and I strongly urge the Bureau to reject them. 

First, removing questions of race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation erases the full scope of my identity when I participate in the Census survey. These data points are not optional. They are the tools we use to enforce civil rights laws, monitor discrimination, and measure the disparities that still affect millions of people. Excluding them from the count does not make them disappear from our society, but it does make our government less equipped to handle big issues when they arise. 

The Constitution is clear: the census must count ALL persons living in the United States, regardless of their immigration or citizenship status. The proposal to exclude non-citizens, including those residents with some type of lawful status, violates more than two centuries of legal precedent. Every person counted in this country contributes to our communities, and every person deserves to be fully seen. 

The consequences of these changes will negatively impact our daily lives. The census affects everything. It determines political representation and the drawing of voting districts. It guides how billions of dollars in federal funding are used to close persistent disparities in schools, hospitals, and other government programs that are designed to improve our lives.  

The census is the foundation of our democracy. It must reflect the complete yet nuanced reality of who we are as a nation. And it must reflect the lives of our friends and neighbors who may not look, think, or speak like we do. I ask the Bureau to withdraw these proposed changes and to preserve a count that includes everyone and represents everyone. 

Thank you for considering my comment.

Sincerely,
d'Anne MacNeil

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I’m writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

As a person who cares about people and our planet, I know how important this data is, and as such, we need a fair and accurate Census. 

First, I ask the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. Significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve more time for members of the public — people like me — to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70 of the proposed rule. I urge you to withdraw the rule for substantial revisions, including:

Count every U.S. resident, including visa-holders, refugees, and asylum seekers.
Establish detailed  guidelines for complex residential situations such as recent movers, people in temporary situations, and children in foster care.
Go back to activity-based residence, not a “one hour” rule.
Drop the January-to-April enumeration period.
Count incarcerated people at home, not at the facility.
Revise the tax records language. Extreme reliance on tax records risks creating inconsistencies in the count.
Drop the ban on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation questions.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of communities like mine. Furthermore, the data collected by the Census determines how billions of dollars of environmental funding is distributed across the country. This includes funding for water and waste disposal systems, public transportation infrastructure, and disaster relief on which we all rely. The data collected will also inform research to identify and address environmental injustices. 

Moving forward with this proposed rule would harm all Americans. Our democracy works best when all people that live within our borders are fully represented in the data collected by the Census.

Sincerely,
KATHY WASON

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. I oppose this proposed rule because it departs from that constitutional mandate, risking severe harm to my community. Excluding noncitizens from the population count used for congressional apportionment and federal funding, while adding a citizenship question designed to deter participation, will suppress response rates across immigrant communities and mixed-status families who fear being targeted. An undercount here would directly strip my community of appropriate congressional representation and our fair share of federal funding for essential safety-net programs like SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, CHIP, and Title I education grants. As someone who cares about fairness and the rule of law, I urge the Bureau to withdraw this proposal and count every person living in our communities, as the Constitution requires. 

I am also concerned that the proposed rule erases vital Census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Decades of demographic data serve as the baseline that public and private institutions rely on to identify inequalities and direct resources where they are needed most. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities.  

Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.  

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Sincerely,
MJ Cooper
Union City, GA

Comment:

Comment:

Every person counted in this country contributes to our communities, and every person deserves to be fully seen. 

The consequences of these changes will negatively impact our daily lives. The census affects everything. It determines political representation and the drawing of voting districts. It guides how billions of dollars in federal funding are used to close persistent disparities in schools, hospitals, and other government programs that are designed to improve our lives.  

The census is the foundation of our democracy. It must reflect the complete yet nuanced reality of who we are as a nation. And it must reflect the lives of our friends and neighbors who may not look, think, or speak like we do. I ask the Bureau to withdraw these proposed changes and to preserve a count that includes everyone and represents everyone. 

Thank you for considering my comment.

Sincerely,
Mark Giese

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment: US Census Bureau,I urge the Census Bureau and Department of Commerce to withdraw the proposed rule changing residence criteria for the decennial Census and restricting demographic questions.The proposal would exclude foreign citizens from the population used for congressional apportionment unless they are also U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents. Overall, this would leave out people who actually live in our community, including many people who are lawfully present in the United States.For all past Census counts, including the 2020 Census, foreign citizens living in the United States were generally counted where they lived and slept most of the time. The 14th Amendment requires congressional representation to be apportioned according to the “whole number of persons in each State.”I am also deeply concerned by the proposal to prohibit race and ethnicity questions, along with sexual orientation, on the decennial Census enumeration questionnaire. It must be complete, accurate, and protected from political manipulation.Please withdraw this proposed rule and preserve a Census that fairly and accurately counts our community.Jim [X] Gardiner, Maine 04345

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Constitution requires the Census to count “the whole number of persons in each State” every ten years—not the whole number of citizens, and not only the people the administration finds convenient. I oppose this proposed rule because it departs from that constitutional mandate, risking severe harm to my community. Excluding noncitizens from the population count used for congressional apportionment and federal funding, while adding a citizenship question designed to deter participation, will suppress response rates across immigrant communities and mixed-status families who fear being targeted. An undercount here would directly strip my community of appropriate congressional representation and our fair share of federal funding for essential safety-net programs like SNAP, WIC, Medicaid, CHIP, and Title I education grants. As someone who cares about fairness and the rule of law, I urge the Bureau to withdraw this proposal and count every person living in our communities, as the Constitution requires. 

I am also concerned that the proposed rule erases vital Census questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Decades of demographic data serve as the baseline that public and private institutions rely on to identify inequalities and direct resources where they are needed most. This data is critical to identify and address critical issues facing our communities, such as the crisis of Black maternal mortality. The loss of this data will impact nearly ALL data collection, public and private, which depends on the Census for a population baseline, in turn compromising vital research that informs evidence-based policymaking and investments that help our communities.  

Proposed changes to the Census would also undercount many women and girls, especially those who are unemployed, survivors of sexual abuse, or under age 18. Collecting bad data can have serious consequences: it can mean less funding for education and for programs that address sexual violence, among other essential services. Erasing these questions does not remove disparities; it simply blinds us to them, making it nearly impossible to allocate research funding, target public services, or hold institutions accountable.  

I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that all underrepresented groups remain visible and accurately counted through the Census.

Sincerely,
NANCY HAIRFIELD
San Diego, CA

I also encourage the Bureau to consult grant professionals and other data users to better understand these practical implications.

Thank you for considering my comments.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

Re: Docket No. 260903-0005, RIN 0607-AA75, USBC-2026-0628. “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions”

I am a resident of Puerto Rico (San Juan). I submit this comment to oppose proposed 15 CFR Parts 60 and 70 because of the harm they would cause to a complete and accurate count of Puerto Rico and of Puerto Ricans.

The fact that they systematically try to erase us, will not make us cease to exist. Count us!

The proposed rule does not mention Puerto Rico a single time, even though the decennial census counts more than 3.2 million U.S. citizens on the island and produces the data used to redraw our legislative districts. Sections 60.5 and 70.3 refer to the “stateside census” and to the “national or state level” without defining “United States.” I ask the Census Bureau to explain in writing how Parts 60 and 70 would apply in Puerto Rico, and not to finalize any rule without doing so.

Section 70.2(a) would prohibit the Hispanic-origin question, which includes the “Puerto Rican” checkbox. More people of Puerto Rican origin now live in the states than on the island, and that question is the only way the decennial census counts them. Without it, our communities in New York, Florida, Pennsylvania, Massachusetts, Connecticut, and elsewhere would disappear from the data used to enforce civil and voting rights and to plan services. I ask that Section 70.2(a) be withdrawn.

Section 60.2(a) says usual residence “should be consistent with, and evidenced by” tax records, but does not say which ones. Most Puerto Rico residents file with the Puerto Rico Department of the Treasury (Hacienda), our local tax authority, not with the IRS; employers issue Form 499R-2/W-2PR. I ask the Census Bureau to state in writing whether it would accept Hacienda returns and Form 499R-2/W-2PR as tax records in Puerto Rico, and how it would obtain and match them.

Even if the Bureau used Hacienda returns, a residence test based on tax records would leave many people in Puerto Rico out. An estimated one-third of the population doesn’t file and works in the informal economy (Caraballo-Cueto), and retirees and low-income households often file no return at all. Moreover, there is concern that a substantial share of the returns that are filed list a P.O. box or rural route as the address, which does not identify the home where the person lives. I ask that tax records not be made the proof of residence in Puerto Rico, and that self-response and field verification be accepted.

The Puerto Rico Community Survey and nearly all surveys are weighted to population estimates based on the decennial census. Section 70.4 says the ACS could still ask about race and origin, but without those data in the census there would be no reliable benchmark. Municipios, agencies, hospitals, universities, nonprofits, and businesses depend on these data, as does the distribution of federal funds for health, nutrition, education, housing, and disaster recovery. I ask that Part 70 not be adopted.

Puerto Rico’s Constitution requires its 40 house and 8 senate districts to be revised after each census, using block- and barrio-level data. The same count is the base for federal funds for health, nutrition, education, housing, and disaster recovery in all 78 municipios. If the rule drops households or places them at a mailing address, the next decade’s maps and funding are distorted. I ask the Bureau to publish an analysis of the rule’s effect on Puerto Rico’s population base before finalizing it.

For these reasons, I ask the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposed rule and ensure that everyone in Puerto Rico and in the diaspora is counted, once, and in the right place.

Thank you for considering this comment.

MGM

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (FDMS Docket Number USBC-2026-0628, published September 10, 2026).  I  strongly oppose the proposed rule’s changes to the residence criteria and demographic items for the 2030 Census.
As the Census Bureau is committed “to counting every person who should be counted once, only once, and in the right place”  the proposed residence requirement should be reconsidered.  The  “census enumeration period” fails to take into account the many citizens who travel to warmer climates during the winter.  By conducting the count from January 3 to April 1, that could easily eliminate people who travel from their “usual residence” to more temperate locations after celebrating with family Christmas/Hanukah and then who return in mid-April to celebrate with family Easter/Passover.  
 When the First Congress said the count should be based on each person’s “usual place of abode”, people were not easily travelling from place to place based on the weather.   As the colonists fought against “taxation without representation” this enumeration period means many people who are taxed as residents of one state will have their representation in Congress misallocated because they took a break in another location.
I recommend the Census Bureau and Department of Commerce:
Withdraw proposed changes to residence criteria, including tying place of residence to tax records and “lawful residence,” and the adoption of a three- month enumeration period. Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).
I am an illustrator and editor at a prominent scientific journal, contributing to hundreds of scientific articles that are published yearly on 40+ different research subjects. Accurate Census data is critical to the work of our authors and researchers, whose work is distributed to and used by many US government agencies to craft policy. I am deeply concerned about the impact of the proposed rules on the fairness and accuracy of the census.
I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw and return with substantial revisions. Specifically:
Abandon any criteria that would exclude U.S. residents, including visa-holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others from the apportionment count. The purpose of the census is to count all people.
Reestablish guidelines for detailed residence situations that encompass the varied living arrangements present in the United States such as for people who have recently moved, people in temporary shelters, and children in foster care.
Eliminate or substantially revise guidelines for the “enumeration period” so that people (such as children in foster care and people in emergency shelters) are not excluded from the count.
Revise the language on tax records. The text “A person's “usual residence” should be consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records (e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms)” ignores the limitations of tax records. For example, tax records reflect a mailing address (such as post office box, business address, or tax preparer's address) rather than residential address and thus are inconsistent with residence for many taxpayers, including for many military personnel and their families. Extreme reliance on tax records also risks missing many dependent children in the count. It also ignores the limitations inherent to linkage of administrative records. It can be difficult, time consuming, and, at times, inaccurate, resulting in both false positive and false negative matches.
Drop the ban on demographic questions. The U.S. has asked about race in every census since our first in 1790. Information on race and ethnicity is critical for public health and civil rights enforcement and should not be banned. Instead, questions on race and ethnicity should be brought into compliance with the 2024 SPD 15 standards. Similarly, sexual orientation, while not currently asked in the census, should not be barred from future censuses. The rule would bar the collection of sexual orientation data on future censuses and could restrict the collection or publication of decennial census data on same-sex couples.
As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of our population. It would result in substantial undercounts in the immediate term and further degradation in quality and reliability over time. Such outcomes are unacceptable and would harm the integrity of American science and research.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
In regards to Docket USBC-2026-0628 — Decennial Census Residence Criteria and Demographic Questions

I am writing in support of the Census Bureau’s proposed changes to residence criteria and demographic questions. I believe these changes would better focus the decennial census on its constitutional purpose of determining population counts for congressional apportionment.

1. **Exclude undocumented/illegal aliens/immigrants and temporary visa holders from congressional apportionment.** I support excluding individuals who are here illegally in the United States, as well as foreign nationals admitted on temporary visas, from the population used to allocate seats in the U.S. House of Representatives. Temporary admission carries an expectation of departure when the authorized stay ends, unless another lawful status is obtained. In my view, temporary presence does not establish the same enduring connection and commitment to the United States as citizenship or lawful permanent residency. Apportionment should reflect those permanent ties.

2. **Support citizenship and immigration-status questions needed to apply these criteria.** I support clear questions that distinguish U.S. citizens, lawful permanent residents, and individuals with temporary or no lawful immigration status. A citizenship question alone would not distinguish permanent residents from temporary visa holders. Collecting the information necessary to apply the proposed residence criteria would help ensure consistent and accurate apportionment counts.

3. **Keep the census focused on counting people.** I support removing questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation from the decennial census questionnaire. Although demographic information has historically been collected, that history alone does not establish that these questions are necessary to determine population totals for apportionment. (What we have always done, doesn't mean it's right, still) Questions about sex, birth date, and household relationships should be limited to what is needed to verify the count and avoid duplication and deceitful entries.

4. **Reduce barriers to participation and prioritize an accurate count.** Additional personal questions may make respondents less willing to participate or complete the questionnaire, potentially undermining the accuracy of the count. A shorter questionnaire focused on necessary information would better serve the census’s central purpose. I urge the Bureau to prioritize direct enumeration, verify supporting records carefully, and transparently explain how it resolves missing, conflicting, or duplicate information.

Thank you for considering my support for these proposed changes and for your work to ensure an accurate and transparent census.
Kristen

 To whom it may concern:
The U.S. Constitution requires a decennial census to count all people living in the United States every ten years. The census serves as a cornerstone of our democracy, determining each state's representation in the U.S. House of Representatives and informing the allocation of hundreds of billions of dollars in federal funding to states and local communities. Census data also guide nonprofits, state and local governments, businesses, and other stakeholders in making critical decisions about resource allocation, service delivery, community investment, and responses to local needs. Accordingly, it is essential that the decennial census produce a fair, accurate, and transparent count consistent with the Constitution's requirements.
The proposed changes threaten the integrity and accuracy of the decennial census by excluding broad categories of people who live in the United States from the population count used to determine congressional representation and allocate federal resources. These categories include international students, H-1B visa holders, refugees, asylum seekers, undocumented immigrants, and others. The proposal would also eliminate questions concerning race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation, departing from longstanding census practices of collecting information that helps policymakers and communities understand the populations they serve. Collectively, these changes risk systematically undercounting communities, diminishing their political representation and access to essential federal funding. Eliminating these data would also impair the ability of governments, nonprofits, researchers, and other stakeholders to identify evolving community needs, evaluate disparities, and develop effective, evidence-based responses to racial, social, and economic inequities.
The consequences of changes that discourage participation or compromise the completeness of census data are well documented. During the first Trump Administration, the Census Bureau sought to add a citizenship question to the decennial census. In 2019, the U.S. Supreme Court rejected the administration's stated rationale for that action. The National Council of Nonprofits submitted an amicus brief opposing the proposed citizenship question, emphasizing the potential harm to individuals and communities. This history underscores the importance of ensuring that census policies promote public trust, encourage participation, and support a complete and accurate count.
For these reasons, we urge the U.S. Census Bureau to reject the proposed changes and preserve a decennial census that accurately reflects the population of the United States. Census policies should strengthen the reliability, transparency, and inclusiveness of the count—not introduce exclusions or eliminate critical demographic information. A complete and accurate census is essential to fair political representation, equitable distribution of federal resources, informed policymaking, and the ability of communities across the country to meet the needs of their residents.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule: Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions, for the reasons outlined next. The census has counted all residents for apportionment regardless of legal status for 230 years. We have always counted native-born U.S. citizens, naturalized U.S. citizens, non-citizen U.S. nationals, lawful permanent residents and temporary migrants, such as foreign students, refugees, asylum seekers and undocumented immigrants. The census has never left out residents because of their immigration status. The census determines the funding and representation of our communities. By not counting all people, communities will not get the resources they need for schools, hospitals, roads, firefighters and other critical services.  This proposal would mean there would no longer be a complete and accurate count of our population, which is unacceptable to me, so I strongly oppose this proposed rule and encourage the census bureau not to enact it.  Thank you for your consideration in this matter.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
A national census cannot fulfill its constitutional purpose if it makes communities less visible in the official record. I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw proposed rule USBC-2026-0628, which would restrict demographic questions on the decennial census short-form and other questionnaires used to enumerate the population. I am a sixth-generation Black American Indian. My ancestors are documented in federal records as full-blooded American Indians and were later reclassified as “Negro.” I do not identify as African American. I ask that my identity be recognized in a manner consistent with my documented American Indian heritage and my identity as a Black American Indian.

    The ability to select both “Black or African American” and “American Indian or Alaska Native,” together with a voluntary tribal write-in field, is essential. It enables people with histories like mine to identify their complete heritage and tribal connection rather than being confined to one broad category that does not accurately describe who we are.

    Government classifications have harmed Native communities when officials substituted racial labels for documented Indigenous identity. Walter Ashby Plecker’s administration of Virginia’s 1924 Racial Integrity Act illustrates that danger: officials classified many Native people as “colored” and altered records identifying them as Indian. This legacy—often described as “paper genocide”—disrupted identity, family documentation, and later recognition efforts.

    That history shows why meaningful self-identification matters. Removing race and ethnicity questions, multiple-response options, and tribal write-in fields risks compounding the displacement and invisibility experienced by Black American Indian and Indigenous communities. It could also revive data practices with effects resembling redlining, where the absence or distortion of community data contributes to our communities being overlooked in planning, investment, and distribution of resources. Historic redlining used racialized neighborhood classifications to deny communities opportunity and resources; public data should not again be structured in a way that makes vulnerable communities less visible.

    Accurate demographic data supports civil-rights enforcement, equitable resource allocation, and informed public policy. The 2030 Census must be able to recognize Black American Indians, multiracial Indigenous people, and specific tribal identities. I urge the Census Bureau to preserve these questions and response options."

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
On behalf of Every Texan, I am writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (FDMS Docket Number USBC-2026-0628, published September 10, 2026). We strongly oppose its changes to the residence criteria and demographic items for the 2030 Census.

Every Texan is a nonpartisan nonprofit that believes good policy must be supported by valid research and data. The proposed changes undermine effective policymaking.

The initial 33-day comment period, ending October 13, 2026, was wholly inadequate. While we support the extension to November 2, 2026, 53 days is still insufficient given the scope of the proposed changes and their effect on census data. Moreover, with the Secretary of Commerce having terminated the Census Bureau’s advisory committees, ample public input is essential to public trust in the census. To give state and local governments, demographers, researchers, and nonprofits sufficient time to evaluate these changes, the Department of Commerce and the Census Bureau must immediately publish a Federal Register notice extending the comment period to at least December 10, 2026.

We are extremely concerned that the proposed changes would undermine the accuracy, integrity, and usefulness of census data, particularly in the following areas:

Excluding noncitizens without lawful permanent residence from apportionment data is unconstitutional and would deprive our communities of their fair share of resources and representation. The Constitution, statutes, and settled law provide that all persons residing in the United States must be counted for apportionment. Research also shows that a citizenship question would chill census participation. An undercount would cost our communities resources for schools, hospitals, transportation, and emergency services, harming the many Texans who rely on Medicaid, SNAP, school meals, and Head Start and child care programs.

Eliminating race and ethnicity data collection is unprecedented, violates statutes, and severely undermines the utility of census data. Every census since 1790 has collected race and ethnicity data in some form. These data underpin other federal datasets and serve as an irreplaceable benchmark for nearly every population-based survey in the U.S. They allow health officials to identify and address differences in health risk factors, are necessary to enforce civil rights laws, give businesses market insights, and help governments and nonprofits target services efficiently. Every Texan relies on them to analyze the impacts of policy on our communities.

The proposed rule would radically redefine “usual residence,” tying enumeration to tax records and “lawful” residence rather than where people actually live, and replacing the April 1 “Census Day” with a three-month enumeration period. These untested changes would increase the risk that seasonal workers, foster youth, people with second homes, shelter residents, and others are missed or counted in the wrong place.

For these reasons, we call on the Census Bureau and Department of Commerce to:
Count all people residing in the United States in the 2030 Census, regardless of immigration status. Excluding noncitizens from apportionment data violates the Constitution and legal precedent, and would erase many communities from critical datasets and deprive them of resources and representation.
Continue collecting race and ethnicity data and implement the 2024 OMB SPD 15 standards. Extensive Census Bureau research and stakeholder engagement show these modernized standards will more accurately represent the nation’s increasingly diverse population.
Withdraw the other proposed changes to residence criteria, including tying residence to tax records and “lawful residence” and the three-month enumeration period. The Bureau must research and consult with stakeholders on the effects of such changes before proposing them for a decennial census.

We appreciate your consideration of these comments. Please contact Coda Rayo-Garza ([X]) with any questions.

Sincerely,
Every Texan

RE: Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions, Docket No. USBC-2026-0628 

I strongly oppose the U.S. Census Bureau's proposed rule to make unprecedented changes to the 2030 Census that would end data collection on race and ethnicity, exclude millions of U.S. residents, and result in an inaccurate count of our population. I ask the Census Bureau to extend the public comment period to December 26, 2026 to give the public a meaningful opportunity to share our input. 

Second, I urge the Census Bureau to withdraw this proposed rule for the harm it would cause to our communities. Data on race and ethnicity are essential to protecting our civil rights and ensuring equal opportunity for all Americans. Ending the centuries-long collection of this data would only make it harder to understand and address the needs of different communities.  

My representation at all levels of government and funding for local schools and hospitals, for example, also depend on census data. Excluding the millions of international students, temporary workers, refugees, and others living in the U.S. from the apportionment count would mean that communities like mine don't get fair representation or resources. 

Though the census does not currently ask about sexual orientation, this proposed rule would prohibit the Census Bureau from ever collecting that data in the future. That decision should be based on research, testing, and input from impacted communities, not on a political agenda. 

The Census Bureau should count all people living in the United States, regardless of immigration status, and continue to collect data on race and ethnicity. I urge the agency to withdraw this proposed rule. Thank you for considering this comment. 

Sincerely,
Mr. Rolf Friis

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I am writing to express strong opposition to the proposed changes to how the Census Bureau conducts the decennial census. Altering the current methodology risks undermining the accuracy and integrity of one of the most essential data-gathering processes in our country.

Accurate population counts are foundational to effective governance. Cities and communities rely on precise census data for planning infrastructure, determining funding levels, allocating resources, and preparing for emergencies. When population numbers are incomplete or distorted, the consequences ripple outward: misallocated federal funds, insufficient public services, weakened disaster response, and long-term planning failures that harm residents.

The census must count everyone living in the United States, regardless of documentation status. People who reside in our communities—who use roads, attend schools, rely on hospitals, and contribute to local economies—must be included. Excluding any group does not make them disappear; it only produces flawed data. Bad data in means bad data out, and decisions made on the basis of inaccurate information can lead to serious harm, including preventable fatalities during crises when resources are misjudged.

If the effect or intent of the proposed change is to exclude certain populations, that is not only impractical but also unethical. A census that does not reflect the true population fails its constitutional purpose and undermines public trust.

The current process, while not perfect, remains the most reliable method for capturing a complete and accurate count. It should be preserved rather than replaced with an approach that risks erasing members of our communities from the data that shapes critical policy decisions.

I urge the Census Bureau to maintain the existing methodology and reject any changes that would compromise the accuracy, fairness, and completeness of the census.

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
The U.S. Census Bureau's proposed rule to strengthen the US Census is critical to fair representation and the future of America.  

The U.S. Census should not include distorted data in its count of Americans.  By including overly generalized ethnic demographic categories, we obscure the true goal of the census and hinder its constitutionally mandated purpose: an accurate count of Americans.  

Additionally, illegal aliens and other non-legal permanent residents should not be included for apportionment. Census data is used for the apportionment of congressional seats. Non-citizens cannot legally vote and should not be used to decrease the voting power of Americans. I support the Census Bureau in advancing the correct understanding of usual residence to recognize an element of allegiance that is antithetical to the inclusion of those not legally present in our country.  

This Census Bureau should also consider adding a citizenship question to the Census survey. The Supreme Court has already held that the Constitution lawfully permits the Census Bureau to at least inquire about citizenship on the census questionnaire. "The census should absolutely include questions related to citizenship and legal presence. 

These changes would strengthen the census in its core purpose of attaining an accurate count of Americans and have my full support. 

Thank you,  

Marvin Moor

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
I write in support of the Census Bureau's proposed rule, "Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions" (Docket No. USBC-2026-0628; RIN 0607-AA75).

The Constitution calls for an "actual Enumeration" every ten years so that representation can be fairly apportioned among the states. The decennial census is meant to be a count, not a survey or a statistical estimate. Americans' voice in Congress depends on that count being right.

In 2020, the Bureau intentionally introduced statistical noise into the population data used to draw congressional and legislative districts. Data that determine political representation should never be deliberately altered. I support proposed  70.3, which directs the Bureau to prioritize the accuracy of the population count and prohibits publishing demographic data when doing so would introduce uncertainty into national or state population counts.

I also support the proposed residence criteria. Being counted at one's "usual residence" has never meant mere physical presence on Census Day. It reflects a lasting connection to a place, which is why service members stationed abroad are still counted in their home states. Counting citizens and lawful permanent residents, and excluding foreign nationals who are here unlawfully or temporarily, follows that principle.

I support keeping the enumeration questionnaire focused on the count itself. The Bureau can continue to produce demographic and statistical information through the American Community Survey and other tools, but those products should remain separate from the constitutional headcount.

To make these reforms durable, I urge the Bureau to state clearly in the final rule that the constitutional enumeration, and the counts used for apportionment and redistricting, are fundamentally distinct from routine federal statistical products and may not be adjusted to serve other statistical purposes.

Please finalize this rule so that the 2030 Census delivers an accurate count and restores Americans' trust in how they are represented.

Respectfully,
Richard Hlabse

Title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-18481
Comment:
To the U.S. Census Bureau:

I’m writing to comment on the proposed rule “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions” (Docket No. 260903-0005, Document 2026-18481, published September 10, 2026).

As a person who cares about people and our planet, I know how important this data is, and as such, we need a fair and accurate Census. 

First, I ask the Census Bureau to extend the comment period until December 10, 2026. Significant regulatory actions such as this one deserve more time for members of the public — people like me — to review and respond.

Second, I oppose both part 60 and part 70 of the proposed rule. I urge you to withdraw the rule for substantial revisions, including:

Count every U.S. resident, including visa-holders, refugees, and asylum seekers.
Establish detailed  guidelines for complex residential situations such as recent movers, people in temporary situations, and children in foster care.
Go back to activity-based residence, not a “one hour” rule.
Drop the January-to-April enumeration period.
Count incarcerated people at home, not at the facility.
Revise the tax records language. Extreme reliance on tax records risks creating inconsistencies in the count.
Drop the ban on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation questions.

As written, the proposed rule would exclude residents, result in an inaccurate count, and prohibit collection of important data on the characteristics of communities like mine. Furthermore, the data collected by the Census determines how billions of dollars of environmental funding is distributed across the country. This includes funding for water and waste disposal systems, public transportation infrastructure, and disaster relief on which we all rely. The data collected will also inform research to identify and address environmental injustices. 

Moving forward with this proposed rule would harm all Americans. Our democracy works best when all people that live within our borders are fully represented in the data collected by the Census.

Sincerely,
James Thoman

The census is the foundation of our democracy. It must reflect the complete yet nuanced reality of who we are as a nation.
